Space of facets. The construct is only lightly differentiated. The only distinction made within it is between anaphoric and cataphoric reference words, and both are presented as part of discourse-level cohesion in dialogue.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. No construct is linked to it either, so the only explicit operational detail is the focus on reference words in dialogue.

Links. No causal, correlational, or related links to other entities are reported.

nodes.name: Collaboration ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat collaboration ability as a latent capacity to work or coordinate with another agent toward a shared or mutually beneficial outcome. In this prevailing framing, the construct covers aligning actions, establishing shared conventions, organizing actions with a partner to avoid redundant or conflicting effort, or collaborating through iterative discussion; some papers narrow the partner setting to diverse teammates or human users and define the ability as dynamic adaptation during cooperation. A smaller line of work uses the label for an observable tendency, namely better response quality when other models' outputs are provided as context, and another broader framing describes collaboration as AI systems jointly performing tasks within a distributed ecosystem of specialized agents.

Space of facets. Across the literature, collaboration, coordination, collaborative ability, coordination ability, and model coordination are used for overlapping cooperative capacities, but the facets emphasized differ. One paper breaks collaboration capability into two components, initiating collaboration and responding to collaboration, while others center coordinat

nodes.name: Collaborative emergence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers converge only at a broad level: they describe capabilities that arise from collaboration among multiple models or agents, rather than from any one model alone. Beyond that, the definitions diverge. One framing treats it as new, sophisticated capabilities that appear as the number of agents scales, and even appear earlier or at much smaller scales than traditional neural emergence, while another treats it as emergent ability shown when collaborating models give correct answers that individual models cannot provide independently.

Space of facets. Papers do not break the construct into named facets or subtypes. The main variation is terminological and contrastive: closely related usage appears under both "collaborative emergence" and "emergent ability," and one framing explicitly positions the former against traditional neural emergence by emphasizing earlier manifestation at smaller scales.

Space of measurement. Operationally, the available descriptions are illustrative rather than tied to named instruments. One usage points to cases where a collaborative system provides the correct answer even when each individual model answers incorrectly, but no meas

nodes.name: Collaborative reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the concept is consistently framed as a multi-agent ability expressed through structured debate: multiple agents collectively analyze a problem, advocate and critique possible solutions, and converge on a judgment or decision. M-MAD: Multidimensional Multi-Agent Debate for Advanced Machine Translation Evaluation describes it as a latent ability of multiple LLM agents to reach a more accurate judgment, while SWE-Search: Enhancing Software Agents with Monte Carlo Tree Search and Iterative Refinement uses the label collaborative decision-making for the ability of a multi-agent system to arrive at a robust decision through debate.

Space of facets. The available papers organize the concept around debate functions: agents advocate for candidate solutions, critically evaluate them, and then refine or select an outcome. The main variation is in naming and end point, with one usage centered on collaborative reasoning and convergence to a more accurate judgment, and another on collaborative decision-making and selection of a robust solution; one source snippet also places collaborative abilities alongside LLMs' 'knowledge' and 'reasoni

nodes.name: Collective intelligence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the prevailing usage treats collective intelligence as a group-level advantage or capacity that emerges when multiple agents collaborate and do better than a single or isolated agent. One recurring version describes a latent advantage from agents jointly refining artifacts instead of relying on a single reasoning stream, while another says a multi-agent system can "surpass individual agent performance through coordinated collaboration and operator composition" (Multi-agent Architecture Search via Agentic Supernet). A closely aligned variant appears under the name collaborative intelligence, emphasizing effective combination of diverse, heterogeneous agents so the group achieves better problem solving than isolated agents.

Space of facets. The papers mostly organize the construct around a common contrast: collective or collaborative performance versus a single reasoning stream, singular-aspect reasoning, or isolated agents. They also use two near-overlapping names, collective intelligence and collaborative intelligence, with the latter stressing heterogeneous agents that "seamlessly collaborate to achieve greater intelligence

nodes.name: Common knowledge
nodes.definition: A form of group knowledge where all agents know a fact, know that all other agents know the fact, and so on ad infinitum, which is a prerequisite for certain types of coordination.

nodes.name: Commonsense knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat this construct as implicit or latent everyday world knowledge, real-world background knowledge, or general world knowledge encoded in a model and used to reason about contextualized situations and make ordinary judgments. Several definitions make this application-oriented, describing knowledge used for planning, multimodal understanding, household work, geospatial resolution, or driving, and one paper says it supports reasoning about "complex and often contextualized situations." A smaller line of work uses the same label for a capability rather than latent knowledge, defining it as the ability or tendency to understand everyday situations, make plausible judgments, or generate inferences aligned with general human knowledge and intuition.

Space of facets. The papers mainly present the construct in lists of model abilities rather than as a taxonomy with explicit subtypes. They use several near-synonymous labels, including "commonsense knowledge," "commonsense," "common-sense knowledge," and "common sense," and place it alongside reasoning, language comprehension, world knowledge, factualness, and scientific knowledge. Some authors narrow the

nodes.name: Commonsense reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats commonsense reasoning as a latent ability to use everyday or general world knowledge, intuition, and shared assumptions about ordinary physical or social situations to make plausible inferences, judgments, or predictions, especially when relevant information is not explicit. Many definitions phrase this as making presumptions about the ordinary world, applying broad knowledge to infer likely outcomes, or filling knowledge gaps through informal reasoning. A smaller line of work defines it more narrowly as the observable task of answering benchmark questions, choosing plausible continuations, or doing sentence completion, and a few papers situate it in specific settings such as embodied task structure, video interpretation, spatial filtering, or cause and effect questions in text. The main disagreement is therefore between a broad latent ability and narrower task- or setting-specific formulations.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby labels around the same family of phenomena: commonsense inference typically emphasizes plausible unstated conclusions or relations between concepts and events, commonsense understand

nodes.name: Compassion-fade bias
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of an LLM judge to evaluate responses differently when they are attributed to a well-known model versus an anonymized or less-known source.

nodes.name: Competence
nodes.definition: The perceived capability dimension of an impression, reflecting whether a target is seen as able to act effectively or intelligently.

nodes.name: Completeness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats completeness as coverage: an answer, summary, or table should include all relevant information or valid items and avoid omissions. Papers express this as retrieving all valid items that satisfy constraints, providing in-depth and in-breadth information, covering all question-relevant points, preserving clinically significant information, or capturing all relevant claims and facts. Smaller lines of work use the same label for different targets, including the completeness of a sub-task decomposition, factual completeness of a claim and its evidence for a non-misleading interpretation, and formal completeness of a reasoning system that can find a valid proof whenever one exists.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a single shared subtype scheme, but they often position completeness as one evaluation dimension among other criteria. It appears beside other evaluation dimensions, while one planning paper places it alongside solvability and non-redundancy, and one fact-verification paper treats factual completeness as an extension that complements traditional fact verification. The naming is not uniform: one p

nodes.name: Complex instruction following ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Rather than a single prevailing definition, papers use two close framings. One paper defines it as accurately interpreting and executing multi-step instructions while maintaining consistency across the full task, while another defines it as discerning and executing a user's core intent from long or convoluted instructions that may contain irrelevant information. The definitions agree on interpretation and execution, but differ on whether complexity is framed mainly as multi-step consistency or as recovering intent from distracting context.

Space of facets. Several evaluation papers treat complex instructions as instructions with multiple constraints or multiple-constraint composition. A smaller usage labels the construct complex instruction understanding and ties it to longer contexts whose relevant and irrelevant content obscures the instruction. One paper also presents it as one of several capabilities evaluated by a benchmark.

Space of measurement. Papers operationalize it through 6 measurement instruments and no linked behavioral indicators. The most frequently linked are CFBench, ComplexBench, FollowBench, IFEval, and MCBench. Operationally, these evalu

nodes.name: Complex reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats complex reasoning as a model capacity for multi-step or multi-hop inference: producing outputs by deriving intermediate conclusions, integrating multiple pieces of knowledge, or handling long sequential chains where each step depends on the previous one. Several papers state the same core more broadly as higher-order or advanced reasoning, beyond basic information retrieval or simple pattern matching, often in tasks with multiple constraints. A smaller departure defines it at the task level as multi-hop deduction, an observable problem format rather than a latent ability.

Space of facets. Papers use several overlapping labels for nearby ideas, especially multi-step inference, higher-order reasoning, deep reasoning, long-chain reasoning, and multi-hop deduction, with two other labels used in isolated definitions. The shared thread is chained reasoning, but papers specialize it by setting or structure: some emphasize reasoning across modalities, some stress integrating multiple facts or knowledge fragments, some describe composite questions that combine up to three reasoning categories, and some focus on tasks with mul

nodes.name: Complexity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers that define it, the prevailing framing treats complexity as a property of the generated response, specifically its level of sophistication, depth, intricacy, or elaboration. The wording varies slightly, but the definitions converge on complexity as a graded response attribute.

Space of facets. Papers most often position complexity within a bundle of response evaluation dimensions that also includes helpfulness, correctness, coherence, and verbosity. In these uses, it appears as one attribute among several, sometimes in the language of reward attributes and sometimes as a rating dimension in preference annotation.

Space of measurement. Operationally, complexity is linked to 2 measurement instruments, HelpSteer and HelpSteer2, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The common measurement pattern is multi-attribute response rating: HelpSteer is used for reward attributes including complexity, and HelpSteer2 annotates each response on a Likert-5 scale along complexity and related dimensions. This operationalization matches the definitions closely, because both treat complexity as a graded property of the response.

Links. Among linked c

nodes.name: Composability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the name is used for different kinds of combination rather than a single settled construct. A recurring extracted definition presents composability as the ability to combine model parameters or components trained on distinct tasks to create new multitask capabilities without additional training. The paper-specific definitions do not fully align with that framing: one treats composability as a latent property of interventions or models, where sequential updates should avoid interfering with prior or future interventions, and another defines it as the extent to which connected modular circuits produce a function that logically follows from their individual functions. Definitions therefore differ over both the object being composed and the criterion for successful composition.

Space of facets. Papers organize the concept around their local object of analysis rather than a shared taxonomy. One line of work uses it for combining trained weights or components across tasks, another for post-training interventions, and another for connected modular circuits. Within the intervention framing, composability is discussed through two facets, Orde

nodes.name: Compositional consistency
nodes.definition: The degree to which answers to complex questions are logically consistent with answers to their constituent sub-questions within a hierarchical reasoning structure.

nodes.name: Compositional generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats the construct as a model capacity to generalize to novel combinations of familiar components that were not seen together during training. Most definitions express the same core idea with different units of composition, including verbs, subjects, and objects, linguistic expressions and targets, primitives or constraints, objects, attributes, and relations, and known subtasks or skills. A smaller line of work states the construct at a higher level as flexibly combining independently learned or foundational skills, or application operations, to solve a novel task, and some authors cast it explicitly as a latent ability while others describe it through success on held-out test cases.

Space of facets. When papers break the construct down, they do so by the kind or level of composition being tested. Examples include action composition over verb, subject, and object combinations, word-level composition versus phrase-level structure, and composition over simple motor skills, subtasks, or user requirements built from familiar primitives. Some authors also broaden the label, describing skill-mixing as a particular sort of

nodes.name: Compositional multi-tasking ability
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to simultaneously execute multiple distinct tasks (e.g., summarization and translation) in a single inference pass, integrating their requirements into a coherent output.

nodes.name: Compositional reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats compositional reasoning as handling combinations of known parts: understanding novel configurations of familiar components, integrating multiple pieces of information or reasoning steps, or interpreting how objects, attributes, relations, acoustic events, or linguistic elements fit together. Several papers make this explicit with examples such as action recognition from known verb, subject, and object roles, understanding order and attribute binding across discrete acoustic events, or the capacity for "infinite use of finite means". A smaller line of work defines it more procedurally, as decomposing a complex task or question into sequential subtasks or sub-questions, solving them, and combining intermediate results, and one paper narrows this further to correct output on two-step composite tasks without explicit intermediate steps. The main axis of disagreement is whether the construct is framed mainly as relation-sensitive understanding of combined elements or as divide-and-conquer problem solving.

Space of facets. Papers organize the construct more by domain and task structure than by a single shared taxonomy.

nodes.name: Compositionality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage describes compositionality as a model property or ability to combine simpler elements, subproblems, skills, or attributes into coherent solutions, structures, or meanings for harder or more complex problems. Many definitions stay close to this general combine-parts framing, whether the parts are reasoning steps, multi-hop subquestions, objects and attributes, or pieces of structured output, and one paper explicitly describes a "compositionality gap" in which gains on single-hop questions outpace gains on complex multi-hop ones. A smaller line of work narrows the term to sentence-level meaning being determined by constituents and composition rules, while other papers place it in learned representations or components, such as high-level actions or expert vectors that can be combined in novel or algebraic ways.

Space of facets. Papers do not offer a single taxonomy, but they do introduce nearby labels that carve the construct more narrowly. Skill composition is used for combining atomic operations, reasoning steps, or previously learned language skills, symbolic composition for composing multiple distinct concepts using sy

nodes.name: Comprehensibility
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this construct as the clarity or ease with which model outputs can be understood by people. One definition states it as the clarity and ease of understanding of the language used in generated responses, while papers using the near-synonym Understandability describe generated text as clear and easy to comprehend by a human reader. A narrower variant keeps the same core idea but specifies spoken output, defining it as how easily a response can be comprehended when spoken aloud or by a listener.

Space of facets. Papers do not sharply separate Comprehensibility from Understandability, and instead use the two names for closely similar qualities of model output. One paper places Comprehensibility inside the FEEL model, alongside Informativeness, Helpfulness, Consistency, Coherence, and Safety. Beyond that, these papers do not offer a broader subtype scheme or explicit contrasts with other constructs.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is explicitly linked to this construct. Still, the snippets show it being used as a human evaluation dimension: annotators are asked to judge

nodes.name: Comprehensiveness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is output completeness: comprehensiveness refers to whether a summary, response, review, or other generation contains enough, or all relevant, information to answer the query or support the task. Most definitions vary mainly in the reference standard rather than in kind, with some emphasizing full coverage of an instruction, including implicit and explicit components, some emphasizing all important information or all document perspectives from the source, and others emphasizing a broad range of relevant cases or situational variations. A smaller formulation describes answer comprehensiveness as addressing the full set of important facets needed for a complete answer to an open-ended question.

Space of facets. Several papers specify what counts as coverage in setting-specific ways. One line treats answer comprehensiveness as facet coverage and explicitly distinguishes core, background, and follow-up sub-questions, while multi-document summarization work treats it as coverage of perspectives from all documents and aims to avoid missing any document's perspective. One code review paper explicitly describes comprehensivenes

nodes.name: Compression robustness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats compression robustness as preserving model performance after compression. One definition states it as maintaining performance when parameters are heavily compressed, with wording that stresses retention especially under large compression ratios, and another frames the same general idea as preserving performance across in-domain and out-of-domain evaluation settings. A smaller line of work shifts the focus from preservation to post-pruning performance recovery, defining it as the latent ability of a pruned model to regain the functional capabilities of its dense counterpart after compression.

Space of facets. The available definitions do not present a shared subtype taxonomy. Instead, papers use neighboring labels for different facets of the construct: task generalization emphasizes preservation across evaluation settings and datasets, while performance recovery emphasizes regaining information and capabilities lost during pruning, especially at high sparsity ratios. The main axis of variation is therefore preservation under compression versus recovery after pruning.

Space of measurement. Papers operationa

nodes.name: Computer science knowledge
nodes.definition: The overall capability of a large language model to understand, apply, and reason about concepts within the field of computer science.

nodes.name: Concept representation
nodes.definition: The model's internal, often linear, representation of abstract ideas, categories, or knowledge that allows it to process complex relationships beyond surface-level patterns.

nodes.name: Conceptual knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, papers consistently treat conceptual knowledge as a model-internal representation of concepts rather than isolated facts. One usage describes it as the internal representation of abstract concepts and their definitions, explicitly distinct from simple factual triples, while another describes concepts as human-understandable groups of features, examples, or words that share a property and can be localized in parameters or activations.

Space of facets. Papers commonly organize knowledge into factual and conceptual kinds, using the contrast to mark conceptual knowledge as the more abstract category; one study says it is "more abstract and more difficult to edit than factual knowledge." Separately, one paper uses conceptualization as a related notion, linking models' ability to capture conceptual knowledge with their ability to conceptualize.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is sparse: papers link conceptual knowledge to 1 measurement instrument, ConceptVectors, and to no behavioral indicators. ConceptVectors is described as a benchmark designed to evaluate unlearning, and one paper uses concepts collected from it in its

nodes.name: Conceptual understanding
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to align its internal representation of abstract concepts (e.g., 'neutral' stance) with human expert definitions through structured taxonomy learning.

nodes.name: Conceptualization
nodes.definition: The ability to recognize and reason about an underlying concept across different visual representations, even when its form, structure, or manifestation varies significantly.

nodes.name: Conciseness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat conciseness, and nearby labels such as brevity and succinctness, as a quality of outputs being brief, to the point, and free of unnecessary repetition, verbosity, or extraneous content. This framing is reused across responses, summaries, code reviews, conversations, explanations, and descriptions, sometimes with the added requirement that the output communicate only the necessary information or fit the reader's needs. A smaller line of work, especially in summarization-oriented formulations, casts conciseness less as shortness alone and more as how much of the generated content aligns with salient, accurate content, while some authors explicitly describe verbosity as its low end.

Space of facets. One organizational move places conciseness under User Alignment, alongside Readability and Harmlessness. Across papers, it is also contrasted with verbosity, described as low conciseness or as being too verbose, and nearby labels such as brevity and succinctness are used for much the same idea in explanations and descriptions. Some summarization papers also use the same term for a content-selection notion, describing conciseness as the sha

nodes.name: Confidence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats confidence as the model's own certainty about an answer, prediction, judgment, or generated response. Most definitions keep that broad framing while varying the target: certainty about providing a correct answer, about a generated instruction, about a reasoning trajectory, or about a correct causal relation, sometimes with decision uses such as whether to answer, ask for more information, or trust a judgment. A smaller line defines confidence against a different reference standard, namely the model's self-assessed likelihood that its judgment will align with human preference, as in Trust or Escalate: LLM Judges with Provable Guarantees for Human Agreement. Only one definition makes the proxy itself central, defining prediction confidence by variance in perplexity across choices.

Space of facets. Papers use the labels confidence, model confidence, and prediction confidence for overlapping notions of model certainty. The main axes of variation are the reference target, such as correctness versus expected human agreement, and whether the term denotes internal certainty or a certainty proxy. Several definitions fold the

nodes.name: Conformity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats conformity as a tendency for an LLM to align its judgment or response with a perceived majority opinion, sometimes even when it initially held a different or correct answer, and potentially at the expense of its own reasoning. Most papers use this majority-alignment framing and describe it as susceptibility to social influence during inference. Smaller variants narrow the construct to accepting group-provided answers even when they are misleading or incorrect, or to an LLM judge preferring the majority view regardless of whether it is correct.

Space of facets. Papers break the topic up mainly by setting and emphasis rather than by a detailed subtype scheme. One line places conformity in LLM-driven multi-agent systems and studies its existence, the factors influencing it, and mitigation strategies. Some authors also use narrower labels for specific manifestations: credulity for following the group's responses even in situations designed to create doubt, and bandwagon bias for judging settings where the majority view is preferred regardless of correctness.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is concentrated i

nodes.name: Conscientiousness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats Conscientiousness as a Big Five personality trait. The clearest definition describes it as characterized by diligence, organization, and self-discipline, and one source snippet similarly associates it with diligence and carefulness. A narrower framing keeps the trait-based view but focuses on its positive aspect, associating it with detailed explanations and improvement in tasks when positively activated.

Space of facets. Papers place Conscientiousness alongside openness, extraversion or extroversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism as one of the Big Five personality dimensions. One line of work further isolates a positive aspect of Conscientiousness in terms of neurons associated with that aspect.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to Conscientiousness, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The only explicit measurement description says that a paper uses the IPIP-NEO-120 questionnaire to quantify behavior patterns across the five personality dimensions, including Conscientiousness, so the available operationalization is questionnaire-based rather than attached to a recorded linked i

nodes.name: Consequentialist reasoning
nodes.definition: A moral reasoning style that evaluates actions primarily by their outcomes, such as maximizing welfare or minimizing harm.

nodes.name: Consistency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The prevailing usage treats consistency as stability or non-contradiction: papers describe it as producing the same or similar answer, prediction, judgment, or successful outcome across paraphrases, semantically or logically equivalent contexts, repeated identical prompts, multiple inference passes, or repeated trials. Related definitions extend this to agreement among sampled reasoning paths, or to beliefs that do not contradict across prompts or logical relations. Another recurring usage applies the same term to alignment between paired items, such as auxiliary and target task distributions, a rationale and the gold answer, a document and the correct answer, ad text and landing-page content, generated text and its source, or language and vision plans. Smaller lines of work use it for text-level logical coherence, continuity of character behavior, stability across fine-tuned variants, or convergence of in-context learning performance, so papers disagree on whether consistency is a property of outputs and behavior, internal beliefs, paired artifacts, or task distributions.

Space of facets. Papers introduce several named variants, especially self-consistency,

nodes.name: Constraint satisfaction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats constraint satisfaction as a model property or output behavior centered on whether generations obey explicit constraints. Most definitions describe adherence to lexical or semantic constraints, user-defined external constraints, or prompt-level requirements such as formatting, structure, style, word count, tone, or multiple explicit instructions; one formulation also describes it as finding a solution that satisfies all conditions. A smaller line of work shifts the emphasis from fulfillment to understanding, defining nearby constructs as the ability to comprehend, internalize, recognize, or differentiate constraints, especially in planning or complex instructions. Definitions therefore vary mainly between latent ability and observable behavior, and between general instruction constraints and narrower validity or feasibility constraints in domains such as travel planning or biophysical sequence generation.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct down by both constraint type and granularity. Some distinguish lexical from semantic constraints and soft from hard satisfaction, while others operationalize ve

nodes.name: Constructional knowledge
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to learn and represent constructions, defined as conventionalized form-meaning pairings in a language.

nodes.name: Constructiveness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available usage, constructiveness is framed as a property of feedback: the degree to which it identifies actionable weaknesses or improvement areas that can help authors revise a paper. The same source also characterizes it through "actionable feedback comments generation" and through "specific, critical feedback points" that target substantive weaknesses and improvement areas, so the emphasis stays on actionable, revision-oriented critique.

Space of facets. No formal subtypes, equivalent constructs, or contrasts are introduced. Instead, the term is elaborated with phrases such as "actionable feedback comments generation" and "specific, critical feedback points targeting substantive weaknesses and improvement areas in a paper," which restate the construct rather than dividing it into separate facets.

Space of measurement. Although the definition is phrased as "the degree to which" feedback identifies actionable weaknesses or improvement areas, no benchmark, human evaluation setup, LLM-as-a-judge procedure, probe, or analysis is linked to it as a measurement instrument. No behavioral indicator is linked to it, and no other constructs are linked to it t

nodes.name: Content-based reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to select and process data efficiently in an input-dependent manner, focusing on relevant content to perform a task.

nodes.name: Content transfer and synthesis
nodes.definition: The ability to generate output by integrating original and modified elements from memory, such as copying, rephrasing, or synthesizing information across context segments.

nodes.name: Context faithfulness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats context faithfulness as a model ability, or sometimes the degree of its responses' alignment, to keep outputs accurate, consistent, and grounded in provided context rather than adding unsupported, irrelevant, or fabricated content. A recurring formulation makes unfaithfulness concrete as responses that contradict the retrieved document or contain material that cannot be verified from it. Many papers further emphasize conflict settings, defining the construct through whether a model follows contextual knowledge when it disagrees with parametric or internal knowledge.

Space of facets. Papers use several closely overlapping labels around this usage, including contextual faithfulness, context-faithfulness, sensitivity to contextual knowledge, context fidelity, and source fidelity, along with other labels for long-context, reasoning, and grounding variants. The distinction that appears most often is between external evidence, such as retrieved documents, source documents, long input context, or dialogue history, and the model's own parametric or internal knowledge. Failure is described in similar terms across t

nodes.name: Context management
nodes.definition: The ability of an LLM agent to maintain a relevant and concise working context during code exploration by filtering out irrelevant or redundant information that could mislead the localization process.

nodes.name: Context retention
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats context retention as maintaining, accessing, and using relevant information or instructions over long contexts, multiple turns, or long sequences of generation. Most definitions differ mainly by setting, long-context fact access, conversational or task continuity, and long-form generation, and one paper makes the boundary explicit by separating retention from sequential reasoning. A smaller line uses the label memory retention for different targets: preserving untargeted knowledge after unlearning operations, or preserving recorded memories for later recall.

Space of facets. Papers do not offer a shared formal taxonomy, but they use several near-overlapping names for similar long-context phenomena: information retention, context retention, sustained context management, and memory retention. The clearest internal contrast is between retaining facts or instructions and reasoning over them in sequence, with one paper describing models as able to store and retrieve large amounts of information while remaining constrained in coherent multi-step inference. Other papers situate the construct in multi-turn instruction transf

nodes.name: Context sensitivity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats context sensitivity as the extent to which outputs or judgments change with contextual information. Most definitions frame it as adaptation of goals, predictions, rationales, or token choices to the current environment, country, preceding context, or other situational cues, rather than to generic response priors or the current input alone. A smaller line of work casts it more normatively, as producing context-appropriate guidance or interpretation, for example when context helps distinguish sarcasm, critique, or non-toxic language from harmful content. Another recurring framing stresses dependence on situational framing itself, as when causal judgments vary across contexts.

Space of facets. The term is applied to several objects: generated goals, survey predictions, rationales, causal judgments, toxicity interpretations, and token-level predictions. The main axis of variation is what counts as context, ranging from agent state, inventory, and environment, to country labels, preceding context, and broader discursive setting. One paper uses the near-synonymous label contextual sensitivity for the same general phenomeno

nodes.name: Context utilization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is the extent or latent ability of a model to make effective use of provided context when generating outputs. Many definitions make this concrete as incorporating relevant information from retrieved or external documents into the final response, leveraging evidence or knowledge on demand, or using the full available input context rather than only a small portion. Smaller lines of work define it more narrowly as answering from input context instead of parametric knowledge when the two conflict, using prior reasoning steps or dialog history, combining textual context with numerical time series, or as an internal memory mechanism for storing and leveraging past information rather than total memory capacity.

Space of facets. Papers use several neighboring labels for overlapping ideas, including context usage, context reliance, knowledge utilization, context utilisation, context integration, and memory utilization. Some papers treat the construct as a property of responses, such as whether retrieved information is incorporated into the final answer, while others phrase it as a model ability or tendency. One line of work contrast

nodes.name: Contextual accuracy
nodes.definition: The model's ability to align translations with visual and auditory context, such as character actions or emotional tone, beyond textual semantics.

nodes.name: Contextual adherence
nodes.definition: The degree to which the model's generated speech conforms to its conditioning inputs, such as the provided text and speaker identity.

nodes.name: Contextual meme understanding
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to interpret the meaning and intent of a meme by integrating information from its surrounding conversational context, such as post text and community comments.

nodes.name: Contextual reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats contextual reasoning as a latent ability to use full, relevant context to make judgments or inferences, rather than relying on literal keyword matching, surface-level cues, or memorization. This appears in definitions about understanding instructions through situational or functional relations, making deontic judgments from full semantic and situational context, using surrounding code and path-sensitive information to judge vulnerability, and using provided context, variable bindings, or sequence structure to infer an answer. Some authors phrase the construct more narrowly as context-specific query reasoning or as sequence reasoning that selectively focuses on relevant context.

Space of facets. Papers characterize the construct by the kind of context being brought to bear: situational and functional relations in instructions, surrounding code and path-sensitive information, roles, relationships, and transmission principles in information flows, user interests and specialized field descriptions in queries, and variable bindings or sequence structure in abstract tasks. Nearby labels, including contextual reasoning, con

nodes.name: Contextual understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this construct as a latent ability to understand, integrate, and use surrounding context so that predictions, responses, or judgments are task-appropriate. Most definitions vary mainly in what counts as context, such as dialogue history, preceding text, retrieved documents, long input sequences, problem descriptions, or multimodal evidence, but keep the same core framing of context use in interpretation or generation. A smaller line of work narrows it to specific settings, including differentiating between groups only when it should, deciding whether answering a query is safe given the context, inferring an image’s true situational context, or solving using only the information available in a puzzle. Another recurring difference is whether papers describe a general model capacity or define the construct through a particular task, such as classification, retrieval, ambiguity resolution, or harmfulness understanding under socio-cultural, historical, or situational context.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for largely overlapping ideas, including context understanding, contextual awareness, con

nodes.name: Continual learning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats continual learning as a model ability to acquire new skills, tasks, or knowledge over time from new or streaming data while retaining performance on what was learned before. Most versions make avoidance of catastrophic forgetting explicit, describing learning without degrading performance or retaining prior information while new tasks arrive "in a streaming fashion." Smaller strands broaden this to lifelong learning from ongoing interaction with an open-world environment, narrow it to learning a sequence of tasks without retraining on past data, or specify continuous updating that integrates new information without parameter updates or retraining.

Space of facets. Papers most commonly organize the construct around sequential, streaming, or episodic task settings, with a single model adapting to task sequences such as {T1, T2, ... TK} or series of novel relations. A smaller line of work places application-specific variants under it, for example few-shot continual relation extraction, described as "a branch of continual information extraction." One paper frames effective continual learning methods around two r

nodes.name: Contract understanding
nodes.definition: The task of processing and interpreting legal contracts to extract specific information or answer questions about their content.

nodes.name: Controllability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the literature, the prevailing usage treats controllability as the ability to steer a model's behavior or outputs toward user-specified requirements, often at inference time. Many papers phrase this as steering by prompts, instructions, or adjustable parameters, for example by choosing and customizing behavior at test time through critique weights or retrieval thresholds, or by making a model adopt desired personas, traits, or target viewpoints. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to controlled generation under syntactic, semantic, length, information-density, validity, or vocabulary-complexity constraints, while another line defines it as intervention on internal representations so a targeted attribute changes without altering others. A few papers specialize the idea further as control over context sensitivity, ethical behavioral correction, targeted execution of design intentions, or simultaneous satisfaction of multiple attributes.

Space of facets. Papers use a broad family of near-synonymous labels for overlapping ideas, including steerability, controllable generation, controlled generation, generation control, prompt steerability, behavio

nodes.name: Conventional-solution bias
nodes.definition: A phenomenon where an LLM-powered error detector shows a significant performance gap between conventional and alternative solutions to a problem, favoring the more common or expected solution format.

nodes.name: Conversational ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats conversational ability as a latent capacity or capability for coherent, context-aware dialogue, usually across multiple turns and sometimes with explicit instruction following. Many definitions fold in neighboring qualities such as fluency, helpfulness, appropriateness, consistency, broad topic coverage, or maintaining prior dialogue context. A smaller line of work frames the construct more as overall chatbot performance or quality, inferred from comparative judgments or focused on setting-specific dialogue quality in domains such as spoken chat, image-authenticity discussion, or medical consultation.

Space of facets. When papers break the notion down, the clearest facet structure is fluency, coherency, and consistency. Some authors place a nearby label, generalist chat capability, as one subcategory of alignment alongside world knowledge and instruction following, which situates conversational ability relative to other evaluated abilities. Papers also use several neighboring names for closely related versions of the construct, including conversational capability, dialogue capability, multi-turn capability

nodes.name: Copyright infringement risk
nodes.definition: The potential for a model to generate content that violates copyright law, particularly through the reproduction of long verbatim quotations from protected sources.

nodes.name: Core knowledge
nodes.definition: The foundational, intuitive understanding of concepts that allows for effective problem-solving and generalization from few examples.

nodes.name: Corrigibility
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of an LLM to acknowledge mistakes and accept correction when prompted with conflicting or incorrect information.

nodes.name: Counterfactual fairness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, usage splits between two framings built on changing a sensitive or demographic attribute while holding the rest of the prompt fixed. One paper defines counterfactual fairness as a latent ability of the model to produce the same output for an individual if the sensitive attribute had been different, with other relevant factors held constant, while another uses the adjacent label counterfactual bias for the tendency to produce semantically different or biased responses when only demographic-sensitive attributes in otherwise matched prompts are changed. The main difference is between a positive invariance requirement and a negative difference or bias framing.

Space of facets. Systematization is minimal and centers on the counterfactual comparison itself. One paper keeps the fairness label for the requirement that the model would have produced the same output under a different sensitive attribute, while another organizes the same setup under counterfactual bias and describes it as assessing semantic differences across LLM responses caused by varying demographic groups mentioned in counterfactual prompts.

Space of measurement. No measurement in

nodes.name: Counterfactual reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats counterfactual reasoning, sometimes also called counterfactual thinking or counterfactuality, as the ability or capacity to reason in hypothetical, contrary-to-fact scenarios: answering what-if questions, considering alternative outcomes under changed conditions, or determining what would have happened if a past event or decision had been different. Several papers tie this directly to causal reasoning, and one definition places it at "the third and highest level of Pearl's causal hierarchy"; a smaller line of work narrows it to settings such as trajectory-level re-evaluation of long-term decisions and credit assignment, or answering under an edited premise or hypothetical knowledge state. Only a minority depart from the latent-ability framing, either describing it as the observable behavior of reasoning about what might have happened differently, or using "counter-factual" language for answer refinement and hallucination avoidance.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels, most often counterfactual reasoning, but also counterfactual thinking and counterfactuality, usually for the same bro

nodes.name: Counting ability
nodes.definition: The cognitive capability to accurately determine the number of objects in an image as specified by a caption.

nodes.name: Coverage
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, Coverage is not used with a single stable meaning. A recurring framing treats it as a support or probability-mass property: how well a base model or offline data cover an optimal response or the support of a benchmark policy, sometimes formalized as how much probability mass is assigned to the arg-max response on average. Other papers use Coverage for completeness of extracted factual claims, defined as capturing verifiable information without explicitly including unverifiable content, or for the inclusion of new patterns from an original dataset in a condensed subset.

Space of facets. The term is broken down differently by task. In claim extraction work it has sentence-level and element-level forms; in sharpening work it is formalized with a coverage coefficient based on 1/πbase(y⋆(x)|x); in offline preference work it appears as a coverage assumption about D_y(·|x) covering the support of π⋆(·|x); and in dataset condensation it refers to samples that introduce patterns not yet covered by the existing condensed subsets. Taken together, papers use the same name for model-level, data-support, extraction-level, and dataset-pattern notions rath

nodes.name: Creativity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats creativity as a model ability or capacity for generating novel, original, diverse, imaginative, or unconventional content, ideas, artifacts, tasks, or solutions. Many definitions also attach a fit condition, describing outputs as coherent, valuable, contextually appropriate, or aligned with user intent rather than merely new. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to constrained text composition, non-obvious problem solving, or adaptive reasoning in unfamiliar environments, while another minority treats creativity as a property of outputs or their judged quality, such as novelty relative to standard responses or ratings of cleverness, remoteness, and uncommonness.

Space of facets. One paper breaks creativity into convergent thinking, defined as purposefulness toward a goal, and divergent thinking, defined as adaptability to explore new environments or constraints. Another paper treats creativity scoring as having two complementary dimensions, the intrinsic qualities of ideas, such as flexibility or diversity, and their extrinsic statistical infrequency, and related human judgments are described throu

nodes.name: Credit assignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing framing is that credit assignment is about tracing later outcomes back to earlier steps or actions in a multi-step process. The definitions agree on localizing where success, failure, or reward came from, but they vary in the bearer of the ability: one paper describes a language agent understanding where it made mistakes in an environment, another a reward model determining where an incorrect reasoning chain went wrong, and another an RL algorithm attributing delayed rewards to earlier actions.

Space of facets. In these papers, the term appears across settings that include agent behavior in environments, reward models over reasoning chains, and RL algorithms facing delayed rewards. A recurring contrast is between coarse outcome-level signals and more local step-level or action-level localization: one study says process supervision gives a richer signal because it marks how many early steps were correct and "the precise location of the incorrect step," while another pairs credit assignment with root cause analysis and understanding where the agent made mistakes.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral in

nodes.name: Critical thinking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat critical thinking as a latent capacity for objective analysis and evaluation that supports reasoned judgment, often adding questioning assumptions, detecting inconsistencies, or independently weighing conflicting viewpoints. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to cases where a model resists incorrect user influence or flawed instructions, including refusing to choose among invalid options, while another task-specific framing casts it as reviewing a proposed solution for deficiencies, overlooked constraints, and constructive critique. Across these definitions, the main agreement is that it is an evaluative reasoning ability, and the main variation is whether it is defined broadly or through specific settings such as debate, solution review, or invalid multiple-choice prompts.

Space of facets. Papers place it in slightly different conceptual neighborhoods. One paper presents critical thinking as part of logical reasoning abilities, while another uses the nearby labels reflective judgment and critical reasoning: reflective judgment is the capacity to question or disregard flawed instructions, and critical reasoning is the und

nodes.name: Critique ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats critique ability as a model's capacity, or sometimes prompted behavior, of evaluating outputs or reasoning, identifying flaws or errors, and often using that feedback to revise or improve the response. Most definitions center on self-critique, where the model critiques its own output or reasoning, though some broaden the construct to critiquing generic responses or other models' reasoning and emphasize "detailed analysis, constructive suggestions, and refinement feedback." A smaller line of work narrows the label to forms such as academic peer review or critical judgment, and some authors frame it as an observable iterative critique-and-revise procedure rather than a latent capability.

Space of facets. Papers split the construct in several ways. One recurring decomposition distinguishes discrimination, the ability to identify or rank mistakes, from critiquing, the ability to provide actionable feedback for improvement, and one paper says discrimination tends to be easier than generation. Another benchmark breaks critique ability into feedback, comparison, correction, and meta-feedback, while other definitions sep

nodes.name: Cross abilities
nodes.definition: The ability to integrate multiple distinct capabilities across different types of expertise to address complex, real-world tasks.

nodes.name: Cross ability
nodes.definition: The ability to integrate multiple distinct capabilities across different types of expertise to address complex, real-world tasks.

nodes.name: Cross-domain generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a model's ability to transfer learned knowledge or maintain performance when training and evaluation come from different domains, topics, targets, prompt distributions, or environments. Most definitions emphasize unseen or held-out settings, such as targets not encountered during training, websites or query settings not seen in training, or movement from one task domain to another. A smaller line of work narrows the transferred object, describing the generalization of learned preferences and concept importance, optimized safety checks and risk patterns, or representations learned from speech and music to bioacoustics. The main variation is therefore in what counts as a domain and in whether the construct is framed as overall task performance or as the transfer of particular learned components.

Space of facets. Rather than a single taxonomy, papers use several near-synonymous labels for closely related uses, including domain transfer, cross-domain transfer, cross-domain adaptability, out-of-domain generalization, domain transferability, and cross-platform generalization. Under these labels, the domain boundary is instanti

nodes.name: Cross-lingual alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats cross-lingual alignment as a latent semantic or representational property: semantically equivalent content in different languages is mapped into a shared space, with sentence embeddings, internal representations, or hidden states brought closer together. Many definitions make this closeness the core of the construct and present it as the basis for cross-lingual transfer. A smaller line of work defines it more by what the shared space enables, such as zero-shot knowledge transfer, language-agnostic reasoning, cross-lingual inference, retrieval, or translation. The main disagreement is whether the construct is the internal closeness itself, the latent ability that follows from it, or a task-specific form of semantic matching.

Space of facets. Papers use several overlapping names for closely related notions, including multilingual alignment, multilingual representation alignment, multilingual semantic alignment, cross-lingual semantic alignment, and language-agnostic semantic processing, alongside other representation-alignment labels. Most of these labels point to the same shared-space formulation, but some authors

nodes.name: Cross-lingual consistency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the term is used in two ways. One usage defines cross-lingual consistency as the degree to which a multilingual model gives semantically equivalent and correct outputs for the same factual query across languages, while another uses it more broadly for whether task or domain performance is stable and comparable across languages, especially within a language family. The papers agree that the construct concerns alignment across languages, but they differ on the reference object: same-query output equivalence and correctness versus cross-language performance stability.

Space of facets. The available papers do not introduce named subtypes, and no construct-to-construct links are reported. The main organizing difference is scope: one framing is narrow and tied to factual queries and parallel facts, while another treats the same label as a broader property of performance across languages and language families.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is narrow in the available work: the construct is linked to 2 measurement instruments, NOVA-63 and XSafety, and to no behavioral indicators. One paper evaluates it with the overlap ratio of co

nodes.name: Cross-lingual generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats cross-lingual generalization as a model ability to transfer knowledge, skills, or representations from one language to another, most often from English or other high-resource languages to low-resource or unseen languages. Many definitions cast it as a latent property of multilingual models, sometimes grounded in aligned multilingual semantic spaces or shared representations, while another common framing defines it through effective performance on other languages without explicit target-language training. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to particular transferred behaviors, such as hallucination mitigation, named entity recognition, reasoning, discourse processing, or document assessment across languages. The main disagreement is scope, broad transfer ability versus task-specific cross-lingual performance, and whether the construct is described as an internal representational property or directly through downstream outcomes.

Space of facets. Papers often use several near-synonymous labels for roughly the same idea, including multilingual generalization, cross-lingual transfer, cross-lingual knowledge trans

nodes.name: Cross-modal grounding
nodes.definition: The ability to correctly align and reference information between visual and textual modalities, ensuring that answers are grounded in the actual content of the image.

nodes.name: Cross-programming-language generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this construct as transfer across programming languages: a model or software-engineering system applies knowledge, skills, reasoning, or problem-solving performance learned in one language to tasks in other, often unseen, languages. Most definitions share that cross-language transfer core. The main difference is scope, because some papers describe a model's learned knowledge or reasoning capabilities, while another frames it as the degree of performance transfer across programming languages and language-specific codebases.

Space of facets. Papers use near-synonymous labels for the same idea, including cross-lingual transferability and cross-language generalization or generalizability. They discuss it through source-target language directions, transfer from Python to other languages, and whether systems move beyond Python repositories toward language-agnostic solutions. One paper also discusses it alongside visual problem-solving limitations and non-Python bugs.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and the only linked behavioral indicator is Knowledge retrieval, but that link is recorded a

nodes.name: Cultural adaptation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers describe cultural adaptation as alignment or adjustment to culture-specific norms, values, rules, and discourse patterns in a given context. Some define it at the model level, as the ability to adjust responses based on a user's cultural context or to adhere to the norms of particular communities, while others define it at the output level, as generated content or dialogue that respects social norms, traditions, sensitivities, and culturally relevant conversational styles. A smaller line of work adds a narrower emphasis on accurately representing diverse norms, especially in non-Western and low-income regions, and on avoiding ethnocentric evaluation.

Space of facets. Papers use several closely related labels for this construct, most often cultural adaptability, cultural appropriateness, and norm following. One line of work breaks it down by levels of norm specificity, "from abstract values to explicit social norms," while another treats it as part of localization beyond literal translation, covering culturally relevant norms, entities, and conversational styles. The main axis of variation is whether papers treat it as a model capacity to

nodes.name: Cultural alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, cultural alignment is most commonly described as correspondence between a model's outputs, responses, judgments, or expressed values and the norms, values, beliefs, or expressions of a particular culture, often with an explicit contrast to defaulting to dominant or Western perspectives. Several definitions instantiate this around specific cultural contexts, including Arab social and political sensitivities, culture-specific image captioning, or culture-specific hate speech judgments, while a smaller line of work broadens the target to pluralistic alignment with diverse human cultures. A minority framing uses the label cultural value adaptation for a latent ability to align behavior with a culture's norms, attitudes, and values, beyond mere language use.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a shared subtype taxonomy, but they do separate a specific-culture framing from a pluralistic one aimed at diverse human cultures. Some authors describe the construct through model values, beliefs, and preferences inferred from responses to culturally sensitive questions, whereas others speak more broadly about outputs or responses reflecting cultural norms

nodes.name: Cultural authenticity
nodes.definition: The degree to which generated stories reflect the sociocultural characteristics specified in the prompt in a way that matches the intended cultural context.

nodes.name: Cultural bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage describes cultural bias as a model tendency to favor some cultural perspectives, knowledge, symbols, values, or norms over others, usually with Western or U.S. content treated as the advantaged case and less prevalent or underrepresented cultures described as receiving limited knowledge, templated outputs, or uneven performance. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to a measurable performance disparity, especially in vision-language image understanding, where an unbiased model is expected to perform similarly across groups and Western bias is computed from relative performance on Western versus East Asian examples. Some definitions further stress stereotyped or implicit associations, such as linking cultural groups to particular traits, settings, or other attributes, so the main disagreement is between broad model-level favoritism or stereotyping and task-level error disparity, and between broad cultural imbalance and explicitly Western-dominant cases.

Space of facets. Papers organize the label through domain-specific manifestations rather than a single fixed taxonomy: culture-conditioned generations, narrative cont

nodes.name: Cultural commonsense
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available papers use two nearby but distinct framings. One paper treats it as shared background knowledge about culturally grounded social expectations that guides appropriate interaction and is "shared within Persian culture but often not intuitive to outsiders" (We Politely Insist: Your LLM Must Learn the Persian Art of Taarof). Another uses the neighboring label "commonsense cultural reasoning" for the capacity to make inferences from everyday, implicit knowledge about cultural norms, practices, and associations, with examples such as attire or food pairing (DRISHTIKON: A Multimodal Multilingual Benchmark for Testing Language Models' Understanding on Indian Culture). The main difference is whether the construct is framed as shared cultural knowledge or as reasoning based on that knowledge.

Space of facets. Within the available uses, one paper presents Taarof as a form of cultural commonsense, while another turns "Common Sense Cultural" into a reasoning category for everyday cultural inference. The labels "cultural commonsense" and "commonsense cultural reasoning" are used for closely related ideas, with the first centered on socially grounded expectati

nodes.name: Cultural competence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats cultural competence, often under the overlapping labels cultural sensitivity or cultural competency, as a model-level capability to understand, recognize, and appropriately respond to culturally specific contexts, norms, values, and practices. Many definitions add that this should help avoid offensive, alienating, or otherwise culturally inappropriate and biased outputs, or enable meaningful engagement with users from different cultural backgrounds. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to accurate capture of culturally nuanced knowledge across cultural groups and prompt conditions, while some papers phrase it as a latent model ability and others as the degree reflected in model outputs.

Space of facets. Papers do not offer a single formal taxonomy, but they repeatedly organize the construct around respect for values, communication styles, practices, norms, taboos, and behavioral or linguistic conventions. The same family of terms is used for several scopes: broad navigation of diverse cultural contexts, meaningful engagement with users from different cultural backgrounds, and narrower domains such as non-verb

nodes.name: Cultural knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats cultural knowledge as a latent or internal model property: stored, implicit, or retrievable understanding of culture-specific facts, norms, values, practices, beliefs, and local context that supports interpreting queries or producing contextually appropriate responses. Most definitions stay close to this framing, though they vary in scope, from broad coverage of history, religion, cuisine, and social norms to narrower settings such as food-related knowledge or culturally specific factual recall in Filipino contexts. One paper instead uses the label cultural literacy for a shared, translinguistic body of community-specific cultural and factual knowledge, and then treats models' knowledge of culturally embedded facts as a proxy for that notion.

Space of facets. When papers spell out the construct, they usually do so by listing domains rather than by proposing formal subtypes. The recurring domains are norms and values, history, cuisine or food, art, religion, legal frameworks, geographical markers, and region-specific practices, and one paper says its coverage spans a wide range of 11 domains. Several papers

nodes.name: Cultural understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats cultural understanding as a latent ability to comprehend, reason about, interpret, or reference culturally specific knowledge, norms, meanings, and contexts tied to a particular audience, language community, or national or regional setting. Many definitions emphasize shared cultural references or context-rich meanings in items such as proverbs, narratives, cuisines, history, and civic norms. A smaller line of work uses nearby labels such as cultural awareness for understanding and navigating social interactions in line with cultural norms, or for recognizing and incorporating culturally specific information in outputs rather than producing Western-centric or generic responses, and one paper narrows the construct to local cultural reasoning as causal reasoning within a specific cultural context.

Space of facets. Papers organize the construct through locale- and task-specific content, including Japanese, Italian, Indian, Persian, and Arabic contexts, as well as domains such as shared cultural references, regional cuisines, figurative language, and region-specific socio-political structures. Some papers separate it from

nodes.name: Culturally grounded safety
nodes.definition: The extent to which a model's safety behavior is aligned with local sociocultural norms, sensitivities, and language-specific context rather than only generic safety standards.

nodes.name: Curiosity
nodes.definition: A model's latent tendency to explore unknowns and identify knowledge gaps through questioning, analogous to epistemic curiosity in humans.

nodes.name: Data analysis ability
nodes.definition: The latent capacity to understand data-centric questions, inspect relevant files and tables, and derive correct answers from complex real-world data analysis settings.

nodes.name: Debuggability
nodes.definition: The capacity to easily identify, diagnose, and correct unwanted behaviors or errors in the model by inspecting its internal concept-based representations.

nodes.name: Deception
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats deception as a latent model tendency, capacity, or disposition to produce misleading, dishonest, or factually incorrect outputs, often in ways that conflict with what the model is described as knowing or believing. Most papers keep this framing, variously emphasizing concealment or manipulation, lies that appear truthful, or deceptive responses under dishonest instructions, and one task-specific formulation describes deceptive evidence as evidence "inconsistent with the information or beliefs you know" (Learning to Discuss Strategically: A Case Study on One Night Ultimate Werewolf). A smaller line of work uses a different definition, deceptive alignment, for a model that behaves well in training but pursues different goals in deployment when it detects it is no longer in a test environment.

Space of facets. Papers most often organize the concept through contrasts with truthfulness: one study examines representations that flip from truthful to deceptive under deceptive versus truthful or neutral instructions, and another reports lies even when the system prompt says the model should not lie. Several papers

nodes.name: Decision-level ability
nodes.definition: The latent cognitive capacity for problem-solving, diagnosis, and planning required to determine a course of action for a given skill.

nodes.name: Decision-making
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats decision-making as a latent or cognitive capability for planning, choosing, and sequencing actions toward goals in an environment. Definitions in this cluster describe support for sequential action selection and policy formation across interactive environments, the ability to plan, make decisions, and take actions autonomously, or the capacity to perceive the environment, make choices, and select appropriate actions to achieve a goal. A smaller line of work uses narrower framings: as an observable process of evaluating candidate activities against internal desire states, as a decision-level problem-solving, diagnosis, and planning capacity distinct from execution, or as high-level reasoning that connects abstract decisions to low-level control.

Space of facets. Papers use several overlapping labels for nearby ideas, including decision-making capability, decision-making ability, decision-level ability, high-level reasoning, and activity evaluation. One strand explicitly decomposes skills into decision-level components such as problem-solving and diagnosis, versus action-level components such as execution an

nodes.name: Decision-making under uncertainty
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the shared core is evaluating or choosing among possibilities when information is incomplete or limited. One framing treats it narrowly as selecting the more likely outcome when evidence is partial, ambiguous, or incomplete, including cases where "the task is to decide which outcome is more likely given C"; another treats it more broadly as iteratively searching for optimal solutions by evaluating possibilities from limited evidence and prior beliefs, especially under incomplete information or large solution spaces.

Space of facets. The main organizing distinction in the definitions is scope: one usage centers a single comparison between outcomes, while the other extends it to an iterative search process that explicitly incorporates prior beliefs and vast solution spaces. Both place the construct in settings of incomplete information, but only the broader framing makes prior beliefs part of the construct itself.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The operationalization that does appear is task-based rather than instrument-based: papers describe deciding which outcom

nodes.name: Defeasible reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats defeasible reasoning as non-monotonic reasoning: an inference or prior conclusion can be revised when new evidence appears. Most formulations share this update-or-retract framing, using language such as inferences being altered in light of new evidence or previously accepted statements being revoked when contradictions emerge. Some authors describe it more specifically as making plausible inferences from incomplete information, where later information can strengthen, weaken, or defeat a conclusion.

Space of facets. Papers consistently place the construct under non-monotonic reasoning, and one paper uses the label non-monotonic reasoning for the capability to revise prior conclusions in light of new evidence. Another naming variation is defeasible inference. The main internal breakdown stated in the definitions is by how new information affects a conclusion, namely strengthening, weakening, or defeating it, and one paper contrasts this kind of reasoning with traditional NLI as a different type of natural language reasoning.

Space of measurement. Papers link it to no measurement instruments, one behavioral indicat

nodes.name: Deontological morality
nodes.definition: A moral framework where the morality of an action is judged based on its adherence to a set of rules or norms, such as not defecting against a cooperator.

nodes.name: Deontological reasoning
nodes.definition: A moral reasoning style that evaluates actions by adherence to moral rules, duties, rights, or principles rather than outcomes.

nodes.name: Depth
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, depth is treated as a property of model outputs: how fully and substantively a response develops its topic, rather than remaining shallow. One definition describes it as generated content that develops topics in a detailed, substantive, and non-shallow way, while another uses the variant name depth of knowledge for the degree to which a response demonstrates substantive expertise or detailed subject-matter knowledge. The shared core is detail and substance in responses, though the emphasis differs between topic development and demonstrated expertise.

Space of facets. Systematization is limited. One paper places depth alongside relevance, breadth, and novelty as parallel evaluation dimensions, while another discusses depth of knowledge together with expertise and reports that both humans and LLMs assign high weight to those attributes. The available material does not describe subtypes of depth or a broader taxonomy beyond these neighboring terms.
