Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to depth, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. In the available uses, papers apply it directly as an evaluation crit

nodes.name: Description correctness
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model's textual description of an image accurately reflects the visual content, including entities, attributes, and relationships.

nodes.name: Detoxification ability
nodes.definition: The underlying capacity of a model to effectively identify and remove toxic content across different forms and contexts without over- or under-correcting.

nodes.name: Diagram understanding ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage frames this as a latent ability to interpret structured information in diagrams, including their components, layout, and semantic meaning. A smaller line of work narrows it to a perceptual ability for diagrams representing physical systems, emphasizing correct interpretation of components, their properties, and their structural relationships. The main difference is scope and framing: broad diagram interpretation in most definitions, versus perception-focused understanding in a physical-science setting in a minority framing.

Space of facets. Papers use closely related labels, namely diagram understanding, diagram comprehension, and physical diagram understanding, with the last functioning as the more specific variant. One paper places physical diagram understanding inside a perception component of expert-level multi-modal reasoning, describing it as understanding the physical context in multi-modal input and handling diagrams with complex physical structures.

Space of measurement. The only linked operationalization uses 1 measurement instrument, the MMMU benchmark, and no behavioral indicators are linked. In that u

nodes.name: Dialogue understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available definition, the construct is framed as processing conversational context and responding to dialogue-based inputs over long contexts. No competing definition or explicit disagreement appears in the papers represented here.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is limited in the papers here: it is linked to 1 measurement instrument and 1 behavioral indicator overall, but only the instrument is explicitly recorded as measuring it. InfiniteBench is the only linked measurement instrument, with evidence coming from a table entry for a "Dialogue" task in An Evolved Universal Transformer Memory. The only linked behavioral indicator is dialogue state tracking, but that link is recorded as related rather than measured_by, so the relationships do not provide a second direct measurement route.

Links. Beyond measurement, one paper reports that dialogue state tracking is related to dialogue understanding. In A Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Pipeline for Dialogue Understanding, the evidence connects dialogue state tracking to understanding user needs and executing appropriate system actions in task-oriented dialogues. No causal or correlational links are rec

nodes.name: Disability bias
nodes.definition: A latent tendency of LLMs to generate systematically less favorable, less accurate, or more stereotypical responses when queries reference disability, reflecting embedded ableist patterns in model behavior.

nodes.name: Disambiguation ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats disambiguation ability as a model's context-sensitive capacity to distinguish among multiple possible meanings or interpretations and respond or translate accordingly. Most definitions instantiate this shared framing in different settings: ambiguous questions with multiple valid readings, words in context, ambiguous terms in translation, entities that share a surface name, superlatives with absolute versus relative readings, and vague or colloquial instructions, sometimes by integrating visual context or common sense. A smaller framing defines it more specifically as sensitivity to same-sense versus different-sense boundaries in a way that mirrors human judgments.

Space of facets. Papers most often systematize the construct by the type of ambiguity being resolved. Some distinguish among alternative readings or meanings, such as multiple valid question interpretations, absolute versus relative superlative readings, or same-sense versus different-sense contexts, while others narrow it to lexical translation, entity disambiguation, or instruction understanding. One survey organizes disambiguation work into th

nodes.name: Discourse understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. A recurring framing treats discourse understanding as understanding the relations and organization that make text coherent: papers describe it as understanding how a text is organized and how its parts contribute to overall meaning and coherence, or as a latent model ability to infer and generate coherent continuations from discourse relations, with one paper noting that such relations involve "longer spans and complex reasoning." Other papers use differently scoped versions of the construct: one defines it as interpreting and reasoning over lengthy, complex narratives to answer questions that require a cohesive understanding of the whole text, while another uses a related label for comprehending and using reply dependency structure in multi-turn dialogue for semantic interpretation and information extraction. Across these definitions, the main differences are whether the construct is framed as a latent model ability or as a task, and whether it targets text organization, discourse relations across argument spans, whole-narrative reasoning, or dialogue reply structure.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a single shared breakdown of the construct, but they

nodes.name: Discrete reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to reason over distinct, separate elements within a text, such as performing multi-step inferences over facts presented in a paragraph.

nodes.name: Disentanglement
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the only explicit framing treats disentanglement as a property of internal representations: distinct, interpretable factors of variation in the data are captured by separate dimensions of the representation. The accompanying usage follows this representational language, describing a rich disentangled orthogonal basis for low-rank adapters, more compact disentangled representations, and a greater tendency to disentangle two adapters. No competing explicit definition is stated.

Space of facets. Papers do not provide a formal subtype taxonomy, but they apply the term to several representational targets. Besides internal representations, they use it for low-rank adapters in the frequency domain, model activations, and task-relevant attributes, with one paper describing activations in human-interpretable features and another describing attributes disentangled for precise control over model behavior.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument and no behavioral indicator are linked to this construct. Instead, papers describe it qualitatively through representational properties, including a rich disentangled orthogonal basis, m

nodes.name: Disparity
nodes.definition: A systematic difference in model behavior across socially or factually contrastive conditions, reflecting either social bias or susceptibility to misinformation, which persists as a latent trait across evaluation instances.

nodes.name: Distraction bias
nodes.definition: A tendency for an LLM judge to be influenced by irrelevant or unimportant details in the prompt or response.

nodes.name: Distribution alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the term is not used in a single way. The prevailing framing describes how closely selected training data matches representative examples from a target task, so that a model can learn the target distribution efficiently; one formulation says the selected data should "match the distribution of the representative examples from the target task." A smaller formulation uses the same label for a student model's ability to replicate a teacher model's output probability distribution across tokens and contexts, described as "fine-grained" and "per-token" alignment. The main difference is whether alignment is defined over training-data selection relative to a target task or over model output probabilities relative to a teacher distribution.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a single stable taxonomy, but they do place the construct in different local structures. One paper treats it as one objective in task-specific data selection and describes a smooth trade-off with generation diversity, while another treats it at a fine-grained, token-wise level through dynamic mixing of divergences. A separate usage contrasts a "distribution alignment setting" wit

nodes.name: Divergent thinking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats divergent thinking as a capacity or cognitive ability to generate multiple distinct ideas, alternatives, or solution pathways from a single task or starting point. Some definitions add novelty or unconventionality, describing alternatives not previously used in the human solution space and exploration of new environments or constraints, while another ties the capacity to varied in-context examples and few-shot prompts. A smaller line of work uses the label divergent reasoning for generating multiple plausible connections and hypotheses from limited expert knowledge by extrapolating to correlated queried concepts.

Space of facets. A recurring framing positions it within creativity, alongside convergent thinking: convergent thinking is described as purposefulness toward a goal, and divergent thinking as adaptability to explore new environments or constraints. In one multi-agent framing, the divergent-thoughts process has two core components, retrieval of relevant tool-usage demos and generation of different few-shot prompts with varied (Q, C, A) tuples, and it proceeds through multiple planning pathways. The terminolog

nodes.name: Document understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a broad capacity to comprehend, extract, and interpret information from documents, often with multimodal or structural content such as text, images, tables, figures, layout, or positional cues. Several definitions explicitly include content, structure, and context, and some narrow the setting to structured visual documents such as forms or invoices or to multi-page documents. A smaller line of work defines it through question answering over a retrieved document or document image, while another paper focuses on synthesizing relationships across an entire document rather than isolated sentences; papers also vary on whether they cast it as a latent ability or as an observable task.

Space of facets. Papers use nearby labels with overlapping but not identical scope. Document comprehension usually carries the broader framing that integrates content with structure, context, layout, or positional cues, whereas document-level understanding is reserved for synthesis across texts, paragraphs, or chapters within a document and for identifying relationships beyond isolated sentences. Some authors also use document understanding as an

nodes.name: Domain knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing treats domain knowledge as a latent understanding, reservoir, or ability to access and apply specialized concepts, facts, terminology, procedures, or entities for a particular field, task, or environment. This includes formulations tied to interpreting observations and choosing actions, handling specialized statistical language and quantitative reasoning, bringing background knowledge to modeling decisions, or using domain-specific information for translation and review. A smaller line of work broadens the construct to a model's repository of professional or comprehensive knowledge across many subjects, while other papers narrow it to localized Chinese professional knowledge, in-domain knowledge acquired through fine-tuning, or circuit component-type recognition. Another recurring split is between knowledge as an underlying model property and knowledge as demonstrated in task performance, such as diagnosis, qualification tasks, tutoring, or paper review.

Space of facets. Papers use many near-synonymous labels, especially professional knowledge, domain-specific knowledge, domain expertise, specialized knowledge, and professi

nodes.name: Domain specialization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers use domain specialization for expert-level selectivity across domains: specific experts preferentially activate for, or are preferentially routed, tokens from particular domains, and in one formulation from distinct modalities as well. Within that prevailing framing, some authors describe it as a latent tendency of experts, while others make it explicitly degree-based, as the proportion of tokens from a domain routed to a given expert. A minority usage applies the same term more broadly to adapting a general-purpose LLM to domain-specific contextual data and domain objectives for a specific field and task.

Space of facets. The papers organize the concept at different levels. In the expert-routing usage, it is defined for a particular expert and domain pair, and one paper makes the scale explicit by stating that a value of 100% means all data from that domain is routed to that expert; another broadens the relevant categories from domains to modalities. By contrast, the broader usage treats domain specialization as a process applied to a general-purpose LLM for a domain and task, rather than as a property of an individual expert.

Space of

nodes.name: Domain-specific performance
nodes.definition: The model's effectiveness on a specific, targeted set of tasks or data distribution, as opposed to general-purpose performance.

nodes.name: Domain-specific reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the shared framing is a latent ability to apply knowledge from a particular domain to interpret dialogue in context. A technical-dialogue usage casts it as interpreting utterances, diagnosing issues, and inferring likely misunderstandings, and describes it as especially needed for subtler, more context-dependent cases of misalignment. Another usage applies the same construct to emotional support dialogue, where the domain knowledge comes from psychological theories and expert-like reasoning about emotional states, causal events, and user intentions.

Space of facets. Papers do not provide a formal subtype taxonomy for this construct. Instead, they position it through nearby ideas: one paper places it alongside pragmatic reasoning when discussing subtle misalignment, while another associates it with psychological theory, expert cooperation, and dialogue analysis from multiple perspectives for extracting user-related information. The main variation across definitions is the target domain, technical troubleshooting in one usage and emotional support in another, while both treat it as a latent ability rather than an observable beh

nodes.name: Domain-specific robustness
nodes.definition: The model's ability to maintain performance and reliability when applied to specialized, high-stakes domains like medicine.

nodes.name: Dynamic adaptability
nodes.definition: The ability of a multi-agent system to adjust expert selection and collaboration strategies in response to evolving task demands and performance feedback over time.

nodes.name: Easy-to-hard generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats easy-to-hard generalization as a model's ability to learn from simpler tasks or instances and then succeed on harder, larger, or more complex ones. The definitions largely keep that core framing while varying the emphasis: some state that the harder cases receive no additional or direct supervision, some describe it as simple-to-hard generalization on unseen instances with longer or more intricate reasoning chains, and others use closely aligned labels such as transferability to more complex circuits or logical extrapolation to larger and more difficult problems.

Space of facets. Authors differentiate the construct mainly by what makes the target case harder. One recurring formulation ties it to reasoning length, with one paper explicitly saying that simple-to-hard generalization is a type of length generalization, while other papers frame the same pattern as logical extrapolation to greater size and difficulty or as transferability to circuits with more components. Across these papers, the labels easy-to-hard generalization, simple-to-hard generalization, transferability, and logical extrapolation are all used f

nodes.name: Editability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the term does not have a single settled definition, but several neighboring ones centered on how well editing can be sustained. One framing treats it as an inherent capacity of a large language model to be successfully and efficiently modified by editing techniques while maintaining overall performance. Another line narrows it to durability under continued updates, either as retaining multiple edits without forgetting or interference, or as continuously integrating a stream of factual updates while retaining prior knowledge. A separate usage treats it as editing reliability, the degree to which a concept editing method consistently and effectively controls a target concept across different inputs.

Space of facets. Papers systematize the construct through different neighboring labels rather than a shared taxonomy. One line uses multiple edits for the property that a system can edit repeatedly without forgetting previous edits, and lifelong knowledge editing for updating a model with a stream of new or revised facts while retaining previously acquired knowledge. Another paper positions editing reliability as one dimension in a broader four-part e

nodes.name: Editing locality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers describe editing locality as a preservation criterion for knowledge editing: the edit should stay local so that unrelated knowledge, inputs, or outputs remain unchanged. Definitions vary mainly in whether they treat it as a latent property of an editing method or as an observable outcome such as "unrelated knowledge preservation", and in scope, from unrelated knowledge alone to untargeted tasks or model capabilities. One paper uses the same term differently, defining locality as a bounded distance between tokens that matter for prediction in work on length generalization.

Space of facets. Papers usually place locality within a broader evaluation bundle for knowledge editing, alongside efficacy or accuracy, generalization, reliability, and sometimes linguistic quality. Most authors use "locality" and "editing locality" interchangeably, while "unrelated knowledge preservation" names the observable maintenance of performance on knowledge not targeted for editing. A recurring contrast is the continual-editing formulation in which reliability, generalization, and locality form an "impossible triangle", and the clearest same-name divergence is the token

nodes.name: Effective receptive field
nodes.definition: The range of preceding tokens from which a model can effectively integrate information when processing a given token in a sequence.

nodes.name: Egocentric video understanding
nodes.definition: The latent capability to comprehend first-person videos by recognizing activities, objects, and other visual details from a self-centered viewpoint.

nodes.name: Elegance
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to capture and reproduce the aesthetic and artistic qualities of the source poetry, such as vivid imagery, concise expression, and emotional depth.

nodes.name: Embodied reasoning
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to understand and reason about physical environments, including objects, their relations, and dynamics, in order to inform action planning.

nodes.name: Emergent abilities
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats emergent abilities as threshold-like changes in task performance with scale: performance stays near chance or improves only slightly in smaller models, then improves sharply or discontinuously beyond a size or pretraining-compute threshold, with capabilities not seen in smaller models. A recurring alternative framing describes them more broadly as latent or qualitatively new abilities in larger, more advanced, or aligned models, including humor interpretation, creative generation, instruction following, few-shot learning, and complex reasoning, without always requiring a sharp threshold. More specialized definitions narrow the term to open-world multimodal and compositional behavior, or make emergence stricter by requiring simultaneous discontinuities across multiple tasks together with learning of underlying data-generating regularities.

Space of facets. Papers do not systematize the term in one way, and several nearby labels are used, including emergent abilities, emergent capabilities, and emergence. One line distinguishes a stricter form in which a capability must show discontinuous improvement on a required task

nodes.name: Emotion understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats emotion understanding as an ability to recognize, perceive, infer, or interpret emotions, sentiment, affective tone, or emotional expressions from visual or multimodal evidence. Several definitions explicitly cast it as a latent model ability, and most differ mainly in whether the target is a person's emotion category, an image's emotional tone, or a scene's emotional or atmospheric qualities. A smaller line of work broadens the construct to complex, coexisting, fine-grained, compound, or culturally specific emotions, and some authors explicitly frame it as going beyond simple classification toward natural-language description or arbitrary emotion categories.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-neighbor labels, including emotional understanding, emotion perception, emotional recognition, fine-grained emotion recognition, and nuanced emotion recognition, for closely related abilities. A recurring distinction is between basic or discriminative recognition and richer understanding: some papers position emotion understanding above basic or discrete category prediction, as a higher-level perceptual task th

nodes.name: Emotional alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats emotional alignment as correspondence between an LLM's emotional responses in specific situations and human responses. A smaller line of work defines it instead through affective appropriateness in emotionally sensitive conversations, emphasizing supportive replies, avoidance of emotional destabilization, and responses tuned to emotional complexity and context rather than generic or overly affirmative ones. The main disagreement is whether the construct is anchored to similarity with human emotions or to context-appropriate, supportive emotional responding.

Space of facets. Systematization is limited. Papers do not give a stable subtype scheme, but they attach the construct to adjacent notions such as emotion appraisal, tone moderation and content adjustment, and emotional calibration, where the contrast case is responses that are generic, overly affirmative, or 'surface-level rather than context-specific empathy.' These usages also highlight handling 'nuanced, multi-layered emotions' as part of how the construct is described.

Space of measurement. Papers link emotional alignment to 1 measurement instrume

nodes.name: Emotional coherence
nodes.definition: The consistency of emotional expression over the course of a dialogue so that responses remain aligned with the character's emotional pattern.

nodes.name: Emotional expression
nodes.definition: The ability of a character to convey emotions vividly and appropriately within the context of an interaction, enhancing user immersion.

nodes.name: Emotional intelligence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats emotional intelligence as a capability or latent ability of a system, agent, or model to perceive, understand or interpret, and respond appropriately to emotions. Most definitions place this in interaction, especially conversation, while some broaden it to social interactions or social situations, and one paper focuses the application on interpersonal conflict resolution. A smaller variation adds managing emotions, and another defines it as responding to the emotions of oneself and others.

Space of facets. Papers do not offer a shared subtype taxonomy. The only explicit part-whole statement treats emotional fidelity as one aspect of emotional intelligence; otherwise, authors mostly locate the construct in task settings such as emotional support dialogue, emotion recognition in conversations, and interpersonal conflict resolution. Beyond emotional fidelity, the papers do not name recurring subcomponents.

Space of measurement. Emotional intelligence is linked to 2 measurement instruments and no behavioral indicators. The named instruments are Chatbot Arena and EQ-Bench, both described as benchmarks, and one paper

nodes.name: Emotional reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to recognize and understand emotions from expressions or context and link them to behavior and decision-making.

nodes.name: Emotional resonance
nodes.definition: The capacity of generated content to evoke genuine emotional responses or reflect sincere feelings that deeply connect with human audiences.

nodes.name: Emotional stability
nodes.definition: The latent disposition of an LLM to generate responses perceived as calm, resilient to emotional influence, and low in emotional variability.

nodes.name: Emotional support
nodes.definition: The ability to provide comfort, encouragement, and understanding to a user experiencing emotional distress.

nodes.name: Emotionality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available usage, Emotionality is framed as a latent tendency of an LLM to express emotional sensitivity and vulnerability. In Exploring the Impact of Personality Traits on LLM Bias and Toxicity, this framing is explicitly tied to generated text: both high and low Emotionality scores are described as leading to an increase in negative responses, and responses are said to "tend to be more negative" regardless of whether the score is high or low.

Space of measurement. Papers do not link Emotionality to any measurement instrument or behavioral indicator.

nodes.name: Empathic concern
nodes.definition: A component of empathy characterized by other-oriented feelings of sympathy and compassion for a person in distress.

nodes.name: Empathy
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats empathy as understanding another person's feelings or perspective and showing that understanding in emotionally attuned, supportive language. Definitions describe models, therapists, advice, or responses as emotionally resonant, compassionate, reflective of users' feelings, or responsive to emotional states. A smaller line narrows empathy to whether a model's own feelings change in ways that match what humans would feel in a situation, and one theoretical account instead presents empathy as a complex, multidimensional psychological construct, so the main disagreement is whether empathy is a model feeling change, a property of generated responses, or a broader construct expressed through language.

Space of facets. When papers systematize the construct, the clearest account treats it as multidimensional rather than unitary. That account identifies Empathic concern and Personal distress as primary targeted facets, and also notes that empathy may be operationalized as a trait, a state, or a social function in conversation. A smaller line distinguishes a broader emotional support quality, defined as overall effectiveness

nodes.name: Engagement
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat engagement, or engagingness, as a response- or dialogue-centered quality: outputs that are interesting, captivating, attention-holding, and likely to elicit further interaction. Within this prevailing framing, some authors cast it as a model ability or capacity, while others describe it as a perceived quality or latent tendency of responses or dialogues, and some narrow it to actively involving the user or maintaining interest over long-term conversation. A smaller line of work instead defines engagement at the discussion level as user participation and interest, combining reciprocity, response diversity, and discussion length, so the main disagreement is between judged output quality and broader discussion participation.

Space of facets. Terminology varies modestly across papers: engagement, engagingness, and interactive engagement are used for closely related notions centered on holding attention and sustaining interaction. Interactive engagement emphasizes drawing the user in and contributing dynamically to the dialogue, while long-term dialogue work emphasizes maintaining interest over time, sometimes through personal and shared history.

nodes.name: Episodic memory
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage centers on recall of specific past events or information rather than general knowledge. Most definitions describe episodic memory as storing and retrieving specific sequence-level or event-level content, often explicitly separated from generalized world knowledge or semantic memory. Some authors make this more specifically autobiographical, defining it through personally experienced events grounded in time and place, past conversations, or historical user engagements. The main variation is between a sequence-storage framing and a personal-event framing, while both preserve specificity and contrast with more general knowledge.

Space of facets. Papers most often systematize episodic memory by contrasting it with semantic or generalized knowledge: one description says it stores sequence-specific information independent of the natural language knowledge a model has, while another contrasts it with semantic memory that stores general knowledge. Some authors also equate it with autobiographical memory or specific personal experiences, including recall of a specific conversation, so the same label is used both for model state

nodes.name: Epistemic uncertainty
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats epistemic uncertainty as reducible, model-specific uncertainty about a model's own prediction, arising from ambiguity or lack of knowledge rather than token-level likelihood alone. Definitions in this vein describe it as the model not knowing something, or as lack of model knowledge within the model's parameters. A smaller line of work instead uses a parameter-focused definition, describing epistemic uncertainty, or weight uncertainty, as uncertainty in model parameters or parameter estimates, represented by a posterior over weights and diminishing with more data.

Space of facets. Papers systematize the concept mainly through contrasts and alternate labels. One recurring contrast separates epistemic uncertainty from token-level or lexical confidence, with next-token likelihood described as lexical confidence rather than epistemic uncertainty. Some authors use parameter uncertainty and weight uncertainty for the parameter-focused version of the construct, and one paper relates it to Parametric Knowledge Boundary by treating it as model-specific lack of knowledge.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is

nodes.name: Epistemic uncertainty awareness
nodes.definition: The tendency to recognize uncertainty caused by missing information or incomplete evidence, where additional knowledge could reduce uncertainty.

nodes.name: Error detection ability
nodes.definition: The latent ability to identify incorrect or flawed reasoning steps within a chain of thought, even when the final answer may appear plausible.

nodes.name: Error propagation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats error propagation as a cascading-error pattern in which mistakes made early in a chain, step sequence, or token sequence spread to later parts of the reasoning process and can yield an incorrect final answer. Definitions largely agree on that pattern, though some phrase it as a tendency for errors to propagate and compound, while others describe it as an observable phenomenon in which early-token or early-step errors lower later accuracy. A smaller line of work applies the same idea to multi-agent communication, defining it as erroneous information from one agent spreading through the network and negatively influencing the system's final output.

Space of facets. Papers use both error propagation and error accumulation for closely related phenomena, but scope varies. Most chain-oriented accounts describe within-trace cascading at the level of reasoning steps or tokens, including a reported pattern of higher token accuracy at the beginning of the chain and lower accuracy at the end, while another account ties the effect to longer outputs that amplify compounding mistakes. A distinct multi-agent framing shift

nodes.name: Error recovery
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this as a latent ability to recover from errors or failures and keep making progress toward task completion. Papers phrase that recovery as handling mistakes in perception, skill execution, or partner actions, adjusting a plan after an invalid action or unexpected state change, or correcting course from execution feedback such as error messages. Some definitions explicitly include error detection, diagnosis, and management, not only correction after the fact, and a smaller line of work narrows the construct either to resynchronizing an internal belief state with the true state after divergence or to observable self-correction during inference after invalid tool calls or flawed reasoning.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby labels for closely related capabilities, including error recovery, failure recovery, error tolerance, error handling, and out-of-sync recovery. The recurring components are error identification or detection, recovery loops, self-correction, fallback strategies, and continued progress after mistakes, with error sources described as perception grounding errors, skill failures, inval

nodes.name: Ethical alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage describes ethical alignment as conformity of a model's responses or behaviors to ethical standards, principles, or values, often coupled with avoiding harmful, misleading, inappropriate, or biased content. Within that common framing, some definitions narrow the reference standard to professional service ethics, while others extend it to safety, privacy, fairness, societal values, and cultural contexts. A smaller line of work instead defines the construct by correspondence between an LLM's moral preferences or value representations and aggregated human preferences, especially in moral dilemmas, and another framing treats it as the model's latent moral orientation revealed by whether outputs conform to or violate value principles.

Space of facets. Papers partition the concept along several facets. One recurring breakdown names safety, privacy, fairness, and harm avoidance as components of ethical considerations, while another treats value issues as social bias, ethics, and toxicity. Across names, the construct overlaps with moral alignment, value conformity, ethical considerations, and ethical values, but these labels do

nodes.name: Ethical bias
nodes.definition: Systematic deviations in moral judgment that may be influenced by factors such as language or culture.

nodes.name: Ethical decision-making
nodes.definition: The capacity to make judgments and choices based on ethical or moral principles, particularly in social dilemmas involving shared resources.

nodes.name: Evaluation ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats evaluation ability as a latent model capacity to accurately assess the quality or correctness of model-generated outputs, responses, or intermediate steps. Most definitions keep this core framing while shifting the evaluation target, including instruction-following responses, coding solutions, text along multiple specified dimensions, and multimodal visual outputs. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to fine-grained evaluation, where judgments are made with user-defined score rubrics and reference materials rather than only coarse preferences, or to checking whether a response satisfies instruction constraints.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for closely related capacities, including evaluation capability, judging ability, judgment capability, text evaluation ability, judge ability, and LLM-as-a-judge ability. The clearest subtype is fine-grained evaluation capability, defined around detailed rubrics and reference answers, and one paper groups reranking, beam search, and refinement under a shared fundamental judging capability. A smaller framing treats judge ability as a

nodes.name: Evaluation bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats evaluation bias as a systematic distortion introduced when a model, or another evaluator, judges outputs or gives feedback. Most definitions locate the distortion in the evaluator's scoring or preferences: papers describe unfair favoring or disfavoring of certain models' responses, the expected gap between a judge's proxy score and a ground-truth score, higher scores for models functionally similar to the judge, or internal unstated preferences that can prioritize style over factuality and safety. A smaller line shifts the construct from evaluator behavior to the assessment setup, defining it as the expected deviation between estimated and true capability caused by flaws in the evaluation protocol, while another broadens it to systematic distortions in human or AI feedback that favor particular perspectives, demographics, or values.

Space of facets. Papers do not share a single taxonomy. One paper decomposes evaluation bias into original, independent, and related terms, and the recorded relational evidence also treats it as related to Self-preference bias. Elsewhere, nearby labels pick out different facets of the

nodes.name: Evaluator self-consistency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available definitions, the construct appears under the name self-alignment and is framed as the extent to which an evaluator's internal reasoning and scoring are consistent with its own task understanding and instructions. The accompanying descriptions tie this consistency to "internal thinking" that aligns the evaluator for better task and preference understanding and for stronger instruction following.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to this construct. Papers instead connect it to two behavioral indicators, Instruction following and Instruction generation, and those connections are recorded as causal rather than measurement links, so the papers do not specify an explicit assessment procedure for it here.

Links. Several papers claim a causal relationship from evaluator self-consistency to Instruction following. In Self-Alignment with Instruction Backtranslation, training on the high quality portion of augmented data is said to lead to increasing instruction following performance, while DreamBench++ says it introduces internal thinking to strengthen task understanding and instruction following capabilities. One paper also cla

nodes.name: Event-level understanding
nodes.definition: The ability to comprehend videos at a fine-grained level by identifying, localizing, and describing individual events, as opposed to providing a single summary for the entire video.

nodes.name: Event understanding
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to correctly identify and interpret event types and their structures from multimodal inputs, integrating relevant textual and visual cues while ignoring irrelevant or misleading features.

nodes.name: Evidence grounding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed definitions, the construct is framed around whether answers are anchored in relevant evidence from the input, rather than being unsupported or shortcut-based. One usage defines it as the ability to support responses with specific, relevant, and accurate references to observable content such as visual scenes, while another, under the label credibility, defines it as answers based on a genuine understanding of relevant evidence within video content rather than shortcuts or biases. The common ground is reliance on relevant evidence, but the emphasis differs: one definition centers on explicit, accurate referencing in the response, and the other centers on whether the answer comes from genuine understanding rather than shortcuts.

Space of facets. The papers use two nearby labels for overlapping material, evidence grounding and credibility. The evidence-grounding label is described through the quality and relevance of the evidence provided, more precise scene descriptions, behavioral insights, and concrete examples that support assertions, while the credibility label is tied to retrieving relevant clues and to answers grounded in genuine unders

nodes.name: Exaggeration
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of an LLM to amplify persona-defining semantic features beyond what is topically necessary, contributing to caricature in identity-conditioned narratives.

nodes.name: Execution feedback utilization
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to effectively incorporate execution outcomes from public tests to improve subsequent code generations across turns.

nodes.name: Executive function
nodes.definition: Higher-level control abilities involved in integrating contextual information and managing task demands.

nodes.name: Expert diversity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats the construct as expert-to-expert distinctness within an MoE model: experts have dissimilar parameters, non-overlapping capabilities or processing preferences, and distinct, non-redundant knowledge, all described as signs of functional specialization. This framing is repeatedly contrasted with overlap in expert functionalities or other forms of redundancy. A smaller line of work uses the alternative label functional similarity, defining the comparison instead by experts producing equivalent outputs for the same input, which reflects redundancy in learned representations.

Space of facets. Papers do not divide the construct into formal subtypes. Instead, they organize it through contrasts: most describe diversity through specialization, uniqueness, and complementary expert roles, while the opposing side is described as overlap, redundancy, functional equivalence, or equivalent outputs on the same input. The terminology is not fully uniform, because most papers use expert diversity for the distinctness side of the comparison, whereas a smaller line of work uses functional similarity for the equivalence and redunda

nodes.name: Expert routing recency bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions here, the most specific usage treats it as a routing tendency in Mixture-of-Experts systems: the router preferentially uses newly added experts or knowledge and neglects older ones. Papers using the broader label recency bias also define it more generally as attention or retrieval favoring more recent, near, or final tokens over earlier context. The main disagreement is therefore about where the bias is located, expert routing over components versus temporal preference over input positions or context.

Space of facets. The papers do not present a shared subtype scheme. Instead, they use the same label across different mechanisms: MoE routing, recent-corpus overfitting, stick-breaking attention or retrieval, single-state linear attention, and long-context attention that is "more strongly concentrated at the tail." In that sense, the term is used for different targets, newly added experts in one usage and recent or near tokens in others.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to this construct. In the papers' descriptions, it is identified through observable patterns such as tokens being "predomi

nodes.name: Expert specialization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats expert specialization as division of labor within a mixture, where individual experts, adapters, or models develop focused capabilities for particular tasks, data patterns, inputs, domains, or parts of the data distribution. Papers describe this as experts becoming adept at a certain type of task or data pattern, learning different skills, or showing distinct task preferences rather than redundant functions. A smaller line of work defines the same term differently, as an expert being specialized when it is mainly co-activated with a small, specific group of other experts, so the main disagreement is whether specialization is about task or input focus or about collaboration structure.

Space of facets. Most papers use closely related labels such as fine-grained specialization, routing specialization, and task-wise specialization for the same general idea that different experts take different roles. Within that usage, papers distinguish specialization by what is separated across experts, including tasks, domains, inputs, parts of the data distribution, and task-specific residuals, often contrasting it with redundant or

nodes.name: Expert utilization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this construct as the extent to which experts are actually used, rather than left underused or concentrated in a small subset. One definition emphasizes whether selected experts are leveraged effectively and whether routing is more balanced, while another, under the name expert activation, emphasizes utilization of distinct experts during optimization and inference and denser use of otherwise underused experts. The main variation is whether the focus is balanced use of selected experts or broader activation of distinct experts as a way of leveraging parameter capacity.

Space of facets. The papers do not offer a broader taxonomy, but they use closely related labels for much the same phenomenon. Expert activation is treated as near-aligned with expert utilization, and one paper explicitly frames denser activation as mitigating low expert utilization and improving use of dead experts. Beyond this terminological variation, the papers do not distinguish formal subtypes or place it under a larger named construct.

Space of measurement. Papers link it to no measurement instruments and no behavioral indicators. Instead,

nodes.name: Explanation faithfulness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, papers split between two framings rather than converging on one. One usage, named causal faithfulness, defines it as whether a feature's interpretation matches its causal role in the model's computation and describes features as interpretable in a way "consistent with their causal role"; another defines explanation faithfulness as the degree to which a textual explanation accurately and reliably describes the behavior of a specific neural network unit, with emphasis on explanations being reliable and truthful. The disagreement is over both the object being evaluated, feature interpretations versus textual explanations of units, and the reference standard, causal role in computation versus accurate description of unit behavior.

Space of facets. Papers do not break the construct into a shared set of facets, but they do use nearby labels for different targets. The label causal faithfulness is used for feature interpretations, while explanation faithfulness is used for textual explanations of units such as neurons, and the latter is described in terms of reliability, truthfulness, and trustworthiness.

Space of measurement. Opera

nodes.name: Explanation quality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats explanation quality as the quality of model-generated explanations or rationales, especially whether they are logical and appropriate for the problem being solved. One definition emphasizes clarity, relevance, logical coherence, and whether the explanation provides meaningful insights into the optimization process and results, while a closely aligned phrasing emphasizes plausibility, logic, and appropriateness for a given query or answer. A smaller framing uses the term more narrowly for the correctness and policy adherence of guardrail explanations.

Space of facets. The clearest structuring in the papers is to treat explanation quality as an overall evaluation aspect that can be set alongside modeling accuracy. Another paper uses the label rationale quality for the generated explanation behind an answer, with criteria that overlap strongly with explanation quality. Across these uses, the object being judged shifts between optimization-focused explanations, answer rationales, and guardrail explanations, and the named criteria shift between insight, plausibility, and policy adherence.

Space of measurement. Papers

nodes.name: Explicit social bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing framing treats explicit social bias as bias that is consciously or intentionally expressed and accessible to direct report or control. One definition ties it specifically to models making overt judgments about demographic attributes, while another states it more broadly as bias that is not automatic, relatively controllable, and captured with direct measures. The shared core is directness, reportability, and non-automatic expression, while the main difference is whether the construct is defined narrowly around overt demographic judgments by models or more broadly as a kind of explicit association or belief.

Space of facets. Papers mainly organize this construct in contrast to implicit bias. On the explicit side, authors describe fairness-related questions and tasks where models make direct judgments, and one paper refers to explicit associations as individual beliefs; on the contrasting side, the same work distinguishes implicit tasks such as image description and form completion. Beyond this explicit versus implicit split, the papers do not introduce finer subtypes.

Space of measurement. Operationally, the construct is link

nodes.name: Exploitation
nodes.definition: The process of refining and improving upon known, promising solutions by leveraging feedback and prior search experience to intensify the search in a local region.

nodes.name: Exploration ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage frames exploration ability as breadth of search: searching broadly across a solution, reasoning, or problem space, generating diverse trajectories or candidate answers, and discovering useful states or solution paths rather than only refining an existing one. Several authors explicitly cast it as a latent ability, capability, tendency, or disposition, while a smaller line defines it behaviorally, as actively searching an environment, visiting new states, or exploring multiple distinct paths in parallel. A narrower variant, self-exploration, focuses on identifying flaws in the model's own reasoning and producing alternative paths without external intervention.

Space of facets. Papers systematize the construct mainly through recurring contrasts and variants rather than a single taxonomy. A common contrast is exploration versus exploitation, with related language about search diversity, sampling diversity, exploratory branches, and breadth before committing to a hypothesis; embodied-task papers instead center exploration of objects, information, or new regions in partially observed environments. Some authors use search for clo

nodes.name: Exploration-exploitation tradeoff
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is a balancing ability or latent tendency between exploration and exploitation. Most definitions describe exploration as trying uncertain actions or generating novel, diverse candidates, and exploitation as selecting immediately promising options or refining known high-quality or high-potential ones. The main variation is the level of description: some papers state it as action choice, while others place it in optimization over sequences or chemical candidates.

Space of facets. Papers consistently organize the construct into two poles, exploration and exploitation. Exploration is described as trying uncertain actions, generating novel solutions, or producing diverse sequences, whereas exploitation is described as choosing promising actions or refining existing candidates; one paper says an agent "intelligently balances exploration and exploitation in the chemical space." Another paper formalizes the balance with a rationality parameter, stating that β controls the explore-exploit tradeoff.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to this construct. Papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator, Action selection

nodes.name: Expressive power
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats expressive power, often under names such as representational capacity, representation power, expressivity, or expressive capacity, as a latent ability of a model, architecture, parameterization, or adaptation method to represent, approximate, or encode complex functions, tasks, signals, or patterns, sometimes under compactness, low-rank, or parameter-sharing constraints. A large theoretical strand defines it in formal terms, as the class of functions, formal languages, or circuits an architecture can realize, sometimes explicitly separate from learnability or inductive bias, with papers describing prompting as Turing-complete and chain-of-thought steps as expanding expressiveness beyond TC0. Smaller strands use the label more locally, for the richness of prompts or embedding spaces, diversity across layer representations, context-sensitive value representations, or complex preference relations, so the main divide is between broad architecture-level capacity and narrower representation- or mechanism-level capacity.

Space of facets. Papers carve the construct into recurring subtypes: representational capacity of lo

nodes.name: External validity
nodes.definition: The extent to which the model’s inferred quantities match ground truth values within a tolerance threshold.

nodes.name: Extraversion
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats Extraversion, sometimes spelled Extroversion, as a personality trait or personality dimension marked by sociability, assertiveness, and being outgoing or energetic. Some papers add seeking stimulation in the company of others, excitement-seeking, or positive emotions, but the overall framing remains the same trait description.

Space of facets. Papers situate Extraversion within broader personality frameworks rather than as a standalone or newly subdivided construct. It appears as Extraversion in HEXACO and as Extraversion or Extroversion in the Big Five, so the main variation is framework placement and spelling rather than a different construct.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to Extraversion. Operationally, papers mention it as a dimension within personality frameworks, but do not link it to a benchmark, human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge setup, probe, or other instrument.

Links. Only one linked construct appears. One paper reports that Extraversion is reported to correlate with Expressive power, stating that "extraversion from HEXACO model shows the stronge

nodes.name: Fact-checking ability
nodes.definition: The overall capacity of an LLM to correctly verify claims and produce sound justifications across diverse and complex real-world scenarios.

nodes.name: Factual grounding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available usage, factual grounding is framed as the degree to which a model's outputs align with real-world distributions and factual information. The same description also says models may be guided toward outputs grounded in factual information and real-world context, so the construct is used through output alignment to real-world context.

Space of facets. The paper systematizes the concept through a desired-distribution lens: real-world distributions are used for factual grounding, in contrast to equal distributions for social equity.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to factual grounding. In the available papers, it is presented conceptually rather than tied to a benchmark, human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge method, probe, or analysis.

Links. The only reported relationship is that factual grounding is related to Social bias. The paper expresses this link by framing bias relative to a desired distribution, equal for social equity and real-world for factual grounding.

nodes.name: Factual knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers describe factual knowledge as the model's ability, or the extent to which it has encoded, stored, and can retrieve accurate world facts from its parameters or pretraining when queried. Closely related labels such as fact recall, knowledge recall, factual knowledge recall, and long-term or parametric knowledge recall are usually used for the same basic idea, often with the added emphasis that the facts are stored internally and can be accessed independent of the current context. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to retrieving specific factual associations, subject-relation-object triples, or entities linked to a subject and relation, and a few papers define recall over edited or injected knowledge rather than over pretraining knowledge. Some authors also extend the construct from retrieval alone to using or expressing those facts in responses or reasoning.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for this family of constructs, including fact recall, knowledge recall, factual knowledge recall, long-term knowledge recall, and parametric knowledge retrieval. The main axis of variation is scope: some definitions stress reca

nodes.name: Factual reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to produce responses grounded in factual knowledge and to avoid generating false claims, especially in the presence of misleading or humorous prompts.

nodes.name: Factual retention
nodes.definition: The ability of an agent to locate and retrieve specific, instruction-relevant pieces of information from within a video to complete a task, even if the information is incidental to the video's main focus.

nodes.name: Factuality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats factuality as output-level factual correctness: model statements, answers, rationales, or reasoning should align with real-world facts or external knowledge and avoid hallucination. Many papers use near-equivalent labels such as factual accuracy, factual correctness, or correctness, and some frame it as a latent ability or tendency of the model rather than only a property of a single response. A smaller line of work changes the reference standard, defining it relative to a source text, image, audio input, annotation, dialogue state, or user question, and a few papers introduce narrower variants such as independent factuality, entity-relation consistency, factuality preservation, or factual and logical correctness.

Space of facets. Papers systematize the term in several overlapping ways. Some place it under background knowledge, or use it as one evaluation dimension alongside retrieval and reasoning, or alongside relevance and adherence in instruction-following evaluation. The clearest contrast is with faithfulness: some definitions reserve factuality for alignment with external or real-world knowledge, whi

nodes.name: Fairness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats fairness as avoiding biased, stereotypical, or prejudicial outputs across social or demographic groups, or more generally as equitable treatment that does not favor or disfavor people based on protected attributes. A smaller line of work states the construct in more formal group terms, such as predictions independent of sensitive attributes, equal false positive and false negative rates, counterfactual fairness, or similar performance across subgroups. Other minority uses narrow it further to no gender preference between paired sentence completions, ideal gender parity in translation, parity across cultures, or a moral dimension centered on justice and reciprocity.

Space of facets. When papers break the construct down, the clearest subtype split is between counterfactual fairness and performance disparity, and one benchmark further divides fairness into stereotype and bias and preference by discriminatory output type. The same label is also used for several neighboring notions: algorithmic fairness for prejudice in candidate comparison, equitability for parity between model performance and user needs across cultu

nodes.name: Faithful calibration
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model's linguistically expressed uncertainty aligns with its intrinsic uncertainty, reflecting a trustworthy and accurate communication of confidence.

nodes.name: Faithfulness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats faithfulness as source- or context-grounded generation: a summary, response, claim, or annotation should be supported by the provided document, passage, graph, image, instruction, or other input, often phrased as factual consistency, entailment, or avoiding hallucination. Many papers use near-equivalent names such as factual consistency, factual accuracy, factual correctness, information accuracy, unfaithfulness, or supportiveness for this same framing. A smaller line of work uses faithfulness for explanations, defining it as whether an explanation reflects the model's actual reasoning, sometimes in causal terms. The main disagreement is whether faithfulness is a property of generated content relative to provided evidence, of explanations relative to model reasoning, or of agent behavior relative to stated intentions, with a few task-specific definitions such as prediction changes under altered conclusions.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct into several subtypes rather than one uniform schema. One negotiation study distinguishes internal faithfulness, based on an agent's own acceptable offers, fr

nodes.name: Faithfulness to decomposition
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model's translation adheres to the specific guidance or analysis provided in a prior decomposition step, reflecting consistency between planning and execution.

nodes.name: Feasibility
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers here, the prevailing and only explicit definition treats feasibility as the extent to which a generated scientific hypothesis can be practically tested or validated through empirical methods. The usage is tied to judging generated research ideas and hypotheses, including references to hypotheses with "high feasibility and impact as judged by human experts" in HypER: Literature-grounded Hypothesis Generation and Distillation with Provenance.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is narrow: papers link feasibility to one measurement instrument, Human evaluation, and to no behavioral indicators. In these studies, human evaluators assess feasibility directly alongside other dimensions of generated ideas or content, with one paper describing evaluation of the "intrinsic quality" of generated content through novelty and feasibility, and another reporting human evaluation of novelty, relevance, and feasibility.

nodes.name: Few-shot generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats few-shot generalization as a model-level capacity to generalize, learn, or adapt from only a few examples or very small amounts of task-specific data. Most definitions keep this broad, describing generalization to new tasks, unseen scenarios, or novel settings under limited data. Some authors add narrower emphases, framing it as leveraging domain-level abstractions rather than surface patterns, inferring broader rules or properties from a few in-context examples, learning effective policies from little task data, or adapting to new prediction tasks with minimal fine-tuning samples.

Space of facets. Across definitions, the term spans several settings: generalization to new tasks from a few examples, inference of general rules or relevant properties from limited in-context examples, low-data policy learning, and adaptation to novel prediction scenarios or frequency bands with minimal fine-tuning. The clearest variation is scope, with some papers using it for broad few-example generalization and others for a more task-specific form of low-data adaptation.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behaviora

nodes.name: Fidelity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats fidelity as a quality dimension of generated outputs, usually visual ones: outputs are described as realistic, high-quality, well-formed, and free from artifacts or unintended distortions. Within that visual framing, scope varies from a narrower focus on realism and artifact-freeness to broader visual quality notions that include clarity, aesthetic appeal, readability, resolution, brightness, and color. Smaller lines of work use the same term for different reference objects: one defines fidelity as preserving the semantic information of the original watermarked text, saying it "reflects the similarity between y and yw," and another defines it as how accurately a natural language concept matches a neuron's activation pattern through precision and recall.

Space of facets. Within visual-generation papers, fidelity is treated as one evaluation aspect among others: one paper groups it with Overall and Alignment, and a benchmark comparison describes existing text-to-video benchmarks as often assessing visual quality and text relevance. Papers use image fidelity, visual quality, and image quality as closely neighboring

nodes.name: Figurative language understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the construct is used in two distinct ways rather than one settled definition. One paper treats it as a latent interpretive ability: understanding utterances whose intended meaning diverges from the literal meaning, including irony or hyperbole, by reasoning about rhetorical strategy, and it describes this as enabling "human-compatible interpretations of non-literal utterances." Another paper uses the nearby label figurative competence for a broader, context-sensitive ability to produce and interpret figurative expressions with pragmatic appropriateness in communicative settings, and explicitly says this requires more than recognizing figurative markers in isolation.

Space of facets. The papers organize the construct around different facets. One framing centers rhetorical strategy, non-literalness, and the communicative goals of speakers and listeners; another reframes it as a usage-level, discourse-level, context-sensitive ability. The naming also varies: one paper speaks of figurative language understanding, while another uses figurative competence for the broader production-and-interpretation framing.

Space of measurement. The re

nodes.name: Financial reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats financial reasoning as a latent ability in the financial domain. Most definitions describe solving finance-related questions or carrying out multi-step computations over financial data, with emphasis on reasoning over documents, text and tables, logical inference, and mathematical computation; one definition further specifies generating executable programs to derive correct answers. A smaller line of work uses a narrower, observable-task framing, defining it as present value calculation, namely determining the current worth of future sums or cash flows given a discount rate.

Space of facets. Papers mainly break the construct down by the steps involved in the reasoning process rather than by named subtypes. In the financial numerical reasoning framing, it includes fact extraction, logical inference, and mathematical computation, and also integrating information from text and tables, applying domain-specific logic, and generating executable programs. Across definitions, the term therefore covers both broad finance-question reasoning over documents or calculations and the narrower case of present value computation.

nodes.name: Fine-grained perception
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats fine-grained perception as a facet or latent ability of visual perception centered on recognizing detailed, specific, or subtle visual attributes from images. Definitions repeatedly illustrate it with object locations, celebrity identities, clothing styles, instance-level features, color and texture, counts, and spatial relations between small objects. A smaller wording difference is whether the emphasis falls on broad detailed visual attributes, instance-level cues, or pixel-level detail, but the definitions otherwise align closely.

Space of facets. Papers usually place fine-grained perception as one capability axis within larger evaluation schemes, alongside coarse perception and, in some cases, OCR, spatial perception, instance reasoning, logical reasoning, attribute reasoning, and relation reasoning. One operational split distinguishes single-instance and cross-instance fine-grained perception, and one paper groups it with localization inside a vision-centric category. The label also appears once as fine-grained visual perception, defined in terms of detailed visual attributes and subtle appearance cues.

Space o

nodes.name: Fine-grained video understanding
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to comprehend and reason about specific, detailed events and their temporal relationships within a video, as opposed to just understanding the overall gist.

nodes.name: Fine-grained visual reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to reason about detailed visual attributes, object relations, and other subtle image features rather than only coarse scene content.

nodes.name: Fine-grained visual understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this construct as a latent model ability to perceive, identify, and interpret detailed local visual information, especially small, pixel-level, point-level, or region-level details that go beyond high-level objects, global summaries, or whole-image semantics. Several definitions make this contrast explicit, describing struggles with 'pixel-level semantic details', small objects, intricate patterns, object attributes and relationships, or subtle local features, and some add that accurate understanding also involves relating local details to broader context. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to more specific settings, such as subtle visual differences in motion, distinguishing confusing or visually similar concepts, or preserving detailed visual information when answering multimodal questions.

Space of facets. Most papers use a cluster of near-synonymous labels for the same general idea, including perception of small visual details, granular visual recognition, detailed scene understanding, fine-grained image understanding, and region-level comprehension. Within that cluster, papers emphasize diff

nodes.name: Flatness
nodes.definition: A property of the solution landscape where a model's parameters reside in a wide, flat region of the loss function, which is correlated with better generalization.

nodes.name: Flexibility
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers do not converge on a single meaning of flexibility. In $R^2$-Guard: Robust Reasoning Enabled LLM Guardrail via Knowledge-Enhanced Logical Reasoning, it is used for a guardrail model's ability to adapt to new or unseen safety categories without complete retraining, with examples that it "shows flexibility to new safety categories by simple PGM graph editing" and can adapt "by simply editing the reasoning graph." In MuseScorer: Idea Originality Scoring At Scale, the term instead refers to response diversity across semantic categories, defined as "distinct semantic category count" or "the number of categories in each participant's responses."

Space of facets. No shared subtype scheme appears across papers. The main pattern is that the same label is used for two different targets, one a model-level adaptation property tied to new safety categories and changes to a knowledge or reasoning graph, the other an output-level count of distinct semantic categories in responses. One paper also mentions Creativity Quotient (CQ) scores alongside the latter usage.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it and no behavioral indicator is linked to

nodes.name: Fluency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats fluency as an output-quality notion: generated text should be grammatical, coherent, natural-sounding, and often smooth or easy to read. Many authors phrase this instead as a model ability or capacity to produce such text, so papers vary between model-centered and output-centered wording. Smaller lines of work narrow fluency to grammatical and orthographic correctness, define it as natural and smooth communication style independent of strict grammatical correctness or context, or treat it as well-formed language independent of whether the content fully captures its source. Another minority framing ties fluency to specific proxies, especially perplexity for language modeling under long or very long contexts; papers also differ on whether fluency includes coherence, readability, lack of repetition, idiomaticity, or translation-specific syntactic and semantic correctness, or whether those are separate criteria.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a single shared taxonomy, but they reuse nearby labels such as language fluency, utterance fluency, and linguistic fluency, and a paper uses linguistic correctness while als

nodes.name: Fluid intelligence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available papers, fluid intelligence is treated as a latent ability for handling novel problems or settings without relying on prior or pre-existing knowledge. The clearest definition adds that this ability involves abstract inductive reasoning and pattern induction from examples, while another paper uses closely matching language and describes it as the capacity to apply learned skills in novel settings. One paper also presents evaluation of fluid intelligence as a way to assess LLM reasoning abilities when memorized knowledge may otherwise be available.

Space of facets. Papers do not break the construct into subtypes. Instead, they define it mainly by contrast with reliance on memorization or pre-existing knowledge, and one paper places analogical reasoning alongside it by saying analogy-making is tightly linked with fluid intelligence. The available usage also connects fluid intelligence to reasoning abilities, but does not treat it as interchangeable with them.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is narrow in the available papers: fluid intelligence is linked to one measurement instrument, the ARC task, and to no behavioral indicators. On

nodes.name: Forecasting ability
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to accurately predict the outcome of future events, typically measured against ground truth resolutions.

nodes.name: Forget quality
nodes.definition: The degree to which an unlearning method successfully removes the influence of specified data from a model, often measured by comparing the unlearned model's outputs to a model never trained on the data.

nodes.name: Formal linguistic competence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The only explicit definition treats formal linguistic competence as an ability to generate fluent and grammatically correct text from statistical patterns in training data. In that framing, it is described as arising from statistical learning on large text corpora and as reflecting surface-level 'data' memory rather than deep semantic understanding; no alternative definition is stated.

Space of facets. The available definition does not break the construct into subtypes or facets. Instead, it is positioned through a contrast: fluent, grammatical text generation is placed on the side of statistical learning and surface-level memory, rather than on the side of deep semantic understanding.

Space of measurement. Formal linguistic competence is linked to 2 measurement instruments and no behavioral indicators. The operationalization is benchmark-based: one paper assesses it with BLiMP and SyntaxGym, explicitly describing them as "two benchmarks" used to assess the construct.

Links. One paper claims a causal relationship from formal linguistic competence to brain alignment, stating that it "actively drives brain alignment during the early phases of training."

nodes.name: Formal reasoning
nodes.definition: The latent capacity to represent and verify mathematical statements using a formal logical system, enabling computer-checked proofs and eliminating reliance on intuitive or ambiguous reasoning.

nodes.name: Format following ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this construct as a model capability to make outputs match requested formatting constraints or predefined structural templates. The examples are concrete, including answers enclosed in bold, structured lists, and outputs with specified tags or sections. One definition makes the scope explicit as adherence to format constraints independent of task performance, while another emphasizes consistent conformity to a strict template such as `<rewrite> rewrite here </rewrite>`.

Space of facets. The papers use closely aligned labels, "format-instruction following" and "format adherence", and do not distinguish them as separate constructs.
