One paper formalizes a "format-instruction following function FC", while another places format adherence alongside reasoning and query rewriting as part of a model's "fundamental capabilities". No further subtype structure is specified in the definitions or snippets.

Space of measurement. The papers do not link this construct to any measurement instrument or behavioral indicator. The only explicit operational detail is a "rule-based heuristic" used to determine a format-instruction foll

nodes.name: Frame-semantic knowledge
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to understand and represent meaning through structured conceptual scenarios (frames) and their associated roles.

nodes.name: Framing divergence
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of an LLM to generate conflicting narrative interpretations of the same event when conditioned on different personas, reflecting epistemic contradictions shaped by perspective.

nodes.name: Full-stack engineering ability
nodes.definition: The ability to engineer solutions across the entire technology stack, including mobile, web, APIs, and browsers, while reasoning about complex inter-codebase interactions.

nodes.name: Functional correctness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing framing is output-level correctness: whether generated code, smart contracts, API calls, or symbolic expressions perform the intended function, satisfy the specification or user request, and pass task-relevant tests or verification. Several definitions make the reference standard explicit through all relevant test cases, functional verification, or equivalence checks by an external solver, and one paper states that functional correctness goes beyond mere syntactic validity. A smaller variation phrases it as the latent tendency of generated code to satisfy the intended specification and pass functional verification, rather than only as the observed degree of success on a task.

Space of facets. Across the papers, functional correctness is most often positioned as a criterion separate from syntactic correctness or well-formedness: one snippet says constrained decoding can improve syntactic correctness without guaranteeing that the output correctly answers the query. Other papers evaluate it alongside design quality, quality attributes, or API hallucination, and one benchmark reports it with Pass@k and Compile@k.

Space of measur

nodes.name: Functional linguistic competence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the defining paper, the concept is framed as a deeper form of language understanding: the model must not only parse surface text but also understand deeper meanings, including semantic integration and reasoning about roles and relationships. The same paper ties this to robust "knowledge" memory, and also notes that what counts as functional linguistic competence is still unclear and under debate.

Space of facets. The paper organizes generalized knowledge memorization into two parts: surface-level "data" memory and deeper "knowledge" memory, corresponding to formal and functional linguistic competence, respectively. Within that framing, functional linguistic competence is paired with knowledge memory and contrasted with a surface-level side of memorization.

Space of measurement. Papers link it to 6 measurement instruments and no behavioral indicators. The linked instruments are all benchmarks: ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, PIQA, and SIQA, plus 1 other instrument. One paper says these benchmarks cover world knowledge, social reasoning, physical reasoning, and common-sense reasoning, so the operationalization centers on benchmark performance in those a

nodes.name: Functional theory of mind
nodes.definition: A behavioral marker indicating that a model produces responses consistent with understanding mental states, without implying the presence of an internal causal model or true cognitive mechanism underlying such understanding.

nodes.name: Gender bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats gender bias as a latent, systematic tendency for model outputs, representations, or reasoning to reflect unfair, skewed, or stereotyped gendered patterns. Several papers describe it broadly as disadvantaging or misrepresenting people on the basis of gender, or as generating harmful assumptions, attitudes, and representations; others specify that this appears in associations between gender and roles or attributes. Smaller lines of work define it more narrowly as reliance on spurious correlations between gender-neutral expressions and gender, as favoring one gender even in stereotype-free text, as gendered clinical reasoning unrelated to clinical relevance, or as unequal attribution of agentic versus communal language. Definitions differ mainly in scope: some papers use a broad unfairness framing, while others define particular stereotype-based manifestations or focus on harms to marginalized genders.

Space of facets. Papers do not converge on a single internal taxonomy, but they do break the construct into recurring manifestations. One explicit subtype is bias against marginalized genders, described as cont

nodes.name: General ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats general ability as broad overall capability, performance, or utility across many tasks and domains, rather than success on a single narrow task. Many papers define it in preservation terms: the broader competence, knowledge, reasoning, question answering, summarization, coding, or instruction-following that should remain intact after editing, unlearning, alignment, steering, continual training, pruning, or quantization. A smaller line of work shifts the construct along two axes, from observable benchmark performance to latent underlying ability, using notions such as a unidimensional trait, a first principal component over benchmark scores, or a capabilities set, and from a model property to the usefulness or correctness of its outputs on legitimate tasks; one paper also uses general abilities for newly enhanced downstream competencies rather than pre-existing broad competence.

Space of facets. Papers use many neighboring labels for this broad construct, including general capabilities, general performance, downstream performance, model capability, model utility, foundational capabilities, all-round capability, and ge

nodes.name: General reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats general reasoning as a latent or unobservable reasoning capacity of the model. A common formulation describes it as the ability to solve individual reasoning tasks or examples, while related definitions describe it more broadly as logically processing information, making deductions, solving problems, and understanding complex relationships across diverse or non-specialized domains. The main variation is whether authors foreground single-example task solving, especially in contrast to generic facts shared across examples, or emphasize broad cross-domain problem solving.

Space of facets. Papers mainly systematize the construct by contrast rather than by subtypes. In Meaningful Learning: Enhancing Abstract Reasoning in Large Language Models via Generic Fact Guidance, abstract reasoning is described as taking examples supported by a generic fact as a whole, whereas general reasoning focuses on each single example, and the paper reports a substantial discrepancy between the two performances. Other papers also position general reasoning against specialized tasks requiring proprietary or domain-specific knowledge, and a

nodes.name: Generality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats generality as post-edit generalization: a model should apply newly edited knowledge to rephrased or semantically equivalent prompts, not only the exact edit prompt. A closely matching wording calls this paraphrase execution, meaning the model produces the correct edited output for a paraphrased version of the original prompt. A smaller line of work extends the same idea across languages, defining it as cross-lingual propagation, the extent to which an edit in one language transfers to semantically equivalent queries in other languages.

Space of facets. Papers most often place generality among the criteria used to evaluate editing, alongside locality and either reliability or efficacy. Some authors use paraphrase execution as an alternative name for the within-language form of the construct, while others use cross-lingual propagation for a multilingual extension of the same broad concern. Beyond these renamings and extensions, papers do not link it to other constructs.

Space of measurement. Papers link generality to 3 measurement instruments and 3 behavioral indicators. The most common operationalizations are eva

nodes.name: Generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats generalization as a model, method, or agent's capacity to maintain useful performance on unseen data, tasks, domains, or conditions, often under distribution shift and often contrasted with memorization or overfitting; one recurring formulation asks whether results reflect "genuine ability or just memorization of the training data." Many papers make this concrete as transfer to new instructions, tools, languages, modalities, environments, users, or harder problems without task-specific retraining. A smaller line uses the same term more narrowly for held-out test performance from the same distribution, for logically or semantically transformed inputs such as reversed relations or rephrased prompts, or for specialized settings like knowledge editing, abstention, attacks, and merged models.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonyms for the broad transfer notion, including generalizability, generalization ability, generalization capability, generalization performance, and British-spelling variants. They also carve out narrower subtypes such as task-agnostic generalizability, domain-generality, single-task general

nodes.name: Generalization to unseen users
nodes.definition: The model's ability to accurately estimate the preferences of new users who were not part of the training data, based on a small number of their annotations.

nodes.name: Generation diversity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats generation diversity as variety and non-repetition in model outputs: responses should differ across samples instead of repeating n-grams, generic phrasing, or a narrow set of completions. Many definitions keep this at the level of wording or unique n-grams, while others broaden the same idea to semantic, syntactic, logical, or structural variation, coverage of the real data distribution, and diverse reasoning chains, plans, or solutions for one problem. A smaller line of work uses diversity for different targets, including balance of yes and no perspectives in summaries, coverage of selected support instances or finetuning tasks, synthesized dialogue coverage, and breadth of model knowledge or capabilities.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-overlapping labels, especially content, response, and output diversity, while task-specific variants shift the focus from responses to other kinds of candidates such as predictions or plans. One explicit breakdown separates multiple distinct responses, linguistic complexity, and coverage of the real data distribution, while other papers speak of lexical, semantic, structura

nodes.name: Generative ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats generative ability as a latent or underlying model capacity for producing fluent, coherent, and contextually appropriate text across generation tasks or open-ended settings. Many definitions add nearby qualities such as diversity, high quality, accuracy, or task relevance. A smaller line of work defines it through the ability to produce free-form, non-multiple-choice outputs in formats such as numbers, phrases, code, JSON, or open-ended text, and a few task-specific formulations narrow or broaden the target to multimodal-conditioned text, detailed object descriptions, text adaptable into jailbreak prompts, or even prompt-satisfying content such as text or images.

Space of facets. Papers mostly use generative ability, generative capability, text generation ability, and language generation as near-equivalent labels for the same latent capacity. The distinctions that appear are mainly by setting and facet: open-ended free-form output versus general task generation, prompt-conditioned or multimodal generation, and qualities such as diversity, coherence, accuracy, and meaning. Some papers pair it with reasoning or evaluat

nodes.name: Geographic bias
nodes.definition: The tendency of models to systematically favor predictions in certain geographic regions—particularly high-density or well-represented urban centers—over others, reflecting uneven learning or data distribution.

nodes.name: Geometric inductive bias
nodes.definition: The model's inherent architectural capacity to capture spatial and geometric relationships among protein residues, such as pairwise distances and angular constraints, which are critical for accurate structure prediction.

nodes.name: Geometric reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats geometric reasoning as a latent ability to understand geometric figures, diagrams, symbols, shapes, and textual problem statements, and then carry out multi-step logical or symbolic inference about properties, relationships, spatial configurations, or theorems to reach a solution. Most definitions cluster around this end-to-end reasoning framing, though some papers use nearby labels for narrower abilities such as geometric comprehension, geometric understanding, geometric structure understanding, or geometric relationship identification, centered on perceiving elements like points, lines, and angles and identifying their relations. A smaller line of work also frames it as the observable task of geometric problem solving, namely taking a diagram-plus-text problem and producing a final, often step-by-step, answer.

Space of facets. Some papers break the construct into lower-level components: geometric comprehension focuses on basic elements and their spatial relations within diagrams, geometric understanding on interpreting diagrams, symbols, and text, and geometric relationship identification on deciding rel

nodes.name: Geospatial reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to interpret and reason about spatial relationships and environmental features, such as distance from epicenter and local site conditions, to infer disaster impact severity.

nodes.name: Geospatial route cognition
nodes.definition: The latent ability of LLMs to understand and reason about sequences of connected landmarks and navigational paths, enabling tasks such as route reversal without relying on global survey knowledge.

nodes.name: Global context understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this construct as whole-context integration or understanding: the ability to use information distributed across the entire input context, sequence, or text, rather than just retrieving isolated facts. Some papers phrase this in more cognitive terms, as comprehending, synthesizing, and reasoning over distributed information, while others describe maintaining awareness of high-level information across long sequences or integrating both preceding and succeeding text into a comprehensive representation.

Space of facets. Papers use closely related labels, including global context understanding, global context awareness, and global contextual awareness, for largely the same whole-sequence idea. One paper explicitly pairs it with local precision and links it to coarse-grained compression over relevant context blocks, while another associates it with long-range dependency handling.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to this construct, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. Where papers describe it operationally, they do so through task demands rather than recorded instruments: one bench

nodes.name: Global reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to perform reasoning that involves integrating information from a large number of input tokens simultaneously, rather than relying on local patterns.

nodes.name: Goal interpretation
nodes.definition: The ability of an agent to understand the overall objective of a task from a natural language description.

nodes.name: Goal misgeneralization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available papers, goal misgeneralization is used in a single explicit sense: a model learns and pursues a proxy goal that is subtly different from the intended goal, which then leads to undesirable behavior in new situations. In Estimating the Probabilities of Rare Outputs in Language Models, it is also mentioned as one possible reason an outcome could occur, alongside an adversarially chosen input, which keeps the focus on a mismatch between the intended goal and the learned proxy goal.

Space of measurement. Papers do not link goal misgeneralization to any measurement instrument or behavioral indicator, and no linked constructs are reported. The papers therefore do not specify an operationalization for it.

Links. No papers report causal, correlational, or other related links involving goal misgeneralization.

nodes.name: Graceful forgetting
nodes.definition: The ability to enhance learning on a new task by selectively discarding irrelevant or outdated knowledge.

nodes.name: Grade-level adaptability
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to adjust its responses in terms of language, complexity, and content to match the cognitive and developmental stage of students at different grade levels.

nodes.name: Grammatical agency
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of an LLM to vary the distribution of syntactic agency in narrative framing, using passive or active constructions to shift attention toward or away from responsible actors based on persona role.

nodes.name: Graph reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats graph reasoning as a facet or latent ability of reasoning over graph-structured data, centered on solving graph problems and inferring properties such as paths, connectivity, or cycles. Several definitions frame it as understanding and solving graph-structured inputs, including natural language descriptions of graphs, and one definition emphasizes understanding, retaining, and manipulating relations among entities. A smaller usage treats it as a task of interpreting and reasoning about data in graphical or chart form, so the definitions vary between a model ability over graph-structured relations and a task label for graphical or chart-form data.

Space of facets. The papers organize the construct mainly through task families. One paper places it under Algorithmic reasoning, and others discuss it through Graph connectivity, Shortest path finding, cycle detection, graph recall, or solving more intricate graph problems by identifying nodes, edges, and constraints and applying graph algorithms. Graph recall is described in one paper as a simple yet fundamental task for understanding graph reasoning abilities, while a

nodes.name: Graph understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the construct is treated as an LLM ability or degree of understanding graph-structured information. The shared core is interpreting structure and relations, but papers place that understanding in different representations: visual graph representations, textual graphs with attributes, or knowledge-graph embeddings with semantic and topological meaning. Scope also varies somewhat, because some definitions include reasoning over subgraphs or neighborhoods, while the visual-graph formulation treats reasoning as a later step after the model understands graph features.

Space of facets. Papers use closely related labels for overlapping variants, including graph comprehension, graph understanding, and graph structure understanding. The main facets are representational, moving from visual graph features and relational information, to textual attributes in real-world textual graphs, to the semantic and topological meaning of graph embeddings, with recurring attention to subgraphs and neighborhoods. One paper also explicitly separates understanding from reasoning by first teaching the model the features of a visual graph and then fine-tuning reasoning wit

nodes.name: Grokking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, grokking is consistently framed as an observable training phenomenon in which test-set or generalization performance improves abruptly only long after a model has already reached near-perfect training performance or memorized the training data. The formulations largely agree on the same delayed shift from memorization to generalization, sometimes phrased as an "abrupt change from random guessing to generalization on the test set" after memorization.

Space of facets. The available descriptions place grokking between memorization and later generalization. One description says it "results from the model learning very structured representations," and another line of work glosses it as "extended training far beyond overfitting" when discussing how transformers learn implicit reasoning.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to grokking, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The operationalization that appears in the snippets is descriptive rather than instrument-based: papers refer to sudden improvement in test-set or generalization performance after near-perfect training performance or memorization, and one study

nodes.name: Grounded reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, grounded reasoning is framed as reasoning or responding that is based on some form of first-hand or actual evidence rather than on abstract knowledge alone or plausible but unsupported content. In Grounded Answers for Multi-agent Decision-making Problem through Generative World Model, the emphasis is on simulated, first-hand experience within an environment's dynamics, with trial and error described as necessary to ground reasoning on complicated problems. In Re-Align: Aligning Vision Language Models via Retrieval-Augmented Direct Preference Optimization, the construct is defined as a latent capacity to base responses on actual visual evidence, with failures described as fabricated details about objects, attributes, and logical relationships in an input image. The main variation is the source of grounding, simulated environmental experience in one usage and visual evidence in the other.

Space of facets. The papers organize the construct through contrasts. One usage sets it against abstract knowledge alone and ties it to trial and error within an environment, while another contrasts it with plausible but unsupported content an

nodes.name: Groundedness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, groundedness is most commonly framed as the degree to which a model response or output comes from provided or retrieved evidence, rather than unsupported internal knowledge, and can be verified against that evidence. Several definitions make this strict by saying the answer should use only the attached documents and that its claims should be supported, sometimes inferable, from inline citations. Smaller variants narrow the construct to generated arguments, defining it as factual support and consistency with retrieved evidence, or shift it to the retrieval and reasoning process itself as avoidance of hallucinated or factually inaccurate content through document-grounded knowledge; definitions also vary in source, from only provided documents to broader verifiable external knowledge such as retrieved context, contract content, or external legal sources.

Space of facets. In these papers, the idea is used at several scopes: groundedness for responses or outputs, argument groundedness for generated arguments, and factual reliability for a document-grounded retrieval and reasoning process. Some authors therefore use adjacent labels for closely relate

nodes.name: Grounding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, grounding is most commonly framed as connecting language or high-level reasoning to concrete visual or environmental referents, especially by localizing image regions, UI elements, or fine-grained video details. Some papers make this explicit through precise spatial outputs such as coordinates or bounding boxes, or through identifying the target GUI element from a natural-language description. A smaller line of work broadens the term to anchoring responses in relevant context or evidence, incorporating retrieved context when judging RAG responses, or grounding abstract user preferences to fixed schemas. Papers also differ on whether grounding is a latent capability or an observable task: several describe an underlying ability, while one GUI line defines tasks such as widget listing, 'find text', and 'find widget'.

Space of facets. Papers often place grounding next to referring under spatial understanding, with one study describing referring and grounding as the two desired capabilities that stem from spatial understanding. In GUI settings, grounding is broken into tasks such as widget listing, finding text, and finding widgets, and some wor

nodes.name: GUI understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat GUI understanding, or neighboring labels such as UI understanding and screen understanding, as a latent capability to interpret visual interface information, including layout, text, icons, structure, and function, and to identify relevant interactive or actionable elements. A smaller line of work narrows the construct either to screen reading comprehension, defined as reading textual and symbolic information on a screen to answer questions, or to GUI action grounding, defined as mapping natural language instructions to specific elements or locations. The main variation is scope: broad interface comprehension versus task-specific question answering or instruction-to-element mapping.

Space of facets. Across papers, the construct is organized through overlapping labels rather than a single fixed taxonomy: GUI understanding, UI understanding, and screen understanding are used for closely similar abilities. Some papers separate it from planning and tool usage as one component of broader agentic abilities, while others treat action grounding as a related dimension or say that action prediction builds on UI understanding. Papers also introduce narr

nodes.name: H-creativity
nodes.definition: The quality of an idea being novel in the context of all of human history, meaning no one else has had the idea before.

nodes.name: Hallucination resistance
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this construct as a latent model-level tendency or ability concerning whether outputs stay factually grounded rather than unsupported, fabricated, or false. Most definitions describe avoiding unsupported knowledge triples, multimodal content, answers, or medical information, and closely related negative framings describe generating 'semantically plausible but factually ungrounded connections' or content inconsistent with actual facts, sometimes explicitly as a failure of knowledge faithfulness. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to specific output domains, such as fabricated citations, or shifts it to molecular generation, where hallucinations are molecules that 'comply with chemical structural rules, yet fail to exhibit practical utility or the anticipated properties.'

Space of facets. Papers mostly organize the idea by output domain and by whether it is named positively or negatively. Positive labels include anti-hallucination, mitigation, and reduction, while negative labels include knowledge hallucination, factuality hallucination, molecular hallucination, and hallucination tendency; most of these still

nodes.name: Harmlessness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats harmlessness as a latent model tendency or response quality defined by not generating harmful, unsafe, unethical, offensive, or toxic content, often even under harmful or adversarial prompts. Many papers make this concrete with examples such as illegal advice, discrimination, misinformation, self-harm, violence, or other socially damaging outputs, and some connect it to refusing harmful requests. A smaller line narrows the setting to particular contexts, including malicious multimodal inputs, advice-seeking, hallucinations in critical applications, or eating-disorder-related content, so definitions differ mainly on model-level disposition versus output-level quality, and on broad safety harms versus task-specific harms.

Space of facets. Most papers place harmlessness beside helpfulness and honesty as one of the recurring 3H or HHH alignment objectives, and some extend this multi-objective framing with humor. Several evaluation setups split data into helpful and harmless subsets, while one advice-focused line treats harmlessness as an evaluation axis independent of helpfulness. A smaller line uses neighbori

nodes.name: Hedonism
nodes.definition: A value orientation focused on pleasure and sensuous gratification for oneself.

nodes.name: Help-seeking
nodes.definition: The disposition of an agent to proactively seek help and engage in productive interactions with collaborators when faced with a problem.

nodes.name: Helpfulness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats helpfulness as a latent quality of model responses: being useful, relevant, informative, supportive, and satisfying relative to a user's query, instruction, or intent. Many papers state this in near-equivalent terms, sometimes adding directness, comprehensiveness, factual accuracy, or alignment with stated or implied goals. Smaller lines of work narrow it to basic task completion or instruction adherence, cast it as perceived helpfulness grounded in a user's own experience and satisfaction during collaboration, or define it through domain criteria such as culturally aware support, subjective advice quality shaped by personal or majority preferences, or tutor guidance that is constructive without giving the full answer. Some authors also use the neighboring term usefulness, either for direct answers to instructions or for retained task performance and compliant responses to benign requests, often alongside safety trade-offs.

Space of facets. Papers most often position helpfulness as one objective in multi-objective or human-preference alignment, commonly alongside harmlessness and sometimes honesty, humor,

nodes.name: Heterogeneous reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to apply different types of logical reasoning—such as temporal, causal, spatial, and numerical—within the same task or context.

nodes.name: Hierarchical concept representation
nodes.definition: The organization of knowledge in LLMs such that high-level task concepts (e.g., 'capital') are encoded in directions orthogonal to low-level, task-specific features, enabling selective attention and compositionality.

nodes.name: Hierarchical generalization
nodes.definition: The model's latent ability to use tree-based syntactic rules to correctly process language, enabling it to generalize to out-of-distribution examples with complex structures.

nodes.name: Hierarchical planning
nodes.definition: The ability to break a complex goal into ordered subgoals and execute them over multiple steps in an interactive environment.

nodes.name: Hierarchical reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, hierarchical reasoning is described in two closely related ways. One paper treats it as the ability to solve problems with multiple dependent reasoning steps organized in a hierarchy or sequence, while another frames hierarchical thinking as a latent ability to decompose complex reasoning problems into multiple levels of sub-tasks through a divide-and-conquer strategy for organized planning. The shared core is hierarchically organized, multi-step reasoning, but the emphasis differs between solving such problems and decomposing them into subproblems.

Space of facets. Papers use both hierarchical reasoning and hierarchical thinking for closely related capacities. The internal structure they emphasize is multi-level organization: dependent reasoning steps, levels of sub-tasks, and a divide-and-conquer process that one paper describes as reducing the length of reasoning chains while maintaining the planning process. Planning is the clearest application context in the hierarchical thinking framing, whereas the other definition is broader and centers on problem solving with hierarchical or sequential dependencies.

Space of measurement. It is lin

nodes.name: Hierarchical understanding
nodes.definition: The model's latent ability to incorporate and leverage the structural relationships between labels in a taxonomy during classification.

nodes.name: Holistic object understanding
nodes.definition: The model's comprehensive ability to not only identify and segment objects but also to generate meaningful descriptive captions, integrating visual and semantic information.

nodes.name: Holistic understanding
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to grasp the overall scene, context, and structure of an image, as opposed to just identifying individual objects.

nodes.name: Honesty
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats honesty as a latent model trait or disposition to give truthful, factually accurate, non-deceptive responses. Many definitions also fold in acknowledging limits, via saying "I don't know," abstaining, declining to answer when information is insufficient, avoiding hallucinations, or candidly disclosing limitations and knowledge extent. Smaller strands narrow it to consistency with the model's own beliefs or internal knowledge, define it as evidence-backed sincerity during cooperation, or frame it as stated confidence matching true accuracy through epistemic markers; most definitions describe a property of the model, though a few describe the degree to which outputs score on preference axes.

Space of facets. Papers usually place honesty alongside helpfulness and harmlessness as one of the 3H or HHH alignment principles, and one paper expands that bundle into five fine-grained alignment perspectives. Some nearby labels are treated as close or overlapping: one survey uses sincerity for doing what one believes to be true without deception and with sufficient evidence. At the same time, papers do not fully collapse adj

nodes.name: Honesty-Humility
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of an LLM to avoid flattery, deception, and self-serving responses, promoting truthful and ethically grounded outputs.

nodes.name: HTML understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats HTML understanding as an ability to comprehend HTML structure and semantics. Most definitions add either the content of HTML documents or the functionality of HTML elements, and one explicitly frames this understanding as informing actions. A smaller line of work uses a broader neighboring framing, structural awareness, as the ability to comprehend and utilize hierarchical and semantic information in document structures such as HTML tags to improve representation quality.

Space of facets. The available definitions organize the construct mainly through recurring components rather than explicit subtypes: structure, semantics, and then either content, functionality, or hierarchical information. "HTML comprehension" and "HTML understanding" are used for closely matching abilities, while "structural awareness" shifts the emphasis toward using structural cues in representations. In one paper, it is discussed as a distinct capability alongside grounded multimodal perception and multi-step reasoning.

Space of measurement. The construct is linked to 1 measurement instrument and 1 behavioral indicator overall. The

nodes.name: Human behavior prediction ability
nodes.definition: The latent capability to infer how individuals will respond in social science experiments from their demographic attributes, experimental condition, and outcome question.

nodes.name: Human-likeness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats human-likeness as resemblance between a model's outputs or behavior and human responses, with emphasis on natural, conversational, believable, or distributionally human patterns rather than only high task accuracy. Papers apply this broad framing to daily activities, role-playing behavior, tutoring responses, and writing style, and one paper makes the contrast explicit by comparing response patterns rather than absolute performance. Smaller lines of work use nearby versions of the construct for language comprehension with human-like depth and nuance, for users' perceived humanlikeness of an agent, or for learning trajectories that mirror human learners, so the main disagreement is whether the construct concerns outputs and behavior, user perception, comprehension, or developmental dynamics.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct into different facets depending on setting: naturalness, coherence, and plausibility for generated daily activities; natural, conversational tutoring responses that do not sound robotic; realism and believability in role-playing, especially emotional expressiveness and personality co

nodes.name: Human preference alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the literature, the prevailing usage treats human preference alignment as a latent degree to which a model's outputs or behavior conform to human preferences, judgments, values, intentions, or desired objectives. Many definitions cash this out in qualities such as helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty, safety, truthfulness, coherence, and appropriateness, and several descriptions tie it to learning from preference data or human feedback so that models present knowledge in a human-preferred way. Smaller variants narrow the reference point to user intentions and expectations, physician preferences, demographic-group aesthetic preferences, or human expertise and therapeutic goals, while a minority use nearby names for observable preference following, meaning responses that rank better with humans or reward models. Another recurring difference is the standard of alignment: most papers appeal to human preferences directly, though some definitions allow model-derived preferences or specified human values.

Space of facets. Papers more often treat this concept as a family of overlapping labels than as sharply distinct constructs: alignment with human preferences,

nodes.name: Humanistic care
nodes.definition: The tendency to communicate respectfully, empathetically, and politely while providing appropriate guidance and respecting patient wishes.

nodes.name: Humor
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, humor is most commonly treated as a stylistic alignment dimension concerning whether responses are witty, amusing, or funny when that style is desired. The definitions largely agree on that core focus: some describe a model's tendency or ability to generate humorous responses, while another describes the quality of a response in being funny or amusing and places it as a secondary objective.

Space of facets. The recurring organization places humor alongside helpfulness and harmlessness as one of three pre-defined or multi-dimensional preference dimensions. Within that framing, some work treats humor as the target reward or as a thresholded secondary objective while helpfulness is the primary objective, whereas other work presents it more generally as one dimension to balance with the others.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is score-based: papers link humor to 2 measurement instruments, HH-RLHF and ArmoRM, and no behavioral indicators. In HH-RLHF-based setups, papers use open-source reward models to score responses on "Harmless", "Helpful", and "Humor", and one setup treats helpfulness as the baseline policy and humor as the target

nodes.name: Humor understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats humor understanding as a latent ability to grasp why something is humorous: papers describe comprehending and interpreting humor's nuances, underlying logic, and context, and in one case cultural cues. Within that shared framing, some definitions center on contradictions and comic juxtaposition, including nonlinear narratives, while others focus on wordplay such as puns and the recognition of ambiguity, contrast, and surprise. A smaller line of work uses a narrower recognition framing, defining it as the ability to identify or detect humor in content rather than to interpret its mechanisms.

Space of facets. Papers subdivide the construct by the kind of humor to be grasped. One strand emphasizes humor through juxtaposition and contradictory narratives, another emphasizes rationales, internal humorous logic, context, and cultural nuances, and another targets puns as context-dependent humor grounded in ambiguity, contrast, and surprise. In one account, humor understanding is contrasted with pattern recognition or memorizing patterns, while the recognition-based usage blurs humor understanding with humor recog

nodes.name: Idea diversity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this construct as within-set diversity among a model's generated ideas: the degree to which solution ideas differ semantically from one another instead of repeating near-duplicate or similar content. The definitions align on the comparison standard, diversity is assessed across the ideas in a generated set rather than against an external reference. One paper further situates the issue as a lack of high-level diversity in model outputs, specifically in candidate plans for solving a problem in natural language.

Space of facets. The main variation is terminological rather than conceptual. One paper uses the name Idea diversity, while another uses Distinctness and describes average idea distinctness for a model in a domain; in both cases, the construct refers to diverse idea generation. The wording also shifts by setting, with one paper framing it in an idea-space for solution planning and another in generated scientific research ideas.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to the construct. Still, the papers operationalize it through direct scoring of difference among gen

nodes.name: Imagination
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, imagination is treated as a visual simulation ability, but the papers split on its target. One framing describes it as generating novel visual representations, specifically intermediate subgoal images corresponding to planned sub-instructions, in support of reasoning before acting. Another framing describes it as mentally simulating or visualizing changes in a scene to infer missing perceptual knowledge and support hypothetical reasoning.

Space of facets. Rather than a shared subtype scheme, the papers place the same label in two nearby systems. In one usage, imagination sits alongside reasoning and action, with imagined subgoal images offering more intuitive guidance for sub-instructions; in the other, it sits alongside hypothetical reasoning, where imagination is used to fill perceptual knowledge gaps by deducing missing details and approximating reality. The main distinction is between subgoal-image generation for planned sub-instructions and scene-change simulation for missing perceptual knowledge.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is sparse: imagination is linked to no measurement instrument and no behavioral indicator.

nodes.name: Impermissible information leakage
nodes.definition: The extent to which a model's outputs, even if individually permissible, reveal dangerous or undesirable knowledge that an adversary can infer.

nodes.name: Implicit personalization
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of an LLM to infer and act upon user demographic attributes based on subtle conversational cues, even when not explicitly stated, thereby tailoring responses in ways that may reflect stereotypes.

nodes.name: Implicit reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Definitions are split between two uses. One paper frames it as a model capacity for inferring unstated assumptions, background knowledge, or indirect logical connections needed to interpret ambiguous or incompletely specified argumentative content, and describes it as "utilizing different background knowledge to complement implicit information" (Identification of Multiple Logical Interpretations in Counter-Arguments). Elsewhere, it is defined as the ability to solve multi-hop reasoning tasks in a single forward pass, without chain of thought, so the main disagreement is between an argumentative-interpretation framing and a multi-hop task-solving framing.

Space of facets. The available papers do not lay out a detailed subtype scheme. The clearest organizing split is between use in identifying logical structure and implicit logic in counter-arguments, including cases where a model "sometimes identifies implicit logic that even annotators did not realize," and use as a capability aligned closely with multi-hop reasoning. In that latter usage, implicit reasoning is treated as closely related to, and sometimes nearly interchangeable with, single-pass multi-hop rea

nodes.name: Implicit social bias
nodes.definition: The tendency of a model to exhibit unconscious, automatic attitudes or stereotypes that influence its decisions and behaviors without being explicitly directed to do so.

nodes.name: Impossible video understanding
nodes.definition: The observable ability of a model to detect, classify, or explain why a video depicts an impossible or counterfactual event, based on visual and temporal analysis.

nodes.name: In-context interference
nodes.definition: The latent tendency for model performance to degrade as the number of in-context demonstrations increases, due to suboptimal action selection rather than format errors.

nodes.name: In-context learning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats it as a model-level ability or capability: adapting at inference time to a new task, function, or query from a few demonstrations in the prompt, usually input-output or input-label pairs, without updating parameters. Many definitions phrase this as few-shot learning from exemplars, sometimes stressing that the model answers a novel query or new task purely from the context it is given. Smaller lines broaden the context to instructions, reference texts, unlabeled inputs, or general prefixes, while a minority use the term more behaviorally, as a prompting procedure or evaluation setup, or more formally, as task-level learnability.

Space of facets. Papers mostly use it as a broad umbrella, but they sometimes split it into model ability or capability, near-synonymous few-shot capability or adaptation, and multimodal extensions such as multi-modal long-context learning, where performance is improved by conditioning on many demonstrations. Narrower variants include selecting causal structure from context, and one formalization recasts the question as task learnability rather than model capacity; another mechanism-focused v

nodes.name: In-context reasoning
nodes.definition: The latent ability to perform inference using only information provided in the context, without relying on internally stored factual knowledge, encompassing arithmetic, symbolic, and logical operations.

nodes.name: In-weights learning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats in-weights learning as a parameter-based form of learning: query-response relationships, or memorized information, are encoded in the model's weights or parameters. Papers agree on that locus and often contrast it with relying on context examples at inference time, using phrases such as "query-response relationships encoded in the weights of the network." A smaller line frames it more broadly as the ability to acquire knowledge by updating parameters during training and thereby encode patterns from training data into the weights.

Space of facets. Papers mostly organize the concept through its contrast with in-context learning, pairing in-weight and in-context predictors as different predictors a model can learn and implement. Some descriptions align it with memorization, including references to memorized information in parameters and to a "memorizing" in-weight predictor. The naming varies slightly, with authors using both "in-weights learning" and "in-weight learning."

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The papers discuss it thr

nodes.name: Inclusivity
nodes.definition: The extent to which generated stories represent diverse sociocultural groups without overemphasizing stereotypes or narrowing representation.

nodes.name: Individuation
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to generate responses that are distinctively aligned with a specific persona, as opposed to a neutral or default narrative stance.

nodes.name: Inductive bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers describe inductive bias as the implicit assumptions, preferences, or tendencies built into a model, its architecture, or its training method that make some solutions or generalizations more likely than others, especially on unseen data or new tasks. Smaller variations keep that core but emphasize different loci: pre-trained LMs as providing assumptions for unseen inputs, transformer architectures as making some behaviors easier to realize, or model-specific tendencies that matter even without explicit instruction. The main variation is whether papers foreground generalization to new data, or a preference for particular solutions or behaviors such as simpler or sparser ones.

Space of facets. Papers usually differentiate inductive bias by source: architecture, training process, pre-training, tuning, and specific components such as butterfly structure or position encodings. Some authors speak of transformer-specific, model-specific, or idiosyncratic inductive biases, while one paper says common LLM architectures and training setups may encode very similar inductive biases. The term is also attached to particular settings, including the inductive bias

nodes.name: Inductive reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats inductive reasoning as inferring general rules, patterns, mechanisms, or high-level abstractions from a small or limited set of specific observations or examples and then applying them to novel situations. Most definitions vary only in scope, for example from general principles or abstract rules to compositional rules or in-context concepts that connect data to labels, but keep the same example-to-rule-to-generalization structure. A smaller line of work makes the procedure more explicit by defining induction as first finding a function or hypothesis that explains the training data before predicting new outputs, or as synthesizing information from multiple reasoning paths into a final answer; another places it within logical inference and associates it with fast, intuitive reasoning, and one paper uses "induction" for detecting and continuing repeated subsequences in context.

Space of facets. Papers often place inductive reasoning inside broader reasoning taxonomies, most commonly alongside deductive and abductive reasoning, and one paper also includes analogical reasoning. Other papers organize it as rule-

nodes.name: Industrial knowledge
nodes.definition: The model's internalized knowledge specific to industrial products, manufacturing processes, and defect types, which is necessary for accurate quality inspection.

nodes.name: Information content
nodes.definition: The amount of information transferred from the training dataset into the model's weights, which the paper argues grows sublinearly with model size.

nodes.name: Information integration
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats information integration as a latent model ability to combine evidence from separated textual units. One paper frames it narrowly as combining evidence across multiple passages to determine relevance in multi-hop retrieval, while another defines it more broadly as combining and using information from different parts of a linguistic context to make predictions, especially across sentence and clause boundaries. The shared core is integration across distinct pieces of text, with the main variation being task-specific multi-passage retrieval versus broader within-context linguistic prediction.

Space of facets. Papers organize the construct by the units over which integration occurs. One usage centers on multiple documents or passages and the relationships between them, while another treats information as distributed across multiple scales of language, including words, sentences, and discourse, and focuses on an "information integration window" that is constrained by sentence and clause boundaries. The same label is therefore used for both cross-document integration and integration across internal linguistic structure.

nodes.name: Information preservation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers are split between two framings rather than using a single prevailing one. One paper defines it as the extent to which an encoder's embeddings retain enough content for an LLM to recover the original input or a downstream signal. Another, under the closely related name information retention, defines it as the degree to which an LLM preserves and transmits its full belief distribution across communication steps rather than discarding uncertainty through discrete token selection, and explicitly says the token sampling step "poses a potential risk of information loss" because it uses one token to represent belief over the vocabulary (Let Models Speak Ciphers: Multiagent Debate through Embeddings). The disagreement is therefore both about where the property resides, embeddings versus communication steps, and about what is preserved, recoverable content versus the model's full belief distribution and uncertainty.

Space of facets. The main pattern is terminological rather than taxonomic. Papers use both information preservation and information retention, but the associated definitions do not fully align: one centers reconstructability from embeddings, while t

nodes.name: Information retrieval ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat the construct as an ability to locate, search for, retrieve, or extract relevant information from text, a long context, memory, or an external corpus. Within that broad framing, many papers focus on finding specific facts or answer spans from earlier input or cross-lingual context, while some define it at the document level as identifying relevant items from a corpus. Smaller lines of work narrow it to reasoning-intensive retrieval, where relevant documents are connected by underlying principles, algorithms, or theorems rather than simple keyword or semantic matching, or broaden it to multimodal search and retrieval using both visual and textual information; one paper further specializes it to finding inspiration papers associated with a research background.

Space of facets. Papers explicitly divide the construct into subtypes such as reasoning-intensive retrieval, multimodal retrieval capability, text retrieval capability, cross-lingual context retrieval, answer retrieval, in-context retrieval, recall capability, and information retrieval and localization. Some works also position it against neighboring constructs: one disentangles ret

nodes.name: Information-seeking ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats the term as a model-side ability to notice missing knowledge and actively gather what is needed by asking questions before answering, especially under uncertainty or ambiguity. In this framing, the construct is tied to proactive questioning, eliciting missing details, and judging whether enough information has been collected to give a confident answer. A smaller line of work uses the same label for a task type instead: responding to queries that ask for factual information or explanations, rather than a latent capability of the model.

Space of facets. The papers mainly organize the concept around question asking and active information gathering rather than around named subtypes. Within the dominant framing, it is described alongside question-asking ability and active information-seeking capabilities, and one paper characterizes success as deciding at each turn whether more information is needed before giving a confident answer. Across papers, the term therefore covers both a latent model property and, in a minority usage, a class of information-seeking questions.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is spars

nodes.name: Informativeness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats informativeness as a quality criterion for model outputs: how much relevant, useful, complete, or adequately detailed information generated text, responses, commentary, or summaries provide. Many definitions add a coverage standard, saying the output should capture the main information without omission, and several also add a non-redundancy standard, describing informative content as new rather than repeated. A smaller line of work uses the same term for preserving useful non-conflicting content during revision, for the usefulness of individual reasoning steps or discovered latent factors, or for the information density of condensed training samples.

Space of facets. Papers most often unpack informativeness into facets such as relevance, completeness, useful detail, and coverage of main information. Some make those facets explicit: chess commentary work defines it through relevance and completeness, multimodal chain-of-thought work treats an informative step as one that adds new information and avoids redundancy, and timeline summarization describes it as the effective volume of information that captures m

nodes.name: Insight
nodes.definition: The ability to generate psychologically meaningful understanding or reframing that goes beyond surface-level support.

nodes.name: Insightfulness
nodes.definition: The tendency of a response to provide useful, thoughtful, or informative content beyond minimal correctness.

nodes.name: Instance-level stability
nodes.definition: The degree to which an accelerated model produces the same predictions for the same inputs as its original, unaccelerated counterpart.

nodes.name: Instance reasoning
nodes.definition: The latent ability to reason about specific instances of objects, their properties, and their relationships within an image.

nodes.name: Instruction following ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this as a latent ability or capacity to understand, parse, and execute natural-language instructions, and to keep outputs aligned with user intent, task goals, and explicit constraints. Most definitions make constraint satisfaction central, often naming format, style, word limits, JSON validity, requested languages, or multi-step procedures, and several extend the same basic idea to multimodal, multilingual, retrieval, agent, and embodied settings. A smaller line of work defines it more behaviorally, as the observable act of producing a compliant response or action, and a few papers narrow it further to exact-specification matching, system-message compliance over turns, or evaluator-side judgment of whether a response satisfies an instruction.

Space of facets. Papers most often organize the concept by what must be followed: guidelines, constraints, rules, system messages, or broader open-ended instructions. Several narrower labels tighten the focus to exact specification matching or condition satisfaction, while one evaluation-oriented line breaks instruction-following into relevance, factuality, and adherence, and s

nodes.name: Instruction understanding
nodes.definition: The model's ability to understand task instructions and map them to appropriate actions in constrained environments.

nodes.name: Intelligence
nodes.definition: The emergent ability of a system to learn effective, generalizable representations and perform well on complex downstream tasks, hypothesized to arise from exposure to and prediction of complex data.

nodes.name: Intelligibility
nodes.definition: The latent ability of synthesized or edited speech to be accurately understood by listeners, reflecting clarity of pronunciation and word-level fidelity.

nodes.name: Intent understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing framing is a latent ability to recover an underlying purpose, goal, task, or information need from an utterance, prompt, or interaction sequence, often when that intent is not stated directly. Most definitions place the construct in context-sensitive inference, for example over conversational turns, GUI trajectories, vague or incomplete queries, or instructions that omit the target object or action. Smaller strands narrow the reference standard to pragmatic speaker meaning beyond literal content, to relevance to social and cultural expectations, or to recognizing malicious versus benign requests.

Space of facets. The construct appears under several neighboring names, including speaker meaning inference, intention inference, intent perception, intention awareness, and user intent understanding, and one paper says the task is sometimes called goal understanding. Across these uses, papers shift the object of inference, from another person's intentions in interaction, to intended meaning and implications, to intended task, to text-based user intentions for recommendation, or to information need in conversational search.

nodes.name: Inter-agent trust
nodes.definition: A latent positive disposition developed by an agent towards its peers based on their historical accuracy, which can increase its propensity to conform to their subsequent judgments.

nodes.name: Interactive reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to use multi-turn dialogue to gather evidence, update hypotheses, and converge on a correct answer.

nodes.name: Interactivity
nodes.definition: The degree to which a system engages the user in its generation process, allowing them to provide feedback and influence the outcome to align with their preferences.

nodes.name: Intergroup empathy bias
nodes.definition: The latent tendency to empathize less with out-group members relative to in-group members, which is inferred from differences in predicted emotion intensity.

nodes.name: Interleaved understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is a latent ability or capacity for understanding interleaved multimodal inputs, especially alternating image and text sequences within a single input, sometimes described as requiring reasoning over those elements and integrating them into a coherent interpretation. A smaller line of work uses a narrower framing centered on long-form intertwined text and multiple images, where the model must identify relevant information and ignore superfluous or distracting content.

Space of facets. Papers use several labels for closely related capacities, including interleaved understanding, interleaved multimodal comprehension, and interleaved image-text comprehension, with scope varying from broad multimodal contexts to specifically image-text settings. Most formulations focus on comprehension or understanding, though one paper explicitly discusses interleaved multimodal comprehension together with generation, and another frames the task around answering questions and following instructions to pinpoint the relevant image.

Space of measurement. Formally, no measurement instrument and no behavioral indicator are linked to the

nodes.name: Interlocutor awareness
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to infer the identity and characteristics of its conversational partner, enabling adaptive behavior based on the interlocutor's model family, reasoning patterns, linguistic style, or alignment preferences.

nodes.name: Internal consistency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available papers, the label is used in two distinct ways rather than one prevailing sense. One paper describes it as agreement between latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers and the final prediction, presenting it as a measure of the model's confidence and as reflecting the stability of the model's internal reasoning process; another defines it as giving equivalent answers to theoretically equivalent queries, regardless of correctness relative to ground truth. The definitions differ mainly on whether internal consistency is located in layerwise internal representations or in answer-level equivalence across matched queries.

Space of facets. The papers do not break the construct into subtypes, but they do use the same name for different targets. In Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency, it is tied to agreement among latent predictions across layers and framed as a measure of confidence; in Compositional Causal Reasoning Evaluation in Language Models, it refers to whether theoretically equivalent quantities are inferred to be equivalent, up to some error δ.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is l

nodes.name: Interpretability and explainability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats interpretability and explainability as human-understandability of a model's internals, learned features, or decision process: representations, sparse features, concept layers, retrieved evidence, and reasoning traces count as interpretable when humans can inspect them, trace outputs to supporting sources, or give concise explanations of activations. A sizable minority uses explainability more narrowly for rationales, critiques, or other justifications that accompany predictions or judgments, sometimes contrasted with systems that provide only labels or numerical scores, while a smaller group uses transparency for inspectable embedding dimensions or identifiable knowledge sources. The main axis of variation is what is being made understandable, internal mechanisms and representations versus output-level rationales, evidence traces, or source attributions.

Space of facets. Papers often place interpretability, explainability, and transparency under the same umbrella, and some explicitly pair the labels or treat interpretability and explainability as interchangeable. At the same time, they carve out narrower variants, su

nodes.name: Intersectional bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats intersectional bias as bias that arises from the interaction or interplay of multiple social or demographic attributes, rather than from a single attribute in isolation. Recurring examples are combinations such as race and gender, physical characteristics and gender, and age and socioeconomic status. The definitions largely align on this core idea, with only a minor shift between describing it as a form of social bias and as a model's tendency to exhibit such bias.

Space of facets. Papers organize the construct around combinations of attributes under study, especially race, gender, physical characteristics, age, and socioeconomic status, and they contrast this with fairness evaluation that examines only one demographic category at a time. One paper further describes it through cases where groups that share one attribute but differ on another are stereotyped differently. The available papers do not introduce formal subtypes or connect it to other named constructs beyond this single-attribute versus multi-attribute distinction.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is sparse: papers link intersectional bias to

nodes.name: Intrinsic bias
nodes.definition: The tendency of a large language model to favor certain types of solutions or options based on patterns in its pre-training data, limiting the diversity of its outputs.

nodes.name: Invariance
nodes.definition: The tendency for a predictor to rely on stable features that remain predictive across environments rather than environment-specific correlations.

nodes.name: Irrelevance detection ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available paper frames this construct as a model-side ability to recognize when none of the available functions or tools matches the user's intent and to refuse the task in that case. In that usage, irrelevance detection centers on judging that "no suitable function exists" and "decline the task, rather than making incorrect attempts" (Robust Function-Calling for On-Device Language Model via Function Masking).

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to it. In the available use, the construct is stated as a capability, but it is not tied to a named benchmark, human evaluation method, judge model, probe, or analysis.

Links. One paper reports that it is correlated with Tool use ability, describing an inverse relationship between accurate function-call execution and irrelevance detection capacity.

nodes.name: Judge sentiment bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definition, the construct is framed as an LLM judge's tendency to have its judgment affected by emotional expression in the content it evaluates. The paper describes this as a preference for positive or negative emotions, and its source language also states that the judge may prefer content without emotional elements.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to this construct, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The available papers therefore do not specify an operationalization for it.

nodes.name: Kanji-rule compatibility
nodes.definition: The model's latent understanding of which mnemonic-creation rules are semantically or visually suitable for a given kanji based on its specific structural or semantic features.

nodes.name: Keyword organization inference
nodes.definition: The latent ability of LLMs to reconstruct the correct semantic organization of keywords from disordered, unnatural inputs by leveraging contextual cues from subsequent natural language questions.

nodes.name: Knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats knowledge as a model-level latent ability or capacity to have acquired, encoded, stored, and recall or retrieve factual information about the world, sometimes with the added condition that the answer is not directly available in the input. A smaller line of work broadens this from recall to correct application or utilization, defining it in terms of applying factual, semantic, procedural, or conceptual information, or of retrieving and using acquired knowledge to solve professional problems. One further framing emphasizes breadth of expert information across subject areas and benchmark items rather than recall alone.

Space of facets. Several recurrent contrasts appear across papers. One paper explicitly divides evaluation into knowledge ability versus inference ability, another says multiple-choice questions mainly assess basic knowledge levels such as recalling, understanding, and applying knowledge, and another treats reasoning and knowledge as part of a broader general ability. The labels knowledge, knowledge ability, and knowledge capacity are used for closely related model properties, although one p

nodes.name: Knowledge acquisition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats knowledge acquisition as learning or internalizing facts, concepts, or associations, often from training data, rather than only as retrieving knowledge at decision time. Several definitions describe a model acquiring facts, concepts, or simple associations from training data, storing them in weights or other internal representations, and in one case absorbing tool-generated solutions into parametric knowledge so problems can later be solved without tool calls; one paper also notes that learning a fact may require "hundreds to thousands of diverse representations". A minority framing treats it as a latent ability to retrieve and use relevant factual or contextual knowledge from external sources or internal representations to support decision-making, and another defines it as knowledge gain, the increase in knowledge or certainty after new information, estimated through shifts in an internal knowledge distribution.

Space of facets. Authors use several neighboring labels for partly overlapping ideas. Fact learning is used for encoding and storing factual information in model weights, with one paper saying it can occur a

nodes.name: Knowledge application
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat this construct as the ability to access and apply knowledge during task performance or reasoning, often described as using pre-trained or stored factual knowledge relevant to the context. A smaller line of work shifts the source of knowledge: some define it as using newly learned facts to answer downstream questions, especially when the query format differs from the training statement, while another defines it as effective use of information supplied in the prompt or retrieved context. Other papers narrow it to domain-specific settings, describing the integration of agricultural knowledge, flexible adaptation of mathematical knowledge rather than rigid memorization, or the application of physical laws and real-world physical theories.

Space of facets. Papers use several neighboring names for the construct, including knowledge utilization, knowledge application ability, and factual knowledge recall. Some descriptions explicitly contrast it with rigid memorization, and one related paper connects it to knowledge memorization; another domain-specific framing treats agricultural knowledge application as something that can occur independ

nodes.name: Knowledge base awareness
nodes.definition: The model's ability to effectively utilize and interact with the information and structure of a knowledge base during task execution.

nodes.name: Knowledge boundary awareness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers describe knowledge boundary awareness as a latent, often internal ability to recognize the limits of the model's own knowledge and to distinguish what it knows from what it does not, whether over questions, statements, or entities. Many of these definitions tie that recognition to response behavior, such as answering only when the model knows, expressing uncertainty, or avoiding false, unsupported, or overconfident claims. A smaller line of work treats the boundary more as a property or limit of knowledge scope, including whether a query needs external retrieval, whether needed information is absent from the image, or, in one case, whether a specific entity is recognized; one survey further defines the boundary across universal, parametric, and outward dimensions.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for overlapping ideas, including knowledge boundary cognition, perception, awareness, knowledge awareness, self-knowledge, and awareness of knowledge limits, and one paper places capability awareness as a facet of self-awareness concerned with assessing knowledge and skills for a task. The clearest subtype scheme splits knowledge

nodes.name: Knowledge conflict resolution
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the shared framing treats knowledge conflict resolution as an ability for handling conflicts between a model's internal knowledge and externally provided context. One paper defines it as reconciling contradictions between parametric knowledge and contextual information, and describes models as facing competing claims between internal knowledge and external evidence. Another uses the name situated faithfulness and defines the ability more specifically as giving the correct answer by dynamically calibrating trust between internal knowledge and external context, regardless of whether the context is correct or incorrect. The main difference is whether the construct is stated broadly as contradiction reconciliation or more specifically as correct answering through trust calibration.

Space of facets. Papers offer only limited systematization. One paper says the construct has a multidimensional nature, while another makes the correctness of the external context an explicit organizing condition by requiring correct answers whether that context is right or wrong. There is also a naming split: some work uses knowledge conflict resolution for the

nodes.name: Knowledge extraction ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this construct as the ability to retrieve knowledge learned during training or pre-training when a model faces information-seeking prompts or other queries. One definition presents it as retrieving and applying "world knowledge" learned from pre-training data, while another narrows the framing to "parametric knowledge extraction," the retrieval of factual knowledge stored in model parameters and learned from documents. The main variation is between a broader world-knowledge-and-application framing and a more specific emphasis on factual, parameter-stored knowledge.

Space of facets. Papers do not lay out an elaborate subtype structure, but they do distinguish a narrower label, parametric knowledge extraction, from the broader notion of knowledge extraction. One paper also ties the construct to prompt type, stating that "knowledge-specific insights" or "information-seeking prompts" engage knowledge extraction learned from pre-training, and it discusses knowledge extraction alongside reasoning as a distinct demand that still "rely on the foundational language model" (Visual Description Grounding Reduces Hallu

nodes.name: Knowledge forgetting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this construct as forgetting that follows model updating: a loss or degradation of previously acquired knowledge, performance, or capabilities after learning new tasks or data.
