Most definitions appear under the name catastrophic forgetting, and describe it in settings such as direct weight updates, sequential learning, fine-tuning, or distribution shift. A smaller line of work narrows the idea to language attrition, where models fine-tuned on one language lose definition-generation ability in other languages despite retained comprehension, or to spurious forgetting, where post-training degradation is attributed to misaligned internal representations rather than complete knowledge loss.

Space of facets. Papers use the broad label for slightly different targets: some definitions focus on previously acquired knowledge, others on capabilities or task performance. Within that family, language attrition is a language-specific variant centered on active generation loss, while spurious forgetting names cases where performance drops even though the paper argues the underlying knowledge may still be present. The sam

nodes.name: Knowledge grounding
nodes.definition: The latent capacity of an LLM to integrate and synthesize external, authoritative information into its responses, enabling factually accurate and traceable outputs in specialized domains.

nodes.name: Knowledge integration
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing framing treats knowledge integration as a latent capacity to update or incorporate new factual knowledge, either by changing internal representations over time or by bringing new facts into internal parameters or retrieval-augmented context while preserving existing knowledge. A smaller line of work uses the same label for combining and leveraging external resources rather than internal updating: one paper describes leveraging external scientific domain knowledge, task-specific instructions, and expert-curated guidance, noting that models "often fail in leveraging extensive broader information" (Large Language-Geometry Model: When LLM meets Equivariance), while another says LLMs "excel at merging structured educational knowledge graphs ... with unstructured textual data" into contextualized instructional content (Position: LLMs Can be Good Tutors in English Education). The main disagreement is between internal knowledge change and the combination of structured, unstructured, or expert-provided external inputs.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a stable facet structure for this construct. Instead, the term spans at l

nodes.name: Knowledge integration efficacy
nodes.definition: The ability of the system to accurately remember and integrate recent events or contexts into its parameters.

nodes.name: Knowledge manipulation
nodes.definition: The ability of a language model to flexibly use factual knowledge memorized from pre-training data to solve downstream tasks that require reasoning, such as classification or comparison.

nodes.name: Knowledge memorization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats knowledge memorization as retention of factual or content knowledge derived from data that should have been forgotten. The definitions agree that unlearning should remove not only verbatim text but also this retained knowledge, with one formulation saying the model should be "incapable of responding to questions about the forget set." Another formulation makes the construct explicitly observable, describing it through correct answers to question-answer pairs generated from the forgetting data.

Space of facets. The available descriptions mostly position the term by contrast rather than by internal subtypes. Papers distinguish it from verbatim memorization and privacy leakage within broader unlearning evaluation, and one snippet glosses it as "general knowledge encoded in the tokens." In that usage, "no knowledge memorization" is presented as one of several desirable properties of an unlearned model, alongside utility preservation, scalability, and sustainability.

Space of measurement. Papers operationalize the construct with 2 measurement instruments and 2 behavioral indicators. The named instruments are MUSE, a

nodes.name: Knowledge reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing treats knowledge reasoning as an ability to answer questions by drawing on factual or world knowledge and integrating that knowledge into inference. Several definitions keep this broad, referring to factual knowledge, conceptual knowledge, or comprehensive knowledge across many subjects, while smaller strands narrow it to implicit geographic, cultural, or encyclopedic facts needed for relevance judgments, or to fact reasoning with open-book information. The main point of variation is the knowledge source: some papers emphasize external facts or corpus-retrieved knowledge, while others describe knowledge-intensive reasoning as retrieving and synthesizing knowledge stored within the model's parameters.

Space of facets. Papers use several neighboring labels for overlapping territory, including knowledge and reasoning, fact reasoning, world knowledge reasoning, and knowledge-intensive reasoning, rather than a single fixed subtype scheme. One line of work treats world knowledge as a narrower case that links textual mentions to external facts and, in one benchmark, sits alongside arithmetic and temporal reasoning; elsewhere knowl

nodes.name: Knowledge retention
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats knowledge retention as a model's capacity to preserve previously learned knowledge, task performance, or general capabilities after later fine-tuning, continual learning, editing, compression, pruning, quantization, unlearning, or other updates. A large parallel usage states the same problem from the loss side as catastrophic or model forgetting: direct weight or parameter updates, distribution shift, or sequential learning can make the model lose previously acquired knowledge, text capabilities, or broad functionality. Smaller definitions narrow the scope to pre-training knowledge, factual and linguistic information in compressed models, shared representations across tasks, or the recall of long-past injected contexts.

Space of facets. Papers introduce several named variants, including retention of pre-training knowledge, knowledge preservation, general capability retention, general knowledge retention, shared knowledge retention, anti-forgetting, and retention as recall of long-past experiences. One paper also separates forgetting into a format-level subtype and a factual-loss subtype, and says the forme

nodes.name: Knowledge storage
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats knowledge storage as a latent, internal mechanism or property of a model's parameters or weights: it is described as how factual information is encoded and retained within the model, including facts from pre-training stored in its 'parametric' memory. A smaller line of work uses a narrower quantitative framing, knowledge storage capacity, defined as the amount of factual information, measured in bits, that a model can store in its parameters and later retrieve. The main difference across definitions is therefore between a mechanistic account of how information is stored and a capacity account of how much can be stored and retrieved.

Space of facets. Papers use closely related names for overlapping ideas: 'information storage' is used for the same general phenomenon and is explicitly equated with a model's 'parametric' memory. One paper uses the name knowledge storage capacity for a quantitative version of the idea, focusing on retrievable factual information in bits rather than the storage mechanism itself. Another paper separates knowledge storage from 'more complicated computations', saying shallow layers likel

nodes.name: Knowledge tracing ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the construct is framed as a latent predictive capacity: correctly forecasting a student's future performance on educational tasks from historical interaction data and evolving knowledge states. No alternative framing appears in the available papers, and the surrounding language keeps the construct tied to future-performance prediction.

Space of facets. The only explicit organizing move is to use the name "Predictive accuracy" for this construct, so the concept is treated in accuracy-centered terms rather than split into separate facets. In that usage, it is organized around forecasting future student performance from prior interactions and evolving knowledge states.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The available operational language, in CIKT: A Collaborative and Iterative Knowledge Tracing Framework with Large Language Models, stays at the level of predictive-performance phrasing, describing whether the model can "accurately predict future performance," "forecast student performance," and enhance "overall predictive performance," rather than naming

nodes.name: Knowledge transfer
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats knowledge transfer as cross-context carryover: something learned in one setting, often prompts, attacks, policies, algorithms, or pre-trained knowledge, is expected to remain effective in another model, task, domain, language, modality, or request set. A common narrower line, especially under the name transferability, focuses on cross-model reuse without retraining or re-optimization, for example whether continuous prompts, jailbreak prompts, or detection methods learned on one model still work on another; one paper defines it as the level at which prompts produced to jailbreak one LLM can successfully jailbreak another model. Smaller lines of work instead define it as task-to-task improvement, including forward and backward transfer in continual learning, exemplar-driven transfer between tasks in in-context learning, or the sharing of domain-specific knowledge within multi-expert systems. The main disagreement is over what bears the property: a model, a prompt or attack, a task pair, or a transfer process between experts, tasks, or domains.

Space of facets. Papers most explicitly divide the construct into forward tr

nodes.name: Knowledge understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat knowledge understanding as a model ability, often described as a latent ability, to comprehend, represent, and correctly apply factual, conceptual, world, or domain knowledge when answering questions, processing inputs, or generating outputs. Some formulations narrow this to information presented in a question or factual knowledge embedded in text, while others broaden it to acquiring, retaining, and applying general world and domain-specific knowledge from training data; one modality-specific variant frames it in spoken interactions across domains such as STEM, social sciences, and humanities. Across these formulations, the recurring core is using knowledge rather than only following instructions.

Space of facets. Papers mostly use near-synonymous labels, including knowledge comprehension and knowledge and understanding, for the same general construct. They usually place it alongside, but not as the same thing as, reasoning, instruction following, problem solving, and general language understanding: one evaluation says it targets knowledge comprehension and reasoning rather than merely instruction following, and another discusses impro

nodes.name: Label noise robustness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats label noise robustness as keeping performance stable when supervision is noisy or corrupted, most often through mislabeled or synthetic label noise in training data. One paper makes this concrete as having the lowest relative drop in performance compared with training on clean data. A smaller line of work extends the same framing to noisy textual descriptions, dialogue annotations or input formulations, noisy in-context demonstrations, and self-generated data with errors, and some of these definitions narrow the outcome to compositional performance or to continuing the self-improvement process.

Space of facets. Instead of a shared subtype taxonomy, papers apply the term across several noise sources and learning settings. The main distinctions in use are between corrupted training labels, noisy captions or textual supervision, annotation or input noise, incorrect labels in demonstrations, and errors in self-generated training data. Some authors also tie the construct to a specific target, either maintaining compositional performance or preserving a self-improvement process under noisy training signals.

Space of m

nodes.name: Language bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats language bias as language-dependent unevenness in model behavior: performance varies by language, models may prefer some languages or language pairs over others, and English, Western, or higher-resource languages are often favored. This framing appears both in task-performance definitions, where similar content can yield different results across languages, and in representation-space definitions, where sentences from the same language can be mapped closer together regardless of semantic similarity. A minority usage applies the same label to large vision-language models, defining it instead as over-reliance on textual inputs and neglect of visual inputs during generation. One paper also broadens the cross-lingual framing from performance alone to equitable computational efficiency across languages.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for the cross-lingual version of the construct, including cross-lingual fairness, anglocentric bias, English-centric bias, language-dependent effectiveness, and linguistic bias. Within that cluster, some authors narrow the issue to English versus other languages

nodes.name: Language modeling ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats language modeling ability as a model's latent or core capacity to predict likely tokens or sequences and to generate coherent, plausible, or fluent text. Many definitions tie this directly to probability-based modeling, describing it in terms of prediction loss, perplexity, token probability distributions, or next-symbol prediction, and one paper explicitly frames it as separate from factual correctness. Smaller lines of work instead define it through performance on broad language-modeling evaluations or predictive performance metrics, narrow it to a retriever encoder's retained capacity to model document text, or specialize it to source-language modeling for translation and transcription.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby labels under this construct, including language modeling ability, capability, quality, predictive capability, and predictive performance. They also refer to general, basic, short-context, masked, and source-language versions, so the term is used both for a broad underlying capability and for more specific settings or scopes. A few papers position it relative to other properties: one sa

nodes.name: Language processing
nodes.definition: The ability to interpret and rewrite natural-language procedural descriptions into more structured task representations.

nodes.name: Language proficiency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats language proficiency as an underlying model capability, usually framed as competence in understanding and generating language and often tied to formal linguistic knowledge such as syntax, morphology, semantics, vocabulary, or orthography. Many definitions describe it as latent or inherent, sometimes as a higher-order or compositional ability that emerges over training, and sometimes as proficiency in a particular language whose level reflects training data amount, quality, or coverage. Smaller lines of work define it more narrowly through acceptable versus unacceptable sentence discrimination or through a target-source language capacity gap, while another broadens it to stable language skills across tasks such as sentiment classification and factual reasoning.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct into formal linguistic facets, including agreement, binding, island constraints, morphology, syntax, semantics, orthography, vocabulary, synonyms and antonyms, and in one case pragmatics; one paper also treats coherent, grammatically accurate sentence generation as part of it. The naming is broad: linguistic compe

nodes.name: Large-scale spatial cognition
nodes.definition: The ability to build and use spatial representations of large environments for tasks like navigation and spatial reasoning.

nodes.name: Latent ability
nodes.definition: A capability that a model possesses but exhibits with low probability by default, which can be revealed through specific elicitation techniques.

nodes.name: Latent reasoning
nodes.definition: The model's capacity to perform internal, non-verbalized cognitive processing in continuous latent space, distilling additional computation into its kv-cache to improve downstream performance.

nodes.name: Latent variable inference
nodes.definition: The model's ability to infer unobserved, low-dimensional parameters or structures that govern the data generation process for a task.

nodes.name: Lateral thinking
nodes.definition: The latent ability to solve problems through indirect and creative reasoning, often involving unexpected shifts in perspective or interpretation of ambiguous cues.

nodes.name: Layout compactness
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to generate layouts that maximize space usage.

nodes.name: Legal accuracy
nodes.definition: The correctness of a model's generated answer according to legal statutes and expert judgment.

nodes.name: Legal compliance
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing framing treats legal compliance, or legality, as a latent model property of adhering to legal rules and regulations. One definition states this broadly for generated responses or instructions, including cases where misalignment yields unlawful instructions, while another narrows it to established regulatory standards in privacy and safety, naming GDPR, the EU AI Act, and HIPAA for how models process or respond to inputs. The definitions differ mainly in scope, broad legal adherence versus compliance under specific privacy and safety frameworks, while agreeing that the construct is a latent disposition or capacity of the model.

Space of facets. Papers use legality and legal compliance as closely aligned names for the same kind of latent adherence property. One paper places legality alongside stereotypes and morality as one of three aspects in an alignment evaluation, while another situates legal compliance within privacy and safety work, emphasizing lawful, safe, and privacy-preserving systems and referring to contextualized legal reasoning. The papers do not explicitly break it into further subtypes beyond this broad versus p

nodes.name: Legal ethics
nodes.definition: Sensitivity to ethical principles, fairness, and moral constraints in legal decision-making and advice.

nodes.name: Legal fidelity
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model's generated answer aligns with the correct legal interpretation of relevant statutory provisions and does not contradict or omit key legal elements.

nodes.name: Legal knowledge
nodes.definition: The extent to which the model has encoded and can accurately retrieve legal principles, statutes, and case law.

nodes.name: Legal language understanding
nodes.definition: The latent ability to interpret legal texts well enough to judge relevance among statutes and precedents in legal retrieval.

nodes.name: Legal reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats legal reasoning as a latent ability to interpret legal texts and apply legal rules or principles to facts so as to reach legally grounded conclusions, judgments, or arguments. Many definitions add that this involves structured, logical inference, with references to well-defined logical flow, professional legal judgment, implicit rules, and procedures such as legal syllogism, not only reading surface text. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to particular settings, such as interpreting legal reporting requirements and deciding whether a statement satisfies them, interpreting legal documents to extract their issues or implications, performing multi-hop inference, computing legally relevant periods or amounts, or applying hierarchical interpretation methods.

Space of facets. Papers often use the label as an umbrella over multiple reasoning types rather than as a single undifferentiated skill. One recurring breakdown names issue-spotting, rule-recall, rule-application, rule-conclusion, interpretation, and rhetorical understanding; other work carves out legal multi-hop reasoning and legal calculation, and another

nodes.name: Legal relevance judgment
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to determine whether a legal statute or precedent is relevant to a given case based on factual and legal alignment, beyond mere lexical or semantic similarity.

nodes.name: Legal relevance judgment ability
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to determine whether a legal statute or precedent is relevant to a given case based on factual and legal alignment, beyond mere lexical or semantic similarity.

nodes.name: Length bias
nodes.definition: A statistical bias where a model learns a spurious correlation between the length of an input and its corresponding class label, using length as a shallow, discriminatory feature.

nodes.name: Length control ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing is an underlying ability to produce outputs that meet explicit length requirements. Several definitions add that this should preserve meaning or content, describing it as "ensuring key information retention while enforcing length constraints" or as maintaining semantic integrity while avoiding premature termination or content distortion. A narrower usage ties the construct specifically to summaries, while another treats response length control as a continuous attribute rather than a discrete category; one generic definition spells out the requirement in terms of word, sentence, or token limits.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby labels, including length control, length-constrained generation, response length control, and aligning, for closely related uses. The distinctions that appear are between summary-focused and general text-generation settings, and between a broad ability to hit a target length and an aligning aspect defined through the discrepancy between a model's perceived length and the target length. In that aligning framing, frequent explicit counting is reported to interfere with semantic mo

nodes.name: Length generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage describes training on shorter sequences and testing on longer ones while maintaining performance, often phrased as applying a model directly to Ltest > Ltrain without performance degradation or effectively processing inputs longer than pre-training exposure. A smaller line of work narrows this to specific settings, such as applying a learned algorithm to longer inputs as evidence of a scalable rather than memorized solution, producing longer programs than seen in training, solving math word problems with extended narratives, or sustaining coherent generation over longer durations. Some authors also broaden the construct from longer inputs alone to varying numbers of context examples, or define it over both upward and downward out-of-distribution lengths.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels, including length extrapolation, long-context generalization, length generalizability, context length generalizability, generative length extrapolation, and size generalisation; one paper explicitly notes that, in language modelling, size generalisation is also known as length generalisation. The construc

nodes.name: Lexical diversity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats lexical diversity as the variety or richness of vocabulary, words, phrases, or n-grams in generated text or in collections of texts. Most definitions locate it in observable outputs, such as text produced across many examples, while one paper shifts the emphasis to the model's capacity to generate varied vocabulary and avoid repetitive n-gram patterns. The main variation is therefore whether it is framed as a property of texts and datasets or as a capacity of the model that produces them, with one paper also narrowing the description to lexical types with shared syntactic properties.

Space of facets. These papers do not present a detailed subtype taxonomy for lexical diversity. Instead, they vary the unit used to describe it, ranging from vocabulary, words and phrases, and n-grams to, in one paper, lexical types. Some authors also distinguish it from other forms of diversity by discussing it alongside diversity in the key points expressed, and one paper places it alongside order diversity in a generation setup.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to lexical diversity, and no behavior

nodes.name: Lexical understanding
nodes.definition: The model's ability to recognize and correctly process individual words or lexical items in spoken language.

nodes.name: Linguistic alignment
nodes.definition: The latent ability of deep layers in an MLLM to refine generated content into grammatically correct and structurally appropriate natural language outputs after cross-modal integration.

nodes.name: Linguistic diversity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available usage, linguistic diversity is framed as a model capacity: generating or recognizing multiple valid phrasings of the same semantic content, as a reflection of natural language variation. The source text elaborates this with alternative expressions of the same idea, such as "There are 12 inches in 1 foot" and "There are 12 inches in each foot," and presents the construct as something SFT often fails to capture. No competing definition appears.

Space of facets. The concept is not broken into named subtypes. The only internal distinction made is between generation and recognition of alternative valid phrasings, and the discussion places linguistic diversity alongside inter-token relationships, with alternative phrasings used to illustrate "nuanced token-level dependencies" that may be overlooked.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to linguistic diversity, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The paper therefore does not specify a benchmark, human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge, or probe for measuring it; instead, it illustrates the construct through examples of multiple valid expressions and describes enriched trainin

nodes.name: Linguistic knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats linguistic knowledge as internal, underlying, or latent knowledge of language that enables understanding, interpretation, generation, or alignment. The papers agree on that core idea, but differ in scope and setting: one frames it around sign language inputs and the generation or alignment of textual outputs, another around understanding and effectively using spoken language, and another around systematic handling of morphological, syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic phenomena, sometimes as knowledge embedded within or intrinsically represented in the model.

Space of facets. When papers break the construct down, they do so mainly by linguistic level. One account names lexical knowledge, syntax, and semantic coherence, another extends the range to morphology, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics, and the sign-language-oriented usage ties the construct to gloss and text data as a way to inject linguistic knowledge into a pre-trained model. No papers link it to any other named construct.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is sparse: papers link linguistic knowledge to one measurement instrument, BLiMP, and to no beha

nodes.name: Linguistic quality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage describes linguistic quality as output quality: generated text should be fluent, coherent, natural, clear, and free of grammatical or spelling errors. Several definitions add related cues such as being logical, smooth, easy to understand, stylistically appropriate, rich in vocabulary, or free of repetition and inconsistency. A smaller group of definitions narrows the construct to grammaticality or syntactic correctness, and one definition treats it as a latent model property reflected in the richness, coherence, and complexity of word transition graphs.

Space of facets. Papers mostly unpack the construct into facets such as clarity, fluency, naturalness, coherence, grammatical correctness, spelling or punctuation, stylistic appropriateness, structural completeness, and the absence of repetition or inconsistency. Across papers, overlapping labels are used for closely related notions, including linguistic quality, linguistic correctness, linguistic coherence, language quality, and grammaticality. The broader labels usually combine several of these facets, while narrower labels isolate grammar-focused evaluation; one paper als

nodes.name: Linguistic similarity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat this construct as cross-lingual similarity inside a model: either the extent to which the model uses shared internal representations and parameters across languages, or the extent to which languages occupy similar positions in the model's internal neural space, inferred from overlapping neuron activations. A smaller line of work defines it instead as relatedness between languages based on script, vocabulary, and grammatical structures, and uses that framing to discuss shared weaknesses across languages. The main disagreement is whether linguistic similarity is anchored in model-internal sharing and overlap, or in language-level similarity described through external linguistic features.

Space of facets. Within the model-internal framing, papers break it down by where similarity appears: one usage focuses on layer-wise inter-language activation similarity, while another quantifies an 'internal linguistic spectrum' from overlapping neurons and computes similarity between language pairs as a measure of language distance. Papers also use nearby labels for closely related ideas, with 'cross-lingual sharing' referring to the use of shared

nodes.name: Linguistic style
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of a model to use language in ways that resemble human conversational wording and discourse patterns.

nodes.name: Local coherence
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to generate text that is logical and consistent within a small, local window of tokens.

nodes.name: Local reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to infer answers from localized chart evidence and chart-specific cues rather than relying on superficial pattern matching.

nodes.name: Localization ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats localization ability as a latent model capacity for accurate spatial localization in visual content: identifying where a target instance or object is, and in one definition, also determining its boundaries. There is little definitional disagreement: both definitions describe a property of the model rather than an observable behavior, and both anchor it in accurate position specification within images or visual content.

Space of facets. Papers do not break the construct into named subtypes. The main naming variation is between "localization capability" and "localization ability," which are used for the same latent property, and one paper contrasts this ability with specific perception models such as SAM in open-ended object detection and segmentation, describing failures as missing objects or producing wrong localization results.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is benchmark-oriented: localization ability is linked to one measurement instrument, MMLongBench-Doc, and two behavioral indicators, Referring expression understanding and Open-vocabulary object detection. Papers use the REC task to evaluate local

nodes.name: Log-likelihood collapse
nodes.definition: The rapid decrease of the log-probabilities assigned to both preferred and dispreferred responses from the training data, often observed in certain offline RLHF methods.

nodes.name: Logical consistency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats logical consistency as internal coherence and absence of contradiction in a model's output or reasoning, often described as logically structured across steps and free of logical errors. Papers use this framing for responses, explanations, dialogues, summaries, programs, and long-form or spoken reasoning, and one evaluation framework adds general applicability during step-by-step reasoning. A smaller line of work defines it more narrowly as adherence to logical relations across paired or decomposed items, such as a statement and its negation, beliefs over related claims, or atomic sub-problems constrained by an overall NLI prediction, while a few papers tie it to conclusions following from premises, invariant decisions across equivalent representations, adherence to domain rules, or human-like operational logic.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby names for closely related ideas, including logical robustness, logical coherence, solution consistency, logicality, and reasoning coherence, while one paper uses a plausibility label for sub-queries. In one framework, logical robustness is a fine-grained sk

nodes.name: Logical correctness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, logical correctness is treated mainly as a property of steps within a reasoning process. The clearest formulation, in MiCEval: Unveiling Multimodal Chain of Thought's Quality via Image Description and Reasoning Steps, defines it as whether a reasoning step is logically deduced from the facts and previous steps, without contradiction, and describes correctness as each step being generated from previously valid information. Another paper uses a broader framing, applying logical correctness to candidate actions, steps, or solutions and describing it in terms of logical feasibility and appropriateness within a reasoning or agentic process.

Space of facets. The papers keep the construct close to step-level or candidate-level evaluation rather than breaking it into named subtypes. In MiCEval, "correctness" is one of the labels collected for reasoning steps. In From Generation to Judgment: Opportunities and Challenges of LLM-as-a-judge, the related activity is described as "logical assessment" of candidate actions or steps, including settings such as API selection, tool using, and LLM routing.

Space of measurement. It is linked to no measurement

nodes.name: Logical reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats logical reasoning as a latent model ability to derive valid conclusions from premises, rules, facts, or constraints by applying formal logic, often through multi-step deduction. Many definitions stay close to this premise-to-conclusion framing, including deduction from rulebases, first-order logic formulas, or natural-language premises, and some papers make the operation explicit with examples such as inferring an equivalent statement like "B is A" from "A is B". A smaller line of work broadens the construct to include inductive or abductive inference, critical thinking and robustness, contradiction detection and internal consistency, or recognition of abstract token patterns, so the main disagreement is between a narrow formal-deductive ability and a broader family of reasoning or coherence abilities, and between latent capacity and observable task performance.

Space of facets. Papers most often systematize the construct into reasoning subtypes rather than a single undifferentiated skill. Several explicitly place deductive, inductive, abductive, and analogical reasoning under logical reasoning, while othe

nodes.name: Logical soundness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the shared core is adherence to valid reasoning, but the scope varies. One line treats it as a model ability in argument generation: producing arguments free from reasoning errors, following valid logical structures, and, in the same paper's logical alignment phrasing, staying aligned with valid reasoning principles as well as the given topic and stance; that study also describes steering models toward 'logically sound arguments' and reporting 'lower fallacy-rates.' Other papers use the nearby label logical correctness for judgments of candidate actions, solutions, or individual reasoning steps, defining these as logically feasible or as deduced from facts and previous steps without contradiction.

Space of facets. The papers organize this area through nearby labels rather than one shared scheme. In argument generation work, logical soundness and logical alignment are treated as closely linked formulations of the same target, whereas other work uses logical correctness for assessing actions or reasoning steps. A recurring distinction is therefore between argument-level alignment to topic and stance and step-level correctness relative to prio

nodes.name: Logical validity
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model's reasoning structure formally supports its conclusions through valid inference, assessed via symbolic logic transformation and inference.

nodes.name: Long context bias
nodes.definition: A model's tendency to exhibit degraded performance on time series analysis tasks as the length of the input sequence (number of tokens) increases.

nodes.name: Long-context multimodal understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this as a model ability, often explicitly a latent ability, to process and comprehend multimodal information over long contexts. Most definitions keep that broad framing but instantiate it with different inputs: interleaved video and subtitles, long documents with text and images or with text, tables, charts, and images, and extended image sequences, sometimes with an added emphasis on reasoning or question answering over those contexts. A smaller framing narrows the scope to long-context visual processing, defined as using information from many visual inputs presented simultaneously, while another paper describes the same area as long-range modeling, emphasizing coherent understanding and performance across extended multimodal sequences.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a shared formal taxonomy, but they use several overlapping labels for nearby abilities: long multimodal document comprehension, long image-sequence understanding, long-context visual processing, long-document understanding, and long-range modeling. The main organizing axis is the form of the long context, such as interleaved video-la

nodes.name: Long-context reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this construct as a latent model ability to process, integrate, and reason over information distributed across long or extended inputs, often emphasizing distant dependencies, use of non-local context, and coherent responses. Most definitions stay close to this framing, describing effective processing of extended text, long sequences, or long textual contexts. A smaller line narrows the scope to particular settings, such as extended conversation histories and long queries, very long HTML or workflow demonstrations, or claim verification over book-length texts. Another minority framing shifts from latent ability to output robustness, defining long-context inference as maintaining stable outputs as input length increases.

Space of facets. Papers more often introduce adjacent labels than a detailed subtype breakdown. "Long-context reasoning," "long-range reasoning," and "context reasoning" are used for closely related notions of modeling dependencies between distant elements and drawing inferences from long contexts, while some descriptions add facets such as logical consistency across extended steps, coherence over lon

nodes.name: Long-context understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats long-context understanding as a latent model ability to process, understand, retain, integrate, and use information across very long input sequences, often while maintaining coherence, relevance, accuracy, or task performance beyond the original context window. Many definitions make the span explicit, from long documents and multi-turn histories to contexts over 100K tokens, and some stress whole-context use, asking whether models can "fully utilize the provided information." A smaller line of work narrows the construct to particular settings or subskills, including cross-page synthesis, recall of specific facts from sparse long inputs, dialogue-history retention, or multimodal long text and video contexts.

Space of facets. Most papers use nearby labels such as long-context comprehension, long-text understanding, long-context capability, long-context modeling, and long-context processing for closely related versions of the same broad ability. More specialized labels carve out narrower facets: cross-page comprehension focuses on reasoning over evidence across pages, recall ability or long-range information access

nodes.name: Long-form text generation ability
nodes.definition: The capability to produce extended, coherent sequences of text, such as the full HTML code for a webpage.

nodes.name: Long-horizon planning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats long-horizon planning as the ability to produce, formulate, or execute extended sequences of interdependent actions to reach a complex, distant, or multi-stage goal. Many definitions add constraints such as concurrent objectives, partial observability, dynamic environments, or the need to maintain coherence across many steps; one benchmark paper describes a relevant setting as combining multiple interactions, concurrent objectives, and error handling in one environment (SmartPlay : A Benchmark for LLMs as Intelligent Agents). A smaller line of work shifts the framing toward long-term or long-horizon reasoning, emphasizing coherent reasoning over multiple interaction rounds or extended action sequences, while some definitions emphasize high-level strategy adaptation over time rather than action sequencing alone.

Space of facets. Papers use several neighboring labels for overlapping formulations, including long-term planning, high-level planning, long-term reasoning, and long-horizon reasoning. The most recurrent internal structure is decomposition: definitions refer to breaking complex objectives into coordinated subt

nodes.name: Long-range dependency modeling
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage describes a model ability or capacity to capture and use dependencies among tokens, elements, or pieces of information that are far apart in a sequence. Most definitions present this same idea under labels such as modeling, capture, handling, or understanding, and some connect it specifically to long texts or long input contexts during response generation. A smaller line of work instead emphasizes special cases or narrower aspects: coordinating distant dialogue states and goals, spatial-temporal interactions in trajectories, preserving distant context for current generation, long-term memorization despite memory decay, or the degree to which earlier context influences current output.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby names for largely the same construct: long-range dependency modeling, capture, handling, understanding, and long-distance dependency capture. Within that broad label, some papers single out semantic dependencies across distant parts of a long context, dialogue dependencies such as keyword order across turns or alignment of early actions with final goals, and spatial-temporal interactions over extended

nodes.name: Long-term memory
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats long-term memory as a model's ability to retain, recall, store, and use relevant information over extended periods, interactions, or multi-step tasks. Most definitions differ mainly by setting, such as financial tasks, dialogue, or multi-session coding, and by whether they stress using retained information for consistency and coherent reasoning or recalling it despite intervening irrelevant content. A smaller variation adds that this memory has a dynamic and interconnected knowledge structure, but it still centers on storing and retrieving information over time.

Space of facets. Papers only lightly systematize the construct. One paper uses the near-variant name "long-term memory retention" for the ability to retain and recall relevant information from prior interactions, while another treats information extraction as one of several core long-term memory abilities. Some descriptions also contrast long-term memory with vector retrieval, stating that vector retrieval does not mimic the "dynamic and interconnected nature" associated with human long-term memory.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked t

nodes.name: Long video understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats long video understanding as a model ability or capacity to comprehend and reason over extended video sequences, especially their content, temporal dynamics, and information spread across long durations. Several definitions add plot, relationships, context, or retrieval and synthesis across long time spans, but stay within that same framing. A smaller line of work describes it instead as the task of processing videos much longer than short clips, often by segmenting them into shorter clips and summarizing them, so the main disagreement is between an ability framing and a task framing.

Space of facets. Papers usually place the construct as a facet of broader multi-modal or video understanding, and one paper explicitly relates it to long-context understanding. The naming varies more than the content: authors also use long video comprehension, long-video understanding, and long-range video understanding for broadly the same phenomenon. Some snippets also describe whole-video settings where models first find the relevant scenes using a hint, and one paper foregrounds target-centric understanding of long videos.

Space

nodes.name: Low-level visual perception
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to accurately respond to questions about low-level visual attributes such as distortions, color, lighting, and composition.

nodes.name: Low-test-error preference
nodes.definition: A disposition where ICL tends to select the pretraining function that minimizes test error rather than adapting to entirely new tasks.

nodes.name: Machine learning knowledge
nodes.definition: The pre-existing, latent understanding of machine learning algorithms that a model possesses from its training.

nodes.name: Manipulation
nodes.definition: A latent tendency for the model to influence users in undesirable ways rather than simply assist them.

nodes.name: Mathematical reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is a latent model ability or capability to understand and solve mathematical problems through step-by-step logical, numerical, or symbolic inference. Most definitions center on math word problems and quantitative tasks, often emphasizing arithmetic or algebraic operations, intermediate reasoning steps, and correct final answers; several explicitly narrow this to grade-school or GSM8K-style problems, and one description says solving such problems requires generating the chain of thought before the answer. Smaller lines of work narrow the construct to specific facets such as arithmetic target-expression generation, numerical reasoning from product metadata, or algebraic manipulation, while others broaden it to formal proof, optimization model formulation, applied asymptotic reasoning, visual mathematical reasoning, or an internal mathematical world-model. Most papers treat it as a latent property of the model, though some define it through observable solving behavior or through benchmark performance meant to reflect mathematical intelligence.

Space of facets. Papers divide the space into arithmetic, numerical or qu

nodes.name: Mathematical rigor
nodes.definition: The quality of a model's generated solution in terms of being logically airtight, providing justification for claims, and adhering to formal proof standards.

nodes.name: Meaningfulness
nodes.definition: The extent to which generated speech preserves grammatical correctness and coherent linguistic content.

nodes.name: Media outlet name bias
nodes.definition: A latent tendency in LLMs to alter their outputs, such as political bias predictions or summary content, based on the name of the media outlet attributed to a news article.

nodes.name: Medical knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats medical knowledge as a latent or embedded body of medicine-related information that a model possesses, including knowledge about diseases, symptoms, treatments, medications, procedures, and related principles or concepts. Several definitions describe this knowledge as encoded within the model and sometimes as something the model can apply, including in interpreting clinical texts. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to preliminary knowledge grasp, meaning memorizing and initially understanding foundational facts and definitions without complex reasoning or application. Papers also differ on whether reasoning belongs inside the construct: some definitions include procedures and reasoning in clinical domain knowledge, whereas other papers contrast medical knowledge with advanced reasoning or with practical capabilities in real-world clinical settings.

Space of facets. Papers often use nearby labels such as clinical knowledge and clinical domain knowledge for overlapping content, centered on diseases, symptoms, procedures, medications, and related concepts. One paper frames this space through clinical concepts,

nodes.name: Medical reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing treats medical reasoning as a latent or cognitive ability for complex, domain-specific reasoning and inference in medicine, usually to support analysis and diagnosis. A common narrower usage labels this diagnostic reasoning and defines it as analyzing patient information, considering differential diagnoses, and inferring an accurate or likely diagnosis from patient data, explicitly contrasted with mere factual recall or pattern matching. A smaller line of work broadens or reframes the construct as scenario-based problem solving in realistic clinical workflows, involving multi-step planning, ordering examinations, and making diagnoses, and one professional-level formulation also includes prognostic thinking and integration of visual information with specialized medical knowledge.

Space of facets. Systematizations in the papers mainly sort the construct by scope. Some authors use nearby labels, especially diagnostic reasoning, for a diagnosis-centered version, while others describe a broader professional-level form that is multi-step and may cover both diagnosis and prognosis, or place it at an "L3" scenario-based problem sol

nodes.name: Medical visual reasoning
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to integrate visual and textual information in a clinically meaningful way, enabling accurate diagnosis and report generation based on medical images.

nodes.name: Memorization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats memorization as a model property or tendency to store specific training examples or associations and later reproduce them, often as exact or near-exact text, benchmark items, or recoverable facts when prompted. A smaller line instead frames it more broadly as encoding and retaining information from context, or over long contexts, in compressed form, sometimes with explicit analogies to human memory. Another recurring framing is memorization capacity, the amount of arbitrary input-output or factual association information a model can store in its parameters without interference. Some reasoning-focused papers use memorization, recall, or statistical recall for performance that comes from retrieved training correlations rather than reasoning, so the main disagreement is between narrow regurgitation, broader storage ability, and reliance-on-recall framings.

Space of facets. When papers break the construct down, the clearest taxonomy separates recitation of highly duplicated sequences, reconstruction of inherently predictable sequences, and recollection of sequences that are neither, as in Recite, Reconstruct, Recollect:

nodes.name: Memory
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats memory as retaining, storing, and later accessing earlier information over long sequences, long contexts, or multi-step interactions. This usage appears under memory capacity, context retention, information retention, and long-context memory, and covers conversation history, earlier frames in video, prior actions, and recurrent or attention state; some papers describe memory failures as failing to retain full history or being unable to remember content across apps. A smaller line of work uses memory more narrowly for retrieving factual knowledge stored in model parameters, independent of reasoning, and one paper defines it as active retrieval and maintenance of information over short sequences. The main difference across definitions is whether memory refers to contextual history versus knowledge in parameters, and whether it is framed over long contexts or short sequences.

Space of facets. Papers subdivide the construct into nearby labels, including memory capacity, context retention, long-term context retention, information retention, and long-context memory, and several of these labels are used for much the sam

nodes.name: Memory management
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the shared core is managing prior information over time: storing, retrieving, and updating earlier experiences or user-specific information so it can be used later. One paper frames this broadly as storing, retrieving, summarizing, and updating past experiences for later decisions, and describes memory as the foundation that accumulates historical experience for other modules; another gives a narrower conversational version, emphasizing accurate storage, retrieval, update, and deletion of user-specific information across turns and topic boundaries. The main variation is scope, broader past-experience management for decision-making versus cross-turn handling of conversational information.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct into memory operations rather than formal subtypes. Storage, retrieval, and update recur across definitions, with some usages adding summarization and others adding deletion; one paper also distinguishes information mentioned minutes earlier from information many turns earlier, and another describes a memory retriever that fetches historically relevant memories from internal memory. Information retrieval is also treat

nodes.name: Meta-cultural competence
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM or AI system to recognize cultural variation, detect when it lacks knowledge about a new culture, and adapt its responses through efficient learning and interaction strategies.

nodes.name: Meta-learning
nodes.definition: The ability to learn how to perform a new task by inferring its rules from a few examples, rather than simply retrieving or copying information from the context.

nodes.name: Meta-reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats meta-reasoning as reasoning about how to reason, with emphasis on selecting and shaping a problem-solving strategy before answering. One paper describes this process as using prompts to "select, adapt, and implement an actionable reasoning structure." A smaller line of work narrows the construct to strategy selection, defined as dynamically choosing between approaches such as text-based reasoning and tool-augmented execution based on the problem.

Space of facets. Papers organize the construct around reasoning procedures before an answer is produced. In the broader framing, its facets include uncovering an "intrinsic reasoning structure" and then selecting, adapting, and implementing that structure; in the narrower framing, it appears as choosing between alternative strategies, including text-based reasoning and tool use. This leaves a broad usage of meta-reasoning alongside a narrower strategy-selection usage for part of the same process space.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is benchmark-based: meta-reasoning is linked to two measurement instruments, MR-Ben and MR-GSM8K, and to no behavioral indicators

nodes.name: Metacognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats metacognition as higher-order self-assessment or self-monitoring: models assess their own knowledge, limitations, competence, uncertainty, or reasoning, and regulate behavior accordingly, such as deciding whether to rely on internal knowledge, use tools, self-verify, abstain, or correct errors. A smaller line of work defines it more narrowly as introspection, the ability to access facts about oneself or internal representations that cannot be derived from training data alone. Other papers extend the term to broader learning processes, including applying prior insights to new tasks, predicting learning progress across goals, recognizing patterns across repeated feedback cycles, and adapting learning plans. Taken together, the main disagreement is over scope: self-knowledge about present capabilities, monitoring of ongoing reasoning and outputs, or regulation of longer-horizon learning.

Space of facets. Papers use metacognition as an umbrella that overlaps with introspection, self-awareness, self-knowledge, self-reflection, cognitive reflection, meta-reasoning, metacognitive monitoring, meta-reflection, and intrins

nodes.name: Misalignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, misalignment is not used in a single way. One framing treats it as a latent unsafe tendency in the model, a safety misalignment that can remain dormant in one setting and become exploitable in another, leading to harmful outputs; this is the usage in Durable Quantization Conditioned Misalignment Attack on Large Language Models. Another framing treats it as the model's failure to follow instructions and produce valid, actionable outputs in a domain, illustrated by broken or incomplete navigation routes and omission of initial directional guidance in TurnBack: A Geospatial Route Cognition Benchmark for Large Language Models through Reverse Route. The disagreement is therefore between a hidden model-level safety tendency and an observable task-level failure of instruction following.

Space of facets. The papers do not present a shared facet structure for the term, and instead attach it to different kinds of phenomena. In the safety-focused usage, authors specifically refer to safety misalignment and to Quantization Conditioned Misalignment, described as dormant in a full-precision model but activated post-quantization. In the route-generation u

nodes.name: Misleading chart reasoning
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to detect, interpret, and reason about visualizations that intentionally manipulate chart representations to support specific claims.

nodes.name: Modality bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is a reliance framing: most definitions describe modality bias as disproportionate dependence on one modality in multimodal inference, with models, and in one case datasets, leaning too heavily on text, vision, or another input while underusing others. A smaller line frames it through uneven capability across modalities, treating better performance on text than on figure or table questions as evidence of bias. The main disagreement is therefore whether the construct is defined by direct reliance on an input modality or by comparative performance differences across modalities.

Space of facets. Papers organize the construct around which modality dominates, with contrasts such as text versus figures and tables, vision versus text, and text versus audio or video. The naming is not fully uniform: 'multimodal bias', 'modality bias', and 'modality reliance' are used for closely overlapping usages. Some authors also extend the construct from models to datasets, describing a dataset as textually biased when many samples can be correctly classified from text alone, and no linked construct is used to nest or equate it with

nodes.name: Modality gap
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing treats modality gap as a discrepancy between source and target modalities, especially a difference in data distributions and, in some wording, underlying model architectures. In Release the Powers of Prompt Tuning: Cross-Modality Prompt Transfer, it is described as one of the gaps a source prompt must overcome across modalities and is interpreted as a distribution difference that comes from different data types. A narrower formulation appears in Understanding the Modality Gap: An Empirical Study on the Speech-Text Alignment Mechanism of Large Speech Language Models, where the term is used for a latent trait reflecting the performance disparity between speech and text inputs within the same model, arising from suboptimal alignment between modalities.

Space of facets. Systematization is limited, but the papers do separate a few uses. One paper places modality gap alongside a distinct task gap in cross-modality prompt transfer, while another instantiates the same label as GAP = Mt - Ms, the overall benchmark-score difference between text and speech inputs. Across these uses, the term is applied both to an underlyi

nodes.name: Modality imbalance
nodes.definition: A phenomenon in multimodal learning where the relative importance of and reliance on different modalities (e.g., text vs. vision) varies by task, potentially causing one modality to dominate the learning process and lead to unbalanced updates.

nodes.name: Mode-seeking behavior
nodes.definition: A property of a model's learned distribution to concentrate its probability mass on a few high-reward or high-preference outputs, rather than covering all possible responses.

nodes.name: Model collapse
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the most recurrent framing treats model collapse as degrading performance in self-consuming, self-improvement, or synthetic-data training loops. In that usage, papers describe worsening generalization, failure to improve with more data, or outputs and training data becoming increasingly deterministic and less diverse. Other papers use the term for different phenomena, including token clustering over transformer layers into a single consensus state that limits output diversity and rapid collapse during optimization under a training loss; a separate theoretical account frames the issue through the capacity to preserve "distributional fidelity" across successive generations of synthesized data. The disagreement is therefore over whether collapse is mainly a problem in recursive synthetic-data training, internal token dynamics, or optimization.

Space of facets. Papers do not use a single internal taxonomy, but they do mark distinct forms and adjacent notions. One line explicitly studies a strong form caused by synthetic data in the training corpus, while other work describes early collapse through loss of distributional tails, homogenized language,

nodes.name: Model selection ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this concept as a model's latent ability to select among candidate functions, algorithms, or function classes on the basis of the task, data, or context, sometimes with implementation of the selected function folded in. One paper describes in-context learning as automatically selecting the best pretraining functions according to downstream context, and another frames transformers as performing model selection between function class families. A smaller usage applies the same label to choosing the optimal LLM from a set of candidate models for a downstream task under resource constraints. The main disagreement is therefore whether the term refers to selection among pre-trained functions or function classes, or to selection among whole LLMs.

Space of facets. Papers systematize the construct mainly through naming and mechanisms. Algorithm selection and model selection are used for closely similar ideas when the focus is choosing among functions or function classes from context, while model selection is also used for choosing among candidate LLMs. One paper further states that the algorithm selection mechanism in

nodes.name: Model similarity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats model similarity as correspondence between two models' outputs: papers define it as statistical resemblance between output distributions, statistically similar or confusable outputs, or closeness between a fine-tuned or draft model and a reference model at the token or output-space level. In that framing, the comparison is often stated to be independent of architecture or size, and one paper notes that models from the same family output more similar distributions than models of similar size. Smaller lines of work use nearby labels for different objects: one defines representation alignment as consistency in hidden-state encoding across layers and tasks during merging, and another uses model alignment to mean adherence to safety constraints and avoidance of harmful outputs.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a single shared taxonomy, but they repeatedly distinguish the notion by what is being aligned and in what setting. The main variants are similarity between arbitrary models' output distributions, token-level alignment between draft and target models in speculative decoding, output-space alignment be

nodes.name: Modularity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats modularity as decomposition into distinct, logical, self-contained, and often reusable components, whether the object is generated code, theorem-proving skills, structured outputs, or internal LM sub-networks. A smaller line of work uses nearby labels such as module reuse, module transfer, and reusability for the tendency to reuse previously learned modules, adapt generic implementations, or transfer modules to new tasks and domains rather than regenerating task-specific solutions from scratch. The main difference is therefore between modularity as a structural property of outputs or computations and modularity as the cross-task usefulness of learned modules.

Space of facets. Papers most often organize the idea around independence, reusability, and composition: modules are described as minimally coupled, independently functional or verifiable, interchangeable, and composable into larger solutions. Several papers also blur modularity and reusability into a joint notion, for example by rating "optimally modular/ reusable programs" or by describing modular skills and lemmas that are added to a library and later retr

nodes.name: Molecular stability
nodes.definition: The degree to which generated molecular structures remain chemically stable and adhere to valency constraints.

nodes.name: Molecular understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the common thread is a latent model ability to understand molecular structures and related chemical information, whether from general molecular representations, molecular text, or 3D geometry. One broad framing describes comprehension of molecular properties, functions, and structures from representations, while another emphasizes "fine-grained chemical understanding" in molecular text, including concepts, structures, nomenclature, and numerical, structural, and semantic aspects of chemical information. A separate line specializes the construct to 3D and cross-modal molecule-text settings, describing the ability to interpret 3D molecular structures, answer questions or generate descriptions from geometry, and align structural data with natural language.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a single taxonomy, but they repeatedly subdivide the construct by modality and granularity. One line uses the neighboring labels "3D molecular understanding," "cross-modal molecular understanding," and "3D molecule-text interpretation" for abilities centered on 3D geometry, molecule-text alignment, and text generation about structure, while another trea

nodes.name: Monosemanticity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats monosemanticity as a feature-level property: a learned feature is more monosemantic when it corresponds to a single word meaning or a single coherent concept, rather than mixing multiple meanings. The shared contrast case is conflation, either of multiple meanings in context or of multiple unrelated behaviors. The small variation in wording is mainly about scope, with one framing centered on word meaning and polysemy, and another using broader language about coherent concepts and behaviors.

Space of facets. Papers mostly use the term at the level of features extracted from activations, speaking of "monosemantic features" rather than a whole-model property. In these uses, monosemanticity is contrasted with "polysemantic activations" and is examined through polysemous words, including whether systems can preserve "the semantic relationship of words" while extracting monosemantic features. Papers also tie it closely to interpretability by describing monosemantic features as interpretable features.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to monosemanticity, and no behavioral indicator is linked to

nodes.name: Moral reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats moral reasoning as a latent or cognitive ability to make judgments in ethically complex situations, especially when principles conflict and actions have consequences. Closely related definitions describe evaluating the moral and consequential implications of actions, sometimes explicitly beyond superficial rule-following, and recognizing or adhering to ethical principles when deciding what is right or wrong. A smaller line of work treats it less as a latent capability and more as an underlying process of weighing considerations such as harm, fairness, and social norms, while other papers narrow it to commonsense moral judgment, principled justification, or moral concept organization through word associations.

Space of facets. Across papers, the construct appears under related labels such as ethical reasoning, machine ethics, ethics, and morality, and the labels do not fully align on whether they refer to a latent capability, adherence in outputs, or an underlying reasoning process. Several papers organize it around trade-offs among competing moral principles or value-based frameworks, and one process-oriented account

nodes.name: Morphological knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available papers, the term does not receive a single identical formulation. One paper describes it as an underlying understanding of word formation rules, centered on decomposing derivational words into meaningful morphemes and assigning their grammatical functions. Another paper uses a neighboring framing of the model's internal representation of word structure, including affixes, tense, and pluralization. The first emphasizes derivational decomposition and functional labeling, while the second names affixes, tense, and pluralization.

Space of facets. The papers break the label into different linguistic contents. One usage focuses on constituent morphemes and their functions in derivational words; another groups affixes, tense, and pluralization under morphology, and places morphology alongside syntax, semantics, and pragmatics. One paper also describes a stage of model features as encoding morphology and basic syntax together.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The only explicit operationalization described in the papers is evaluating the ability to segment derivational w

nodes.name: Morphosyntactic competence
nodes.definition: The model's integrated ability to process and understand both morphological (word structure) and syntactic (sentence structure) information in context.

nodes.name: Motion reasoning
nodes.definition: Inferring higher-level information from a motion sequence, such as the likely identity or context of the motion.

nodes.name: Multi-chart comprehension
nodes.definition: The underlying capacity to understand, integrate, and reason over information presented across multiple semantically related charts.

nodes.name: Multi-hop reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats multi-hop reasoning as a latent ability to connect, integrate, or synthesize multiple pieces of evidence through sequential inferential steps to reach an answer, conclusion, or verification decision. Most definitions keep this broad framing across documents, passages, tables, charts, and other sources; for example, "Hybrid Graphs for Table-and-Text based Question Answering using LLMs" describes a case where a system must extract a marathon finisher from raw text and then link that result to a database to determine placement. Most papers cast it as an ability, though some describe it more behaviorally as generating inference chains, decompositions into intermediate questions and answers, or iterative retrieval steps, and a smaller line narrows it to verification-oriented relation tracing, explicit two-hop fact composition, or associative reasoning through shared entities or concepts.

Space of facets. Papers systematize the construct mainly by hop structure and evidence form. One narrower subtype is two-hop reasoning, defined as composing two factual associations into a distant relation, while other papers u

nodes.name: Multi-image reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing framing describes a latent ability to integrate information across multiple images, then answer questions or infer relations that require cross-image comparison and synthesis. Closely related definitions recast it as multi-image comprehension or understanding, emphasizing processing, integrating, and reasoning over multiple images, sometimes with interleaved text and sometimes with attention to shared or consistent elements across a group of images. Another framing calls it multi-frame integration and defines it as accumulating geometric and visual cues across non-overlapping frames to form a unified understanding of a scene, with one snippet saying models must "mentally" reconstruct the scene.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for overlapping uses: multi-image reasoning, multi-image comprehension, multi-image understanding, and, in one line of work, multi-frame integration. Within these labels, the targeted relations are variously described as spatial, temporal, or logical relationships among multiple images, while example prompts focus on similarities between images or temporal progression across them.

nodes.name: Multi-session reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to synthesize information spread across multiple sessions in order to answer questions that require aggregation or comparison.

nodes.name: Multi-step planning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage describes multi-step planning as forming or selecting an ordered sequence of actions, steps, or subgoals to reach a goal across multiple steps or an extended horizon. Most definitions agree on the ordered, goal-directed sequence, while some stress execution and future outcomes, including plans that receive high reward, and others stress decomposition into intermediate subgoals or reasoning steps before solution generation. Some definitions also label this natural planning or step-by-step planning and frame it as a latent ability to break complex problems into simpler subtasks.

Space of facets. Some authors use nearby labels, especially natural planning and step-by-step planning, for the same general idea of ordered subgoals or reasoning steps. One paper explicitly contrasts natural planning with classical AI planning and, in the recorded links, relates it to Task decomposition by defining it as decomposing an input problem into ordered intermediate subgoals. In challenge-oriented usage, it is described alongside pathfinding, logic skills, spatial navigation, rule understanding, and constraint satisfaction.

Space of measure

nodes.name: Multi-table reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a latent or general ability to integrate information across multiple related or interdependent tables and reason over it. Most definitions converge on cross-table understanding as the central idea, while a narrower framing in nvAgent: Automated Data Visualization from Natural Language via Collaborative Agent Workflow makes this concrete through correct joins, filtering conditions, and aggregations for complex queries, and other papers phrase the same ability more broadly as unified analysis or support for downstream tasks.

Space of facets. Papers do not offer a detailed taxonomy of subtypes. Instead, they use nearby labels, multi-table reasoning, cross-table comprehension, and multi-table understanding, for closely overlapping descriptions centered on integrating information from multiple tables; one paper further specifies query-oriented components such as joins, filters, and aggregations, while another explicitly pairs understanding with reasoning in multi-table tasks.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Information retrieval, through a causal
