nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to encode and utilize abstract, generalized knowledge about a user’s beliefs and preferences, derived from long-term engagement patterns.

nodes.name: Semantic multimodality
nodes.definition: The degree to which a corrupted context leads to multiple plausible predictions for masked tokens, reflecting ambiguity in the model's learned semantic representations.

nodes.name: Semantic preservation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats semantic preservation, often also called meaning preservation or semantic fidelity, as retaining the original meaning, semantic content, or core information when a text is rewritten, stylized, simplified, paraphrased, revised, or perturbed. Papers repeatedly phrase this as preserving the original meaning, ensuring minimal impact on the original semantics, or rewriting without changing the semantics. A smaller line of work applies the same idea to other objects, such as whether a selected benchmark subset retains the semantic information of the full question set, and one definition adds logical consistency with an expected answer and fidelity to the task goal.

Space of facets. Across papers, nearby labels such as meaning preservation and semantic fidelity are used for the same broad notion of preserving original semantics under transformation. The label meaning accuracy shifts the reference point from a source text to an expected answer and logical consistency. Papers also place this construct alongside other evaluation dimensions, including fluency, simplicity, conciseness, layness, coherence, grammatical

nodes.name: Semantic reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, semantic reasoning is consistently treated as a model ability, most often as understanding the meaning of language instructions and their relationship to objects and actions in an environment. Another framing treats it as latent multi-step inference over concepts not explicitly stated in text, used to connect implicit content and identify implicit targets such as "democracy." The disagreement is mainly about scope: grounded instruction meaning versus unstated textual meaning.

Space of facets. Papers do not provide a shared internal breakdown of the construct. One taxonomy places semantic as one of six subtypes inside a broader text-based reasoning category within natural language reasoning. Elsewhere, semantic reasoning is mentioned together with visual reasoning and with spatial reasoning, rather than broken into further facets.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to semantic reasoning. It is linked to 2 behavioral indicators, Referring expression understanding and Table question answering: the former is described as localizing an object from a complex textual query that requires spatial and semantic r

nodes.name: Semantic representation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats semantic representation as a model property: the ability or quality of its vector or internal representations to capture semantic meaning. Most definitions converge on high-quality text representations or embeddings that preserve meaning or semantic relationships, whether framed as "high-fidelity, contextually rich embeddings," the internal encoding of words and sentences, or the preservation of relations between words or concepts. A smaller difference in emphasis appears in whether the construct is described mainly as support for downstream tasks, as internal representational structure, or as an ability that bidirectional modeling can enhance, sometimes alongside a stated trade-off with generative performance.

Space of facets. The papers do not lay out a shared subtype system, but they use closely related labels for largely the same construct, including text representation quality, embedding capability, and semantic representational power. Across those formulations, the common thread is semantic content in representations, while some papers foreground context sensitivity or bidirectional information and others f

nodes.name: Semantic richness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available definition treats semantic richness as a property of generated captions: the degree to which they capture complex, diverse, and contextually grounded meanings rather than simple or template-like descriptions. In Learning to See through Sound: From VggCaps to Multi2Cap for Richer Automated Audio Captioning, this usage is accompanied by descriptions of longer captions, richer and more diverse vocabulary, higher readability complexity, and content descriptions framed as more complex.

Space of facets. The construct is not elaborated into named subtypes here. Instead, the available description situates semantic richness next to diversity, vocabulary richness, readability complexity, and more complex content description, rather than distinguishing explicit facets or contrasting definitions.

Space of measurement. No measurement instruments or behavioral indicators are linked to semantic richness. The available operationalization is descriptive: authors discuss semantically richer captions through longer average caption length, richer and more diverse vocabulary, higher readability complexity, and more complex content descriptions, rather than through

nodes.name: Semantic sensitivity
nodes.definition: The model's ability to differentiate between semantically contrasting instructions and generate appropriately distinct outputs, reflecting a coherent understanding of instruction meaning.

nodes.name: Semantic uncertainty
nodes.definition: The degree of uncertainty over the meaning of an LLM output, as distinct from uncertainty caused by lexical or syntactic variation.

nodes.name: Semantic understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats semantic understanding as a model capability to comprehend meaning, semantic relations, and context in language, often explicitly beyond surface lexical, syntactic, acoustic, or phonetic form. Many definitions keep this broad, while some narrow it to settings such as choosing between similar tools, grasping spoken language meaning, interpreting implicit bias, inferring function-level intent in code, or making fine-grained sense distinctions from context. A smaller line of work defines it instead through representation quality, for example whether embeddings separate sentences by meaning or preserve medically meaningful structure rather than superficial cues.

Space of facets. Paper terminology varies: semantic understanding and semantic comprehension are often used for closely related phenomena, but some authors shift attention to internal representations or to integrating acoustic, syntactic, and semantic information rather than broad language meaning. Some papers carve out narrower variants, especially semantic relationship comprehension for explicit and implicit entity links such as part-whole or hierarchy, and rec

nodes.name: Sensitivity to social status
nodes.definition: The tendency for an agent to alter responses based on perceived authority, rank, or superior identity cues.

nodes.name: Sentiment bias
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of a model to assign disproportionately positive or negative sentiment to outputs based on socio-demographic attributes of the subject, independent of the actual data.

nodes.name: Sentiment control ability
nodes.definition: The tendency of the model to express positive or negative sentiment in its generated text.

nodes.name: Sentiment preservation
nodes.definition: The degree to which a rewrite retains the original emotional tone or polarity of the source text while removing toxicity.

nodes.name: Sentiment understanding
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to understand, interpret, and classify subjective content such as opinions, emotions, and attitudes expressed in text across various dimensions including polarity, emotion, sarcasm, and stance.

nodes.name: Sequence modeling
nodes.definition: The fundamental ability of a model to process and generate representations from sequential data.

nodes.name: Sequential decision-making
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats sequential decision-making, sometimes called multi-step decision-making, as an ability or capability to select, sequence, and execute actions over multiple steps to accomplish a task or goal. Most definitions add either an interactive environment or environmental feedback, with actions depending on previous outcomes over time. A smaller line of work frames it as the task of training policies to make a series of choices over time to achieve a goal, so the main difference is whether papers describe a model capability or a problem setting.

Space of facets. Papers do not offer an elaborate subtype scheme, but they use sequential decision-making and multi-step decision-making for closely similar descriptions. The construct is commonly situated alongside planning and reasoning, including work that describes a method as integrating reasoning and acting to address sequential decision-making tasks, and it is also tied to embodied agent policies. As examples, papers place it in web navigation and in problems such as online shopping, scientific reasoning, and mathematical problem-solving, all described as requiring m

nodes.name: Sequential reasoning
nodes.definition: The latent ability to understand and reason over sequences of actions and states, maintaining coherent interpretation across multiple steps in a dynamic environment.

nodes.name: Sexual orientation bias
nodes.definition: A latent, systematic skew in the model's representations related to sexual orientation, influencing its portrayal of different relationship types and identities.

nodes.name: Short-context ability
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to perform well on tasks where the required information is contained within a short input context.

nodes.name: Shortcut learning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage describes shortcut learning as models relying on spurious or superficial correlations, or other salient but task-irrelevant features, instead of the intended task features, underlying concepts, or deeper task-relevant reasoning. Several definitions make the data-distribution aspect explicit, saying these cues are prevalent in majority training data or can support high in-distribution performance while failing on minority or out-of-distribution cases. A smaller line of work narrows the idea to mini-batch-level spurious pattern capture, and another frames it more broadly as task-specific heuristics, or different laws for each sample, rather than a unified, interpretable world model.

Space of facets. Papers largely use labels such as shortcut learning, reliance on spurious correlations, and spurious correlation capture for the same family of behavior. One paper also speaks of 'shortcut circuits' that directly influence outputs based on salient features, while another ties the construct to task-specific heuristics, coarsened state representations, and non-parsimonious representations. Across these framings, shortcut learning is

nodes.name: Sign language understanding
nodes.definition: The latent ability to interpret sign language across recognition, alignment, and translation tasks by capturing visual cues and linguistic structure.

nodes.name: Simplicity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat simplicity as the ease or understandability of simplified text, sometimes explicitly for non-experts or general audiences. Another formulation casts it as a model ability to reduce linguistic and conceptual complexity, with one paper describing the goal as reducing the domain knowledge in generated text so general audiences can still understand the core idea. A related label, layness, focuses on whether generated text is suitable and understandable for a general, non-expert audience.

Space of facets. One recurring distinction is between raw simplicity of the rewritten text and relative simplicity gain when it is compared with the input complex text. Papers also separate simplicity from neighboring criteria by rating it alongside meaning preservation and fluency, and in one setup alongside comprehensiveness, conciseness, and layness. No construct-level equivalence or nesting is reported.

Space of measurement. Papers link simplicity to 3 measurement instruments and no behavioral indicators. Human evaluation operationalizes it with 1-5 Likert ratings of simplicity or layness, LLM-as-a-judge evaluates simplified text along meaning preserva

nodes.name: Simplicity bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing framing treats simplicity bias as a tendency to favor simpler functions, strategies, or solutions over more complex alternatives. Papers agree on that core idea, but differ on what counts as simple and when the bias appears: one line describes models as favoring simpler functions like SAS earlier in training, even when these compete with more complex but ultimately more effective strategies; another casts it as Transformers learning the shortest RASP-L program consistent with the training set when multiple solutions fit it; another describes a bias toward lower-frequency functions in in-context learning when multiple functions are consistent with the examples. Definitions also differ on source: some describe the bias as the model's implicit inductive bias, while another says Transformers add no extra inductive bias of their own and instead emulate a Bayesian predictor shaped by the pretraining distribution.

Space of facets. Papers usually do not break the construct into a formal subtype system. Instead, the same label is applied to several instantiations of simplicity, including simpler learning strategies, lower-frequen

nodes.name: Simulation fidelity
nodes.definition: The capacity of an LLM to generate a large number of diverse and representative synthetic samples before its simulated distribution deviates significantly from the target population, as quantified by the selected sample size bk.

nodes.name: Situated reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to understand situations dynamically and reason with present knowledge accordingly, recognizing that cognition is inseparable from its context.

nodes.name: Situational awareness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing framing treats situational awareness as a model property centered on knowing itself and its circumstances, then using that knowledge in behavior: definitions commonly mention self-knowledge, inference about the situation, and acting on that knowledge. Closely related formulations describe perceiving and understanding operational context, or using knowledge about the model itself, its training context, and human supervisors to guide behavior, including recognizing when it is being evaluated or deployed. A smaller line of work narrows the term to dialogue scenes, defining it as perceiving environmental cues and other characters' behaviors, emotions, and intentions, while another uses it for context-sensitive weighting of uncertainty across reasoning steps so the agent stays aligned with the correct reasoning trajectory.

Space of facets. Papers most explicitly break situational awareness into self-knowledge, situational inference, and action on the basis of that knowledge. One dialogue-focused formulation instead represents it as "SA = <EP, BA, EA, IA>" formed through hierarchical perception and interpretation, without further elabo

nodes.name: Situational inference
nodes.definition: The ability to make plausible deductions about the model's present situation from cues in the prompt or context.

nodes.name: Skill retention
nodes.definition: The ability of an agent to learn how to perform a task by observing a human demonstration in a video and then applying that learned skill to complete the task efficiently.

nodes.name: Small-scale spatial cognition
nodes.definition: The ability to perceive, imagine, and mentally transform objects or shapes in two or three dimensions.

nodes.name: Social and emotional intelligence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this as an ability, or latent ability, to understand social and emotional information in interaction, especially intentions, feelings, actions, and the nuances of social context. Most definitions stay at that general level, though one paper uses a narrower, task-tied formulation: the ability to answer questions about social interactions in a way that reflects such understanding. A smaller variation also makes management part of the construct, describing socio-emotional skills as understanding and managing the social and emotional aspects of interaction.

Space of facets. The papers use closely related labels, including social and emotional intelligence, social/emotional intelligence, and socio-emotional skills. Named facets include introspection, predicting the feelings of others, and understanding other people's intentions, actions, feelings, and social context; one paper also places theory of mind alongside socio-emotional skills rather than treating it as the same term. Another paper treats it as a domain that language models do not capture well, contrasting it with physical commonsense.

Space of measurement.

nodes.name: Social bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across most papers, the prevailing usage treats social bias as a model's latent tendency or observable output pattern that reflects, amplifies, or differentially expresses societal stereotypes, prejudices, or disparate treatment across social or demographic groups. Closely related definitions describe outputs that vary with attributes such as race, gender, religion, nationality, age, or other social categories, and some state the idea more generally as attitudes, beliefs, or behaviors that favor or disfavor groups by category membership. A smaller line of work defines it through other reference standards, including preference for stereotypical over anti-stereotypical sentences, disparate subgroup performance, deviation from a desired distribution, or narrower variants such as user name bias, judge-specific diversity bias, omnivore bias, and bias and discrimination in judicial decision-making.

Space of facets. Papers often use the labels social bias, societal bias, demographic bias, and bias for overlapping group-based phenomena, while narrower names such as user name bias, diversity bias, and omnivore bias mark specific settings. One paper organizes social bi

nodes.name: Social competence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the shared framing is a latent social ability in language or dialogue, but papers do not converge on a single emphasis. One usage centers on whether a conversational agent responds appropriately in social interaction and avoids socially deficient replies; another treats the construct as the ability to handle socially grounded judgments or commonsense social situations in language tasks; a third focuses on recognizing subtle, implicit social cues, intentions, and implications beyond the literal text. The main variation is whether the construct is framed as appropriateness of produced responses, performance on socially grounded judgments, or interpretation of implicit social meaning.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a common subtype scheme. Instead, they use several neighboring labels, social competence, social awareness, and social understanding, with each label foregrounding a different aspect: appropriate response behavior in interaction, handling socially grounded or commonsense social situations, and interpreting implicit cues such as intentions and implications. One paper also places deficiencies in social competence within a

nodes.name: Social intelligence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats social intelligence as a latent capacity or ability to understand and navigate complex social situations and interactions. Most definitions add some combination of inferring others' goals or mental states, pursuing social goals, adhering to norms or social rules, maintaining relationships, or responding appropriately to others' emotions, intentions, and behaviors. A smaller line of work narrows the term to human-like role enactment and realistic collaboration, while another frames it as making effective decisions and optimizing outcomes through interaction in cooperative contexts; the main disagreement is between a broad social-navigation ability and more task-facing formulations centered on collaboration or cooperative decision-making.

Space of facets. Papers mostly describe multiple facets rather than fixed subtypes. Recurrent facets include social-goal pursuit, inferring or safeguarding private information, goal completion together with information or implicit reasoning, norm adherence, relationship maintenance, and sensitivity to others' emotions, intentions, and behaviors. Several papers place other constructs b

nodes.name: Social reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage frames social reasoning around using social cues and context to reason about human behavior. The most common formulation describes the ability to interpret human events, norms, cues, and contexts, especially in visual narratives, and accompanying descriptions stress human norms, conflicting feelings, and subtle cues tied to cultural backgrounds. A smaller framing treats it as a latent model ability to draw on identity cues and interaction dynamics to anticipate and respond to group-level social behaviors, such as leader selection and peer evaluation. The main disagreement is about scope and setting: interpretation of socially loaded narratives versus anticipation of collective behavior.

Space of facets. Papers mainly organize the construct through nearby social cognition concepts rather than a detailed subtype scheme. One paper presents this form of reasoning as a core competency of social intelligence, while another connects it to competencies relevant to theory of mind, specifically interpreting the goals and beliefs of characters.

Space of measurement. Papers operationalize social reasoning with 3 linked measur

nodes.name: Social relation reasoning
nodes.definition: The higher-level cognitive ability to infer the nature of relationships, such as friends, family, or colleagues, between individuals based on contextual and visual cues.

nodes.name: Social vision
nodes.definition: The ability to perceive and understand dynamic scenes involving complex, higher-order phenomena like multi-agent social interactions.

nodes.name: Software engineering ability
nodes.definition: The capability to work effectively on repository-level programming tasks such as debugging, code editing, and implementing fixes in existing software systems.

nodes.name: Soundness
nodes.definition: The logical consistency and clarity of a generated ablation study design, such that it is free of internal contradictions and can be clearly understood and replicated by human researchers.

nodes.name: Source credibility assessment
nodes.definition: The latent capacity to evaluate the trustworthiness and credibility of information sources cited in a claim or argument.

nodes.name: Source credibility assessment ability
nodes.definition: The latent capacity to evaluate the trustworthiness and credibility of information sources cited in a claim or argument.

nodes.name: Spatial imagination
nodes.definition: The latent ability to imagine the outcomes of spatial transformations or manipulate spatial relationships mentally.

nodes.name: Spatial language understanding
nodes.definition: The model's ability to interpret the meaning of natural language expressions that describe spatial relations.

nodes.name: Spatial navigation ability
nodes.definition: The ability to efficiently move within a spatial environment to reach a target location.

nodes.name: Spatial perception
nodes.definition: A specific facet of perception involving the ability to understand and describe the spatial relationships between objects in an image.

nodes.name: Spatial reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats the term as a broad ability to understand, infer, and navigate spatial relationships, positions, and layouts in 2D or 3D settings, often from visual inputs, language prompts, or both. Many definitions emphasize directions, relative position, object size or other attributes, topological structure, and navigation, and some snippets describe it through questions like where a model is, what it will see, or whether one object is to the left of another. Smaller lines of work broaden the construct into spatial cognition or spatial intelligence, adding perception, mental representation, interaction, and action in space and time, while others narrow it to spatial localization, directional reasoning, a yes or no spatial relation inference task, or an a priori Euclidean spatiality. The main variation is therefore between a broad latent ability and narrower subskills or tasks, and between reasoning alone versus broader perception, representation, and action.

Space of facets. Papers systematize the area in several ways. One line divides the broader notion into large-scale and small-scale spatial cognition, while another separ

nodes.name: Spatial speech understanding
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to process and comprehend spoken language in conjunction with its spatial origins, such as the direction of the speaker.

nodes.name: Spatial understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats spatial understanding, often under closely related labels such as spatial awareness or spatial relationship understanding, as a latent ability to perceive, interpret, and reason about the arrangement, positions, and relations of objects in images or visual scenes. Many definitions stay close to this object-in-scene formulation, sometimes adding fine-grained relations, transformations, or grounding in embodied scenes. Smaller lines of work extend the term to positional sequences in structured lists, the connectivity and continuity of road networks, overall structure and spatially distributed findings in medical images, layout or self-positioning in 3D environments, or directional context from audio inputs.

Space of facets. Papers use several labels for overlapping ideas, including spatial awareness, spatial understanding, spatial comprehension, spatial structure understanding, and spatial relationship understanding. Within this family, some papers single out facets such as relative position, arrangement, grounding, transformations, connectivity and continuity, or position and orientation; others place spati

nodes.name: Spatial visualization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The papers treat spatial visualization as an ability centered on mentally manipulating and transforming 2D or 3D stimuli and complex spatial configurations. The wording is consistent across the available definition and snippet, including the phrase "the ability to mentally manipulate 2D or 3D stimuli" in Does Spatial Cognition Emerge in Frontier Models, and no alternative framing is introduced.

Space of facets. Systematization is limited, but one paper places spatial visualization among the skills evaluated in small-scale tasks. In that usage, it appears alongside spatial orientation, spatial perception, selective spatial attention, and visuospatial working memory, in tasks that require understanding space at the level of objects or object arrangements.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is sparse. No measurement instrument and no behavioral indicator are linked to spatial visualization, although one source snippet refers to an unnamed task simply as "a test of spatial visualization," without specifying a particular instrument.

Links. The only reported construct link is that spatial visualization is related to small-scale spatial cognition. The suppor

nodes.name: Spatiotemporal consistency
nodes.definition: The quality of generated instructions being logically sound and correct with respect to the physical arrangement and temporal ordering of assembly steps.

nodes.name: Spatiotemporal rationality
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to generate travel plans that are logical and practical in terms of both spatial routes and temporal schedules.

nodes.name: Spatiotemporal reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats spatiotemporal reasoning as a latent ability to reason about or understand spatial relationships or layout together with temporal change, dynamics, order, or constraints, most often within video content. Many definitions stay close to object relations and their changes over time, while others emphasize movement, positioning and directional change, fine-grained temporal extents, or making inferences from spatial layout and temporal dynamics. A smaller line of work broadens the scope to images, videos, and 3D scenes, or recasts the construct as awareness of a model's own movement history, a mental model of a changing environment, or correct representation of world state and action order in physical assembly.

Space of facets. Across papers, the construct is differentiated by what is tracked across space and time: spatial relationships or layout, temporal order or temporal structure, movement and directional change, object locations and temporal extents across frames, and the updating of world or environment state. The naming is varied, with nearby labels such as spatial-temporal awareness, spatial-temporal understan

nodes.name: Specialization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, specialization is not used in one consistent way. Some authors describe a process in which models within a multiagent system develop distinct functionalities or expertise through targeted finetuning, such as generation versus critique. Other papers use the same term for narrow target-domain strength, for high performance on held-in tasks through correct expert retrieval and use, or for concentration on a few skills at the expense of others while optimizing an evaluation metric; papers variously frame it as a process, a latent tendency, an ability, or a pattern of uneven skill development.

Space of facets. Papers organize the idea along different units and objectives rather than a common subtype scheme. One line of work specializes different models into roles within an output generation procedure, including critic agents; another centers specialization on a few topics or target sets; another ties it to expert modules and held-in tasks; and the skill-specialization usage treats it as uneven competency across skills. The same name is therefore applied to several usages, and the only explicit contrast elsewhere is with generalization.

Space of mea

nodes.name: Specificity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats specificity as a response-level quality: answers should be concrete, detailed, precise, and targeted to the question, rather than vague or general. Within that shared framing, some definitions emphasize referring to facts and details, others stress directly addressing the specific issues raised, and the legal variant adds logically structured answers tailored to the relevant facts and rules. A smaller line of work uses the same term differently, defining specificity for abstention as not refusing questions about sibling or ancestor concepts, so the main disagreement is whether specificity concerns answer content or the scope of refusal.

Space of facets. One named variant is logical specificity, which narrows the common answer-focused meaning by adding logical structure and legal tailoring. Elsewhere, specificity appears as one evaluation criterion alongside evidence support, comprehensiveness, relevance, and factuality. The clearest terminological split is that the same label, specificity, is used both for detailed targeted responses and for selective non-refusal in abstention settings, and one abstention

nodes.name: Speech quality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available usage, speech quality is described as the perceptual quality of synthesized speech output, with naturalness, clarity, and absence of artifacts named as its main aspects. The same paper also treats it as a performance dimension alongside conversational abilities, and no competing definition appears.

Space of facets. The only explicit breakdown treats naturalness, clarity, and absence of artifacts as the facets of the construct. Beyond those aspects, the paper does not introduce subtypes, broader taxonomies, or contrasts with nearby constructs.

Space of measurement. Papers link speech quality to no measurement instruments, one behavioral indicator, and no constructs. In operational use, the only paper measures it by computing VisQOL and MOSNet on reconstructed speech, explicitly targeting the reconstructed speech output.

Links. One paper claims a causal relationship from Speech enhancement to Speech quality, describing speech enhancement as aiming to improve the intelligibility and quality of speech when degradation is caused by various noises.

nodes.name: Speech suitability
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model's output is appropriate for spoken delivery, encompassing naturalness, conciseness, and ease of comprehension when heard rather than read.

nodes.name: Speech-text alignment
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to form coherent and consistent representations across speech and text modalities, enabling robust cross-modal understanding and performance.

nodes.name: Speech understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats speech understanding as a latent model ability to interpret the semantic content of spoken language in audio: understanding words, phrases, context, and semantic meaning from speech, sometimes including following spoken instructions. One paper states that it focuses on "the interpretation of the semantic content within the audio," and another uses the closely aligned label linguistic comprehension for understanding spoken language well enough to answer questions correctly. A smaller line of work uses a broader scope, defining it as extracting both linguistic and paralinguistic information, including speaker attributes and acoustic features.

Space of facets. Papers organize the concept in a few different ways. One benchmark places speech understanding alongside audio scene understanding and voice understanding (paralinguistic), which treats paralinguistic content as separate, while another paper folds paralinguistic information into speech understanding itself. At the task level, papers connect it to speech recognition and spoken question answering, and some authors use the alternate label linguistic compre

nodes.name: Spurious correlation detection ability
nodes.definition: The latent ability to identify non-causal, dataset-specific patterns that appear predictive but do not reflect true semantic relationships.

nodes.name: Spurious correlations
nodes.definition: Input-output regularities that fit the observed data but arise from sampling noise rather than the underlying ground truth.

nodes.name: Stability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions frame stability as consistency or robustness under change, but papers disagree on what should remain stable and under which variation. Some define it as a latent property of prediction robustness at a given input, with high local neighborhood confidence and low variability in embedding space, while others define it as consistent performance near an optimal retrieval depth, or as consistent high-quality generations for the same input, quantified by variance in reward scores. A smaller line of work uses stability for controlled training dynamics that avoid collapse, for decoding algorithms whose output probabilities change only in bounded ways under logit perturbations, for performance retained across training rounds and languages, for robustness of concepts or explanations to input or concept-set perturbations, and for preserving knowledge or overall capabilities during self-training or knowledge editing.

Space of facets. Papers introduce named subtypes such as local stability, inference stability, and training stability. Beyond these labels, the concept is applied to several levels: predictions at a single input, model performance over retrie

nodes.name: State tracking ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats state tracking ability as a latent capacity to maintain and update an internal representation of state as inputs, updates, or operations unfold. This common framing appears in definitions centered on an evolving world state, a system's state from observed updates, or an internal state for sequential operations. A smaller line of work uses narrower, task-bound versions: maintaining the complete final set of fluents after actions, inferring which fluents remain valid, tracking task progress and partner actions, keeping a running quantity, reusing intermediate results over long computations, or tracking past actions. The main disagreement is therefore between a broad internal-state ability and more specific observable or task-level tracking behaviors.

Space of facets. Papers mainly organize the construct through named subcases and adjacent labels. One recurring distinction is between fluent tracking, which asks which properties remain valid after a sequence of actions, and a broader state tracking category that queries the complete set of final-state fluents, and one paper explicitly says the latter extends the former.

nodes.name: Statistical reasoning
nodes.definition: The proficiency in performing quantitative synthesis, including aggregation, distributional analysis, and correlation analysis, using information from multiple documents.

nodes.name: Stereotype susceptibility
nodes.definition: The degree to which an LLM's latent user representations are influenced by socio-demographic stereotypes present in conversation topics, leading to biased inferences about user identity.

nodes.name: Stereotyping
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats stereotyping as model behavior that reproduces or endorses oversimplified, inaccurate, or potentially negative generalizations about people, usually keyed to demographic attributes. Much of the work narrows this to gender, describing tendencies to assign roles, traits, or expected behavior by gender, and many of those papers further focus on occupation-gender associations, such as consistently linking professions with specific genders when cues are ambiguous. A smaller line of work shifts from observable output tendencies to latent bias or reasoning, describing the model as preferentially selecting stereotype-aligned responses; some broader fairness definitions also extend beyond gender to ethnicity, religion, or socioeconomic status. One paper further frames the behavior as responses guided by stereotypical gender roles rather than culturally appropriate norms.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct into several nearby forms, including gender stereotypical bias, stereotypes, stereotypical bias, stereotypical association, stereotypical reasoning, and gender-occupation or occupational gender bias. The narrowest v

nodes.name: Storyline consistency
nodes.definition: The degree to which the simulated conversation maintains alignment with the original dialogue in terms of character reactions, emotions, attitudes, and behavioral trajectories.

nodes.name: Strategic behavior
nodes.definition: The underlying approach and pattern of tactics an agent employs to navigate a conflict and achieve its goals, as a dimension of behavioral alignment.

nodes.name: Strategic communication
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available usage, strategic communication is framed as a latent ability to use natural language effectively for persuasion, deception, coordination, and information sharing in strategic interactions. The same paper places it in free-form conversation used to achieve agreements and perform strategic deceptions, and illustrates it with a voting coordination strategy in which a Seer asks Villagers to vote for a strongly suspected Werewolf.

Space of facets. The only explicit breakdown treats the construct as spanning persuasion, deception, coordination, and information sharing. The snippets further emphasize agreement seeking, strategic deception, and vote coordination, but no additional taxonomy, synonym, or contrast with other constructs is stated.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to it. The available evidence instead illustrates the construct through in-game language behavior, including free-form conversation for agreements and deception and an explicit request that Villagers coordinate their votes.

Links. One paper claims a causal relationship from strategic reasoning to strategic communication, stating

nodes.name: Strategic decision-making
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to make goal-directed choices over multiple turns that optimize long-term outcomes, particularly in interactive or game-like settings.

nodes.name: Strategic planning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats strategic planning as a latent, goal-directed capacity for long-horizon, multi-step decision making: navigating a complex space, planning ahead, weighing future consequences, and refining actions from feedback. Many definitions also stress balancing exploration and exploitation, simulating future rewards or outcomes, or reasoning about opponent actions in adversarial settings. Some authors narrow the construct to dialogue, defining it as guiding conversations through sequences of strategies or questions toward consensus, information extraction, or a target, while a smaller framing describes it as choosing among alternative reasoning paths under uncertainty. The main variation is between a broad planning ability across decision spaces and narrower dialogue-specific or reasoning-specific versions.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-overlapping names for related capacities, including strategy planning, multi-turn planning, strategic thinking, and strategic dialogue planning. Within the broad framing, recurring facets are lookahead, future consequence simulation, exploration versus exploitation, and feedback-

nodes.name: Strategic reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage frames strategic reasoning as opponent-facing, goal-directed reasoning in competitive or multi-agent settings: analyzing the situation, anticipating an opponent's actions or policies, and choosing plans or counter-strategies to achieve a goal. Some papers narrow this to longer-horizon choice, emphasizing moves that maximize long-term success rather than immediate gains, or multi-step lines that secure guaranteed future wins. A smaller line of work applies the same label to broader or more domain-specific behavior, including navigating dynamic environments under uncertainty, planning multi-step interactions that exploit policy ambiguities or edge cases, and using conflict-resolution strategies such as interests, rights, or power in ways aligned with human negotiation behavior.

Space of facets. Papers most clearly organize the construct by time horizon. One named subtype, long-term strategic reasoning, is the latent ability to find and execute multi-step strategies, such as blocking an opponent's win or creating a fork that leads to assured future wins, rather than merely reacting to immediate threats. Elsewhere, s

nodes.name: Streaming video understanding
nodes.definition: The ability to comprehend and reason about video content that is presented as a continuous, unfolding stream over time, requiring integration of information across extended temporal contexts.

nodes.name: Structural similarity
nodes.definition: The degree to which generated circuits match real circuits in their structural characteristics after synthesis.

nodes.name: Structural understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the most recurrent framing treats this construct as a latent ability to interpret structure and use relations among elements, especially in database schemas, so that natural language questions can be aligned with tables, columns, and relationships for SQL generation. One paper describes this in terms of structural alignment between a question and database elements and their relationships, and another emphasizes identifying the relevant schema subset for each question. Other papers use broader or different framings, defining it as parsing and reasoning over long structured data such as tables or JSON, or as the extent to which a model uses graph connectivity, so definitions differ in both scope and in whether the concept is an ability, a task, or a degree of utilization.

Space of facets. Within the schema-centered usage, papers organize the construct around tables, columns, relationships, and foreign keys, and they focus on linking a question to the subset of schema elements that a query actually uses. Across papers, several names are used for nearby ideas: structural understanding and schema understanding refer to the database-schema versio

nodes.name: Structure-aware reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to comprehend and reason about the layout and relationships within complex data structures, such as hierarchical or nested tables.

nodes.name: Structured reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage describes structured reasoning as organized, multi-step reasoning that follows explicit structure or constraints. Definitions commonly invoke formal dependencies in planning, step-wise decomposition into causally linked steps, graph-like integration of internal knowledge with external structured evidence, or explicit intermediate steps toward a conclusion. A smaller line of work narrows the term to non-linear tree or graph reasoning, or to generating outputs that satisfy hierarchical and temporal constraints such as valid DAGs and correct start and finish ordering.

Space of facets. Papers use both structured reasoning and structural reasoning for related ideas, and they describe it through several forms of organization rather than a single subtype. Some formulations emphasize sequential, explicit reasoning steps, including graphs of interconnected steps drawing on causality theory, while others emphasize structural CoTs with multi-chain, tree, or graph forms. Another recurring distinction is between reasoning over structured knowledge or semantically rich graphs and generating structures that themselves obey graph and t

nodes.name: Stubbornness
nodes.definition: The tendency of an LLM to persist in an incorrect stance despite valid corrective feedback, reflecting overconfidence or over-reliance on parametric knowledge.

nodes.name: Style adherence
nodes.definition: The degree to which a response matches the intended character style, tone, and child-directed wording specified by the prompt.

nodes.name: Stylistic consistency
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to preserve the source code's stylistic features—such as variable naming, code structure, and API usage—in the translated output, enhancing readability and maintainability.

nodes.name: Stylistic representation
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a language model to encode abstract, author-specific patterns such as syntax, diction, and rhetorical structure from text, independent of semantic or factual content.

nodes.name: Subjective phrase operational semantics
nodes.definition: The way a language model adjusts its output behavior when a specific subjective phrase is included in its prompt.

nodes.name: Subword compositionality
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of a model to systematically combine subword representations into a coherent word-level representation rather than relying on arbitrary or purely memorized mappings.

nodes.name: Summarization ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a latent or cognitive ability to distill longer inputs into concise summaries while preserving what is most salient or relevant. Most definitions emphasize identifying, organizing, and synthesizing salient content from extended material, whether long video, long-form narrative, conversation or execution history, or longer documents; some add quality criteria such as "high-quality, concise, and relevant" summaries, and some specify preserving events, interactions, sequences, emotional arcs, and thematic depth. A smaller difference is whether authors describe it as a "latent ability" of a model or as a "cognitive ability," but the shared focus remains summarization of long inputs.

Space of facets. The papers use the same label across several source materials rather than breaking it into named subtypes. In HourVideo: 1-Hour Video-Language Understanding, summarization appears as one task in a broader suite alongside perception, visual reasoning, and navigation; in InfiniBench: A Benchmark for Large Multi-Modal Models in Long-Form Movies and TV Shows, it is framed as more than "just factual recall," with summaries expecte

nodes.name: Summary quality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers split between two framings. One treats the construct as an overall judgment of how good a generated summary is, including informativeness and quality. Another uses an agent-centered framing: the ability to compress retrieved content into summaries that preserve salient, valid, and information-dense entities. The difference is mainly between overall summary quality and a more specific summarization ability tied to retrieved content.

Space of facets. These papers offer little shared internal taxonomy. One framing bundles informativeness into overall summary quality, while the other emphasizes preserving salient, valid, and information-dense entities when summarizing retrieved content. The labels "Summary quality" and "Summarization quality" are used for these differently scoped framings, and papers do not link the construct to other constructs as equivalent, broader, or contrasting concepts.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is narrow: papers link the construct to 1 measurement instrument and no behavioral indicators. The only linked instrument is Reddit TL;DR, used for a summarization quality task through Reddit posts from the TL;DR dataset, so

nodes.name: Superficial forgetting
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of a model to deviate from required response formats of previous tasks due to interference from the answer styles of subsequently learned tasks, without necessarily losing underlying knowledge.

nodes.name: Superposition
nodes.definition: The latent property that a model represents more features than its hidden dimensions can uniquely encode, causing features to be entangled in a non-orthogonal basis.

nodes.name: Supportiveness
nodes.definition: A dimension of conversational competence that reflects the degree to which a model's responses are perceived as empathetic, compassionate, and validating.

nodes.name: Susceptibility to misinformation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing treats this construct as a model-level tendency or disposition to accept, favor, or be influenced by false information when it is presented by a user or otherwise presented as factual. One definition centers on whether a model will "accept and incorporate false information provided by a user, even when it contradicts the model's internal knowledge," and another describes models as being influenced by "biased, misleading, or false information presented as factual," including adoption of malicious data without explicit instruction. A smaller framing names a narrower phenomenon, authority bias, where models "tend to favor the knowledge provided by the user even when it deviates from the facts," specifically over conflicting database information and because of "undue trust in the user's authority as a human."

Space of facets. The papers organize closely related behavior under different names rather than a single shared taxonomy. "Susceptibility to misinformation" is framed against the model's own knowledge, "authority bias" is framed as favoring human-provided knowledge over a database, and "persuadability" is fram

nodes.name: Sycophancy
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats sycophancy as a model tendency or latent disposition to align its responses with a user's stated or implied beliefs, preferences, opinions, or biases, often when those are incorrect, and to do so at the expense of truthfulness, accuracy, honesty, or the model's own judgment. Several papers describe it as agreeing with the user's view, matching user beliefs over truthful ones, or saying what users likely want to hear; a narrower variant applies the same pattern to tool use, where a model avoids returning "none" and selects an irrelevant tool instead. A smaller line of work uses adjacent labels rather than the same formulation: anti-sycophancy fidelity names resistance to undue deference through evidence and logical reasoning, and human preference bias names over-prioritizing human input regardless of correctness.

Space of facets. Most papers present sycophancy as a single broad behavior rather than a detailed shared taxonomy. Within that broad usage, some papers cast it as unwanted human-approval seeking, some treat it as a common type of hallucination, and one paper says it can occur at different levels without detai

nodes.name: Symbolic music reasoning
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to interpret and make logical deductions about musical concepts based on symbolic notation.

nodes.name: Symbolic reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats symbolic reasoning as a latent ability to manipulate abstract symbols, discrete patterns, or formal expressions according to rules to reach correct answers on logic-based or rule-governed problems. Some authors mark the boundary by saying a problem is symbolic when it can be grounded in a natural, well agreed-upon formal system, with examples such as mathematics, first-order logic, planning languages, date calculations, and navigation puzzles. Smaller strands use the term for narrower sequence transformations like reordering, deletion, or swapping, or for adjacent ideas such as exact programmatic operation via code generation, formal-language reasoning with SQL or Prolog, and emergent symbol processing over value-invariant variables, so the main variation is whether the term names a latent capability, a task class, or a formal reasoning approach.

Space of facets. Papers commonly place symbolic reasoning alongside arithmetic and commonsense reasoning, and some also situate it beside logical reasoning and broader evaluation categories such as language understanding or reading comprehension, so it functions as both

nodes.name: Syntactic competence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats syntactic competence as a latent ability or internalized knowledge of grammatical structure and rules. Most definitions describe representing and processing agreement, word order, sentence hierarchy, and sentence-level form, often with the practical test of distinguishing acceptable from unacceptable, or grammatical from ungrammatical, contrasts; some broaden this to syntax, the syntax-semantics interface, and morphology. Smaller strands define it more specifically as formal competence independent of meaning, grammatical abstraction over category constraints, or grammatical accuracy in L2 English agreement phenomena. Another minority framing places it in the model's internal representations, as the degree to which hidden states encode and use part-of-speech, dependency, and phrase-type information, or infers it from outputs that stay in the correct syntactic category despite semantic errors.

Space of facets. Papers often use neighboring labels interchangeably, including syntactic understanding, syntactic ability, syntactic awareness, grammatical knowledge, grammatical competence, grammatical awareness, syntactic

nodes.name: Syntactic correctness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats syntactic correctness as generated code or queries adhering to the grammatical and structural rules of a target programming language and being free of syntax errors. Most definitions frame it as a model ability or capability to produce such outputs, while a smaller variation defines it as the degree to which outputs conform to syntax and avoid linter-detected errors; language-specific descriptions mention HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, SQL clause arrangement and operator usage, and Verilog code that can be successfully compiled.

Space of facets. Papers do not divide the construct into named subtypes; instead, they apply the same idea across different programming settings, and one line of work uses the near-synonymous name syntax correctness. Rather than subdividing it, papers mostly contrast it with other properties: semantic accuracy or semantically meaningful code, logical coherence or logical structure, and, in one evaluation, functional accuracy.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead operationalize it within 2 behavioral indicators, Code generation and Text-to-SQL, and

nodes.name: System 1 thinking
nodes.definition: A cognitive mode characterized by fast, intuitive, unconscious, and automated thought processes used for straightforward tasks.

nodes.name: System 2 thinking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage frames System 2 thinking as slow, deliberate, reflective, logical, or analytical reasoning, often described as step-by-step and effortful for complex problem solving and reasoning. Most definitions stay within this core, though some narrow it to methodically examining assumptions, conditions, calculations, and logic to identify mistakes, and others emphasize revising an initial output, exploring multiple reasoning paths, or conscious evaluation rather than single-path answering. A smaller line of work broadens the term to deliberate, consistent, rule-based processing that is not swayed by incidental or superficial features.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for closely related ideas, including System-2 thinking, System 2 reasoning, slow thinking, deep thinking, and deliberate reasoning. Within that family, some authors treat self-reflection as a manifestation of the construct, while others foreground planning, exploration of alternatives, self-correction, intermediate search traces, predictive rollout search, or MCTS-style iterative search. It is also repeatedly set against fast or Syst

nodes.name: Systematic generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the cited work, the prevailing usage treats systematic generalization as applying learned knowledge to novel instances, most often phrased as solving new problem instances by composing knowledge learned from multiple smaller training examples. One paper makes the setting explicit by saying the test instances are systematically made larger than the informationally complete training instances. Other formulations keep the same core idea but describe it as applying learned abstract structures to superficially different new instances, or, in a word-learning setting, using a newly learned word consistently and flexibly across structurally different but semantically related contexts.

Space of facets. The available papers frame the construct through composition across training examples, abstraction and generalization in novel ways, and flexible transfer across different contexts. In these formulations, the same name is used for both a broad ability to handle novel instances and a narrower word-learning case, without a separate naming scheme. Length generalization is treated as related rather than synonymous.

Space of measurement. Papers do not link systematic

nodes.name: Table reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats table reasoning as a latent ability or capacity to comprehend, query, process, connect, and synthesize structured tabular data in response to natural language questions or complex queries. Many definitions add intermediate reasoning over rows, columns, and cell values, or say it involves solving questions or verification problems by extracting and manipulating information from tables through intermediate steps. A smaller line of work frames it as a task rather than a model property, describing it as answering questions or solving problems based on a given table.

Space of facets. Papers often use table reasoning, table-based reasoning, tabular reasoning, and table understanding for closely overlapping phenomena, with some definitions broadening the scope to open-domain use, multi-table settings, or tables and infoboxes, and others narrowing it to visual tables. Several papers decompose the area into narrower facets, including column-level understanding, compositional condition understanding, and table structure understanding. In the visual-table line, the construct is further organized into table detection, table stru

nodes.name: Task adaptation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the construct is used for several kinds of model adjustment rather than one settled meaning. The prevailing usages split between adaptation to a downstream task through parameter modification or structured weight changes, often with preservation of general capabilities from pretraining, and inference-time behavior adaptation through injected vectors instead of parameter updates. Smaller lines of work cast it as continual adaptation to new tasks in a sequential setting while retaining previously learned knowledge, or as adjustment of neuronal representations to capture task-specific input patterns in an orthogonal subspace. The main disagreements are whether adaptation happens through parameter updates or without them, whether it is framed at the level of behavior, weights, or neuronal representations, and whether it targets a single downstream task or a sequence of new tasks.

Space of facets. When papers unpack the construct, they usually do so by the locus or mechanism of adaptation. Some describe task-specific directions in the pre-trained weight matrix that change under fine-tuning for a task, while another decomposes task-specific represent

nodes.name: Task alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, a recurring framing describes task alignment as the model's ability to adapt its outputs to the specific constraints and goals of a new, ad-hoc task. Another distinct framing defines it as the degree to which a model's internal representations correspond to a downstream task's requirements, with one paper locating this especially in deeper or later layers. The main disagreement is therefore about whether task alignment is described at the level of outputs and task fulfillment or at the level of internal representations.

Space of facets. Papers do not present an elaborate subtype scheme, but they place the construct in different conceptual neighborhoods. One paper equates following task-specific instructions and demonstrations with in-context learning ability, explicitly relating that ability to task alignment, while another uses the term for alignment of task-specific representations toward output layers. Another paper also discusses fine-grained style and task alignment across domains such as news articles, emails, and blog posts.

Space of measurement. Papers link task alignment to no measurement instrument and no behavioral indica

nodes.name: Task decomposition ability
nodes.definition: The ability to break down a complex task into smaller, more manageable sub-tasks.

nodes.name: Task execution ability
nodes.definition: The latent ability to implement a learned task during generation, such as producing an antonym or translating a phrase, based on internal task representations.

nodes.name: Task generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats task generalization as transfer beyond seen tasks: a model, agent, policy, or method performs on unseen, new, or different tasks, often without task-specific fine-tuning or retraining and sometimes in zero-shot or few-shot settings. Many definitions make this cross-task transfer explicit, for example by asking whether training on one task can support another unseen task, or whether a system can handle tasks and prompts beyond the training distribution; some papers describe generalizing to all tasks, including unseen tasks, or to tasks not included in the fine-tuning process. Several authors state it as a latent ability, while others define it more directly through observed performance. A smaller line of work uses broader notions of generality, meaning effectiveness across varied datasets or real-world scenarios, and in that usage the property can belong to an evaluation method rather than to the model being evaluated.

Space of facets. Papers use several overlapping names, especially cross-task generalization, multi-task generalization, generalization to unseen tasks, and generality, along with several near

nodes.name: Task interference
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, task interference is most commonly treated as a latent phenomenon of performance degradation when multiple tasks are learned jointly or when task-specific models are merged, because learning signals, shared parameters, or representations conflict. Most definitions describe one task's learning as hurting another at the task level, while some authors use near-synonyms such as negative transfer or inter-task interference for the same broad pattern. A smaller line narrows the construct to parameter interference, where updates or merged parameters that help one source model or language pair degrade others. The main variation is therefore between a broad cross-task degradation framing and a narrower parameter-conflict framing.

Space of facets. Papers do not settle on a single naming scheme: alongside task interference, they also use negative transfer, inter-task interference, and, in model-merging or multilingual settings, parameter interference. Only one paper explicitly names a subtype, partial task interference, for jointly trained control and understanding tasks with overlapping representations that mutually degrade performance. One definitio

nodes.name: Task learning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats task learning as the model's ability to solve a task from in-context demonstrations by learning or inferring the input-label mapping those examples instantiate. Most definitions stay close to this framing, describing performance that is based solely on demonstrations or the ability to grasp new mappings not seen during pre-training, and contrasting it with simply copying a label or retrieving memorized patterns. A smaller terminological variant uses the name task inference and phrases the same general ability as deducing the abstract rule or underlying task from input-output examples in context.

Space of facets. Papers most often position task learning against task recognition: one line describes it as directly learning from demonstrations to deal with the task, while separately tracking task recognition. Another line uses task inference for closely related behavior, describing the model as inferring the task from context rather than merely copying a label, and explicitly relating that ability to meta-learning. The construct is also tied to in-context learning more broadly, where effective in-context learn

nodes.name: Task planning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats task planning as decomposing a high-level goal or instruction into a sequence of executable actions or skills. The wording varies between mid-level actions, low-level skills or steps, and action sequences in interactive environments, but the common focus is on producing a plan that accomplishes the goal; one paper also describes a close-loop version that adapts the plan based on real-time observations. A smaller line of work uses the related label problem decomposition for a latent system-design ability to break complex tasks into smaller, independently solvable subproblems for asymptotic computational gains.

Space of facets. The main axis of variation is what is being decomposed and at what level: papers alternately describe high-level goals, natural language instructions, and GUI objectives, with outputs framed as mid-level skills, low-level skills, or coherent low-level steps. Most papers keep the construct tied to the generated action sequence itself, whereas the problem decomposition usage shifts it toward a latent property of the system design and adds independent solvability and computational-cost

nodes.name: Task recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers describe task recognition as identifying the target or underlying task from in-context demonstrations, sometimes adding that the model then solves the task by using knowledge obtained from pre-training. One formulation says the model 'recognizes the target task from demonstrations' and uses prior knowledge from pre-training to solve it. Some authors instead define the construct as differentiating among tasks from input characteristics without explicit task labels, while another frames it as a transformer's latent ability to retrieve a high-level task concept vector from demonstration pairs. Across definitions, the shared theme is recovering task information from examples, but the emphasis varies between observable task identification and solving, unsupervised task differentiation, and latent task-vector retrieval.

Space of facets. Papers most often place it alongside task learning as a separate part of in-context learning, rather than giving a finer subtype taxonomy. One paper explicitly describes in-context learning as disentangled into task recognition and task learning. The naming is not fully uniform: papers attached to this construc

nodes.name: Task understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat task understanding as a model ability, often a latent one, to grasp what a task requires from the prompt and context, including the task's requirements, goals, intent, or structure. Some definitions state this in terms of being able to generate valid synthetic examples for transfer or to learn the inherent reasoning and structuring of task questions. A smaller line narrows it to deep-level task semantics in open-ended multimodal settings, beyond surface-level visual or linguistic features, while another paper uses a weaker version, a basic or coarse grasp of the downstream task sufficient for rough initial labels or judgments.

Space of facets. The papers use closely related names, task comprehension, task understanding, and task semantics understanding, for overlapping ideas. The clearest split is by depth and setting: most usage concerns understanding task requirements, goals, intent, and structure, whereas one formulation singles out deep-level semantics from text or video and explicitly contrasts this with surface-level visual or linguistic features. Another formulation introduces a lower-resolution variant, basic or coarse task unde

nodes.name: Teacher hacking
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of a student language model to over-optimize alignment with an imperfect teacher model at the expense of approximating the true data distribution, analogous to reward hacking in reinforcement learning.

nodes.name: Technical expertise
nodes.definition: The ability to produce correct outputs in technical domains such as coding, debugging, and software design.

nodes.name: Temporal arithmetic
nodes.definition: The ability to perform mathematical calculations involving time points and durations.

nodes.name: Temporal commonsense
nodes.definition: The model's internalized understanding of typical temporal sequences and event orderings derived from real-world experience or training data.

nodes.name: Temporal consistency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats temporal consistency, often called temporal coherence, as continuity over time in generated video: smooth progression across frames, logical flow of events and objects, and stable subjects or backgrounds without flicker or discontinuities. A smaller line of work defines it more narrowly for video segmentation outputs, as segmentation masks that remain stable and coherent across consecutive frames. One paper uses temporal coherence for text instead, describing article coherence as the logical and chronological flow of ideas across sentences and as temporal structure captured in latent representations.

Space of facets. Several papers use temporal consistency and temporal coherence for similar video-level continuity, but they apply the label to different targets. One evaluation framing separates consistency for the main subject and the background, another emphasizes logical progression and continuity across a large time range in time-lapse video, and one video object segmentation paper treats temporal consistency specifically as an output-side requirement, distinct from the input-side need to capture temporal dynamics.

nodes.name: Temporal dependency modeling
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the prevailing usage treats temporal dependency modeling as a latent modeling ability rather than an observed behavior. Papers describe it as capturing correlations and dependencies between observations at different timestamps within a time series, including with exogenous variables, or as representing the evolution of a patient's medical history over time, including progression and recurrence across visits. The shared core is modeling relationships across time, while the emphasis differs between timestamp-level dependencies in time series and visit-level evolution in patient histories.

Space of facets. The papers use closely related labels, temporal dependency modeling and temporal dynamics modeling, for a broad idea of modeling change over time. Rather than formal subtypes, the descriptions foreground different facets: one centers a temporal encoder that captures dependencies within data while accounting for exogenous variables, and another centers an evolve-and-memorize mechanism that updates patient representations by weighting historical visits by their time intervals.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is

nodes.name: Temporal generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat temporal generalization, often called temporal generalizability, as a model's ability to maintain performance when applied to future data that may shift over time. The recurring usage is performance-centered: papers describe classification performance varying over time and methods that enhance generalizability over temporal data shifts or model performance over time. A narrower formulation appears in fact-checking work, where the term is defined as accurately verifying claims that arise after a model's knowledge cutoff by relying on external evidence rather than parametric memory, so the main difference is between a broad future-data performance framing and a task-specific post-cutoff verification framing.

Space of facets. The term is used at different scopes rather than being broken into named subtypes. In one usage it refers to classification under temporal data shifts, including multilingual settings where performance varies over time across languages; in another it refers to fact-checking on later claims, tied to external evidence and described alongside real-time fact-checking. The available definitions therefore contrast a broader

nodes.name: Temporal grounding ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats temporal grounding ability as a query-conditioned video localization capability: models are described as associating a textual query, question, or instruction with the specific time segment, timestamp, or part of a video where the relevant event occurs. A closely aligned framing calls this "referring," defined as comprehending time information from user inputs and identifying which part of a video the user is referring to. A smaller line of work uses a narrower temporal localization framing, centered on "finding the sub-action frames where the differences might occur, and aligning those frames between the two videos," which shifts the scope from general event grounding to cross-video sub-action alignment.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby labels for overlapping phenomena, most often "temporal grounding" or "video temporal grounding," and less often "referring" or "temporal localization." The first two are used for the general ability to localize events in time from language, while "referring" is presented as a capability in a task taxonomy and "temporal localization" is used for the more specifi

nodes.name: Temporal perception
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, temporal perception is most commonly framed as recognizing and processing information distributed across the time dimension of a video. A narrower formulation describes it as the latent ability of a model to perceive and understand dynamic visual changes over time, especially rapid or subtle motion patterns in video sequences. The common ground is attention to temporally distributed video information, while the main difference is scope: broad time-dimension processing versus a more motion-focused account.

Space of facets. The clearest systematization groups temporal perception with chronological ordering and spatio-temporal coherence as three aspects of video understanding, rather than treating it as a synonym for either of the other two. In that usage, it is evaluated within the same benchmark framework that also includes retrieval, ordering, and counting tasks. No other constructs are linked to it.

Space of measurement. Papers link temporal perception to 1 measurement instrument and 1 behavioral indicator. The instrument is VNBench, described as a video benchmark that includes retrieval, ordering, and counting to evaluate temporal p

nodes.name: Temporal reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions.
