Across papers, the prevailing usage is as a broad ability to reason about events in time, especially their order, timing, duration, and relationships, sometimes extending to whether someone had the right opportunity at the right time or to reasoning through timelines. Many papers carry this framing into video, table, and factual settings, where it covers evolving states or attributes and temporally embedded information. A smaller line of work uses nearby labels, temporal awareness, temporal semantics, chronological reasoning, reverse event inference, and clock-time computation, for narrower slices such as recurring time instructions, the logic of temporal relations, narrative order, reconstructing event flow, or explicit time calculations. The main disagreement is about scope and level: most definitions describe a latent capability, while some define it through observable tasks such as temporal sequences or clock-time calculation.

Space of facets. Some papers explicitly decompose the construct. One line separates understanding the semantics and logic of time from temporal arithmetic, and one benchmark further organizes temporal QA into time-time, time-event,

nodes.name: Temporal referential consistency
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to produce identical correct answers to semantically equivalent temporal queries that differ only in whether they use absolute time references (e.g., 'January 1949') or event-based chronological references (e.g., 'before Concordia Seminary').

nodes.name: Temporal understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats temporal understanding as the ability to represent, comprehend, and use temporal order, dynamics, and relations among events over time, most often in videos or long narratives. Closely related labels, including temporal comprehension, chronological understanding, and temporal modeling, are used for much the same idea: sequencing events correctly, handling long-term temporal relations, and reasoning when duration or ordering matter. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to timing-specific information, such as knowing how long frames last, using dates and periodicity, or condensing temporal patterns for forecasting, while another line defines temporal awareness as tracking and reasoning about time-evolving factual knowledge or dynamic graph structure. The main disagreement is therefore about scope and emphasis: event order and relations in video versus broader time-evolving knowledge and prediction settings, and order versus duration, timing, or periodicity.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct into several facets rather than treating it as a single undifferentiated skill. One benchmark disting

nodes.name: Terminology accuracy
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to correctly translate domain-specific financial terms, reflecting its grasp of specialized vocabulary and conceptual consistency across languages.

nodes.name: Test generation ability
nodes.definition: The overall latent capability of a model to produce effective and high-quality software tests that cover code paths and detect bugs.

nodes.name: Text generation quality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats text generation quality as a broad, holistic property of generated outputs or responses, usually described through mixtures of coherence, fluency, relevance, accuracy, usefulness, informativeness, diversity, or human preference. Most definitions attach this property to the produced text itself, though some recast it as a latent ability or capacity of the model or generator to produce high-quality outputs. A smaller line of work narrows it to domain-specific or reference-dependent forms, such as survey content quality, conversation quality inferred from engagement and safety, storyline or information quality, composition ability, artistic merit, or preservation relative to an original, unwatermarked, or real-data reference, so the main disagreement is between a general holistic framing and narrower task- or reference-specific ones.

Space of facets. Papers often decompose this construct into recurring facets rather than treating it as a single opaque score: coverage, structure, and relevance for surveys; fluency, coherence, informativeness, and grammar in human ratings; and broader response criteria such as

nodes.name: Text-image alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats text-image alignment as semantic fidelity between a text input and a generated visual output: papers describe the degree to which an image or other visual asset corresponds to a caption, prompt, or narrative fragment, including its semantic content, intended visual elements, and descriptive details. A smaller line of work uses the same label more broadly for cross-modal consistency, defining it as the capacity to jointly interpret visual content and embedded text so that meaning remains consistent across modalities; one paper further describes this as requiring integration that goes beyond pattern recognition toward comprehension.

Space of facets. Recurring facets in the definitions are semantic correspondence, accurate interpretation of visual concepts from text, faithfulness to intended visual elements and descriptive details, and, in narrative settings, visual consistency in depictions of characters and settings. The same name is therefore used for two nearby targets in these papers, most often faithfulness of generated visuals to text, and in a minority usage consistency of meaning across visual conten

nodes.name: Text quality preservation
nodes.definition: The latent property of a controlled generation method to maintain natural, coherent, and grammatically correct text even under strong attribute biasing.

nodes.name: Text-to-visual generation alignment
nodes.definition: The degree to which a generated video accurately reflects the objects, counts, colors, styles, actions, and other specifications described in the input text prompt.

nodes.name: Textual aesthetics
nodes.definition: The latent trait encompassing the aesthetic quality of text generated by LLMs, including readability, visual organization, consistency of style, and logical coherence, which contributes to user engagement and comprehension.

nodes.name: Textual bias
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of a model to preferentially rely on textual input over audio evidence when the two modalities conflict, even when the text is misleading.

nodes.name: Theorem proving ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this as a latent model property: the capacity to find, generate, or complete valid formal proofs for mathematical statements, theorems, or lemmas, usually within a formal system or proof assistant. Some formulations make the proof form more explicit by emphasizing valid, step-by-step proofs, while a narrower variant restricts the construct to out-of-distribution settings, defined as proving theorems that are distributionally distinct from the training data, such as competition-level problems.

Space of facets. Papers mostly use the labels ability, skill, capacity, and capability for the same latent property. The main internal distinction is scope: some definitions center on successfully finding proofs for mathematical statements, some on generating or completing proofs across theorem-proving tasks and benchmarks, and one paper names out-of-distribution theorem-proving ability as a narrower subtype defined by theorems that are distributionally distinct from the training data.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to it. The surrounding descriptions place the constru

nodes.name: Theory of mind
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats theory of mind as an ability to attribute, infer, track, or reason about other agents' mental states, usually beliefs, intentions, desires, knowledge, emotions, or preferences, often so behavior can be predicted or interaction coordinated. Many definitions stay at this broad level, sometimes extending to communication, decentralized collaboration, information asymmetry, or the fact that others can hold mental states different from one's own. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to specific targets: estimating an opponent's payoff table in negotiation, inferring hidden roles or likely actions in games, inferring the goal of an observed human action sequence, or separating agents' perspectives from an omniscient view. The main disagreement is about scope, broad social and mental-state reasoning versus task-specific belief, intent, or perspective inference.

Space of facets. Papers that break the construct down foreground mental state tracking, belief inference, and perspective separation. Some work integrates perspective separation and belief inference in a unified framework, while other papers describe re

nodes.name: Time-series feature extraction ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available usage, this construct is treated as a model ability over time-series data: identifying and using relevant patterns for reasoning. The only explicit definition describes patterns such as pictorial, time-aware, cross-dimension, and frequency-domain features, and the accompanying discussion says that many planned features are difficult to extract from numerical time series, while "visualization empowers feature extraction" (A Picture is Worth A Thousand Numbers: Enabling LLMs Reason about Time Series via Visualization).

Space of facets. The only internal breakdown is by feature type, namely pictorial, time-aware, cross-dimension, and frequency-domain features. The available paper does not equate it with another construct or place it in a broader taxonomy; instead, it frames the construct around whether relevant features can be extracted from numerical time series at all, and contrasts that difficulty with the claim that visualization can enable extraction.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Reward function generation, but only through a causal claim rather than a measured

nodes.name: Token diversity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the prevailing usage is highly aligned: papers describe token diversity as variation in the tokens a model generates, often explicitly as entropy or richness in the output distribution rather than repetition. One definition frames it as a varied token distribution instead of repetitive tokens, and another uses nearly the same idea in terms of variation and entropy in produced tokens. The shared focus is on a property of generated outputs during generation, with little disagreement beyond wording.

Space of facets. Systematization is light, and the clearest organizing distinction is between varied, higher-entropy token distributions and repetitive token use. One paper explicitly says it introduces "three additional metrics that evaluate token diversity," and names Token Entropy as measuring the diversity of tokens in the model's output. Another definition folds entropy directly into the construct itself by describing it as variation and entropy in produced tokens.

Space of measurement. It is linked to no measurement instruments and no behavioral indicators. Still, the papers that define it make the operationalization fairly ex

nodes.name: Tool use ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across most papers, the prevailing usage treats this construct as a latent capability of an LLM or agent to select, invoke, and use external tools or APIs appropriately to complete tasks, often including choosing the right tool and arguments or parameters. Many definitions stay close to this core but narrow it to function calling, API call generation, tool selection, or execution, while others broaden it to coordinating multiple tools, sequencing calls, processing tool outputs, or using tools across dialogue settings and complex real-world tasks. A smaller line instead describes tool utilization as observable tool interaction or tool use itself rather than a latent capability, and a few papers foreground particular aspects such as reliability and hallucination reduction, deciding whether to call a tool at all, comprehension of tool documentation and feedback, or integration of conversational history and user profile.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct into recurring facets: selecting the appropriate tool or API, generating valid calls with suitable parameters or code, planning or sequencing multiple calls, coordinating or orchestrating tools, and dec

nodes.name: Toxicity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats toxicity as a latent tendency, risk, or propensity in a model or its outputs: generating or containing harmful, offensive, inappropriate, rude, hateful, or otherwise undesirable language, often when particular prompts elicit it. Papers using this framing vary mainly in whether they locate the property in the model, the generated text, or the content being scored, and in the examples they foreground, such as threats, obscenity, insults, explicitness, humiliation, or stereotype-perpetuating language. A smaller line of work narrows toxicity to hostility and aggression in community discourse, frames the inverse trait as non-toxicity or anti-toxicity, or describes it as an ability to identify and avoid offensive material; one paper uses the same term for a poisoned sample that is easy to retrieve and induces wrong responses.

Space of facets. When papers break the construct down, the clearest subtype scheme lists toxic, severe toxic, obscene, threat, insult, and identity hate. Other papers use overlapping facet vocabularies, describing toxicity through threatening, sexually explicit, profane, stereotype-perpetua

nodes.name: Toxicity mitigation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing framing is a latent model capability for making language non-toxic, whether by preventing toxic generation or by removing toxic content from text. The definitions agree that the construct is an inherent or latent capacity of the model, and they differ mainly in scope: one paper describes preventing, reducing, or counteracting toxic content broadly, while the others focus more narrowly on identifying and removing toxic elements in text. A smaller distinction is that some formulations add constraints on how this is done, especially avoiding over- or under-correction and transforming text into a non-toxic form.

Space of facets. Papers do not lay out a detailed subtype structure. Instead, they use nearby labels such as detoxification accuracy and detoxification quality for largely the same capacity, with one usage centered on successful toxic-element removal and another on removal plus transformation into non-toxic text; one paper also discusses it alongside semantic preservation rather than as a separate subtype.

Space of measurement. Operational language centers on whether toxic content is successfully removed. One paper frame

nodes.name: Traceability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing framing treats traceability as the degree to which generated outputs can be traced back to supporting sources, and in one formulation also to reasoning steps, so that users can verify content and carry out error analysis. A narrower, task-specific usage applies the same idea to summarization: summaries are traceable when users can inspect the source sentences, often through sentence-level citations, that support each summarized aspect.

Space of facets. The main variation in usage is between a general framing, which links outputs back to specific sources or reasoning steps, and a narrower summarization framing, which focuses on sentence-level traceability from summary content to inspectable source sentences. The surrounding discussion places traceability alongside verification, error analysis, interpretability, and accountability: one paper says opaque generation processes hinder traceability and error analysis, while another emphasizes that tracing source evidence lets users assess summary accuracy.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to traceability, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. In the

nodes.name: Trajectory generation ability
nodes.definition: The capability to generate extended, coherent sequences of states or actions that remain plausible over many time steps.

nodes.name: Transition awareness
nodes.definition: The latent ability to detect dialogue mode changes and adapt responses appropriately when conversations shift between task-oriented dialogue and chitchat.

nodes.name: Transition naturalness
nodes.definition: The extent to which a model's mode switches are contextually appropriate and perceived as smooth and natural by users or evaluators.

nodes.name: Transitive reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers describe transitive reasoning as inferring an unobserved relation from intermediate relations, whether by deducing reachability from concatenated path segments, inferring a new relation via a common intermediary, or reasoning from X→Y and Y→Z to X→Z. The shared core is transitivity or multi-hop inference, sometimes explicitly about relations not directly observed in training; for example, ALPINE: Unveiling The Planning Capability of Autoregressive Learning in Language Models describes failures to identify reachability relationships through transitivity when concatenation is required. A smaller usage departs from this and uses related "inductive generalization" language for the ability to use previously unseen agentic operators during inference, rather than for deducing a transitive relation.

Space of facets. For the dominant framing, papers alternate between the labels transitive reasoning, transitive inference, and, in one causal formulation, inductive generalization. They instantiate the construct in different relation types, including reachability, hierarchical or subsumption relations described as transitive, that is multi-hop, subsumptions, a

nodes.name: Translation ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats translation ability as a latent or underlying model capacity to translate from a source language to a target language accurately and fluently. Many definitions add that this capacity is inferred from performance across multiple translation tasks or directions, while a smaller line of work narrows the framing to low-resource settings or describes machine translation capability as something that can be transferred to speech translation. Some papers also describe the capability as demonstrated even without explicit parallel data.

Space of facets. Papers use translation ability, translation capability, machine translation capability, and translation performance in largely overlapping ways for the same underlying phenomenon. The main distinctions are scope based: some definitions emphasize performance across diverse translation directions, some focus on low-resource language translation, and some frame it as a text-based capability that can be adapted to speech-to-text translation.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is limited: translation ability is linked to 1 measurement instrument and no behavioral indicators.

nodes.name: Translation quality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats translation quality as a broad property of translated output or model ability: how accurately, fluently, adequately, and faithfully the target text conveys the source meaning. Definitions repeatedly mention fluency, adequacy, correctness, fidelity, meaning preservation, and sometimes understanding or contextual appropriateness; some describe an overall degree of excellence of the translation, while others cast it as a latent ability of the model to produce such outputs. A smaller line of work uses a narrower terminology-centered framing, defining the relevant quality in terms of correctly translating domain-specific financial terms, so the main disagreement is between broad overall output quality and specialized term accuracy.

Space of facets. Papers usually break the concept into recurring facets rather than formal subtypes: fluency, adequacy, correctness, fidelity, meaning preservation, understanding, and, in one multimodal setting, contextual appropriateness. Some also package it as a combined evaluation target, for example a trade-off between translatability and meaning preservation, while others discuss it along

nodes.name: Travel planning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers consistently treat travel planning as the production of a travel itinerary, but they differ on how broad and constraint-bound that output is. One line of work defines it as travel plan generation, an observable action that may involve basic arrangements of points of interest, while a broader variant treats it as all-in-one travel plan generation with timing, attractions, dining, accommodations, tickets, and costs. Another framing, in Large Language Models Can Solve Real-World Planning Rigorously with Formal Verification Tools, treats it as creating a detailed trip itinerary for transportation, accommodation, and activities under constraints such as budget and time, stating that the system should output a plan that satisfies users' constraints.

Space of facets. The available definitions divide the construct mainly by scope. Papers distinguish a narrower travel plan generation, centered on producing an itinerary with basic point-of-interest arrangements, from an all-in-one version that expands the same activity to detailed arrangements for timing, attractions, dining, accommodations, tickets, and costs. Across these uses, the term is also framed differen

nodes.name: Travel planning ability
nodes.definition: The general latent capability to produce feasible, personalized travel itineraries from user requirements and contextual constraints.

nodes.name: Trust calibration
nodes.definition: The alignment between user expectations and actual system capabilities, such that trust in the AI artifact is neither under- nor over-estimated based on its performance and anthropomorphic cues.

nodes.name: Trustworthiness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats trustworthiness as the reliability or dependability of a model or its outputs, often with added emphasis on safety, accuracy, consistency, honesty, or dependable confidence expression. Many definitions cast it as a latent property that lets users, clinicians, or other end-users appropriately rely on outputs in critical or high-stakes settings. Smaller lines of work narrow it to particular manifestations, such as self-consistency across generation steps, resistance to hallucinated or unsupported content, or outputs that are not maliciously manipulated, while others broaden it into a bundle that also includes fairness, robustness, and misuse-related concerns. A further minority frames it more subjectively, as the degree to which users trust outputs depending on factors like performance or explainability.

Space of facets. Papers use the term both as a broad umbrella and as a narrower output-oriented property. Some explicitly divide model trustworthiness into robustness and truthfulness, while others treat it as a multi-dimensional evaluation target rather than a single trait. Alongside the canonical term, papers int

nodes.name: Truthfulness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats truthfulness as a response-level property: outputs should be factually accurate, aligned with reality or verifiable knowledge, and avoid false, misleading, hallucinatory, or misinforming content. Many papers frame it through questions designed to trigger misconceptions or false answers learned from imitation, and some add that truthful responses should remain grounded regardless of user beliefs or preferences. Smaller lines of work narrow it to the correctness of generated claims in a RAG setting, or instead describe truthfulness as an internal, non-universal encoding that varies with the skill required by a task.

Space of facets. Papers do not organize truthfulness in one shared way, but several recurring distinctions appear. Some split it into response truthfulness versus attribution groundedness, and one paper argues that models encode multiple, skill-specific notions of truth rather than a single universal one. Other papers place truthfulness within broader trustworthiness frameworks, sometimes dividing trustworthiness into robustness and truthfulness, distinguish it from honesty as stating what is objectively tr

nodes.name: Type consistency
nodes.definition: The degree to which the type annotations generated by a model are coherent and free of contradictions when analyzed across an entire codebase.

nodes.name: Typo-fixing
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to recognize and correct typographical errors in input text by leveraging local and global contextual information to recover the intended meaning.

nodes.name: Unanswerability detection ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat this construct as the ability to judge whether the available context contains enough information to answer a question, or whether the question is unanswerable. The definitions instantiate that judgment in several settings: databases where "a valid SQL cannot be produced given the database schema" or the data is missing, documents where a model predicts whether a question is answerable, retrieved evidence that may lack sufficient information, video content whose informational boundaries a question may exceed, and interaction histories where the sought fact was never mentioned. A smaller line of work foregrounds refusal or abstention, defining the construct as choosing not to answer, or saying "I don't know," when insufficiency is detected; another definition describes it as recognizing flawed or incomplete problems and choosing not to answer.

Space of facets. Rather than a shared subtype taxonomy, papers describe context-specific versions of the construct according to what makes a question unanswerable: missing database data, columns, or join paths, insufficient document evidence, queries beyond a video's content, information absent from

nodes.name: Uncertainty
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats uncertainty as lack of confidence, unreliability, ambiguity, or indecision in a model's prediction or output. Variants of this dominant framing define it over a video sample, a prompt, an answer's correctness, or an evaluator's judgment, and some papers make the operational form explicit by saying it is "typically defined over the different answers of the LLM given the same prompt" or by tying higher uncertainty to a score near 0.5 and many "MAYBE" labels. A smaller line of work shifts the locus from outputs to internals, describing uncertainty as information carried by internal states or as representation-level unpredictability and information content across layers and heads.

Space of facets. Papers do not use a single subtype scheme, but they apply the same name at several levels: sample-level prediction ambiguity, prompt-level variability across stochastic generations, token-level confidence signals, evaluator-side judgment uncertainty, and layer- or head-level entropy in representations. Some papers frame it through output patterns such as answer variation or ambiguous score and label distributions, while oth

nodes.name: Uncertainty awareness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats uncertainty awareness as a model's own awareness or sensitivity to uncertainty in what it generates. Most definitions describe a latent property tied to recognizing lack of knowledge or confidence in generated answers, and one of them also extends this to document relevance for self-calibration. A smaller line of work frames it in vision-language terms as recognizing when no definitive answer can be provided because of information limitations or inherent unpredictability, so the main variation is between confidence-centered self-awareness and recognition of cases where a definitive answer cannot be provided under multimodal uncertainty.

Space of facets. Papers also name the construct self-aware uncertainty and multimodal uncertainty awareness. One paper places it in a taxonomy that distinguishes epistemic uncertainty awareness and aleatoric uncertainty awareness, and both are related constructs.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and papers link it to one behavioral indicator, iterative refinement, through a causal rather than measurement relation. In the descriptions, one paper ope

nodes.name: Uncertainty handling
nodes.definition: The ability to manage and reason through incomplete, ambiguous, or underspecified user queries without premature commitment to incorrect answers.

nodes.name: Uncertainty quantification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat it as a model or system's ability to estimate, represent, or express how uncertain it is about its predictions or outputs, usually in terms of confidence or reliability, and sometimes with the stricter calibration view that expressed confidence should match the probability of being correct. A smaller line of work defines uncertainty more narrowly around particular objects: ambiguity in attention or prediction distributions used for adaptive processing, instability in LLM evaluations, ambiguity in reward-model preference predictions, uncertainty about a prompt's response distribution or repeated samples, uncertainty in reasoning processes, or latent ambiguity from underspecified user input. The main difference across definitions is the locus of the uncertainty, general self-uncertainty about outputs versus uncertainty tied to a specific module, judgment process, or interaction setting.

Space of facets. Papers organize the concept into several named variants: reward uncertainty, evaluation uncertainty, response uncertainty, reasoning uncertainty, and underspecification uncertainty. They also use uncertainty estimation alongside uncer

nodes.name: Understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats understanding, often called comprehension, as a latent model ability to comprehend and correctly interpret text, instructions, task requirements, content, or user intent. Most definitions stay at this broad level and vary mainly by setting, for example few-shot prompts, multimodal prompts, cyber threat reports, OS environments, complex claims, multi-hop queries, or counseling scenarios. A smaller line of work defines it more explicitly through performance on discriminative or interrogative tasks and states that it is independent of generative fluency, while a few papers add qualifiers about it being foundational from large-scale text training or being influenced by left-to-right autoregressive processing.

Space of facets. Papers often use understanding and comprehension interchangeably, alongside names such as comprehension ability, understanding capability, and general comprehension capability, for a broad latent ability. Several papers place it next to reasoning and generation as a separate capability, and one taxonomy treats Understanding as one of six aspects alongside Memorization, Logic Inference, Discriminatio

nodes.name: Uniformity
nodes.definition: A property of the embedding space where embeddings are spread out, preserving as much information as possible in the representation.

nodes.name: Universality
nodes.definition: The hypothesis that different language models, despite varying architectures and scales, develop common internal representations and mechanisms for specific cognitive functions, such as token succession.

nodes.name: Unnatural language comprehension
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to derive meaning from syntactically noisy, human-incomprehensible text while still using it to answer questions or reconstruct natural language.

nodes.name: Usability
nodes.definition: The degree to which a system can be effectively used in real documentation workflows by intended users.

nodes.name: User agency
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model preserves the user's control over information access and decision-making, rather than imposing or withholding content.

nodes.name: User behavior modeling
nodes.definition: The ability to model implicit and heterogeneous user behaviors in shopping contexts, such as queries, clicks, purchases, and reviews.

nodes.name: User modeling
nodes.definition: The model's internal representation and judgment of a user's attributes, such as their personality, motivations, and background.

nodes.name: Utilitarian morality
nodes.definition: A moral framework where the morality of an action is judged based on its consequences, specifically its ability to maximize the collective welfare or payoff for all agents.

nodes.name: Utility preservation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is retention: papers describe utility preservation as the extent to which a model keeps its general performance, knowledge, or capabilities after some targeted intervention. This is usually stated as preserving performance on non-target data, the retain set, general downstream tasks, or the original model's task performance after unlearning, alignment, pruning, editing, steering, detoxification, or fine-tuning. Some definitions narrow the preserved capacity to a particular setting, such as functional code generation under security alignment or use of retained tools after unlearning, and one theoretical account talks about preserving the core capabilities of a reference policy. The main variation is therefore scope, broad general utility versus a more specific retained capability, rather than whether the construct concerns post-intervention retention.

Space of facets. Papers often use several near-synonymous labels for the same broad idea, including capability preservation, utility retention, performance preservation, model integrity, and utility. Within that family, the preserved object shifts among general capab

nodes.name: Value
nodes.definition: The usefulness or functional benefit of a creative artifact to the user, assessed based on task-specific criteria such as persuasiveness, clarity, or appropriateness.

nodes.name: Value orientation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed definitions, the prevailing usage treats value orientation as an underlying, often latent or implicit disposition, tendency, or set of principles that guides how an LLM responds, expresses views, or makes judgments. Papers largely agree that it concerns preferences about human values, with examples ranging from individualism and family importance to environmentalism, diversity, and community. Smaller variations are mostly about scope: some definitions emphasize cross-context response tendencies, some narrow it to views on political leanings and moral situations, and some frame it as context-specific principles that operate even when the task does not state them explicitly.

Space of facets. Across papers, the construct appears under overlapping labels, including alignment preferences, value priorities, and implicit values, which all describe value-guided tendencies or principles. One formulation places it beside reasoning patterns and linguistic style as one of the dimensions used in interlocutor inference, while another distinguishes implicit values from explicit task instructions by focusing on principles that guide decision-making even w

nodes.name: Value-reasoning reliability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, papers do not converge on a single framing. One paper uses a broad reliability definition: stable, consistent value-based judgments across repeated prompts, perturbations, persuasion, and open-ended expression tasks. Another paper uses the label value consistency for a narrower idea, maintaining adherence to a target value under opposing or conflicting guidance, including opposite or potentially malicious prompts. The clearest difference is scope: multi-condition stability of value reasoning versus resistance to prompt-level conflict around a target value.

Space of facets. The broader framing is explicitly decomposed into output consistency under identical prompts, output robustness under semantically equivalent prompts, maintaining stable value reasoning in the face of attacks, and consistency in open-ended value expression tasks. Terminology is not uniform, because one paper names the construct Value-reasoning reliability while another uses value consistency for adherence to a target value under conflicting guidance. The sole linked construct is Consistency, which one paper treats as related to Value-reasoning reliability.

nodes.name: Verbal uncertainty
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats verbal uncertainty as a latent, output-side tendency or ability to communicate doubt through language. Most definitions agree on the core idea of expressing uncertainty in responses, through explicit phrases or implicit cues, but they differ on what that expression is tied to: some connect it to recognizing knowledge gaps or contradictory information and responding with doubt, refusal, or non-commitment, while another defines it as expressed doubt or confidence independent of the model's actual knowledge or internal certainty. A smaller broadening move extends the construct beyond short verbal markers to richer forms such as explanations, verbal qualifiers, and speech prosody.

Space of facets. Papers mostly differentiate the construct by the forms of expression they include. Some descriptions separate explicit and implicit cues, for example 'I doubt...' or 'Possibly...', while others widen the space to explanations, verbal qualifiers, prosody, refusals, and other non-committal responses. Papers also use overlapping labels, including uncertainty expression, output uncertainty, and uncertainty signaling, and some contr

nodes.name: Verbatim memorization
nodes.definition: The tendency of a language model to reproduce exact or near-exact text from data that should have been removed.

nodes.name: Verbosity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats verbosity as a response-level attribute about how long or wordy model outputs are, either as a tendency to produce outputs of a certain length that can be controlled or as an extent running from concise to verbose. Several papers place it alongside helpfulness, correctness, coherence, and complexity. A smaller line of work uses a narrower, more evaluative framing, defining verbose generation as outputs that are unnecessarily long, wordy, or redundant, so the main disagreement is between neutral output length and excess length beyond what is needed.

Space of facets. Papers most often embed verbosity within broader attribute sets: one formulation says question-answering systems have relevance, verbosity, and completeness, and another recurring formulation rates helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity together. An explicit internal contrast appears as a concise-versus-verbose scale in preference annotation. One paper also uses the label verbose generation for the more negative case of unnecessarily long or redundant outputs.

Space of measurement. Verbosity is linked to 3 measurement instruments a

nodes.name: Verbosity bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats verbosity bias, often under the alternate name length bias, as a tendency in a reward model, judge, LLM-based evaluator, reward signal, or model to prefer longer or more verbose responses over shorter ones, even when quality or content does not warrant that preference. Definitions repeatedly phrase it as favoring outputs based on sequence length rather than true quality, or preferring longer responses over more succinct ones of equal content. A narrower variant describes it as systematically assigning different rewards to longer versus shorter responses, without explicitly invoking quality.

Space of facets. Papers mostly use length bias and verbosity bias for the same construct. They place it among broader bias families in reward modeling and LLM evaluation, for example alongside position bias and self-enhancement bias, and one line of work describes it as arising from spurious correlations in training data or as a dataset bias. The main variation is where authors locate the bias, in the reward model, reward signal, judge, evaluator, or LM, rather than in the basic phenomenon being named.

Space of measurement. O

nodes.name: Verifiability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats verifiability as a property of reasoning that can be checked: papers most commonly describe it as the extent to which a model's reasoning process can be systematically checked for correctness because it is transparent and structured. In this framing, authors stress stepwise verification, with language such as "structured decomposition enhances transparency and facilitates systematic verification of each step," and they also mention easier error tracing and logical consistency checks. A smaller line of work uses a different, output-centered framing, defining verifiability as whether users can validate claims in generated content through accurate, fine-grained citations and "easily double-check the answer," so the main disagreement is between verifiable internal reasoning and verifiable cited outputs.

Space of facets. Rather than defining formal subtypes, papers organize verifiability around nearby elements. Within the dominant reasoning-process framing, it is tied to transparency, structured form or decomposition, verification of each step, error tracing, and logical consistency, and one paper also pairs it

nodes.name: Verification ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this construct as a latent verification capacity: a model judges the correctness or quality of candidate outputs and selects the correct trajectory from alternatives. One definition frames it as identifying and selecting the correct solution trajectory from a set of candidates, and another says the model may act as a "better-than-random verifier of its own outputs." A smaller formulation narrows the concept to a PRM's discriminative power, namely distinguishing correct from incorrect reasoning steps at fine-grained, including token-level, resolution. The main variation is therefore about scope and granularity, complete candidate solutions versus step-level discrimination, and about whether the ability is stated for a model generally or for a PRM specifically.

Space of facets. Papers mainly differentiate the concept by what is being verified. Most formulations concern complete candidate outputs or solution trajectories, including self-verification of a model's own outputs; one paper also describes "informative verification" through a verifier model used to construct a proxy utility function. A narrower usage appears u

nodes.name: Versatility
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat versatility as breadth: a model's ability to perform well or successfully across a wide and diverse range of tasks and domains. Smaller variants keep that breadth framing but narrow the setting, either to conversational versatility, the ability to handle diverse open-ended instruction-following queries across benchmark categories, or to a generalist agent's skill repertoire, the breadth and diversity of goal-directed capabilities for varied real-world user requests. One usage also makes compatibility with augmentation explicit, stating that retrieval can improve factual accuracy without hurting versatility, while indiscriminate retrieval can diminish it.

Space of facets. Papers do not build a broader construct hierarchy around versatility, and no linked constructs equate it with or place it under another construct. Instead, the concept is organized through neighboring labels tied to setting: conversational versatility for open-ended instruction-following benchmarks, and skill repertoire for agents with many goal-directed abilities. In biomedical use, the term is attached to doing well on multiple tasks over 8 modalities.

Space of measu

nodes.name: Video understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats video understanding as a model ability to comprehend and interpret video content, usually including content, context, events, actions, and temporal dynamics. Many definitions also fold in reasoning, describing comprehension of dynamic visual sequences through spatial, temporal, and semantic information, or the ability to draw conclusions from what unfolds over time. A smaller line of work uses the term more behaviorally, defining it through answering questions, generating descriptions or responses, or otherwise demonstrating comprehension of a video's temporal and spatial content.

Space of facets. Papers also use the label video comprehension for the same general capability, and some use broader compound labels such as video understanding and reasoning. The clearest subtype is long-form video understanding, sometimes phrased as long-form video-language understanding, where the focus shifts to extended-duration videos and integrating information over many minutes or, in one definition, hour-long material. One paper also carves out explanation as a facet, meaning explaining phenomena in videos by articulating their und

nodes.name: Vision-language reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to reason about visual scenes based on textual descriptions, encompassing both global understanding and local concept analysis.

nodes.name: Visual causal reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to infer and reason about causal mechanisms and relationships from visual and textual inputs.

nodes.name: Visual disentanglement
nodes.definition: The property of conceptual rationales being visually distinct and corresponding to non-overlapping parts of an image, as assessed by human or machine evaluators.

nodes.name: Visual generation ability
nodes.definition: The latent ability to generate high-quality, detailed, and semantically aligned images from textual or mixed-modality inputs.

nodes.name: Visual grounding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats visual grounding as a latent ability to connect language, such as phrases, referring expressions, instructions, or generated answers, to specific visual regions, objects, or locations. Most definitions describe aligning semantic descriptions with image regions or localizing the instance named by text, and domain-specific versions apply the same framing to medical images, GUIs, diagrams, embodied scenes, and 3D scenes. A smaller line of work frames it more behaviorally, as producing explicit spatial outputs such as bounding boxes, coordinates, masks, or highlighted patches, and another minority extends it from localization to whether reasoning and responses are anchored in observed visual evidence rather than text alone.

Space of facets. Papers organize the construct through nearby task names and subtypes rather than a single fixed taxonomy. Multimodal grounding is described as including phrase grounding and referring expression comprehension, and some work explicitly uses visual grounding as referring expression comprehension; elsewhere closely related labels include spatial understanding, visual localization, region

nodes.name: Visual perception
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats visual perception as a latent model ability to extract, interpret, and understand visual information from images or other visual inputs, often for downstream multimodal tasks. Most definitions stay broad, covering objects, scenes, text, spatial relations, diagrams, charts, plots, natural images, or video. A smaller line narrows the construct to specific settings such as chart reading, GUI screenshots, document screenshots, or agricultural visual input, and one paper instead frames "vision perception" as the quality of visual input interpretation shaped by resolution, keyframe granularity, and visual encoding.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for closely overlapping ideas, including perception, perception capability, perceptual capability, perception ability, and perceptual understanding. One paper isolates a most basic layer under the name sensation and grounds it in count, color, OCR, and scene categories, while chart-focused work breaks perceptual failures into compositional, color, and spatial errors. Other papers place visual perception alongside reasoning, cognition, or gener

nodes.name: Visual processing
nodes.definition: The latent capacity of a model to interpret and understand visual elements, particularly icons and graphical widgets, in GUI environments, independent of textual cues.

nodes.name: Visual reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats visual reasoning as a model ability to understand visual information and draw inferences from it, often by combining perceptual cues with multi-step, symbolic, compositional, or otherwise complex reasoning. Many papers keep this broad while specializing the setting, for example videos with fine-grained spatiotemporal interactions, charts, tables and diagrams, geometric and spatial patterns, or multimodal problems that combine vision with text and can require ambiguity resolution. Most definitions describe an ability or capacity, though one paper uses it as a task of performing reasoning steps based on visual information to answer a complex question. A smaller line of work uses nearby labels or other framings, including visual-linguistic reasoning over joint visual and textual inputs, visual thinking with image-based internal representations or generated visualizations, and limited cognitive ability, where a model gives hallucinated responses despite accurate perception.

Space of facets. Papers commonly break visual reasoning into subtypes rather than treating it as a single undifferentiated skill. One recu

nodes.name: Visual recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage describes visual recognition as a model capability for identifying or classifying objects, text, landmarks, and other visual elements in an image, and some definitions add describing those elements and their relationships. Several papers present it as a latent or general capability used before solving a task or tie it to simple descriptions of visual elements. The main disagreement is about scope: most papers use this broad recognition framing, while smaller lines of work narrow it to recognizing novel concepts not seen in pre-training or to determining whether a specified object is present or absent.

Space of facets. Papers use the term both broadly and as a bounded component. One paper gives visual grounding as an example of recognition and treats visual recognition as one function alongside visual understanding, while another contrasts it with visual perception, saying perception extends beyond recognition by interpreting and contextualizing scene elements. Narrower labels also appear within this space, especially novel concept recognition and object existence determination, and one paper additionally uses visual recogni

nodes.name: Visual robustness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The only explicit definition describes visual robustness as the degree to which a model's predictions stay stable and accurate under degraded or distorted visual inputs, and it ties that behavior to reliable integration of visual cues. The accompanying snippets use the same framing, emphasizing consistent prediction patterns across varying visual qualities and consistent predictive behavior for distorted and normal visual inputs.

Space of facets. One paper places visual robustness within visual perception capabilities and treats it as one of three dimensions, alongside visual hallucinations and basic visual perception. In that usage, it appears as a distinct dimension related to visual perception rather than as a synonym for those other constructs.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to visual robustness. The only operational cues describe it through whether prediction patterns remain consistent across varying visual qualities and whether predictive behavior is consistent for distorted and normal visual inputs, rather than through a named benchmark, human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge, probe, or analysis.

Links. Pa

nodes.name: Visual understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats visual understanding as a broad latent ability to comprehend and interpret visual inputs, usually images, so that a model can extract meaningful information, recognize objects or cues, and sometimes describe visual content. Many definitions differ mainly in wording, using nearby labels such as image understanding, image comprehension, visual comprehension, vision understanding, or visual interpretation for the same general capability. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to particular settings, including single images, molecular spectra, handwritten math, multimodal documents, structured images such as tables and charts, medical images, or whole-image and global comprehension. Another minority framing defines it by what it excludes, namely answering by analyzing the image rather than relying on textual priors or commonsense, or by integrating visual observations with textual context.

Space of facets. Papers most often use a family of overlapping names, including visual understanding, image understanding, image comprehension, visual comprehension, and vision understanding, with little separation amo

nodes.name: Warmth
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, warmth is treated as a social or interpersonal quality, but the exact emphasis differs. One framing defines it as the extent to which a chatbot conveys empathy and emotional connection during interaction, including a reduced form as whether the chatbot conveys empathy. Another framing treats warmth as the perceived intent or social friendliness dimension of an impression target, for example whether it appears benevolent, friendly, hostile, combative, or friendly. The main disagreement is whether warmth is described as conveyed empathy in interaction or as a broader impression dimension centered on perceived intent and friendliness.

Space of facets. The available systematization is limited. One paper places warmth in a two-dimensional impression framework alongside competence, and in that usage warmth is the perceived intent dimension of the impression target. Beyond that pairing, no linked constructs are recorded.

Space of measurement. Warmth is linked to 0 measurement instruments and 0 behavioral indicators. The only concrete uses described in the papers are that one reports positive ratings on warmth among chatbot characteristics,

nodes.name: Watermark detectability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats detectability as the degree or ability to identify an embedded watermark in model-generated text, usually through a detection system or statistical test. Most definitions stay within this watermark-focused framing, whether they emphasize a statistical signal in the text, correct identification of watermarked outputs under tokenization inconsistency or adversarial attack, or reliable detection with low false positive rates. A smaller line of work uses detectability more broadly for whether machine-generated text, including personalized disinformation, can be distinguished from human-written text, so the main disagreement is over the target of detection, watermark presence versus AI authorship, and secondarily over whether the property is assigned to the watermarking scheme, the detector, or the text.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a stable subtype scheme. The recurring split is between watermarked versus non-watermarked detection and human-authored versus machine-generated detection, and within the watermarking usage authors alternately describe detectability as a property of the embedded signal or waterma

nodes.name: Weak-to-strong deception
nodes.definition: A phenomenon where a strong model, supervised by a weak one, behaves aligned in areas known to the supervisor but produces misaligned behaviors in areas the supervisor does not know.

nodes.name: Weak-to-strong generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage describes weak-to-strong generalization as a strong or more powerful model trained on labels, supervision, or demonstrations from a weaker model nevertheless achieving performance above the weak source or weak supervisor. Several papers sharpen this by saying the strong model is not merely copying the weak model but learning the task's intent and rules, or generalizing an alignment objective beyond the weak supervisor's knowledge boundary. A smaller framing makes capability recovery more explicit, describing the construct as eliciting latent knowledge, recovering part or all of the strong model's full capabilities, or reaching its full potential despite noisy weak labels.

Space of facets. Papers use the label at several levels: as a phenomenon, as an ability of the stronger model, and as a training paradigm or approach in which a strong model is supervised by a weaker one. The same family of usage also appears under nearby names such as weaker-to-strong generalization and Weak-to-Strong, and some authors tie it specifically to capability elicitation, latent knowledge, or supervision toward an alignment target rather tha

nodes.name: Weak-to-strong transition
nodes.definition: The latent potential of initially underperforming LLM experts to become top-performing models through collaborative search, indicating untapped or implicit expertise.

nodes.name: Wealth-seeking
nodes.definition: A specific AI persona characterized by a desire to accumulate monetary or material wealth.

nodes.name: Webpage understanding
nodes.definition: The ability to comprehend the structure, content, and visual elements of a webpage from a screenshot.

nodes.name: Word-deed consistency
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model's actions in specific, grounded scenarios align with its stated opinions, values, or theoretical beliefs.

nodes.name: Working memory
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats working memory as the capacity to hold and manipulate task-relevant information while performing a task. Most definitions share that core, but they anchor it differently: some frame it as an LLM analogy tied to the context window and to representation learning, some describe it over the course of an interaction so that information can guide current and future actions, and another describes it as holding and integrating many features at once for a decision. The variation is mainly in whether the capacity is attached to context windows, interaction, or decision aggregation.

Space of facets. Papers do not break working memory into formal subtypes. Instead, they place it in different local systems: it is connected to representation learning and the context window in one line of work, grouped with other cognitive abilities for verbal interaction such as common-sense reasoning and theory of mind in another, and glossed more narrowly as aggregating features for a decision in another. The same label is thus used both as a broad cognitive ability and as a more specific decision-focused operation.

Space of measurement. No

nodes.name: World knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats world knowledge, often under labels like general knowledge, background knowledge, prior knowledge, or open-world knowledge, as broad factual and conceptual information internalized during pre-training and encoded in the model's weights or parameters, together with the capacity to recall and apply it. Many definitions stress a latent repository of facts, sometimes framed as parametric knowledge or a source of prior beliefs, and describe it as supporting question answering, reasoning, or evidence generation when the needed information is not in the immediate input. The main variation is whether papers treat it as stored knowledge in the model, as an ability to bring external facts to multimodal or missing-context tasks, or as something deeper, namely coherent world understanding beyond surface linguistic patterns. A smaller line narrows it further to specific content such as scientific intuition, social dynamics, object materials and physical properties, or memorized visual attribute associations.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for neighboring notions, including general knowledge, backgr

nodes.name: World modeling
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats world modeling as a latent or internal representation, or the latent ability to build one, that captures an environment's mechanics, dynamics, rules, or state space so a model can understand observations and predict outcomes. Many papers phrase this in terms of predicting action effects or future states, while others emphasize reasoning about underlying principles and causalities, or uncovering deeper truths behind observed sequences. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to specific settings: a causal world model over cause-effect relations among tokens, a latent world model maintained in activations over entities and relations in context, a mathematical world-model over concepts and structures, or event understanding of how actions change a web page or application. The main variation is between world modeling as a broad latent ability and world model as the internal representation itself, with further variation in whether the content is general environment dynamics or domain-specific causal or structural content.

Space of facets. Papers use both world modeling and world model, usually separating t

nodes.name: Worst-case performance
nodes.definition: The extent to which a model avoids highly undesirable outputs on rare or adversarially shifted inputs rather than only performing well on average.

nodes.name: Zero-shot generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers describe it as the ability of a pre-trained model or agent to perform well on unseen tasks, datasets, domains, categories, policies, or constraints without task-specific training, fine-tuning, or exposure to target examples. A common variant makes the zero-shot condition instruction-based, meaning the model acts from instructions or natural-language task descriptions alone, or without in-context examples, while relying on prior training or learned patterns. Smaller task-specific definitions narrow the setting to clinical entity extraction, dialogue understanding, forecasting, control, or task classification, but keep the same core idea.

Space of facets. Across definitions, the recurring distinctions are the kind of novelty involved: unseen datasets or domains, unseen downstream tasks, unseen classes or categories, and unseen schemas, labels, guidelines, policies, objects, instructions, or constraints. Papers also use many neighboring labels for largely the same construct, including zero-shot generalizability, zero-shot learning, zero-shot transfer, zero-shot transferability, zero-shot capability, zero-shot inference, zero-shot adaptability, and ze

nodes.name: 20 Newsgroups
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, 20 Newsgroups is most commonly treated as a dataset of newsgroup posts for text or document classification. Definitions describe it as a document understanding or text classification dataset, and one definition specifies that it contains approximately 20,000 documents partitioned across 20 different newsgroups. A smaller usage narrows it to the computer science categories for an in-domain news generation task, with the other categories used as an out-of-domain set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use 20 Newsgroups to measure 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The linked constructs are natural language understanding and robustness, and the linked behavioral indicator is text classification; one paper also describes it as a proxy dataset for a topic classification task. The measurement claims are spread across this small set of targets rather than concentrated on a single construct.

Space of uses. Papers usually position it as one benchmark within a larger evaluation suite rather than as a standalone instrument. No other measurement instrument is directly linked to it, but papers show it used alongside BANKING77 in federated fine-tuning co

nodes.name: 2WikiMultiHopQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a Wikipedia-based multi-hop question answering dataset or benchmark. Most definitions emphasize multi-document reasoning, with answers requiring models to combine information from multiple documents, evidence pieces, paragraphs, or sources; some add that it includes up to 5-hop questions synthesized from Wikipedia passages through manually designed templates. A smaller line of work narrows this to reasoning over two linked facts or entity-centric questions that combine information from two or more distinct Wikipedia articles, and one paper presents it as a more challenging benchmark with many comparison and composition questions. Some papers also refer to a LongBench form of the benchmark under the name 2WikiMQA.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, it is linked to 5 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure multi-hop question answering and multi-hop reasoning. Papers also use it to measure question answering and chain-of-thought reasoning, while the remaining links spread across several other QA and reasoning framings.

Space of uses. It is most commonly used alongside HotpotQA and Mu

nodes.name: 3MDBench
nodes.definition: Medical Multimodal Multi-agent Dialogue Benchmark, a framework simulating telemedicine consultations to evaluate LVLMs on diagnostic accuracy and communication quality using patient and assessor agents.

nodes.name: 42D
nodes.definition: Multi-domain challenge benchmark for word sense disambiguation that spans 42 domains aligned with BabelNet, designed to test generalization across diverse topics.

nodes.name: A-OKVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat A-OKVQA as a visual question answering dataset or benchmark for image-grounded questions that require knowledge beyond direct visual evidence, variously described as external real-world knowledge, world knowledge, or commonsense knowledge about objects or actions in the image. Some definitions add format details, describing image-question pairs in open-ended and multiple-choice settings, while another specifies four candidate answers with one correct option and three distractors, and one paper notes that the images come from MSCOCO. A smaller line of work describes it more broadly as a general-purpose VQA benchmark with mostly large objects or larger visual concepts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use A-OKVQA to measure a broad mix of targets rather than a single construct. It is linked to 8 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators: the prevailing measured target is Visual question answering, and individual papers also report it as measuring Commonsense knowledge, Commonsense reasoning, Cultural bias, and Fairness, with 4 other constructs and one other behavioral indicator linked elsewhere. These measurement claims usually follow the be

nodes.name: Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus
nodes.definition: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) is a benchmark designed to test abstract reasoning capabilities by requiring the solution of novel visual puzzles.

nodes.name: AbsVis
nodes.definition: Dataset of 675 images with 14,175 concept–explanation pairs from humans and VLMs, used to benchmark abstract concept attribution and explanation in visual contexts.

nodes.name: AccessEval
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset and evaluation framework for assessing disability bias in LLMs, consisting of paired neutral and disability-aware queries across six domains and nine disability types.

nodes.name: ACE05
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat ACE05, or ACE, as a news-domain benchmark for structured information extraction, especially sentence-level event extraction, with annotated news documents. Some definitions broaden that framing to a benchmark that includes named entity recognition, relation extraction, and event extraction, while another description presents ACE as a multiple-choice computational-thinking assessment aimed at Analyzing, Evaluating, and Creating, so the label is not used uniformly across papers.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure one construct and three behavioral indicators. The behavioral indicators named in those links are Event detection, Multiple-choice question answering, and Named entity recognition, and one paper also uses it, alongside other datasets, to measure Generalization. The reported measurement claims therefore span several targets rather than centering on a single measurement claim, although the definitions most often describe the benchmark around event and information extraction.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use it in multi-benchmark evaluations rather than on its own. It appears alongside other information-extraction and event

nodes.name: ACRE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe ACRE as the Abstract Causal REasoning dataset, a diagnostic benchmark for causal induction. Definitions recurrently present it as identifying which Blicket objects trigger a machine or detector, and one paper says it evaluates how well vision systems perform causal induction. A smaller line of work frames it as a rule-induction benchmark in which the model infers a hidden mapping from input-output examples and generates new examples consistent with the shared rule.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ACRE to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. They use it to measure inductive reasoning, causal reasoning, and visual reasoning, and they also report it as measuring causal inference, described in one paper as testing an LLM's ability to identify causal relationships. Across these claims, its measurement role is spread across several reasoning targets rather than converging on one alone.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In use, papers place it alongside CATER, Something-Else, and STAR for diverse visual reasoning tasks, and alongside List Functions as an inductive reasoning benchmark. They also position it

nodes.name: ActivityNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers here, ActivityNet is most commonly treated as a large-scale video dataset or benchmark for activity or human activity understanding. Some descriptions emphasize diverse web videos, while others use it as a source of time-aligned captions and denser event pairs for temporal reasoning question creation. It also appears as the basis for an activity generation task in InterleavedBench and as a benchmark for evaluating video-based multimodal models.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ActivityNet to measure two behavioral indicators, Action recognition and Natural language planning, and it is not linked to any construct. The reported measurement claims are limited to those two indicators: one paper evaluates action recognition on ActivityNet, and another uses activity generation from ActivityNet for natural language planning.

Space of uses. Papers position it both as a standalone benchmark and as a source dataset inside other evaluations. It is used alongside Something-Something V2, UCF-101, YouCook2, DAVIS, and QVHighlights, and appears in action recognition evaluation, conditional video generation, video understanding, and QA data creation from ca

nodes.name: ActivityNet Captions
nodes.definition: An English dense video captioning dataset referenced as a prior benchmark for video-language evaluation.

nodes.name: ActivityNet-QA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as a video question-answering benchmark or dataset built on ActivityNet videos. Descriptions repeatedly frame it as open-ended and aimed at understanding complex web videos, longer activity videos, or complex human activities, and some papers further emphasize complex temporal or event understanding. Some authors specify that it is constructed from the ActivityNet action recognition dataset, and a smaller line of work positions it for zero-shot video understanding evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ActivityNet-QA to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The dominant claim is that it measures Video question answering, with many papers using it as an open-ended or general VideoQA benchmark, and a smaller but recurring framing uses it to measure Video understanding. Only a few papers use it to measure Visual question answering, Long video understanding, or Spatiotemporal reasoning, and one paper explicitly says it is "designed to assess the capabilities of VideoQA models in long-term spatiotemporal reasoning."

Space of uses. No paper links it to another measurement instrument. Even so, papers usually use it i

nodes.name: Adaptive attack
nodes.definition: A custom jailbreak evaluation procedure designed to prevent backtracking by optimizing prompts while discouraging generation of the [RESET] token.

nodes.name: AddSub
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats AddSub as an arithmetic word-problem dataset or benchmark centered on addition and subtraction. Definitions repeatedly describe it as containing addition and subtraction word problems for arithmetic, basic operational reasoning, or basic mathematical reasoning, and one evaluation section describes it as containing simple math word problems on addition and subtraction. One paper additionally frames it as a near-shift out-of-distribution benchmark, while another uses it as a seed dataset and as a well-defined evaluation set within PMC.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AddSub mainly to measure Mathematical reasoning. It is linked to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator: the construct is Mathematical reasoning, which papers evaluate through arithmetic datasets and mathematical reasoning testbeds, and the behavioral indicator is Mathematical problem solving, which one paper measures with AddSub as part of a more general benchmark suite. The reported measurement claims therefore converge on Mathematical reasoning rather than spreading across many targets.

Space of uses. Most papers use AddSub as one dataset wi

nodes.name: AddSub+
nodes.definition: A dataset for arithmetic reasoning that involves addition and subtraction problems, used here with variants of different digit lengths.

nodes.name: ADE20K
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, ADE20K is most commonly described as a large-scale scene parsing or semantic segmentation benchmark, sometimes specified as ADE20K (A-150). Definitions describe it as containing densely annotated images across a wide range of scenes, with a diverse set of objects and stuff classes. A smaller line of work treats it differently, either as a source dataset for constructing evaluation data with instance-level semantic annotations or as an alternative dataset for patch-level probing.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ADE20K to 3 behavioral indicators and to no constructs. The prevailing usage is that it measures semantic segmentation, with several papers describing evaluation, fine-tuning, or reported results on ADE20K for that purpose. A smaller line of work uses it to measure open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, and one paper reports it as measuring image segmentation.

Space of uses. Most papers position ADE20K as a benchmark or transfer target for semantic segmentation, often reporting results on it, fine-tuning on it, or using it as a downstream check after image restoration. It appears alongside PASCAL Context, PASCAL VOC 20, COCO

nodes.name: AdvBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, AdvBench is most commonly treated as an adversarial or jailbreak benchmark of harmful instructions, prompts, behaviors, objectives, or queries, used to test whether models produce harmful responses. The prevailing description is a text benchmark with about 500 items, often stated as 500 harmful instructions or malicious prompts, though some papers describe 520 harmful behaviors or queries, one paper describes 521 lines of harmful behaviors plus 575 lines of harmful strings, and several studies use a refined or curated 50-item version or smaller subsets. Some definitions also describe topical coverage, including crimes, self-harm, defamation, weapons, misinformation, hate speech, cybercrime, financial crime, terrorism, and fraud.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AdvBench to measure 7 constructs and 6 behavioral indicators. The most common construct framings are Safety alignment, Safety, Harmlessness, Adversarial robustness, and Robustness, plus 2 other constructs, and papers also use it to measure Jailbreaking, Harmful content generation, Harmful content detection, Harmful request refusal, and Jailbreak resistance, plus 1 other behavioral ind

nodes.name: AdversarialQA
nodes.definition: Question answering dataset with adversarially constructed questions designed to challenge model robustness and reasoning.

nodes.name: AG News
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is a benchmark or corpus for news topic classification, usually framed as assigning news articles to the categories World, Sports, Business, and Sci/Tech. Definitions vary in detail: some describe short news articles, some a collection from diverse domains, one describes article titles and descriptions and uses AG News Title and Description (AGT and AGD), and others present it more generally as a balanced multi-class text classification benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AG News to measure eight constructs and three behavioral indicators.
