The most common behavioral uses are text classification, downstream task performance, and news categorization; among constructs, it is most frequently linked to zero-shot generalization, adaptability, adversarial robustness, calibration, and general ability, plus generalization, in-context learning, and language modeling ability. Overall, papers use it for both task-level classification behavior and a broad spread of model properties rather than only one construct.

Space of uses. The prevailing use is as one benchmark within multi-dataset evaluation suites, especi

nodes.name: Agent-as-a-Judge
nodes.definition: Framework that uses agentic systems to evaluate other agentic systems by analyzing step-by-step task-solving processes, incorporating modules for reading, locating, retrieving, and judging based on hierarchical requirements.

nodes.name: AgentBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, AgentBench is most commonly treated as a benchmark or evaluation suite for LLMs acting as agents. Papers describe it as comprehensive or multi-dimensional, and one description characterizes it as having 8 distinct environments for assessing reasoning and decision-making abilities. The content is described broadly rather than uniformly: some definitions stress tasks such as OS interaction, web browsing, and web shopping, while others emphasize intrinsic reasoning and adaptation to environment feedback or broader coverage across code and web environments. Papers also describe task-specific reporting with success rate, F1 score, and reward score.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AgentBench to measure 7 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators, so its measurement claims are spread across multiple targets rather than converging on one. The construct links include agency, reasoning, and planning, with 4 other constructs also reported, and the behavioral-indicator links include action selection and instruction following, with 2 other behavioral indicators also reported. Papers also describe it as assessing reasoning and decision-making abilities and

nodes.name: AgentBoard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is of AgentBoard as a standardized or comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM agents. Definitions describe it as a unified, open-source evaluation framework for multi-turn agents, with diverse tasks in partially-observable environments and analytical metrics beyond success rates; other papers describe it more broadly as a collection of diverse tasks, or as a benchmark spanning various environments to assess agent performance in tasks such as reasoning and planning.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims converge on a single construct: papers use AgentBoard to measure Agency. The linked evidence describes it as a collection of diverse tasks for evaluating language models' agentic capabilities, and another paper places it under real-world applications; no behavioral indicators are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers position AgentBoard as a benchmark and evaluation framework for agent evaluation, including analytical evaluation of LLM agents. In use, it appears alongside AgentBench in standardized agent evaluation setups, and some descriptions also group it with ToolBench in broader benchmark suites for assessing agent

nodes.name: AgentDojo
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, AgentDojo is most commonly described as an evaluation benchmark or framework for agents in dynamic environments, especially for testing agent vulnerabilities to prompt injection attacks. Some descriptions are broad, calling it a dynamic environment for testing prompt injection or agent vulnerabilities, while a more specific one presents a benchmark of stateful, multi-turn tool-use tasks in realistic environments such as email clients, online banking systems, and Slack channels. That narrower description says the benchmark contains 97 tasks across the Workspace, Slack, Travel, and Banking domains.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AgentDojo to measure four constructs, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The measurement claims spread across adversarial robustness, robustness, security, and utility preservation: papers describe it as measuring the adversarial robustness of AI agents, evaluating the utility and security of AI agents in dynamic tool-calling environments with untrusted data, and demonstrating utility preservation under indirect prompt injection.

Space of uses. Papers use AgentDojo as an evaluation benchmark for methods in s

nodes.name: AgentHarm
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, AgentHarm is treated as a safety benchmark for harmful or malicious agent behavior. Papers describe it in two ways: as malicious tasks for general agents that evaluate general agent safety and vulnerability to harmful instructions, and as a benchmark for tool-using LLMs that provides detailed safety measurements through harmful and benign examples, including multi-step trajectories with injected harmful tool outputs to test refusal behavior.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link AgentHarm to 2 constructs, Harmlessness and Robustness, and no behavioral indicators. The reported measurement claims are split across those constructs: some work uses it to measure harmfulness or harmlessness in LLM agents, while other work reports that it measures the potential harm from agents executing malicious tasks under Robustness.

Space of uses. In the available uses, papers position AgentHarm as a safety evaluation benchmark, and no other measurement instrument is linked to it. One framing uses it for general agents and harmful instructions, while another uses it to test safety in tool-using settings, especially refusal behavior when multi-step tool

nodes.name: AggreFact
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, AggreFact is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for evaluating factual consistency in summarization. Definitions portray it as providing fine-grained annotations and summary-level labels across multiple domains, while a narrower description presents it as a summary evaluation benchmark built around the CNN and XSum datasets. One paper also refers to the AGGREFACT-FTSOTA split, indicating use of a named split or subset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AggreFact to evaluate factual consistency in summarization, and some also frame it more broadly as a benchmark for summary evaluation. The recorded links do not connect it to any construct or behavioral indicator, so the explicit measurement claims here do not extend beyond those benchmark descriptions.

Space of uses. The available snippets position AggreFact as one benchmark used alongside other summarization evaluation datasets, especially TRUE and SUMMAC, in model testing. Papers also use it with specific summarization datasets, describing it as consisting of or evaluating CNN or CNN/DM and XSum, and one paper specifies evaluation on the AGGREFACT-FTSOTA split.

nodes.name: AGIEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, AGIEval is most commonly described as a benchmark for evaluating foundation or language models on human-centric standardized exams and related human-centric tasks. Definitions usually characterize its content as exam-style questions drawn from sources such as the Gaokao, SAT, GRE, law school admission tests, college admission tests, and civil service examinations, and some descriptions narrow this further to reasoning-oriented exams in English, Math, Law, and Logic. A smaller line of work describes it more broadly as an aggregated or broad-range suite for overall model capabilities across tasks and skills, and one paper specifically calls it a bilingual benchmark for exam performance.

What it is claimed to measure. In recorded relationships, papers use AGIEval to measure two constructs, Generalization and Reasoning, and it is not linked to any behavioral indicator. One paper says it runs all English tasks in AGIEval under zero-shot settings to verify Generalization, while another places it among public benchmarks spanning natural language understanding and Reasoning tasks. These uses are split across those two constructs rather than centered on a single

nodes.name: AGIEval-Math
nodes.definition: Out-of-distribution test set used to evaluate mathematical reasoning generalization beyond the training domain.

nodes.name: AI2-THOR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, AI2-THOR is most commonly described as a simulation environment or interactive 3D simulator for embodied AI in realistic or photorealistic home-like indoor scenes. Definitions emphasize household tasks with natural language instructions and egocentric visual observations, where agents navigate and interact with household items; a smaller line of work presents it as the base environment for multi-agent setups and for benchmarks built on top of it, including MAP-THOR.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AI2-THOR to measure one construct, Planning, and one behavioral indicator, Causal inference. These claims are concentrated on that small set of targets: one paper reports "planning results" and "N-step causal inference accuracies" across environments and step lengths using AI2-THOR.

Space of uses. Papers position AI2-THOR as an evaluation environment for embodied agents. In the snippets, it is used for evaluations across multiple scenarios, including alongside LEGENT, and as the underlying simulator for open-ended, long-horizon home-like tasks in a multi-agent setup.

nodes.name: AI2D
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, AI2D is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset of diagrams, usually science or textbook diagrams, for diagram understanding and question answering. Many descriptions also treat it as an evaluation of diagram comprehension, interpretation, or reasoning, and one paper frames it around scientific knowledge and mathematical reasoning. Some authors add format detail, describing diagrams paired with questions and answers, exhaustive annotations of constituents and relationships, and multiple-choice questions; papers also mention named forms such as AI2D-Test and AI2D-RST.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link AI2D to 5 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on one construct. The prevailing use is diagram-focused: papers use it to measure Diagram understanding, Chart and diagram understanding, Multiple-choice visual question answering, and Visual question answering. Broader construct-level uses are also reported, with AI2D used to measure Document understanding and 4 other constructs.

Space of uses. Papers do not claim direct links from AI2D to other meas

nodes.name: AIAH
nodes.definition: A benchmark used to evaluate the safety-alignment of Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) against harmful questions across audio-text, text-only, and audio-only modalities.

nodes.name: AIME
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, AIME is commonly treated as the American Invitational Mathematics Examination, used as a challenging benchmark or dataset for advanced mathematical reasoning and problem solving. Definitions differ on the exact instantiation: some papers use an AIMO validation set with 90 questions from AIME 22, 23, and 24, while others evaluate on AIME 2024 with 15 competition math problems or on AIME 2025, Parts I and II. One description also frames it as exams designed to challenge high school math students in America.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AIME to measure 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Mathematical reasoning, with a smaller recurring use for Reasoning more generally. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Mathematical problem solving, and isolated papers use it to measure Chain of thought and General ability.

Space of uses. Papers frequently include AIME in multi-benchmark evaluations and describe it as challenging, widely used, or standard for math-focused evaluation. It is used alongside MATH500, GPQA, AMC, MATH, and Omni-MATH, and other papers pair it with additional math and reasoning benchmark

nodes.name: AIME 2024
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats AIME 2024 as a benchmark of problems or questions from the 2024 American Invitational Mathematics Examination, usually described as challenging competition-level mathematics for advanced reasoning or problem solving. Papers variously call it AIME24, AIME2024, AIME'24, or AIME 24, and a few add details such as coverage of algebra, counting, geometry, number theory, and probability, answers that are integers between 0 and 999, or a size of 30 questions or examples. Most descriptions frame it as high-school, competition-level, out-of-distribution, or Olympiad-level math, though one paper describes AMC2023 and AIME2024 as middle school math competitions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link AIME 2024 to 4 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so its reported use is spread across several targets rather than concentrated on one. The most common claims are that it measures mathematical reasoning and reasoning. It is also reported as measuring mathematical problem solving, with smaller lines of work linking it to generalization, problem-solving ability, and one other behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Papers most often

nodes.name: AIME 2025
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe AIME 2025, sometimes written AIME25, as a benchmark or benchmark dataset derived from the 2025 American Invitational Mathematics Examination. The definitions converge on its use for testing advanced mathematical problem-solving skills or evaluating mathematical reasoning performance, and one study also classifies AIME25 among "smaller benchmarks."

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the dominant use is to measure Mathematical reasoning: it is linked to two constructs overall, most often Mathematical reasoning and, in a smaller line of work, Self-improvement. This appears in language such as evaluations of "performance (%) on mathematical benchmarks" and of models' "mathematical reasoning capabilities"; one paper instead uses this recent mathematics benchmark to examine test-time learning capabilities in solving high-level mathematical problems, which is recorded as measuring Self-improvement. Papers do not link it to any behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Reported evaluations often place AIME 2025 alongside other mathematics benchmarks. Papers commonly pair it with AIME24, and some also include AMC23, MATH500, Minervamath, and

nodes.name: AIR-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats AIR-Bench as a benchmark or aggregated evaluation suite for large audio or audio-language models, aimed at audio understanding in a relatively holistic way. Most descriptions place its content across speech, audio, and music, and one survey specifically describes it as an open-ended question-answering benchmark for general auditory processing. Papers also mention named components or tracks within it, including AirBench-Chat for conversational ability and a foundation track for evaluating foundation models; one separate usage describes AIR-Bench instead as a retrieval benchmark whose test data is automatically generated by large language models.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AIR-Bench to evaluate a spread of targets rather than a single recorded construct. In descriptions and snippets it is reported as evaluating audio understanding, audio comprehension, general auditory processing, conversational ability in AirBench-Chat, and, in one paper, retrieval performance; another paper highlights its foundation track for evaluating foundation models. No constructs and no behavioral indicators are linked to it.

nodes.name: AIR-Bench 2024
nodes.definition: A language-model safety benchmark containing 5,694 risky instruction prompts grounded in the AIR 2024 taxonomy of regulation- and policy-derived risk categories.

nodes.name: AIR-Bench (information retrieval)
nodes.definition: An information retrieval benchmark that covers a range of out-of-domain topics, including long document and question-answering sections, to test model generalization.

nodes.name: AitW
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat AitW as a large-scale dataset or benchmark for Android device control, used to evaluate mobile or GUI agents. Definitions also describe it as containing diverse natural language instructions and operation trajectories, with subsets such as General and Web Shopping, and some authors add that it provides an evaluation environment for real-world tasks. A smaller line of work presents it more specifically as a mobile navigation benchmark, and one paper describes it as an open-source mobile control dataset that lacks UI trees.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, claims about what AitW measures are concentrated on a small set of outcomes: papers link it to 2 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing usage is to use it to measure GUI automation, papers also use it to measure task completion, and a smaller line of work reports that it measures Adaptability.

Space of uses. Papers commonly position AitW as an evaluation benchmark for Android, mobile, or GUI control agents. Some also use it as a training or fine-tuning source and then evaluate on test subsets derived from AitW, while others use it as a comparison point or evalua

nodes.name: ALERT
nodes.definition: An evaluation dataset designed to test the safety of responses generated by large language models.

nodes.name: ALFRED
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a benchmark or dataset for embodied household tasks in simulation, used for planning and instruction following with human-annotated, formally verifiable tasks that involve object manipulation and state changes such as heating, cooling, and cleaning. Definitions and snippets variously place it in a simulated Unity environment or describe it as built on the AI2-THOR simulator, and some papers also present it as providing vision-and-language navigation and rearrangement tasks for everyday household settings. A smaller usage writes it as ALFRed and emphasizes long-horizon embodied tasks and task decomposition, while another paper curates an ALFRED test set for 3D evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is limited and split across 2 constructs, with no linked behavioral indicators. One paper uses it to measure 3D perception through a curated ALFRED test set for "3D evaluation" (LLaVA-Interleave: Tackling Multi-image, Video, and 3D in Large Multimodal Models), while another uses it to measure robustness by reporting experiments in "VirtualHome, ALFRED, and CARLA" (Exploratory Retrieval-Augmented Planning

nodes.name: ALFWorld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a text-based household or housework benchmark for interactive agents, often framed as an embodied environment aligned with or based on ALFRED and accessed through a text-only or low-level text action interface. Agents are described as following high-level language instructions to complete tasks such as finding hidden objects, moving and manipulating items, and more broadly picking, cleaning, heating, or cooling objects. Some papers specify six task types and either 134 unseen environments or 134 evaluation tasks, while a smaller line of work treats ALFWorld as a text-based world simulator with interaction logs for next action prediction.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ALFWorld to measure 9 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role spans multiple capabilities rather than a single shared target. Recurring construct-level uses are Generalization and Decision-making, while recurring behavioral uses are Action selection, Task completion, and Embodied planning. Other papers also report it as measuring several additional constructs.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to ALF

nodes.name: AlignBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a Chinese benchmark of 683 samples for evaluating LLM alignment. It is commonly presented as multidimensional, with a rule-calibrated LLM-as-judge procedure and Chain-of-Thought reasoning for evaluation, and some descriptions add that different question types have manually set evaluation dimensions. One paper also treats it as a benchmark from which Clarity, Completeness, and Factuality are drawn.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to evaluate alignment, variously phrased as LLM alignment, alignment capabilities of LLMs in Chinese, or model alignment across multiple dimensions. One paper further reports using Clarity, Completeness, and Factuality from AlignBench for quality assessment. No constructs and no behavioral indicators are linked to it in the reported relationships.

Space of uses. Most papers position it as an evaluation benchmark rather than alongside other named instruments. A smaller use treats it as a source of metrics, where a model predicts instruction and instruction-response scores based on Clarity, Completeness, and Factuality from AlignBench. No other measurement instruments are linked to it.

nodes.name: Alpaca instruction dataset
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats Alpaca as an instruction-following or instruction-tuning dataset, often described as 52K instruction-response pairs or demonstrations, sometimes in instruction, input, output form. One definition says the examples were generated from text-davinci-003, while a smaller line of work describes it as a hybrid question-answer dataset or uses parts of it as code prompts, complex advice queries, seed data, or model-editing prompts. Papers also refer to specific variants such as the training dataset, a cleaned version, and subsets without unsafe instructions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Alpaca to 5 behavioral indicators and 5 constructs. The dominant measurement claim is instruction following; papers also use it to measure question answering, refusal, text generation, and text summarization. On the construct side, it is reported as measuring helpfulness most often, and is also used for general ability, in-context learning, language modeling ability, and semantic consistency. Overall, the reported measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than confined to one construct.

Space of uses. No measurement

nodes.name: AlpacaEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, AlpacaEval is most commonly described as an automatic benchmark or evaluation framework for instruction-following and open-ended generation, typically using a strong LLM, most often GPT-4, to make pairwise judgments between a model output and a reference response or reference model and to report a win rate. Many definitions mention 805 prompts, instructions, or questions from diverse domains, and v1.0 or 1.0 is described as comparing against text-davinci-003 with GPT-4 as annotator; papers also mention AlpacaEval 2.0, length-controlled AlpacaEval 2, and the 129-prompt helpful_base subset. Some papers instead emphasize it as a dataset, an out-of-distribution test set curated from open-source instruction-following and dialogue data, or a leaderboard with archived outputs, and one paper describes it as a human preference evaluation with crowdworker judgments rather than an LLM judge.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the dominant measurement claim is instruction following, variously phrased as instruction following or instruction-following ability. Papers link AlpacaEval to 14 constructs and 7 behavioral indicators overall, with the most frequen

nodes.name: AlpacaEval 2.0
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats AlpacaEval 2.0 as an automatic, LLM-as-a-judge benchmark for open-ended instruction following and chat evaluation, often described as a simulated human preference evaluation. Most definitions describe pairwise comparisons in which a strong judge model such as GPT-4 compares a model response against a reference or baseline response, although one paper instead calls it a reference-free instruction-following benchmark. Several descriptions say it contains 805 questions or instructions from five datasets, while another describes 805 representative instructions from real user interactions; recurring variants include length-controlled AlpacaEval 2.0 or Alpaca-Eval V2, and smaller lines of work describe it as an updated conversation-quality version, a text-only human preference alignment benchmark, or a leaderboard.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AlpacaEval 2.0 to measure 9 constructs and 6 behavioral indicators. The dominant framing centers on instruction following, especially instruction following ability, and recurring uses extend to human preference alignment, helpfulness, and alignment; one paper also says it approxim

nodes.name: AlpacaFarm
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat AlpacaFarm as an evaluation framework or benchmark for open-ended conversation and instruction-following models, though some describe it as a dataset, codebase, or software framework. Across definitions and snippets, it contains instructions, output pairs or model responses, and human preference annotations for pairwise comparisons, and papers say it uses human or model-based comparisons to assess response quality and instructability. Several papers refer to a test set of 805 instructions, training or validation splits, and a full collection of 9.69k instructions; one paper also uses a variant with separate splits for different RLHF stages.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link AlpacaFarm to two constructs and one behavioral indicator. They use it to measure Helpfulness and Instruction following ability, and one paper also reports it as measuring Pairwise comparison by placing it among benchmarks that primarily rely on that task. Definitions in the same literature also describe it as assessing response quality and instructability.

Space of uses. In use, papers apply AlpacaFarm both as an evaluation benchmark and as a dataset with traini

nodes.name: Amazon Books
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers treat Amazon Books as an Amazon dataset centered on products in the Books category, with user-item interactions and product metadata. In the available definition, it is described as being used to evaluate recommendation performance, and no versions or subsets are described.

What it is claimed to measure. The only explicit measurement claim in the available material is that papers use Amazon Books for evaluating recommendation performance. No construct is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it, so the recorded claims do not converge on any named construct beyond that general evaluation use.

Space of uses. The available paper positions Amazon Books as an evaluation dataset rather than describing it alongside other instruments. No other measurement instrument is linked to it in the recorded relationships.

nodes.name: Amazon Mechanical Turk
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats Amazon Mechanical Turk as a crowdsourcing platform for collecting human annotations and human evaluations. Most definitions describe it as a platform, while one frames it as a crowdsourced evaluation procedure; the reported uses include collecting valid versus invalid labels to train critic models, rating generated plans, comparing outputs on fluency and descriptiveness, evaluating model outputs across a test set, building an annotation platform for splitting and labeling interaction sequences, verifying benchmark samples and human performance, and collecting open-ended answers and ratings for visual riddle tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Across these papers, Amazon Mechanical Turk is not explicitly linked to named constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, it is used to gather task-specific human judgments and annotations, including fluency and descriptiveness comparisons, ratings of generated plans, subjective ratings on generated diagrams, human verification and human performance on image-caption matching tasks, and human answers and ratings for visual riddles.

Space of uses. Papers position Amazon Mechanical

nodes.name: Amazon Polarity
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats Amazon Polarity, or simply Amazon, as a text or sentiment classification benchmark on product reviews. One paper states, "We study text classification using four datasets: sentiment analysis using SST-2 and Amazon" (Privacy-Preserving In-Context Learning for Large Language Models). Some authors describe it more broadly as an NLP classification dataset, and one debiasing paper uses the surface form AmazonPolarity for a downstream classification check. A smaller line of work uses the name Amazon differently: one paper describes a product co-purchasing network for node classification, while another describes a temporal point process benchmark for predicting the timestamp and category of the next reviewed product among 16 categories.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link Amazon Polarity to any constructs or behavioral indicators through explicit measurement relationships. Most often, they use it to evaluate sentiment analysis or product-review text classification, while some papers frame it more broadly as an NLP classification or semantic understanding task. Separate descriptions of Amazon use the same name for no

nodes.name: Amazon Reviews
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a widely used public dataset of Amazon product reviews. One description presents it as reviews across multiple categories, used for sentiment analysis and for evaluating model performance on commercial user feedback, while another describes an adapted version that adds simulated user consultation texts, user profiles, and interaction behaviors for evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to evaluate sentiment analysis performance on commercial user feedback, and one adapted use supports evaluation with consultation texts, user profiles, and interaction behaviors in work on users’ search motivations. Papers do not explicitly link it to any construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. The reported uses are task-specific rather than presented alongside other named instruments. In one line of work it serves as a product review dataset for sentiment analysis, and in another it is adapted with simulated consultation text and interaction data for evaluation; no other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: Amazon Reviews 2023
nodes.definition: A dataset of user reviews on Amazon products, used here for the task of personalized review generation, covering categories like Books, Movies & TV, and CDs & Vinyl, and preprocessed with splits from the DPL framework.

nodes.name: Amazon Video Games
nodes.definition: An Amazon dataset containing user-item interactions and metadata for products in the 'Video Games' category, used for evaluating recommendation performance.

nodes.name: AMBER
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, AMBER is most commonly described as a hallucination benchmark that extends POPE beyond existence checks to cover attribute and relation hallucinations as well. Several papers also present it as spanning both discriminative and generative tasks, and one description says it evaluates multimodal hallucinations through 15,220 yes-or-no questions. Smaller descriptions treat it as a dataset for image description tasks, or note implementation details, such as the use of CHAIR as the evaluation metric; one paper further describes it as designed to be evaluated without LLM assistance, with metrics including response-level hallucination and human cognition hallucination.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AMBER to measure 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing use is to measure hallucination, especially hallucination and object hallucination, with papers also using it to measure hallucination resistance and visual recognition. These links are concentrated on hallucination-related targets, while visual recognition appears as a smaller additional use.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers usually position AMBER as

nodes.name: AmbigNQ
nodes.definition: A dataset of naturally occurring ambiguous questions from Google search logs, which served as the origin for the queries used in AmbigQA and subsequently CondAmbigQA.

nodes.name: Ambrosia
nodes.definition: A benchmark containing human-crafted databases and questions specifically designed to incorporate ambiguities for evaluating semantic parsing.

nodes.name: AMC 2023
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the literature, AMC 2023 is most commonly treated as a benchmark or dataset drawn from the 2023 American Mathematics Competitions, sometimes written as AMC, AMC2023, or AMC23. Most definitions describe challenging, competition-level math problems at the high school level, with one definition presenting it as a 2023 exam of standardized math problems and another describing it as a middle school competition covering arithmetic, algebra, and geometry with 40 questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link AMC 2023 to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is to measure Mathematical reasoning, with papers reporting it as a mathematical or olympiad benchmark for evaluating reasoning performance; a smaller line of work uses it to measure Mathematical problem solving, and one paper uses it to measure Reasoning. Overall, the measurement claims mostly converge on Mathematical reasoning rather than spreading evenly across several constructs.

Space of uses. Most papers use AMC 2023 as part of a broader benchmark suite rather than on its own. It is commonly reported alongside GSM8K, MATH500, AIME2024, OlympiadBench, and Omni-MATH, and papers vari

nodes.name: AndroidControl
nodes.definition:
What it is. Definitions mostly treat AndroidControl as a benchmark for evaluating mobile agent tasks on Android platforms. One description is more specific, calling it an offline GUI benchmark and an in-distribution offline dataset, while another highlights two variants: AndroidControl-Low, where both low-level and high-level instructions are provided, and AndroidControl-High, where only high-level instructions are given. One paper also describes it as a UI control dataset with 14,548 unique tasks over 833 Android apps.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AndroidControl to measure three constructs, Agency, Generalization, and Out-of-distribution generalization, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. These measurement claims are spread across those constructs rather than centered on one: one paper presents it as a mobile-agent benchmark, another frames evaluation on it as a test of out-of-distribution performance because only 20 of the 833 apps had been encountered during data synthesis, and another says its task and app coverage allows analysis of performance in and out of the training domain.

Space of uses. When papers place AndroidControl within broader evaluation

nodes.name: AndroidWorld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is of an online or dynamic Android benchmark for mobile or autonomous agents, usually running in Android emulators or a virtual Android environment. Definitions mostly converge on a suite of 116 tasks across 20 real-world apps, with reward signals or automated evaluation based on final device states, and with task-specific initialization, success-checking, and tear-down logic; one paper also describes a Pixel 6 phone simulator. A smaller line of work treats it more broadly as an Android virtual agent benchmark used for both trajectory collection and evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three constructs and no behavioral indicators. The most common claim is that it measures adaptability: papers say it enables finer-grained analyses of agent adaptability and use results on AndroidWorld to report adaptability across real-time dynamic OS tasks. Smaller uses report it as measuring robustness, through performance across different random seeds and task parameters, and chain-of-thought reasoning, in work that describes AndroidWorld as an online environment requiring multi-step reasoning. Overall, the measur

nodes.name: ANLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ANLI is most commonly described as Adversarial Natural Language Inference, a benchmark or dataset for natural language inference. Several definitions add that it was collected iteratively through an adversarial human-and-model-in-the-loop, or human-in-the-loop, process and designed to challenge contemporary or state-of-the-art models; other descriptions place it in a classification benchmark set or describe it as a textual entailment task for natural language understanding and reasoning. Some work uses the challenging subsets ANLI-A2 and ANLI-A3, and one paper describes the data as open-domain questions enhanced via an iterative adversarial procedure.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ANLI to two constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claim is natural language inference: papers use ANLI, sometimes alongside MNLI or e-SNLI, to benchmark understanding of entailment, contradiction, and neutrality or simply for natural language inference. A smaller line of work reports ANLI as measuring natural language understanding and commonsense reasoning, so the linked uses extend beyond one target to those two additional constructs

nodes.name: ANLI R2
nodes.definition: The second round of the Adversarial Natural Language Inference (ANLI) dataset, a challenging benchmark for sentence pair classification.

nodes.name: AnnoMI
nodes.definition: Expert-annotated counseling dataset with 133 dialogues and 9 therapist strategies, used for evaluating emotional support dialogue strategy prediction.

nodes.name: Anthropic Red Team
nodes.definition: An adversarial dataset of potentially harmful queries designed to test the safety of language models.

nodes.name: API-Bank
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, API-Bank is most commonly treated as a benchmark or dialogue-style dataset for evaluating tool calls by LLMs in conversational or tool-augmented settings. Definitions vary in scope: some emphasize single- and multi-turn scenarios, one describes calling predefined local Python tools from user requirements, and others frame it as evaluating planning, retrieval, and API calling. Several papers distinguish two retrieval-call variants, either Call versus Retrieve + Call or L-1, invoking a known API, versus L-2, retrieving and calling from multiple candidates; reported contents also differ, from 314 tool-use dialogues and 753 API calls to 2,138 distinct APIs, 1,888 dialogues, and 4,149 API calls, with another description emphasizing general-purpose tools across 1,000 domains.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link API-Bank to one behavioral indicator and two constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure Tool use and Tool use ability: papers describe it as evaluating tool use, tool-utilization capabilities, or tool-calling capability, including planning, retrieval, and API-calling proficiency. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Generalization, speci

nodes.name: APIBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark focused on APIs that load machine learning models, used to train and evaluate LLMs' ability to interface with ML services.

nodes.name: APPS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, APPS is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for code generation or program synthesis built from algorithmic or competitive programming problems. The recurring description is that each problem comes with a natural language description and test cases or unit tests, and some definitions add solutions, often Python solutions; several papers also describe it as 10,000 problems split into 5,000 training and 5,000 testing examples across introductory, interview, and competition levels. A smaller line of work uses subsets rather than the full benchmark, such as 500 interview-level problems, 500 sampled test questions, or the competition split of 1000 problems, and some papers refer to it as the Automated Programming Progress Standard.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link APPS to 3 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing use is to measure code generation, with papers describing it as evaluating generic code synthesis, program implementation, or coding tasks, often by pass@1 or pass@k and by checking solutions against test cases. Smaller uses treat it as measuring code debugging and neural self-repair, and one paper reports it as

nodes.name: AQuA-RAT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing treats AQuA-RAT, often written AQuA or AQUA-RAT, as a dataset or benchmark of algebraic word problems in multiple-choice format. Many definitions add rationales and multi-step reasoning, and one study describes it as containing approximately 100,000 algebraic word problems, each with a rationale leading to one of five answer options, while others characterize it more broadly as algebraic and quantitative reasoning or as reasoning over quantitative and qualitative relationships. Papers also differ slightly in presentation, with one calling it a 4-option multiple-choice benchmark and another a five-option one, and with difficulty described both as relatively simple and as harder math word problems.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing usage is as a measure of Mathematical reasoning: papers say it is used to assess varying levels of mathematical reasoning abilities, mathematical reasoning capacity, and arithmetic reasoning. Papers link it to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator overall, with claims concentrated on Mathematical reasoning; a smaller line of work uses it to measure Mathematical problem solving, and single paper

nodes.name: ArabicMMLU
nodes.definition: An Arabic-specific variant of MMLU that evaluates knowledge across subjects with regional relevance to Arab countries, used in a zero-shot setting with option logit probability.

nodes.name: AraEval
nodes.definition: A comprehensive Arabic multi-task evaluation suite assessing knowledge, reasoning, truthfulness, and instruction-following in LLMs, comprising seven datasets with 24,378 samples.

nodes.name: ARC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across most papers, ARC is treated as the AI2 Reasoning Challenge, a multiple-choice science question benchmark drawn from grade-school or similar school-level exams and used to study knowledge and reasoning. The prevailing description includes ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge, also written Arc-E and Arc-C, and some papers focus specifically on the challenge split. A smaller line of work uses the same name for the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus or Challenge, a visual or grid-based benchmark where models infer transformation rules from input-output grids and apply them to a test grid; descriptions also differ on educational level, since most papers say grade-school while one paper describes graduate-school science questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ARC to 15 constructs and 11 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement claims are spread across many targets. The most common framing is that it measures commonsense reasoning and reasoning, typically through multiple-choice question answering and question answering; papers also link it to 13 other constructs and 9 other behavioral indicators. In smaller lines of work, especially when ARC is used in the

nodes.name: ARC-AGI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe ARC-AGI as a benchmark of grid-based reasoning tasks in which models infer a transformation rule from example input-output pairs and then produce the correct output for a test input. One description adds that the original dataset consists of 900 reasoning tasks, and a source snippet states that the objective of each task is to discern the rule from the examples and apply it to new input grids.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ARC-AGI to measure 4 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is reasoning: papers describe ARC as a benchmark designed to challenge AI models' core reasoning capabilities and list ARC-AGI among novel reasoning tasks. Smaller strands report it as measuring abstract reasoning, core knowledge, and generalization, and one paper uses it to measure code generation by treating ARC as a strong testbed for program synthesis.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to ARC-AGI. Papers position it directly as a benchmark or testbed: one source says it poses a challenge for large language models, and another treats it as a strong testbed for program synthesis because it was designed to resist patte

nodes.name: ARC-Challenge
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, ARC-Challenge is most commonly treated as the harder challenge split of the AI2 Reasoning Challenge, a multiple-choice science question answering benchmark built from scientific or grade-school exams and designed to be difficult for simple retrieval or word co-occurrence methods. Papers refer to it under several spellings, including ARC-Challenge, ARC-C, ARC-c, ARCC, and ARC_C, and usually contrast it with ARC-Easy. Descriptions vary slightly: some emphasize commonsense or scientific reasoning, some describe it as open-book QA, and another frames it as a closed-set reasoning dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, ARC-Challenge is linked to 16 constructs and 14 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims are spread across many targets rather than concentrated on a single one. The prevailing use is to measure commonsense reasoning and broader reasoning, with recurring claims that it also measures general ability, generalization, natural language understanding, and scientific reasoning. On the behavioral side, papers most often use it for multiple-choice question answering, language understanding task performance, qu

nodes.name: ARC-Easy
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ARC-Easy is most commonly described as the easy split or easy subset of the AI2 Reasoning Challenge, used as a multiple-choice science question answering benchmark. Definitions usually frame the items as grade-school or elementary-level science questions, often as easier than ARC-Challenge and sometimes as answerable with simple retrieval or text-matching, though some papers instead emphasize reasoning, commonsense reasoning, or basic factual knowledge. One paper gives the most specific dataset description, stating that the full ARC collection has 7,787 multiple-choice science exam questions and that the Easy subset contains 5,197 relatively easier questions; most reported uses are zero-shot, though one paper refers to ArcEasy-3-shots.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ARC-Easy to measure 13 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators, so the claimed target is spread across many framings rather than concentrated on a single one. The prevailing construct-level links are to Commonsense reasoning, Reasoning, and General ability, while the most frequent behavioral framings are multiple-choice question answering and question answering.

Space of uses. In

nodes.name: Arena-Hard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Arena-Hard is most commonly described as a challenging benchmark of technical problem-solving and open-ended instruction-following prompts, often drawn from challenging user queries or live chatbot data. The prevailing setup uses pairwise comparison against a strong baseline, with GPT evaluators or other LLM judges selecting preferred responses and reporting win rates, and several definitions emphasize close agreement with human preference rankings. Some papers use the name more broadly for versioned releases and automated variants, including LLM-judge forms, while a smaller line of work treats one release as a pool of prompts and system responses for judge-ranking studies.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Arena-Hard to measure a broad spread of targets, it is linked to 9 constructs and 7 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is for instruction following ability and instruction following, with recurring claims that it measures human preference alignment, alignment, and technical problem solving rather than only one outcome. Other constructs and indicators appear less often.

Space of uses. Most papers use Arena-Hard alongside MT-Bench and Al

nodes.name: ARES
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, ARES is described in two ways. In Probabilistic Soundness Guarantees in LLM Reasoning Chains, it is introduced as Autoregressive Reasoning Entailment Stability, a probabilistic framework that evaluates each reasoning step by its expected entailment probability, conditioned only on previously verified premises or previously occurring sound claims. RAGChecker: A Fine-grained Framework for Diagnosing Retrieval-Augmented Generation instead describes ARES as an automated evaluation framework for RAG systems that uses LLM-based classifiers to predict fine-grained scores, and says it followed the RAG Triad concept and improved score prediction approaches on different datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement claims are concentrated on one construct: papers link ARES to 1 construct, Error propagation, and to no behavioral indicators. That link is recorded as a measured_by relation, so papers use ARES to measure Error propagation, with one study reporting that it "excels at identifying propagated errors, especially in long chains."

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The available descriptions position it either

nodes.name: ArgCMV
nodes.definition: A key point extraction benchmark dataset comprising ~12K arguments from real multi-turn debates on Reddit’s r/ChangeMyView, spanning ~3K topics, designed to evaluate long-context argument understanding and summarization.

nodes.name: ArgKP21
nodes.definition: ArgKP21 is a prior key point extraction benchmark consisting of crowd-sourced arguments on controversial topics with human-created gold key points and argument-to-key-point mappings.

nodes.name: Arithmetic
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is an arithmetic evaluation task or dataset, though its format varies across uses. One recurring framing uses natural-language addition and subtraction questions involving at most 5-digit numbers. Other papers describe Arithmetic as mathematical expressions built from six unique two-digit numbers with addition, multiplication, and subtraction, or as a set of 1,000 generated problems of the form a + b · c + d − e · f.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers attach several measurement claims to Arithmetic rather than one shared linked construct. Definitions describe it as assessing generator-validator consistency through correctness randomization, and as evaluating arithmetic reasoning or basic mathematical reasoning. No construct or behavioral indicator is explicitly linked to it in the recorded relationships.

Space of uses. Papers use Arithmetic in different evaluation setups. One use asks a generator to produce either a correct or an incorrect response and then has a validator check that response, instantiating generator-validator consistency through randomized correctness. Another paper positions it as one of several d

nodes.name: ARITHMETIC context-sensitivity dataset
nodes.definition: A synthetically generated dataset of simple arithmetic expressions where contexts provide reassignments of subexpressions to create counterfactual answers.

nodes.name: ArmoRM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats ArmoRM as an automated reward model or judge for evaluating LLM responses, often described as multi-dimension or multi-objective and as assessing outputs from multiple perspectives. Some authors describe it more specifically as 8B or Llama3-8B variants, including ArmoRM-8B, ArmoRM-Llama3-8B, and ArmoRM-Llama3-8B-v0.1, used to score model outputs, filter synthetic preference data, or create preference pairs. One paper also describes it as producing both a scalar reward value and human-interpretable fine-grained attributes.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ArmoRM to 4 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so it is reported as measuring several targets rather than only one. The most common construct links are to Helpfulness and Text generation quality, followed by Harmlessness and Humor; the behavioral-indicator links are to Instruction following and Preference ranking. In these uses, papers report it as assessing response quality, evaluating responses from various perspectives, and, in one case, using its instruction-following dimension as the main evaluation metric.

Space of uses. Most commonly, papers positi

nodes.name: Arxiv
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Arxiv is most commonly treated broadly as a dataset of scientific or academic texts from the arXiv repository, but the format varies by task. Some definitions present it as a directed citation network of Computer Science papers, while others use the same name for a long-document summarization corpus of scientific articles, a subset of paper abstracts used through validation splits, a citation recommendation benchmark derived from arXiv preprints, or a short-form academic-text dataset. The prevailing usage is therefore task-specific rather than tied to a single format.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Arxiv to measure 2 constructs, Length generalization and Zero-shot generalization, and 1 behavioral indicator, Node classification. For node classification, one paper frames the task as predicting which arXiv CS sub-category a paper belongs to. Other papers report Arxiv as part of real-world or out-of-domain evaluations for length generalization and zero-shot generalization, so the measurement claims span several targets rather than converging on one.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is explicitly linked to Arxiv through instrument relation

nodes.name: ArxivCorpus
nodes.definition: Dataset of Arxiv paper abstracts used for pretraining and evaluating text regeneration, with test sets containing texts published after January 2024 to ensure strict unseen evaluation.

nodes.name: ArXivQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats ArXivQA as a question answering resource built from arXiv or academic-paper figures, most commonly as a VQA dataset consisting of questions about figures from ArXiv academic papers. A smaller line of work instead frames it as a page-level retrieval task, where the question is used as the query and the associated page as the gold document, or as a multiple-choice dataset for document visual question answering in closed- and open-domain settings. One survey describes ArxivQA differently again, as a QA test set generated from recent arXiv abstracts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. Its measurement claims are spread across information retrieval, question answering, and visual question answering: papers use it as a QA benchmark where answers are produced in natural language, as a VQA dataset targeting figure types, and as question-document pairs for retrieval evaluation.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is directly linked to it. Papers often use it alongside ChartQA, InfographicsVQA, PlotQA, MP-DocVQA, and SlideVQA in document or figure evaluations, and one QA setu

nodes.name: ASAP
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available description treats ASAP as the Hewlett Foundation Short Answer Scoring dataset, containing short essay responses across science and biology topics for evaluating automated scoring systems. The description does not mention versions or subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. The available paper describes ASAP as a dataset used for evaluating automated scoring systems, but papers do not link it to any named constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. No other measurement instruments are linked to ASAP. The available paper presents it as a dataset of short essay responses on science and biology topics for evaluating automated scoring systems.

nodes.name: Asch conformity experiment
nodes.definition: A series of classic social psychology experiments studying how individual judgment is influenced by a majority group opinion, which inspired the design of the Trust and Doubt protocols.

nodes.name: ASDiv
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats ASDiv as a benchmark dataset of diverse arithmetic or math word problems. Definitions variously call it "A Set of Diverse Math Word Problems", "Another Solved Dataset of Diverse Word Problems", or "Another Simple Math Word Problem Set", and several descriptions emphasize varied problem types, operations, and difficulty levels for evaluating robustness, comprehension, or numerical reasoning. A smaller line of work presents it as an out-of-distribution or out-of-domain evaluation set, and one paper describes it as an English math word problem corpus with 2,305 instances, typically found in elementary schools.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ASDiv to measure 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures Mathematical reasoning, with additional measured_by links to broader Reasoning and, less often, Generalization through out-of-domain generalizability. Among behavioral indicators, papers use it for Mathematical problem solving, and some also treat it as a held-out test for Instruction following.

Space of uses. No paper links ASDiv to another measurement instrument. In practice, paper

nodes.name: ASQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ASQA is most commonly treated as a benchmark or dataset for long-form question answering, especially ambiguous factoid questions. Definitions describe it as an attributable long-form QA benchmark, an open-domain dataset for ambiguous factoid queries collected from AmbigQA, and a benchmark that requires answers to cover multiple possible interpretations of a question. A smaller line of work describes it more specifically as question-answering data for long-form, multi-hop answers with supporting evidence and citation quality, and papers mention both test-set evaluation and use of the training split as a question source.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than centering on one recurring target. Papers link ASQA to 3 behavioral indicators and 3 constructs; named uses span ambiguous question answering, long-form question answering, factuality, trustworthiness, and unanswerability detection ability, plus 1 other behavioral indicator. In these uses, one paper follows ASQA's official metrics, Disambiguous-Rouge with ROUGE-L and Disambig-F1, to report factual correctness, while another evaluates on ASQA wit

nodes.name: AssoCiAm
nodes.definition: A multimodal benchmark designed to evaluate the associative ability of MLLMs by presenting multiple-choice visual association tasks where ambiguity has been systematically mitigated.

nodes.name: ATIS
nodes.definition: The Air Travel Information System (ATIS) dataset, used for intent classification to source seed samples and evaluate downstream classifier performance.

nodes.name: AudioBench
nodes.definition: Open-ended QA benchmark assessing LALMs’ performance on a range of auditory processing tasks, including speech and environmental sound understanding.

nodes.name: AudioCaps
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats AudioCaps as an audio captioning benchmark or dataset of AudioSet clips paired with human-written captions or natural-language descriptions. Some definitions add that the captions are in English, and one specifies one or two captions per clip. A smaller line of work also describes it as being used for audio retrieval, semantic retrieval, or question answering, and a few papers refer to AudioCapsZS, AudioCaps-QA, or an AC evaluation set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AudioCaps to measure 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant use is for Audio captioning: papers evaluate generated captions on AudioCaps, sometimes on its test set, and report conventional captioning metrics such as CIDEr. More occasionally, papers report it as measuring Cross-modal retrieval through semantic retrieval on AudioCaps, and Text-to-audio generation through evaluation on the AC evaluation set, so the measurement claims extend beyond captioning but remain centered on it.

Space of uses. In practice, papers most often use AudioCaps alongside Clotho or Clotho v2, and some also report it together with MusicCaps or Clo

nodes.name: AUTO-J
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat AUTO-J as an LLM-based automated judge. Definitions describe it as a 13B-parameter generative judge model that rates the helpfulness of model responses on a numeric scale and is used to evaluate model responses. A smaller usage refers to AutoJ Eval, an in-domain pairwise-comparison test set from AUTO-J with 58 prompts and 1,392 response pairs, where human annotators label outcomes as win, tie, or lose.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers present AUTO-J as rating response helpfulness and, in another description, as assessing the distance between a reference answer and a model’s output. No constructs are linked to it, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it.

Space of uses. In use, papers position AUTO-J as a judge alongside other evaluators. One paper uses both AUTO-J and GPT-4 to evaluate model responses, while another places it with LLM judges such as ARES and PROMETHEUS for comparing a reference answer with a model output. A separate usage names AutoJ Eval as an in-domain pairwise-comparison test set.

nodes.name: Auto-J test set
nodes.definition:
What it is. The prevailing description treats Auto-J as a curated benchmark for meta-evaluation of LLM judges. A smaller line of work describes AutoJ as an automated judge benchmark for evaluating reward models, especially their correlation with human expert judgments. Some papers further refer to "Auto-J (Eval-P test set with ties)", describing it as a pairwise evaluation benchmark that includes ties.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported links are spread across 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator rather than centered on a single target. Papers use it to measure helpfulness, with AUTO-J providing 1-to-10 ratings, and text summarization, where the Auto-J model is used to measure win rates of model-generated summaries against human ones. Beyond those measurement uses, one paper records a causal relationship from the Auto-J test set to critique ability.

Space of uses. Papers position it both as a benchmark and as an evaluator used inside broader evaluation setups. One paper uses AutoJ alongside RewardBench and MT-Bench as one of several reward model benchmarks, another uses AUTO-J together with GPT-4 to rate responses, and another uses the Auto-J model to score summary wi

nodes.name: AutoDAN
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, AutoDAN is most commonly described as a jailbreak attack or procedure for generating adversarial prompts that bypass LLM safety alignment, usually with a genetic or hierarchical genetic algorithm. Several definitions add that it searches from human-designed attack prompts, can produce high-perplexity or human-readable prompts, and may use controllable text generation or an added loss term for stealthiness or interpretability; some papers also frame it as a white-box or optimization-based attack, while another describes instruction-based or query-based AutoDAN for jailbreak evaluation. A smaller line of work treats AutoDAN differently, including as a public dataset for jailbreak detection or as an attack included in the EasyJailbreak dataset for transferability evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link AutoDAN to 2 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators overall. Papers use it to measure adversarial robustness, safety robustness, and jailbreak resistance, typically by testing defenses against jailbreak attacks and reporting robustness or attack success rates; these measurement claims spread across several robustness-related targets rather than

nodes.name: Automated interpretability
names: Automated simulation evaluation with language models
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions describe it as an LLM-based evaluation procedure for SAE latents: the judge is given activating examples, works from a proposed or generated textual feature description, and is used to predict when the latent will activate or to score the explanation's predictive success. Some papers specify GPT-4o or GPT-4o-mini, one paper frames the protocol as automated interpretability classification with validation on new activating and non-activating examples, and another describes a related automated simulation evaluation that measures the correlation between actual activations and activations predicted from the explanation. One paper also applies the same prompting pattern to explain meta-latent groupings.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, claims converge on one construct: it measures Interpretability and explainability. The linked evidence describes this as evaluating the human-understandability of learned latents with an LLM as judge, or as using GPT-4o for automated interpretability classification. It is linked to one construct and no behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims do not spread across multiple constructs.

Space of use

nodes.name: AUXDATASET
nodes.definition: A 10-terabyte web-text corpus used as a proxy for proprietary training data when searching for exact substring matches in model outputs.

nodes.name: AV-Human
nodes.definition: The human-annotated subset of AVUT containing 698 videos and 1,734 question-answer pairs created by trained annotators.

nodes.name: bAbI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is to treat bAbI as a reasoning benchmark. One description presents it as a benchmark of 20 synthetic tasks designed to evaluate basic aspects of reasoning, while another uses it more narrowly for deductive reasoning questions requiring inference from a short passage; a smaller line of description cites it as a set of prerequisite toy question-answering tasks and an example of a language-based reasoning benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, bAbI is used to measure three constructs and one behavioral indicator. The most common claim is that it measures Logical reasoning, and smaller lines of work also report it as measuring Spatial reasoning and Temporal reasoning; one paper further links it to the behavioral indicator Coreference resolution, describing the benchmark as assessing "spatial and temporal reasoning, deduction, and coreference resolution" ("BABILong: Testing the Limits of LLMs with Long Context Reasoning-in-a-Haystack").

Space of uses. In use, papers link bAbI to one other measurement instrument, BABILong, and characterize that instrument as extending bAbI. Outside that relation, authors employ

nodes.name: BABILong
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, BABILong is most commonly described as a long-context benchmark for reasoning and retrieval, where models must find and reason over multiple pieces of evidence or supporting facts distributed in long sequences or extremely long documents. Some authors frame it as a long-context extension of bAbI over extended narratives, while one comparison description mentions it more broadly as a benchmark for evaluating long-context language models. Descriptions also differ on its task makeup: one paper calls it a benchmark of 5 tasks, while another says it includes 20 reasoning tasks such as fact chaining, simple induction, deduction, counting, and handling lists or sets.

What it is claimed to measure. Its claimed measurement targets are spread across several reasoning and context-related targets rather than centered on a single construct. Papers link it to 8 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators; among constructs, the recurring links are Long-context reasoning, Commonsense reasoning, and Context utilization, and among behavioral indicators they are Counting and Factual question answering, with 5 other constructs and 2 other behavioral indicators also linked. Relat

nodes.name: BabiStories
nodes.definition: A dataset of simple stories, which is a reproduction of TinyStories, used for training and evaluating language models in a controlled setting.

nodes.name: BabyAI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, BabyAI is most commonly described as a procedurally generated, partially observable 2D gridworld for evaluating agent capabilities on tasks given as textual or visual goals, especially navigation and object manipulation. Some authors describe it more specifically as an interactive 20x20 grid with a limited sight range for text-based agent evaluation, while others frame it as a grid-world benchmark with discrete navigation and interaction actions where an agent completes an instruction, including evaluation on instructions rephrased with synonyms.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BabyAI to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing measurement use is Navigation, with papers describing grid-world tasks in which agents navigate and interact with objects, and one paper referring to five types of navigation tasks. Smaller lines of work use it to measure Embodied planning and Instruction following, including natural language goal instructions such as Go to the tile (3,2) and Look behind the green locked door.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Across the papers, BabyAI is used as an embodied or grid-world ev

nodes.name: BACE
nodes.definition: A dataset from the MoleculeNet benchmark for the binary classification task of predicting binding results for the inhibition of human β-secretase 1.

nodes.name: Bamboogle
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Bamboogle is most commonly treated as a question answering benchmark for complex questions, often described as a multi-hop dataset involving web search and reasoning over multiple documents. It is also used as an unseen or out-of-domain evaluation task for RAG-tuned models, and one paper describes it as containing questions that Google answers incorrectly. The descriptions vary on coverage: some authors place it with datasets "derived from Wikipedia documents", while another says it "requires knowledge beyond Wikipedia's coverage".

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Bamboogle to 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure multi-hop question answering, with a broader question answering framing also recurring. A smaller line of work reports that it measures compositional reasoning and generalization, including out-of-domain generalization.

Space of uses. Papers usually use Bamboogle directly alongside other question answering benchmarks, especially HotPotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, WebQuestions, and PopQA. They variously position it as one of several established or widely used multi-hop QA datasets, as an unseen

nodes.name: BANKING77
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, BANKING77 is most commonly treated as a banking-domain intent classification benchmark containing customer or online banking queries. Most descriptions specify 77 intent classes or categories, and papers variously frame it as fine-grained intent detection, customer service intent classification, or a benchmark for domain-specific language understanding. Papers refer to it as BANKING, Banking-77, or Banking77; one paper instead uses Bank77 and describes it as an intent discovery dataset for finding unknown intents in user utterances.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use BANKING77 to measure two behavioral indicators and two constructs. The prevailing claim is that it measures intent classification, sometimes worded in the papers as intent detection, and it is also used for text classification. A smaller line of work uses it to measure robustness, in one case under various data heterogeneity settings, and reasoning, in a study evaluating reasoning accuracy across prompt engineering and demonstration selection techniques, so the linked measurement claims are spread across more than one target.

Space of uses. Most papers position BANKING77 as an e

nodes.name: BBBP
nodes.definition: A dataset from the MoleculeNet benchmark for the binary classification task of predicting whether a molecule can penetrate the blood-brain barrier.

nodes.name: BBH Object Counting
nodes.definition: A benchmark task used here as one of the general evaluation tasks for zero-shot and in-context performance.

nodes.name: BBQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is of BBQ as a question-answering benchmark or dataset for evaluating social bias, societal bias, or stereotype reliance. Most definitions describe ambiguous and disambiguated, or ambiguous and unambiguous, contexts with closed-ended answer choices, often multiple choice; one paper specifies three labels, Stereotyped, Unknown, and Unstereotyped. Papers also differ on scope and size, describing nine social dimensions or protected groups in several places, but also 11 bias categories in one account, and giving totals of 31,372 question-answer pairs or 58,492 unique questions in others.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers connect BBQ to three constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is to measure social bias: several papers describe it as evaluating biases against protected classes or groups, sometimes across nine social dimensions. Smaller lines of work use it to measure stereotyping and, in one case, social reasoning, while papers also report it as measuring question answering when bias is operationalized through QA tasks.

Space of uses. Papers usually position BBQ as a direct evaluation benchmark for bias, for e

nodes.name: BBQ Lite
nodes.definition: The Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) Lite, a subset of the full benchmark designed to measure social biases in language models across various demographic axes.

nodes.name: BC5CDR
nodes.definition: A document-level biomedical relation extraction dataset focused on binary relations between chemical and disease entities.

nodes.name: Beaver
nodes.definition: An enterprise database benchmark with 99 tables used to evaluate ambiguous and unanswerable semantic parsing tests in a real-world setting.

nodes.name: BeaverTails
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, BeaverTails is most commonly treated as a safety and alignment benchmark for model responses, often described as having human annotations over 14 harm or safety categories. Definitions vary on its format: some describe an evaluation subset of 700 prompts for query-answer interactions and helpfulness or harmlessness judgments, some describe advice queries with candidate answers, and others describe a larger resource of 330k annotated sentences; papers also frame it as containing safe and unsafe samples for alignment and attack simulation. One description states that the evaluation dataset comprises "700 prompts spanning 14 harm categories" (Aligner: Efficient Alignment by Learning to Correct).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use BeaverTails to measure 5 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so its reported role spans several targets rather than centering on only one. The prevailing claims concern harmlessness and helpfulness, with papers saying it categorizes annotations into helpfulness and harmlessness and that corresponding prompts are used for those evaluations; a smaller line of work reports it as measuring safety alignment, safety, and adver

nodes.name: BeaverTails-Evaluation
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is of an evaluation benchmark for LLM harmlessness on harmful instructions, with definitions emphasizing both content safety and refusal behavior. One paper also refers to its 700 test prompts that can potentially elicit harmful responses. A smaller line of work uses the name Beaver-eval for a public dataset of malicious instructions and describes it as one source used to construct SG-Bench.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to two constructs and no behavioral indicators. The dominant use is to measure Harmlessness: papers say it is used to evaluate a model's harmlessness, and one paper uses its harmful-response prompts for that purpose. A smaller usage treats it as measuring Safety more broadly, with one paper listing it among benchmarks that address safety.

Space of uses. Most papers use it directly as an evaluation benchmark. One paper includes it in a broader safety benchmark suite alongside XSTest, while another treats Beaver-eval as source material for constructing SG-Bench. No measurement instruments are linked to it.

nodes.name: BEHAVIOR-1K
nodes.definition: A benchmark of 1,000 everyday activities in realistic simulation, cited to show that daily tasks often involve multiple objects.

nodes.name: BEIR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat BEIR as a diverse benchmark suite for information retrieval, used for zero-shot or out-of-domain evaluation across domains. Papers describe it as a collection of diverse or public retrieval datasets, sometimes emphasizing ranking or re-ranking performance, and one definition names Covid, SciFact, DBpedia, and NFCorpus as included datasets. The coverage is described differently across papers, with references to 18 datasets, 14 public retrieval datasets excluding MS MARCO, or more generally a standard suite of retrieval benchmarks.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, its measurement claims cluster around retrieval-related outcomes. BEIR is linked to 2 constructs, most often Generalization and also Retrieval effectiveness, and to 2 behavioral indicators, Information retrieval and Ranking. Papers use it to measure out-of-domain or zero-shot retrieval performance, the generalization ability of ranking models, and re-ranking or retrieval effectiveness.

Space of uses. Papers often use BEIR as a main evaluation suite alongside MS MARCO, TREC Deep Learning benchmarks, and MTEB, and they describe it as a standard or widely used benchmark for do

nodes.name: Belebele
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Belebele is most commonly described as a multilingual reading comprehension benchmark, usually framed as multiple-choice questions over short passages. Definitions variously present it as assessing basic language understanding across many languages, as a multiple-choice machine reading comprehension dataset spanning 122 language variants or language-dialect combinations with parallel passages and questions, and as a corpus of questions over passages sourced from FLORES-200.
