Papers also describe its language coverage differently, including 122 languages, 122 language variants, and in one case translation into over 200 languages including 50+ African languages, and some note official or adapted Moroccan and Egyptian dialect sets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Belebele to one construct and four behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure machine reading comprehension, with additional uses for multiple-choice question answering, language understanding task performance, and question answering; one paper also uses it to measure multilingual ability. In these claims, the measurement focus stays mostly on reading comprehension and QA,

nodes.name: BFCL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, BFCL is most commonly described as a comprehensive benchmark or leaderboard for evaluating LLM function calling and tool use, often framed as executable function-call evaluation. Most definitions describe categories such as single-turn, multi-turn, hallucination, and executable function calling; other papers recast these as Non-live, Live, Multi-turn, and Hallucination, or emphasize simple, multiple, and parallel function calls with AST accuracy, execution, and relevance detection. Some authors also describe it as covering multiple programming languages, application domains, and real-world APIs, and papers refer to versioned releases and to the live&simple category.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BFCL to 2 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The measurement claims concentrate on Tool use and Tool use ability, with BFCL described as assessing whether models can call functions or tools accurately; additional papers use its Hallucination category to measure Hallucination and its multi-turn portion to measure Context retention. A separate paper also relates BFCL to Tool use ability by discussing its focus on tool-calling accuracy.

Space of u

nodes.name: BFCL-v2
nodes.definition: A tool-calling benchmark with Python-style tool call data across four categories (Simple, Multiple, Parallel, Parallel Multiple) to evaluate a model's ability to correctly call tools.

nodes.name: BIG-bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is of BIG-bench as a large, collaboratively built benchmark suite of over 200, often specifically 204, diverse tasks for probing the capabilities and limitations of language models. Papers usually describe broad coverage, often emphasizing reasoning, comprehension, traditional NLP tasks, and novel problems. A recurring variation is that authors work with named subsets or slices, including BIG-BENCH LITE, BBII, UICL categories, Date Understanding, and a verb tense subset, rather than treating it as a single fixed task set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use BIG-bench to measure 8 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims are spread across many targets rather than centered on one construct. At the construct level, papers report it as measuring Calibration, Emergent abilities, General ability, Logical reasoning, and Mathematical reasoning, and 3 other constructs. At the behavioral level, papers use tasks from BIG-bench to measure Word sorting, Date inference, and Table question answering, while Object counting is only reported as related to BIG-bench rather than measured by it.

Space of uses. In

nodes.name: BIG-Bench Hard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, BIG-Bench Hard is most commonly described as a challenging subset of BIG-Bench used for reasoning-focused evaluation. Most definitions emphasize hard tasks requiring complex or multi-step reasoning, though some also describe it as covering semantic understanding, language understanding, world knowledge, or general language understanding. Papers describe its makeup differently: many refer to 23 tasks, some to 27 tasks or 27 tasks across 23 task types, one to 21 tasks, and one to 23 multiple-choice tasks plus 4 free-form generation tasks. Some studies use only selected BBH tasks or categories, such as DATE, Navigate, Boolean Expression, Dyck Language, or sports_understanding, rather than the full suite.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BBH to 20 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure reasoning, with recurring construct claims around general ability and generalization, while other construct claims are more dispersed. On the behavioral side, the most recurrent named uses are complex reasoning question answering and instruction following, and the remaining 10 indicators are spread across other behaviors.

nodes.name: BIG-Bench Logical Deduction
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions treat BIG-Bench Logical Deduction as a task from BigBench for deductive or logical reasoning. Definitions describe it as testing deductive reasoning from a set of premises, and one paper further frames it as a symbolic reasoning benchmark for deduction over structured premises; a smaller framing describes it more generally as a benchmark for evaluating logical reasoning capabilities. Papers also use the shorter label "Deduction" and place it among BigBench datasets such as Date Understanding, Penguin, and Colored Objects.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to four constructs and one behavioral indicator. Its use as a measure does not converge on a single construct: papers use it to measure logical reasoning and symbolic reasoning, for example by including it among "seven logical reasoning tasks" or selecting it as one of four BigBench datasets for symbolic reasoning. A smaller set of links reports it as related to mathematical reasoning and to the reversal curse, and one paper claims a causal relationship from Chain of thought to BIG-Bench Logical Deduction.

Space of uses. Papers link it to two other measurement instruments, BIG-Bench Hard

nodes.name: bigcode-evaluation-harness
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, bigcode-evaluation-harness is most commonly treated as an evaluation framework or harness for running code-generation benchmarks and assessing models on coding tasks. Definitions largely converge on that role, while a smaller variation describes it as a software library, one paper highlights its use for HumanEval because it supports safe code execution, and others mention use with benchmarks such as HumanEval and MBPP and for assessing non-Python versions of APEval.

What it is claimed to measure. The measurement claims are narrow rather than spread across many targets: papers use it to measure Code generation, and it is linked to one behavioral indicator and no constructs. In relationship evidence, authors describe using the Bigcode Evaluation Harness as the evaluation tool for coding tasks, with one example reporting Pass@1 and Pass@10.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use it alongside Eleuther Harness or lm-evaluation-harness, with those paired with natural language tasks while bigcode-evaluation-harness is used for coding tasks; one paper also says evaluations are run under the same settings with lm-evaluation-harness and bigcode-evaluation-harness

nodes.name: BigCodeBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, BigCodeBench is most commonly described as a code generation benchmark centered on completion or function completion tasks that require correct use of library APIs and multiple function calls. Definitions also portray it as a Python benchmark with execution-based evaluation over 1,140 fine-grained, rich-context, multi-tool-use tasks drawn from 139 libraries and 7 domains, while another paper describes 148 function completion problems requiring multiple Python libraries. Some papers further describe it as covering diverse problems from cryptography to data visualization, and a smaller usage mentions the BigCodeBench Leaderboard plus the BigCodeBench-Hard and BigCodeBench-full subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BigCodeBench to 3 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing use is to measure code generation, with papers describing it as a benchmark for code generation, a harness for running and evaluating LM-written code, and a dataset attached to the code generation task. A recurring secondary framing says it measures tool use and instruction following, especially in tasks that require using tools and following complex instruc

nodes.name: BigCodeBench-Complete
nodes.definition: The structured-docstring version of BigCodeBench used to evaluate code generation from verbose programming prompts.

nodes.name: BigCodeBench-Instruct
nodes.definition: A variant of BigCodeBench that evaluates instruction-to-code generation, where models generate code from short, natural-language-oriented instructions.

nodes.name: BigMath
nodes.definition: Dataset of multi-step math problems used to evaluate tutoring models, containing problems of medium-to-high difficulty with annotated solve rates.

nodes.name: BioASQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat BioASQ as a biomedical question answering dataset or challenge, often tied to scientific literature or PubMed abstracts, while some definitions frame it more broadly as a resource for biomedical semantic indexing and question answering. Papers describe its contents in several ways, including human expert-written question-answer pairs with ground truth documents based on PubMed abstracts, and they vary in the question types they foreground: several mention factoid, list, and yes/no questions, while another mentions factoid, list, and summary questions. A narrower use focuses on Tasks 2B, 3B, and 4B and disregards long answers to assess the precision of short responses.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the prevailing measured use is question answering. BioASQ is linked to 2 behavioral indicators, Question answering and Text generation, and to no constructs; the more common claim is that it measures question answering, including PubMed-based biomedical QA for specialized domains and biology and medicine tasks. A smaller line of work also uses it to measure text generation in the biology and medicine domain.

Space of uses. Papers commo

nodes.name: Biography
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe Biography as a fact-seeking long-form generation dataset, or biography-generation task, centered on biographical information. In those descriptions it is used to evaluate factual consistency in narrative generation, factual long-form generation, and factual precision. One paper instead presents it as an out-of-domain test set and uses a subset with 183 questions about biography generation, whereas another definition specifies 181 prompts; a separate paper also describes the Biography dataset as synthetic and constructed for controlled experiments on spurious forgetting.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Biography to two constructs, Factuality and Knowledge forgetting, and to one behavioral indicator, Biography generation. The prevailing measurement claim is factuality: definitions describe it as evaluating factual consistency in narrative generation or out-of-domain factuality, and one paper reports FactScore on the Biography dataset for this purpose. Smaller uses treat it as measuring knowledge forgetting and biography generation directly.

Space of uses. The only named instrument linked to Biography is FActScore. Papers describe

nodes.name: BIRD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, BIRD is most commonly described as a large-scale, cross-domain, database-grounded Text-to-SQL benchmark, often framed as more challenging than earlier datasets because it includes complex databases, difficult questions, and reliance on external knowledge. Definitions also emphasize real-world coverage, with descriptions ranging from databases drawn from 37 domains to 95 databases, diverse cell-value formats, dirty values, and value-based reasoning; one sizing gives 9,428 training, 1,534 development, and 1,789 test pairs, while another describes over 12,751 unique question-SQL pairs totaling 33.4 GB. A smaller naming variant calls it BIRD-Bench, and some papers refer specifically to the development set, including a 1,534-example dev split with 11 databases or a dated 20240627 BIRD-dev version.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BIRD to 2 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing use is to measure Text-to-SQL, with papers evaluating natural language queries to SQL generation on it; a smaller line of work uses it to measure schema linking, and one paper reports it as measuring cross-domain generalization, explicitly describing traini

nodes.name: BiRdQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for question answering that, according to the paper's analysis, contains a non-trivial amount of answer ambiguity.

nodes.name: BizsRE
nodes.definition: BizsRE is a multilingual dataset created using machine translation models like Google Translate.

nodes.name: BLEnD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, BLEnD is most commonly described as a culture-specific benchmark dataset for everyday knowledge questions across diverse cultures and languages, with data sourced from authentic, real-world scenarios in native-speaking regions. Some authors describe it through particular parts or settings, such as its short-answer questions in native languages, while another presents it as a traditional annotation setup in which annotators answered fixed questions from 500 pre-defined templates for Indonesian and Nigerian cultural knowledge. One description also expands the name as the Benchmark of Linguistic and ENcyclopedic Diversity and frames it around culturally diverse inputs.

What it is claimed to measure. Most descriptions frame BLEnD as testing everyday knowledge across cultures and languages. One paper describes it as designed to measure model performance on culturally diverse inputs, and another uses it to assess generalization of cultural awareness in LLMs. Papers do not explicitly link BLEnD to any constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. BLEnD appears as a standalone evaluation benchmark in the available papers. Reported uses include adoptin

nodes.name: BLiMP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, BLiMP is most commonly described as an English benchmark, corpus, dataset, or test suite of linguistic minimal pairs for grammaticality or acceptability judgments. The prevailing setup is pairs of minimally different acceptable and unacceptable sentences, used to test whether a model identifies the grammatical sentence or assigns lower perplexity to it. Most descriptions refer to 67 paradigms or subtasks with 1,000 pairs each, spanning syntax, morphology, and semantics, though some describe 12 grouped categories or phenomena, one paper states 13 phenomena, and some emphasize template-generated or manually crafted materials totaling 67,000 pairs; one study further restricts BLiMP to 11 datasets usable for generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use BLiMP to measure six constructs, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The most frequent uses are to measure syntactic competence, language proficiency, explanation faithfulness, formal linguistic competence, and linguistic knowledge, with one additional construct also linked. Across relationships, the claims are spread across several construct labels rather than a single exclusive label.

Sp

nodes.name: BLINK
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is of BLINK as a multi-image benchmark, or benchmark suite, for visual perception and reasoning, especially multi-view and spatial relationships. Several papers also describe it as a collection of 14 visual perception tasks that humans can quickly solve, covering indoor, outdoor, and natural scenes; some tasks involve multiple images, including visual similarity and multi-view reasoning, and papers mention Jigsaw and Multi-view reasoning splits. A smaller line of work frames it more generally as a benchmark meant to test whether multimodal language models can perceive as well as see.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BLINK to five constructs and one behavioral indicator. The most common claim is that it measures multi-image reasoning, with papers using it in multi-image understanding, multi-image tasks, and multi-image analysis settings; smaller strands also use it to measure spatial reasoning, visual perception, and visual reasoning. One survey further reports it as measuring hallucination, and a separate paper treats it as related to long-context understanding rather than as a direct measure, so the report

nodes.name: Blocksworld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Blocksworld is most commonly treated as a classical planning benchmark or domain in which blocks are rearranged from an initial or source configuration to a specified goal configuration, often on a table and sometimes with the explicit rule that only one unstacked block may be moved at a time. Definitions vary at the margins: some papers formulate it in PDDL, some describe it as a symbolic or commonsense domain, some call it a planning dataset, and some place it within PlanBench or describe it as a real-world task planning benchmark that corresponds to path-finding in a state transition graph. A smaller line of work also defines task-specific splits inside it, including plan-length train, validation, and test partitions and in-distribution versus out-of-distribution block-count ranges.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement use is concentrated on Planning. Papers use Blocksworld to measure 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator, with Planning the prevailing target, described in relationship evidence as a real-world task planning benchmark, a symbolic planning problem, or simply the planning task on which a framework is evaluated. Smalle

nodes.name: BMIKE-53
nodes.definition: BMIKE-53 is a multilingual dataset created using LLMs for translation.

nodes.name: BOLD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the prevailing description is an open-ended language generation benchmark, or bias evaluation dataset, for fairness and bias assessment in model outputs. Definitions describe English prompts for bias benchmarking, sometimes specified as Wikipedia-derived prompts spanning five domains, race, gender, profession, religion, and politics; some authors say it assesses sentiment or the affective properties of generated text, and another describes a large-scale setup that prompts models with diverse demographic terms. A smaller line of work also frames it as a fairness and toxicity benchmark, particularly for analyzing gender bias.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BOLD to 2 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The most prevalent claim is that it measures social bias, and a smaller line of work treats it as measuring stereotyping, including analyses of LM gender bias; individual papers also report it as measuring biased content generation and text generation. Across these links, the reported uses stay centered on bias in open-ended generation.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked directly to it, but papers also deploy it al

nodes.name: Bongard Problems
nodes.definition: A family of abstract reasoning tasks consisting of two sets of six images each, where the model must identify the conceptual rule distinguishing the sets and express it in natural language.

nodes.name: BookMIA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the prevailing description is of BookMIA as a membership inference benchmark built from book text, and one definition also calls it a prior temporal detection dataset. Papers describe its contents somewhat differently: some define it as text excerpts from books published in 2023, after the knowledge cutoff of the studied models, paired with passages from popular books as memorized examples, while another describes paragraphs extracted from copyrighted books. A smaller usage keeps only the items labeled "unseen," defined as paragraphs from books published after the release of the models.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BookMIA to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The construct-level use is Memorization, where it is reported as evaluating unseen book excerpts against potentially memorized popular-book passages; at the behavioral-indicator level, papers use it to measure Pre-training data detection and, in a smaller use, Creative writing, where one study uses book snippets from BookMIA as human texts. Papers also describe it as measuring Membership inference attack, so the reported measurement claims span memorization and pretraining

nodes.name: Books3
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats Books3 as a large collection of books used as a dataset or benchmark for language model evaluation, especially on long-context or extremely long documents. Definitions describe it as an extensive collection of books, a large-scale dataset of text from a wide variety of books, or a large dataset for long-context sequences, and one paper uses the spelling Book3.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Books3 to one construct and no behavioral indicators, and the measurement claims converge on length generalization. In that usage, Books3 is reported as measuring length generalization through language modeling evaluations such as perplexity, with one snippet stating that perplexity on Books3 'shows better extrapolation' and another using Books3 among real-world datasets when reporting length generalization gains.

Space of uses. Most papers position Books3 as an evaluation dataset or benchmark rather than as a standalone target. It is used alongside PG-19 or Gutenberg in evaluations over book datasets and alongside Arxiv in model-performance experiments, and papers link it to one other measurement instrument, The Pile, thro

nodes.name: BookSum
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, BookSum is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for book or long-form narrative summarization on long inputs. The descriptions differ on granularity and content: some papers frame it as evaluating summaries of entire books, others call it a collection of datasets for long-form narrative summarization over novels, plays, and stories, and another describes each example as a book chapter paired with a summary of that chapter’s content.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use BookSum to measure Text summarization, and it is linked to one behavioral indicator in total. No constructs are linked to it, so the reported measurement claims are concentrated on summarization rather than spread across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers use BookSum as a standalone evaluation dataset rather than alongside other linked measurement instruments. In the available descriptions, it is used to assess long-context and long-response generation capabilities, to evaluate models on a book summarization dataset, and to evaluate takedown methods in the books domain.

nodes.name: BookTection
nodes.definition: A membership inference benchmark for book excerpts used as a prior temporal detection dataset.

nodes.name: BoolQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, BoolQ is most commonly described as a yes/no question-answering benchmark or dataset, typically with a question paired with a passage or short context and a binary answer, and often framed as reading comprehension or commonsense reasoning. Several definitions add that the questions are natural or naturally occurring and unprompted; some descriptions say the questions are about Wikipedia articles, and one paper describes BoolQ as a closed-book QA dataset. One paper spells out the format and size, stating that each example has a question, a passage, and a binary answer, with 15942 examples split into train, validation, and test.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use BoolQ to measure a broad range of targets rather than a single one: it is linked to 9 constructs and 10 behavioral indicators. The prevailing construct-level framing is commonsense reasoning, and other recurring uses frame it as measuring machine reading comprehension, question answering, reasoning, and language understanding task performance. The remaining links are spread across additional construct and task framings, so papers do not present a single exclusive measurement claim.

Spa

nodes.name: BorderLines
nodes.definition: Benchmark containing multilingual questions about disputed territories, designed to test model consistency and handling of conflicting claims.

nodes.name: BRIGHT
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the available work, BRIGHT is treated as a text retrieval benchmark centered on reasoning in retrieval. It is described as focusing on complex queries that require deep reasoning to identify useful passages beyond simple semantic relevance, and one abstract presents it as the first text retrieval benchmark requiring intensive reasoning to retrieve relevant documents.

What it is claimed to measure. Its measurement claims are narrow rather than spread across many targets. Papers link BRIGHT to 1 construct, Information retrieval ability, and to no behavioral indicators; the recorded relationship is that Information retrieval ability is measured by BRIGHT. In those uses, BRIGHT is presented as benchmarking retrieval on challenging, reasoning-intensive queries.

Space of uses. Papers position BRIGHT as a challenging benchmark for evaluating retrieval systems. In LimRank: Less is More for Reasoning-Intensive Information Reranking, it is used alongside FOLLOWIR, with BRIGHT covering reasoning-intensive retrieval and FOLLOWIR covering instruction-following retrieval. No other measurement instrument is linked to it in the recorded relationships.

nodes.name: C3
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, C3 is most commonly treated as a Chinese reading comprehension benchmark or dataset, described both as Chinese Cloze-style Reading Comprehension and as a Chinese machine reading comprehension benchmark for evaluating reading comprehension in Chinese. A smaller variation in wording presents it as a modern Chinese reading comprehension dataset used to test the generalizability of a procedure, while other descriptions add that it covers Chinese passages and questions and is a free-form multiple-choice dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Its measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers link it to one behavioral indicator and one construct. One paper uses it to measure Machine reading comprehension, describing C3 as a free-form multiple-choice Chinese machine reading comprehension dataset, and another reports it as measuring Chinese language understanding through Chinese comprehension.

Space of uses. Papers use C3 as an evaluation benchmark or test set. One study explicitly marks it as a test benchmark, and another uses it to evaluate a procedure on a modern Chinese reading comprehension dataset to demonstrate th

nodes.name: C4
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, C4 is most commonly treated as a large, cleaned web-text corpus derived from Common Crawl, sometimes described more specifically as English text and sometimes as a general-domain dataset. The prevailing use is as a language-modeling benchmark where papers report perplexity or loss, though some papers also present it as calibration data for quantization or pruning, as pretraining or continual-training data, as a source of prompts for open-ended generation, and as material for neuron-activation analysis. Papers also refer to variants and subsets such as the en subset, c4 en-validation, the C4 validation set or C4 validation loss, the C4 Corpus, the first shard, and subsets of validation data.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link C4 to four constructs and one behavioral indicator. The most recurring reported use is to measure Text generation, with several papers evaluating it on C4, usually through perplexity; individual papers also report C4 as measuring Generative ability, Language modeling ability, Length generalization, and Quantization robustness. Overall, the measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than concentrated on a

nodes.name: C-Eval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, C-Eval is most commonly described as a comprehensive Chinese evaluation benchmark, or a multi-level, multi-discipline suite for foundation models. Definitions often say it covers 52 subjects or academic disciplines, including STEM, humanities, and social sciences; one paper further describes four difficulty levels, and another says it contains 13,948 multiple-choice questions. A smaller line of work frames it more by task, as a benchmark for cross-linguistic multi-task language understanding, Chinese instruction-following, or general knowledge and problem solving, and some studies use only subsets such as the logic subject or selected subjects.

What it is claimed to measure. Use claims are centered on general ability, but not limited to it. Papers link C-Eval to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators: it is most often used to measure General ability, while smaller lines of work use it to measure Generalization and Multilingual understanding, and single-paper uses report it as evaluating Chinese instructions or as a source of subjects for Multiple-choice question answering. Overall, the recorded claims converge most on a broad general-capability framing

nodes.name: CAA
nodes.definition: Contrastive Attribute Analysis, a method and dataset for extracting steering vectors using binary-choice contrastive prompts and evaluating model behavior via output probabilities and GPT-4o mini scoring.

nodes.name: Caltech101
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions describe Caltech101 as an image or object classification dataset or benchmark with 101 object categories, used for visual recognition evaluation. Papers also place it in broader evaluation setups, for example among nine benchmark datasets for image classification and in an 11-dataset image-classification suite, and one paper reports 4,331 test images from 101 classes.

What it is claimed to measure. Across reported links, papers use it to measure one behavioral indicator and two constructs. The recurring claim is that it measures image classification, while a smaller line of work reports that it is used to measure personalization and generalization, so the recorded uses extend beyond a single construct.

Space of uses. Papers commonly include it as one dataset within larger image-classification suites rather than presenting it on its own. It appears alongside datasets such as ImageNet, StanfordCars, Flowers102, CUB, and OxfordPets, with several other classification datasets also used, and papers position it in zero-shot and linear-probe evaluations as well as in multi-dataset studies of personalization and generalization.

nodes.name: Candle
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, CANDLE is most commonly treated as a cultural benchmark or dataset, though one definition instead describes Candle as an international research program studying human values that is used with the World Values Survey to select sensitive topics. Papers describe the benchmark form as a multiple-choice question benchmark, larger in sample size at 1.1M, with a focus on cultural norms and commonsense knowledge. Another paper frames it as a prior dataset for culture-specific items that extracts cultural commonsense knowledge from web-scale corpora.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers link it to 1 construct, Cultural knowledge, and to no behavioral indicators. In that usage, it is reported as measuring general cultural knowledge, and no other construct is linked to it here.

Space of uses. Papers most often position it as part of a suite of cultural evaluations. One study says it is used with CULTURALBENCH as a multiple-choice benchmark, and another places it alongside CULTURALBENCH and ETICOR for general cultural knowledge evaluation; elsewhere it is used as

nodes.name: CapsBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark used to evaluate fine-grained captioning and visual perception.

nodes.name: CASIE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage is as a cybersecurity event extraction or event detection dataset. Definitions describe it as focused on cybersecurity incidents with trigger and argument annotations, and some descriptions specify five event types, Databreach, Phishing, Ransom, Discover, and Patch; one paper also describes it as identifying security-related incidents from technical reports and news, while another places its evaluation setting in cyber threat reports.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CASIE to one construct and one behavioral indicator. It is used to measure Event argument extraction, and one paper also uses it in an evaluation framed as measuring Generalization, describing results from "extensive evaluations across six datasets" to demonstrate generalizability. In the surveyed work, these measurement claims center on those two targets rather than a wider spread of constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to CASIE. Across the cited uses, papers place it within broader experimental suites, for example as one of "16 IE benchmarks" or within evaluations spanning six datasets, and one table

nodes.name: CausalVLBench
nodes.definition: A comprehensive benchmark for evaluating visual causal reasoning in Large Vision-Language Models, encompassing tasks of causal structure inference, intervention target prediction, and counterfactual prediction.

nodes.name: CB
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats CB, often expanded as CommitmentBank, as a SuperGLUE natural language inference or textual entailment benchmark over short premises and hypotheses or other short texts. Several definitions add that it evaluates whether a sentence or statement commits the author to a belief or entailment, some specify entailment, contradiction, and neutrality between a premise and a hypothesis, and one paper frames it more broadly as a general NLU classification task.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what CB measures are concentrated rather than spread out: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Natural language inference, and to no constructs. Papers use it to measure Natural language inference, and related descriptions also say it evaluates textual entailment, in one case with an emphasis on pragmatic inference.

Space of uses. Papers usually position CB as one task within larger evaluation suites rather than as a standalone protocol. It is linked to one other measurement instrument, SuperGLUE, and papers commonly describe it as part of that benchmark; across examples it appears alongside RTE and COPA, and also with BoolQ and Wi

nodes.name: CC3M
nodes.definition: The Conceptual Captions 3M dataset, containing millions of image-URL/alt-text pairs, used for pretraining and, in this paper, for a large-scale compositional evaluation.

nodes.name: CCBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark used to assess the general multimodal capabilities of models.

nodes.name: CelebA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a large-scale face or facial attributes dataset of celebrity images, often described as having over 200K images with 40 attribute annotations or binary labels. Some authors frame it more specifically as a face-image classification benchmark, while others use it for facial attribute recognition or for building emotion-comparison examples from facial cues such as smiling. A smaller line of work describes task-specific protocols or preprocessing, such as taking Blond Hair as the target and Male as the sensitive attribute, or cropping, resizing, and flattening pixel values into space-separated numerical sentences.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CelebA to two behavioral indicators, Image classification and Image reconstruction, and no constructs. The recorded measured_by links do not converge on a construct; instead, papers use CelebA to measure those two behavioral indicators. In their own descriptions, papers also report using it to evaluate fairness, robustness under distribution shifts and spurious attribute correlations, early-exit diffusion-based image generation, disentanglement, and attribute-scoring reliabili

nodes.name: CFBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, CFBench is most commonly described as a complex instruction-following benchmark built around instructions with multiple constraints. Definitions emphasize coverage of a comprehensive range of constraint types, including format, content, and style. A less common description presents it as a comprehensive Chinese benchmark for evaluating constraint comprehension and following capabilities through a multi-dimensional evaluation framework, and shared definitions also state that it is evaluated with GPT-4 as a judge.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CFBench to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing claim is that it measures Complex instruction following ability, with papers using it for evaluations where instructions consist of multiple constraints and for comprehensive assessment of model capabilities. Papers also use it to measure Instruction following ability and the behavioral indicator Instruction following, so the linked uses are concentrated on instruction following, especially formulations centered on multiple constraints.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use CFBench alongside FollowBench, and some evaluations also place it w

nodes.name: CHAIR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, CHAIR is most commonly described as a benchmark, metric, or evaluation protocol for hallucination in image captioning, especially object hallucination. The prevailing description is that it compares generated captions with ground-truth objects or annotations and computes the proportion or ratio of mentioned objects that are not present in the image; most papers describe instance and sentence variants, written as CHAIRi and CHAIRs, for hallucinated object instances and sentences containing hallucinated objects. Some papers describe the same evaluation as open-ended captioning on sampled MS-COCO images, and a smaller line describes broader sentence- or image-level checks such as object, attribute, count, or positional correctness.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CHAIR to five behavioral indicators and one construct. The most frequent use is to measure Hallucination, Image captioning, and Object hallucination, with papers saying that CHAIR assesses hallucination by comparing objects mentioned in generated captions with ground-truth or reference objects; additional links treat it as measuring Text generation in open-ended generation

nodes.name: Charades-STA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats Charades-STA as a benchmark dataset for temporal grounding: localizing a video segment, or identifying the start and end timestamps of video content, from a natural language sentence. A smaller framing describes it as a temporal activity localization dataset, and one definition says it is used as a source for event-caption alignment and temporal video grounding. One paper summarizes it as "temporal activity localization via language query" (E.T. Bench: Towards Open-Ended Event-Level Video-Language Understanding).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Charades-STA to measure temporal grounding, the only linked behavioral indicator; no constructs are linked to it. The relationship evidence describes this as evaluating the ability to locate specific activities described in text, including moment retrieval with recall at IoU thresholds and tasks that identify start and end timestamps from a query sentence. In these links, claims converge on this single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers position Charades-STA mainly as an evaluation benchmark or test set for tempora

nodes.name: ChartGaze
nodes.definition: A high-precision eye-tracking dataset for chart question answering that pairs chart images and questions with human gaze annotations.

nodes.name: ChartMimic
nodes.definition: Benchmark for evaluating chart-to-code generation, assessing both code executability and chart fidelity through high-level (image similarity) and low-level (code similarity) metrics.

nodes.name: ChartQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, ChartQA is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for question answering about charts, often framed as requiring both visual perception and logical reasoning. Several descriptions make that more specific by mentioning item comparison, counting, numerical computation, or even complex, multi-step logical and visual reasoning; a smaller set of papers frames it more broadly as figure QA or a document task dataset, and one paper refers to it as VQAChart. Papers also vary in how they describe its contents, including real-world charts from sources such as Statista and Pew Research, human-created and LLM-augmented questions in one account, and a mixture of handwritten and machine-generated questions in another; one reuse paper states that it contains 18K real-world charts and 23.1K human-authored QA pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ChartQA to 5 behavioral indicators and 4 constructs, so its reported measurement role is spread across chart-specific evaluation and broader multimodal assessment rather than concentrated on a single target. Among behavioral indicators, papers most often use it to measure chart and diagram understanding

nodes.name: ChartX
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing framing is a chart-to-code benchmark for assessing text and data reproducibility in generated code, with attention to accurate rendering of chart content. A smaller usage treats ChartX as a figure description dataset, specifically as one of the sampled sources for F2TBenchmark. One paper further describes it as providing fixed instructions to GPT-4 to write code that procedurally generates predefined chart types and settings in bulk.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ChartX to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The recorded uses are Code generation, where one paper says it evaluates MLLMs' code generation ability, especially for text and data reproducibility, and Figure-to-text generation, where another paper lists it under figure description. The measurement claims therefore spread across 2 behavioral indicators rather than converging on a construct.

Space of uses. In chart-to-code work, papers use ChartX alongside ChartMimic and Plot2Code as one of the benchmarks on which methods are evaluated. In figure-to-text work, one paper uses it differently, as one of the sampled sources for F2TBenchmark.

Concerns raised. A

nodes.name: CharXiv
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe CharXiv as a benchmark or evaluation suite for chart understanding and complex visual reasoning. Definitions present it as using real-world chart data from arXiv preprints, and one definition specifies 2,323 natural, challenging, and diverse charts with hand-curated descriptive and reasoning questions. Across these descriptions, some authors call it a benchmark dataset, while others call it a comprehensive evaluation suite.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CharXiv to measure one construct and two behavioral indicators. The linked construct is reasoning, and the linked behavioral indicators are chart and diagram understanding and complex reasoning question answering. The relationship evidence also describes its reasoning questions as requiring synthesizing information across complex visual elements.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to CharXiv. In use, papers report validation-set results on it to compare systems across domains, particularly on tasks involving complex visual reasoning and interpretation of charts and graphs, and one survey positions it as expanding chart-understanding scenarios through real-

nodes.name: Chatbot Arena
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the dominant framing is a crowdsourced, open or public evaluation platform and leaderboard for anonymous pairwise battles between model responses. Definitions usually describe users comparing two side by side outputs in open-ended conversational tasks, with human preference votes turned into Elo rankings or pairwise win-rates that support system ranking; some papers also describe it as a large human preference dataset or a collection of user prompts and tasks. A few definitions instead cast it as an evaluation framework using LLM judges, as a multimodal arena variant, or as an evaluation set or dataset of real-world user-assistant interactions, including a 5.2k-instance set and multilingual data; one paper uses the name ChatArena for a multi-agent language game framework.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Chatbot Arena to 7 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement target is spread across several concepts rather than only one. The prevailing use is to measure human preference alignment, with conversational ability and general ability also recurring; papers also report it as measuring emotional intelligence and multi

nodes.name: Chatbot Arena Conversations
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available papers, it is most commonly described as the LMSys Chatbot Arena Conversations dataset, a collection of real-world user preferences gathered from user votes on pairwise comparisons of LLM outputs. Another paper describes it as a dataset of human-annotated pairwise model comparisons.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers do not link this dataset to any named constructs or behavioral indicators. In their own descriptions, they use it to capture real-world user preferences and to compute human agreement with LLM judge decisions.

Space of uses. One paper positions it as a usage dataset for broader real-world preferences, stating that "the usage datasets capture broader real-world preferences" (HumT DumT: Measuring and controlling human-like language in LLMs). Another uses it to compute human agreement and evaluates agreement on held-out test instructions not used for model selection; the papers do not link it to other measurement instruments.

nodes.name: ChatEval
nodes.definition: ChatEval is an evaluation framework that uses multi-agent collaboration to assess model outputs, aiming for preference judgments that are better aligned with humans.

nodes.name: ChatRAG-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats ChatRAG-Bench as a benchmark for retrieval-augmented generation and conversational question answering. Definitions differ on the task framing: some describe short-context evaluation within a 4K token window, including "nine short context (within 4K) tasks," while others describe multi-turn question answering with retrieved text chunks; another paper-level description presents it as a benchmark for evaluating RAG and conversational question answering capabilities of LLMs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, conversational question answering, and to no constructs. The recorded measurement claim uses ChatRAG-Bench to measure conversational question answering, with one paper describing it as "the RAG benchmark for conversational QA tasks within a 4K context window," so the reported measurement use is focused on that single behavioral target rather than spread across multiple constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation benchmark for conversational QA and short-context RAG settings. One paper states, "We use ChatRAG Bench (Liu et al., 2024) as our benchmark for

nodes.name: ChEBI-20
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, ChEBI-20 is most commonly described as a dataset used in molecule-text tasks: one definition says it is widely used for text-based molecule generation, where a model generates a molecular sequence from a textual description, and another says it contains molecules and their corresponding text descriptions for molecule-text alignment and caption generation. A smaller line of work describes it differently, as the molecular graph VQA ChEBI-20 used for fine-tuning and copyright-tracking evaluation. One paper also reports using a restricted subset by selecting molecules containing fewer than 100 atoms.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement use is concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers use ChEBI-20 to measure one behavioral indicator, Molecule captioning, and it is not linked to any constructs. The evidence is performance-focused, with papers reporting the performance of molecule captioning on ChEBI-20 and using it to test molecule description generation.

Space of uses. Papers use ChEBI-20 both as a direct evaluation dataset and in conjunction with other resources. In captioning evaluations, it is used alongs

nodes.name: CheckEval
nodes.definition: Checklist-based LLM-as-a-Judge framework that evaluates text generation by decomposing criteria into binary yes/no questions and computing scores based on the proportion of affirmative responses.

nodes.name: ChemProt
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a biomedical labeled dataset for chemical-protein interaction tasks in scientific literature. Most definitions frame it as a relation extraction or classification dataset, with one paper specifying that it features five relation classes and describing the up regulator and down regulator classes as mutually exclusive. A smaller line of work describes it instead as a named entity detection resource with annotations for chemical compounds and gene or protein-related objects from article paragraphs, and derives the subsets ChemProt-Chem and ChemProt-Gene.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ChemProt to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The construct-level use is Adaptability, where it is included among labeled downstream tasks in biomedicine. At the behavioral level, papers use it to measure Relation extraction and Text classification, so the recorded measurement claims cover more than one task framing.

Space of uses. Papers often use ChemProt as one item in broader biomedical evaluation suites or downstream task collections. It appears alongside RCT, and in one biomedical evaluation setup also alongside PubMedQA,

nodes.name: CHENGYU-BENCH
nodes.definition: A comprehensive benchmark for Chinese idiom understanding, assessing models across three tasks: evaluative connotation (sentiment classification), appropriateness (misuse detection), and open cloze (idiom generation in context), with 2,937 human-verified examples covering 1,765 idioms.

nodes.name: Chess
nodes.definition: An evaluation task using a textual representation of the game of chess, where the agent's goal is to make moves that result in victory.

nodes.name: ChID
nodes.definition: A large-scale cloze test dataset for Chinese idiom comprehension, containing 581k passages with multiple-choice idiom selection tasks from news, novels, and essays.

nodes.name: CHIME
nodes.definition: CHIME (Hsu et al., 2024), a taxonomy-generation baseline that extracts claims and frequent entities and prompts an LLM to build a hierarchical structure.

nodes.name: Chinese SimpleQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark introduced by Alibaba Group comprising concise, fact-oriented questions to assess the factual capabilities of LLMs in a Chinese context, focusing on general knowledge.

nodes.name: CIFAR-10
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a standard or benchmark image classification dataset, most often described as 60,000 32x32 color images in 10 classes. Some definitions compress this to a 10-class object recognition or small-image classification benchmark, while a few papers describe it more situationally, for example as a testbed for clustering comparisons, automated accuracy prediction under synthetic and natural shifts, dirty-sample detection under poisoned or noisy samples, or zero-shot adversarial robustness.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator and 3 constructs. The prevailing use is to measure Image classification, with studies using it for finetuning, zero-shot classification, linear probing, and downstream performance evaluation. One paper each also uses it to measure Generalization, Label noise robustness, and Multimodal alignment, so the measurement claims are centered on image classification rather than distributed evenly across several constructs.

Space of uses. Most papers position it as one benchmark within broader image-evaluation suites, often alongside CIFAR-100 and ImageNet, and also with STL-10, CUB, and Pla

nodes.name: CIFAR-100
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, it is most commonly described as an image classification benchmark or dataset with 100 classes, often framed as 100 fine-grained object classes or categories. Some definitions add that it consists of 32x32 color images, and several papers explicitly contrast it with CIFAR-10 as a more challenging or more complex setting; papers also use both spellings, CIFAR-100 and CIFAR100.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing use is to measure Image classification, which is the only linked behavioral indicator and the one attached to most papers, covering finetuning, zero-shot classification, linear probing, transfer learning, and downstream performance. Papers also link it to 2 constructs, Generalization and Multimodal alignment: one paper evaluates the generalization of discrete prompts on CIFAR-100, and another reports alignment scores on CIFAR-100 to measure multimodal alignment. Overall, the measurement claims concentrate on image classification rather than spreading evenly across constructs.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to other measurement instruments directly, but they commonly use it inside multi-benchmark evaluation suites, most often along

nodes.name: CipherChat
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats CipherChat as a jailbreak method or framework that encodes prompts in cipher, most often a Caesar cipher, to bypass safety alignment and probe a model's intrinsic or inherent characteristics. Most descriptions emphasize the cipher-based prompting itself, with some specifying a three-letter Caesar shift, while one paper gives a fuller procedural account: user instructions are enciphered, a system prompt and few-shot enciphered demonstrations are added, the model is checked for responding in cipher, and the output is then deciphered.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CipherChat to one construct and no behavioral indicators. The linked construct is Safety alignment, and the claims converge on that single target: papers use CipherChat to measure or examine safety alignment, including a report that it is used to "systematically examine the generalizability of safety alignment to non-natural languages, ciphers" (GPT-4 Is Too Smart To Be Safe: Stealthy Chat with LLMs via Cipher).

Space of uses. Papers use it by encoding user instructions or questions in cipher, commonly a Caesar cipher with shift three, and the

nodes.name: CiteSeer
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, CiteSeer is most commonly described as a real-world citation network dataset of scientific papers or publications. The prevailing usage treats its nodes as papers and uses the dataset for node classification evaluation. A smaller line of work describes a modified CiteSeer for link prediction, with nodes from the original node classification test set removed.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CiteSeer to measure two behavioral indicators, with claims concentrated on node classification and a smaller usage for link prediction. Across the papers, the dominant framing is that CiteSeer measures node classification, while a single paper reports it as evaluating link prediction. No constructs are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers commonly place CiteSeer in multi-dataset evaluations, most visibly alongside Cora and, in broader benchmark suites, PubMed, ogbn-arXiv, ogbn-products, and Wiki-CS. In node classification studies it appears as one dataset among several benchmark datasets, while in the link prediction use it is paired with a modified Cora and treated as an evaluation dataset after removing the original node classification test nodes.

nodes.name: CLAIR
nodes.definition: Automated evaluation metric that measures overall caption quality by assessing alignment with reference captions using GPT-4o.

nodes.name: ClassEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the dominant framing is of a benchmark for object-oriented, class-level code generation. Definitions describe it as assessing object-oriented programming skills and class-level code generation abilities, and some descriptions add that it is a manually crafted collection of 100 class-level Python code generation tasks. Papers also describe it as containing 100 standalone programming tasks from seven domains, and one evaluation setup further specifies 100 classes, 410 methods, an average of 33 tests per class, and 8 tests per method.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure one behavioral indicator, code generation, and do not link it to any constructs. The prevailing claim is specifically class-level code generation: papers state that they evaluate code LLMs on class-level code generation using ClassEval and list it with other benchmarks for code generation, so the reported measurement role converges on that single indicator rather than spreading across multiple targets.

Space of uses. In use, papers usually place it within broader benchmark suites, listing it alongside LiveCodeBench, BigCodeBench, HumanEval, MBPP, and DevEval

nodes.name: CLEVR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, CLEVR is most commonly treated as a visual reasoning benchmark or diagnostic dataset, often framed around compositional language and elementary visual reasoning. Some definitions instead describe it as question answering about 3D scenes, and one paper uses it as an image classification task. A smaller line of work specifies a particular subset, using the val split with 15,000 images of cylinders, cubes, and spheres in different sizes and colors for multimodal data understanding and retrieval.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CLEVR to one construct and no behavioral indicators. The measurement claims converge on a single target: one paper claims that Chain-of-thought reasoning is measured by CLEVR, describing the setting as complex reasoning in CLEVR. No other construct is linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers use CLEVR in several roles, and no measurement instrument is linked to it. Some include it as one task within a broader evaluation suite, for example among image classification tasks, while others use it as a scene reasoning domain for inductive program synthesis or for multimodal data understanding and retrieving. Another recu

nodes.name: Climate-FEVER
nodes.definition: Climate-FEVER is a benchmark for fact checking focused on claims about climate change.

nodes.name: CLIMATEVIZ
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for scientific fact-checking over climate-related charts, containing 49,862 claims paired with 2,896 expert-curated visualizations, each labeled as support, refute, or not enough information, and including structured knowledge graph explanations.

nodes.name: CLINC150
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant description of CLINC150 is an English intent classification or intent detection benchmark organized around 150 intents or classes. Papers agree on the 150-class framing but describe the domain structure differently: one definition says 10 domains, another says multiple domains such as banking and travel, and one paper describes 150 classes across five domains. A smaller line also treats it as an intent clustering benchmark, and one dataset-construction paper uses sample sentences from CLINC while extracting 40 intents from five domains for culturally adapted utterance generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CLINC150 to one behavioral indicator, Intent classification, and one construct, Reasoning. The prevailing usage is to measure Intent classification or intent detection: one relationship says it is designed for intent classification, and another paper reports using CLINC for intent detection. A smaller usage reports it as measuring Reasoning, describing evaluations of reasoning accuracy across benchmark datasets that include CLINC150.

Space of uses. Papers often position CLINC150 as one benchmark among several. It appears a

nodes.name: ClinTox
nodes.definition: A dataset from the MoleculeNet benchmark for the binary classification task of predicting the clinical toxicity of a molecule.

nodes.name: Clotho
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats Clotho as an audio captioning dataset or benchmark, though one definition also frames it as a benchmark for audio-retrieval tasks. Definitions consistently describe paired audio and text data: audio clips with natural-language captions, with some papers adding that it contains long, diverse soundscapes, is human annotated, and is composed of FreeSound samples. A more detailed description gives 6,000 clips of 15 to 30 seconds with five captions per clip, and another paper likewise describes each sample as having five different captions. A smaller usage refers to Clotho Caps, and one retrieval study explicitly uses the original, non-spatial version.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Clotho to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures Audio captioning, with several papers evaluating models on Clotho for audio captioning tasks; a smaller line of work uses it to measure Cross-modal retrieval through semantic retrieval scores such as R@1, R@5, and R@10. One paper also reports that Clotho measures Generalization, stating that a model trained solely on AudioSet’s audio excerpts and

nodes.name: ClothoAQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe ClothoAQA as an audio question-answering benchmark or dataset derived from Clotho for evaluating audio-language understanding. One definition gives more detail, describing 1,991 audio samples from the Clotho dataset, each paired with six crowdsourced questions and corresponding answers, and says it is used to evaluate natural language understanding of general audio content.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers here, its use converges on one target: Audio question answering is measured by ClothoAQA. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Audio question answering, and to no constructs; the definitions also describe it as evaluating audio-language understanding or natural language understanding of general audio content.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead use it as the audio question-answering evaluation, with one paper listing it among "foundational benchmarks" and another using it as the audio question-answering task in a broader audio evaluation setup.

nodes.name: CLTE
nodes.definition: Chinese Language Teaching Evaluation benchmark, a comprehensive framework assessing LLMs across three dimensions: basic knowledge, international teacher certification, and teaching practice via student model improvement.

nodes.name: CLUTRR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers variously describe CLUTRR as a benchmark or dataset for reasoning over family relations in text. Definitions frame it as relation inference from partial graph descriptions in natural language, family relation path reasoning, and a diagnostic benchmark for inductive reasoning from text; other descriptions call it a deductive reasoning dataset requiring multi-hop reasoning over family relationships or a relational reasoning benchmark based on human-written stories about family relations. One paper also uses the CLUTRR dataset as the basis for the NoRa-Commonsense task.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CLUTRR to 4 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The recorded measured_by links span Inductive reasoning, Logical reasoning, Multi-hop reasoning, and Relational reasoning, so papers use it to measure several reasoning constructs rather than a single one. In the relationship evidence, authors describe it as a "deductive reasoning dataset requiring multi-hop reasoning over family relationships" and as a relational reasoning benchmark.

Space of uses. Papers do not link CLUTRR to any other measurement instrument. Instead, they position it as a direct bench

nodes.name: CMATH
nodes.definition: Chinese math reasoning benchmark assessing mathematical problem-solving ability in Chinese, evaluated under 0-shot or 5-shot settings.

nodes.name: CMB-Clin
nodes.definition: Open-domain medical Q&A dataset used to assess LLM performance on real-world clinical consultation scenarios.

nodes.name: CMB-Exam
nodes.definition: Medical examination dataset used for evaluating LLMs on standardized medical knowledge and clinical reasoning tasks.

nodes.name: CMedCalc-Bench
nodes.definition: CMedCalc-Bench is a Chinese clinical calculation benchmark containing 69 calculators and 1,143 real-world patient cases for evaluating medical LLMs.

nodes.name: CMMLU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat CMMLU as a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating knowledge and reasoning in Chinese, often under the name Chinese Massive Multitask Language Understanding. Several descriptions add that it covers 67 subjects from basic to advanced or professional levels, and one definition says it uses multiple-choice questions across diverse academic disciplines. A smaller set of papers frames it more specifically as Chinese language understanding or proficiency, while a few describe it differently, including as multilingual or multimodal, and one snippet mentions a 5-shot setting.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, its measurement claims are spread across 4 constructs and no behavioral indicators, rather than concentrating on a single target. The most frequently linked constructs are Chinese language understanding, general ability, reasoning, and generalization. Papers use it to assess "Chinese language understanding," to check that general capabilities are not compromised, and in one out-of-domain evaluation to test generalization.

Space of uses. CMMLU is usually used as one component of a broader evaluation suite, commonly alongside MMLU and also with

nodes.name: CNN/DailyMail
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, CNN/DailyMail is most commonly described as a widely used news summarization dataset or benchmark, built from CNN and Daily Mail articles paired with human-written summaries, often described as multi-sentence summaries or highlights. Definitions usually frame it as text or abstractive summarization, though some papers describe it more specifically as document-level or single-document summarization, and one paper describes it as an English-language dataset with just over 300k unique news articles. A few studies refer to particular subsets or uses, such as the test set, 100 randomly sampled texts, or the first 300 entries, and one paper uses the article-highlight pairs to evaluate citation attribution.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 4 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing measured use is Text summarization, and smaller lines of work report it as measuring Abstractive summarization, News summarization, and Text generation. The recorded links are concentrated on summarization tasks; the only construct link is Out-of-distribution generalization, where a paper treats CNN/DailyMail as the out-of-distribution test set for summar

nodes.name: CoBia
nodes.definition: A suite of lightweight adversarial attacks using constructed conversations to expose hidden societal biases in LLMs, with two main variants: history-based constructed conversation (HCC) and single-block constructed conversation (SCC).

nodes.name: COCO Caption
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a COCO-based image captioning benchmark or dataset used to evaluate models that generate textual descriptions for images. Definitions vary at the margins: some describe a large-scale captioning benchmark, some describe the captioning portion of a broader object detection and segmentation dataset with multiple short human-written descriptions per image, and some use it as a source of prompts for text-to-image evaluation. Specific descriptions mention the validation set, the validation split, and the karpathy-test split, and one paper describes over 330,000 images with more than 1.5 million captions and five human-generated captions for each image.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure image captioning, with several papers explicitly evaluating caption tasks on this benchmark and reporting caption metrics such as BLEU, METEOR, CIDEr, SPICE, ROUGE-L, or BertScore. Smaller lines of work also use it to measure image generation, fine-grained perception, and visual understanding.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers usuall

nodes.name: CodeAttack
nodes.definition: CodeAttack is a jailbreak attack method used to embed harmful requests in seemingly harmless task templates.

nodes.name: CodeContests
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat CodeContests as a benchmark or dataset of challenging competitive programming problems for code generation. Definitions also describe it as a competitive programming dataset in which each problem comes with multiple human-written correct and incorrect solutions, and one line of work further divides the test problems into basic and advanced levels by difficulty tags. Some papers describe the task as generating code from natural language problem statements, sometimes with public test-case descriptions, with evaluation against private test cases, and some studies use subsets rather than the full benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Across reported relationships, papers link CodeContests to 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing use is to measure code generation, and a smaller line of work reports it as measuring coding; these claims are framed through benchmark performance or pass@k evaluation on test problems. Single-paper claims also report that it measures algorithmic reasoning, because competition-level benchmarks "require algorithmic reasoning," and factuality, where generated code is checked against private test cas

nodes.name: Codeforces
nodes.definition: A competitive programming website that serves as a longitudinal benchmark for code generation, featuring problems released over time with public and private test cases for evaluation.

nodes.name: CodeMixBench
nodes.definition: A comprehensive benchmark introduced in this paper for evaluating the performance of LLMs on multilingual code-mixing, encompassing eight tasks and 18 languages.

nodes.name: CodeNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the dominant framing treats CodeNet as a source corpus for code research rather than as a standalone evaluation protocol. Definitions describe it as a competitive programming dataset, and one paper adds that it "collects data from online judge websites" (DCE-LLM: Dead Code Elimination with Large Language Models). Papers use different slices of that corpus: C++ submissions and problem trajectories for constructing PIE, material for extending a code-to-code semantic search evaluation set to more languages, and source code for a dead-code dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link CodeNet to any constructs or behavioral indicators through explicit measurement claims. Instead, they report it as underlying data for resources such as PIE, a code-to-code search evaluation set, and a dead-code dataset, so these papers do not state that CodeNet measures a particular construct.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The recurring use is as upstream data for derived resources: one paper states, "Our dataset is constructed based on performance-improving edits (PIE) made by human programmers in a range of competitive programm

nodes.name: CodeParrot
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available definitions, CodeParrot is treated as a code-focused evaluation resource. One paper describes it as a "code-oriented long-context benchmark" used in length extrapolation evaluation, while another describes it as a code modeling dataset for assessing language modeling performance on programming language sequences.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one construct, Length generalization, and to no behavioral indicators. The measurement claim is concentrated on that single construct: one paper places CodeParrot within "length extrapolation on six long benchmarks," so it is reported as measuring Length generalization.

Space of uses. The available papers position it in two ways: as part of a long-benchmark suite for length extrapolation, and as a dataset on which perplexity is evaluated. In the latter use, one paper evaluates perplexity on it alongside PG19 and Proof-Pile, and beyond that co-usage papers do not report links to other measurement instruments.

nodes.name: CodeQL
nodes.definition: A semantic code analysis engine used as an instrument to automatically detect security vulnerabilities in the code generated by a model.

nodes.name: CodeSearchNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the dominant framing is as a benchmark for function-level text-to-code retrieval, using natural language queries and code snippets. Some papers describe it more broadly as a dataset for evaluating code generation and understanding, with code snippets and natural language descriptions across multiple programming languages. One definition presents the CodeSearchNet Corpus as covering six programming languages and containing over 2 million (comment, code) pairs extracted from GitHub.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims stay with behavioral indicators rather than constructs: papers link it to three behavioral indicators, Code generation, Code retrieval, and Ranking, and to no constructs. Papers use it to measure Code retrieval and Ranking in text-to-code retrieval evaluation, while one paper reports using the CodeSearchNet dataset for Code generation evaluation.

Space of uses. Where evaluation setups are described, it appears alongside AdvTest as a text-to-code retrieval benchmark. Some work also uses code search and summarization datasets from CodeBERT that are described as extensions of CodeSearchNet, while another paper selects

nodes.name: CodeXGLUE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, CodeXGLUE is most commonly treated as a benchmark for code tasks, but its scope is described in more than one way. Some authors present it narrowly as a code-to-text benchmark for evaluating natural-language explanations of code snippets, where the task is to generate a natural language explanation from a code snippet. Others describe it more broadly as a benchmark suite for code intelligence, including code defect detection in C, or as a public benchmark for programming language models with single-file code completion datasets such as PY150 and Github Java Corpus.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CodeXGLUE to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing recorded use is to measure vulnerability identification, through the CodeXGLUE code defect detection task in C, which papers describe as a binary defect detection setting with a label for whether code is insecure and may attack software systems. A smaller usage links it to code summarization, with papers reporting that they use the CodeXGLUE benchmark for that task.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers use it directly as a benchmark,

nodes.name: CoGS
nodes.definition: Construction Grammar Schematicity corpus, a dataset of 10 construction types used to evaluate model performance on partially substantive and schematic constructions.

nodes.name: Coin Flip
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats Coin Flip as a simple symbolic or rule-based reasoning benchmark in which a model tracks a coin's state through a sequence of flips and non-flips and gives a binary answer, usually Yes or No or the final face, heads or tails. Definitions often make the setup explicit, including questions with named agents performing or not performing flips; one paper uses versions with 2, 3, and 4 rounds of potential flips, and another describes scalable versions. A smaller line of work instead describes it as testing simple probabilistic scenarios or as a knowledge-free reasoning task without factual knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Coin Flip overwhelmingly to measure Symbolic reasoning: it is linked to one construct, Symbolic reasoning, and the recurring description is a symbolic reasoning benchmark or dataset. The measurement claims converge on that single construct rather than spreading across many. It is also linked to one behavioral indicator, State tracking, but only as a related indicator rather than as something the benchmark directly measures.

Space of uses. Papers commonly pair Coin Flip with Last Letter when ev

nodes.name: CoIR
nodes.definition: CoIR, a benchmark covering code-to-text, code-to-code, hybrid code retrieval, and text-to-code retrieval tasks.

nodes.name: CoLA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats CoLA as the Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability, a GLUE benchmark or task for judging whether an English sentence is grammatically acceptable. Papers commonly describe it as a single-sentence, often binary classification setting, with sentences labeled as acceptable or unacceptable, or as grammatically correct or incorrect. A smaller line of work describes GLUE-CoLA as a dataset of text from books and journal articles used inside TDDBench, and one paper refers to CoLA-dev in its evaluation setup.

What it is claimed to measure. In the papers that connect it to broader concepts, CoLA is used to measure one construct, Generalization, and it is not linked to any behavioral indicators. One paper treats GLUE-COLA as one of several "unseen tasks" when reporting Generalization, so the measurement claims converge on a single construct rather than spreading across several.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Most papers position CoLA as one task inside broader benchmark suites or downstream checks, including GLUE development-set reporting, fine-tuning and parameter-efficient adaptation, out-of-domain close

nodes.name: Cola (compositional image retrieval)
nodes.definition:
What it is.
