Across the definitions, Cola is most commonly described as a compositional text-to-image retrieval benchmark: papers say it assesses compositional ability or compositional reasoning by retrieving the correct image for captions about relations between entities, or for specific configurations of attributes and objects, from candidates that include distractors. One paper makes the procedure explicit by saying it computes a perplexity score between a caption and all candidate images and predicts the image with lower perplexity. A minority usage applies the name COLA to the Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability, a dataset for judging whether English sentences are grammatically acceptable.

What it is claimed to measure. Although the definitions mostly frame it as compositional retrieval, papers link it to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims span several targets rather than converging on one. The most common construct link is Natural language understanding, while papers also use it to measure Compositional reasoning and, less often, General ability; among behavioral indicators, Grammatical acceptability judgment is the most common link, w

nodes.name: COLD
nodes.definition: Chinese Offensive Language Dataset, a benchmark dataset that categorizes sentences into fine-grained types such as personal attacks and anti-bias expressions concerning race, gender, and region.

nodes.name: Collab-Overcooked
nodes.definition: A benchmark built on the Overcooked-AI game, designed to evaluate LLM-based multi-agent systems on 30 collaborative tasks that require resource isolation and asymmetric task knowledge.

nodes.name: CollegeMath
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions frame CollegeMath as a college-level mathematical reasoning benchmark, often presented as a more challenging or out-of-domain evaluation set beyond high school material. Papers variously describe it as college-level math problems, advanced topics beyond the high school curriculum, or an out-of-domain benchmark for generalization; one description in DART-Math specifies 2,818 test problems drawn from 9 textbooks across 7 domains such as linear algebra and differential equations. A smaller line of description differs: Logits-Based Finetuning calls it "a mathematical reasoning dataset created using MathScale, containing two million math question-answer pairs."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CollegeMath mainly to measure mathematical reasoning. Across recorded relationships it measures 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator: mathematical reasoning is the prevailing target, while a smaller number of papers use it to measure generalization and mathematical problem solving. The reported measurement claims therefore center on reasoning, with only limited extension to other targets.

Space of uses. Papers typically use CollegeMath inside multi-bench

nodes.name: CommonGen
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, CommonGen is most commonly described as a commonsense-guided or constrained text generation benchmark or dataset. Papers consistently define the task as generating a coherent or natural sentence from a given set of concepts or keywords, often three to five per example, with the sentence required to contain all of them; some frame this as describing an everyday scenario or as a struct-to-text task, and one definition notes that inflections of the keywords are allowed. A smaller usage modifies the data split by restricting the training set to samples having "man" while leaving validation and test unchanged.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CommonGen to measure 3 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than centered on one. The linked constructs are Constraint satisfaction, Evaluation ability, and Generative ability, and the linked behavioral indicators are Commonsense generation, Constrained decoding, and Text generation. In these uses, papers describe CommonGen as a way to compare text generation and evaluation abilities, to evaluate commonsense generation and constrain

nodes.name: Commonsense170K
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat Commonsense170K as a large supervised fine-tuning dataset for commonsense reasoning, often described as a combined collection or mixture of eight commonsense reasoning datasets. Definitions commonly present it as training data built from tasks such as BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy or ARC-Challenge, and OpenbookQA, while some papers instead call it a composite benchmark or evaluation suite and describe it as used for both training and evaluation. One paper further specifies a train split of 170020 samples and a validation split of 400 samples.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it mainly to measure commonsense reasoning: it is linked to 1 construct, Commonsense reasoning, and papers describe it as a comprehensive collection of commonsense reasoning questions or a commonsense reasoning benchmark. Its measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread widely, with 1 linked behavioral indicator, Commonsense question answering, which one paper also reports it as measuring.

Space of uses. Most papers use it as the fine-tuning dataset in commonsense experiments, then test models on downstream tasks or on the component dataset

nodes.name: Commonsense reasoning benchmark
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the dominant framing is a composite suite of eight commonsense reasoning tasks or datasets used to evaluate model performance. Most descriptions enumerate BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC material, and OBQA, with the main variation being whether ARC appears as ARC-e plus ARC-c or simply ARC. Papers describe the suite as targeting reasoning about everyday situations, commonsense question answering and inference, and factual, physical, social, and scientific inference; some also note combined training with separate test evaluation, or that the training sets from the eight datasets are aggregated.

What it is claimed to measure. Across linked uses, papers primarily use this benchmark to measure Commonsense reasoning, and it is linked to one construct and one behavioral indicator overall. The prevailing claim is that papers evaluate on commonsense reasoning benchmarks or report performance on commonsense reasoning tasks, so the measurement claims converge mostly on that construct rather than spreading across many. A smaller line of work uses five component benchmarks, SIQA, PIQA, Arc-Easy, Arc-Challenge, and OBQA, to measure Instruction

nodes.name: CommonsenseQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, CommonsenseQA is most commonly described as a multiple-choice question answering benchmark or dataset for commonsense reasoning or commonsense knowledge. Definitions usually portray it as everyday or daily-life questions with distractor answers, often in a 5-choice format, and some papers say it has more than 10K questions or specifically 12,102; a smaller line describes it as assessing general understanding or general knowledge. Some papers further describe it as built upon ConceptNet, and a few add that the questions are intended to resist superficial cues or simple fact retrieval.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CommonsenseQA to measure 14 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The dominant construct target is commonsense reasoning, with smaller lines also using it for general ability, general reasoning, generalization, and reasoning. The behavioral-indicator links keep it mostly inside question-answering formats, so the reported measurement claims spread beyond a single construct even while commonsense reasoning remains the prevailing framing.

Space of uses. Most papers use CommonsenseQA as one benchmark within a larger evaluat

nodes.name: CommonsenseQA 2.0
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited work, CommonsenseQA 2.0 is treated as a dataset for commonsense reasoning. Definitions converge on that framing, with one study describing CSQA2 as containing "a large number of questions about entity knowledge and commonsense reasoning" (UniCoTT: A Unified Framework for Structural Chain-of-Thought Distillation), and another describing it as a multiple-choice dataset used to evaluate commonsense reasoning capabilities.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to two constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure Commonsense reasoning, with papers evaluating on it as one of several commonsense QA datasets; a smaller use links it to Factuality, where one paper places CSQA2 within a "Factual Reasoning Task."

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the available papers, it is used within broader evaluation suites: one study evaluates on it alongside CREAK and StrategyQA, and another includes it among widely utilized commonsense QA datasets alongside CommonsenseQA, OpenBookQA, and ARC-Easy.

nodes.name: CommonsenseQA-CoT
nodes.definition: A version of the CommonsenseQA dataset augmented with 8.1k Chain-of-Thought examples generated by GPT-4o-mini to facilitate CoT-based training.

nodes.name: ComplexBench
nodes.definition: Evaluation suite for complex instruction-following abilities, focusing on multi-step and multi-constraint reasoning, assessed via GPT-4 judgment.

nodes.name: ComplexOR
nodes.definition: A benchmark for optimization problem solving that requires models to use an optimization solver, focusing on linear programming without explicit input numbers.

nodes.name: ComplexTempQA
nodes.definition: A large-scale dataset of over 100 million temporal question-answer pairs used to evaluate temporal reasoning, with questions categorized into attribute, comparison, and counting types, and enriched with metadata such as time span and popularity.

nodes.name: CompreCap
nodes.definition: Evaluation framework using a Directed Scene Graph to assess the correctness of object mentions, attributes, and their relationships in image captions.

nodes.name: ComVE
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available paper describes ComVE as a natural language reasoning dataset where the task is to identify which of two sentences violates common sense. In that same description, it is presented as being used to evaluate commonsense reasoning and explanation generation, and it is also grouped with ECQA and e-SNLI as a widely used natural language reasoning dataset with NLEs (Self-Critique and Refinement for Faithful Natural Language Explanations).

What it is claimed to measure. The available definition says that papers use ComVE to evaluate commonsense reasoning and explanation generation. Beyond that definition-level claim, papers do not explicitly report that it measures any construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. In the available usage snippet, ComVE is used alongside ECQA and e-SNLI: the paper says its experiments were conducted on these three natural language reasoning datasets with NLEs. This positions ComVE as one of the datasets on which the study's experiments are run.

nodes.name: ConceptARC
nodes.definition: An ARC-style benchmark where each task is designed to exemplify a single, isolated high-level concept, allowing for more targeted evaluation of specific reasoning abilities.

nodes.name: ConceptVectors
nodes.definition: A benchmark designed to evaluate unlearning, used as a source of concepts for the erasure experiments.

nodes.name: CondAmbigQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark and dataset of 2,000 ambiguous questions with condition-answer-citation triples, designed to evaluate models' ability to resolve ambiguity through explicit condition identification and conditional answer generation.

nodes.name: ConflictingQA
nodes.definition: Benchmark dataset containing controversial yes/no web search queries and labeled support/refute web pages, used to evaluate model performance on debatable query summarization.

nodes.name: ConflictQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing treats ConflictQA as a contradiction-checking benchmark built around questions paired with both aligned and conflicting evidence. Most descriptions emphasize samples containing a PopQA question, correct aligned evidence, and ChatGPT-generated contradictory evidence; one benchmark-oriented description adds that each question also comes with matched and contradictory evidence plus the answer. Some authors instead foreground its counterfactual contexts, noting that these questions often lack descriptors, and some studies report using only a subset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ConflictQA to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators. The measurement claims converge on a single construct, Context utilization: one paper uses ConflictQA as a measurement instrument for context utilization, in a comparison that places it alongside CounterFact rather than spreading its use across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation dataset for contradiction checking and for testing performance under conflicting or unhelpful contexts, and some explicitly work with a subset rather than the full benchmark. It is linked

nodes.name: ConflictQA+
nodes.definition: An extension of the ConflictQA dataset, constructed to evaluate LLM performance by adding distracting, ambiguous, and duplicated contexts to the original set of counterfactual contexts.

nodes.name: CoNLL-2003
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, CoNLL-2003 is most commonly described as a named entity recognition benchmark or dataset. When papers specify its content, they describe news text and four entity types, persons, locations, organizations, and miscellaneous, and one paper further says these are tagged using the IOB scheme, resulting in nine distinct IOB labels. One definition also presents it as an English flat NER dataset for benchmarking sequence labeling models, while another broadens its use to token-level representation learning through tasks such as NER, chunking, and POS tagging.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, its measurement claims concentrate on 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs: papers use CoNLL-2003 to measure named entity recognition. This framing is consistent across the relationship evidence, which repeatedly presents it as the dataset used for NER experiments. A broader evaluative role for token-level representation learning appears in one definition, but no additional behavioral indicators or constructs are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers use it mainly as an experimental dataset for named entity recognition, and one paper explicitly st

nodes.name: Consensual Assessment Technique
nodes.definition: A psychometric method for evaluating creative products through holistic judgments by domain experts, adapted here for LLMs to assess poetry across criteria like creativity and quality.

nodes.name: ContextHub
nodes.definition: A benchmark for propositional logic, used to evaluate the generalization of the model's complex logical reasoning capabilities to an unseen domain.

nodes.name: ConvAI2
nodes.definition: A multi-turn open-domain dialogue dataset with persona profiles and conversational history.

nodes.name: COPA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, COPA is most commonly described as The Choice of Plausible Alternatives, a benchmark or dataset for commonsense causal reasoning, usually framed as choosing the more plausible cause or effect for a given premise or situation. Definitions vary slightly in task format: some call it a multiple-choice task, while others describe a sentence completion setup with a premise event, a causal query, and two choices; one paper says the dataset includes 1000 causal questions. Papers also place it within SuperGLUE, mention a zero-shot form, and in one multimodal adaptation convert it into multi-image cause-and-effect questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link COPA to 3 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure causal reasoning, often described more specifically as commonsense or commonsense causal reasoning, while a smaller line of work uses it to measure general ability. Claims about behavioral indicators are more dispersed: papers report using COPA to measure causal discovery, downstream task performance, multiple-choice question answering, sentence completion, and zero-shot task performance.

Space of uses. Papers link COP

nodes.name: COPAL-ID
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, COPAL-ID is treated as an Indonesian evaluation resource. One definition describes it broadly as a benchmark used to assess downstream model performance after safety fine-tuning, while another paper describes it more specifically as an Indonesian causal reasoning dataset written from scratch by native speakers in both standard and Jakartan Indonesian. Papers therefore describe it both as a benchmark and as a task-specific dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link COPAL-ID to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The construct links are divided between causal reasoning and cultural understanding: one paper reports that COPAL-ID measures causal reasoning, and the same line of work uses it to assess models' ability to reason within the Indonesian cultural sphere, treating it as a measure of cultural understanding. Another paper uses COPAL-ID as one of the benchmarks that measure downstream task performance after safety fine-tuning.

Space of uses. In use, papers position COPAL-ID as part of broader model evaluation. One study includes it in a suite of Indonesian benchmarks alongside IndoMMLU, IndoCareer, IndoCulture, MAPS, and IndoCl

nodes.name: Copy-paste attack
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is a watermark-robustness test built around mixing texts. Most definitions describe inserting a watermarked or machine-generated span into a larger human-written or hand-written document, while one definition instead describes inserting copied original text before generated text. Reported setups vary, including embedding watermarked fragments in a surrounding un-watermarked document, inserting 600 tokens from the origin text before generated text, or inserting a 200-token watermarked span into a 1000-token human-written passage.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure Robustness, the only linked construct, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. One paper explicitly assesses the robustness of different watermarking methods under various attacks, including the copy-paste attack, so the available claims converge on robustness rather than spreading across multiple targets.

Space of uses. Papers use it as a scenario-based attack within broader watermark evaluations, and some describe the same setup as text mixing or a Copy-Paste scenario where watermarked text appears inside a larger hand-written passag

nodes.name: CoQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, CoQA is most commonly described as a conversational question answering benchmark or dataset for evaluation, often framed as dialogue-based question answering or reading comprehension. Definitions repeatedly describe understanding a text passage or dialogue context and answering a series of interconnected questions in conversation, with some adding multi-turn reading comprehension, short-answer questions, or conversational comprehension requiring coreference and pragmatic reasoning. Papers mention the development split, the validation set, and the coqa-dev-v1.0 version; many descriptions call it open-book, though one paper labels it a closed-book reading comprehension dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CoQA to 5 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The dominant use is for question-answering related indicators, especially Question answering, Conversational question answering, and Machine reading comprehension; it is also used for Extractive question answering and Knowledge generation. These claims are concentrated on behavioral indicators rather than multiple constructs, since the only linked construct is Reasoning, with one paper assess

nodes.name: Cora
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing framing is of Cora as a citation network benchmark: nodes are described as scientific publications, documents, or academic papers, and edges as citation links. Most definitions place it in text-attributed graph or node classification settings, though some papers also use it for node-level and edge-level tasks, and one paper evaluates perplexity, structural understanding, and zero-shot node and link classification on forms labeled Cora-Node and Cora-Link. A smaller line of work also mentions an expanded version of Cora.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Cora to three behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant use is to measure node classification, with papers reporting node classification accuracy on Cora and describing it as widely adopted for that task; smaller lines of work report it as measuring link prediction and graph partitioning, including multi-scale graph partitioning datasets based on Cora. Overall, the measurement claims are concentrated on node classification rather than spread evenly across tasks.

Space of uses. Papers do not explicitly relate Cora to another measurement instrument, but they

nodes.name: CosmosQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a large-scale dataset or benchmark for commonsense-based reading comprehension. Most definitions present it as multiple-choice questions based on reading comprehension passages that require commonsense reasoning, while one paper specifies four answer options and highlights questions about human behaviors, intentions, and social interactions. A smaller line of work describes it more broadly as a real-world NLP classification dataset or as a resource for narrative understanding and inference.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CosmosQA to measure one construct, commonsense reasoning, and three behavioral indicators, chain of thought, machine reading comprehension, and question answering. The construct-level usage is concentrated on commonsense reasoning, while the behavioral-indicator links are spread across several framings rather than converging on one. In these claims, papers variously describe it as an evaluation dataset for machine reading comprehension, a common sense reasoning dataset used when measuring chain of thought, and one of the question answering datasets in a broader task collection.

Space of uses. Acr

nodes.name: CoSQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, CoSQA is most commonly described as a natural-language-to-code semantic search or code search benchmark, using natural language queries to retrieve relevant code and to evaluate alignment between code and intent expressed in natural language. A smaller line of work treats CosQA as a code-oriented question answering dataset of natural language-code pairs, used to test model performance on a code question-answering task and, in one definition, a model's ability to understand and reason about code semantics.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing usage presents CoSQA as evaluating natural-language-to-code semantic search, code search, and alignment between code and natural language intent. One paper also describes it as testing code question answering and understanding and reasoning about code semantics. No paper explicitly links it to a named construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Papers commonly position CoSQA as one benchmark within a small group of code search evaluations, most often alongside AdvTest and a third benchmark named as CSN in one paper and CodeSearchNet in another. In that role it is described as one of the "

nodes.name: CoSQL
nodes.definition: CoSQL is a conversational text-to-SQL dataset referenced as prior work with limited ambiguous and unanswerable questions.

nodes.name: CounterFact
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing treatment is as a dataset for knowledge editing built around counterfactual facts, though some authors describe it more broadly as a question-answering or factual recall dataset. Definitions variously present it as (subject, relation, answer) tuples with three paraphrased prompts, factual prompt pairs, or counterfactual statements, sometimes explicitly false facts, used as new knowledge for editing; some papers also mention neighboring datapoints, rephrased and unrelated queries, and old versus new knowledge partitions. Individual studies sometimes use subsets, such as the first 1000 examples filtered to correctly recalled facts or prompts sharing one relation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CounterFact to 12 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure factual recall, knowledge editing, fact checking, editing locality, and factual knowledge; beyond these, papers link 10 other constructs to it, so the measurement claims are spread across many constructs rather than centered on one. A separate paper also reports CounterFact as related to fact checking through knowledge triplets.

Space of uses. Ma

nodes.name: CoVoGER
nodes.definition: A multilingual multitask benchmark for speech-to-text generative error correction, covering ASR and ST across 15 languages and 28 language pairs, using N-best lists from Whisper and SeamlessM4T models.

nodes.name: CoVoST 2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, papers treat CoVoST 2 as a multilingual speech-to-text translation corpus or benchmark, commonly described as derived from Common Voice and used for training and evaluation. Descriptions differ in which slices they foreground: one describes 15,500 English examples translated into seven typologically diverse languages, another uses its French-English and German-English subsets as a general-domain benchmark, and CoVoGER uses 14 non-English source languages paired bidirectionally with English for 28 source-target directions and N-best list generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers primarily use CoVoST 2 to measure Speech translation, and the links are more concentrated on that behavioral indicator than spread across many targets. Papers link it to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators, with Speech translation the prevailing target, Speech recognition a smaller usage, and Cross-lingual alignment the linked construct. One study also reads CoVoST 2 results as confirming "superior cross-lingual alignment and translation performance."

Space of uses. Papers use CoVoST 2 both as a direct evaluation benchmark and as source material for downstream be

nodes.name: CR
nodes.definition: Customer Reviews sentiment classification benchmark used to evaluate polarity labeling.

nodes.name: Creak
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing framing is a fact-checking dataset or benchmark. One paper describes Creak as a dataset for "evaluating the verification of claims against a knowledge graph, using Wikidata" (Reasoning of Large Language Models over Knowledge Graphs with Super-Relations), while another treats CREAK as a benchmark "for fact-checking and commonsense reasoning ability" that assesses whether statements are supported by commonsense knowledge (Weak to Strong Generalization for Large Language Models with Multi-capabilities).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure one behavioral indicator and two constructs. The most common claim is that it measures Fact checking, while a smaller line of work also uses it to measure Commonsense reasoning, and a more limited framing reports it as evaluating Factuality through a "Factual Reasoning Task." Overall, the reported measurement claims cluster around fact checking, commonsense reasoning, and factuality rather than spanning many constructs.

Space of uses. Papers position it mainly as an evaluation dataset within broader benchmark suites. It appears alongside FEVER in fact verification settings, and

nodes.name: CREPE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, CREPE is not described in one uniform way. The prevailing benchmark-style usage treats it as an evaluation dataset for reasoning: some papers describe a causal reasoning dataset for identifying cause-effect relationships in natural language, while others describe CREPE or Crepe as a compositional reasoning benchmark that tests systematicity and productivity, including an image-text retrieval dataset with hard negatives for compositional understanding. A separate paper uses the same name for a different instrument, CREPE as "Rapid Chest X-ray Report Evaluation by Predicting Multi-category Error Counts," described as a domain-specific BERT-based, multi-head regression metric that predicts error counts in six clinical categories.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CREPE to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The recorded measurement claims are spread across Causal reasoning, Compositional reasoning, and Compositionality, rather than converging on a single construct: one paper uses it for causal reasoning, one reports it as evaluating compositional reasoning, and one uses it for compositionality with a focus on systematicity and productivi

nodes.name: CRITICTOOL
nodes.definition: A self-critique evaluation benchmark for LLMs in tool-calling scenarios, assessing performance across internal and external error types using evolved data strategies.

nodes.name: CrossCodeEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats CrossCodeEval as a repository-level, cross-file benchmark. One definition describes it broadly as evaluating code generation and understanding, while another presents it more narrowly as a diverse, multilingual benchmark, and also as a repository-level code completion dataset, for cross-file code completion.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator, Code completion, and to no constructs. The recorded use converges on that single indicator: one paper uses CrossCodeEval to measure code completion in repository-level, cross-file settings, specifically for code Fill-in-the-Middle scenarios.

Space of uses. In use, papers report performance on CrossCodeEval as an evaluation dataset for repository-level code completion. One paper uses it alongside CrossCodeLongEval and RepoEval to evaluate repository-level code Fill-in-the-Middle in cross-file scenarios, and a survey mentions it together with RepoBench when discussing repository-level tasks.

nodes.name: CrossNER
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for evaluating zero-shot NER that includes five domains: Movies, AI, Literature, Politics, and Science.

nodes.name: CrowS-Pairs
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of a crowdsourced benchmark or dataset of minimal or contrastive sentence pairs, with one sentence more stereotypical and the other anti-stereotypical or less stereotypical, used by checking which sentence a model prefers or assigns higher probability to. Definitions variously frame the judgment as which sentence is more likely, more natural or reasonable, and some specify pairs that differ by a single word or by social group references; several papers also describe coverage of historically disadvantaged groups and nine social bias categories, with 1,508 English examples. A smaller line of work refers to multilingual or language-specific versions, including French, Dutch, German, Spanish, and Catalan, and one paper mentions English CrowS-Pairs, Multilingual CrowS-Pairs, and a Spanish subset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 4 constructs, with the most common claims linking it to Social bias and then Stereotyping. Smaller lines of work report it as measuring Aesthetic bias and Toxicity, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. Across these claims, papers describe it as evaluating social bias, ster

nodes.name: CRUXEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, CRUXEval is most commonly described as a benchmark for code reasoning, understanding, and execution, often framed through predicting a program's input, output, or execution result. Papers also describe input and output prediction tasks, and one paper names these variants CruxEval-I and CruxEval-O. A smaller line of work uses it to validate deductive and abductive code reasoning, and one definition adds concrete benchmark content by describing 800 Python functions created with a generate-and-filter approach using CodeLlama.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is as a measure of code reasoning, while smaller lines of work use it to measure abductive code reasoning and reasoning more broadly. On the behavioral side, papers use it to measure code output prediction and code input prediction, and one paper reports it as related to code execution by stating that a code execution scenario is based on CRUXEval's output-prediction setup. Overall, the measurement claims stay concentrated on a small cluster of code reasoning and execution-oriented prediction tasks.

Space of uses.

nodes.name: CSCD-NS
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available definitions treat CSCD-NS as a Chinese Spelling Correction benchmark dataset, described as high-quality and as containing character errors that primarily stem from pinyin input methods, with many homophonic and word-level errors. In Enhancing Character-Level Understanding in LLMs through Token Internal Structure Learning, it is grouped with LEMON as one of two newer CSC benchmarks, in contrast to earlier datasets such as SIGHAN.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it in a focused way rather than across many targets: it is linked to 1 behavioral indicator, Chinese spelling correction, and to no constructs. One paper explicitly uses CSCD-NS as one of two CSC benchmarks for evaluating Chinese spelling correction.

Space of uses. Usage is shown mainly as a paired benchmark: papers use it alongside LEMON, and one study says the pair was selected to address limitations identified in previous datasets like SIGHAN. No other measurement instruments are linked to it.

nodes.name: CSRT
nodes.definition: Code-Switching Red-Teaming, a framework that synthesizes multilingual code-switching adversarial prompts to evaluate both safety and multilingual understanding of LLMs.

nodes.name: CTC
nodes.definition: An automated evaluation procedure used to compare generated chain-of-thought rationales against manually created golden references.

nodes.name: CUAD
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the cited papers, CUAD is described as the Contract Understanding Atticus Dataset, a corpus of commercial legal contracts used to evaluate automated contract review and provision extraction. One characterization also presents it as a specialized contract understanding dataset with 510 labelled documents spanning 25 contract types.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CUAD to two constructs and no behavioral indicators. It is reported as measuring contract understanding, and it is also linked to general ability, so the measurement claims are not confined to a single construct.

Space of uses. The cited papers do not link CUAD to any other measurement instrument. Where it is discussed, authors position it as a specialized dataset for contract understanding evaluation and for automated contract review and provision extraction.

nodes.name: CUB-200-2011
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats CUB-200-2011, also written as CUB-200, CUB, CaltechUCSD Bird-200, Birds-200-2011, and Caltech-UCSD Birds, as a fine-grained bird image benchmark or dataset for 200 bird species. Most definitions frame it as an image classification or fine-grained visual classification benchmark, often within FGVC, while some papers also describe it as a fine-grained image dataset used for image captioning and generation, or as a source of bird attributes for evaluating attribute relativity in the animal domain. A smaller line of work describes it in terms of detailed visual understanding, localization, and concept-based evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to 5 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The dominant measurement claim is image classification, while smaller lines of work use it to measure cross-modal retrieval, image captioning, image reconstruction, and object recognition. Papers also report it as measuring interpretability and explainability, with one study stating that CUB offers image-level concept annotations that enable quantitative evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers usually use it as one data

nodes.name: CultSportQA
nodes.definition: A multilingual, multicultural benchmark containing 33,000 multiple-choice questions across text and image modalities, assessing models on history-based, rule-based, and scenario-based understanding of traditional sports from 60 countries and 11 languages.

nodes.name: CURIE GEO
nodes.definition: Geospatial Dataset Extraction task in the CURIE benchmark where the model must identify all datasets used in a research paper, including their sources, variables, and time/spatial ranges.

nodes.name: CV-Bench 2D
nodes.definition: A vision-centric benchmark specifically for evaluating 2D visual understanding capabilities of models.

nodes.name: CVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat CVQA as a culturally diverse, multilingual visual question answering benchmark, sometimes calling it the Cross-lingual Visual Question Answering dataset. Definitions describe it as a large-scale resource for culturally specific images and questions across 31 languages and 30 countries, written in English and local languages. Its questions are usually presented in multiple-choice form, with one correct answer and three plausible distractors, though one paper also says it is convertible to free-text open-ended QA; question types range from simple identification to multi-hop reasoning and local common-sense knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the prevailing measurement claim centers on cultural understanding: CVQA is used to assess a model's ability to "reason about and understand culturally diverse visual content," and one paper says it can probe the cultural capability and bias of multimodal models. More broadly, papers link it to 6 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. These claims spread across several targets rather than converging on just one, with named links to cultural understanding, visual question answering, cul

nodes.name: CWQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, CWQ is most commonly treated as ComplexWebQuestions, a benchmark dataset for multi-hop knowledge base or knowledge graph question answering. The prevailing description places it on Freebase and frames it as testing complex, compositional, or knowledge-intensive reasoning over a knowledge graph, with some definitions noting conjunction, composition, comparison, or superlative reasoning and natural language questions paired with SPARQL queries. A smaller line of work describes it instead as multi-hop, web-based questions for reasoning over web content.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CWQ to measure three constructs and two behavioral indicators. The most common use is to measure Knowledge graph question answering, and papers also report it as measuring Multi-hop reasoning; less common links use it to measure Reasoning, World knowledge, and Question answering. Overall, the reported measurement claims cluster around KGQA and multi-hop reasoning, while the other uses appear as smaller framings.

Space of uses. In use, papers usually include CWQ in a small suite of KGQA benchmarks, most often alongside WebQSP and often GrailQA; some also pair it

nodes.name: D4RL
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available paper treats D4RL as Datasets for Deep Data-Driven Reinforcement Learning, described as a benchmark suite for offline reinforcement learning. In that usage, it appears specifically in risk-sensitive variants, with experiments run on four risk-sensitive D4RL tasks using public human preferences, as described in A Distributional Approach to Uncertainty-Aware Preference Alignment Using Offline Demonstrations.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers represented here do not report D4RL as measuring any construct or behavioral indicator, and no measured_by relationship is recorded for it.

Space of uses. Usage is illustrated in one paper as an experimental benchmark: the authors report that they "conduct experiments using public human preferences from Yuan et al. (2024) on four risk-sensitive D4RL tasks." No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: DailyDialog
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is of a dataset of human-written dialogues or human conversation transcripts about everyday life, used to evaluate dialogue generation or conversational performance. Definitions variously say it covers "various topics of daily life," consists of "transcripts of conversations between humans," or comprises sequences of everyday conversations. A minority description adds that it contains 13,118 dialogues annotated with 7 emotions for emotion recognition and dialogue generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use DailyDialog to measure one behavioral indicator, Dialogue generation, and do not link it to any constructs. The claims converge on dialogue generation rather than several outcomes: papers describe "dialogue generation with the DailyDialog dataset" and report using it to "assess performance in conversation scenarios."

Space of uses. Papers position it both as a case-study setting and as one dataset within multi-dataset evaluations. One line of work describes "a single setting as a case study: dialogue generation with the DailyDialog dataset," while other work evaluates systems across diverse datasets or d

nodes.name: DAN
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats DAN, also called DoAnythingNow, as a benchmark or dataset for safety evaluation: papers describe a benchmark collection of jailbreak-enhanced instructions, or a benchmark for testing resilience against malicious instructions and jailbreak attacks. Some authors narrow it to a specific jailbreaking prompt, with one study using the latest DAN 13.0 prompt as a baseline that overrides AI safety restrictions, and another describing a dataset of forbidden prompts from the Do Anything Now jailbreak family. One paper instead uses the same name for Expose Backdoors on the Way (DAN), a feature-based textual backdoor defense method evaluated against query-triggered and observation-triggered agent backdoors.

What it is claimed to measure. In papers that make explicit measurement claims, DAN is used to measure three constructs and no behavioral indicators. The linked constructs are Backdoor vulnerability, Safety, and Safety robustness, so the claims are spread across several constructs rather than centered on one repeated target. Papers use AdvBench and DoAnythingNow to assess safety, report results on the DoAnythingNow benchmark

nodes.name: DART
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, DART is most commonly described as a dataset or benchmark for structured-data-to-text generation: definitions call it a large, open-domain resource with 82,191 examples from various domains, and describe the task as turning structured records, graphs, or RDF triples into natural language. Most descriptions use struct-to-text, data-to-text, or graph-to-text language, though one paper describes it as employed for evaluating text-to-data generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The linked indicators are Data-to-text generation and Text generation, both via measured_by relations; one paper further specifies RDF-to-text generation in that usage, while another places it inside a Natural Language Generation task and says it is employed for evaluating text-to-data generation.

Space of uses. Papers most often position it as an evaluation benchmark. As one study states, "We conducted all of our experiments on the following three benchmarks: WebNLG17, WebNLG20, DART", while other papers use it in broader NLG evaluation and in LoRA merging evaluation for converting structured data to na

nodes.name: Databricks Dolly-15k
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing treatment is as an instruction-following dataset, often described as open-source, human-generated, and used for fine-tuning or evaluation. Definitions variously describe it as a 15k collection of human-written instruction-response pairs, a manually crafted instruction dataset, and a benchmark dataset for federated LLM fine-tuning experiments. A narrower description emphasizes its coverage of categories such as brainstorming, classification, closed QA, generation, information extraction, open QA, and summarization, and one paper uses a 500-sample test split from the dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one construct and two behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role is spread across a few targets rather than centered on one. It is reported as measuring helpfulness when papers use general-domain Dolly samples to assess whether models retain usefulness after fine-tuning, and as measuring dialogue generation when it is used as the dialogue generation task. A smaller line of work also uses it to measure refusal in an AutoPoison-refusal setting.

Space of uses. Papers use it alongside other datasets, including A

nodes.name: Date Understanding
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, Date Understanding is most commonly treated as a task from BigBench for reasoning about dates and temporal information. Definitions describe it as evaluating calendar dates and temporal relationships, answering date-related questions, understanding dates in natural language, and in some cases inferring dates from contextual clues and calendar logic. A smaller line of work describes it as a benchmark dataset for commonsense or logical reasoning, and one paper places it in the BIG-Bench-Hard suite rather than referring only to BigBench.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Date Understanding to measure four constructs, Calibration, Commonsense reasoning, Logical reasoning, and Symbolic reasoning, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The measurement claims are spread across these different constructs rather than centered on one framing: some papers position it as a commonsense, logical, or symbolic reasoning measure, while another uses it for Calibration. One paper also describes the date understanding task in Big-bench as a testbed used to measure commonsense reasoning ability.

Space of uses. Papers present Date Understanding as one t

nodes.name: DBPedia
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, DBPedia is most commonly described as a Wikipedia-derived benchmark for topic or ontology classification. The prevailing description is a 14-way or 14-class setup, sometimes phrased as classifying articles into 14 non-overlapping classes or ontology types, and some authors describe it more generally as "multi-class classification of Wikipedia articles" for text categorization. A smaller line of work describes it differently, as Wikipedia articles organized in a three-layer taxonomy tree with 9/70/219 classes for hierarchical text classification.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link DBPedia to 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure text classification, with several papers introducing it as a classification task or dataset; a smaller line of work reports it as measuring hierarchical text classification. At the construct level, papers also use it to measure in-context learning and prompt sensitivity, so the claims are centered on classification and also include those two constructs.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to DBPedia. In practice, papers usually place it inside multi-dataset evaluat

nodes.name: DBpedia Class
nodes.definition: A dataset used to examine watermark decryption accuracy by analyzing word frequencies within specific semantic classes.

nodes.name: DCLM
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available definition treats DCLM as the pre-training data of the DCLM-7B model, and one paper explicitly uses it as a calibration source. Another paper uses a subset of DCLM and describes DCLM as a high-quality corpus carefully curated with complex pipelines.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked uses, papers use DCLM to measure Language modeling ability, and this is the only construct tied to it. It is reported as testing language modeling capability on a subset of DCLM, "to examine how well LMs capture broad and diverse knowledge," and no behavioral indicators are linked to it.

Space of uses. In the available papers, DCLM is positioned both as calibration data and as an evaluation subset for language modeling tests. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: DDXPlus
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, DDXPlus is most commonly described as a medical diagnosis dataset or benchmark used to evaluate models on complex and diverse conditions. Definitions differ in how they describe its contents: one treats it as a large-scale Electronic Health Record dataset, another as clinical vignettes with synthetic patient information for differential diagnosis, and another says agents must choose among 49 diagnoses from patient profiles detailing symptoms (StreamBench: Towards Benchmarking Continuous Improvement of Language Agents).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use DDXPlus to measure 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing claim is that it measures Medical diagnosis, with papers saying it tests models on diagnosing complex and diverse medical conditions and requires a diagnosis from symptom profiles. Smaller uses report it as measuring Medical reasoning, through clinical vignettes that evaluate diagnostic reasoning abilities similar to a clinical setting, and Domain knowledge, through assessing continuous improvement in applying expert knowledge.

Space of uses. Across the papers, DDXPlus is used as an evaluation dataset for models or ag

nodes.name: DecodingTrust
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, DecodingTrust is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for evaluating LLM trustworthiness or related properties. Definitions and snippets emphasize both broad coverage, described as assessing models from several perspectives, and specific components, especially a privacy dataset with the Enron email extraction task and a stereotypes partition about demographic groups. A smaller line of work describes it differently, as a public leaderboard that integrates massive amounts of new test data, or as a benchmark that collects red-teaming instructions for safety and trustworthiness evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link DecodingTrust to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The most frequently linked constructs are Aesthetic bias and Trustworthiness, and the linked behavioral indicator is Privacy leakage. The uses are spread across these targets rather than centered on one alone: papers report that it measures Aesthetic bias through a stereotypes-focused use, measures Trustworthiness through a comprehensive assessment framing, and measures Privacy leakage through the privacy dataset, especially the Enron email extraction

nodes.name: DeepCAD
nodes.definition: A dataset of CAD parametric sequences used as the source for training and test data in the sequential learning stage.

nodes.name: DeepInception
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available definitions, the prevailing usage treats DeepInception as a manually crafted jailbreak prompt template that uses imaginary scenes and characters to attack target LLMs. One paper describes it as a meticulously crafted manual prompt template that incorporates imaginary scenes with various characters. Other papers use a broader framing, treating it as a jailbreak method or as one of the evaluated state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link DeepInception to one construct, Harmlessness, and to no behavioral indicators. The recorded relationship is that Harmlessness is measured by DeepInception, with supporting evidence coming from an evaluation table that compares harmfulness scores for jailbreak attacks and shows attack success rates in brackets. The measurement claims are therefore concentrated on Harmlessness rather than distributed across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. In the available usage examples, papers place DeepInception inside multi-attack evaluations rather than presenting it by itself. One study evaluates it alongside GCG and PAIR, and another lists it with AutoDAN, ReNeLLM, and CodeAttack among jai

nodes.name: Defects4J
nodes.definition: Real-world Java bug-fix benchmark containing 806 bugs from 15 open-source projects, used to evaluate automated program repair systems on repo-level debugging tasks.

nodes.name: DeliData
nodes.definition: A dataset of multi-party, problem-solving dialogues where participants propose and score solutions, used to evaluate controlled dialogue generation and hallucination.

nodes.name: Detoxify
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat Detoxify as an automatic toxicity scoring or classification model for text outputs. Definitions describe it as a model-based system that assigns a toxicity score to generated text, a machine learning model and library for toxicity detection, and a tool for scoring continuations or responses where higher scores indicate more toxic generation. Some papers threshold that score, including at 0.1 and at ≥0.7, while others use the score directly; one paper also describes a retrained Detoxify model on a biased subset of the Jigsaw Unintended Bias in Toxicity Classification dataset, and another specifies six attributes, toxicity, severe toxicity, obscene, threat, insult, and identity attack.

What it is claimed to measure. Its use is concentrated on Toxicity rather than spread across many targets. Papers link it to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator, most often using it to measure Toxicity by evaluating or scoring generated text, responses, continuations, or tweets, sometimes through derived quantities such as Toxicity Probability and Expected Maximum Toxicity. Smaller uses link it to Harmlessness via toxicity scores, and to Harmful content generation via

nodes.name: DialogSum
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat DialogSum as a dialogue summarization dataset or benchmark. Definitions and snippets describe it as a large-scale resource of dialogues paired with manually labeled summaries, and one description adds topics and a total of 13,460 dialogues. A smaller line of work uses it beyond dialogue summarization evaluation, rebuilding it for instruction tuning, using it as dialogue context for grammar analysis, or using it for summary-to-dialogue generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, DialogSum is linked to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing use is to measure Dialogue summarization, and papers also use it to measure Text summarization and, in a smaller framing, Abstractive summarization. All 3 linked behavioral indicators are summarization-related.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers most often position it as an evaluation benchmark, including zero-shot generative evaluation, decoding-stage experiments, assessment of efficient inference methods, and evaluation after coreset selection or alignment; some papers instead rebuild it for fine-tuning an event summary module, use it as context

nodes.name: Dictator Game
nodes.definition: A one-shot bargaining game used to measure altruism and fairness, where one player unilaterally decides how to split a sum of money with a passive recipient.

nodes.name: DiDeMo
nodes.definition: Describe, Detect and Moment dataset focused on moment-level video grounding and retrieval, where models must align natural language queries with specific video segments.

nodes.name: DiscoveryBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for data-driven analysis that uses expert-curated analytics to assess agent performance against human experts.

nodes.name: DIWALI
nodes.definition: A large-scale dataset of Culture Specific Items (CSIs) for India, containing approximately 8,000 concepts from 17 cultural facets across 36 sub-regions, used for evaluating cultural text adaptation.

nodes.name: DMDTEval
nodes.definition: A systematic evaluation framework for assessing LLMs' disambiguation capabilities in multi-domain translation, including a multi-domain ambiguous word dataset, disambiguation prompt strategies, and disambiguation accuracy metric.

nodes.name: DnD
nodes.definition: Role-playing dataset involving 10 fantasy characters and 129 in-game situations with 3 possible actions each, used to evaluate alignment with character-specific behavioral preferences.

nodes.name: DocBench
nodes.definition: Document understanding benchmark containing 229 long documents and 1,102 questions across five domains—Academia, Finance, Government, Laws, and News—with evaluation by evidence source and document type.

nodes.name: DOCCI
nodes.definition: A dataset containing 15,000 image-caption pairs with highly detailed, hallucination-free captions, used for evaluating caption quality.

nodes.name: DocVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat it as a document visual question answering benchmark or dataset for document images, often framed as a standard benchmark for document understanding. Definitions commonly say models answer questions from document text and layout, and one paper describes an extractive QA format for span or segment extraction over scanned or photographed documents; one variant name, VQADoc, is used once for an image-based question answering benchmark on document images. Descriptions diverge on scope: some papers say it can only assess single-page documents, while one definition presents it as evaluating single-page and multi-page document QA and retrieval.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 4 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The prevailing construct framing is document understanding, and on the behavioral side it is most often used for optical character recognition, document question answering, information retrieval, and machine reading comprehension. Overall, papers distribute it across multiple constructs and indicators rather than tying it to a single target.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it in explicit relationshi

nodes.name: Dolos
nodes.definition: A state-of-the-art plagiarism detection tool used to assess the degree of copying or approximate memorization in generated code.

nodes.name: DOSA
nodes.definition: A community-driven dataset of cultural artifacts for a sub-regional culture in India, built through a gamified data collection process.

nodes.name: DOTA
nodes.definition: A large-scale dataset for object detection in aerial images.

nodes.name: DoTA (traffic accident analysis)
nodes.definition: An academic benchmark dataset for traffic accident analysis, providing annotations for captions, temporal localization, and bounding boxes.

nodes.name: DreamBooth
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers commonly treat DreamBooth as a subject-focused text-to-image resource, but they describe its format in several ways: as a dataset and method for fine-tuning on subject-specific data, as a subject-driven image generation benchmark or test set, and as a text-to-image personalization evaluation setup. The described contents center on subject examples and reference images, including a DreamBooth dataset that "includes 30 different subjects" and settings with "30 new concepts" from DreamBooth used as reference images; some descriptions also frame the setup around subject-driven generation with special identifier tokens.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers do not explicitly link DreamBooth to any named constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, they describe it in task terms, reporting its use for subject generation evaluation in diffusion models, for evaluating reference-based image compositing on test images and generated variants, and for text-to-image personalization or subject-driven generation.

Space of uses. In use, papers position DreamBooth mainly as an evaluation setup, benchmark, or test set, rather than alongside any linked measurement instrument

nodes.name: DRISHTIKON
nodes.definition: A multimodal, multilingual benchmark for evaluating cultural understanding in vision-language models, consisting of 64,288 aligned text-image multiple-choice questions across 15 Indian languages and all 36 states and union territories, covering cultural themes like festivals, attire, cuisine, and heritage.

nodes.name: DroidTask
nodes.definition: An existing benchmark for GUI agents consisting of 162 tasks across 12 English-language Android applications.

nodes.name: DROP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe DROP as a reading comprehension benchmark or dataset that requires discrete reasoning over paragraphs or passages, with recurring examples such as addition, counting, and sorting over paragraph-level content to answer questions. A smaller set of papers frame it more specifically as grounded or open-book question answering, and one paper describes it as a generation task for phrase or numeric answers. Definitions also mention variant uses, including decontextualized versions of a subset, and one paper says its queries mainly address History, Politics, Sports, Demographics, and Societal Issues.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, DROP is linked to 7 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so its measurement use is spread across several targets rather than centered on one. The prevailing usage is to measure reasoning and machine reading comprehension; recurring secondary uses are discrete reasoning, question answering, and contextual understanding, and other papers report it as measuring further targets as well.

Space of uses. Papers often place DROP inside broader evaluation suites alongside MMLU, BBH, SQuAD, NQ, and TriviaQA. In

nodes.name: DS-1000
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe DS-1000 as a benchmark of 1000 data science coding problems, workflows, or challenges, usually spanning seven widely used Python libraries such as NumPy and Pandas. The prevailing framing is data science code generation, though some definitions narrow this to code completion of partial snippets, and one description adds two evaluation modes, completion and insertion. Several papers also describe the problems as real-world StackOverflow questions with unit tests or test cases, while one paper characterizes them as non-standalone functions with contextual dependencies.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, papers use DS-1000 to measure code generation, and it is linked to one behavioral indicator and no constructs. The claims concentrate on that single indicator: authors describe tasks as generating Python code for data science questions written in natural language, using standard data science libraries, and passing executable test cases. Some papers frame the same use more specifically as data science code completion.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to DS-1000. In use, papers often place it alongside o

nodes.name: DTD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, DTD is most commonly described as the Describable Textures Dataset, a dataset or benchmark for texture classification and texture recognition. Some definitions add that it contains texture images in the wild annotated with describable attributes and is used for fine-grained visual classification based on descriptive attributes, while another frames it as a benchmark for recognizing and differentiating textures within images. A smaller line of work refers to it simply as Texture and uses it as an out-of-distribution texture dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, DTD is linked to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. The recurring claim is that papers use DTD to measure Image classification: they report image recognition or classification evaluations on DTD in settings such as fine-tuning, transfer learning, and zero-shot or linear-probe image classification. The measurement claims therefore center on one behavioral indicator rather than multiple constructs.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to DTD directly. In practice, papers usually place it inside multi-dataset evaluation suites alongside benchmarks such as CIF

nodes.name: DUDE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, DUDE is most commonly described as a benchmark for multi-page document understanding, with documents limited to up to 20 pages. One paper describes it more specifically as a multi-page visual question answering dataset containing financial reports, and papers also refer to its diverse domains and complex document structures.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link DUDE to one construct, Long-context understanding, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The measurement claim is narrow rather than spread across many constructs: one paper reports that Long-context understanding is measured by DUDE, noting that the benchmark includes a small percentage of cross-page questions (2.1%) and unanswerable questions (12.7%).

Space of uses. Usage evidence shows DUDE being used alongside MPVQA, CUAD, and MOAMOB in a multi-dataset evaluation. In that example, papers use it to evaluate retrieval and QA performance, and beyond that co-usage example papers do not relate DUDE to any other named measurement instrument.

Concerns raised. Papers note a scope limit: DUDE is described as not assessing documents exceeding 20 pages. One paper also notes that the benc

nodes.name: DynaMath
nodes.definition: Benchmark evaluating dynamic mathematical reasoning with visual inputs, used to assess model performance on evolving problem structures.

nodes.name: DynamicNER
nodes.definition: A multilingual, multi-granular Named Entity Recognition dataset with dynamic categorization, designed to evaluate LLM-based NER methods across varying entity type lists and granularity levels.

nodes.name: DynamicQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to handle knowledge conflicts arising from evolving real-world information, including static, temporal, and disputable cases.

nodes.name: E2E NLG Challenge
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a benchmark or dataset for natural language generation from structured input in the restaurant domain. Authors variously refer to it as E2E NLG Challenge, E2E NLG, or simply E2E, and most describe the task as generating natural language from structured meaning representations; some instead phrase it as data-to-text or table-to-text generation, and one description specifies that it verbalizes key-value attribute pairs in English.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to two behavioral indicators and no constructs. The more prevalent recorded use is to measure Text generation, with papers describing it as an NLG or text generation benchmark, and it is also used to measure Data-to-text generation, including table-to-text generation and verbalizing structured attributes, so the recorded claims cluster around those two behavioral indicators rather than a broader construct set.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers often use it alongside WebNLG, and one text generation setup also groups it with CommonGen and an Adidas product description dataset; a recurring usage is as a benchmark

nodes.name: E-GSM
nodes.definition: Extended Grade-School Math, a benchmark of math word problems with lengthy narratives, created by iteratively extending problems from the GSM8K test set.

nodes.name: e-SNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, e-SNLI is most commonly described as an extension of the SNLI corpus or dataset that adds human or human-annotated explanations to premise-hypothesis pairs. The prevailing description emphasizes entailment-style natural language inference, including labels such as contradiction, neutral, and entailment, while another recurring framing treats it as a multi-premise setting because the premise and explanation are described as jointly entailing the hypothesis. A smaller usage highlights it as a held-out test for generalization.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link e-SNLI to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The most common claim is that it measures natural language inference, with papers describing its task as determining the logical relationship between a premise and a hypothesis; papers also report it as measuring logical reasoning ability and interpretability and explainability, including through human explanations that support explicit reasoning and interpretability benchmarks. Taken together, the reported uses are spread across this small set rather than tied to only one target.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linke

nodes.name: ECL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats ECL, often called Electricity, as a benchmark electricity-consumption time series dataset. Most descriptions say it contains hourly data for 321 clients or customers, sometimes specifying 2012 to 2014 and a 1-hour recording frequency, and papers place it in real-world or benchmark suites for long-term forecasting. A smaller line of work describes ECL as a subset of the Electricity dataset with hourly kilowatt-hour consumption from 19 clients, and one paper describes Electricity as a dataset for evaluating self-healing adaptation strategies across different data distributions.

What it is claimed to measure. Most papers report ECL as a benchmark for evaluating long-term time series forecasting, forecasting models, or forecasting accuracy. One paper instead describes Electricity as being used to evaluate the performance of self-healing adaptation strategies across different data distributions. No construct is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers usually use ECL as one member of a broader benchmark suite rather than as a standalone instrument. It appears alongside ETTh1, Weather, T

nodes.name: ECQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ECQA is most commonly treated as a commonsense question-answering dataset or benchmark that requires models to answer questions and provide explanations. Definitions differ in how they expand the name, including Explainable CommonsenseQA, Explanations from Commonsense Knowledge Acquisition, and Explanation-based Commonsense Question Answering. One paper additionally describes it as a knowledge QA dataset with chain-of-thought reasoning, while another uses it as source data for constructing fine-tuning datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ECQA to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is to measure commonsense reasoning, with papers describing it as used for explainable commonsense reasoning and including it in commonsense evaluations; a smaller use treats it as measuring question answering by adopting its test split for evaluation. These claims concentrate on commonsense reasoning and question answering rather than spanning many targets.

Space of uses. Most papers position ECQA as an evaluation set, either as a benchmark or through its test split. No measurement instrument is linked to it, but papers use it alongs

nodes.name: EDUADAPT
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset of nearly 48,000 grade-labeled question-answer pairs across nine science subjects for Grades 1–12, designed to evaluate grade-level adaptability in LLMs through both multiple-choice and open-ended questions.

nodes.name: Ego4D
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, Ego4D is most commonly described as a large-scale egocentric video dataset. Definitions frame it as a source dataset from which other benchmarks are curated or recast: one paper says HourVideo uses videos from Ego4D and notes that "HourVideo consists of 500 videos from the Ego4D dataset, covering 77 daily life scenarios" (HourVideo: 1-Hour Video-Language Understanding), while another describes Ego4D as a large-scale egocentric video dataset for everyday activities with dense annotations that is recast into an offline mistake detection format for Ego4D-PMD.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Ego4D to no constructs and to one behavioral indicator. The reported use is concentrated on Temporal grounding: one paper states that Temporal grounding is measured by Ego4D, describing Ego4D as offering human-annotated videos and labels for certain egocentric video understanding tasks.

Space of uses. The available descriptions position Ego4D mainly as a source dataset rather than a standalone evaluation protocol. Papers use it to curate downstream benchmarks, including HourVideo and Ego4D-PMD, and one description says the latter is built from in

nodes.name: EgoSchema
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, EgoSchema is most commonly treated as a benchmark, often called a benchmark dataset, for long-form or long video question answering on egocentric videos. Some descriptions frame it more broadly as a benchmark for very long-form or long-context video-language understanding, but the recurring details are multiple-choice questions over egocentric videos, often described as over 5K videos or 5000 questions and as three-minute videos or videos with an average length of 3 minutes. Some papers further specify evaluation slices such as a 500-question subset, the full test split, or a 5031-video test set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link EgoSchema to 4 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claims are that it measures video understanding and long video understanding, and papers also use it to measure egocentric video understanding, temporal reasoning, and the behavioral indicator video question answering. Overall, papers use it across several targets rather than tying it to only one.

Space of uses. Papers do not describe EgoSchema through direct instrument-to-instrument relationship claims. Instead, they usually deploy it as

nodes.name: EHRNoteQA
nodes.definition: A clinical benchmark comprising 962 QA pairs linked to distinct patients' discharge summaries from MIMIC-IV EHR, evaluated in both open-ended and multi-choice formats.

nodes.name: EIFBENCH
nodes.definition: Extremely Complex Instruction Following Benchmark, a multi-instruction, multi-constraint evaluation framework assessing LLMs across diverse task types and constraint categories in plain text, dyadic dialogue, and multi-party dialogue scenarios.

nodes.name: ELI5
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ELI5 is most commonly described as an open-ended, long-form question-answering dataset. Definitions usually emphasize user-generated questions about science, history, and everyday life, often sourced from the Reddit "Explain Like I’m Five" forum, with answers expected to be simple and easy to understand, paragraph-length, or otherwise comprehensive and multi-aspect. Some papers foreground factual question answering and helpfulness, while others describe complex QA or LFQA settings, including a WebGPT-collected version with questions, model-generated answers, and supporting context.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ELI5 to two behavioral indicators and two constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure long-form question answering, and more broadly question answering. A narrower use treats evaluations on ELI5 as measuring trustworthiness and unanswerability detection ability, with table-based evaluations referring to TRUST-SCORE and Grounded Refusals F1.

Space of uses. Papers usually position ELI5 as an evaluation benchmark or prompt source for long-form QA and retrieval-augmented generation. It is often used alongside ASQA, and also with NQ-Op

nodes.name: EMBODYGUARD
nodes.definition: A PDDL-grounded benchmark containing 942 LLM-generated scenarios for evaluating physical safety in embodied decision-making, split into EMBODYGUARDmal (malicious commands) and EMBODYGUARDsit (situational hazards).

nodes.name: Emotion (dair-ai)
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats Emotion (Saravia et al., 2018) as a text classification dataset or benchmark for fine-grained emotion classification. One definition specifies six classes, joy, sadness, anger, fear, love, and surprise, and one study describes these as six "nuanced" classes in a more complex evaluation. Another definition also presents it as a six-category emotion benchmark but lists anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, and surprise, so papers do not describe the label set identically.

What it is claimed to measure. Most papers use it to measure Text classification, describing Emotion among "Text Classification datasets" and text classification benchmark suites. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Sentiment analysis, with one paper describing it as text data labeled with various emotions and suitable for sentiment analysis tasks. Papers link it to 2 behavioral indicators, Text classification and Sentiment analysis, and to no constructs.

Space of uses. Papers often place it inside multi-dataset evaluation suites. In those setups it appears alongside other text classification datasets such as CoLA, AG News, Stanford Sentiment Tr

nodes.name: EmpatheticDialogues
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, the prevailing treatment is as a dialogue dataset centered on emotional situations. Papers describe it as conversations grounded in specific emotional situations and, more specifically in one definition, as 24,850 multi-turn speaker-listener conversations annotated with one of 32 emotions for fine-grained emotion classification. Another naming variant in the papers, E-Dialogue, is described as a benchmark for evaluating empathetic capabilities in open-domain conversation models, so the descriptions emphasize either fine-grained emotion labels or empathetic evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it most often as a task or evaluation dataset for fine-grained emotion classification and emotion detection in dialogue, while another definition says it evaluates empathetic capabilities in open-domain conversation models. No construct or behavioral indicator is linked to it, so the papers here describe its measurement role through tasks rather than explicit construct mappings.

Space of uses. Papers position it as a benchmark or task dataset. No measurement instrument is linked to it, but one paper reports using E-Dialogue alongside

nodes.name: Enron email dataset
nodes.definition: A standard dataset of emails from which personally identifiable information is sampled to construct prompts for privacy evaluation.

nodes.name: EntityQuestions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe EntityQuestions as a question answering dataset.
