The prevailing description is a closed-book QA specific dataset containing knowledge across 24 topics extracted from Wikipedia and used to construct training and testing sets, while another paper frames it more broadly as a fact-seeking QA dataset centered on entity-related factual knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Closed-book question answering, which is measured by EntityQuestions, and no constructs are linked to it. Separately, one definition describes it as being used to evaluate non-factuality prediction in fact-seeking question answering.

Space of uses. Papers use EntityQuestions in different evaluation roles. One paper uses it to construct training and testing datasets for experiments, while another poses questions from it alongside PopQA and Natural Questions as one of three widely-used QA datasets; papers do not link it to any other measurement instrument.

nodes.name: Enwik8
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat Enwik8 as a Wikipedia language modeling benchmark built from 100 million bytes of unprocessed English-language text. Definitions usually frame it as byte-level and as a dataset for compression and sequence prediction, with one paper noting long-term dependencies that can span tens of thousands of bytes and another describing it as a standard English Wikipedia dataset for training and evaluating compression models. A smaller line describes EnWik-8 as a character-level language modeling benchmark for evaluating pretraining performance, so the prevailing framing is byte-level but not uniform. One paper also contrasts it with enwik9, described there as an extension, while enwik8 contains the first 100 million bytes.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers do not explicitly report Enwik8 as measuring any named construct or behavioral indicator. Instead, they use it as an evaluation setting and report outputs such as test bits-per-byte and, in the character-level framing, test bytes-per-character.

Space of uses. Across the papers, Enwik8 is used for both training and evaluation: one paper states that it trains vanilla Transformer models on enwi

nodes.name: EQ-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe EQ-Bench in two different ways. One treats it as a benchmark for creative writing, specifically a creative writing leaderboard scored by other LLMs. Another describes it as an emotional intelligence benchmark that incorporates human survey ratings and allows multiple correct answers through cosine similarity to weighted choice distributions.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, EQ-Bench is linked to three constructs and no behavioral indicators. Those measurement claims are spread across emotion understanding, emotional intelligence, and social and emotional intelligence: papers report using it to evaluate emotional understanding ability, treat it as a benchmark from a similar emotional-intelligence domain, and place it within socio-emotional evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers use EQ-Bench as an evaluation benchmark. No measurement instrument is linked to it, though one paper groups it with LM-Pragmatics, SocialIQA, and SimpleToM under a socio-emotional category, and another uses it as a comparison point alongside other benchmarks from a similar domain.

nodes.name: EquiBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark consisting of 2400 program pairs in Python, C, CUDA, and x86-64, designed to evaluate an LLM's ability to reason about program semantics via equivalence checking.

nodes.name: ESC-50
nodes.definition: Environmental sound classification benchmark with 50 classes, used to evaluate zero-shot audio classification performance.

nodes.name: ESC-Judge
nodes.definition: An automated, LLM-driven evaluation framework that compares emotional-support LLMs using synthetic help-seeker roles and a judge model guided by Hill’s Exploration–Insight–Action rubric across nine fine-grained dimensions.

nodes.name: ESConv
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe ESConv as a benchmark dataset for emotional support conversations. The available definition presents it as collected in a help-seeker and supporter mode, with approximately 1K conversations and 31K utterances, and with utterances annotated with one of eight support strategies.

What it is claimed to measure. In the linked work, ESConv is used to measure 1 behavioral indicator, Text generation, and it is not linked to any constructs. The reported measurement claim is narrow rather than spread across multiple outcomes: one paper says it conducts experiments on ESConv when applying IntentionFrame to enhance downstream response generation.

Space of uses. Across the cited work, ESConv is positioned as an experimental benchmark for emotional support conversation systems. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers use it for experiments on response generation and framework evaluation, including studies that report experiments on ESConv when assessing emotional support performance and support strategy selection.

nodes.name: ESOL
nodes.definition: A dataset from the MoleculeNet benchmark for the regression task of predicting the log water solubility of a molecule.

nodes.name: ETHICS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as a benchmark dataset for machine ethics or ethical reasoning built around scenario-based moral judgments. Definitions commonly describe morally charged or common-sense scenarios; one paper says they are first-person descriptions of morally relevant actions with binary labels, and another uses the benchmark to categorize scenarios as "wrong" or "not wrong." Some papers refer specifically to Commonsense, Justice, or Deontology subsets, while a smaller framing presents it as a zero-shot benchmark scored by accuracy.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ETHICS to measure 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, with the dominant use centered on moral reasoning. Several papers claim it measures moral reasoning, describing it as analyzing machine ethics, evaluating commonsense moral recognition, or "mainly measures LLM's moral reasoning ability," while a smaller line of work uses it to measure ethical decision-making. Single papers also use it to measure zero-shot task performance and binary classification, and one paper reports ETHICS as related to helpfulness.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers u

nodes.name: ETHOS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available definitions, ETHOS is treated as a dataset for detecting hate speech. The only description provided places it in binary classification experiments where papers report F1 score under optimized prompts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link ETHOS to any construct or behavioral indicator. In the available usage, it is reported as an evaluation dataset for F1 score in hate speech detection, rather than being tied to a broader set of measurement claims.

Space of uses. The available paper uses ETHOS alongside ArSarcasm, Liar, and BBH-navigate, reporting F1 score across these benchmarks. In that usage, ETHOS appears as one item in a multi-dataset evaluation setup for prompt optimization.

nodes.name: ETTh1
nodes.definition: A real-world benchmark dataset for long-term time series forecasting, consisting of seven factors related to electricity transformers.

nodes.name: ETTm1
nodes.definition: A time series benchmark dataset used in long-term forecasting evaluations, part of the Electricity Transformer Temperature datasets with hourly and minute-level sampling.

nodes.name: EuroGEST
nodes.definition: A multilingual dataset for measuring gender stereotypes in 30 European languages, consisting of gendered minimal sentence pairs (EuroGESTG) and gender-neutral sentences (EuroGESTN) that can be placed in gendered templates.

nodes.name: EuroSAT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, EuroSAT is most commonly described as a satellite imagery or satellite image classification benchmark or dataset used for image classification. Some definitions narrow this to land use and land cover classification, with one description calling it a dataset and deep learning benchmark for that task, and another specifying Sentinel-2 satellite images covering 10 land use and land cover classes. A smaller line of description frames it through particular evaluation settings, such as remote sensing image understanding or the evaluation of descriptions for rare or abstract visual concepts.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded links, papers use EuroSAT to measure the behavioral indicator Image classification. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Image classification, and to no constructs. Several papers describe evaluations on EuroSAT as part of image recognition or classification benchmarks, including formulations such as satellite image classification and standard benchmark datasets for multiple classification domains.

Space of uses. Papers usually position EuroSAT as one dataset within broader benchmark suites for image recognitio

nodes.name: EvalPlus
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description treats EvalPlus as an augmented or upgraded version of HumanEval and MBPP, with HumanEval+ and MBPP+ adding many more test cases for more rigorous code-generation evaluation. One paper states that HumanEval+ has 'an average of 774.8 test cases per problem,' while MBPP+ expands test cases 'by over 35 times'; another says the suite reports both base scores on HumanEval and MBPP and plus scores on HumanEval+ and MBPP+. A smaller line of description frames it as an evaluation framework, or specifically as the test set used to augment HumanEval for more comprehensive functional-correctness testing, particularly for Python.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use EvalPlus to measure 3 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is code generation, often via its plus variants for function-level evaluation; other papers use it for three other behavioral indicators and three constructs, including code debugging, vulnerability identification, and inductive reasoning, with one paper explicitly saying that the abundance of test cases allows MBPP+ to serve as an inductive reasoning dataset. Overall, the reported measu

nodes.name: Event-Bench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating long video understanding, with a specific focus on the challenging task of episodic reasoning.

nodes.name: EvoEval
nodes.definition: Benchmark with 828 programming problems evolved from HumanEval using GPT-4, including semantic-altering and semantic-preserving variants to test robustness and efficiency.

nodes.name: Evol-Instruct
nodes.definition: Evol-Instruct, an instruction-following benchmark used to compare model responses under pairwise judgment.

nodes.name: EVOUNA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe EVOUNA as a question answering benchmark, though some also refer to it as a dataset. The prevailing description is that it augments QA datasets with LLM-generated responses and uses human annotations of whether each response is semantically equivalent to the golden answer; one paper further describes it as including human evaluations of five reader models across two QA datasets and as a source for constructing EMBERQA.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, EVOUNA is linked to one behavioral indicator and no constructs. Papers use it to measure question answering, so the reported use converges on that single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across multiple constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers position EVOUNA as an evaluation source for QA tasks. One paper uses it alongside EQAE as one of two sources for question answering data, and another uses it as source data when constructing EMBERQA; no measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: Execution-based evaluation
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is an evaluation procedure that verifies success by execution rather than by static demonstrations or string matching. Most descriptions say it runs model outputs and checks results through scripts or test cases: one line checks the final state of a computer environment, another runs generated code in a secure, isolated, Docker-based sandbox against test cases, and another describes an execution-based focused evaluation in which scripts programmatically obtain database results and judge the core answer components while ignoring non-essential columns.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use it to measure one behavioral indicator, Code generation, and no constructs. The measurement claims therefore center on code generation rather than being spread across multiple constructs; one study states that the method "executes generated code against test cases to measure the success rate."

Space of uses. Papers also link it to one other measurement instrument, OSWorld, which is described as supporting "execution-based evaluation of open-ended computer tasks" and as providing example-wise execution-based evaluat

nodes.name: Expert evaluation
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a human evaluation protocol in which domain experts review model outputs or benchmark items against ground truth, predefined criteria, or paired alternatives. Definitions vary in who the evaluators are, from SQL experts, medical professionals, clinicians, radiologists, legal experts, translators, psychotherapists, and domain researchers to trained students or native speakers in some studies, and the format also varies, including independent judgments, pairwise comparisons, blind or randomized reader studies, rubric or Likert scoring, and consensus adjudication. A smaller line of work uses the same label for expert annotation or validation of benchmark data, unit tests, captions, or adversarial items, and some papers use it to establish human performance baselines on sampled benchmark questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, expert evaluation is used to measure 9 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so the recorded measurement claims are spread across many targets rather than centered on one. The most frequently listed construct links are Accuracy and Clinical interpretability, with 7 other constructs also linked

nodes.name: FActScore
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a factuality evaluation procedure or benchmark for long-form generation, especially biographies, that breaks outputs into atomic facts or claims and verifies each one against a knowledge source, often Wikipedia or retrieved passages. Most definitions present it as a fine-grained, reference-based method that reports the percentage or proportion of supported atomic facts, a precision score, or the numbers of true and false facts. Some papers describe it more specifically as an automated retrieval augmentation pipeline, a suite and fact evaluator for faithful biography generation, or a decomposition policy with annotated demonstrations; a smaller set of definitions also refer to FACTSCORES as citation-supported sub-facts and to FactScore-Bio as a long-form QA dataset of biography questions from Wikipedia.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure Factuality, with papers using it as a representative reference-based truthfulness score, to evaluate factual long-form summaries and biographies, and to assess the factuality of model-generated responses.

nodes.name: FairEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat FairEval as a benchmark dataset for open-ended question answering: definitions describe 80 open-ended questions drawn from a wide array of categories, including common-sense, counterfactual, and coding, with corresponding human annotations. Some papers describe it differently, casting it as a meta-evaluation benchmark for assessing the performance and biases of LLM evaluators, while another paper uses it as a fairness-oriented evaluation procedure adopted to eliminate positional bias.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, the recorded measurement claim concentrates on one behavioral indicator: papers use FairEval to measure Open-ended question answering. No construct is linked to it, so the reported use converges on that single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across multiple constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. Papers use FairEval both as a benchmark in model evaluation and as a reference point in evaluator meta-evaluation. One paper evaluates a system on FairEval alongside Topical-Chat, where FairEval represents the open-ended question answer category, another compares evaluator accuracies on FairEval agains

nodes.name: FaithEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe FaithEval as an evaluation benchmark designed to measure and reduce model hallucination across challenging scenarios. Another description presents it as a novel, comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the faithfulness of LLMs in contextual scenarios, and says it comprises 4.9K high-quality problems built through a four-stage context construction and validation framework.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FaithEval to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The main measurement claim is context faithfulness: one paper describes it as a benchmark tailored to evaluate the faithfulness of LLMs in contextual scenarios. It is also reported as measuring document question answering, and another paper uses FaithEval in an ablation study while discussing reduced hallucinations, treating the benchmark as a measure of hallucination.

Space of uses. Papers connect FaithEval with two other instruments, Human evaluation and LLM-as-a-judge. One description says its problems were validated with both LLM-based auto-evaluation and human validation, and another says a separate LLM judge was used to verify whether a new answer was valid given the context. Beyo

nodes.name: Fann or Flop
nodes.definition: A benchmark comprising 6,984 poem-explanation pairs across 12 historical eras and 14 genres of Arabic poetry, designed to evaluate semantic, metaphorical, prosodic, and cultural understanding through QA-style tasks.

nodes.name: FANToM
nodes.definition: A theory-of-mind dataset containing questions based on multi-party dialogues, some of which rest on false premises, to test a model's ability to handle such scenarios.

nodes.name: Fashion-MNIST
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe Fashion-MNIST as a dataset of Zalando article, or clothing, images with 60,000 training examples and 10,000 test examples. The prevailing framing presents it as an image-classification dataset, while another definition describes it as a drop-in replacement for MNIST; papers also use both the "Fashion MNIST" and "FashionMNIST" spellings.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the reported relationships, papers use it to measure one behavioral indicator, Image classification, and they do not link it to any constructs. One paper records the directional claim that Image classification is measured by Fashion-MNIST, in a setting that considers models trained on MNIST and the Fashion-MNIST dataset of clothing images.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the usage snippets, papers place it alongside MNIST: one uses MNIST for pretraining and FashionMNIST for fine-tuning, and another considers models trained on both MNIST and Fashion-MNIST.

nodes.name: FB15k-237
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, papers most commonly treat FB15k-237 as a benchmark dataset, or standard benchmark, for knowledge graph completion, derived from Freebase or from the original FB15k. The prevailing description is that it is a subset built by removing inverse relations to reduce or prevent test set leakage, and one definition adds that it focuses on common knowledge. A smaller line of work instead describes it as a large-scale knowledge graph with complex relational semantics.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FB15k-237 to measure four behavioral indicators and do not link it to any constructs. It is most often used for link prediction, and is also reported as measuring fact checking, graph partitioning, and knowledge graph completion. Overall, the reported uses spread across multiple behavioral indicators rather than converging on a single linked construct.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use it alongside WN18RR, and some also pair it with YAGO3-10, PrimeKG, FB15k-237N, or the FEVER fact verification challenge. In these studies it is positioned as one of the benchmark datasets used for experimental evaluation, for example as one of "two large datasets" f

nodes.name: FB-Bench
nodes.definition: A fine-grained, multi-task benchmark in Chinese for evaluating LLMs’ responsiveness to human feedback across error correction and response maintenance scenarios, using a weighted checklist evaluated by GPT-4o.

nodes.name: Feedback Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, papers treat Feedback Bench as a benchmark for evaluating judge models or LLM-as-a-judge. The fuller description presents it as the official test set of Feedback Collection, with 1K responses to evaluate and instructions and scoring rubrics that do not overlap with the training set, while a briefer description frames it as a benchmark for single-instance rating tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. In the reported relationships, papers use it to measure one construct, Evaluation ability, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The claims therefore converge on a single construct rather than spreading across many: one paper reports measuring evaluation ability by checking correlation with GPT-4 across customized score rubrics on Feedback Bench.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation benchmark for judging tasks, including single-rating evaluation. One study places it alongside MT Bench, Vicuna Bench, and Flask Eval when measuring correlation with GPT-4 across multiple benchmarks, which positions it as one component of a broader evaluation setup.

nodes.name: Ferret-Bench
nodes.definition: A benchmark of multimodal dialogue-style VQA tasks for referring and grounding, constructed with GPT-4.

nodes.name: FeTaQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, FeTaQA is most commonly described as a table question answering benchmark or dataset with open-ended, free-form, long-form natural-language answers. Definitions repeatedly say that answering requires fetching multiple entities from a table, aggregating or reasoning over them, sometimes across multiple table sections, and producing a coherent response; one paper also describes it as an English dataset of Wikipedia tables paired with questions, answers, and supporting table cells. A smaller use treats FetaQA as table-language data adapted into training formats for table-language interleaved learning and for training column embeddings, rather than only as an evaluation benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FeTaQA to 3 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing use is to measure Table question answering, with several papers explicitly naming it as a TableQA benchmark or dataset. Smaller lines of work also report it as measuring Data-to-text generation and Long-form question answering, and one paper uses it to measure Table reasoning, so the recorded links are concentrated on table question answering with a few additional fram

nodes.name: FEVER
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant treatment of FEVER is as a fact verification, or fact extraction and verification, benchmark built from claims that are checked against evidence from Wikipedia. The prevailing formulation is a three-way classification task, Supported, Refuted, and NotEnoughInfo, though one definition instead uses supported, refuted, and neutral, another frames it as a natural language inference benchmark, and some descriptions add that claims may require multiple evidence pieces; one paper also describes it as a large-scale resource with 185,000 annotated claims.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FEVER to measure one behavioral indicator, Fact checking, and they do not link it to any constructs. This use is concentrated rather than spread across many targets: relationship evidence repeatedly calls FEVER a fact-checking or fact verification task, and definitions say it assesses whether a model can determine the veracity of claims from evidence, while a smaller set of papers also describes it as testing world knowledge, factuality, or factual consistency.

Space of uses. Papers link FEVER to one other measurement instrument, BEIR, with one study listin

nodes.name: FEVEROUS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, FEVEROUS is most commonly described as a fact-verification or complex claim-verification dataset or benchmark built around mixed evidence. Definitions usually say it combines structured or semi-structured tables with unstructured text or sentences, often from Wikipedia, and several descriptions add complex or multi-hop reasoning, sometimes with evidence annotated at the sentence or table-cell level. A smaller line of work adapts it for open-domain table reasoning by restricting attention to table-only claims and framing the task as identifying relevant evidence tables.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FEVEROUS to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure fact checking: papers describe it as a fact verification, claim verification, or fact-checking benchmark for deciding whether evidence supports or refutes claims. Smaller usages treat it as measuring table reasoning, through an open-domain adaptation, and entity disambiguation, through a reported FEVEROUS partition.

Space of uses. Papers do not link FEVEROUS to another measurement instrument. It is nevertheless used alongside other benchmarks, most commonly HOVE

nodes.name: FewEvent
nodes.definition: A dataset for type discovery focused on identifying event types from text.

nodes.name: FewRel
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat FewRel as a benchmark dataset for few-shot relation extraction, used to evaluate model performance in low-resource relation classification settings. In continual relation extraction work, it is also described as an FCRE benchmark and is repeatedly paired with TACRED for method and baseline comparisons. A smaller framing describes it as a dataset for type discovery, focused on identifying relation types from text and grouped with FewEvent and FewNerd under information extraction tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. One paper reports FewRel as measuring relation extraction. In the surveyed work it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Relation extraction, and to no constructs, so the reported measurement claims center on that single indicator.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Even so, papers frequently use FewRel alongside TACRED when evaluating methods, and one paper explicitly describes FewRel and TACRED as "widely used benchmarks"; across these examples, it is positioned as a benchmark dataset for comparing methods and FCRE baselines.

nodes.name: FFHQ
nodes.definition: A high-resolution face image dataset used for unconditional and conditional image generation evaluation.

nodes.name: FGSM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe FGSM as the Fast Gradient Sign Method, an adversarial attack method. The definitions converge on the same mechanism: it generates adversarial examples by adding a small perturbation in the direction of the sign of the loss gradient with respect to the input, and one definition explicitly presents it as a white-box attack.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not use FGSM to measure any construct or behavioral indicator, and no measurement links connect it to linked outcomes.

Space of uses. Where papers describe its use, they apply FGSM as an adversarial attack procedure. One paper reports using it together with SI-NI-FGSM and varying the attack strength, stating, "We apply two adversarial attacks FGSM and SI-NI-FGSM with various attack strengths."

nodes.name: FGVC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, FGVC is treated as a Fine-Grained Visual Classification benchmark for specialized image classification, covering bird, flower, dog, and car recognition. Definitions describe it as five specialized tasks; one source names CUB-Birds, NA-Birds, Oxford Flowers, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars, while a related description says FGVC includes CUB-200-2011, Oxford Flowers, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FGVC to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator, both centered on image-focused evaluation. The prevailing usage is to use FGVC to measure Image classification, and one paper also reports Visual recognition as measured by FGVC.

Space of uses. Papers use FGVC alongside other evaluation settings: one evaluation quote groups it with VTAB-1K, few-shot learning, and domain adaptation as visual classification adaptation tasks, and another reports evaluation on VTAB-1k and the FGVC benchmark. Papers also relate FGVC to 4 instruments, CUB-200-2011, Oxford Flowers-102, Stanford Cars, and Stanford Dogs, describing them as included datasets within the benchmark.

nodes.name: FGVC-Aircraft
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, FGVC-Aircraft is most commonly described as a fine-grained aircraft image classification dataset or benchmark. Definitions converge on aircraft model recognition, with papers variously describing it as focusing on aircraft categories and as containing images of 100 or over 100 different aircraft model variants. A smaller framing specifies the evaluation setting rather than the content, describing it as used for few-shot learning performance, while another definition says it is used to assess visual classification and explanation quality.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to two behavioral indicators and no constructs. The reported measurement claims center on fine-grained visual recognition and image classification: one paper uses FGVC-Aircraft to measure image classification, describing it as part of "12 image recognition datasets" for "aircraft model classification," and another uses it to measure fine-grained visual recognition as one of several "popular FGVR datasets."

Space of uses. Papers typically include it within broader benchmark suites, for example alongside CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, OxfordPets, StanfordCars, and Flowers1

nodes.name: FigStep
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, FigStep is most commonly treated as a multimodal safety benchmark, sometimes described as a harmful-question dataset, for testing vision-language or multimodal models on unsafe prompts. Definitions vary in what they foreground: attacks involving figures and text, harmful-response behavior from image-based prompts, typography that transfers unsafe text into images, and adversarial step-by-step harmful task instructions, with one definition also noting unsafe and benign variants. One paper adapts it by excluding legal, medical, and financial advice categories and converting the questions to speech.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FigStep to measure three constructs: Safety alignment, Safety, and Safety robustness. The recorded links are all measured_by relations from those constructs to FigStep, and it is not linked to any behavioral indicator. In the papers' own terms, it is used to evaluate safe alignment, multimodal safety, or jailbreak robustness.

Space of uses. FigStep is usually deployed alongside other safety benchmarks, most often MM-SafetyBench and SIUO, and also JailBreaKV, VL-Guard, and MOSSBench. Papers generally position it as o

nodes.name: FilBench
nodes.definition: FILBENCH, a Filipino-centric benchmark suite that evaluates LLMs across cultural knowledge, classical NLP, reading comprehension, and generation tasks in Filipino, Tagalog, and Cebuano.

nodes.name: FIMO
nodes.definition: A formal dataset for automated theorem proving containing challenging Olympiad-level math problems.

nodes.name: FinanceBench
nodes.definition: An English-language financial benchmark consisting of 1 dataset for 1 task.

nodes.name: Financial PhraseBank
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats Financial PhraseBank, also written as FPB or FP, as a benchmark dataset for sentiment analysis or text classification in financial text. Definitions consistently describe sentences from financial news, and one definition broadens this to financial statements and news, annotated for sentiment. Most descriptions specify positive, negative, and neutral categories, while one paper describes its task setup on the dataset as positive or negative.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Financial PhraseBank to measure 2 behavioral indicators and link it to no constructs. The dominant claim is that it measures sentiment analysis, with papers describing it as extracting positive, negative, or neutral sentiment from financial texts. A smaller but recurring line of work uses it as a text classification benchmark, describing it among several text classification datasets.

Space of uses. Papers often use it within multi-dataset evaluations, for example alongside FiQA-SA and TSA in financial sentiment analysis, or alongside Tweet Irony and MRPC in broader text classification comparisons. Some papers also frame it as a focused t

nodes.name: FineDiving
nodes.definition: A dataset of Olympic diving performances, used as a source for the 'Diving' category videos in the VidDiffBench benchmark.

nodes.name: FinEval
nodes.definition: Benchmark for evaluating financial domain understanding and reasoning in language models.

nodes.name: FineWeb
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, FineWeb is most commonly described as a web-text corpus or LLM pretraining dataset. Definitions present it as a corpus for analyzing bilinear transformer feature interactions at different model sizes, a high-quality dataset used to generate prompts for base LLMs, and a large corpus of deduplicated English web documents used for negative log-likelihood evaluation. Some papers also work with study-specific variants or subsets, including 'two FineWeb models with 12 and 16 layers' ('fw-small' and 'fw-medium') and a 10k-example sample from the corpus.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FineWeb to measure one construct, Generalization, and two behavioral indicators, Text continuation and Text generation. The linked claims are distributed across these uses: one paper employs the FineWeb dataset during pre-training for Text continuation, another uses prompts from FineWeb to synthesize new texts for Text generation, and another reports evaluating a model on FineWeb as one of several datasets for Generalization.

Space of uses. Papers position FineWeb in several roles rather than as a single fixed evaluation protocol. It appears as pretraining data, as a pr

nodes.name: FineWeb-Edu
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, FineWeb-Edu is most commonly described as a curated educational web-text dataset used in language model training and evaluation. Definitions present it as high-quality educational text from CommonCrawl, while one paper instead treats Fineweb-Edu as an English LLM-annotated dataset with approximately 450,000 document assessments of educational value. Another description presents it as educational text filtered from FineWeb, comprising 1.3T tokens with documents up to 339K tokens long, and mentions a curated subset of 1,000 texts of 128K tokens each for perplexity assessment.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers do not link FineWeb-Edu to any construct or behavioral indicator through measured_by relations, so no prevailing claim appears about what it measures. In the available descriptions, it is used as training, evaluation, sampling, or perplexity material rather than being tied to a recorded construct-level or behavioral measurement claim.

Space of uses. Papers position it mainly as source material rather than as an instrument used alongside other named instruments, and no other measurement instrument is linked to it. The recurring uses are tr

nodes.name: FinQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description treats FinQA as a financial question-answering dataset, often used as a held-out benchmark, that requires generating a Python-executable math expression from a question and a financial table. Some authors describe it more broadly as a financial benchmark for knowledge-based question answering, while another paper also presents it as a financial question-answering dataset used for reranking tasks and as a benchmark that primarily assesses text generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Its measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets. Papers link it to one construct, Financial reasoning, describing datasets such as FinQA as benchmarks for numerical reasoning tasks in the financial domain, and to one behavioral indicator, Table question answering, where it appears as benchmark data for evaluating table tasks.

Space of uses. Papers mainly position FinQA as an evaluation resource: one study uses it as a held-out dataset to test generalization ability, and another uses financial question-answering datasets such as FinQA to construct reranking tasks. No measurement instrument is linked to it, though

nodes.name: FINTRUST
nodes.definition: A comprehensive benchmark with 15,680 question-answer pairs across textual, tabular, and time-series data, designed to evaluate LLM trustworthiness in finance through seven dimensions: truthfulness, safety, fairness, robustness, privacy, transparency, and knowledge discovery.

nodes.name: FiQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, FiQA is most commonly described as a BEIR retrieval dataset, often used as a single-hop retrieval benchmark. One paper states that its retrieval corpus consists of human-written responses to the search queries in the dataset. Some papers instead describe it as a financial question answering benchmark for downstream evaluation, and one paper refers to FiQA as a financial-domain sentiment analysis task.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FiQA to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing usage is that it measures Financial question answering, while a smaller line of work uses it to measure Sentiment analysis, described as predicting positive, neutral, or negative sentiments in financial texts. Taken together, the measurement claims spread across these behavioral indicators rather than converging on a construct.

Space of uses. FiQA is linked to 1 other measurement instrument, BEIR, and papers frequently position it as part of the BEIR benchmark rather than a standalone protocol. Beyond that broad placement, papers use it to generate and evaluate adversarial passages in corpus-poisoning experiments, to evaluate methods alon

nodes.name: FiQA-SA
nodes.definition: A dataset for sentiment analysis in the financial domain.

nodes.name: FLAN
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, FLAN is described as a benchmark or dataset of diverse tasks, including free-form generation tasks such as translation and summarization. Some descriptions further frame it as a collection of datasets expressed via natural language instructions for evaluating model performance on a wide variety of NLP tasks, and papers also position it as a large multi-task evaluation set or a mix of multiple NLP tasks. A reported use samples 100 questions from each of its 66 tasks as a "whole benchmark."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FLAN to measure 2 constructs and link it to 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claim is that it measures Generalization, while a smaller line of work uses it to measure Robustness, with both claims framed through evaluation across multiple tasks. Beyond those measurement links, FLAN is also related to Open-ended question answering.

Space of uses. In use, papers position FLAN as a reference dataset or multi-task evaluation set for checking performance across varied tasks. Reported uses include sampling 100 questions from each of its 66 tasks as a "whole benchmark" and evaluating it alongside Wikitext a

nodes.name: FLAN Collection
nodes.definition: The FLAN Collection is a dataset composed of various tasks formatted as instructions, used to evaluate instruction-following, chain-of-thought, and few-shot learning capabilities.

nodes.name: FLASK
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat FLASK as a fine-grained benchmark or evaluation protocol for particular LLM skill sets. Definitions vary in emphasis: some describe it as a benchmark for single-instance rating or for assessing LLM-as-a-judge performance, while another describes it as a protocol for both human-based and model-based evaluation. One definition specifies 200 test prompts and 2000 responses from Alpaca-7B, Vicuna-13B, Bard, and GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613, and another highlights a logical thinking category with logical correctness, logical robustness, and logical efficiency.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FLASK to measure 7 constructs and no behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than centered on one. The prevailing framing is granular evaluation: one paper says it offers 12 skill-specific scores, and papers report that it measures Factuality, Completeness, Insightfulness, Logical consistency, and Metacognition, plus 2 other constructs. One paper further narrows this use to the logical thinking category when using FLASK to measure Logical consistency.

Space of uses. Papers link FLASK to 3 other measurement instru

nodes.name: FLenQA
nodes.definition: Flexible Length Question Answering, a benchmark that assesses a model's reasoning capabilities over contexts of varying lengths by asking True/False questions.

nodes.name: FLEURS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats FLEURS as a multilingual speech benchmark or dataset, often for automatic speech recognition, and one definition expands its name as the Few-shot Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech. Some papers narrow this to the English test split or test subset, where WER is computed, while a smaller line of work describes it as a multilingual or massively multilingual speech translation benchmark, including translation between English and German, Spanish, and French in both directions. One paper describes it as speech for 102 languages, and another says it covers 21 African languages.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FLEURS to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs, so the claims about what it measures concentrate on behavioral indicators rather than constructs. The most common claim is that it measures Speech recognition, including ASR evaluations and WER on the English test split, and a smaller line of work also uses it to measure Speech translation through ST tasks on several language pairs.

Space of uses. Papers commonly position FLEURS as a standard multilingual benchmark for ASR and AST

nodes.name: FLEURS-ASL
nodes.definition: A benchmark for American Sign Language to English video translation, extended from the multilingual FLORES/FLEURS benchmarks and featuring vocabulary from Wikipedia articles.

nodes.name: Flickr30k
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, Flickr30k is most commonly treated as a benchmark built from 30,000 Flickr images paired with captions, usually described as five descriptive sentences or captions per image. The prevailing framing is image captioning, including image-level and zero-shot caption generation, though several papers also describe it as an image-text retrieval benchmark where models match images to captions or the reverse. A smaller line of work uses it for text-to-image generation, and one paper specifies the Flickr30k Karpathy split test set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Flickr30k to measure five behavioral indicators and two constructs. The most common claim is that it measures Image captioning, with papers using it to assess image-level caption ability, zero-shot caption generation, and general image captioning; Cross-modal retrieval is the next most frequent usage, including image-to-text and text-to-image retrieval. Smaller lines of work report it as measuring Image generation, Information retrieval, and Synthetic recall, and papers also use it to measure the constructs Multimodal understanding and Visual perception, so the reported measurement claims e

nodes.name: Flickr30k Entities
nodes.definition: Benchmark dataset for phrase grounding, where models are evaluated on their ability to localize text phrases in images; uses recall at K (R@1, R@5, R@10) with IoU > 0.5.

nodes.name: FLORES
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, FLORES is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for machine translation, often framed as multilingual or massively multilingual and used across many languages. Definitions describe it as evaluating text-to-text translation across over 200 languages, with one paper paraphrasing it as a set of short documents translated into 200 languages, while other papers emphasize low-resource evaluation, translation across languages and scripts, or high-quality translation between language pairs. A smaller line of work describes Flores as a dataset for bitext mining where the same sentences are shared across several language pairs, and some papers refer specifically to FLORES devtest for npi and gug.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FLORES to one behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and one construct, Translation quality, so the named measurement claims focus on these outcomes rather than a wider set. The prevailing usage is to measure machine translation: papers say they use or adopt FLORES to assess machine translation performance, including English to non-English and non-English to English settings and experiments on 100 languages. A smalle

nodes.name: Flores-101
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats Flores-101 as a multilingual benchmark dataset built from aligned translations, or human-written translation pairs, across 101 languages. Definitions differ slightly in emphasis: some describe professionally translated sentences used for qualitative evaluation of interventions in a machine translation context, while others frame it as a benchmark for machine translation and cross-lingual generation, and one paper specifies BLEU and COMET as the translation-quality metrics. Source snippets also mention both the general dataset and the devtest split, and describe inputs as sampled from Flores-101.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the recorded relationships, papers use Flores-101 to measure 2 behavioral indicators and do not link it to constructs. The dominant link is to Machine translation: papers describe it as the evaluation set for translation tasks, translation performance, or bidirectional machine translation, with some reporting BLEU scores and others discussing Eng→X and X→Eng settings. A smaller line of work reports it as measuring Coreference resolution, illustrated by an example where the prediction of the pronoun

nodes.name: FLORES-200
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions treat FLORES-200 as a multilingual machine translation benchmark spanning 200 languages, often emphasizing low-resource coverage. Papers variously use its development, test, and devtest splits; some explicitly describe it as parallel text, and one definition says it contains short paragraphs sampled from Wikimedia and translated by skilled human translators into 204 languages, whereas most others describe 200 languages. A smaller line of work also uses its development and test sets as high-quality parallel training data, and one paper notes that Belebele passages are sourced from FLORES-200.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked claims, papers use FLORES-200 to measure 1 behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and 1 construct, Generalization. The prevailing usage is machine translation evaluation, including low-resource, multilingual, English-to-X, X-to-English, and many-to-many settings; papers report chrF1, spBLEU, COMET, or BLEU on the benchmark. Only one construct link appears: one paper uses Flores200 for zero-shot evaluation as a measure of generalization in En-Zh and En-De translation.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is l

nodes.name: FLORES+
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the available definitions, FLORES+ is treated as a multilingual parallel-sentence dataset. The only described use frames it as an out-of-domain dataset for visualizing cross-lingual alignment with t-SNE, and one paper says it "randomly sample[s] 100 parallel sentences" for that examination (Debiasing Multilingual LLMs in Cross-lingual Latent Space).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers in the available evidence do not link FLORES+ to any construct or behavioral indicator through explicit measurement claims. The only stated evaluation target is cross-lingual alignment in a visualization setting, where authors examine sentence representations with t-SNE rather than report it as measuring a broader construct.

Space of uses. The documented usage is narrow: papers use FLORES+ as an out-of-domain set for visualization. In the reported procedure, authors sample 100 parallel sentences and inspect their cross-lingual alignment with t-SNE; no linked instruments are reported alongside it.

nodes.name: FLUID QA
nodes.definition: A multilingual benchmark that evaluates figurative language usage in multi-turn dialogue across English, Korean, and Chinese, using a cloze-style multiple-choice format to assess pragmatic appropriateness.

nodes.name: FM2
nodes.definition: Fact verification benchmark assessing whether models can verify claims using retrieved evidence.

nodes.name: fMoW
nodes.definition: The Functional Map of the World (FMOW) dataset, a satellite imagery benchmark for object classification that includes multiple classes and spurious groups, used to test model performance in complex settings.

nodes.name: FoCus
nodes.definition: A dialogue dataset focused on conversational information-seeking scenarios, used for developing and evaluating personalized dialogue systems.

nodes.name: FOLIO
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat FOLIO as a benchmark dataset for natural language reasoning with first-order logic, where models infer or assess conclusions from given premises. Several definitions emphasize that it is human or expert annotated and includes first-order logic annotations, while a smaller translation-oriented use describes it as English statements paired with logical forms for NL-FOL generation. Papers describe it at different granularities, from around 1,000 human-annotated deductive reasoning questions overall to a validation split of 203 expert-written natural language reasoning instances with corresponding first-order logic annotations, and some mention evaluation on the validation set or an original and perturbed version.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the prevailing usage is that FOLIO measures Logical reasoning. It is linked to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators, and the other reported measurement claims are less common: some papers use it to measure Chain-of-thought reasoning or Reasoning more broadly. Overall, the measurement claims converge mainly on logical reasoning rather than being spread evenly across many constructs.

Sp

nodes.name: FollowBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats FollowBench as an instruction-following benchmark, most commonly described as a fine-grained constraint-following benchmark with five levels of difficulty. Definitions emphasize diverse, open-ended instructions that require evaluation by strong LLMs, sometimes described specifically as GPT-4-based evaluation. Some papers stress complex, multi-constraint tasks, while others place it among benchmarks for more general instructions that need LLM-based judgment.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FollowBench to four constructs and one behavioral indicator. The dominant use is to measure instruction following, framed either as instruction following ability or as the behavioral indicator instruction following, and several papers also use it to measure complex instruction following ability, especially where instructions consist of multiple constraints. Smaller lines of work report it as measuring generalization, with one paper saying it can fully examine generalization to more general instructions not verifiable by simple code executions, and conversational ability.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is lin

nodes.name: FollowIR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, FollowIR is most commonly described as a benchmark for instruction-following document retrieval, or more broadly for instruction following in information retrieval, used to assess how well models adapt to user instructions in search queries. A narrower description adds that it is built from three TREC collections and uses a pairwise evaluation framework to measure how models respond to altered instructions. One paper also presents FOLLOWIR as more than a benchmark alone, pairing it with training data that includes diverse and realistic instructions.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement claims converge on a single behavioral indicator: papers use FollowIR to measure Instruction following, describing it as a benchmark that explicitly measures the instruction-following ability or capabilities of retrieval models. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Instruction following, and to no constructs.

Space of uses. Papers use FollowIR as an evaluation benchmark for retrieval models, including reporting performance on instruction-following retrieval tasks and evaluating models' instruction-following capabilities on the benchmark. One paper

nodes.name: Food-101
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe Food-101 as a food image classification dataset or benchmark organized around 101 food categories. Several definitions also frame it as a fine-grained image classification or recognition resource, and some add that it contains 101,000 images and is challenging. Some papers describe it more specifically as being used for zero-shot class descriptions, zero-shot transfer, or few-shot learning performance, while others use it more generally for image classification and prediction-correctness evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Food-101 to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. The reported relationship is consistent: papers use Food-101 to measure Image classification, and no other behavioral indicators are linked to it. The measurement claims therefore converge on a single behavioral target rather than spreading across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers usually place Food-101 within larger benchmark suites rather than using it alone, often alongside CIFAR-100, CUB, Caltech101, OxfordPets, and SUN397. The reported settings include fine-tuning, transfer learning, zero-shot and linear-probe evaluation, and fine-grained imag

nodes.name: FrameNet 1.7
nodes.definition: An expanded FrameNet benchmark with more annotated examples, more defined frame definitions, and increased lexical diversity, used for frame identification evaluation.

nodes.name: FreebaseQA
nodes.definition: A question answering dataset where questions are centered around entities and relations in the Freebase knowledge graph.

nodes.name: FreeSolv
nodes.definition: A dataset from the MoleculeNet benchmark for the regression task of predicting the hydration free energy of a molecule.

nodes.name: FreshQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the dominant framing is a question-answering dataset or benchmark. Definitions converge on questions with varying time sensitivity and complexity, with papers describing it as assessing factuality and reasoning; some add paired correct and incorrect contexts, while others emphasize up-to-date information and questions whose answers change over time, framing it as a benchmark for freshness and factuality of LLM responses.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FreshQA to measure 4 constructs, and it is not linked to any behavioral indicators. The measurement claims are spread across compositional reasoning, factuality, generalization, and knowledge conflict resolution rather than centered on a single construct: papers variously list it among factuality benchmarks, use it in benchmarking situated faithful reasoning on question-answering tasks, and report it as evaluating compositional reasoning or generalization.

Space of uses. Papers do not link FreshQA to another measurement instrument, but they do use it alongside NaturalQA, TriviaQA, PopQA, CuQA, and MultiHop-RAG. In those uses it is positioned as one of several question-answering tasks, and in

nodes.name: FreshWiki
nodes.definition: A dataset of high-quality, recent Wikipedia articles used to evaluate a model's ability to perform deep research and generate comprehensive articles on a given topic.

nodes.name: FrontierMath
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe FrontierMath as a benchmark used to evaluate the complex problem-solving and reasoning abilities of large language models. It is also described as a new benchmark developed through a collaboration with over 60 expert mathematicians, containing around 300 problems across 23 categories.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, FrontierMath is linked to two constructs, General ability and Reasoning, and no behavioral indicators. Papers use it to measure Reasoning, including one statement that it is used "to evaluate reasoning on several families of LLMs," and they also report it as measuring General ability.

Space of uses. Papers position FrontierMath as a reasoning benchmark. One study mentions "reasoning benchmarks, e.g. FrontierMath and ARC-AGI," so it appears alongside ARC-AGI in benchmark discussions, and no other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: FSD50K
nodes.definition: A benchmark for audio event classification.

nodes.name: Functional MATH
nodes.definition: Functional MATH is a transfer evaluation dataset used to test whether reasoning improvements generalize beyond the original training benchmark.

nodes.name: FUNSD
nodes.definition: The Form Understanding in Noisy Scanned Documents dataset, used to evaluate key information extraction and form parsing capabilities.

nodes.name: G-Eval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, G-Eval is most commonly described as an LLM-based automated evaluation protocol for generated text, usually using GPT-4 to assign criterion-specific scores or 1 to 5 Likert-scale ratings from a prompt. Some descriptions emphasize step-by-step chain-of-thought or auto-CoT prompting, and one variant frames it as a logit-weighted method that reweights score tokens by the model's predicted probabilities to refine scoring granularity. Papers also mention variants and adaptations, including G-Eval-4, where GPT-4 is sampled 20 times and the average score is used, and GCC-Eval, which modifies and extends G-Eval for chess commentary.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 11 constructs and link it to one behavioral indicator. The most commonly linked constructs are coherence, fluency, relevance, ambiguity handling, and completeness, with additional reported uses for empathy, engagement, faithfulness, interpretability and explainability, naturalness, and patient-centricity. Overall, the reported measurement claims are spread across many qualitative dimensions rather than centered on one target, and the only linked behavioral indicator is chain of

nodes.name: GAIA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, GAIA is most commonly treated as a benchmark for general AI assistants and tool use, with multimodal and information-seeking tasks as the dominant framing. Definitions describe it either as a multi-modal benchmark with 446 tasks and 109 files for document understanding, web surfing, logic reasoning, and answer summarization, or as 466 human-designed and annotated questions covering reasoning, multimodal comprehension, coding, and tool usage. A smaller line of work describes it more narrowly as diverse tool-use and information-seeking tasks such as web browsing and file reading, and one comparison paper characterizes it as focused solely on question answering tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GAIA to 5 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The most recurrent use is to measure tool use, with other recurring claims that it measures reasoning and web navigation; papers also report it as measuring generalization, multimodal understanding, robustness, and tool use ability. The reported measurement scope is spread across several abilities, often framed through real-world questions or scenarios that require reasoning, web browsing, multi-modali

nodes.name: Game of 24
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a mathematical reasoning benchmark, also called Game 24 or Game24, in which a model or agent must combine four given numbers with basic arithmetic operations to produce an expression equal to 24. Several definitions add search or planning language, describing it as a mathematical reasoning and search benchmark or a planning and reasoning benchmark, and multiple snippets specify that each of the four numbers is used exactly once. A few descriptions vary the starting items, speaking of a given set of integers, poker cards, or the 4nums.com task, but they consistently describe the goal as reaching 24 from four values with arithmetic operations.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported uses spread across several targets rather than converging on one: papers link it to 6 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators overall. The most common measured_by claims treat it as measuring Mathematical reasoning, followed by Reasoning and Planning, with smaller lines of work using it to measure 3 other constructs. Among behavioral indicators, papers use it to measure Mathematical problem solving, while one paper reports it as related to Self-verifi

nodes.name: GaoKao
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat GaoKao as an exam-oriented dataset tied to the Chinese National College Entrance Examination. Definitions describe it either as derived from exam questions or as simulating the exam, but they converge on academic subject coverage and reasoning demand: it is used for Chinese physical, chemical, and mathematical reasoning, and is described as requiring complex or high-level reasoning and knowledge integration.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the prevailing usage is that GaoKao measures Mathematical reasoning. It is linked to 1 construct, Mathematical reasoning, and no behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims converge on a single construct rather than spreading across many. Relationship evidence also describes GAOKAO, alongside ZHONGKAO, as enabling measurement of "a wider range of abilities," while using it to assess model accuracy under chain-of-thought reasoning settings.

Space of uses. The available usage examples place GaoKao alongside other datasets rather than in isolation. Papers use it together with ZHONGKAO and CN Middle School 24 in broader evaluation setups, and one reported protocol assesses model acc

nodes.name: GaoKao 2023 En
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description treats this as an English-language or English-translated benchmark or dataset of mathematics problems from the 2023 Chinese National College Entrance Examination, often phrased as the Gaokao math test in English. Papers also frame it as an out-of-domain or out-of-distribution evaluation set. A smaller description is looser, calling it an out-of-distribution mathematics benchmark drawn from major 2023 exam sources for testing generalization.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure two constructs and no behavioral indicators. The dominant claim is that it measures Mathematical reasoning, as papers report results on it among advanced math benchmarks, while a broader reasoning framing also appears in diverse reasoning task suites. Overall, the linked claims are concentrated on Mathematical reasoning and Reasoning rather than spread across many constructs.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Across the available papers, it is used alongside other evaluation benchmarks such as Minerva Math, OCWCourses, GSM8K, MATH or MATH500, and CollegeMath, and it is positioned as part of broader be

nodes.name: GAVIE
nodes.definition: An evaluation procedure for assessing generative hallucinations by prompting models to produce open-ended captions.

nodes.name: GCG
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the literature, GCG is most commonly described as Greedy Coordinate Gradient, a white-box or gradient-based jailbreak attack that uses greedy coordinate descent or related gradient optimization to craft adversarial prompts. Definitions usually frame the output as an adversarial suffix, sometimes a universal suffix, appended to a harmful query to elicit unsafe or target responses, though one paper describes attack strings prepended to harmful prompts and another treats successful GCG outputs as a filtered set of jailbreak prompts. A smaller line of work refers to nanoGCG as a lightweight variant and to individual or transfer variants of GCG attacks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GCG to four constructs and three behavioral indicators. The prevailing measurement use is for robustness-oriented outcomes, especially Adversarial robustness, with additional use for Harmlessness, Jailbreak resistance, and Harmful content detection, while two other robustness-related constructs are also measured by it; overall, the claims spread across several outcomes rather than converging on a single target. Separate from those measurement links, several papers claim a cau

nodes.name: GEMBA-MQM
nodes.definition: A prompting-based automatic evaluation metric that uses an LLM to detect translation quality errors based on the Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) framework.

nodes.name: GenEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, GenEval is most commonly described as a benchmark for whether a model can generate an image that accurately depicts a given prompt. Some authors also treat it as a score or metric for the quality and alignment of generated images with input text, with one description saying it is based on human preferences and semantic accuracy.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GenEval to 2 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure visual generation ability, with papers evaluating text-to-image or visual generation capabilities on it; other papers use it to measure prompt understanding, saying improvements on GenEval reflect enhanced prompt-following capabilities. It is also reported as measuring image generation and multimodal generation.

Space of uses. Papers typically position GenEval as a visual generation benchmark for model comparison, including comparisons with recent diffusion models and with other state-of-the-art systems. Papers do not link it to another measurement instrument, though some use it alongside MS-COCO and DSG, and one paper presents it as part of a move to report more comprehensive benchmarks r

nodes.name: Geometry3K
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, Geometry3K is most commonly described as a geometry benchmark or dataset centered on plane geometry problems. Definitions differ slightly: one paper calls it an early multimodal reasoning benchmark, while another describes a geometry dataset with human-annotated logical forms that is used to generate factual QA pairs and to evaluate geometry problem solving.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The linked constructs are geometric reasoning and mathematical reasoning, so the measurement claims focus on reasoning tasks: one paper evaluates effectiveness with “the problems from the Geometry3K dataset,” and another includes Geometry3K in geometry sub-task evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers most often position it as an evaluation source. One study uses its problems directly for evaluation, while another also treats it as source material, stating that “the factual QA pairs in the alignment data are generated using Geometry3K”; the same paper places it alongside GeoQA+, UniGeo, and GEOS in geometry-focused evaluation, and notes that the testmini split of MathVista is collected from GeoQA

nodes.name: GeoQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, GeoQA is most commonly described as a geometry question-answering or geometry problem benchmark for evaluating multimodal geometric problem solving. Definitions vary slightly in what they foreground: one emphasizes questions and images, while another emphasizes diagrams, textual descriptions, and the need for complex reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, GeoQA is linked to one construct, Geometric reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators. In G-LLaVA: Solving Geometric Problem with Multi-Modal Large Language Model and Theorem-Validated Reverse Chain-of-Thought Problem Generation for Geometric Reasoning, it is used to measure Geometric reasoning, so the measurement claims converge on a single construct rather than spreading across many.

Space of uses. In the cited evaluations, papers use the test set of GeoQA alongside the geometry problem solving task, testmini split, of MathVista. One paper also compares model performance on GeoQA with traditional methods in the geometry problem solving domain, which positions it as an evaluation benchmark for model comparison.

nodes.name: GeoQA+
nodes.definition: An enhanced version of the GeoQA dataset for geometric problem solving.

nodes.name: GEOS
nodes.definition: A dataset for geometry problem solving, included as a subtask within the MathVista benchmark.

nodes.name: Global-MMLU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe Global-MMLU as a multilingual extension of MMLU covering 42 languages, with improved translation quality, expanded language coverage, and subsets labeled as culturally sensitive and culturally agnostic. The fuller description presents it as a comprehensive test set containing MMLU's 14K samples in 42 languages, totaling 589,764 samples.

What it is claimed to measure. The cited papers do not explicitly claim that Global-MMLU measures any construct or behavioral indicator, and no construct or behavioral-indicator links are reported for it.

Space of uses. Across the papers, Global-MMLU is positioned as a multilingual benchmark or comprehensive test set for broader language coverage. One paper cites it as part of broader initiatives extending coverage to 42 languages, and no measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: GlobalOpinionQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, GlobalOpinionQA is most commonly described as a dataset or benchmark built from the World Values Survey and the Pew Global Attitudes Survey, with questions and answers intended to capture diverse perspectives on global issues. Several descriptions present it as a multiple-choice evaluation of model opinions against aggregated population opinions from different countries, while another describes it as a benchmark for human values and opinions across regions with around 2.5K questions. Some work also treats it as a template for preserving original questions and response options, uses selected country sets such as C′1 and C3, or notes that the original data contains answer distributions from multiple respondents within a country.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, its measurement claims are spread across several constructs rather than centered on one. It is linked to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators, and papers use it to measure In-context learning, Personalization, and Social bias. The recorded measurement language varies, including quantifying distributional alignment, assessing steerability for specific users or social grou

nodes.name: GLUE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat GLUE as a benchmark suite, or collection, of diverse natural language understanding tasks, often described as covering sentence-level classification, inference, paraphrase, similarity, sentiment analysis, textual entailment, and linguistic acceptability. A recurring framing is that it is a multi-task evaluation benchmark, sometimes even an analysis platform, though papers differ on its exact composition: several describe nine tasks, others refer to eight tasks or datasets, and many use subsets such as four binary classification datasets, five challenging tasks, or six selected subtasks. A smaller line of work describes it more narrowly as shorter-sequence NLU evaluation, as a source of classification and entailment tasks, or as including question answering and coreference resolution.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use GLUE mainly to measure natural language understanding. It is linked to 10 constructs and 9 behavioral indicators overall, and the most recurrent additional uses are for text classification, language understanding task performance, sentiment analysis, and natural language inference. The claims therefore converge most clearly on nat

nodes.name: GLUE-X
nodes.definition: An extension of the GLUE benchmark specifically designed to evaluate the out-of-domain robustness and generalization of language models.

nodes.name: GMAI-MMBench
nodes.definition: Medical multimodal benchmark assessing visual question answering across 38 modalities and four clinical tasks including attribute, blood vessel, bone, and cell recognition.

nodes.name: GoEmotions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, GoEmotions is most commonly described as a multi-label emotion recognition benchmark or dataset with 27 fine-grained emotions. Several definitions say it contains human-annotated Reddit comments, with one paper describing 58,000 comments from popular English subreddits and labels drawn from 27 emotions plus neutral, while a smaller line of work describes it more generally as texts with fine-grained emotions and one definition instead refers to human annotations of tweets. Several papers also use pooled variants, usually seven labels formed by hierarchical clustering, and one paper notes an average of 3.6 annotators per sample.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GoEmotions to one behavioral indicator and no constructs, and the linked indicator is emotion analysis. The claims are concentrated rather than spread across multiple outcomes: several papers use it to measure emotion analysis, describing it as a multilabel emotion recognition benchmark with 27 emotions.

Space of uses. The prevailing use is as an evaluation benchmark for emotion classification or emotion recognition, including fine-grained, multi-label, and open-set setups. Some papers ad

nodes.name: GossipCop
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, GossipCop is most commonly treated as a factuality-labeled dataset for entertainment and celebrity gossip content. The prevailing description is a collection of English-language celebrity gossip news articles, labeled for factuality or as true or false, and one definition also describes it as containing related social media posts alongside news articles.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use GossipCop to measure one behavioral indicator, Misinformation detection, and no constructs are linked to it. The measurement claims converge on that single target: papers describe it as a benchmark for fake news or misinformation detection in entertainment-related domains.

Space of uses. Papers position GossipCop as a benchmark dataset for fake news detection tasks. One study presents it as the second of two benchmark datasets used to evaluate a framework, and another applies open-ended rewriting to fake news and rephrases real news from GossipCop alongside PolitiFact.

nodes.name: GovReport
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat GovReport as a long-document summarization dataset or benchmark built from U.S. government reports. Definitions variously describe congressional and U.S. Government reports, long reports from the U.S. Government Accountability Office, and a SCROLL benchmark dataset for summarizing long government reports; one paper names a task variant, SUM-GOVREPORT, for long government reports with complex structure and content. Where papers give details, they describe 19,402 reports, corresponding summaries, and an average document length of 7,866 tokens.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing claim is that GovReport measures Text summarization: papers describe using it for the summarization task and as a generic summarization dataset. A smaller line of work reports it as measuring Length generalization, via length extrapolation on six long benchmarks. Overall, papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Text summarization, and one construct, Length generalization.

Space of uses. Papers usually use GovReport as one benchmark within broader long-context evaluations. They pair it with Proof-pile for language modeling on long or long-

nodes.name: GPQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, GPQA is most commonly described as a graduate-level, "Google-proof" question answering benchmark, usually centered on biology, physics, and chemistry and written by domain experts or PhD-level experts. Several definitions make its multiple-choice format explicit, and some describe it as consisting of 448 questions. Most descriptions keep the focus on those science domains, though one paper says it spans various disciplines and another emphasizes difficult physics and chemistry questions; a smaller line of work refers to it more generically as a reasoning or general-purpose QA benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use GPQA to measure 10 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Reasoning, followed by Generalization and General ability; at the behavioral level, the recurring framings are Multiple-choice question answering and Question answering. Overall, papers report it as evaluating a broad spread of targets rather than a single construct alone.

Space of uses. Papers usually place GPQA inside broader benchmark suites rather than using it alone, often alongside MMLU, ARC-C, BBH, and GSM8K. They typically positi

nodes.name: GPQA-Diamond
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is as a challenging, expert-level science or STEM question answering benchmark for deep reasoning.
