Definitions commonly describe graduate-level multiple-choice questions across biology, physics, and chemistry, with one description specifying 198 questions, and papers refer to it as GPQA-Diamond, GPQADiamond, or GPQA Diamond. A smaller descriptive variant treats GPQADiamond as a challenging subset of GPQA used for zero-shot generalization on unseen expert-level reasoning tasks, and some authors additionally specify pass@1 accuracy.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to five constructs and one behavioral indicator. The dominant claim is that GPQA-Diamond measures reasoning, often when authors describe it within broader reasoning benchmarks or reasoning ability evaluations; smaller lines of work use it to measure chain-of-thought reasoning, generalization, mathematical reasoning, and problem-solving ability. One paper also uses it to measure the behavioral indicator long chain-of-thought generation, describing it as part of a benchmark set for long trace reasoning ability.

Space of uses. In practice, papers usually inclu

nodes.name: GPT-4 Head-to-head Comparison
nodes.definition: An evaluation protocol where an evaluator, such as GPT-4, is prompted to directly compare the outputs of two different models for the same input and decide which is better.

nodes.name: GQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, GQA is most commonly described as a visual question answering benchmark or dataset for real-world visual reasoning and compositional question answering over images. Many definitions emphasize complex, compositional, or multi-hop questions, and some describe it as grounded question answering or as focusing on scene understanding and reasoning. A smaller line of papers gives a more structural description, saying it uses scene graph structures to generate balanced question-answer pairs with one ground-truth answer, and that each image is paired with a scene graph and each VQA pair has a SQL-like reasoning path. Papers also refer to variants or evaluation splits such as GQA balanced, test-balanced, and balanced-testdev.

What it is claimed to measure. The measurement claims are spread across many constructs rather than a single target: papers use GQA to measure 12 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The most recurrent links are to visual understanding, compositional reasoning, visual perception, fine-grained visual understanding, and visual question answering, while the remaining links are distributed across other reasoning, understanding, gene

nodes.name: GrailQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing description is a Freebase KBQA or KGQA benchmark aimed at complex, compositional, and zero-shot reasoning. Papers also describe it as a dataset for evaluating KBQA generalizability, with I.I.D., compositional, and zero-shot splits; one definition adds that it contains 64,331 questions with target S-expressions and includes complex questions requiring up to 4-hop reasoning. A smaller framing presents it as used to evaluate semantic parsing systems.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to five constructs and one behavioral indicator. Most commonly, papers use it to measure generalization and knowledge graph question answering; other reported uses are multi-hop reasoning, compositional generalization, robustness, and zero-shot generalization. Overall, the reported measurement claims are spread across several related targets, though generalization is the most recurrent framing.

Space of uses. In practice, papers usually place it inside multi-dataset evaluations, most often alongside CWQ and WebQSP, and some also pair it with Simple Questions, WebQuestions, or SimpleQA. They position it as one of the representative or widely

nodes.name: Granite Guardian
nodes.definition: IBM’s Granite Guardian, an open-source LLM designed to detect risks in prompts and responses, including societal bias, harmful content, and unethical behavior, used as a binary classifier for bias detection.

nodes.name: GREEN
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe GREEN as an evaluation procedure, Grounded-factual-correctness Evaluation for radioloGy reports, for radiology report evaluation. The available definition says it uses a finetuned LLM to assess the factual correctness of generated radiology reports, and one paper further characterizes it as a metric based on a "single-answer reference-guided LLM-as-a-Judge mechanism."

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, GREEN is linked to one construct and one behavioral indicator. Papers use it to measure Clinical accuracy, and they also report Radiology report generation as measured by GREEN; the accompanying language emphasizes factual correctness in generated radiology reports and describes it as a metric for radiology report evaluation.

Space of uses. The papers here position GREEN as a primary evaluation metric. One paper calls it a "state-of-the-art metric for radiology report evaluation," and another says results are "primarily" reported with GREEN and F1-SRR-BERT Score to assess clinical accuracy and structural consistency; no other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: gRefCOCO
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for generalized referring expression segmentation, which includes expressions that refer to multiple objects or no objects at all.

nodes.name: GSM8K
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of GSM8K as a benchmark or dataset of text-only, open-ended grade-school math word problems used for mathematical or arithmetic reasoning, often emphasizing multi-step solutions or step-by-step reasoning. Many definitions say it contains about 8.5K problems, and some specify 7,473 training and 1,319 test examples or the 1.3k official test set, though a few papers instead describe over 8,000, about 8K, or 8.8K problems. Most papers place it at the grade-school level, but a few describe middle-school, elementary-level, or high school-level problems; smaller lines of work mention a multilingual version with English and 9 other high-resource languages, GSM8K-tsn, and text-completion or exact-match style evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GSM8K to 25 constructs and 13 behavioral indicators. The dominant use is to measure mathematical reasoning, and recurring work also uses it for reasoning and general ability; at the behavioral level it is used for mathematical problem solving and chain of thought. Beyond this core framing, the recorded links cover many additional constructs and indicators.

Space of uses. Pap

nodes.name: GSM8K-Aug
nodes.definition:
What it is. Definitions describe GSM8K-Aug as an augmented version of GSM8K with a 385k training set, where intermediate reasoning steps are represented as mathematical equations. A source snippet further states that it "uses only math equations as the reasoning steps."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one construct and no behavioral indicators. The only recorded measurement claim is that it measures Mathematical reasoning, with one study referring to GSM8K-Aug as a "complicated mathematical reasoning benchmark."

Space of uses. In the available snippets, GSM8K-Aug appears alongside GSM8K-Aug-NL as one of the datasets used in experiments. Papers also position it as a main fine-tuning dataset, stating that they mainly fine-tune models on GSM8K-Aug for mathematical reasoning.

nodes.name: GSM-Hard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, GSM-Hard, also written GSM-HARD or GSMHard, is most commonly described as a harder GSM8K benchmark or test set of grade-school math problems. Most definitions present it as a more challenging subset or version of GSM8K, while some are more specific and say it is created by replacing the original question numbers with larger-magnitude values to increase calculation difficulty. A smaller line of work describes it as an extended or out-of-distribution version with more complex arithmetic problems, and one definition says it contains problems that state-of-the-art models struggle with and is designed to test the limits of mathematical reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GSM-Hard to three constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing claim is that papers use it to measure Mathematical reasoning, with several papers also reporting it as measuring the broader construct of Reasoning; a smaller line uses it to measure Robustness, often in out-of-distribution or perturbation settings, and one paper reports it as measuring Mathematical problem solving. Overall, the linked uses lean most toward mathematical reasoning.

Space of

nodes.name: GSM-IC
nodes.definition: A benchmark of math word problems with irrelevant context, used to evaluate the generalizability of the proposed methods.

nodes.name: GSM-NoOp
nodes.definition: A dataset derived from GSM-Symbolic templates where seemingly relevant but ultimately inconsequential statements are added to problems to test a model's ability to discern relevant information.

nodes.name: GSM-Plus
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a grade-school math benchmark framed as an adversarial version of GSM8k. Definitions also describe it as an extension of GSM8K and, in one paper, as a held-out test suite of grade-level math problems; across these formulations, it is presented as a more challenging benchmark for mathematical reasoning and as a benchmark for evaluating robustness in mathematical problem solving.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use GSM-Plus to measure 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. Among constructs, it is most often linked to mathematical reasoning, followed by robustness and verification ability; among behavioral indicators, the listed links are mathematical problem solving and instruction following. The measurement claims are spread across several targets, although the recurring framing stays centered on math-related evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers typically use GSM-Plus inside broader math evaluation suites rather than on its own. It appears alongside MATH, SVAMP, ASDiv, GSM8k, and TheoremQA, is sometimes treated specifically as a robustness benchmark using original evaluation scripts with GPT-4o, is used in one case as a held

nodes.name: GSM-Symbolic
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, it is described as a benchmark for symbolic math word problems. One description presents it as a dataset where names and numerical values are replaced with symbolic variables, so models must generate correct symbolic expression solutions; another presents it as an enhanced benchmark built from symbolic templates of GSM8K questions, able to generate diverse variants for more controllable and reliable evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 1 construct, Mathematical reasoning, and 1 behavioral indicator, Mathematical problem solving. The reported targets are concentrated rather than spread across many outcomes: one paper says it provides more reliable metrics for measuring models' reasoning capabilities, and another uses it to assess mathematical reasoning skills through correct symbolic expression generation.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the recorded relationships. In use, one paper places it among "challenging symbolic reasoning benchmarks" alongside FOLIO and uses it as an evaluation benchmark for CRANE, while another positions it as an improved benchmark that generates diverse question variant

nodes.name: GTA
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating multi-modal agents on tasks that require a combination of perception, operation, logic, and creativity using visual data.

nodes.name: GTZAN
nodes.definition: A music genre classification benchmark.

nodes.name: GuessingGame
nodes.definition: An open-domain, open-ended evaluation protocol where a 'Guesser' LLM identifies a hidden object by asking free-form questions to an 'Oracle' LLM.

nodes.name: GUI-Odyssey
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating mobile agent capabilities, assessing step-wise task completion on Android platforms.

nodes.name: GUI-WORLD
nodes.definition: A comprehensive video dataset and benchmark designed to evaluate MLLMs on GUI understanding across six scenarios, with a focus on dynamic and sequential tasks.

nodes.name: HADES
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the available definitions, HADES is described as a multimodal jailbreak benchmark designed to probe multimodal safety under adversarial conditions. Papers characterize it as using crafted images and accompanying typography, with malicious intent embedded and amplified in those materials, and as targeting harmful scenarios.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link HADES to one construct and two behavioral indicators: it is used to measure Safety alignment, and is also reported as measuring Jailbreak resistance and Harmful content detection. The linked uses span a small range of outcomes rather than only one framing, with papers describing it as a typographical jailbreak dataset for Safety alignment, as one of several jailbreak attack methods or datasets for evaluating defense capabilities against jailbreak attacks, and as an instrument involving images and text queries where the text itself is harmful.

Space of uses. In the cited uses, HADES is presented as part of broader jailbreak evaluation setups rather than only on its own. It appears alongside MM-SafetyBench, SafeBench, MML, and HIMRD in one defense evaluation, and another paper groups it with MM-SafetyBench

nodes.name: HAGRID
nodes.definition: A long-form question answering dataset for attributed generation, containing information-seeking questions with answers that are generated by LLMs and subsequently evaluated by humans.

nodes.name: HallusionBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a benchmark, sometimes written as HallBench or HallB, for assessing hallucination in multimodal or vision-language models. Definitions also describe it as a diagnostic suite for entangled language hallucination and visual illusion, a tool for distinguishing VLM reasoning error modes, and a benchmark for image-context reasoning; some descriptions specify 346 images paired with 1129 questions, while others emphasize question type, difficulty level, or real-world and multi-discipline contexts. A smaller line of work describes HallBench more broadly as evaluating multimodal understanding with an emphasis on hallucination-related performance.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link HallusionBench to 4 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing use is to measure hallucination, with relationship evidence describing evaluation of language or knowledge hallucination together with visual illusion; other papers use it to measure hallucination detection, visual hallucination, and visual question answering. Papers also report it as measuring hallucination resistance and visual reasoning, so its reported measurement claims extend

nodes.name: HaluEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, HaluEval is most commonly described as a large-scale benchmark or dataset for evaluating hallucination, often factual hallucination, in model-generated responses. Some papers narrow this to language-only dialogue contexts or to question answering, including judging whether an answer contains a hallucination with yes/no accuracy, while others use dialogue and summarization subsets called HaluDial and HaluSum. Papers variously describe its contents as synthetically generated hallucination data, as user queries paired with factual and hallucinated LLM responses annotated by human evaluators, and, for a QA track, as 10000 questions with reference knowledge, a right answer, and a hallucinated answer automatically generated by ChatGPT.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use HaluEval to measure 4 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure Hallucination, with additional uses for Hallucination detection, Text summarization, Generalization, and Factuality. Overall, the linked claims span several targets rather than one construct, although hallucination-focused uses are the most common.

Space of uses. In practice, HaluEv

nodes.name: HANNA
nodes.definition: Dataset for evaluating short stories generated from prompts, with human ratings on narrative qualities such as surprise and coherence.

nodes.name: HANS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, HANS is most commonly described as an adversarial or stress-test natural language inference dataset. Definitions converge that it probes sensitivity to lexical overlap and related artifacts or heuristics: one description says it is generated so that examples cannot be solved through simple heuristics like lexical overlap, and another says it manipulates lexical overlap, subsequence, and negation to expose reliance on syntactic heuristics rather than semantic understanding. A smaller framing presents it as part of binary classification experiments, and one paper specifies that it contains 30K examples.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link HANS to one behavioral indicator, natural language inference, and one construct, robustness. In one paper it is explicitly employed "for NLI," and the same line of work describes the evaluation data as reflecting adversarial distribution shifts relative to the training data, which it reports as making HANS suitable for evaluating OOD robustness. The measurement claims are concentrated on these two targets rather than spread across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers typically use HANS as an evalua

nodes.name: HardEN
nodes.definition: Challenging word sense disambiguation benchmark consisting of instances that were not correctly disambiguated by any system in prior evaluations, used to assess performance on difficult or out-of-distribution examples.

nodes.name: HarM
nodes.definition: Harmful Meme dataset focused on COVID-19-related memes, used to evaluate zero-shot detection of harmful content in a public health context.

nodes.name: HarmBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, HarmBench is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset of harmful instructions, questions, or behaviors for evaluating jailbreak success and safety behavior under adversarial attacks. Several definitions specify a standard set of 200 harmful behaviors or instructions, including tasks such as chemical synthetization, cybercrime, misinformation, harassment, and physically harmful behaviors, while one paper treats it as an out-of-distribution test set distinct from AdvBench and others report using 400 questions, 300 malicious queries, 100 sampled harmful questions, 80 cases, or a 27-point subset from JBB-Behaviors. A smaller line of descriptions foregrounds the evaluation protocol rather than the prompt set, referring to an official HarmBench classifier, a default judge, or automated assessment of jailbreak success with GPT-3.5-turbo.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link HarmBench to 6 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The most prevalent reported behavioral use is to measure jailbreaking, often through attack success rate and harm judges or classifiers; among constructs, papers most often use it to measure harmlessness, adversarial robus

nodes.name: HarmBench-adv
nodes.definition: An adversarial evaluation set used to test prompt and response classification under jailbreak attacks.

nodes.name: HarmBench classifier
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats the HarmBench classifier as an LLM-based safety judge for model responses. Definitions variously call it a classifier, evaluator, or judge, but they converge on assessing whether outputs are harmful or unsafe, including whether a response to a harmful instruction matches malicious intent and counts as a successful jailbreak. One description calls it "the official HarmBench classifier of model response harmfulness" and says it is fine-tuned from Llama-2-13B, while another names the variant HarmBench-Llama2-13B-Chat and uses it to label responses as harmless or harmful.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims are narrow rather than spread across many targets: papers link it to 1 construct, Harmlessness, and 1 behavioral indicator, Harmful content generation. Papers use it to measure harmful content generation when computing attack success rate, and they also report percentage of harmless responses based on the HarmBench-Llama2-13B-Chat classifier. Across these uses, the recorded framing is response safety, either as harmfulness or harmlessness.

Space of uses. Papers position it both as the evaluator used for HarmBench

nodes.name: Harmful instructions
nodes.definition: A safety benchmark used to evaluate VLM behavior under harmful multimodal jailbreak prompts.

nodes.name: Harry Potter dataset
nodes.definition: A copyrighted-text unlearning evaluation dataset built from Harry Potter book passages used to test whether the model stops reproducing the source text.

nodes.name: HateCheck
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for evaluating hate speech detection models, used in this paper as a source of unsafe, hate-speech-related prompts for the LITMUS benchmark.

nodes.name: Hateful Memes
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, Hateful Memes is most commonly described as a multimodal meme benchmark or dataset for deciding whether a meme image together with its text or caption is hateful. Definitions also frame it as detecting hate speech or harmful content in memes, and one description says it was a challenge hosted by Meta to classify whether an image and caption "describes hateful intentions." A smaller line refers to it specifically as the Facebook Hateful Memes, or FHM, dataset and presents it as a binary yes or no task that can require reasoning beyond simple unimodal signals.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing use is hate speech detection, with papers describing it as a benchmark for multimodal hate speech detection; smaller lines of work use it to measure harmful content detection, multimodal reasoning, and toxicity, including use to see whether a model can distinguish toxic from non-toxic images. Overall, papers report it as evaluating several closely related targets rather than only one construct.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to other measurement instruments. In use, they prese

nodes.name: HateXplain
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a natural-language or toxic text classification benchmark or dataset. It is most commonly framed as classifying sentences as normal versus hateful or offensive, with one snippet specifying that the target label is 0 for normal sentences and 1 for those considered hateful or offensive. Some authors describe it more specifically as a dataset with demographic correlation shifts and unwanted correlation between toxicity labels and mentions of demographics, while others present it as a subjective single-label dataset or as a source task for transfer learning in harmful content detection.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it primarily to evaluate classification of normal versus hateful, offensive, or toxic text. Some also report using it to evaluate fairness with respect to gender-related sensitive information, and another paper uses it to evaluate zero-shot robustness in the presence of demographic correlation shifts. No construct or behavioral indicator is explicitly linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers position it as an evaluation dataset in several roles. It appears as one of several text classification datasets us

nodes.name: HC3
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats HC3 as a ChatGPT text detection corpus, described as up-to-date, bilingual in English and Chinese, and organized at multiple text lengths, with full or long-text data and sentence-level or short-text variants for multiscale evaluation. Papers explicitly mention the short-text subsets HC3-English-Sent and HC3-Chinese-Sent. A smaller line of work instead frames it as the Human ChatGPT Comparison Corpus, a set of responses or question-and-answer pairs from humans and GPT-3.5 or ChatGPT to the same questions, used to compare their characteristics or for human-AI text discrimination.

What it is claimed to measure. Among recorded links, papers use HC3 to measure AI-generated text detection. It is linked to 1 behavioral indicator, AI-generated text detection, and to no constructs, so the recorded measurement claims are concentrated on that single indicator. One paper describes using a learned kernel from HC3 to test unseen HC3 texts "to mimic the MGT-detection."

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position HC3 as an evaluation benchmark or corpus: methods are evaluated on its long or full and short

nodes.name: HealthCareMagic
nodes.definition: Medical consultation dataset containing single-turn patient queries paired with licensed professional responses, used for in-distribution evaluation of medical QA systems.

nodes.name: HellaSwag
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, HellaSwag is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for commonsense natural language inference, commonsense reasoning, or sentence and context completion. The prevailing format is multiple-choice selection of the most plausible ending or continuation for a sentence, text snippet, event, or everyday scenario, often from four options. A smaller set of definitions instead emphasize grounded or physically situated commonsense, next-event prediction, or text completion with adversarially filtered or generated alternatives.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link HellaSwag to 17 constructs and 17 behavioral indicators, so the measurement claims spread across many targets. The dominant use is as a measure of Commonsense reasoning and broader Reasoning, with smaller but recurring uses for General ability, Generalization, and Natural language understanding. Some papers simply call it a test of commonsense inference, while another says it aims to measure a model's ability to understand language; at the behavioral level, the most common links are to language understanding task performance and zero-shot task performance.

Space of uses. Pa

nodes.name: HelloBench
nodes.definition: A comprehensive, in-the-wild, and open-ended benchmark designed to evaluate the performance of large language models in generating long text.

nodes.name: HELM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat HELM as Stanford's Holistic Evaluation of Language Models, a large-scale, comprehensive benchmark or framework for evaluating language models across a wide range of scenarios and metrics, often described as covering capabilities, limitations, and risks. Some papers further position it as an aggregate benchmark, and one paper uses it specifically as the source of rankings for LLM performance on MMLU. A smaller usage in one paper instead labels "HELM" as a non-adaptive watermark-evasion baseline that randomly adds typos, lowercasing, or contractions.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, HELM is linked to 0 constructs, 1 behavioral indicator, and 2 other instruments. The recorded measurement claims center on a single behavioral indicator rather than multiple constructs: multiple-choice question answering is measured by HELM in one paper, which says HELM uses MMLU questions "with multiple choice questions and labeled correct answers," and MMLU is measured by HELM in another paper through HELM-based ranking of MMLU performance. Beyond that, the other instrument-level link is not another measurement claim but a reported correlation with LiveBen

nodes.name: HELMET
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, HELMET is most commonly described as a long-context benchmark for assessing model performance on extended text processing tasks. Papers describe it at different granularities: one account says it covers seven diverse, application-centric categories, while another reports evaluation across five task types, synthetic recall, retrieval-augmented generation, many-shot in-context learning, passage re-ranking, and long-document QA, covering 17 sub-tasks. A recurring detail is that it includes portions from other long-text benchmarks, especially RULER and ∞Bench, and one paper also refers to HotpotQA, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA as factoid QA tasks curated by HELMET for 128k-token benchmarking.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link HELMET to several long-context constructs and behaviors rather than only one target. It is linked to 4 constructs, length generalization, long-context understanding, long-range dependency modeling, and memory, and to 4 behavioral indicators, in-context prediction, synthetic recall, document question answering, and ranking. The relationship evidence also places many-shot in-context learning and synthetic recall directly

nodes.name: HelpSteer
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe HelpSteer as a multi-attribute dataset for aligning or evaluating LLM outputs against human-preferred characteristics, with human-annotated ratings for helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity. Some authors frame it more specifically as a model alignment and steering dataset, while a smaller line of work describes it as a QA dataset for evaluating instruction following across five dimensions, including informativeness and factuality, or as a multi-attribute helpfulness dataset. One paper also treats it as an unpaired dataset with around 35K samples, where each prompt has a single response scored on attributes.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use HelpSteer to measure 6 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than centered on one. The most frequently linked constructs are helpfulness, coherence, complexity, factuality, and faithfulness. Additional papers also report it as measuring other recorded targets beyond those five.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position HelpSteer in several ways: as a dataset used

nodes.name: HelpSteer2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats HelpSteer2 as a multi-aspect preference or alignment dataset used in alignment experiments and reward-model training. Definitions vary by slice and framing: one line describes a validation split of 1,000 prompts, while another describes a permissively licensed CC-BY-4.0 release with 10,681 prompts and 21,362 annotated samples, each prompt paired with two responses annotated for helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity. Other papers describe it as prompts and completions with Likert-5 scoring, as binary-labeled human preference pairs across multiple assessment dimensions, as an instruction-following dataset from Nvidia, or as a subset used to synthesize judge-training data.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, it is linked to six constructs and one behavioral indicator. Among the measurement claims, coherence appears most often; other papers use it to measure complexity, helpfulness, model collapse, and personalized alignment, with one other construct linked as well, so the claims are spread across several constructs rather than centered on one target. One paper also relates HelpSteer2 to multi-tu

nodes.name: HESEIA
nodes.definition: A Spanish-language dataset of 45,416 sentences created by high-school teachers and students in Latin America to evaluate social biases in LLMs, organized by school subject and annotated for intersectional demographic biases.

nodes.name: HEx-PHI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, HEx-PHI is most commonly described as a harmful query or safety benchmark: a dataset of 330 harmful instructions or queries spanning 11 harmful categories or use cases. Definitions converge on its use for testing whether models comply with harmful requests, produce unsafe outputs, or generate harmful or privacy-invasive responses, though one description narrows this to privacy-harming and personally harmful instructions. A smaller line of work refers to it as the Policy-Oriented Safety Evaluation Benchmarks or the POSE benchmark, describing its categories as derived from Meta's and OpenAI's usage policies or prohibited use cases.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three constructs and one behavioral indicator. Most often, it is used to measure Harmlessness, followed by Safety and Safety alignment, and the only linked behavioral indicator is Harmful content generation. The recorded relationships keep these claims within safety evaluation, with papers describing the benchmark as assessing harmfulness or evaluating whether a model complies with harmful requests, so its use is spread across three constructs rather than centered on

nodes.name: HEXACO-60
nodes.definition: A 60-item personality inventory used to measure six major dimensions of personality: Honesty-Humility, Emotionality, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Openness to Experience.

nodes.name: HH-Golden
nodes.definition: A preference dataset, modified from HH-RLHF, used to evaluate a model's alignment with a broad spectrum of human preferences.

nodes.name: HH-RLHF
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is an Anthropic human preference dataset or benchmark for helpful and harmless assistant behavior, usually built from human-assistant conversations or prompts paired with two responses and a human preference label. Definitions vary between paired responses, paired conversations, multi-turn dialogues, and single-step human-assistant interactions, and several papers treat helpfulness and harmlessness as separate portions or subsplits. Smaller usages refer to a helpfulness-only portion, a harmlessness-focused setup, an out-of-domain subset called HH-RLHF*, or an Anthropic HHH version described as adding honesty.

What it is claimed to measure. Most papers use HH-RLHF to measure helpfulness and harmlessness, and the strongest convergence is around those two constructs. It is linked to 10 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators overall: beyond helpfulness and harmlessness, the most common additional construct links are alignment, humor, and human preference alignment. On the behavioral side, it is used most often for dialogue generation, and more occasionally for multi-turn dialogue and text generation.

Space of uses. Papers do not l

nodes.name: HH-RLHF harmless subset
nodes.definition: A binary human-preference dataset of harmlessness-oriented response comparisons used to test reward-model explanations.

nodes.name: HH-RLHF helpful subset
nodes.definition: A binary human-preference dataset of helpfulness-oriented response comparisons used to test reward-model explanations.

nodes.name: HiTab
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe HiTab as a benchmark or table reasoning dataset built around hierarchical or otherwise complex tables from government reports and Wikipedia pages. Definitions emphasize multi-level headers, implicit relationships, and complex structural relationships, and they describe the dataset as used for table transformation and question answering; one paper specifies 3,597 tables from HTML government reports and Wikipedia pages and 10,672 QA pairs. One paper also presents it as designed for table-based question answering and table-to-text generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use HiTab to measure 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The construct link is table reasoning, while the behavioral indicator links are data-to-text generation and table question answering. Taken together, papers report it as evaluating several related table tasks rather than only one.

Space of uses. Papers use HiTab as an evaluation benchmark in experiments on table reasoning, question answering, and generation, and one paper places it among three widely used table reasoning datasets. No other measurement instrument is linked to it, though papers evaluate it

nodes.name: HotpotQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description treats HotpotQA as a multi-hop question answering benchmark or dataset, usually based on Wikipedia, where answering requires finding, combining, or reasoning over multiple supporting documents, paragraphs, passages, or facts. Some authors instead frame it as multi-hop reading comprehension, open-domain or search-based QA, and a smaller line describes it either as an open-ended task with long answers or as a closed-ended task with short entity or yes or no answers. Papers also mention several settings and subsets, including open-domain fullwiki, distractor or distractor dev, closed-book evaluation, the KILT subset, the train-hard split, and variants where paragraph ordering changes retrieval difficulty.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use HotpotQA to measure 9 constructs and 11 behavioral indicators. The dominant claims are that it measures multi-hop reasoning and multi-hop question answering, and it is also used for question answering, reasoning, and complex reasoning question answering. Beyond these, the measurement claims spread across 15 other constructs and indicators rather than converging on only one target.

Space

nodes.name: HotpotWikiQA-mixup
nodes.definition: Multi-hop QA dataset derived from Wikipedia, combining elements of HotpotQA with long-context requirements.

nodes.name: HoVer
nodes.definition: Multi-hop fact verification benchmark requiring evidence aggregation across multiple documents, based on Wikipedia, with claims structured in 2-hop, 3-hop, and 4-hop reasoning paths.

nodes.name: How2Sign
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is as a large-scale American Sign Language dataset drawn from instructional videos and used as a benchmark for translation. Some descriptions make the domain more specific as "how to" instructional videos and as ASL-to-English translation, and another adds that it contains 35,191 samples with a vocabulary of 16K English words.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant measured-by use is sign language translation, with papers reporting How2Sign as one of the datasets or benchmarks for that task; a smaller use is sign language identification, where results are reported with top-1 accuracy, while sentence-level translation in the same benchmark setup is scored with BLEURT-20.

Space of uses. Papers commonly mention How2Sign alongside other sign language datasets: the recurring companions are CSL-Daily, with some mentions of OpenASL, PHOENIX14T, and FLEURS-ASL. In these descriptions it is positioned as one of the benchmarks on which models report results in sign language translation experiments or broader benchmark suites, and no measurement instrument is formally li

nodes.name: HSSD
nodes.definition: A dataset of synthesized, single-floor indoor scenes used to create environments for the Habitat-MAS benchmark.

nodes.name: Human annotation study
nodes.definition: A human evaluation protocol where 84 participants each analyzed and classified 18 news stories (9 real, 9 fake) as either real or fake without using the internet.

nodes.name: Human baseline
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a human evaluation protocol run on the same benchmark tasks as a model, to provide a performance reference, baseline, or upper-bound. Most definitions describe people completing prompts, puzzles, questions, web or OS tasks, extraction tasks, or meal-estimation examples, with variants ranging from independent annotators and native speakers to domain experts, authors, volunteers, Prolific participants, and humans acting as LLM agents. A smaller line of work uses closely related procedures such as expert forecasts or an offline survey in which participants view clues, submit a guess after each clue, and indicate whether they would buzz. Some implementations cover the full task set, while others are restricted to subsets such as 100 randomly selected table-updating pairs, 75 abstracts, or 1000 questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not record this instrument as measuring any construct or behavioral indicator: it is linked to no constructs and no behavioral indicators. The only explicit relational claim is that one paper uses a human baseline to measure OSWorld, and reports that the human performance study shows OSWorld ex

nodes.name: Human evaluation
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, definitions treat human evaluation as a family of manual assessment protocols with many formats. Most papers describe annotators, experts, clinicians, users, or crowdworkers scoring, ranking, comparing, or labeling model outputs, with formats ranging from pairwise preferences and rubric-based Likert scoring to categorical labels, manual verification, and spot-checking. Some studies use it as a human baseline where people solve the same tasks as models, and one large variant reports over 10,000 judgments from verified English speakers on Wikipedia and fictional story continuations.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 58 constructs and 27 behavioral indicators, so its claimed targets are spread across many qualities and tasks rather than centered on one. The most recurrent construct-level uses are helpfulness, harmlessness, conciseness, faithfulness, and fluency. Papers operationalize these targets through pairwise preferences, accept or reject judgments, and task-specific rating rubrics, and the behavioral links are likewise dispersed across many indicators.

Space of uses. Many papers position human evaluation as a gold sta

nodes.name: Human preference evaluation
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a human pairwise comparison protocol, variously described as side by side comparisons, A/B testing, pairwise evaluation, or preference voting. Evaluators usually see two outputs for the same input and choose the better one, often with tie or no-difference options, and some papers summarize results as win rates or win:tie:lose ratios. The compared content varies by task, from model responses and table descriptions to arguments, video captions, and audio outputs, and a smaller line of work describes the evaluation instead as Mean Opinion Score ratings of naturalness and meaningfulness on a 5-point Likert scale.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this protocol to four constructs and one behavioral indicator. The construct links span Human preference alignment, Engagement, Faithfulness, and Helpfulness, and Instruction following is the only linked behavioral indicator, so the recorded uses are spread across several targets rather than centered on one. In the linked claims, papers use human choices to measure Human preference alignment and Instruction following, to judge whether a description is more faithful to a table, and to

nodes.name: Human subject study
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, this label covers several direct-participant methods rather than a single fixed protocol. The prevailing usage is survey-based: papers describe a community survey to gather perspectives on harmful model behaviours and ideal responses, a mixed-methods user survey with open-ended questions and Likert ratings to identify adoption patterns, use cases, and challenges, and a questionnaire on frustrations and the perceived helpfulness of clarifications, entity graphs, and relationship graphs. A smaller line of work uses open-ended interviews to elicit detailed feedback on participants’ experience and workflow fit.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not report this instrument as measuring any linked constructs or behavioral indicators, and no construct or behavioral indicator is linked to it. In practice, the studies use it to elicit participants’ perspectives, frustrations, adoption patterns, perceived helpfulness, and experience in the papers’ own terms.

Space of uses. Most papers position human subject studies as an elicitation or validation step alongside broader system or model work, for example to broaden a list of harms, identify user ch

nodes.name: HumanEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a Python code generation benchmark, usually described as 164 handwritten or hand-crafted programming problems whose outputs are checked by unit tests and often reported with pass@1. Definitions commonly describe function-level synthesis or completion from function signatures and docstrings, and some add reference code, automated tests, or an average of 7.7 or 9.6 test cases per problem. A smaller line of work describes it more specifically as code completion, Python function completion, or single-line code infilling, and some papers use named variants such as HumanEval-Python, HumanEval+, HumanEvalSynthesize, and HUMANEVALPACK.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use HumanEval to measure a broad set of outcomes: it is linked to 13 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The dominant claims center on coding ability, reasoning, functional correctness, code generation, and code completion. Taken together, the recorded uses spread across many outcomes, although coding-focused uses are the prevailing ones.

Space of uses. Among explicit instrument links, papers relate HumanEval to 2 other instruments, EvalPlus and MultiPL-E; one pape

nodes.name: HumanEval-Decompile
nodes.definition: A decompilation benchmark derived from the C-language adaptation of HumanEval, containing 164 C functions compiled with O0–O3 optimization flags and disassembled into X86-64 assembly.

nodes.name: HumanEval+
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, HumanEval+ is most commonly treated as an extended or improved version of HumanEval for code generation, with stronger, more comprehensive unit tests or test cases for more rigorous functional-correctness evaluation. Papers variously describe its contents as handwritten Python programming questions with ground-truth unit tests, or as function-level problems with docstrings, code headers, and input-output examples; one paper also describes it as 164 hand-crafted programming problems with function signatures, docstrings, and unit tests. A recurring description is that the extension substantially enlarges testing, with one paper stating that it scales the number of test cases by 80×.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link HumanEval+ to two behavioral indicators and two constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure Code generation, with some papers also using it for Coding; at the construct level, papers link it most often to Coding ability, with Factuality also appearing. Across these links, the clearest convergence is on evaluating code generation capabilities and functionally correct code, and some studies report pass@1 on the benchmark.

Space

nodes.name: HumanEval-X
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats HumanEval-X as a multilingual benchmark for evaluating code generation capabilities. Some definitions make this more specific by calling it a comprehensive benchmark across Python, C++, Java, JavaScript, and Go, while another describes it as a multilingual extension of HumanEval that translates its Python problems into multiple languages. A smaller line of work uses the name HumanEval-Multi for the multilingual version of HumanEval and frames it as a test dataset for utility and for the functional correctness of model-generated code.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link HumanEval-X to one construct and two behavioral indicators. It is most commonly used to measure Code generation: papers report pass@1 on HumanEval-X and describe it as evaluating multilingual code generation abilities. More narrowly, one paper reports it as measuring Code translation, and one paper links the HumanEval-X (CPP and Java) dataset to measuring Factuality through reported code efficiency and pass@1.

Space of uses. Papers position HumanEval-X mainly as an evaluation benchmark or test dataset, often by reporting pass@1 results on it

nodes.name: HumanEvalFix
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing description is a benchmark for fixing bugs in provided functions with accompanying test cases. Papers also frame it as function-level bug fixing, and one usage narrows it to the Python subset and lets models or agents self-debug over multiple turns with feedback from test execution.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use HumanEvalFix to measure one behavioral indicator, Code debugging, and one construct, Code editing ability. The linked claims center on bug fixing and debugging: several papers describe it as measuring Code debugging through tasks where an incorrect function with unit tests is given and the system is asked to fix it, while one paper also reports using it to evaluate Code editing ability.

Space of uses. In the available papers, it is used as an evaluation benchmark for code-editing tasks. One paper uses it alongside CanItEdit, NoFunEval, Aider, and Aider Polyglot, while another applies it in a multi-turn setup where the system solves bugs by self-debug using test-execution feedback.

nodes.name: HumanEvalPack
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe HumanEvalPack as a code benchmark used to supply prompts for code-domain evaluation. In RM-Bench: Benchmarking Reward Models of Language Models with Subtlety and Style, authors state that prompts for the code domain are sourced from HumanEvalPack. Some authors discuss the HumanEvalSynthesize variant instead, describing it as adapted for instruction-following models, where the task is framed as a natural language instruction to generate a complete program.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 1 behavioral indicator, Code generation, and link it to no constructs. The reported measurement claims converge on code generation, including a setup where, given a natural language docstring or comment describing the desired code, the model is tasked to synthesize the correct code.

Space of uses. Papers relate it to 1 other instrument, RM-Bench, where it is used as a source of prompts for the code domain or code split. Generative Representational Instruction Tuning uses the HumanEvalSynthesize variant and describes that choice as more adequate for instruction-following models.

nodes.name: Humanity’s Last Exam
nodes.definition: Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) is a challenging benchmark consisting of difficult exam questions across various academic and professional domains.

nodes.name: HumanML3D
nodes.definition: HumanML3D benchmark of human motions and textual descriptions used for evaluating text-to-motion and motion-to-text performance.

nodes.name: Humor Style Questionnaire
nodes.definition: Standardized 32-item psychological assessment measuring four humor styles—affiliative, self-enhancing, aggressive, and self-defeating—using a 5-point Likert scale, used here to probe LLMs' representation of humor-related constructs.

nodes.name: HybridQA
nodes.definition: HybridQA is a question answering benchmark combining table evidence with textual passages for hybrid reasoning.

nodes.name: Hypersim
nodes.definition: A photorealistic synthetic dataset used as a transfer task to evaluate the model's fine-tuned performance on semantic segmentation.

nodes.name: HyPoradise
nodes.definition: A generative error correction benchmark for LLM-enhanced ASR containing over 316K hypotheses-transcription pairs from mainstream ASR corpora, used to evaluate H2T mapping.

nodes.name: ICL CIPHERS
nodes.definition: A cryptographic evaluation framework that applies bijective and non-bijective token-level substitution ciphers to in-context learning inputs to assess task learning by comparing performance gaps between reversible and irreversible mappings.

nodes.name: iCliniq
nodes.definition: Real-world medical consultation records from the iCliniq platform, used as an out-of-distribution test set to evaluate generalization in medical QA.

nodes.name: IconQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat IconQA as a visual question answering dataset for diagram understanding. One definition also describes it as "a new benchmark for abstract diagram understanding and visual language reasoning," and another places it as one task within the CMIT benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link IconQA to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. The reported measurement claim is consistent: IconQA measures visual question answering, with the task described as diagram understanding VQA, rather than being used for a wider spread of constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. Within the reported uses, papers position IconQA as a visual question answering task for model comparison, including comparisons that pair it with ScienceQA and multi-task settings that include both ScienceQA and IconQA. No other measurement instrument is linked to it, and one definition frames it as a task used inside the CMIT benchmark.

nodes.name: IEMOCAP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe IEMOCAP as the Interactive Emotional Dyadic Motion Capture database, used as a benchmark for emotion recognition from speech, and one paper further presents it as a multimodal dataset for emotion classification from spoken dialogue. In that usage, it is also used to evaluate text-based emotion detection in long conversational sequences. The cited evaluations also refer to IEMOCAP Session 5, and one paper specifies 1,241 utterances.

What it is claimed to measure. Among linked entities, papers connect it to one behavioral indicator, Emotion analysis, and to no constructs. The recorded relationship is that Emotion analysis is measured by IEMOCAP, with supporting snippets describing emotion recognition as being assessed on IEMOCAP and reporting accuracy for "ER | IEMOCAP Session 5". Its reported measurement role therefore centers on a single named behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation benchmark, sometimes alongside other datasets. One study assesses emotion recognition on IEMOCAP and MELD, while another reports "consistent improvements on MultiWOZ 2.2 and IEMOCAP" and reports IEMOCAP accuracy gains over DEEPSEEK and MODERNBERT

nodes.name: IFEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the prevailing description is a targeted benchmark for instruction following, especially for checking whether model outputs follow explicit instructions or satisfy verifiable constraints embedded in prompts. Definitions often emphasize precise textual constraints on format, style, or content, and some papers describe a standardized and automated assessment with a built-in evaluation methodology. A smaller line of work treats it more specifically as part of the TÜLU-2 evaluation suite, adapts data from it into single-turn rule-following tasks, or uses both the original text-based benchmark and a synthesized spoken version.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, its measurement claims converge most strongly on instruction following. It is linked to 6 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, and the most common claims are that papers use it to measure instruction following ability, instruction following, and constraint adherence; smaller strands also report it as measuring complex instruction following ability, helpfulness, and 3 other constructs. Several descriptions sharpen this framing by stating that it evaluates instruction adherence or whe

nodes.name: iGSM
nodes.definition: A synthetic dataset of program-generated, elementary-school level math reasoning problems with step-by-step solutions, designed to be controllable and verifiable.

nodes.name: IIRC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, IIRC is treated as a benchmark dataset for reading comprehension, expanded in one definition as Iterative Information Retrieval and Comprehension. A more specific description frames it as focused on information integration and reading comprehension, where models answer questions by linking information across document sections, testing retrieval and contextual understanding. One paper also reports evaluation on decontextualized versions of a subset of IIRC.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what IIRC measures are concentrated rather than spread across many targets. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Question answering, describing it as one of the QA datasets used for measurement, and to one construct, Mathematical reasoning, which a smaller line of work treats as measured by IIRC.

Space of uses. Papers use IIRC for evaluation, including as one of four QA datasets in one study and in decontextualized subset form in another, where it is used alongside DROP. The available descriptions also position it as a setting where methods are compared across metrics, with one paper reporting a consistent advantage on IIRC across metrics.

nodes.name: IIW-400
nodes.definition: A dataset consisting of 400 image-caption pairs with highly detailed, hallucination-free captions, used for evaluating caption quality.

nodes.name: ImageNet-100
nodes.definition: A subset of the ImageNet dataset used for evaluating image classification performance.

nodes.name: ImageNet-1k
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is a large-scale image classification or object recognition benchmark, usually under the names ImageNet, ImageNet-1K, ImageNet1k, ImageNet-1k, or ImageNet-2012. Definitions commonly specify 1,000 categories or classes, and some add scale details such as over 1.2 million images, or over a million training images plus 50,000 validation images. Although most uses are classification-oriented, some papers also treat it as a standard class-conditional image generation setting, and a few rely on narrower slices or transformations such as the ILSVRC2012 validation split or flattened grayscale image patches.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 3 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The dominant link is image classification, with many papers using it for classification evaluation, sometimes explicitly through top-1 accuracy or core classification accuracy. Smaller strands report it as measuring multimodal alignment, image generation, adaptability, and generalization, plus 3 other linked behavioral indicators: object recognition, synthetic recall, and zero-shot classification. Some alignment-oriented work also states th

nodes.name: ImageNet-A
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe ImageNet-A as an out-of-distribution benchmark for ImageNet that contains natural adversarial examples and is challenging for standard models. Across the available definitions, that is the only characterization provided.

What it is claimed to measure. No papers link ImageNet-A to any construct or behavioral indicator, so the available literature here does not specify what it is claimed to measure.

Space of uses. The available evidence only shows the benchmark being named in Section 5.1 of "LiNeS: Post-training Layer Scaling Prevents Forgetting and Enhances Model Merging". No papers link it to any other measurement instrument, so its use alongside other benchmarks is not specified.

nodes.name: ImageNet-C
nodes.definition: A standard procedure and dataset used to generate corrupted versions of images with perturbations like snow, brightness changes, and motion blur to test model robustness.

nodes.name: ImageNet-R
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description treats ImageNet-R as an image classification or out-of-distribution benchmark built from artistic renditions of ImageNet object classes. Definitions repeatedly mention forms such as paintings, cartoons, sculptures, embroidery, and graffiti, and one paper describes these renditions as domains; the benchmark is framed as testing generalization to novel styles, different artistic forms, or transformed visual appearances.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most commonly present ImageNet-R as evaluating robustness to out-of-distribution images or out-of-distribution robustness, with adjacent descriptions of generalization to novel styles, different artistic forms, and transformed visual appearances. No constructs and no behavioral indicators are linked to it in the recorded relationships, so the available claims stay at the level of benchmark purpose rather than explicit construct or behavior mappings.

Space of uses. Papers use it mainly as an evaluation benchmark for out-of-distribution images and artistic renditions of ImageNet classes. Learning from Teaching Regularization: Generalizable Correlations Should be Easy to Imi

nodes.name: ImageNet-Segmentation
nodes.definition: A dataset providing pixel-level segmentation masks for a subset of the ImageNet dataset, used for evaluating semantic segmentation and object localization.

nodes.name: ImageNet-Sketch
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, papers treat ImageNet-Sketch mostly as an out-of-distribution ImageNet benchmark made up of sketch-like images. The prevailing description is a dataset of sketch-like, sometimes explicitly black-and-white, images derived from ImageNet classes, used to test robustness and generalization; one definition phrases it as an out-of-distribution benchmark for ImageNet, while others describe it as a dataset for evaluating image classification under out-of-distribution conditions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Image classification, and to no constructs. The only measured_by claim treats ImageNet-Sketch as measuring Image classification, so the reported measurement use is confined to that single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple linked targets.

Space of uses. In the cited uses, papers place it alongside ImageNet, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-Rendition when evaluating models. One snippet describes evaluating ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 on ImageNet-R and ImageNet-Sketch to investigate out-of-distribution robustness, and another places it among the image datasets used to evaluate TIMM; papers do not li

nodes.name: ImageNetV2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, papers treat ImageNetV2 as an ImageNet-derived benchmark or test set rather than a new task. The prevailing descriptions say it is used to test robustness under natural distribution shift and to measure generalization to new, similarly distributed data, and one definition also specifies that it was collected with a replicated protocol. Papers use both spellings, ImageNetV2 and ImageNet-V2.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ImageNetV2 to one behavioral indicator and no constructs. The only recorded measurement claim is that image classification is measured by ImageNetV2, so the reported use converges on a single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across multiple constructs. In the definitions, this evaluation is framed as testing robustness under natural distribution shift or measuring generalization to new, similarly distributed data.

Space of uses. Across the cited uses, papers position ImageNetV2 as one dataset within broader evaluation suites. One paper includes it among a larger collection of image recognition datasets, and another uses it alongside ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, and ImageNetSketch for evaluation. No measurement instr

nodes.name: IMDb
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe IMDb as a movie-review sentiment benchmark, usually for binary or sentiment classification, with positive and negative labels. Some definitions are narrower, calling it a sentiment-related GRUE dataset or an out-of-distribution target-domain benchmark, while one paper describes movie reviews and ratings used for sentiment analysis and recommendation-system research. Some papers instead use it for controlled generation of positive movie reviews, and one such setup uses a positive and negative sentiment-control subset.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, IMDb is linked to 4 behavioral indicators and 5 constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure sentiment analysis and text classification: papers present it as a sentiment classification task, a text classification dataset, or a benchmark for binary polarity over movie reviews. A smaller but recurring line of work uses it to measure controlled sentiment generation, and one paper uses it for text generation. Construct claims are more spread out, with papers reporting it as measuring generalization most often, and also adaptability, general ability, in-context learning, and out-of-distributio

nodes.name: IMHI
nodes.definition: In-distribution dataset for MentaLLaMA consisting of approximately 105,000 instruction-response pairs for mental health analysis, including depression detection and wellness classification.

nodes.name: IMPLIRET
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating retrieval and reasoning capabilities when relevance depends on implicit facts in documents, covering arithmetic, temporal, and world knowledge reasoning across uni- and multi-speaker discourse styles.

nodes.name: In-context attack
nodes.definition: A baseline evaluation setting that uses few-shot demonstrations of immoral or harmful behavior to induce the target model to endorse similar unethical behaviors.

nodes.name: INCLUDE
nodes.definition: INCLUDE, a native multilingual benchmark cited as culturally aware but lacking discipline balance and difficulty control.

nodes.name: IndoCulture
nodes.definition: An Indonesian benchmark used to assess downstream model performance after safety fine-tuning.

nodes.name: IndustryOR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is of IndustryOR as an open-source dataset of commercial Operations Research problems. Definitions also frame it as the basis for a novel benchmark dataset for explainable OR, and one description specifies that it consists of 100 real-world optimization problems spanning linear, integer, and mixed-integer programming at various difficulty levels.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link IndustryOR to one construct, Accuracy, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The only recorded measurement claim is that Accuracy is measured by IndustryOR, with evidence described as formulation correctness results on benchmarks containing LPs and MILPs.

Space of uses. In the available papers, IndustryOR is positioned as an evaluation resource, either as the basis for a new benchmark dataset or as a benchmark of optimization problems at varied difficulty levels. No other measurement instruments are linked to it.

nodes.name: InfiAgent-DABench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for data analysis containing 257 challenges with CSV inputs and multi-level (easy, medium, hard) analysis questions.

nodes.name: InfiniBench
nodes.definition: A large-scale benchmark for long-form video understanding in multi-modal models, assessing eight skills across 87.7K question-answer pairs from 1,000+ hours of movies and TV shows, using both multiple-choice and open-ended formats.

nodes.name: InfiniteBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a long-context benchmark or benchmark suite for evaluating LLMs on ultra-long inputs, usually described as exceeding 100K tokens. Most descriptions treat it as a diverse collection of synthetic and real-world tasks, sometimes stated as 10 tasks, while narrower descriptions focus on particular subsets such as En.QA, En.MC, En.Sum, Inf.QA, Inf.MC, or specific retrieval tasks. Papers differ in emphasis: some describe long-book or long-novel QA and multiple-choice tasks, while others include multilingual QA, code debugging, dialogue, math, and retrieval, and reported average lengths vary across descriptions, including 100K, 145.1K, 190k, 214k, and 184K tokens for particular setups.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use InfiniteBench to measure 4 constructs and 9 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures Long-context understanding, while smaller lines of work also report it as measuring Length generalization, Long-context reasoning, and Dialogue understanding. At the behavioral level, the named links are spread across several targets rather than one, most often Text summarization, Code debugging, Document

nodes.name: InfoBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is an instruction-following or instruction-adherence benchmark that decomposes complex instructions into simpler sub-instructions for granular evaluation. One description says it introduces the Decomposed Requirements Following Ratio and contains 500 diverse instructions with 2,250 decomposed questions across multiple constraint categories. A smaller line of work describes it as a direct-scoring dataset with a Likert scale from 1 to 5, Easy and Hard English subsets, and expert annotations across 50 tasks, while another paper uses an Expert split for classification. Some authors also place it among benchmarks for more general instructions that need LLM-based judgment.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most commonly use InfoBench to measure Instruction following: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, and descriptions say it assesses instruction-adherence capabilities and evaluates a model’s ability to comprehend and execute detailed directives. Its construct links are narrower, with two constructs recorded, Instruction following ability and Generalization. Overall, the measurement claims are centered on instruction following,

nodes.name: InfoSeek
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available definitions, InfoSeek is treated as a visual question answering dataset centered on knowledge-seeking questions. The recurring description is that it requires identifying an entity in an image and then querying for a related fact, and one paper also places it among "three popular KB-VR benchmarks" alongside A-OKVQA and OK-VQA.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link InfoSeek to two constructs, Generalization and Commonsense knowledge, and no behavioral indicators. In SearchLVLMs: A Plug-and-Play Framework for Augmenting Large Vision-Language Models by Searching Up-to-Date Internet Knowledge, it is used to evaluate "the generalization capability of our framework across datasets that do not necessitate up-to-date knowledge," and the same paper also reports that "InfoSeek and A-OKVQA Rely on Commonsense Knowledge (RCK)," so the available uses are split across these two constructs rather than concentrated on one.

Space of uses. The available papers use InfoSeek alongside A-OKVQA, OK-VQA, and GQA. One paper positions it as one of three popular KB-VR benchmarks in model evaluation, while another selects it with GQA and A-OKVQA specifically to assess

nodes.name: InfoVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe InfoVQA, sometimes written as InfographicVQA or InfographicsVQA, as a visual question answering benchmark or dataset for infographics or infographic images. Some descriptions instead frame it as information visual question answering on document images, emphasizing information localization, extraction, or extracting specific information, and one definition places it among prior single-page document understanding datasets. One paper also characterizes the infographics setting as high-resolution and requiring interpretation of charts and graphical data.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing claim is that papers use it to measure document understanding, while smaller lines of work also report it as measuring fine-grained visual understanding and optical character recognition. Beyond document understanding, its reported measurement use therefore extends to OCR-related and fine-grained visual evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers usually deploy it within broader benchmark suites, commonly alongside DocVQA, ChartQA, TextVQA, and OCRBench, and sometimes with STVQA. In the

nodes.name: InjecAgent
nodes.definition: A red-teaming framework that uses a large language model (GPT-4) to automatically generate adversarial injection prompts for attacking LLM agents.

nodes.name: InstruSum
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, InstruSum is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for evaluating instruction-controllable summary generation. Definitions describe it as containing articles or a source article, summary requirements expressed as a specific or complex instruction, and model outputs; one description also says it contains human annotations, and another states that it contains 400 samples. A smaller line of work instead frames it as a summarization-focused pairwise comparison benchmark for evaluating instruction-following and content quality in summaries.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link InstruSum to one behavioral indicator, Pointwise scoring, and to no constructs. The reported use is that it measures pointwise scoring of instruction-controllable summarization, so the measurement claims are concentrated on that single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. Papers use InstruSum as an evaluation benchmark for instruction-controllable summarization. In one evaluation setup it appears alongside LLMBar, with the two benchmarks described as respectively representing pairwise evaluation of ins

nodes.name: IOI task
nodes.definition: The Indirect Object Identification task, used to evaluate model understanding of internal circuits by testing if a model can identify the indirect object in sentences with a known structure.

nodes.name: IPIP-NEO-300
nodes.definition: A 300-item personality questionnaire from the International Personality Item Pool used to measure the Big Five personality traits, used in this paper as a generalization target for models aligned on IPIP-NEO-120 data.

nodes.name: Isaac Gym
nodes.definition: A GPU-accelerated physics simulation environment for reinforcement learning, used to evaluate performance on nine challenging robotic locomotion and manipulation tasks.

nodes.name: IU-Xray
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a chest X-ray dataset paired with associated medical or radiology reports and used in evaluation. Most definitions frame it around medical report generation, while one definition also explicitly presents it as being used for medical visual question answering. One paper further specifies that its test set contains 590 samples.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link IU-Xray to three behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant use is to measure Medical report generation: several papers describe evaluating report generation on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray or list IU-Xray among report generation datasets. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Medical visual question answering, and one paper uses it to measure Radiology report generation, so the reported measurement use is concentrated in generation tasks with an additional VQA use.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In reported experiments, papers most commonly use IU-Xray alongside MIMIC-CXR, and broader evaluation suites also place it with Harvard-FairVLMed, PMC-OA, Quilt-1M, and OmniMedVQA. Papers position it as an evaluation dataset, for

nodes.name: IWSLT 2017
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as a benchmark dataset from the International Workshop on Spoken Language Translation 2017 for evaluating machine translation systems, papers treat IWSLT 2017 as a translation benchmark rather than defining it in broader terms. Some definitions are more specific, describing parallel documents sourced from TED talks, and one paper focuses on the tst2017 test sets covering 12 language pairs. A smaller line of usage calls it an international speech translation benchmark and notes its use in zero-shot prompting experiments, while another paper refers to extracting its training and test sets and using it to evaluate translation performance for low-resource language pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed papers, the measurement claim converges on one behavioral indicator: Machine translation. IWSLT 2017 is linked to one behavioral indicator and no constructs, and papers use it to measure machine translation in settings described as text translation, context-aware machine translation from English to French, and additional translation evaluation in a generation scenario. The reported use is therefore concentrated on this single indica

nodes.name: JailbreakBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat JailbreakBench as a standardized or open benchmark for evaluating a model's safety, robustness, or vulnerability under jailbreak attacks. The prevailing description is a dataset of harmful queries, instructions, or unsafe behavior prompts, often described as 100 selected prompts or instances, and one paper describes it as adversarial prompts collected from multiple sources, including GCG and PAIR attacks. A smaller line of work emphasizes the procedure around the dataset, describing an LLM-as-judge protocol, a classifier-based setup with a pretrained Llama-3-70B-Instruct model, or a leaderboard of submitted attacks, and one paper distinguishes template and direct forms.

What it is claimed to measure. Across recorded relationships, papers use it to measure 4 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The construct links cover Harmlessness, Adversarial robustness, Safety, and Safety robustness, while the behavioral links include Jailbreaking and 1 other indicator, so the reported measurement claims are spread across several safety-oriented targets rather than a single named construct.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use it alongside HarmBench and AdvBench,

nodes.name: JailbreakV
nodes.definition: A multimodal safety dataset used to evaluate jailbreak resistance and safety performance, identified in the paper as suffering from visual safety information leakage.

nodes.name: JAMA Clinical Challenge
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats JAMA Clinical Challenge as a benchmark or dataset drawn from the JAMA Network Clinical Challenge archive, made up of challenging or complex real-world clinical cases for diagnosis or treatment decision-making. Definitions agree on a multiple-choice format built from case narratives: papers describe a long or detailed patient case followed by a clinical question, four answer choices, and a discussion or expert explanation; one description also includes the correct answer index and a medical speciality classification. One paper further specifies a size of 1,524 cases.

What it is claimed to measure. The measurement claims are concentrated on a small number of targets: papers link it to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. Most commonly, papers use it to measure Clinical decision-making, with the cases described as testing decision-making skills in realistic clinical scenarios; it is also reported as measuring Multiple-choice question answering, since the benchmark is described as structured as a multiple-choice question-answering task with expert-written explanations.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it.
