nodes.name: JEEBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe JEEBench as a mathematics benchmark or challenging dataset used to benchmark LLM performance on math problems. Some definitions are more specific, describing coverage of college-level topics such as simple ODEs and multivariable calculus, while another frames it as a collection of Indian Institute of Technology entrance exam problems assessing advanced mathematical reasoning. Papers also place it among more challenging, exam-style problem sets.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the recorded links, the measurement claim converges on one construct: one paper uses JEEBench to measure Mathematical reasoning. It is linked to one construct and no behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement use here is concentrated rather than spread across multiple targets.

Space of uses. Papers position it as part of broader hard-math evaluation setups rather than as a standalone protocol description. One study includes JEE-Bench among hard tasks spanning from high school competition to college-level exams, alongside Olympic-Arena and MATH, and another treats it as an additional challenging dataset alongside OmniMATH; no measurement instrument is f

nodes.name: Jigsaw
nodes.definition: A toxicity classification dataset where each sample is a sentence and sensitive attribute value is identified by humans.

nodes.name: JIGSAWS
nodes.definition: A dataset of surgical activities, used as a source for the 'Surgery' category videos in the VidDiffBench benchmark, featuring procedures like knot tying.

nodes.name: JudgeBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as a benchmark for challenging evaluation cases, most often for evaluating LLM-based judges on difficult response pairs or questions. Definitions repeatedly emphasize advanced reasoning demands, including coverage of knowledge, reasoning, math, and coding, and one description speaks more broadly of harder questions for various reasoning tasks rather than judge evaluation alone. A smaller usage frames it as an additional case study for judge behavior and agreement under uncertainty, and another describes it as testing the robustness and accuracy of LLM-as-a-Judge systems.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, JudgeBench is linked to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The most frequently linked constructs are Factuality, Mathematical reasoning, and Reasoning: papers say it focuses on "the factual and logical correctness of complex responses to challenging questions," use it because it includes response pairs involving factual correctness, and describe it as evaluating difficult response pairs that require advanced reasoning abilities or span knowledge, reasoning, math, and coding. The reported measurement links there

nodes.name: JudgeLM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers treat JudgeLM as a judge model for automated evaluation of LLM responses, with outputs assessed either by scoring or by selecting among responses. They also mention model variants JudgeLM-7B, JudgeLM-13B, and JudgeLM-33B.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not explicitly present JudgeLM as measuring any behavioral indicator, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. It is linked to one construct, Generalization, but that link is recorded as related rather than measured_by, so papers do not clearly frame JudgeLM as a measure of a named construct.

Space of uses. Papers place JudgeLM alongside PandaLM and GPT-4 as one of several judge models used for automated evaluation. The stated use is to evaluate LLM responses by scoring them or selecting outputs.

Concerns raised. One paper relates JudgeLM to Generalization and reports that judge models demonstrate poor generalization when evaluating different LLMs and benchmarks.

nodes.name: Just-Eval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat Just-Eval as an evaluation framework or benchmark for scoring model outputs, though one paper also presents it as a dataset of diverse instructions. Across these descriptions, the recurring content is the same five dimensions, helpfulness, clarity, factuality or factual accuracy, depth, and engagement, and one paper says the official prompt is used with GPT-4 scoring each dimension from 1 to 5. Papers also use subsets of the instructions, with examples of 1,000 and 800 diverse instructions.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the reported links, Just-Eval is connected to one construct, Helpfulness, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. Papers use it to measure Helpfulness by evaluating outputs in terms of helpfulness, clarity, factuality, depth, and engagement, and one description explicitly says it is used to measure the helpfulness of edited LLMs. The reported measurement claims therefore center on Helpfulness rather than on multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Most usages present Just-Eval as a direct output evaluation: papers score responses on the named dimensions and report Just-Eval scores, often for edited or defended LLM outp

nodes.name: K-QA
nodes.definition: A real-world medical question-answering benchmark, with a subset of responses verified by physicians.

nodes.name: Keirsey Temperament Sorter
nodes.definition: A self-assessment personality questionnaire, based on the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, used to classify individuals into one of four temperament groups: Rationals, Idealists, Guardians, and Artisans.

nodes.name: Kitchen
nodes.definition: A simulated benchmark (Gupta et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2020) designed to test an agent's ability to handle sparse terminal rewards and perform long-horizon manipulation in a kitchen setting.

nodes.name: KnowEdit
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available descriptions, papers treat KnowEdit as an integrated benchmark for evaluating knowledge editing methods. The benchmark is described as containing six datasets for different evaluation types, and one paper notes that experiments are conducted on the KnowEdit benchmark (Precise Localization of Memories: A Fine-grained Neuron-level Knowledge Editing Technique for LLMs).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers describe KnowEdit as evaluating knowledge editing methods across criteria such as success, portability, locality, and fluency. Beyond those benchmark criteria, no construct links or behavioral-indicator links are recorded, so the available usage does not connect it to a broader spread of named constructs.

Space of uses. The available paper uses KnowEdit as an experimental benchmark for assessing knowledge editing methods. No other measurement instruments are linked alongside it in the available relationships.

nodes.name: Konwinski Prize
nodes.definition: A benchmark designed to fairly evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs by using only new GitHub issues, thereby mitigating data contamination.

nodes.name: L-Eval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats L-Eval as a benchmark, often described as a standardized long-context evaluation suite for language models. Most definitions frame it around long-context capability or performance, with closed-ended tasks, especially multiple-choice and true or false question answering, while some papers describe a broader suite with both closed-ended and open-ended tasks for understanding, reasoning, summarization, and open-format question answering over long inputs. A smaller line of work specifies its contents as 508 long documents from various domains, divided into 20 subtasks or "20 smaller long sequence datasets," and one paper notes that its tasks appear at varying input lengths.

What it is claimed to measure. Relationship claims are concentrated rather than spread broadly: papers link L-Eval to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The dominant claim is that it measures long-context understanding, with several papers describing it as a commonly used long-context benchmark or as part of a "comprehensive evaluation of long-context understanding." A smaller usage links it to long-context generation, where one paper report

nodes.name: LAION-1k
nodes.definition: A set of approximately 1,000 LAION-derived text-image pairs related to human names and personal life, used to assess training data memorization.

nodes.name: LAMBADA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, LAMBADA is most commonly described as a language modeling, word prediction, or next-word benchmark in which a model predicts the final word of a passage, paragraph, or sentence from broad discourse or long-range context. A recurring formulation is that it tests long-range dependencies, long-term context recall, or contextual understanding, and several papers evaluate it in zero-shot settings. A smaller line of work describes it as a reading comprehension benchmark, and papers also refer to variants such as LAMBADA-standard (LS), LAMBADA (OpenAI), the OpenAI variant, and LAMBADA_OPENAI.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use LAMBADA to measure a broad range of targets rather than a single recurring construct: it is linked to 11 constructs and 8 behavioral indicators. The most frequently linked constructs are Commonsense reasoning, Contextual understanding, General ability, Natural language understanding, and Reasoning, with 6 other constructs also linked: Zero-shot generalization, In-context learning, Language modeling ability, Logical reasoning, Long-context understanding, and World knowledge. Among behavioral indicators, the most frequent links are D

nodes.name: Lambada-OpenAI
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available definitions treat Lambada-OpenAI as a benchmark for language understanding, specifically for evaluating the ability to model long-range dependencies in text through a text completion task. The only direct format detail reported is a 0-shot setup, noted as "Lambada-OpenAI (0-shot)" in Parameters vs FLOPs: Scaling Laws for Optimal Sparsity for Mixture-of-Experts Language Models.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked uses, papers use Lambada-OpenAI to measure Language understanding task performance. Its reported measurement role is narrow rather than spread across many targets: it is linked to a single behavioral indicator, Language understanding task performance, and no constructs are linked to it; papers place it under "Language Understanding (LU)" when reporting this role.

Space of uses. In use, papers place Lambada-OpenAI alongside Hellaswag-0-shot, Winograd-3-shots, and WinoGrande-5-shots as part of a broader language understanding evaluation bundle. The observed configuration is 0-shot, and one paper labels the relevant result panel "(a) Language Understanding Lambada-OpenAI (0-shot)".

nodes.name: LaMP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, LaMP is treated as a benchmark or dataset for short-form personalization evaluation. The prevailing descriptions frame it around short-form personalized text generation, including tasks such as news headline generation, scholarly title generation, and tweet paraphrasing, while another description presents it as a public LLM personalization benchmark with named subsets, LaMP-1 through LaMP-5, covering citation identification, movie tagging, Amazon product rating, news headline generation, and scholarly title generation, and says these tasks test surface-level personalization on short-context queries. A broader framing in another paper describes LaMP as consisting of various text classification and generation tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use LaMP to measure 4 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The linked behavioral indicators are headline generation, scholarly title generation, text classification, and text generation, so the recorded uses are spread across several task types rather than converging on any linked construct. In the more task-specific descriptions, papers explicitly tie it to the headline and scholarly title generation s

nodes.name: LaMP-QA
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating personalized long-form question answering, covering questions from Arts & Entertainment, Lifestyle & Personal Development, and Society & Culture, using user profiles and aspect-based evaluation derived from question narratives.

nodes.name: Lap14
nodes.definition: A dataset for aspect-based sentiment analysis from the SemEval 2014 shared task, requiring classification of sentiment towards a particular entity or aspect.

nodes.name: LASER
nodes.definition: An LLM-based ASR evaluation rubric that uses detailed prompts with error type examples to assign no, minor, or major penalties based on semantic impact, producing a sentence-level score.

nodes.name: Last letter concatenation
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of a symbolic or reasoning benchmark in which a model concatenates the last letters of words or names in an input sequence. Definitions vary between a reasoning task, dataset, benchmark test set, string-manipulation benchmark, and text-processing benchmark, but they converge on the same format: taking the last letters from a series of words, sometimes specified as a 4-word sequence or a set of names, for example 'Amy Brown' to 'yn'. A smaller line of work describes it as a string-manipulation benchmark used to evaluate algorithmic reasoning and length generalization in verification settings.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to two constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure symbolic reasoning, with papers explicitly grouping it under symbolic reasoning benchmarks or datasets; a smaller usage treats it as measuring more general reasoning, as in one paper's reference to 'standard reasoning datasets (GSM8K, CSQA, and LLC)'. The reported measurement claims are concentrated on those two constructs rather than spread across many.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use it inside broader eva

nodes.name: LastFM
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for recommendation research derived from a popular music service, containing user-artist interaction histories.

nodes.name: LawBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the available usage, LawBench is treated as a benchmark focused on Chinese laws, with 20 diverse legal tasks. The definition and source text specifically mention charge prediction and prison term prediction, and the paper places LawBench alongside LegalBench when evaluating LLMs' generalization capability across legal domains.

What it is claimed to measure. The available paper links LawBench to 2 behavioral indicators, charge prediction and prison term prediction, both through measured_by relationships. Its quoted use narrows LawBench to these two tasks, and no constructs are linked to it.

Space of uses. The available paper uses LawBench as part of a broader legal-domain evaluation and positions it alongside LegalBench. Within LawBench, it concentrates on the two challenging tasks of charge prediction and prison term prediction. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: LeanDojo
nodes.definition: LeanDojo is a Lean theorem-proving benchmark and data-extraction ecosystem used as a comparison point for premise-based theorem proving.

nodes.name: LeetCode
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, LeetCode is most commonly treated as a collection of programming problems from the LeetCode platform, either used directly as a coding benchmark or used as source material for derived tasks. One description uses approximately 2,000 coding problems, covering solutions in Python, Java, and C++, to build fill-in-the-blank items. A smaller framing treats Leetcode as a benchmark of recent problems scraped from the website, described as recent enough that models released before July 2023 would not have been trained on them.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link LeetCode to two behavioral indicators and to no constructs. The recorded uses are to measure Code completion, through fill-in-the-blank tasks built from LeetCode problems, and Code generation, with LeetCode grouped with HumanEval for coding. The measurement claims therefore stay with these two behavioral indicators rather than any linked construct.

Space of uses. Papers position LeetCode in two main ways. In one use, it serves as an upstream source corpus inside a broader evaluation, where LeetCode problems are converted into fill-in-the-blank tasks. In another, it is used as a standalone co

nodes.name: LeetCode Contest
nodes.definition: A benchmark consisting of programming contest problems categorized by difficulty (Easy, Medium, Hard) to assess performance on complex problem-solving.

nodes.name: LegalBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe LegalBench as a benchmark or benchmark suite for evaluating legal reasoning in language models, and one paper says it consists of 162 tasks covering various aspects of legal reasoning. A smaller line of work calls it a dataset for evaluating reasoning and hallucination in legal contexts and for assessing domain-specific factual accuracy. Papers also refer to specific parts of the benchmark, including the International Citizenship Questions sub-task and the Definition Extraction task, and one paper presents LegalBench-Instruct as derived from LegalBench through prompt refinement.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, claims converge on a single construct: LegalBench is used to measure legal reasoning. It is linked to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators, and several papers describe it as evaluating various aspects of legal reasoning, measuring legal reasoning in large language models, or providing problem templates for profiling legal reasoning. One definition also extends its use to reasoning and hallucination in legal contexts, but the linked measurement claim centers on legal reasoning.

Space of uses. No measurement instrume

nodes.name: LEMON
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers here, LEMON is described as a large-scale, multi-domain Chinese Spelling Correction dataset built from real-world spelling errors. Definitions emphasize seven sub-domains, with examples including game, encyclopedia, contract, medical care, and car, plus two others, and one paper says it typically tests domain correction capabilities in a zero-shot setting. Another paper characterizes it as having test sets from seven domains without in-domain training sets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure two constructs and one behavioral indicator. The construct links are both generalization-oriented, Cross-domain generalization and Generalization: one paper describes LEMON as an ideal benchmark for evaluating a model’s cross-domain generalization capability, and another says it serves as a cross-domain dataset for evaluating generalization capabilities. A separate paper also uses it as a benchmark for Chinese spelling correction.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In use, papers position it as an evaluation benchmark centered on cross-domain testing: one definition says it typically assesses domain correction capabilit

nodes.name: LexEval
nodes.definition: Legal domain evaluation suite containing Legal Translation and Legal EssayQA tasks, assessing bilingual translation and open-ended legal reasoning.

nodes.name: LFQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the dominant framing treats LFQA as a long-form question-answering dataset drawn from Reddit. Definitions say it was created by scraping Reddit questions and pairing them with human-written answers, and one paper further specifies that it is curated from posts and responses on Reddit's "Explain Like I'm Five" forum. A smaller framing presents LFQA as a pairwise comparison benchmark for evaluating long-form question answering.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link LFQA to any constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, they describe it at the task level, as being used for evaluating watermark robustness in question answering settings and for pairwise comparisons in long-form question answering.

Space of uses. Papers position it mainly as an evaluation set or prompt source. One paper says LFQA was adopted as prompts for a human paraphrasing study, while other definitions describe it as part of evaluation for watermark robustness and as an evaluation set for pairwise comparisons. No other measurement instruments are linked alongside it.

nodes.name: LIAR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available definitions, papers treat LIAR as a dataset for evaluating claim verification. One paper also places it among "7 standard datasets" used for evaluation and describes its role here as assessing F1 score in true/false classification under prompt optimization.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded relationships do not link LIAR to any construct or behavioral indicator as a measurement instrument. In the available descriptions, its stated evaluative role is claim verification and F1 assessment for true/false classification.

Space of uses. Papers use LIAR as one dataset within a broader evaluation setup alongside other standard datasets, including WSC, Ethos, and ArSarcasm. In the reported use, it appears in prompt optimization experiments, with one result summarized as "improving F1 score by 10.1 on LIAR dataset" (Efficient and Accurate Prompt Optimization: the Benefit of Memory in Exemplar-Guided Reflection).

nodes.name: LIAR2
nodes.definition: Benchmark dataset of approximately 23,000 short statements manually labeled by professional fact-checkers for truthfulness, used for fake news detection evaluation.

nodes.name: LibriSpeech
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe LibriSpeech as a large corpus, dataset, or benchmark of read English speech derived from audiobooks, often aligned and segmented, and commonly framed as clean read speech for ASR. Definitions usually mention 960 hours of English reading audio, though one paper says it contains roughly 1000 hours and another extracts chunks from it to form a 1GB audio dataset for compression experiments. Papers use several subsets and settings, including train-clean-100, dev-clean, dev-other, test-clean, test-other, and 100-hour and 960-hour setups, while a smaller line simply describes Librispeech as a speech recognition dataset for closed-ended audio evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, LibriSpeech is linked to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure Speech recognition: relationship evidence calls it an automatic speech recognition benchmark, a benchmark dataset of clean read speech for standard ASR tasks, and a test set that demonstrates ASR performance in a clean scenario. A smaller line uses it to measure Speech reconstruction, and one paper uses it to measure Utility preservation as part of a general utili

nodes.name: LIMA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, LIMA is described as a natural language dataset organized around instruction-response pairs. Papers portray it in two main ways: as a non-code dataset used to study memorization and test whether findings generalize beyond code, and as an instruction fine-tuning dataset with curated prompts and responses designed to teach specific instructional formats. One paper further characterizes its training split as 1,030 diverse instruction-response pairs covering a wide range of downstream scenarios.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use LIMA to measure three constructs and one behavioral indicator. The linked constructs are General ability, Instruction following ability, and Memorization, and the linked behavioral indicator is Text generation. These claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on one recurring construct: one paper computes language-model loss on the training split of LIMA for General ability, another studies memorization on LIMA, another uses LIMA to investigate instruction-following capabilities, and one paper reports Text generation as measured by an evaluation described as similar to the evaluation process in LIMA.

Space

nodes.name: LINGOLY
nodes.definition: Benchmark consisting of linguistic puzzles from the United Kingdom Linguistics Olympiad (UKLO), covering six topics: phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, number systems, and compounding, used to evaluate LLM performance on puzzle solving.

nodes.name: LiRA
nodes.definition: Likelihood Ratio Attack, a membership inference attack that formulates the problem as hypothesis testing, comparing the likelihood of a model's output score under the hypotheses that the sample was or was not in the training data.

nodes.name: List Functions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a dataset or benchmark for list transformation, where a model infers a rule that maps an input list to an output list from examples. Definitions and snippets variously describe the target rule as primitive, compositional, or a general transformation function, and they frame the benchmark as evaluating human and machine concept learning ability and inductive reasoning ability. A smaller line of work presents "List Function" as a Programming by Example task about computable list to list functions using GPL rules. Some descriptions further specify integer-list inputs and outputs, including the possibility of an empty list.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked work, papers use List Functions to measure inductive reasoning. It is linked to one construct, Inductive reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators or other measurement instruments. The claims converge on that single construct, with papers describing the benchmark as evaluating "inductive reasoning ability in inferring list transform functions" and as one of the "inductive reasoning datasets" used in experiments.

Space of uses. Papers most often position i

nodes.name: LITRANSPROQA
nodes.definition: An LLM-based question-answering framework for literary translation evaluation that uses professionally curated questions to assess translation quality across multiple dimensions including literary devices, cultural understanding, and authorial voice.

nodes.name: LiveBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed definitions, LiveBench is most commonly described as a dynamic, contamination-limited benchmark from Abacus AI: papers say it evaluates models on questions with ground-truth answers, compiles items from recent sources such as math competitions, and refreshes the dataset regularly. A recurring description is that it spans multiple domains, most commonly data analysis, language, reasoning, math, instruction following, and coding, while some definitions emphasize the large test set and others stress periodic updates to reduce contamination.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 5 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The construct links are led by Reasoning, with additional claims for Coding ability, General ability, Mathematical reasoning, and Natural language understanding, while the behavioral-indicator links cover Data analysis, Instruction following, and Language understanding task performance. Overall, the measurement claims are spread across several abilities rather than concentrated on one construct, in line with the benchmark's multi-domain task descriptions.

Space of uses. It is linked to 6 other measurement instruments.

nodes.name: LiveCodeBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, LiveCodeBench is most commonly described as a contamination-free benchmark for code generation built from recent competitive programming problems, often from LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces, with careful segregation by date to avoid contamination. Some descriptions emphasize continual collection of new human-authored problems to maintain freshness, while others frame it more broadly as a holistic evaluation for code that includes code generation and code execution tasks, including a code execution component called LCB-Exec. Papers also describe different slices and sizes: LiveCodeBench-v1.0 appears in one study, its "easy" subset is used for efficiency and accuracy comparisons, and other papers variously describe over 711 coding problems, 400 recent Python algorithm challenges, or over 300 challenging questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Most papers use LiveCodeBench to measure code generation, and one paper explicitly says the benchmark continues to evolve and add new code generation tasks. Papers link it to 6 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators overall. Beyond code generation, smaller lines of work use it to measure code debugging and code ou

nodes.name: LiveSum
nodes.definition: A synthetic football game comments dataset designed for text-to-table tasks, featuring multi-instance and dynamic data where team statistics are aggregated from individual player scores mentioned in the text.

nodes.name: LIWC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, LIWC is described either as Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count, a psycholinguistic feature extraction tool, or as LIWC-22, a text analysis program. Definitions converge on its role in categorizing words into linguistic and psychological dimensions such as emotion, cognition, and formality, and in calculating the percentage of words in a text that fall into such categories. A narrower versioned usage names LIWC-22 specifically, while another paper refers to LIWC more generally as providing psycholinguistic characteristics.

What it is claimed to measure. The only reported measured_by link treats LIWC as measuring Stylistic variation, with the paper describing it as a traditional stylometric feature set that provides psycholinguistic characteristics. In these papers, it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Stylistic variation, and to no constructs, so its reported measurement use is concentrated on that single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers use LIWC as an analysis tool applied to text or responses. One paper reports segment comparison results using LIWC alongside WritePrint features, whi

nodes.name: Llama Guard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats Llama Guard as an LLM-based or model-based safety classifier, guardrail, or safeguard for prompts and responses. Definitions describe it as judging whether outputs are harmful, unsafe, safe, or harmless, and also as an evaluation tool that can calculate Attack Success Rate by classifying response harmfulness. A smaller line names 7B variants, LLaMA Guard 7B or LlamaGuard-7B, as open-source guard models or dedicated safety classifiers; other papers describe it as a pretrained content-moderation guardrail, an input-output safeguard used as an NSFW filter, or a safety mechanism deployed on selected communication edges in multi-agent systems.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Llama Guard to 2 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The most recurring measurement claim is Harmlessness, where papers use Llama-Guard to determine the safety of the responses; other papers report it as measuring Toxicity, Harmful content generation, Jailbreaking, and Safety classifier evasion. Overall, the measurement claims are spread across several safety-related targets rather than centered on a single construct.

Space of uses. Papers t

nodes.name: Llama Guard 2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the prevailing treatment is as an automated safety classifier and LLM-as-a-judge for judging whether model outputs are safe, unsafe, harmful, or toxic. Definitions commonly describe it as a model fine-tuned from Llama-3-8B, with named variants such as Llama-Guard-2-8B and LLaMA Guard 2 8B, and one definition also describes it as an 8-billion-parameter open-source guard model. Most uses focus on classifying responses or conversations, though some papers additionally use it to identify unsafe documents, derive soft safety scores for rejection sampling, or use its feature layer as a semantic embedding source.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers link it to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Safety, for example by classifying responses or conversations as safe or unsafe and by reporting unsafe response rates; a smaller line of work reports it as measuring Harmful content generation, including attack success rate based on output safety, and Jailbreaking, by classifying responses as jailbreak or non-jailbreak.

Space of uses.

nodes.name: Llama Guard 3
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the dominant framing is Llama Guard 3 as an automated content safety classifier or judge for prompts and model responses. Most descriptions refer to an 8B variant and describe it as a content safety classification LLM that labels text as safe or unsafe, scores harmfulness or toxicity, or identifies harmful categories such as violence, self-harm, illegal activities, and inappropriate sexual content; one paper also specifies it as a Llama-3.1-8B-based model fine-tuned for content safety classification. A smaller line of work treats it as a moderation defense or external guardrail for detecting jailbreak attempts and unsafe content.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator and three constructs. The recurring use is to measure harmful content generation by evaluating the harmfulness of model responses, while other papers report that harmlessness, safety, and safety alignment are measured by it, often through content safety classification or harmfulness scoring. The linked claims therefore center on several named outcomes rather than a single target.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers m

nodes.name: LLaVA-Bench-in-the-Wild
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats it as an in-the-wild, open-ended benchmark for multimodal dialogue, image understanding, and real-world visual questions. Definitions often describe challenging images and questions, and several specify 24 images with 60 questions organized around conversation, detailed description, and complex reasoning; some papers describe it more narrowly as conversational VQA, visual conversation, or single-image long-form reasoning. A recurring detail is model-based scoring, with GPT-4, GPT-4V, or GPT-4o used for evaluation, and one paper also treats the Wild variant as a dataset for varying visual input semantics alongside a COCO version.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the relationships reported for it are entirely measurement claims, and papers link it to 6 constructs and 10 behavioral indicators. The most frequently linked behavioral indicators are complex reasoning question answering, visual question answering, detailed image description, multi-turn dialogue, and catastrophic forgetting, with five other behavioral indicators also present. On the construct side, papers report it as measuring helpfulness, visual understa

nodes.name: LLaVA-Med
nodes.definition: A large-scale instruction-tuning dataset for biomedical vision-language processing, used for training.

nodes.name: LLF-Bench Meta-World
nodes.definition: A simulated benchmark environment featuring a Sawyer robot manipulator for testing an agent's ability to learn from language feedback on tasks like reach, pick-place, and push.

nodes.name: LLM-as-a-judge
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing treats LLM-as-a-judge as an automated evaluation protocol in which one language model, often GPT-4 or GPT-4o, judges another model's output. Most definitions describe pairwise comparisons or direct scoring for open-ended responses, usually with the prompt, candidate output, and sometimes a reference answer, rubric, dialogue history, or checklist; smaller variants use binary correctness decisions, stepwise grading, task-completion checks, or semantic classification such as harmful or benign. A smaller line of work extends the same pattern to multimodal judges, including GPT-4V, VLMs, and MLLMs, and to specialized forms such as verifiers, success detectors, meta-judges, and judge ensembles.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 66 constructs and 38 behavioral indicators, so the claims are spread across many targets rather than concentrated on one. The most common construct links say it measures helpfulness, harmlessness, factuality, text generation quality, and fluency. The most common behavioral links say it measures text generation, hallucination, instruction following, harmful content generation, and jailbreaking.

nodes.name: llm-foundry
nodes.definition: Evaluation suite for benchmarking pretrained language models in an in-context few-shot learning setup across multiple task categories.

nodes.name: LLM Guard
nodes.definition: LLM-Guard, a safety evaluation procedure used to measure safety rates on safety benchmarks.

nodes.name: LLMBar
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, LLMBar is most commonly described as a meta-evaluation benchmark, or dataset, for assessing LLM evaluators' discernment of instruction-following outputs. Definitions converge on natural and adversarial pairwise comparison samples, and one paper specifies that it contains one Natural subset and four Adversarial subsets, Neighbor, GPTInst, GPTOut, and Manual (SaMer: A Scenario-aware Multi-dimensional Evaluator for Large Language Models). A smaller framing emphasizes that it consists of high-quality human annotations with high inter-annotator agreement.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link LLMBar to 2 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, and the dominant claim is that it measures instruction following, often through pairwise comparison tasks. The linked constructs are evaluation ability and instruction following ability, the linked behavioral indicators are instruction following and pairwise comparison, and papers also link it to 1 measurement instrument, LLM-as-a-judge. One relationship describes it as using response pairs with clear ground truth preference labels based on adherence to instructions rather than subjective preferences, wh

nodes.name: LLMEval
nodes.definition: An LLM-based evaluation pipeline used to judge whether model responses are correct, abstentions, or hallucinations.

nodes.name: LM1B
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers treat LM1B as a dataset. One description names it the One-Billion Word Language Model Benchmark and uses it for language modeling evaluation, while another uses it to run experiments and check whether results seen on C4 also appear on a different data source.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link LM1B to one construct and no behavioral indicators. The only reported measurement claim is that it measures Zero-shot generalization: a paper describes out-of-domain unseen datasets as validating models' ability in zero-shot generalization, and LM1B is linked to that evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to another measurement instrument. In use, LM1B appears alongside C4, where authors report 'observed similar results,' and alongside the OpenWebText test set in an evaluation that uses out-of-domain unseen datasets to validate zero-shot generalization; elsewhere it is presented as a language modeling benchmark.

nodes.name: lm-evaluation-harness
names: Eleuther AI Language Model Evaluation Harness
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is as a standardized, open-source evaluation framework, library, or software suite for running language-model benchmarks in a reproducible and comparable way. Most definitions describe a broad suite of downstream tasks, while some narrow it to zero-shot or few-shot settings, multiple-choice tasks, or text-only and short-context subsets, with examples such as ARC, BoolQ, HellaSwag, Wikitext, and LAMBADA. A smaller line of work presents it as the common protocol for leaderboard-style assessments or as a unified framework for evaluating generative language models.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 11 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims span many targets rather than a single construct. Most commonly, papers use it to measure commonsense reasoning, general ability, reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and in-context learning. Across the behavioral-indicator links, the same broad pattern appears, with papers using it for capability evaluations such as zero-shot and downstream-task performance.

Space of uses. Most commonly, papers use it as a common framework for benchmark suites, ofte

nodes.name: LMR-BENCH
nodes.definition: A benchmark designed to evaluate an LLM agent's ability to reproduce code from language modeling research papers by implementing masked functions in a provided code repository.

nodes.name: LMSYS-Chat-1M
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of a large dataset of real-world conversations or interactions, used as a source of prompts and dialogue for chat-oriented work. Definitions vary in emphasis: some describe user prompts, user-model conversations, or broader LLM conversations, while others specify an open-access collection from the Chatbot Arena platform or real-world conversations with state-of-the-art LLMs. Across these descriptions, papers mainly treat it as a source of real-world chat data for fine-tuning and evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link it to any construct or behavioral indicator, so there is no recurring named measurement target in the recorded relationships. Instead, definitions and snippets present it as a source of real-world inputs for assessing non-adversarial reproduction, analyzing usage patterns, representing realistic use cases, and testing classifier generalization.

Space of uses. Most papers use it by sampling prompts or conversations from it for fine-tuning or for another analysis, such as rerunning an evaluation, drawing out-of-distribution prompts, or assembling prompt sets meant to reflect real-world use.

nodes.name: LoCoMo
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, LoCoMo is most commonly treated as a long-term conversation benchmark for assessing long-term conversational memory over very long dialogue histories. Definitions describe it as including 50 long-term chat histories with questions, and one paper also calls it the longest conversation dataset to date, while another quoted description instead refers to 30 multi-session dialogues between two speakers. Papers also vary in how they describe its question categories: some list single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, commonsense, world knowledge, and adversarial reasoning, while another lists single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, and open-domain.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use LoCoMo to measure one behavioral indicator, Question answering, and it is not linked to any constructs. The measurement claims converge on that single target: papers report QA performance on LoCoMo and describe it as a dataset for evaluating question answering.

Space of uses. Papers commonly position LoCoMo as one of the long-term conversation benchmarks and mention it alongside Long-MT-Bench+, including in performance comparison tables. No measurement in

nodes.name: LOFT
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating long-context models on real-world retrieval tasks, including argumentative retrieval, fact-checking, web search, and multi-hop reasoning question answering.

nodes.name: LogicBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark comprising various logic questions in both binary classification and multiple-choice formats to assess logical reasoning.

nodes.name: LogicNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat LogicNLI as a logical reasoning benchmark, and some describe it more specifically as an NLI-style or natural language inference dataset. Across definitions, the recurring framing is that it assesses hypothesis verification from facts and rules and isolates first-order logic reasoning from commonsense inference; as one study notes, "LogicNLI effectively separates the targeted FOL reasoning from common-sense inference" (Few-Shot Natural Language to First-Order Logic Translation via Code Generation).

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement targets are concentrated: papers link it to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is to measure Logical reasoning, with several papers evaluating models on LogicNLI as a logical reasoning dataset, while a smaller usage treats it as measuring Natural language inference, including a paper that selects LogicNLI "for natural language inference."

Space of uses. Most uses here position LogicNLI as one member of a broader evaluation suite rather than a standalone protocol. Papers use it alongside RobustLR, PrOntoQA-OOD, ProofWriter, ParaRules, and ProntoQA in logical reasoning

nodes.name: LogiQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, LogiQA is most commonly described as a logical reasoning benchmark or dataset, often as multiple-choice machine reading comprehension in which a model chooses the correct option from a passage, a logic puzzle text, or stated premises. Several definitions say it uses expert-written questions to test human logical reasoning, and some specify deductive, inductive, and abductive inference or a broader mix of categorical, conditional, disjunctive, and conjunctive reasoning. A smaller line of work describes it instead as a commonsense reasoning benchmark, and one paper frames it as NLI-style questions that require inferring a conclusion from premises.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link LogiQA to 5 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure Logical reasoning, and more broadly Reasoning, while additional papers use it to measure Commonsense reasoning, Generalization, and Temporal reasoning. It is also used to measure Question answering and Zero-shot task performance, so papers most often treat it as a logical reasoning measure, while also attaching it to several adjacent targets.

Space of uses. Most papers position LogiQA a

nodes.name: LogiQA 2.0
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats LogiQA 2.0, often written as LogiQA2 or LogiQA 2, as a benchmark or dataset for logical reasoning and logical question answering. Papers describe it as requiring logical reasoning over text, and some specify a multiple-choice format, including "logical reasoning multi-choice QA" and multiple-choice questions derived from professional exams that require deductive reasoning. A smaller strand presents it as an improved version of LogiQA for machine reading comprehension, and one relationship snippet describes LogiQA2 as a revision and re-annotation of LogiQA.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 5 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The most common claim is that it measures Logical reasoning; other papers use it to measure Commonsense reasoning, Executive function, Generalization, and Reasoning, and one paper uses it for the behavioral indicator Multiple-choice question answering. Overall, its reported measurement role is spread across several reasoning-related constructs rather than confined to a single framing.

Space of uses. Across papers, it is usually one component of broader evaluation suites rather tha

nodes.name: Logistics
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Logistics is consistently treated as a PDDL planning benchmark or domain centered on transporting packages between locations with trucks and airplanes. Definitions do not diverge on this core description. One paper also places it among four PDDL tasks used in experiments, alongside BlocksWorld, Minigrid, and Tetris, and another describes it as a widely used benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Its use as a measurement instrument converges on a single construct: papers use Logistics to measure Planning. Papers link it to one construct, Planning, and to no behavioral indicators. The accompanying descriptions frame this as evaluating plan generation in the domain, including references to generating simple plans or valid plans.

Space of uses. Papers position Logistics as a planning evaluation benchmark. One paper uses it alongside BlocksWorld, Minigrid, and Tetris as part of a set of PDDL tasks, while another uses it to test whether many-shot in-context learning can improve the ability to generate simple plans on the domain. Papers do not link it to other measurement instruments.

nodes.name: Long Range Arena
nodes.definition: Long Range Arena (LRA), a pioneering benchmark for long context modeling with tasks ranging from 1k to 16k tokens.

nodes.name: LongBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat LongBench as a multi-task benchmark or benchmark suite for long-context understanding in LLMs, though some describe it more loosely as a dataset or collection. The prevailing description emphasizes diverse tasks, especially question answering, summarization, and code completion or generation, while some papers also add few-shot learning and retrieval, and one study calls it a 'collection of long context benchmark datasets.' Papers also describe its scope differently: some definitions give evaluation lengths of 5k to 15k tokens, while others refer to 32K maximum length, average context around 18K, bilingual or multilingual coverage, or a medium-context framing around 10K tokens.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the dominant measurement claim is that LongBench measures long-context understanding. It is linked to 7 constructs and 14 behavioral indicators: beyond that main construct, papers sometimes use it for general ability and length generalization, while task-level use most often targets text summarization and few-shot task performance. The claims therefore concentrate on one main construct but are spread across many specific task behavi

nodes.name: LongBench-E
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe LongBench-E as a benchmark covering 13 real-world long-context applications, including coding, question answering, and few-shot learning. Some authors instead describe it as the English-language subset of the LongBench benchmark, used for evaluating long-context understanding. One recurring characterization also calls it a multitask benchmark for long-context understanding, with task lengths averaging between 5k and 32k tokens.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing claim is that LongBench-E measures Long-context understanding: it is linked to one construct, and papers describe it as evaluating large language models' ability to understand long contexts or to find key information within a long multi-document context. It is also linked to two behavioral indicators, Coding and Few-shot task performance, through papers that use its coding and few-shot learning applications. Overall, papers use it mainly for one construct, with two additional task-level indicators attached to it.

Space of uses. Papers use LongBench-E as an evaluation benchmark for comparing models and methods, including experiments with propose

nodes.name: LongBench v2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a multiple-choice benchmark for long contexts, with contexts ranging from 8K to 2M words. One fuller account specifies 503 multiple-choice questions spanning six tasks, single-document QA, multi-document QA, long in-context learning, long dialogue history understanding, code repository understanding, and long structured data understanding, and presents it as designed to evaluate deep long-context comprehension and reasoning, while a shorter description emphasizes its use for assessing long-context performance and efficiency.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, it is linked to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The only linked construct is long-context reasoning, and the linked behavioral indicators are document question answering and text summarization; one paper describes it as a benchmark for challenging long-context question-answering, another uses it for long-context reasoning, and another groups it with datasets that primarily assess retrieval and summarization rather than complex reasoning.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. In use, papers position it as a long-

nodes.name: LongEmbed PasskeyRetrieval
nodes.definition: A synthetic benchmark from the LongEmbed study used to evaluate long-context retrieval by requiring the model to retrieve a random 'passkey' from a long, distracting document.

nodes.name: LongEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a benchmark for long-context performance in language models. Most definitions specify topic retrieval and line retrieval tasks with varying prompt lengths, while another paper summarizes it more broadly as including various long context retrieval tasks and presents it as an early benchmark for long-context models.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers describe it as measuring long-context performance, and one paper frames this as evaluating tasks that require understanding of long-span context. No constructs or behavioral indicators are linked to it, so the papers' claims about what it measures stay at that broad performance level.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation benchmark for long-context analysis, and no measurement instrument is linked to it. One study reports additional experiments on LongEval to provide a more comprehensive analysis of scalability, and another says the StreamEval dataset was inspired by the LongEval benchmark.

nodes.name: LongEval (summarization faithfulness)
nodes.definition: Evaluation benchmark for long document summarization factuality, used to assess performance on scientific texts with summary-level correlation metrics.

nodes.name: LongFact
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, LongFact is most commonly treated as a benchmark for long-form factuality and fact-seeking long-form generation. Papers describe it differently: one definition presents it as a dataset with 250 prompts, while another presents it as a GPT-4-generated prompt set with 2,280 fact-seeking questions or prompts that solicit long-form responses across 38 manually selected topics in open domains.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers mainly use LongFact to measure behavioral indicators rather than constructs. It is linked to three behavioral indicators and no constructs; the direct measurement claims center on long-form text generation and hallucination, while instruction following appears in a separate causal claim about the quality of LongFact prompts rather than as something LongFact measures.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position LongFact as a benchmark for long-form factuality in open domains, and one study groups it with "four fact-seeking long-form generation datasets" (Improving Factuality with Explicit Working Memory).

Concerns raised. One paper raises a caution about how LongFact is produced: because Lo

nodes.name: LongGenBench
nodes.definition: Benchmark designed for extreme-length generation with multi-shot in-context examples, testing long-context reasoning and comprehension.

nodes.name: LongLaMP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat LongLaMP as a benchmark dataset for long-form personalized text generation. The prevailing description is that it covers tasks such as abstract generation, topic writing, and review generation; another description presents it as an extended version of LaMP with longer-form, open-ended, and more subjective personalized generation tasks, including abstract and topic writing.

What it is claimed to measure. In these papers, LongLaMP is not linked to named constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, papers describe it at the task level as evaluating long-form personalized text generation, with one description further characterizing its tasks as involving more subjective or user-specific expression.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use LongLaMP alongside LaMP, positioning the pair as resources for long-form and short-form personalized text generation, respectively. One study also places it within a set of open-ended personalized text generation tasks drawn from LaMP and LongLaMP.

nodes.name: LongMemEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Definitions treat LongMemEval as a long-term, multi-session conversation dataset used to evaluate response generation and memory utilization. Across other papers, it is more often framed as a chat-form benchmark for chat assistants' long-term or long-context memory, described either as a comprehensive benchmark for five core abilities, information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention, or as a challenging benchmark spanning six memory tasks. These descriptions agree on its use for memory-focused evaluation, while differing on whether it is called a dataset or a benchmark and on the stated task count.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims span 5 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The most recurring construct links say it measures multi-session reasoning and temporal reasoning; papers also use it to measure length generalization, memory, and multi-hop reasoning. On the behavioral side, it is reported as evaluating information extraction, knowledge editing, and abstention.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is directly linked to it. Papers position it as an adopted benchmark for assessing l

nodes.name: LongReport
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset created for this paper, containing 12 complex prompts designed to elicit comprehensive, long-form reports on time-sensitive topics.

nodes.name: LongVideoBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, LongVideoBench is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for long video or long-context video-language understanding, usually framed as video question answering on very long inputs, sometimes explicitly hour-long. The most specific description presents it as a question-answering benchmark with interleaved video-language inputs up to an hour long, containing 3,763 web-collected videos with subtitles and 6,678 human-annotated multiple-choice questions in 17 fine-grained categories. A smaller group of papers characterizes it more narrowly as a referred reasoning benchmark, and one paper uses the variant name "LongVideo-Bench".

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use LongVideoBench to measure 5 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so the reported use spreads across several closely related targets rather than a single one. The most common construct link is video understanding, followed by long video understanding, long-context multimodal understanding, long-context understanding, and multimodal understanding. Papers also use it to measure video question answering and visual question answering, and some descriptions make this more specific by c

nodes.name: LooGLE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats LooGLE as a benchmark or workload for long-context evaluation. Definitions describe it as evaluating long document question answering with prompts containing extensive text from which answers must be derived, and more broadly as evaluating long-context understanding through extremely long documents, diverse domains, short- and long-dependency tasks, and long-range dependencies over the full sequence. Papers differ slightly in emphasis, with some foregrounding long document QA and others framing it as a broader long-context benchmark; the descriptions also note documents with over 24,000 tokens and data primarily around 32,000 tokens.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use LooGLE to measure long-context understanding, and this is the only linked construct. It is linked to 1 construct, long-context understanding, while no behavioral indicators are linked. The claims converge on this single construct rather than spreading across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers position LooGLE both as a standalone workload and as part of broader evaluation suites. Some descriptions treat it as one workload among others, f

nodes.name: LoraxBench
nodes.definition: A multitask, multilingual benchmark suite covering 20 Indonesian languages and 3 register variations across 6 tasks: reading comprehension, open-domain QA, natural language inference, causal reasoning, cultural QA, and machine translation.

nodes.name: LSMDC
nodes.definition: Large-Scale Movie Description Challenge dataset featuring movie clips with textual descriptions, designed for evaluating multimodal understanding and retrieval in narrative contexts.

nodes.name: LV-Eval
nodes.definition: Bilingual benchmark assessing long-context understanding through single-hop and multi-hop question answering across 11 datasets, designed to evaluate model performance at varying context lengths.

nodes.name: LVIS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, LVIS is most commonly described as a large-vocabulary instance segmentation dataset or benchmark used for evaluation. Definitions repeatedly emphasize a long-tail version with annotations for over 1000 object categories, while one paper describes a commonly used zero-shot LVIS with 1,203 categories. Papers also refer to its validation dataset or validation sets, and some describe it as being used to evaluate object-level classification when a model is prompted with a visual region.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use LVIS to measure 2 behavioral indicators, Instance segmentation and Open-vocabulary object detection, and no constructs are linked to it. These linked claims stay at the behavioral level, though some definitions also describe LVIS as assessing object-level classification performance, including referring classification scored with Semantic Similarity and Semantic Intersection over Union.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to LVIS. Papers mainly position it as an evaluation benchmark: they report results on object detection, instance segmentation, and open-vocabulary recognition or segmentation, and in one usage the

nodes.name: M3Exam
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers here, M3Exam is most commonly described as a multitask, multilingual benchmark used to evaluate multimodal models. A narrower description in Is Translation All You Need? A Study on Solving Multilingual Tasks with Large Language Models treats it as a multilingual, multi-subject, multiple-choice exam benchmark built from real-world national exam questions, with questions drawn from different languages rather than translated from English.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link M3Exam to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims converge on a single construct rather than spreading across many targets. Its linked construct is Cultural knowledge: one paper uses M3Exam to measure it, stating that the questions require strong multilingual proficiency and cultural knowledge to perform well.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the recorded relationships. In use, papers present M3Exam as an evaluation benchmark or dataset: R2-MultiOmnia: Leading Multilingual Multimodal Reasoning via Self-Training uses it together with XMMMLU and MAXM to study multimodal reasoning performance, while another paper sel

nodes.name: M4
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe M4 in two distinct ways. Some definitions present it as a short-term time series forecasting benchmark containing marketing data at different sampling frequencies, and one snippet describes it as a testbed with a collection of marketing data in different sampling frequencies. Several source snippets instead use M4 for a machine-generated text detection dataset or benchmark: documents generated by multiple LLMs in five domains, a multilingual resource with languages such as Chinese, Russian, Urdu, Indonesian, Arabic, and Bulgarian, and in some cases the Urdu subset or a large-scale multi-domain benchmark for cross-domain scenarios.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use M4 to measure two behavioral indicators, AI-generated text detection and time series forecasting, and no constructs are linked to it. The recorded measurement links are split across these two behavioral indicators: one paper reports AI-generated text detection as measured by the Urdu subset of M4, and another reports time series forecasting as measured in work on transfer learning between the M3 and M4 competitions.

Space of uses. Across the papers, M4 is positioned either as an evalu

nodes.name: M-LongDoc
nodes.definition: A benchmark of 851 samples designed to evaluate multimodal long-document understanding through open-ended question answering over real-world documents spanning hundreds of pages, with questions requiring in-depth reasoning across text, figures, and tables.

nodes.name: M-RewardBench
nodes.definition: A multilingual benchmark for evaluating reward models across 23 languages, assessing chat, safety, reasoning, and translation capabilities through human-validated preference triples.

nodes.name: MAGE
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available definition treats MAGE as a supervised fine-tuned model for AI text detection. It is described as classifying text as human or machine-generated through binary classification on linguistic features.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link MAGE to any constructs or behavioral indicators, so the available evidence does not specify broader concepts it is used to measure.

Space of uses. The available usage evidence places MAGE among other AI text detectors rather than as a standalone protocol. In Beyond Checkmate: Exploring the Creative Choke Points for AI Generated Texts, it is evaluated as part of a suite of prominent detectors alongside GPT-Zero, Radar, Binoculars, and GPT-Who.

nodes.name: MagicBrush
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe MagicBrush as a benchmark or manually annotated dataset for instruction-guided image editing, in one case specified as real image editing and in another as evaluation for image editing within an interleaved generation context. Some descriptions emphasize that its editing queries can demand a series of complex edits to an image, and one paper reports using the full test set. A smaller line of work repurposes it to form paired images with subtle differences for existence comparison.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, claims about what MagicBrush measures converge on a single behavioral indicator: papers use it to measure Image editing, often by describing evaluation of image editing capabilities on MagicBrush. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Image editing, and no constructs are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers mainly position it as an evaluation set for image editing. One paper uses it alongside EVR and MA5K when evaluating image editing capabilities, another reports an additional evaluation on the full test set, and another adapts it for comparative reasoning by constructing paired images with subtle differences.

nodes.name: MAGPIE
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the surveyed work, MAGPIE is described as a corpus of potentially idiomatic expressions labeled as figurative or literal. The definition also presents it as a resource used to test whether global affinity distinguishes figurative from literal usage.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MAGPIE to one behavioral indicator, Idiom identification, and to no constructs. The recorded use is as a measure of idiom identification, with one study stating that it adapts the dataset for the identification task.

Space of uses. The reported use treats MAGPIE as a task dataset, with one study noting that it adapts the dataset for the task and applies some filtering. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: MaliciousInstruct
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat MaliciousInstruct as a harmful benchmark or dataset of malicious instructions for testing LLM safety defenses on out-of-domain or out-of-distribution inputs. Definitions converge on that role, while varying in wording between a dataset, a benchmark, and an out-of-domain test set. Another definition states that it contains 100 broader harmful instructions and is used to assess transferability.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, MaliciousInstruct is linked to one construct, Safety, and to no behavioral indicators. The reported measurement claim converges on that single construct: papers use it to measure Safety, including as an out-of-domain test set for evaluating safety defenses and in evaluations that check whether responses lacked keywords indicating instruction rejection.

Space of uses. Papers use MaliciousInstruct alongside AdvBench, and also with HEx-PHI and AdvExtent. It is typically positioned as one of several harmful benchmarks for evaluating defense strategies, or as an OOD check for transferability. A paper also uses jailbreak attacks on MaliciousInstruct and then applies string matching to identify whether respons

nodes.name: MAMI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, MAMI is most commonly treated as a publicly available dataset or benchmark of memes for evaluation, especially around misogyny and abusive or harmful content. The prevailing description says it contains memes that are predominantly derogatory towards women, while another recurring framing presents it as a shared-task resource for multimedia automatic misogyny identification with binary and multi-label misogyny classification. Some papers describe it more broadly as a dataset of multimodal abusive memes used to benchmark detection of abusive language and imagery in social media content.

What it is claimed to measure. Across reported links, papers use MAMI to measure one behavioral indicator, Harmful content detection, and it is not linked to any construct. The recorded measured_by relation says Harmful content detection is measured by MAMI, with the dataset used for evaluation in that role. The measurement claims therefore converge on a single reported target rather than being spread across multiple constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. In use, a paper places MAMI alongside HarM and FHM as part of a set of publicly available meme datasets for

nodes.name: MAMO
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is as a benchmark for mathematical or optimization modeling. Some descriptions add that it benchmarks modeling with code solvers and focuses on linear programming problems, while others present it through EasyLP and ComplexLP, either as two optimization datasets or as subsets of varying difficulty.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MAMO to evaluate mathematical modeling, mathematical optimization modeling, or LLM performance on those tasks. No constructs or behavioral indicators are linked to it in the surveyed papers.

Space of uses. In the surveyed papers, MAMO appears as one benchmark within broader evaluation suites. It is used alongside NL4OPT, IndustryOR, OptiBench, and OptMATH-Bench in one evaluation setup, and another study includes Mamo, specifically EasyLP and ComplexLP, among real-world optimization and operation task datasets; one snippet also places it among established modeling benchmarks.

nodes.name: Mantis-Eval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, papers most commonly describe Mantis-Eval as an evaluation dataset or benchmark for multi-image reasoning. The prevailing framing is an evaluation set of high-quality, human-annotated multi-image reasoning samples: one description specifies 207 examples and mentions tasks such as size perception and weight comparison, while another highlights co-reference, reasoning, and comparison. A smaller line of work refers to it simply as Mantis and treats it as a multi-image benchmark used to assess performance on multi-image inputs.

What it is claimed to measure. In relationship claims, papers use it to measure 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The most common measured target is multi-image reasoning, and papers also report it as measuring multimodal reasoning and multi-image visual question answering. Overall, these links cluster around reasoning over multiple images rather than spreading across many different targets.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead position it as one benchmark within broader multi-image evaluation suites, most often alongside MMMU and BLINK, and sometimes with QBench, NLVR2, or MVBench. In

nodes.name: Manual error analysis
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is a human evaluation protocol in which annotators manually inspect model outputs and identify errors with predefined questions, categories, or a taxonomy. The described applications vary in scope: native English speakers assess model-generated rationales for context, word-sense, and pun pair mistakes; human annotators count errors in generated instructions across four categories; other papers annotate generated text for linguistic and non-linguistic errors, or analyze a random sample of incorrect generations.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to one construct, Linguistic quality, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The recorded measured_by relationship centers on Linguistic quality: manual annotation of outputs is used to investigate inconsistencies and linguistic quality, and no other construct links are recorded.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers use it as a manual check on generated text, sometimes positioned beyond standard metrics through fine-grained annotation, and sometimes as a reference point when another metric is reported to correlate with manua

nodes.name: MASSIVE
nodes.definition: Multilingual dataset for intent and slot detection covering 15 low-resource languages, used to evaluate zero-shot performance on unseen label schemas.

nodes.name: Massive(I)
nodes.definition: A dataset for intent discovery, aiming to identify unknown intents within user utterances.

nodes.name: MATH
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MATH is most commonly described as a benchmark of challenging high school or competition-level mathematics problems used for evaluation, often traced to AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and similar sources. Several definitions add that it contains 12,500 problems, spans subjects such as algebra, geometry, number theory, counting and probability, and related areas, and includes difficulty levels from 1 to 5; some papers also note step-by-step solutions, boxed answers, or exact string and SymPy matching for correctness. A smaller line of work uses specific forms such as the algebra subset, MATH-Algebra-Easy, a multiple-choice version, or names it as Hendrycks-MATH or Hendrycks MATH.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure a wide spread of targets, with 11 linked constructs and 4 linked behavioral indicators. The dominant convergence is on mathematical reasoning, and many papers also use it for reasoning, generalization, general ability, and mathematical problem solving. Definitions repeatedly frame it as assessing mathematical reasoning and problem solving, and some descriptions add that it spans a range of difficulty levels.

Space of uses. The preva

nodes.name: MATH-500
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats MATH-500 as a subset of the MATH benchmark that serves as a test set for evaluation. Most papers describe it as a representative and challenging selection from the MATH test set, while a smaller set of definitions describes the content more directly, as high school competition problems across subjects such as algebra and number theory with graded difficulty. Some papers also motivate using this subset when full MATH evaluation is computationally expensive.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure four constructs and two behavioral indicators. The most frequent construct links are Mathematical reasoning and Reasoning, followed by Problem-solving ability; the behavioral-indicator links are Mathematical problem solving and Long chain-of-thought generation, and papers report one additional construct link. Papers therefore report it as evaluating reasoning, mathematical reasoning, or problem-solving ability, depending on the study.

Space of uses. In practice, papers usually place MATH-500 in multi-benchmark evaluations rather than using it alone, frequently alongside GSM8K, AIME 2024, GPQA, and MMLU. Several pa

nodes.name: Math Hard
nodes.definition: A difficult mathematics benchmark used to assess complex mathematical reasoning.

nodes.name: MathBench
nodes.definition: Chinese mathematics benchmark requiring models to solve school-level math problems in Chinese, used to evaluate complex task learning.

nodes.name: MathDial
nodes.definition: MathDial, a dataset of tutoring conversations collected by human teachers interacting with simulated students, used for tutoring evaluation and preference data.

nodes.name: Mathematics Dataset
nodes.definition:
What it is. Definitions usually treat Mathematics Dataset, also referred to as Mathematics or DeepMind-Mathematics, as a dataset or benchmark of mathematical problems for evaluating mathematical reasoning. The content is described as covering diverse mathematics topics, including algebra, arithmetic, calculus, and probability, with one description also listing comparison, measurement, and numbers; another says the problems are based on a national school mathematics curriculum up to age 16. A smaller variation in description is whether papers emphasize a curriculum-based generation process, a benchmark format, or a test set of 1000 problems.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure Mathematical reasoning. The measurement claims converge on one construct rather than spread across many: it is linked to one construct, Mathematical reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. Papers use it both as an out-of-domain evaluation dataset, alongside SVAMP and SimulEq, and as part of HUMANBENCH, which contains 7 datasets from the Mathematics Dataset. Another paper describes DeepMind-Mathematics directly as a test set.

nodes.name: MathGAP
nodes.definition: MathGAP (Mathematical Generalization on Arithmetic Proofs), a synthetic evaluation framework that generates arithmetic word problems and chain-of-thought solutions with controllable proof-tree complexity for out-of-distribution testing.

nodes.name: Mathlib
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as Lean's largest community-maintained repository, Mathlib is also treated as the Lean mathematical library that serves as the formal environment for compiling and checking theorem statements and proofs. Papers use it both as a source of evaluation theorems for testing generalization, including newly added theorems in one study, and as the library against which correctness tests are run in a matching Lean and Mathlib setup.

What it is claimed to measure. In the available relationships, Mathlib is not claimed to measure any construct, and it is linked to one behavioral indicator, theorem proving.
