That connection is reported as a related link rather than a direct measurement claim, with one paper stating that most neural theorem provers based on Lean are primarily trained on Mathlib.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Across the definitions and snippets, papers use Mathlib as shared infrastructure: a repository models may have trained on, a source of evaluation theorems for generalization tests, and the formal environment used to compile, check, and run correctness tests for theorem statements and proofs.

nodes.name: MathOdyssey
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is of a math benchmark for LLM reasoning made up of problems with varying difficulty, including olympiad-level competition questions, and papers refer to it as MathOdyssey or Math Odyssey. One paper says it 'consists of problems of varying difficulties' and, in that study, uses the 148 problems belonging to olympiad-level competitions, while another places it among multiple olympiad benchmarks for evaluating olympiad-level mathematical reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure one behavioral indicator and two constructs. The named targets are Mathematical problem solving, Generalization, and Mathematical reasoning, so the reported measurement claims do not converge on a single target: a paper uses it as a held-out benchmark when assessing mathematical problem solving and generalization, and another reports it as part of competition and olympiad-level benchmarking for mathematical reasoning.

Space of uses. In use, papers position MathOdyssey as a held-out evaluation benchmark and as one of several olympiad benchmarks in comparative tables. It appears alongside Hendrycks MATH and Functional Math in h

nodes.name: MathQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MathQA is most commonly described as a math question answering benchmark or dataset of math word problems used to assess multi-step quantitative or mathematical reasoning. Definitions usually present it as multiple-choice, and one paper notes that it "contains more diverse problems in geometry, physics, probability, and algebra" and "provides 5 options to choose from for each problem." Some authors also emphasize operation-based or interpretable formalisms, while a smaller line of work, under the name MQA, describes a benchmark containing GRE and GMAT exam questions for more diverse and complex quantitative reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MathQA to 6 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Mathematical reasoning, and one paper also reports MathQA as related to Mathematical reasoning; smaller lines of work use it to measure Commonsense reasoning and Reasoning. The two recorded behavioral indicators are Mathematical problem solving and Classification, and papers also link it to 3 other constructs.

Space of uses. Papers do not link MathQA directly to another measurement instrument. In practice, they

nodes.name: MathTutorBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for measuring open-ended pedagogical capabilities of LLMs in mathematics tutoring, involving task prompts, human evaluation, and scaffolding-focused metrics.

nodes.name: MathVerse
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MathVerse is most commonly described as a multimodal or visual math benchmark for assessing mathematical reasoning with visual inputs and diagrams. Definitions variously emphasize geometry-related mathematical reasoning, quantitative reasoning, and diagram interpretation, and a description specifies 2,612 visual math problems. Papers also mention a multiple-choice evaluation setup, and some describe different presentation modes, including a Vision-Only mode where questions are presented in images; a smaller line of work refers to it as a prior static visual math benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MathVerse to measure 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claim is mathematical reasoning, including descriptions of mathematical abilities and visual mathematical reasoning, while smaller uses treat it as measuring generalization and geometric reasoning. It is also reported as measuring chain of thought, with a snippet describing "CoT evaluation and accuracy" on the benchmark, so papers spread its measurement role across several targets rather than tying it to only one.

Space of uses. In use, papers often place

nodes.name: MathVerse-mv
nodes.definition: A multi-image mathematical reasoning benchmark used for out-domain evaluation.

nodes.name: MathVision
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, MathVision is most commonly described as a visual mathematical reasoning dataset or benchmark for multimodal problem solving. Definitions present it as covering algebra, geometry, combinatorics, and logic, with evaluation by accuracy on complex multimodal problems, while another description says it involves interpreting diagrams and solving quantitative problems. One source also refers to the testmini subset of the MATH-Vision dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MathVision to 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Mathematical reasoning: papers place it among math-related benchmarks and describe such benchmarks as designed to evaluate the mathematical abilities of MLLMs. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Calibration under visual mathematical reasoning.

Space of uses. It is frequently used alongside MathVista, and in some benchmark suites also with MathVerse, DynaMath, MMStar, and CharXiv. Papers position it as one benchmark within broader visual reasoning or math-related evaluations, and one paper pairs it with MathVista specifically to evaluate calibration under visual mathematic

nodes.name: MathVista
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MathVista as a benchmark for mathematical reasoning in visual or multimodal contexts. Definitions emphasize image-based puzzles and evaluation across reasoning types, including logical, arithmetic, and geometric reasoning, and across image contexts such as natural images, line plots, and scientific figures. Some authors describe it more broadly as combining mathematical and visual understanding across 31 existing multimodal datasets and 3 newly created datasets, totaling 6141 examples, and as including both math-related reasoning and general visual question answering tasks. A smaller line of work uses particular portions of the benchmark, especially the geometry problem solving task on the testmini split.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the prevailing use is to measure mathematical reasoning. Papers link it to 8 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators; beyond mathematical reasoning, recurring links include reasoning and geometric reasoning, and the two behavioral indicators are visual question answering and chart and diagram understanding. Five other construct links are also reported, so the claims center on mathematical reaso

nodes.name: MAWPS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MAWPS is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset of math word problems, often framed as arithmetic problems in natural language or as Math Word Problem Solving. Several definitions present it as a standardized collection of arithmetic word problems, while a smaller line of work describes it as an out-of-distribution or out-of-domain benchmark repository. One paper uses the label differently, reporting the average of SingleEQ, SingleOP, AddSub, and MultiArith under the collective term MAWPS, so papers do not use the name in exactly the same way.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MAWPS to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is to measure Mathematical reasoning, with papers describing it as part of arithmetic reasoning, math reasoning, or broader mathematical reasoning evaluations; a smaller line of work also reports it as measuring In-context learning and Problem-solving ability, and the linked behavioral indicator is Mathematical problem solving. Overall, the measurement claims are concentrated on Mathematical reasoning rather than spread evenly across many targets.

Space of uses. In use, papers usually place

nodes.name: Maze
nodes.definition: A text-based navigation task in which an agent must choose moves in a maze, including partially observed and fully observed variants.

nodes.name: MBPP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, MBPP is most commonly described as a Python code-generation benchmark of short, entry-level or beginner-level problems, where a model produces code from a natural language description, textual context, or docstring and the result is checked with automated tests or unit tests. Some papers describe each item as including a task description plus reference code or a code solution, while papers variously report around 1,000 tasks, 974 problems with about three test cases each, 500 test problems, 427 tasks, 399 held-out problems, 378 problems, and sanitized subsets of 257 or 400 problems. A smaller set of papers names variants such as MBPP+, MBPP-pro, and EvalPlus versions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MBPP to 10 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure code generation and coding ability, often framed as generating short or functionally correct Python code from natural language; one paper states, "Given a textual context, the model is prompted to generate the corresponding code snippet." Smaller lines of work use it for reasoning, generalization, and algorithmic reasoning, so the recorded claims spread a

nodes.name: MBXP
nodes.definition: The MBXP benchmark is a multilingual dataset for evaluating code generation models across multiple programming languages.

nodes.name: mC4
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, mC4 is most commonly described as the multilingual Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus, or multilingual C4, a large multilingual web-crawl dataset derived from Common Crawl. Papers variously present it as multilingual pre-training data, as a benchmark spanning high-, medium-, and low-resource languages, and as a multilingual partition of CommonCrawl web scrapes; some descriptions focus on particular portions or slices, such as Arabic and English portions, selected linguistically diverse languages, or tokens used to record feature activation ranges.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, mC4 is not explicitly linked to any named construct or behavioral indicator, so it is not presented as measuring a single construct. The reported measurement uses are instead task specific: evaluating multilingual pre-training behavior, computing model perplexity across 50 languages, reporting validation loss on selected languages, and approximating entity occurrence in pre-training data.

Space of uses. The papers do not explicitly relate mC4 to other named measurement instruments. They use it as multilingual experimental data: for pre-training distillation

nodes.name: MCBench
nodes.definition: Metric Calculating Benchmark, a code-verifiable evaluation suite that tests LLMs on their ability to follow complex step-by-step rubrics for computing string-matching NLP metrics, with objective assessment via parallel reference code.

nodes.name: MD-Judge
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available papers, MD-Judge is treated as an automated, LLM-based evaluation procedure for safety judgments. The descriptions converge on its role as an evaluator or classifier, but differ in scope: one paper describes it as assessing whether generated responses appropriately handle fairness and privacy concerns in terms of safety and appropriateness, while another describes it more generally as evaluating the safety of instruction-response pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MD-Judge to one construct and to no behavioral indicators. The only recorded measurement claim is that it measures Privacy awareness: one paper reports using it to assess generated responses regarding Qf and Qp, so the measurement claims here are concentrated on that single construct rather than spread across multiple linked outcomes.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it here. Papers instead position MD-Judge as the evaluator itself, either by directly employing it to assess model outputs, as in The Tug of War Within: Mitigating the Fairness-Privacy Conflicts in Large Language Models, or by describing it as an evaluation procedure built around an

nodes.name: Mean Opinion Score
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, Mean Opinion Score is most commonly treated as a subjective human rating protocol on a 1 to 5, 5-point, or Likert-like scale. The prevailing usage is in speech and audio, where listeners rate synthesized speech or generated responses for naturalness or overall quality, while a smaller usage applies the same format to text, where raters judge quality and diversity.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MOS to rate a range of output qualities rather than tying it to one named target. The recurring claims are that it gauges naturalness and quality in synthesized speech or generated audio, and quality and diversity in text, with some definitions further describing perceived fluency and coherence; however, papers do not explicitly link it to any construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Papers typically position MOS as a subjective human evaluation step. In the audio-focused work, it is described as a commonly used crowd-sourced listening test, including collection through Amazon Mechanical Turk, and one paper reports using MOS alongside a separate prosody mean opinion score, P-MOS, when evaluating prosody and naturalness; in the t

nodes.name: MEBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark comprising 4,780 question-answer pairs designed to evaluate LLMs and RAG systems on cross-document, multi-entity question answering across comparative, statistical, and relational reasoning tasks.

nodes.name: Medbullets
nodes.definition: A question answering dataset based on online medical questions.

nodes.name: MEDFACT
nodes.definition: A large-scale Chinese dataset for evidence-based medical fact-checking of LLM-generated claims, containing 1,321 questions and 7,409 claim-evidence pairs with veracity labels across five categories: Supported, Partially Supported, Refuted, Uncertain, and Not Applicable.

nodes.name: MedHallu
nodes.definition: A benchmark of 10,000 medical question-answer pairs with systematically generated hallucinated answers, stratified by difficulty (easy, medium, hard) and hallucination type, used to evaluate medical hallucination detection in LLMs.

nodes.name: Media Frames Corpus
nodes.definition: A dataset of news articles annotated for policy frames such as 'Economic' or 'Morality', used to evaluate alignment with human-constructed framing schemes.

nodes.name: MediaSum
nodes.definition: A summarization dataset used as part of the faithfulness evaluation setup for intrinsic and extrinsic refinement experiments.

nodes.name: Medley-solos-DB
nodes.definition: A benchmark for instrument-related audio classification.

nodes.name: MedMCQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MedMCQA is most commonly treated as a large-scale, multi-subject medical multiple-choice question answering benchmark or dataset. Definitions consistently place it in the medical domain and often specify that it is built from Indian medical entrance examinations, especially AIIMS and NEET or NEET PG, while one paper further describes it as a 4-way multiple-choice dataset. Some descriptions are more generic, referring to it simply as a domain-specific or knowledge-intensive medical QA benchmark, and one paper notes that it provides plain-text explanations for QA tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MedMCQA to 2 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure question answering and medical knowledge: several papers use it to assess question-answering performance in specialized or knowledge-intensive settings, and several others report it as evaluating medical knowledge, including clinical domain knowledge or preliminary knowledge grasp. Additional papers use it to measure medical question answering and multiple-choice question answering, while single papers report it as measuring chain of thought and calibration th

nodes.name: MedQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, MedQA is most commonly treated as a medical multiple-choice question answering benchmark built from United States Medical Licensing Examination questions, often described as professional medical board exam content used to evaluate model knowledge and reasoning in medicine. Some definitions add that it consists of USMLE-style questions curated by medical examination experts from various medical question banks (Rationale-Guided Retrieval Augmented Generation for Medical Question Answering), while a smaller line describes it as a standard single-turn benchmark with patient records followed by exam-style multiple-choice questions. Papers also use variant names such as MedQA-USMLE and MedQA-US: MedQA-USMLE is described as sourced from the National Board of Medical Examiners or from USMLE preparatory tests, and one paper notes that MedQA also included questions from Medbullets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MedQA to measure 5 constructs and 6 behavioral indicators. The prevailing construct-level framing is medical knowledge, and papers also use it to measure medical reasoning, domain knowledge, reasoning, and zero-shot generalization;

nodes.name: MedQuAD
nodes.definition: A question-answering benchmark with long free-form answers used to evaluate uncertainty methods.

nodes.name: MeetingBank
nodes.definition: A dataset for summarization tasks, specifically from meeting transcripts, used for both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation of model refinement.

nodes.name: MELD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MELD is most commonly described as a multimodal dataset of TV show dialogues annotated for emotion and sentiment, used for evaluating emotion recognition in conversational speech. Some descriptions are more specific, calling it a multimodal multi-party Speech Emotion Recognition dataset from the TV series Friends with over 1,400 dialogues and 13,000 utterances, annotated with seven emotion labels and sentiment, while another paper reports assessing emotion recognition on 2,608 utterances.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MELD to measure two behavioral indicators, Emotion analysis and Speech emotion recognition, and two constructs, Emotion understanding and Utility preservation. The prevailing usage is emotion-focused: papers describe it as an emotion recognition or emotion classification benchmark, and one paper interprets MELD results as showing "strong emotion perception and contextual understanding"; the links therefore center on emotion-related outcomes, though a smaller line of work also uses it in general utility evaluation.

Space of uses. In the papers here, MELD is positioned as an evaluation benchmark and is used alongside other be

nodes.name: Membership inference attack
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats membership inference attack as an evaluation or auditing procedure for asking whether a specific example was used in a model's training, alignment, or unlearning setting, usually by distinguishing member from non-member examples from model behavior. Some authors narrow this to black-box settings that rely only on output texts or output behavior, without logits or token probabilities, while others describe loss-based variants and heuristics such as loss, perplexity, lowercase probability, zlib compression, and Min-k% probability. A smaller line of work extends the framing from single examples to document-level attacks or to suspect datasets, defining it as detecting whether a suspect dataset was used in training.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use this procedure to measure 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The most common measurement claims are privacy-focused: papers report that privacy leakage and privacy preservation are measured by membership inference attacks, and one paper describes them as established practice for quantifying privacy. Other papers use them to measure forget quality and knowledge memorizati

nodes.name: MemeReaCon
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating contextual meme understanding in vision-language models, consisting of 1,565 annotated Reddit posts with meme images, post text, and top comments, assessed across four tasks probing interplay, stance, connections, and intent.

nodes.name: Mercury
nodes.definition: Code generation evaluation used as a validation set for tuning hyperparameters in code-related tasks.

nodes.name: MERLIN
nodes.definition: A benchmark focused on entity recognition in multilingual multimodal settings, evaluating the model's ability to identify culturally relevant entities from image-text pairs.

nodes.name: Meta-World
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats Meta-World as a MuJoCo-based robotic manipulation benchmark, often also framed as a multi-task and meta-reinforcement-learning benchmark. Papers describe an agent controlling a Sawyer robot to manipulate objects such as doors, drawers, and windows, or more generally manipulating an object to achieve a given goal, and they use the benchmark to evaluate generalization across robot manipulation tasks. Some papers refer to specific subsets or settings, including ML10, ML45, MT10, MT50, the ML-45 version with 45 tasks, and a setup with 10 different robot manipulation goals.

What it is claimed to measure. Where papers make explicit measurement claims, they use Meta-World to measure one behavioral indicator, Robotic manipulation, and they do not connect it to any constructs. The reported use is concentrated rather than spread across many targets: relationship evidence describes Meta-World as a robotic manipulation benchmark suite and as a tabletop manipulation benchmark, so the measurement claim converges on robotic manipulation.

Space of uses. Papers position Meta-World mainly as an evaluation or verification benchmark for rob

nodes.name: MetaICL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, MetaICL is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset or evaluation framework for in-context learning. Definitions repeatedly describe it as covering 142 NLP tasks, with papers variously emphasizing meta-training and meta-testing partitions, seven partitions, or task types such as text classification, question answering, natural language inference, and paraphrase detection. A smaller line of description focuses on a high-to-low resources setting with 61 training tasks and 26 unseen test tasks, where evaluation uses multiple-choice accuracy.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the reported relationships, papers link MetaICL to one construct, In-context learning, and to no behavioral indicators. The claims converge on that single construct rather than spreading across many: papers describe MetaICL as "designed for in-context learning scenarios," use it for "short finetuning and evaluation," and report results as a "MetaICL in-context learning evaluation."

Space of uses. Papers use MetaICL as an evaluation benchmark to validate methods, and some follow its short-finetuning-and-evaluation setup. One paper reports average accuracy across 2

nodes.name: MetaQA
nodes.definition: Multi-hop KBQA dataset requiring reasoning over multiple relations in a knowledge base, available in 1-hop, 2-hop, and 3-hop variants.

nodes.name: MetaTool
nodes.definition: A dataset used to evaluate an LLM's ability to select the correct tool for a given task, assessing a key component of agent-oriented capabilities.

nodes.name: MFCAQ
nodes.definition: The Moral Foundations Character Action Questionnaire, a 16-item instrument designed to assess the moral dimensions of a fictional character's behavior based on Moral Foundations Theory, using a 5-point Likert scale.

nodes.name: MFQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MFQ is described as the original Moral Foundations Questionnaire, a psychometric or psychological survey designed for humans. One definition says it measures how individuals evaluate abstract moral scenarios in relation to their own values, while another describes it as a survey that has been used to analyze which morals are most expressed in language model outputs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MFQ mainly in terms of moral evaluation and moral expression: one definition frames it as measuring evaluations of abstract moral scenarios relative to personal values, and another says it has been used to analyze which morals are most expressed in model outputs. The papers do not explicitly link it to any construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. The usage described in the papers treats MFQ as a human psychological survey that is brought into LLM analysis. The papers do not report it being used alongside any other named measurement instrument.

nodes.name: MFRC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MFRC is described as the Moral Foundations Reddit Corpus, a dataset of 16,123 English Reddit posts from 12 subreddits, categorized into US politics, French politics, and everyday moral life. Another description presents it as a multi-label moral foundation corpus covering six moral foundations, with three annotators assigned to each sample, so the prevailing usage combines a Reddit post collection with a multi-label annotation setup.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MFRC to measure one behavioral indicator, Moral foundation classification, and no constructs are linked to it. The measurement claim converges on that single use: papers describe MFRC as a corpus of six moral foundations and, in one definition, as an evaluation resource for subjective multi-label classification and distribution alignment.

Space of uses. Papers do not link MFRC to any other measurement instrument. The available descriptions present it as a Reddit-based, multi-label corpus, and one description notes that each sample received three annotators.

nodes.name: MFTC
nodes.definition: The Moral Foundations Twitter Corpus, a dataset of 32,218 tweets annotated for moral dimensions across sociopolitical and cultural contexts including Black Lives Matter and the 2016 US presidential election.

nodes.name: MGSM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, MGSM is most commonly described as a multilingual grade-school math benchmark or dataset of word problems, used to evaluate mathematical or arithmetic reasoning across languages. Several papers further describe it as extending or translating GSM8K into multiple languages, but the reported coverage differs: some definitions mention 10 languages, others 11 languages, and another refers to nine non-English languages; one relationship statement specifies 250 manually translated GSM8K test problems, and another paper describes 250 QA pairs. A smaller line of work treats it as the source for AfriMGSM, while other papers mention related resources such as MGSM-SYMBOLIC and MGSM8KInstruct, and one definition says evaluation is done with exact match.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MGSM to measure five constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is to measure Mathematical reasoning, and papers also report using it for Multilingual reasoning, Reasoning, Generalization, and the behavioral indicator Mathematical problem solving, plus one other construct. Overall, the linked claims concentrate on reasoning-oriented constructs rat

nodes.name: MHellaSwag
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe MHellaSwag, also referred to as MHELLASWAG or Okapi-HellaSwag, as a multilingual commonsense reasoning benchmark. The prevailing description presents it as sentences or paragraphs where models must choose the most likely continuation or ending, and one paper says it "aims at collecting the multilingual understanding abilities" (P-MMEval: A Parallel Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Consistent Evaluation of LLMs). Another definition uses slightly different wording, framing Okapi-HellaSwag as evaluating event prediction and situational understanding.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, claims converge on one linked construct: multilingual ability. Papers report it as measuring multilingual ability in evaluations of models' capability across languages, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers position it as one benchmark within broader multilingual evaluation efforts rather than alongside any named companion instrument. One paper groups it with multilingual benchmarks that rely on English translation for cross-language evaluation, and no other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: MileBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models on tasks involving multiple images, categorized into temporal, semantic, needle-in-a-haystack, and image retrieval tasks.

nodes.name: MIMIC-CXR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats MIMIC-CXR as a chest X-ray or chest radiograph dataset paired with free-text radiology reports, mainly for report generation and grounded report evaluation. Several definitions add that the studies are de-identified and publicly available, and some describe each study as accompanied by labels as well as a report. A smaller line of work refers to processed or subset versions, and one paper points to a VQA variant, MIMIC-CXR-VQA, for chest-radiograph question answering.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MIMIC-CXR to 3 behavioral indicators, and to no constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure medical report generation, with additional use for radiology report generation, while a smaller line of work uses it to measure medical visual question answering. These links are all to behavioral indicators, especially report generation tasks, not to any construct.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it directly, but papers commonly use MIMIC-CXR alongside IU-Xray, and sometimes alongside CT-RATE, CheXpert Plus, Harvard-FairVLMed, or PMC-OA. Snippets describe it as used for both training and evalu

nodes.name: MIMIC-III
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, MIMIC-III is most commonly described as a large, publicly available, de-identified in-patient or critical-care EHR dataset from the MIMIC project. Most descriptions emphasize health data from patients who stayed in critical care units, while some specify the materials used in a study, including discharge summaries, medical notes and time-series lab tests, or radiology reports for summarization. As one study puts it, it "comprises de-identified Electronic Health Records of patients who were admitted to the ICU ... from 2001 to 2012" (Knowledge-Empowered Dynamic Graph Network for Irregularly Sampled Medical Time Series).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MIMIC-III to 1 construct and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing uses are to measure medical diagnosis and mortality prediction, with papers evaluating diagnosis-related methods on MIMIC-III and one study explicitly focusing on "the binary in-hospital mortality prediction task" to assess classification performance. Smaller lines of work report it as measuring hospital readmission prediction and length of stay prediction, and one paper uses it to measure privacy preservation through

nodes.name: MIMIC-IV
nodes.definition:
What it is. A common description in the papers is a large-scale multimodal clinical dataset, and one definition specifically says it is used to evaluate multimodal fusion strategies for patient outcome prediction. Some papers also frame it as a public or real-world EHR dataset and mention 28,900 EHRs. The named tasks include length of stay and 48-hour in-hospital mortality, and one paper says its records are converted into test samples for a full-path clinical diagnosis task.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MIMIC-IV to measure 4 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The behavioral uses are medical diagnosis, mortality prediction, hospital readmission prediction, and length of stay prediction, while the only construct link is multimodal integration. Overall, the reported uses spread across several clinical prediction tasks rather than concentrating on a single behavioral outcome.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In use, papers mostly position MIMIC-IV as an evaluation dataset for EHR methods, and papers also use it alongside MIMIC-III to verify the effectiveness of compared methods or to evaluate prediction and diagnosis systems across mortality

nodes.name: MIMIR
nodes.definition: A challenging benchmark for pretraining data detection that contains "seen" and "unseen" text samples from the Pile dataset, specifically constructed to have high n-gram overlap between classes.

nodes.name: MIND
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MIND as a hallucination detection method whose distinctive feature is automatic label creation during detection, rather than reliance on pre-annotated data. One definition presents it as classification-based, while another describes it as unsupervised; the more detailed account says it truncates Wikipedia articles, prompts an LLM to continue the next sentence, and generates truth labels by matching named entities between the response and the original succeeding sentence.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded links, papers do not specify MIND as measuring any behavioral indicator, and they link it to one construct only, Generalization, through a related claim rather than a measured_by claim. The definitions frame it as a hallucination detection method, but the explicit network links are concentrated on that single construct rather than spread across many named constructs.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to MIND. In the usage descriptions, papers position it as an alternative to approaches that rely on pre-annotated datasets, and one comparison states that unlike SAPLMA, MIND labels data during the detection proc

nodes.name: Mind2Web
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat Mind2Web as a real-world web navigation benchmark or dataset for agents following language instructions on real websites. Definitions commonly describe human demonstrations or action-annotated tasks, often citing about 2K instructions from 137 websites, and they emphasize cross-task, cross-website, and cross-domain generalization, with one description presenting these as three test categories. The prevailing framing is an offline evaluation setting, though some papers narrow it to action prediction or multi-step planning, and one paper recasts each task as a dynamic how-to question with multiple possible outcomes per step. Papers commonly mention step success rate and element accuracy, while some also include action F1, task-level success rate, or step accuracy.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, Mind2Web is linked to 4 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure web navigation, with papers using it to evaluate agents performing complex instructions on real-world websites, and a smaller recurring line uses it to measure action prediction, especially generalization across tasks, websites, and domains. Papers al

nodes.name: Minecraft
nodes.definition: A 3D open-world video game environment used as a platform for evaluating generally capable agents on tasks involving resource gathering, crafting, and exploration.

nodes.name: MineDojo
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is a Minecraft-based simulation suite and benchmark for open-ended embodied agents, with thousands of natural language-specified or language-prompted tasks. Definitions consistently place those tasks in navigation, harvesting, combat, and crafting, and a smaller framing also describes MineDojo as a research framework for embodied-agent research.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MineDojo to measure two constructs, Generalization and Long-horizon planning, and one behavioral indicator, Navigation. These measurement claims are spread across both constructs rather than centered on one: MineDojo is reported as measuring Generalization and Long-horizon planning, while its task set is also used to measure Navigation.

Space of uses. Papers mainly position MineDojo as a validation environment for embodied-agent methods. One study validates in both MineDojo and Mineflayer environments, while another selects certain long-horizon tasks from MineDojo to test its approach; papers do not otherwise link it to another measurement instrument.

nodes.name: Minerva Math
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, papers attach the Minerva Math label and closely neighboring names, including Minerva, MinervaMATH, OCW, OCWCourses, and OCW-Math, to two recurring benchmark descriptions. One common framing presents a mathematical reasoning benchmark for scientific and mathematical questions, including undergraduate- or Olympiad-level problems that require advanced quantitative reasoning. Another common framing describes an OpenCourseWare-based benchmark with 272 undergraduate STEM problems with automatically verifiable solutions, spanning areas such as chemistry, information theory, differential equations, and special relativity, and often characterized as requiring multi-step reasoning or serving as an out-of-domain benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is to measure Mathematical reasoning, with many papers listing it among mathematical-reasoning benchmarks or mathematical reasoning datasets; a smaller line of work uses it to measure the broader construct Reasoning, and another reports it as evaluating Mathematical problem solving. Overall, the reported measurement claims are concen

nodes.name: miniF2F
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, miniF2F is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for formal theorem proving, often for neural theorem proving, used to evaluate whether models can generate proofs verifiable by a theorem prover. Definitions usually portray it as formal mathematical problems or statements drawn from competition mathematics, often high-school or Olympiad-level; several descriptions give 488 items split into 244 validation and 244 test problems, and some say it spans multiple formal systems or four formal languages. Papers also mention a miniF2F-test variant for Lean-based evaluation, while a smaller line of work describes it as standalone competition problems that do not require external context, and one description extends it to Olympiad and undergraduate-style coursework.

What it is claimed to measure. Across surveyed uses, papers use miniF2F to measure 4 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The most frequently linked behavioral indicators are Formal theorem proving, Theorem proving, and Autoformalization, and the most frequently linked constructs are Mathematical reasoning, Generalization, Autoformalization ability, and Formal reasoning. The measurement c

nodes.name: Minimal-pair ABX task
nodes.definition: A training-free, zero-shot evaluation framework where a model must determine if a test item X is representationally closer to item A or item B, used to measure the structure of embedding spaces.

nodes.name: MiniWoB++
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions treat MiniWoB++ as a simulated or interactive web benchmark for computer control or web navigation, with diverse tasks that simulate human-computer interaction through natural-language instructions and browser actions. Several descriptions emphasize simplified or minimalist web pages and low-level tasks, while others specify 56 simulated tasks, 125 minimalist web interfaces, or keyboard and mouse interaction; one paper also calls it "a standard task suite." A smaller line of work, using the name MiniWob, describes it differently, as 2000 open-ended tasks from 137 real web environments and as a multimodal benchmark requiring multi-step actions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 1 construct and 3 behavioral indicators. The named targets are GUI automation, task completion, and web navigation, plus the construct adaptability, so the measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on a single construct. In the relationship language, one paper reports task completion through success rates on MiniWoB++, another uses MiniWob to validate adaptability, another treats it as measuring GUI automation through tasks wi

nodes.name: MinosEval
nodes.definition: Framework for evaluating medical question answering, including Top-1 Hit Rate (GPT-4o ranking) and Average NLI Score using a ClinicalBERT model on MedNLI.

nodes.name: MINT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MINT as a multi-turn interactive agent evaluation framework or benchmark that adapts existing datasets into interactive, feedback-rich environments. The prevailing description centers on evaluating task-solving through multi-turn interaction, especially by using tools and leveraging natural language feedback; definitions also mention agent capabilities such as tool use and self-debugging, and a curated subset of reasoning, code generation, and decision-making tasks with GPT-4-simulated feedback. Some uses refer to a part of the MINT dataset focused on tool-utilization for reasoning, another use only considers coding and math problems, and related work also refers to it as Mint-Bench.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what MINT measures are concentrated rather than spread across many targets. It is linked to 1 construct, Responsiveness to human feedback, and 1 behavioral indicator, Multi-turn interaction: papers use it to measure responsiveness to human feedback through "leveraging natural language feedback," and to measure multi-turn interaction. More generally, papers describe it as evaluating performance or task-solving ability

nodes.name: MIntRec2.0
nodes.definition: Large-scale multimodal intent recognition dataset with 30 fine-grained intent labels across text, video, and audio modalities, used to evaluate performance in complex semantic understanding scenarios.

nodes.name: MIRACL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed definitions, MIRACL is most commonly described as the Multilingual Information Retrieval Across a Continuum of Languages dataset for multilingual retrieval evaluation. Papers describe it as covering 18 languages, with native questions and relevance judgements of retrieved passages; another formulation presents it more generally as a dataset for evaluating retrieval systems across 18 diverse languages.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MIRACL to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The construct link is Multilingual ability, with MIRACL used to assess multilingual retrieval capability; a separate reported link treats it as measuring Synthetic recall, citing MIRACL among multilingual and cross-lingual IR resources.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to other measurement instruments. In use, MIRACL is positioned both as a main evaluation dataset used alongside BEIR for retrieval assessment, and as a base resource that another benchmark builds on top of, reusing its native-language questions while generating responses with diverse large language models.

nodes.name: MixEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a hybrid benchmark for language models built by mixing existing ground-truth tasks. Definitions consistently say it combines 18 ground-truth-based tasks across a diverse mix of tasks and domains, and one paper says it was created by matching real-world user queries mined from the web with similar queries from a pool of existing ground-truth benchmarks. Another source characterizes it as "a hybrid of 18 ground-truth-based tasks" with a 0.96 correlation to human preferences.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MixEval to measure six constructs and one behavioral indicator, and these links are spread across multiple targets rather than centered on one. The named construct links include Alignment, Conversational ability, General ability, and Instruction following ability, alongside two other constructs, and it is also reported as measuring Classification as a behavioral indicator. In the relationship evidence, authors describe it as evaluating "general capabilities," "alignment effectiveness," and "generalist chat capabilities," while another paper says it "contains downstream tasks" when used for safety robustness.

Space

nodes.name: MixEval-Hard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, MixEval-Hard is most commonly treated as the hard subset of MixEval. Papers describe it as a challenging or more challenging subset for difficult tasks or queries, and one definition says it was derived to better differentiate strong language models; a smaller formulation presents it more generally as a benchmark for challenging general-domain tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MixEval-Hard to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators. The only linked construct is Reasoning: one paper uses MixEval-Hard among datasets spanning instruction-following, reasoning, mathematics, and coding, so in the recorded relationships it is reported as measuring reasoning rather than a wider spread of constructs.

Space of uses. The available uses place it within broader evaluation suites. Papers use it alongside several other benchmarks, for example MT-Bench, AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena Hard Auto, and MixEval, and another paper treats it as one of several general-domain tasks. One paper also reports that this harder subset shows a higher correlation of 0.96 with Chatbot Arena Elo.

nodes.name: MKQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MKQA as a multilingual or cross-lingual question-answering benchmark or dataset. Definitions vary slightly: some present it as a multilingual open-domain benchmark derived from Natural Questions, some as a multilingual open-ended benchmark for assessing retrieval-augmented answering, and another treats it as a knowledge retrieval dataset for interpretability analysis. One study further characterizes it as a multilingual knowledge QA task with 10k question-answer pairs aligned across 26 languages, and some papers place it among benchmarks built by translating or aligning parallel questions across languages.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the prevailing use is to measure multilingual question answering. It is linked to 2 behavioral indicators and 1 construct overall, most often multilingual question answering, with smaller usages as a measure of knowledge retrieval and as measuring cross-lingual alignment capability. The reported measurement claims are concentrated on question answering rather than spread across many different targets.

Space of uses. Papers frequently use MKQA alongside other multilingual QA benchmarks, espec

nodes.name: MLaKE
nodes.definition: MLaKE is a multilingual dataset created using LLMs for translation.

nodes.name: MLDR
nodes.definition: Long-context information retrieval benchmark consisting of over 200,000 long documents, used to evaluate single- and multi-vector retrieval performance in out-of-domain and in-domain settings.

nodes.name: MLogiQA
nodes.definition: Multilingual logical reasoning benchmark derived from LOGIQA, assessing the ability to make logical inferences from complex texts.

nodes.name: MLQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MLQA as a multilingual question answering dataset or benchmark with extractive question-answer instances in SQuAD format across seven languages. One recurring description says it contains over 5K instances in English, Arabic, German, Spanish, Hindi, Vietnamese, and Simplified Chinese, and another emphasizes its aligned structure, with each question-answer pair present in multiple languages. Smaller descriptions frame it more functionally, as a benchmark for cross-lingual reading comprehension, answer extraction, or comprehension skills across seven languages, and one study uses it as the source for the MLNeedle test.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, MLQA is linked to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure multilingual question answering: several papers describe it as facilitating cross-lingual evaluation of QA systems or as representing multilingual open-ended question-answering tasks, and one definition says it evaluates extractive question answering capabilities in multiple languages. Smaller usage treats it as measuring question answering more generally, or natural language understan

nodes.name: MLVU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, MLVU is most commonly described as a long-video understanding benchmark for evaluating performance on long-form video tasks. The prevailing descriptions frame it as multi-task or question-answering oriented, with multiple-choice accuracy used in some papers; several definitions specify videos ranging from 3 minutes to 2 hours, one adds a test set of over 500 QA pairs, and another reports an average video duration of 15.5 minutes. A smaller set of papers describes it more broadly as a multimodal long-video benchmark for extended temporal reasoning, complex scene dynamics, or long-context comprehension.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MLVU to measure five constructs and two behavioral indicators. The most common reported target is video understanding, and papers also use it to measure long video understanding, long-context understanding, multimodal understanding, and temporal reasoning; among behavioral indicators, it is linked to video question answering and, more narrowly, counting. Overall, the reported measurement claims spread across several closely related long-video and question-answering targets rather than converging on a sing

nodes.name: MM-ID
nodes.definition: A benchmark designed to evaluate a model's ability to remember and recognize instance identities across four tasks: matching, location, question-answering, and captioning.

nodes.name: MM-NIAH
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MM-NIAH is described as a benchmark for long multimodal or mixed-modality haystacks in which needles of information are embedded and the model must locate or comprehend them. One framing presents it as a mixed video-text retrieval benchmark, with text segments inserted across different frames in long-video inputs, 25% of the input made up of these inserted text segments, and input lengths reaching 4.5k frames, or about 1.1M tokens. Another framing presents it as a benchmark for long multimodal documents of interleaved text and images, with retrieval, counting, and reasoning tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, MM-NIAH is linked as measuring 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The constructs are long-context multimodal understanding, long-context understanding, and multimodal reasoning, and the behavioral indicator is synthetic recall. In the papers' own terms, it is used to systematically evaluate comprehension of long multimodal documents, through retrieval, counting, and reasoning tasks, and to detect image or text needles within hybrid long contexts.

Space of uses. Papers position MM-NIAH both as a benchmark introduced for mixed-

nodes.name: MM-SafetyBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MM-SafetyBench as a multimodal safety benchmark for testing whether vision-language models produce unsafe responses to harmful inputs and for assessing safety in vision-language settings. More specific descriptions present it as a benchmark with 5,040 text-image pairs across 13 scenarios for multimodal jailbreak attacks, or as a dataset of typographical images, stable diffusion-generated images, Typo + SD images, and text-based attack samples. Other papers frame it as a safety-critical evaluation framework against image-based manipulations and visual prompt attacks. Papers also mention an official tiny version with 168 samples, and one paper abbreviates it as MMSafe.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, MM-SafetyBench is linked as a measurement instrument to three constructs, Safety, Safety alignment, and Safety robustness, and to three behavioral indicators, Harmful content detection, Harmful content generation, and Jailbreak resistance. Papers use it to judge resiliency when models are prompted with harm-inducing instructions, to calculate average attack success rate following MM-SafetyBench, and to evaluate defense capabilities

nodes.name: MM-Vet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing treats MM-Vet as a multimodal evaluation benchmark for the integrated capabilities of large multimodal models, often described as covering visual reasoning and understanding across diverse scenarios. Several definitions make this concrete as an open-ended or free-form benchmark, sometimes described as an in-the-wild, zero-shot setting, and one paper states that it contains 217 challenging open-ended tasks requiring detailed perception, cross-modal reasoning, and world knowledge. Papers also describe it through recurring core capabilities, with recognition, OCR, knowledge, spatial awareness, language generation, and math repeatedly named, while some narrower descriptions cast it as a visual question answering benchmark or as an evaluation of visual conversations judged with GPT-4.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MM-Vet to measure a broad spread of outcomes rather than a single construct: it is linked to 9 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is for visual understanding, followed by multimodal understanding, reasoning, spatial understanding, and fine-grained visual understanding, while other papers also

nodes.name: MMAU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MMAU as a benchmark for expert-level audio reasoning, with sound and music subsets rather than a basic classification setup. The available definitions portray it as the Massive Multi-Task Audio Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark, aimed at complex understanding beyond basic classification, and they note that it includes information extraction and reasoning questions. One survey also places it among benchmarks for auditory expertise and musical understanding, including melodic structure, harmony, instrument identification, and contextual music interpretation.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the measurement claims are spread across six constructs and three behavioral indicators rather than converging on a single target. MMAU is reported as measuring audio perception, audio reasoning, domain knowledge, knowledge retrieval, and tool use, with four other linked targets also recorded. The recorded descriptions frame these uses in terms such as evaluating "expert-level multimodal reasoning and knowledge-retrieval capabilities" and emphasizing "advanced perception and reasoning with domain-specific knowledge."

Space of uses. No ot

nodes.name: MMBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats MMBench as a comprehensive, all-around multimodal benchmark for large vision-language models, used for complex vision-language tasks spanning perception, knowledge, commonsense, and reasoning. A common concrete description is a multiple-choice visual question answering benchmark with diverse question types and topics, while a smaller line of work frames it more specifically as a general VQA or instruction-following evaluation. Several papers also refer to English and Chinese variants, a Chinese version, or a dev split.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMBench to measure 17 constructs and 6 behavioral indicators, so the claims about what it evaluates are broad rather than centered on a single target. The dominant construct links are visual understanding and multimodal understanding, followed by fine-grained visual understanding and general ability, with many additional constructs also linked. Among behavioral indicators, visual question answering is the most common use, while the remaining indicators appear in smaller lines of work.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it, but papers often use MMBench

nodes.name: MMBench-CN
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat MMBench-CN, also written as MMBench-Chinese, MMBCN, or MMB-CN, as the Chinese version of the MMBench benchmark for evaluating multimodal models. Some descriptions narrow this to answer robustness under shuffled multiple-choice answers, while others frame it more broadly as evaluating multimodal tasks, multimodal understanding and generation in a Chinese-language context, or vision-language capabilities in a non-English setting. A smaller usage presents it as a standard evaluation for single-image QA performance, and one paper refers specifically to the MMBCN dev split.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MMBench-CN to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The construct claims are split across Multimodal understanding and Robustness: one paper says MMBench and its CN version evaluate a model's answer robustness with all-round shuffling on multiple-choice answers, while another uses MMBCN for comprehensive evaluation of multimodal understanding. The behavioral-indicator claim is narrower, with one paper placing MMB-CN among conventional visual question answering and single-image QA tasks.

Space of uses. Papers typically use MMBench-

nodes.name: MMBench-Video
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat MMBench-Video as a video-focused version of MMBench for evaluating multimodal understanding. A more detailed framing presents it as a quantitative benchmark built from long-form, multi-shot web videos and human-annotated, free-form questions, intended to evaluate LVLMs' video understanding capabilities across a hierarchical taxonomy. Papers also describe the videos as long-form and diverse, covering a broad spectrum of topics.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMBench-Video to measure 6 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than concentrated on one. The most frequently named construct links are Commonsense reasoning, Long video understanding, Spatial understanding, Temporal reasoning, and Temporal understanding; papers also connect it to 1 other construct and 2 behavioral indicators. In the relationship evidence, it is described as probing models through human-annotated ability taxonomies and free-form questions.

Space of uses. Across the available papers, MMBench-Video is positioned as a benchmark for evaluating LVLMs on longer, multi-shot video tasks, and as a

nodes.name: MMC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MMC as a benchmark for evaluating chart understanding, with charts drawn from diverse sources. Another definition frames it as a recent benchmark for multimodal chart understanding and notes that some questions require external domain-specific knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MMC to one behavioral indicator and to no constructs. The recorded measurement claim centers on Chart and diagram understanding, with one paper explicitly labeling MMC as chart understanding.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is formally linked to MMC. In practice, papers use or discuss it alongside other multimodal and chart benchmarks: one paper includes it in a broader benchmark suite and contrasts it with MMMU and MathVista by noting that those include mathematical figures, whereas MMC contains charts from diverse sources, and another discusses it alongside ChartBench and ChartX3 as a recent chart-understanding benchmark.

Concerns raised. Concerns appear in one paper, which says that some MMC questions require external domain-specific knowledge. The same paper also groups MMC with benchmarks that have issues with the source or diversi

nodes.name: MMCU-Medical
nodes.definition: Multi-task medical dataset used to evaluate LLM performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning.

nodes.name: MME
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, MME is most commonly described as a comprehensive multimodal or vision-language benchmark for large multimodal language models. Definitions consistently frame it around perception and cognition, with papers sometimes reporting separate MME-Perception and MME-Cognition scores, or an aggregate MME*, and task descriptions that include OCR, color, counting, scene understanding, and commonsense reasoning. Smaller variations describe it as using single-image instructions, as open-ended yes/no or true/false questions, as human-annotated, or as including a hallucination subset for existence, count, position, and color.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MME to measure 15 constructs and 6 behavioral indicators, so its measurement claims are spread across many targets rather than centered on one alone. The prevailing construct-level uses are visual understanding, multimodal understanding, and visual perception, while the most recurrent behavioral-indicator uses are visual question answering and hallucination. Papers also link it to many other constructs and several other behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. Papers frequently use MME inside broa

nodes.name: MME-P
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe MME-P as a multimodal benchmark for visual understanding, with one definition specifying OCR and fine-grained visual reasoning as prominent task types. A second description treats MME Perception as a sub-benchmark of the MME suite for evaluating visual perception capabilities, and one paper explicitly inspects OCR-related tasks within MME-P.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the reported relationships, papers use it to measure Visual understanding, and this is the only construct linked to it. No behavioral indicators are linked to it, so the reported measurement claims concentrate on a single construct rather than spreading across multiple outcomes.

Space of uses. No other measurement instruments are linked to it. In use, one paper includes MME Perception among several mainstream benchmarks in a broader evaluation suite, while another reports an overall MME-P score under visual understanding benchmarking and then examines OCR-related tasks within the benchmark.

nodes.name: MME-RealWorld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MME-RealWorld as a manually curated or manually annotated multimodal benchmark for real-world scenarios, used to assess vision-language performance across categories such as monitoring, autonomous driving, OCR, property, and text or address tasks. Descriptions converge on five primary categories or real-world domains and 43 subtasks, and one paper adds an average resolution of 2000x1500. Another recorded use specifies a multiple-choice format with four manually constructed answer options, and some work refers to a Reasoning subset and an MME-RealWorld-Lite Reasoning subset.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what it measures are spread across several targets rather than centered on one alone. Papers link it to 2 constructs, Generalization and Reasoning, and to 6 behavioral indicators, including Agent intention prediction, Color recognition, Diagram understanding, Multiple-choice question answering, and Object counting, plus 1 other behavioral indicator. The relationship evidence also frames it as covering perception and reasoning subtasks, and one paper uses the Lite Reasoning subset and the remaining Reasoning subset to test gene

nodes.name: MMHal-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MMHal-Bench is most commonly described as a benchmark for multimodal or vision-language hallucination. Most definitions portray it as 96 image-question pairs, or questions, spanning eight question types, including object attributes, adversarial objects, comparisons, counting, and spatial relations; one paper additionally describes 12 object topics, and some authors frame it as a question-answering or generative benchmark. Many papers also describe GPT-4-based evaluation, variously for hallucination severity, response quality, hallucination rate, or agreement with human responses, object labels, or ground-truth answers, and a few papers add response informativeness or information richness.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, it is linked to six behavioral indicators and one construct. The prevailing usage is to measure hallucination: papers say it quantifies hallucinations, evaluates the degree of hallucination, or assesses response-level hallucination rates. Smaller lines of work also use it to measure attribute recognition, hallucination detection, object hallucination, and, in one paper, faithfulness by identifying hallucinations in outputs,

nodes.name: MMLongBench-Doc
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is of a benchmark dataset for multi-modal long-context document understanding or document question answering on lengthy, information-rich documents. Definitions describe extensive or long PDF documents with complex layouts and diverse multi-modal elements, where expert-annotated questions may require integrating text, images, and charts across many pages; some papers refer to it as MMLongBench. The descriptions that give dataset details agree on 135 documents averaging 47.5 pages, with one reporting 1073 questions and another saying the documents span 7 categories.

What it is claimed to measure. Most commonly, papers use it to measure long-context document understanding and nearby capabilities rather than a single narrow target. Papers link it to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators: the construct links are Localization ability, Long-context multimodal understanding, and Long-context understanding, and the behavioral-indicator links are Document question answering and Hallucination. One benchmark description further says its question types assess complementary aspects of long-context document understanding, and s

nodes.name: MMLU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a broad multiple-choice benchmark, usually expanded as Massive Multitask Language Understanding, spanning 57 subjects across STEM, humanities, social sciences, and other academic or professional areas. Definitions variously call it a benchmark, dataset, test set, or quiz bank of exam-style questions, and one paper states that all questions are multiple choice with four options. Most descriptions say it covers 57 subjects, though papers differ on scale, citing 14,042 questions, 14,079 questions, about 16,000 questions, 14,421 problems, or 15,439 multiple-choice problems, and one paper instead describes general knowledge questions across 22 high-school subjects. A smaller line of work uses subject subsets, such as four subjects for distribution shift, legal-specific tasks, medical or scientific subsets, or slices like College Physics, College Chemistry, and Clinical Knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the dominant framing is broad capability measurement rather than a single narrow construct. Papers link MMLU to 47 constructs and 21 behavioral indicators: the most common construct claims are general ability

nodes.name: MMLU-Math
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the dominant description treats MMLU-Math as the mathematics subset of the Massive Multitask Language Understanding benchmark, used in a multiple-choice format to evaluate knowledge and problem-solving skills. Definitions vary in how they specify its coverage: some describe it broadly as covering topics from elementary to advanced math or various math subjects, while another specifies Algebra, Probability, Number Theory, and Calculus and says its evaluation setup follows MAmmoTH.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MMLU-Math to one behavioral indicator, Mathematical problem solving, and one construct, Mathematical reasoning. The prevailing usage is as a measure of Mathematical problem solving, with papers reporting evaluation on MMLU-Math when assessing models on math benchmarks across different domains; a smaller line of work reports it as measuring Mathematical reasoning by including it among representative math datasets. The reported measurement claims are concentrated on these two targets rather than spread across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. No paper links it to another measurement instrument. Across the papers,

nodes.name: MMLU-Med
nodes.definition: A medical examination question-answering dataset used to evaluate retrieval performance in the medical domain, part of the broader MMLU benchmark.

nodes.name: MMLU-Medical
nodes.definition: A subset of the MMLU benchmark containing exam questions from nine subjects relevant to medicine, used to assess broad medical knowledge.

nodes.name: MMLU-Pro
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of an enhanced, more challenging version of MMLU for multi-task or multi-discipline language understanding and reasoning. It is repeatedly described as a multiple-choice benchmark, in one source with up to ten options, covering 14 domains or categories and a wide range of academic and professional subjects. Definitions commonly emphasize more complex reasoning questions and more distractor answer choices, and some also mention reduced dataset noise, a different evaluation protocol, or the use of subject subsets rather than the full benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMLU-Pro to measure a broad set of targets rather than one shared construct: it is linked to 14 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The most recurrent claims are that it measures natural language understanding, reasoning, and world knowledge, while some papers use it for multiple-choice question answering and language understanding task performance. The remaining links spread across additional constructs and indicators rather than converging on a single measurement claim.

Space of uses. Papers relate it to two other instruments, JudgeBench

nodes.name: MMLU-Pro Math
nodes.definition: A subset of the MMLU benchmark focused on professional-level mathematics problems.

nodes.name: MMLU-ProX
nodes.definition:
What it is. Available definitions describe MMLU-ProX as a multilingual benchmark of parallel multiple-choice questions for advanced LLM evaluation. It is presented as covering 29 languages, with 11,829 questions in its full version, and as maintaining the high difficulty level and reasoning focus of MMLU-Pro while assessing advanced reasoning in diverse linguistic and cultural contexts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMLU-ProX to measure two constructs, multilingual ability and multilingual reasoning, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The claims cluster around cross-lingual capability and reasoning: one paper says it "enables comprehensive evaluation of LLMs’ cross-lingual reasoning abilities" (MMLU-ProX: A Multilingual Benchmark for Advanced Large Language Model Evaluation), while another places it among benchmarks used "to evaluate the LLMs’ capability across languages."

Space of uses. In the available relationships, no other measurement instrument is linked to MMLU-ProX. Papers position it as a benchmark for evaluating LLMs across languages: one introduces it as "a comprehensive benchmark covering 29 languages," while another cites it alongside other mu

nodes.name: MMLU-Redux
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat MMLU-Redux as a general knowledge and reasoning evaluation benchmark derived from MMLU, often explicitly as a zero-shot variant. Some papers instead foreground its format and curation, describing a revised or manually re-annotated multiple-choice, closed-form question answering subset spanning a wide range of subjects, from elementary to professional level. Papers do not describe the subset identically: one line says it contains 3,000 manually re-annotated questions across 30 subjects, while another says 5,700 questions across all 57 subjects; elsewhere it is described more broadly as assessing language understanding and knowledge across domains.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMLU-Redux to measure 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claim is Reasoning, with papers calling it a logical reasoning benchmark and a reasoning benchmark used to elicit chain-of-thought performance; additional work uses it to measure Robustness, including robustness to order swapping of choices, and Mathematical reasoning by focusing on mathematics subjects. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Error detection, with one pa

nodes.name: MMLU-STEM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a STEM-focused subset of the MMLU benchmark, covering science, technology, engineering, and mathematics subjects. Most definitions present it as evaluating broad STEM knowledge and reasoning, while some narrow this to mathematical and scientific reasoning or to knowledge and problem-solving skills. Format details are only occasionally made explicit: papers describe it as a multiple-choice dataset or as multiple-choice questions for human exams across math and other STEM disciplines; Llemma: An Open Language Model for Mathematics specifies a subset of 18 out of 57 MMLU subjects, and another paper reports a STEM subset with 3.13K problems.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Mathematical reasoning and Reasoning, while a smaller line of work reports it as measuring Domain knowledge. Correspondingly, relationship evidence places it in evaluation suites for reasoning abilities across domains and for mathematical reasoning, and one paper treats performance on it as evidence about specialized knowledge.

Space of uses. Although no measurement

nodes.name: MMMLU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats MMMLU, sometimes written M-MMLU or m-MMLU, as a multilingual version of MMLU, often explicitly a human-translated or professionally translated variant. Papers commonly describe it as covering multiple languages and subjects for general language understanding or knowledge comprehension; one description adds multiple difficulty levels, and another frames it as a world-knowledge benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMMLU to measure 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on one. The construct links are multilingual ability, knowledge understanding, and multilingual reasoning, and the behavioral-indicator links are language mixing and multiple-choice question answering. The surrounding definitions also present it as testing general language understanding and reasoning performance across languages and subjects.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is directly linked to it. Papers nevertheless use it alongside other benchmarks, especially Belebele and m-ARC in multilingual evaluation bundles, and alongside MMLU

nodes.name: MMMU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats MMMU as a massive multi-discipline multimodal understanding and reasoning benchmark. Definitions usually place it at college or university level, with questions requiring advanced subject knowledge and reasoning across diverse domains; several papers specify six core disciplines or 30 college-level subjects, some say it contains 11.5K questions while one says about 12.5K, and others note that it includes both single- and multi-image items drawn from exams, quizzes, and textbooks. Papers variously describe its format as VQA or image+text-to-text, and they also refer to MMMU-dev and the validation set as separate splits, often used through multiple-choice questions, while a smaller minority frame it more narrowly as college-level subject knowledge, expert knowledge assessment, or, in one definition, a university-level mathematics understanding benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMMU to measure 17 constructs and 6 behavioral indicators, so its claimed targets are spread across many labels rather than concentrated on one. The dominant framing is that it measures multimodal understanding, reasoning, visual rea

nodes.name: MMMU-Med
nodes.definition: The medical subset of the Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding (MMMU) benchmark, used for evaluating advanced comprehension.

nodes.name: MMMU-Pro
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, papers treat MMMU-Pro as a challenging multimodal benchmark for advanced, professional-level vision language model capability. The prevailing description emphasizes complex knowledge and reasoning tasks across disciplines, with a vision component that requires deep understanding of images. Some authors further frame it as an advanced version of MMMU, with more challenging questions and stricter evaluation settings, including a 10-option multiple-choice format, and one reported setting is MMMU-Pro-std with 10 options.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 4 constructs and no behavioral indicators. It is used to measure calibration, general ability, multimodal reasoning, and multimodal understanding: one paper adopts it to measure calibration on complex, multidisciplinary image understanding and reasoning problems, another says it is designed to assess true multimodal understanding and reasoning across a wide range of academic disciplines, and another uses it among comprehensive benchmarks and VQA datasets to evaluate the general capabilities of VLMs. Across these claims, papers position it against several broad capabilities rather than a s

nodes.name: MMStar
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MMStar is most commonly described as a single-image or multimodal benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models, often framed as vision-indispensable and built from 1,500 human-selected or curated samples. Several papers say it is designed so that visual content is necessary for the correct answer, and some descriptions add that it evaluates 6 core capabilities with 18 detailed axes. Most definitions cast it broadly as assessing visual-language understanding, general understanding, reasoning, or advanced capabilities, though some papers describe it more narrowly as an image question-answering benchmark, and a smaller line of work places it among math-related benchmarks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMStar to measure a broad set of targets rather than a single outcome. It is linked to 12 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator; the most frequent construct links frame it as measuring logical reasoning, reasoning, visual perception, and fine-grained perception, and papers also report it as evaluating visual question answering. Other links extend to additional reasoning and perception constructs.
