Space of uses. Papers commonly use MMStar

nodes.name: MMT-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat MMT-Bench as a multimodal benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models on multitask performance. The most specific description says it "covers 162 concrete sub-tasks" drawn from existing datasets, is primarily focused on perception, uses a multiple-choice question format, and enables in-depth analysis through its "taskonomy" and diverse input forms (MEGA-Bench: Scaling Multimodal Evaluation to over 500 Real-World Tasks). Another paper places it among widely-adopted VLM benchmarks and also refers to it as a visual question answering benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, MMT-Bench is used to measure 1 behavioral indicator, Visual question answering, and no constructs are linked to it. The claims therefore concentrate on a single behavioral use, with a paper presenting MMT-Bench as a visual question answering benchmark.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In use, papers report results on MMT-Bench alongside other widely-adopted VLM benchmarks, and a paper positions it within a comparative table of visual question answering benchmarks for leading methods.

nodes.name: MMToM-QA
nodes.definition: A real-world multimodal dataset combining video and text to assess machine learning models’ ability to infer mental states, used here to validate the generalizability of probing methods.

nodes.name: MMVP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MMVP is most commonly described as a benchmark for fine-grained visual recognition or visual detail understanding, built from CLIP-blind pairs of visually similar images with a binary-option question for each pair. Definitions also describe it as containing 150 image pairs and covering 9 visual patterns, with paired classification accuracy used for evaluation. A smaller line of work places it under single-image VQA or, more broadly, among multi-image benchmarks for probing visual shortcomings, and one paper notes converting it to paired image-text format without altering the content.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMVP to measure a broad range of targets rather than one shared construct: it is linked to 9 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The constructs most often listed are Visual understanding, Compositional reasoning, Fine-grained perception, Fine-grained visual understanding, and Multimodal perception, with 4 other constructs also linked, while the behavioral indicators are Fine-grained visual recognition and Visual question answering. In the relationship evidence, papers also frame it as evaluating visual perception, visual reasonin

nodes.name: MNIST
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is of MNIST as a benchmark or classification dataset for handwritten digits. Most descriptions treat it as a handwritten digit recognition or image classification benchmark, while some position it more narrowly as a dataset for controlled finetuning experiments, shallow-network training and evaluation, or robust hyperparameter optimization. A smaller usage treats it as a test of digit recognition and number comprehension from images, with one study noting that models "struggle on simple digit recognition and counting tasks, e.g. MNIST."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MNIST to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The reported measurement claims are spread across image classification, optical character recognition ability, model collapse, and visual perception, rather than concentrated on one target. In these accounts, papers use it to measure image classification, to assess "the models’ ability to identify digits and count objects within images" for optical character recognition ability, to measure model collapse in experiments with shallow networks fully trained on MNIST, and to test visual perception.

Space of uses.

nodes.name: MNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, MNLI is most commonly treated as a natural language inference benchmark or corpus of premise-hypothesis sentence pairs for entailment classification. Definitions usually describe three labels, entailment, contradiction, and neutral, and often add that it is large-scale, crowdsourced, and spans multiple genres; one paper paraphrases the third label as unrelated, and another presents it as a multi-class classification problem. Some authors refer to match and mismatch variants, including MNLI-(m/mm) and hard-match versus hard-mismatch splits, while a smaller line of work describes MultiNLI as supervision for fine-tuning NLI-adapted models.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing measurement claim is that papers use MNLI to measure natural language inference. Beyond that, papers link it to 4 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators: alongside natural language inference, it is used to measure natural language understanding, generalization, in-context learning, and reasoning, and to evaluate language understanding task performance, text classification, and zero-shot task performance. The measurement claims therefore converge most clearly on NLI, with

nodes.name: ModelNet40
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset consisting of 3D CAD models from 40 categories, used for tasks like 3D point classification.

nodes.name: Mol-Instructions
nodes.definition: Mol-Instructions is a benchmark dataset for molecular generation tasks including retrosynthesis, reagent prediction, and forward reaction prediction.

nodes.name: MoleculeNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers consistently treat MoleculeNet as a benchmark suite, or benchmark dataset, for molecular machine learning and molecular property prediction. The prevailing description emphasizes a collection of tasks and public datasets, sometimes used for classification evaluation on multiple molecular datasets; some papers additionally describe its tasks as spanning properties from quantum mechanics, physical chemistry, biophysics, and physiology. Papers often work with subsets rather than only the full resource, commonly naming BBBP, BACE, ClinTox, ESOL, and FreeSolv.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the reported measurement target converges on a single behavioral indicator: MoleculeNet is used to measure Molecular property prediction. It is linked to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs, so papers do not link it to other constructs or behavioral indicators. Relationship evidence frames this use as evaluation, validation, or fine-tuning on MoleculeNet for molecular property prediction tasks.

Space of uses. In use, papers most often position MoleculeNet as an evaluation benchmark: models are evaluated on it, validated on datasets drawn from it, or fine-tuned

nodes.name: MOLERR2FIX
nodes.definition: A structured benchmark assessing LLMs on chemical error detection, localization, explanation, and revision using 1,193 expert-annotated molecular description errors.

nodes.name: MORABLES
nodes.definition: A human-verified benchmark built from fables and short stories from historical literature, designed to assess abstract moral reasoning in LLMs through a multiple-choice question answering task.

nodes.name: MORBENCH
nodes.definition: Multilingual Over-Refusal Benchmark, a large-scale, automatically constructed evaluation set designed to assess overrefusal behaviors in LLMs across 7 languages and 12 safety categories by targeting prompts near the safety decision boundary.

nodes.name: MovieChat
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat MovieChat, often named MovieChat-1K, as a long video or long-form video understanding benchmark built from movie clips. Definitions vary slightly between calling it a dataset and a benchmark: one describes 1,000 movie clips with an average duration of 9.4 minutes and 14K annotations, while several others describe roughly 10-minute movie clips. A smaller description emphasizes question-answer pairs about movies, and another adds two evaluation modes, a global mode for overall long-term understanding and a breakpoint mode for detailed analysis of specific moments.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MovieChat to evaluate long-form or long video understanding rather than to measure a named construct. It is described as evaluating long-form video understanding, overall long-term understanding in a global mode, and detailed analysis of specific moments in breakpoint mode. No papers explicitly link it to any construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. In use, papers position MovieChat as one of the long video benchmarks for model evaluation, sometimes alongside EgoSchema and MovieNet-QA. One paper reports evaluations on more challengin

nodes.name: MovieLens
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat MovieLens as a benchmark dataset for recommendation systems research, centered on user movie ratings and often described as including movie metadata. Across the definitions, it is used in movie recommendation settings and, in some papers, also includes user demographics and covers; one paper specifies that the dataset includes 86K movies, 0.3M users, and 3.3M ratings.

What it is claimed to measure. Across these papers, MovieLens is used as an evaluation dataset for recommendation tasks, including sequential recommendation, query modification in LLM-based recommenders, dynamic recommender simulation, and personalized cover generation. Papers do not explicitly link it to any constructs or behavioral indicators, so they present it as a task benchmark rather than as measuring a named construct.

Space of uses. Papers usually position MovieLens as one dataset in a broader evaluation suite. It is used alongside LastFM and Steam in sequential recommendation experiments, alongside LastFM for LLM4Rec evaluation, alongside Google Local and AmazonBook in simulation-platform experiments, and as one of two public datasets for short-video and movie recomme

nodes.name: MovieLens-25M multi-tabular
nodes.definition: A multi-tabular dataset adapted from the MovieLens-25M dataset, used to evaluate graph construction methods on a relation attribute prediction task.

nodes.name: MP-DocVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available definition treats MP-DocVQA as a benchmark for multi-page document question answering. The same description limits it to documents under 20 pages, and a paper further states that benchmarks such as MP-DocVQA do not assess documents exceeding 20 pages. In retrieval-oriented uses, papers also describe it as covering industrial documents.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MP-DocVQA to measure two behavioral indicators, Visual question answering and Information retrieval, and no constructs are linked to it. These claims are spread across those two task framings rather than centered on a linked construct, and both uses rely on question-document pairs drawn from MP-DocVQA.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it, but papers use MP-DocVQA alongside other VQA datasets. One paper groups it with DUDE as a current multi-page document question answering benchmark, while another combines its question-document pairs with ArXivQA, ChartQA, InfographicsVQA, and SlideVQA, plus another figure-focused dataset, to target different document types.

Concerns raised. The stated concern is page-length coverage. Papers note that MP-DocVQA is limited to d

nodes.name: MPQA
nodes.definition: The Multi-Perspective Question Answering dataset, used for opinion and sentiment analysis tasks.

nodes.name: MQAR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat MQAR as Multi-Query Associative Recall, a benchmark or task for assessing whether a model can retrieve values associated with keys from a context. Definitions commonly describe contexts with multiple key-value pairs, query positions, and sometimes distractors; a smaller line of work states the task more operationally as identifying multiple query tokens in a sequence and outputting, for each, the value token that followed the key's first appearance. One description also frames it as a synthetic diagnostic benchmark for retrieving multiple associative key-value pairs from context.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MQAR to one behavioral indicator and one construct. The prevailing claim is that it measures Key-value retrieval, with the task described as predicting the value associated with the corresponding key at query positions; a smaller use treats it as measuring Long-context understanding, where papers say a model's recall capability is assessed using MQAR. The measurement claims therefore center on one named retrieval indicator and one named construct, rather than a wide set of targets.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked

nodes.name: MQM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat MQM as a framework or guided error annotation scheme for translation evaluation that defines categories, dimensions, and severities for translation errors. Papers describe it as covering dimensions such as accuracy, fluency, and style, and one description specifies six major categories: terminology, accuracy, fluency, style, locale-convention, and non-translation. A smaller use treats the MQM evaluation framework as a source from which manual metrics, in that case fluency and idiom translation, are derived.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, MQM is linked to one construct, Translation quality, and one behavioral indicator, Machine translation. Papers use it to measure translation quality, and one paper also treats machine translation as measured by MQM, describing that setting as having substantial amounts of fine-grained MQM data already available. No other construct or behavioral indicator is linked to it.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to MQM by the surveyed papers. Papers position it as guided human error annotation, where evaluators read a source and candidate translation, identify error span

nodes.name: MQP
nodes.definition: The Medical Question Pairs dataset, a benchmark for detecting duplicate questions in a medical domain.

nodes.name: MQuAKE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MQuAKE is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for evaluating model or knowledge editing through multi-hop knowledge questions. Definitions converge on question answering over edited facts: some emphasize reasoning over edited knowledge, while others emphasize whether edited knowledge propagates to related facts or supports knowledge editing generalization through multi-hop questions; one paper describes each case as a multi-hop question built from a chain of single-hop subquestions. A smaller line of description adds versions that vary in hop count and temporal knowledge, and one source snippet specifies questions with 2 to 4 hops and different positions of the knowledge used in the questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MQuAKE to 4 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is to measure Multi-hop reasoning and Multi-hop question answering: papers describe it as evaluating multi-hop reasoning over edited knowledge, and one relationship states that Multi-hop Accuracy on MQuAKE measures the accuracy of multi-hop question answering. Smaller lines of work use it to measure Counterfactual reasoning, Context f

nodes.name: MQuAKE-CF
nodes.definition: A dataset used for evaluating multi-hop reasoning capabilities in the context of model editing.

nodes.name: MR-Ben
nodes.definition: A benchmark for error detection covering domains such as natural sciences, coding, and logic.

nodes.name: MR-GSM8K
nodes.definition: A benchmark for reasoning step error detection based on a subset of the GSM8K dataset, with manual annotations for the reason behind the first error.

nodes.name: MRDA
nodes.definition: ICSI Meeting Recorder Dialog Act corpus, a multiparty dialogue dataset with 50 fine-grained DA classes, used to evaluate dialogue act classification and related pre-tasks.

nodes.name: MRPC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, MRPC is most commonly described as the Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus, framed either as a benchmark or as a dataset for paraphrase detection or paraphrase identification. Definitions usually describe the task as deciding whether two sentences are paraphrases of each other, while some papers phrase it as determining the semantic equivalence relationship between two sentences. A recurring secondary framing treats it as a binary sentence-pair text classification task, often as a GLUE task.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims center on paraphrase detection: papers explicitly use MRPC to measure the behavioral indicator Paraphrase detection, often under nearby labels such as paraphrase identification or paraphrase tasks. Papers also use it to measure 3 constructs, Natural language understanding, General ability, and In-context learning, so the broader construct-level use is spread across several constructs even though the task-level framing converges on paraphrase detection. Overall, it is linked to 1 behavioral indicator and 3 constructs.

Space of uses. Papers most commonly position MRPC as one task within broader evaluation s

nodes.name: MS-COCO
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is MS-COCO as Microsoft Common Objects in Context, usually a large-scale object detection, segmentation, and captioning dataset, and often more specifically its validation split for zero-shot captioning or text-to-image evaluation. Some definitions foreground image captioning with complex scenes and multiple objects, while others extend the scope to keypoint estimation or region-level classification. Papers also use several named subsets and versions, including MSCOCO-2014, the COCO-2017 validation set, COCO-Val, and the Karpathy test split, and one captioning-oriented description specifies 5 captions per image under the Karpathy split.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MS-COCO to measure 11 behavioral indicators and 4 constructs, so the claimed targets are broad rather than concentrated on a single construct. The prevailing behavioral uses are image captioning, cross-modal retrieval, image generation, object detection, and instance segmentation, with additional measured uses beyond these. On the construct side, papers report it as measuring multimodal alignment, in-context learning, multimodal understanding, and visual gener

nodes.name: MS MARCO
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MS MARCO is most commonly treated as a large-scale retrieval and question answering benchmark built from queries or questions and passages. Definitions variously describe it as a question answering dataset, a machine reading comprehension dataset, a passage-ranking benchmark, or a collection used for reading comprehension and information retrieval; several descriptions mention real-user Bing queries, and one specifies that the public dev split has 101.09k examples, each with a simple question and 10 relevant passages. A smaller line of work narrows attention to particular parts or variants, such as only the question-and-answer pairs, the passage set, the MARCO QA subset, or the TREC Deep Learning subsets DL19 and DL20.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MS MARCO to 4 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs, and all recorded relationships treat it as a measuring instrument. Among the named behavioral indicators, the most common use is to measure Information retrieval, followed by Open-domain question answering, Question answering, and Ranking; the linked constructs are Retrieval effectiveness and Robustness. These claims are spread across several r

nodes.name: MSR-VTT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MSR-VTT as a large video description or video captioning benchmark for video-language evaluation. Several definitions frame it as an English, open-domain collection of videos paired with natural language descriptions, while one paper more specifically treats it as a text-to-video retrieval benchmark and another as a short-video understanding benchmark. Across these descriptions, the prevailing framing is a benchmark that bridges video and language, though papers differ on whether they foreground captioning, retrieval, or understanding.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MSR-VTT to three behavioral indicators and two constructs. The most common claim is that it measures Video captioning, with additional uses for Video generation and Cross-modal retrieval; papers also report it as measuring Video understanding and, in one benchmark comparison, Fidelity. Overall, the reported measurement claims are spread across several tasks and constructs rather than concentrated on a single target, although video captioning is the prevailing use.

Space of uses. Papers often use MSR-VTT alongside MSVD, and also place it with VATEX, LSMDC, DiDeMo, a

nodes.name: MSRVTT-QA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a video question answering benchmark based on or derived from the MSR-VTT dataset, also expanded in some definitions as Microsoft Research Video to Text. Definitions differ mainly in label and emphasis: some call it a benchmark, others a dataset or benchmark dataset, and several specify that it is open-ended, testing comprehension of video content through associated questions or answers about video clips. One description also notes that MSRVTT-QA, together with MSVD-QA, is derived from video retrieval datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets. Papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator, Video question answering, and this is the dominant usage: relationship evidence describes MSRVTT-QA as a benchmark for open-ended or zero-shot video question answering. Papers also link it to 1 construct, Video understanding, typically when placing it inside broader video understanding benchmark suites.

Space of uses. No paper directly links it to another measurement instrument, but papers usually use it alongside other video QA benchmarks, most often MSVD-QA and Activit

nodes.name: MSVD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, MSVD is most commonly treated as a video understanding benchmark, including use for assessing short video comprehension. Some authors describe it more specifically as a video captioning dataset: one definition states that it contains 1,970 open-domain videos collected from a commercial video search engine, each paired with about 41 human-annotated captions. The descriptions therefore converge on a video benchmark framing, with a narrower captioning-oriented characterization in some work.

What it is claimed to measure. In the surveyed papers, it is linked to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is as a measure of video understanding, with papers also using it to measure cross-modal retrieval and video question answering. Overall, the reported measurement claims are centered on video understanding but extend to multiple task-specific behaviors.

Space of uses. Papers often use MSVD alongside other benchmarks rather than on its own. In the available examples, it appears with MSR-VTT and TGIF in video understanding evaluation, with MUSIC-AVQA in open-ended VideoQA evaluation, and with MSR-VTT, LSMDC, and DiDeMo in cross-

nodes.name: MSVD-QA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MSVD-QA is most commonly treated as a video question-answering benchmark, often described as open-ended and frequently used for zero-shot evaluation. Definitions repeatedly tie it to the Microsoft Video Description dataset or the Microsoft Research Video Description Corpus, and the name also appears as MSVDQA and, in one formulation, MVSD-QA. Some descriptions add that it assesses understanding of video content through natural-language answers to video-based questions, sometimes over short video clips, and one paper notes that MSVD-QA is derived from video retrieval datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MSVD-QA to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Video question answering, with many papers explicitly calling it a video QA, open-ended VideoQA, or zero-shot video question answering benchmark. A smaller line of work reports it as measuring Video understanding by placing it among video understanding benchmarks, and a minority framing uses it for Visual question answering. These claims concentrate most strongly on Video question answering rather than spreading evenly across targets.

Space of uses.

nodes.name: MT-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MT-Bench is most commonly described as an LLM-judged benchmark for multi-turn conversation and instruction following, usually using GPT-4 or another strong LLM to score model responses. The prevailing description is a set of 80 high-quality or human-crafted multi-turn, often two-turn, questions across eight domains or categories such as writing, roleplay, reasoning, math, coding, extraction, STEM, and humanities, with scores often given on a 1 to 10 scale; several papers restate this as 160 prompts or 160 open-ended questions by counting the follow-up turns. A smaller line of work instead treats it as a dataset for pairwise comparison or judge evaluation, emphasizing expert human annotations, human preference judgments, or its use as a meta-evaluation benchmark for LLM judges.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MT-Bench to measure a broad range of outcomes, with links to 23 constructs and 17 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure instruction following ability and conversational ability, and papers also frequently use it for helpfulness, generalization, and general ability; on the behavioral side, instruction following, multi-t

nodes.name: MT-Bench-101
nodes.definition: Multi-level benchmark using multi-turn questions to assess model understanding and consistency in complex dialogues.

nodes.name: MTEB
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MTEB is most commonly described as a comprehensive or general-purpose suite for evaluating text embedding models, and some papers also refer to it as a leaderboard plus a collection of benchmarks. The most detailed description presents it as 56 English tasks across 7 types, including classification, clustering, retrieval, semantic textual similarity, and summarization, plus 2 other task types. A smaller line of work describes it differently, as covering 8 task types, or uses narrower subsets such as the retrieval set or ten STS tasks; one definition also frames it as spanning multiple tasks and languages.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MTEB to measure 6 behavioral indicators and 3 constructs. These reported uses span several embedding-related outcomes rather than a single target: text clustering and information retrieval are the most frequently linked behavioral indicators, semantic textual similarity is also a recurring reported use, and 3 other behavioral indicators are additionally reported. On the construct side, representation quality is the most frequently linked construct, with 2 other constructs also measured through MTEB.

Space of us

nodes.name: MTOP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers here, MTOP is most commonly treated as a benchmark dataset for multilingual task-oriented semantic parsing, with definitions centering on intent and slot filling. It is also described as containing compositional representations for complex nested queries across multiple languages and domains, and one description says it covers 6 languages and 11 domains.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MTOP to measure one behavioral indicator, Semantic parsing, and no constructs are linked to it. The linked claims converge on semantic parsing: papers describe MTOP as a semantic parsing benchmark and as a benchmark for multilingual task-oriented semantic parsing, with attention to intent and slot filling.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to MTOP, but papers do use it alongside other semantic parsing benchmarks. One paper presents it with SM-CalFlow and GeoQuery as part of "three popular diverse semantic parsing benchmarks," and another evaluates across four semantic parsing tasks that span "intent and slot filling (MTop)."

nodes.name: MTOP(I)
nodes.definition: A dataset for intent discovery, aiming to identify unknown intents within user utterances.

nodes.name: MUCAR
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating multilingual cross-modal ambiguity resolution, consisting of 1278 samples in Chinese, English, and Malay, including dual-ambiguity cases where both text and image are ambiguous but jointly resolve to a single interpretation.

nodes.name: MuirBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Definitions treat MuirBench as a multimodal, multi-image benchmark for evaluating understanding or reasoning across multiple images. Papers describe it as a comprehensive benchmark for assessing multi-image understanding by multimodal LLMs, as testing a model's ability to integrate information from diverse visual inputs, and as assessing various image relationships; one description explicitly adds that it does not cover spatial relationships.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on one alone. Among the named links, MuirBench measures multi-image reasoning, scene understanding, visual grounding, chronological ordering, and counting; relationship descriptions further frame these as abilities such as ordering images from text and counting specific objects across multiple images.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers use it as a benchmark for multimodal LLM evaluation and comparative performance reporting: one study reports "13.3% on MuirBench" in its abstract, and another passage says a model stil

nodes.name: Multi30k
nodes.definition: Multilingual dataset for machine translation, containing image captions in English and German.

nodes.name: Multi-IF
nodes.definition: Benchmark designed to evaluate instruction-following with multiple independent constraints.

nodes.name: Multi-Needle-in-a-Haystack
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats this as a long-context retrieval variant of Needle-in-a-Haystack: a model must locate multiple needles, hidden targets, or pieces of information within a single long context, sometimes with multiple distractor facts mixed in. A smaller line of usage casts it as a multi-turn evaluation in which different specific pieces of information are retrieved from the same long context across successive conversational turns, with questions issued one-by-one.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to one construct, Long-context understanding, which is reported as being measured by it. No behavioral indicators are linked to it, and no other constructs are named, so the measurement claim converges on that single construct rather than spreading across several targets.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Where papers describe its role, they present it as a more complex or harder needle retrieval evaluation by mixing multiple needles and by running multi-NIAH alongside single-NIAH in longer contexts; another paper uses it following NeedleBench and frames it as a multi-turn conversation setti

nodes.name: MultiArith
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MultiArith is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset of arithmetic word problems, often grade-school or general math word problems that require multiple operations or multi-step reasoning. Some definitions frame it more broadly as a quantitative or mathematical reasoning dataset, and one paper describes it as a subset of MAWPS containing multi-step mathematical word problems. A few papers add corpus details, reporting either a data size of 600 or a split of train: 420 and test: 180.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MultiArith to 2 constructs, Mathematical reasoning and Robustness, and to 1 behavioral indicator, Mathematical problem solving. The prevailing usage is to measure Mathematical reasoning, with papers using it to verify mathematical reasoning capacity or assess arithmetic reasoning tasks. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Robustness through out-of-domain evaluation, and it is also used to measure Mathematical problem solving on general benchmark suites.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers usually evaluate MultiArith alongside GSM8K and, in smaller benchmark suites, SVAMP, AddSu

nodes.name: MultiHiertt
nodes.definition: A question answering dataset in the finance domain designed to support compositional reasoning by encoding hierarchical table structures for multi-step questions.

nodes.name: MultiHop-RAG
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats MultiHop-RAG, also written MultiHopRAG or M-RAG, as a benchmark or multi-hop QA dataset for retrieval-augmented generation and multi-hop question answering. Definitions describe it as requiring integration of information across multiple documents or articles to answer questions, and one paper says it is used to assess the capability of LLMs to extract and synthesize relevant information from multiple documents. A smaller descriptive difference is that some authors emphasize its format as a dataset of 2,556 multi-hop questions, while another paper highlights four question types: Inference, Comparison, Temporal, and Null.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure one behavioral indicator, multi-hop question answering, and three constructs: generalization, multi-hop reasoning, and temporal reasoning. The construct-level claims are spread across several targets rather than centering on one: some papers report it as assessing multi-hop reasoning performance, others use it as an out-of-distribution benchmark for temporal reasoning or to assess generalization.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is formally li

nodes.name: MultiJail
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a multilingual benchmark for adversarial or harmful prompts across languages. One definition describes it as a red-teaming dataset covering nine languages, used to sample and translate adversarial prompts for non-English safety evaluation, while another describes it as a multilingual harmful-prompt benchmark; one paper further mentions 315 queries when using it as seed data.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is narrow rather than spread across many targets. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, harmful content detection, and to no constructs, using it specifically to evaluate the accuracy of detecting harmful prompts in multilingual benchmarks.

Space of uses. Papers position it both as a benchmark in multilingual safety evaluation and as seed data for another dataset. It is related to one other instrument, CSRT, which one paper constructs by leveraging MultiJail's 315 queries as seed data, and another paper evaluates on it alongside other text attack benchmarks such as RTP-LX and AyaRedTeaming.

nodes.name: Multimodal Mind2Web
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat Multimodal Mind2Web as a multimodal extension of Mind2Web used for offline evaluation of web or GUI agents. Papers describe it as evaluating web agent task completion from cached screenshots and high-level task instructions, with a test split of 1,013 tasks spanning over 100 websites; another recurring framing is that it evaluates increasingly difficult cross-task, cross-website, and cross-domain generalization. A smaller line of work describes it as an in-distribution offline dataset for GUI-agent tasks involving web browsers.

What it is claimed to measure. Where papers make explicit measurement claims, they use it to measure 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. One paper uses it to measure Generalization, stating that it evaluates generalization across cross-task, cross-website, and cross-domain settings. Another paper uses it to measure Action grounding, using its test data to further assess GUI grounding models after alignment.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position it as an offline evaluation benchmark for realistic web tasks, and one paper also describes it as a challenging benchmark on which evaluati

nodes.name: MultiNERD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the dominant framing is a named entity recognition dataset. Definitions describe it as a pre-training dataset based on Wikipedia and Wikinews, with an English split and multiple label names, and some authors also present it as a baseline for IE pre-training. Another use treats it as a named entity recognition dataset for few-shot open-set classification, including chain-of-thought prompting on the dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure a single behavioral indicator, Named entity recognition, and it is not linked to any constructs. The recorded claims therefore converge on that one behavioral indicator rather than spreading across several targets.

Space of uses. Papers position it both as a baseline for IE pre-training and as an evaluation dataset for chain-of-thought prompting under few-shot open-set conditions. In that latter use, a study reports the highest F1-score across many settings for both seen and unseen classes. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: MultiNews
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, MultiNews is most commonly described as a dataset or benchmark for multi-document summarization. One description specifies that it consists of news articles and human-written summaries from newser.com, and one source further describes 56k article-summary pairs with summaries written by professional editors (GraphRouter: A Graph-based Router for LLM Selections). A smaller line of description places it within LongBench as a multi-document summarization dataset, while another simply frames it as a dataset for summarization tasks that require synthesizing multiple documents.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MultiNews to measure 1 behavioral indicator, Text summarization, and link it to no constructs. The recorded uses converge on summarization rather than spreading across multiple outcomes: papers describe it as a summarization task, use it in summarization evaluations, and report it as evaluating multi-document summarization. One paper adds that the task "requires synthesizing information from the entire context" (APE: Faster and Longer Context-Augmented Generation via Adaptive Parallel Encoding).

Space of uses. In the cited evaluations, Mult

nodes.name: MultiPL-E
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats MultiPL-E as a multilingual code generation benchmark formed by translating HumanEval, and often MBPP, into multiple programming languages. Several definitions describe parallel datasets in 18 programming languages, sometimes as translations of two unit-test driven Python benchmarks to 18 other languages; as one paper puts it, it is "translated from the Python benchmark ... into parallel datasets in 18 programming languages" (Knowledge Fusion of Large Language Models). Some authors also call it a multi-language parallel benchmark for text-to-code generation, and papers report evaluations on subsets such as 8 languages, 5 languages, or cpp/go. A smaller line of work describes it more narrowly as translated HumanEval problems, while one paper instead describes a Bash-focused benchmark with 540 scripting tasks checked by unit tests.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MultiPL-E to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant claim is that papers use it to measure code generation, with evaluations reported on MultiPL-E using metrics such as pass@1, pass@k, Avg. Pass@(1+10), and pass@100. A smaller line uses i

nodes.name: MultiRC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat MultiRC as a Multi-Sentence Reading Comprehension dataset or benchmark for question answering, usually described as requiring reasoning or synthesis across multiple sentences in a passage or text. The prevailing description presents it as a multiple choice dataset, and one recurring definition adds exact-match accuracy as the evaluation format. Some authors place it within SuperGLUE, note that questions may have multiple correct answers, or describe multi-sentence reading comprehension as the task itself rather than the dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked claims, papers connect MultiRC to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. It is more commonly used to measure Machine reading comprehension, with papers describing it as a question-answering dataset testing reading comprehension and as part of validation sets that cover reading comprehension. A smaller line of work uses it to measure General ability by including it among many tasks drawn from different general domains.

Space of uses. Papers use MultiRC alongside Arc-Easy, Arc-Challenge, OpenBookQA, MMLU, and HellaSwag. In those settings it is usually one task among br

nodes.name: MultiWOZ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers commonly treat MultiWOZ as a task-oriented, multi-domain Wizard-of-Oz dialogue dataset or benchmark. Definitions describe conversations where one human acts as a booking system for domains such as hotels and restaurants and the other acts as the user, while other papers frame it more broadly as a large-scale dataset for bookings and information requests. Papers also describe it differently by evaluation task: some use it as a dialogue state tracking benchmark, and another uses a later version built on an earlier release with corrections and enhancements to the test set.

What it is claimed to measure. No constructs or behavioral indicators are formally linked to MultiWOZ. Even so, papers use it to evaluate several targets rather than one recorded construct: dialogue state tracking, user satisfaction estimation, and first-order uncertainty quantification, including prediction of how certain the user is that they are more satisfied than would occur by chance, with average crowd-worker user-satisfaction annotations treated as ground truth.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is formally linked to MultiWOZ. In practice, papers position it both as a widely

nodes.name: MUSE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MUSE as a comprehensive machine unlearning evaluation benchmark, expanded in one definition as Machine Unlearning Six-Way Evaluation for language models. The prevailing description says it evaluates unlearned models across six desiderata or facets, using news and book corpora with verbatim-text and question-answer knowledge sets. Some authors frame it more specifically as a benchmark for erasing copyrighted information, with two unlearning scenarios, Books from the Harry Potter series and News from BBC News, while another description focuses on the News setup in which passages are split into Forget and Retain sets for question-answering based evaluation of knowledge removal and utility preservation.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on one. Papers link MUSE to four constructs and one behavioral indicator, namely knowledge memorization, robustness, utility preservation, verbatim memorization, and privacy leakage. One definition also presents it as evaluating six desirable properties of unlearning: no verbatim memorization, no knowledge memorization, no

nodes.name: MUSE-Books
nodes.definition:
What it is. The only available paper treats MUSE-Books, under the name BOOKS, as a dataset within the MUSE benchmark. In Catastrophic Failure of LLM Unlearning via Quantization, it is described as featuring the Harry Potter series, with the original novels as the forget set and related FanWiki materials as the retain set.

What it is claimed to measure. The available paper does not explicitly report that MUSE-Books measures any construct or behavioral indicator, and papers do not link it to any constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers position it as a component of the MUSE benchmark rather than as a standalone protocol. The described use pairs the original Harry Potter novels as the forget set with related FanWiki materials as the retain set, with the retain set used to preserve domain knowledge post-unlearning, and no other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: MUSIC-AVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe MUSIC-AVQA as a multimodal question answering benchmark over audio and video. One definition calls it an open-ended VideoQA dataset used for multimodal question answering, while another paper uses the name MUSIC-QA and frames it as a benchmark for music-related audio-visual understanding and reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, it is linked to two behavioral indicators and no constructs. Papers use it to measure Audio-visual question answering and Video question answering, with one paper presenting fine-tuning results on Audio-Video Question Answering using MUSIC-AVQA and another listing it among open-ended VideoQA datasets.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it through the recorded relationships. In practice, papers evaluate with it alongside other benchmarks, for example with MSVD as an open-ended VideoQA dataset, and in a broader audio-visual QA suite that also includes AVSD, AVSSD, MSVD-QA, and MSRVTT-QA, along with other benchmarks.

nodes.name: MusicCaps
nodes.definition: Benchmark for music captioning with rich textual descriptions, used to evaluate open-domain music understanding and description.

nodes.name: MuSiQue
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats MuSiQue as a challenging multi-hop question answering benchmark or dataset for questions that require connecting multiple pieces of information across multiple paragraphs, passages, or documents. Most descriptions emphasize questions composed from single-hop questions, often as composable pairs, with up to four-hop reasoning and design choices meant to reduce reasoning shortcuts; smaller lines of work also mention adversarially written paragraphs, bridge-entity construction, minimal lexical overlap, and supporting plus distracting evidence. Papers also refer to variants or slices such as the answerable version, a 2-hop evaluation subset, and MuSiQue-Ans, and one paper specifically uses its 3-hop and 4-hop data.

What it is claimed to measure. In the linked usage, papers report MuSiQue as measuring 4 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The dominant claims center on multi-hop reasoning and multi-hop question answering, and papers also use it for question answering, generalization, and chain-of-thought evaluation, with some broader reasoning and long-context framings as well. Overall, the reported uses converge most clearly on

nodes.name: MuSR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats MuSR as a benchmark from the Open LLM Leaderboard for reasoning-oriented evaluation, with some definitions specifically placing it in Open LLM Leaderboard v2. Definitions describe it as evaluating reasoning over social or multi-step scenarios, while one paper more specifically presents it as a semi-symbolic benchmark for probing soft-reasoning performance and notes that all tasks are multiple-choice. Relationship evidence further describes its domains as murder mysteries, object placement, and team assignment, involving physical and social situations, theory-of-mind, and commonsense reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, measurement claims are spread across six linked constructs and no linked behavioral indicators rather than concentrated on one target. The most common framing is that papers use MuSR to measure commonsense reasoning; papers also use it to measure chain-of-thought reasoning, logical reasoning, physical world understanding, and social reasoning, plus one other construct. A separate paper relates MuSR to commonsense reasoning without recording it as a measurement claim, describing it as semi-sym

nodes.name: MuST-C
nodes.definition: A multilingual speech translation corpus created from English TED Talks, widely used for evaluating speech translation systems.

nodes.name: MuTual
nodes.definition: A dataset for multi-turn dialogue reasoning, adapted from Chinese high school English listening comprehension exams.

nodes.name: MVBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a video or video-language understanding benchmark centered on temporal-sensitive tasks. Definitions most commonly describe nine core temporal tasks with 20 subtasks that cannot be solved using a single frame, while other papers describe it as a reorganized benchmark covering 20 challenging video understanding tasks, or as a multiple-choice QA benchmark with 4,000 question-answer pairs drawn from 11 public video benchmarks. A smaller line of work narrows attention to action-related subsets, including Action Antonym, Action Count, Action Sequence, Action Prediction, Action Localization, Fine-grained Action, and Unexpected Action, and one paper characterizes the benchmark as predominantly human-centric.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MVBench to four constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claim is that it measures video understanding, while other papers use it to measure long video understanding and temporal reasoning, and a smaller line treats it as measuring multi-image reasoning. One paper also uses it to measure action localization through an Action Localization subtask, so the recorded mea

nodes.name: MVSA-M
nodes.definition: A multimodal sentiment analysis benchmark for post-level sentiment classification on image-text posts.

nodes.name: MVSA-S
nodes.definition: A multimodal sentiment analysis benchmark for post-level sentiment classification on image-text posts.

nodes.name: Mystery Blocksworld
nodes.definition: An obfuscated version of the Blocksworld planning domain from the PlanBench suite, designed to be more challenging by obscuring the commonsense nature of the task.

nodes.name: MzsRE
nodes.definition: MzsRE is a multilingual dataset created by translating full sentences with Google Translate.

nodes.name: NarrativeQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of NarrativeQA as a long-context question-answering or reading-comprehension benchmark over narrative texts, especially entire books and movie scripts or transcripts. Definitions usually describe questions paired or concatenated with long text and require free-form answers, sometimes as full stories with corresponding QA pairs. Some papers place it within the SCROLL benchmark, while one paper instead describes annotators reading novel summaries to write the questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use NarrativeQA to measure 3 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The dominant measurement claims are for question answering and document question answering, with a smaller line using it for machine reading comprehension. Among constructs, papers most often use it for long-context understanding, and a smaller line uses it for length generalization, including length extrapolation or evaluations with different input context lengths. Overall, the reported uses spread across several closely related QA and long-context targets.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use NarrativeQA as one benchmark within broader long-context evalua

nodes.name: Natural Instructions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited work, Natural Instructions is described as a dataset for evaluating a model's ability to follow natural language instructions across a wide range of tasks. One usage snippet also places it in generation-task testing, where papers report testing method effects on Natural Instructions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Natural Instructions to measure Instruction following. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Instruction following, and to no constructs, so the available measurement claims converge on that single target rather than being spread across multiple outcomes.

Space of uses. In the available usage evidence, papers position Natural Instructions as a training and evaluation dataset alongside XSum and the WMT-14 en-de translation dataset. Another paper uses it to test generation-task effects of different methods.

nodes.name: Natural Questions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Natural Questions is most commonly described as a question answering benchmark built from real user queries to Google Search, typically paired with Wikipedia-based short or long answers, sometimes described as human-annotated. The prevailing framing is open-domain QA, often single-hop or knowledge-intensive, though some authors instead use it as a closed-book or fact-recall benchmark, and others describe retrieval, open-book, long-form QA, or multi-document QA uses. Papers also refer to variants such as NQ, NaturalQA, NaturalQuestions, and NQ-Open or NaturalQuestions-Open, with reported settings including 0-shot, 3-shot, 5-shot, and 32-shot.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Natural Questions to measure 12 constructs and 9 behavioral indicators, so its claimed measurement role is spread across many targets rather than concentrated on one. The dominant uses are to measure question answering and open-domain question answering, and papers also use it to measure world knowledge, factuality, and editing locality, with additional work reporting other behavioral and construct-level targets beyond these.

Space of uses. Natural Questions is linked to 4 o

nodes.name: NBA
nodes.definition: Natural Backdoor Attacks (NBA), a baseline backdoor attack method that injects fixed, non-learnable 'natural triggers' like rain or a whistle at the beginning of an audio waveform.

nodes.name: Nectar
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers treat Nectar as a dataset used in evaluation. The fullest description presents it as containing human-labeled responses in seven distinct rankings and using those responses to evaluate question answering performance; one study says it "includes human-labeled responses categorized into seven distinct rankings." Some authors use the name Berkeley Nectar and describe it more narrowly as a dataset used in direct and indirect transfer evaluations of decoding-time alignment, without adding further content details.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, the measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets. Nectar is linked to no constructs, to one behavioral indicator, Question answering, and to no measurement instruments. In the recorded relationship, Question answering is measured by Nectar, and the same line of work defines the dataset as being used to evaluate question answering performance.

Space of uses. Papers describe using Nectar in experiments and evaluations. One paper says it began experiments with the Nectar dataset, and another uses Berkeley Nectar in direct and indirect transfer evaluations of decoding-time alignment

nodes.name: Needle-in-a-Haystack
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of a popular synthetic long-context retrieval benchmark, variously called a test, task, evaluation procedure, pressure test, or stress test. Most definitions describe inserting a fact, statement, answer, sentence, or key-value pair, the "needle", into a long distracting, irrelevant, or random context, the "haystack", often at controlled or varying depth positions, and then querying the model to retrieve it. Some papers mention variants such as NIAH1, a 4-needle setting with multiple inserted items, or a version that asks for random numbers assigned to randomized cities, and a smaller line of work describes it as a task used within RULER.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 5 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is for long-context understanding, and the most common behavioral framing is synthetic recall; other recorded uses include contextual understanding, visual information retrieval, and context retrieval. Overall, papers report it as evaluating several retrieval- and context-centered constructs and indicators.

Space of uses. In use, papers commonly position it as a long-context

nodes.name: NeedleBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats NeedleBench as a long-context evaluation, described either as a benchmark for models' ability to comprehend and retrieve information from long input sequences or, in closely related terms, as "a suite of recall-intensive tasks" for long-context retrieval and information finding (Rodimus*: Breaking the Accuracy-Efficiency Trade-Off with Efficient Attentions). One paper also places it among synthetic benchmarks, and another description specifies three subtasks: Single-Needle Retrieval, Multi-Needle Retrieval, and Multi-Needle Reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The construct link treats NeedleBench as measuring Long-context understanding, while the behavioral indicator link treats it as measuring Synthetic recall; across both framings, the recurring emphasis is retrieval, recall, and reasoning in complex or long contexts.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. In use, papers discuss it alongside Needle-in-a-Haystack and Ruler as benchmarks focused on understanding long-context input sequences, and alongside MQAR when assess

nodes.name: NegHalu
nodes.definition: A constructed dataset for evaluating hallucination detection in negated text, derived from HaluEval, BamBoo, and SelfCheckGPT-WikiBio by applying post-negation transformations and reassigning hallucination labels based on logical consistency.

nodes.name: NESTFUL
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset designed to evaluate LLMs on nested sequences of API calls in mathematical reasoning and generic coding domains, assessing five dimensions of performance including F1 scores and sequence accuracy.

nodes.name: NewsQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, NewsQA is most commonly described as a news-based question answering or machine comprehension dataset. Papers characterize it as requiring answers from long passages, with some emphasizing comprehension and extraction from long, realistic passages, while another specifies CNN articles paired with questions and answers; one study also refers to the MRQA version of NewsQA.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, NewsQA is used to measure two behavioral indicators, machine reading comprehension and question answering, and it is not linked to any constructs. The linked measurement claims concern these two behavioral indicators only.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to NewsQA. Where papers describe its use, they include it among evaluated datasets for answering questions from long news passages, sometimes as the MRQA version, and one paper uses it specifically for the news articles domain with CNN article question-answer pairs.

nodes.name: NExT-QA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is as a video question answering benchmark, often described as multiple choice, for evaluating causal and temporal reasoning over video events. Several definitions add that it targets everyday activities, natural videos, or explanations of temporal actions, and some descriptions also mention descriptive question types; one paper additionally names a subset, NExT-GQA, with timestamp annotations to locate the answer moment. Papers describe its video scope somewhat differently: some call it a long-form or minute-long video dataset with thousands of multiple-choice questions, while others describe it as measuring temporal dynamics over short clips or focusing on short videos.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Video question answering, and to seven constructs. The dominant measurement claim is that papers use NExT-QA to measure video question answering, while construct-level uses are spread across long video understanding and video understanding, followed by causal reasoning, compositional reasoning, reasoning, spatiotemporal reasoning, and temporal reasoning. The recorded relationship language

nodes.name: NFCorpus
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe NFCorpus as a medical information retrieval dataset or benchmark. A smaller line of work refers to it more generally as a retrieval or IR dataset, including as one of the BEIR datasets and as a dataset used to generate and evaluate adversarial passages in corpus-poisoning experiments. One definition adds that NF-Corpus contains queries in simple English and technical documents extracted from PubMed, with 323 queries in the test split and 3.6k total documents, while another uses it for domain-specific factual questions involving single entities.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use NFCorpus to measure 2 behavioral indicators, Factual question answering and Information retrieval, and no constructs are linked to it. The measurement claims stay at the level of task behavior: one paper evaluates long-document retrieval scenarios, while another says NFCORPUS is among the datasets consisting of factual questions involving single entities.

Space of uses. In practice, papers position NFCorpus mainly as an evaluation dataset, for query generation and retrieval, long-document retrieval, and adversarial passage generation and evaluation. It is

nodes.name: NL4OPT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats NL4OPT as a benchmark or benchmark dataset for optimization modeling from natural language. Definitions describe it as evaluating a model's ability to construct or extract mathematical or optimization formulations from natural language questions or descriptions, with one description specifying named entity recognition to extract entities and numerical values before formulating the model. A smaller line of work describes it more simply as a dataset from the NL4Opt competition for solving optimization problems stated in natural language, and one paper characterizes it as a curated set of 244 linear programming problems used to evaluate autoformulation systems.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link NL4OPT to one construct, Accuracy, and to no behavioral indicators. In the recorded relationships, Accuracy is measured by NL4OPT, described through "formulation correctness results on four benchmarks containing LPs/MILPs," so the available claims concentrate on accuracy rather than a broader spread of measured targets.

Space of uses. The available usage places NL4OPT inside broader benchmark suites. Papers describe ev

nodes.name: NLGraph
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, NLGraph is most commonly described as a benchmark or evaluation framework for graph reasoning tasks presented in natural language. Some definitions frame it broadly as assessing whether language models can handle graph tasks and basic graph properties, including counting node degrees or finding shortest paths, while one usage narrows to the shortest-path subset, where models find the shortest path between two nodes in a weighted undirected graph.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement claims link NLGraph to two constructs, Reasoning and Generalization, and no behavioral indicators. Papers use it to measure Reasoning in benchmark suites, and another paper reports that simpler tasks in NLGraph evaluate Generalization, so the measurement claims are spread across more than one construct rather than centered on a single one.

Space of uses. Papers position NLGraph as an evaluation benchmark for graph-task performance, sometimes as an extensive framework and sometimes through a specific subset or simpler tasks. One line of use employs only the shortest-path subset, and another refers to the simpler tasks in NLGraph when evaluating generalizati

nodes.name: NLP4LP
nodes.definition: A benchmark for solving linear programming problems where models must use an optimization solver, with problem data presented implicitly in the text.

nodes.name: NLVR2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description treats NLVR2 as an extension of the NLVR dataset built from pairs of real-world photographs and natural language statements, used to test visual reasoning. A compatible framing presents it as a benchmark for evaluating reasoning over paired visual inputs and related language statements, and some papers refer to it simply as a dataset for visual reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use NLVR2 to measure three constructs: Multi-image reasoning, Visual reasoning, and Visual understanding, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. These claims are spread across those constructs rather than concentrated on one: some papers place NLVR2 among multi-image benchmarks, another uses it for visual reasoning, and another reports it as measuring visual understanding.

Space of uses. Across the papers, NLVR2 is commonly positioned as one item in a broader evaluation suite rather than as a standalone protocol. As one study notes, "we select five multi-image benchmarks" including NLVR2, while another uses it within a broader set of image-text tasks; papers do not link it to any other measurement instrument.

nodes.name: NoCaps
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, NoCaps is most commonly treated as an image captioning benchmark or dataset for testing captions on novel objects or classes not seen during training, often in zero-shot settings. Some authors describe it as large-scale or open-domain; one paper labels it a captioning task for natural images, another says it is derived from Open Images, and another uses it as an out-of-domain benchmark for transferability and robustness tests. The recurring content description is images with diverse objects and scenes, especially categories not seen frequently in training.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use NoCaps to measure 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing use is Image captioning: papers describe it as evaluating image-level caption ability, zero-shot image captioning, or image-to-text captioning. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Object hallucination, with one paper evaluating object hallucination in visual caption and checking transferability and robustness on out-of-domain images.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers commonly report it alongside Flickr30K and COCO, and some also place i

nodes.name: NormAd
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, NORMAD is most commonly described as a benchmark or hierarchical evaluation framework for LLM cultural adaptability, though one paper also refers to it as a dataset. Definitions converge on a multi-country set of free-text or short social situations, reported as 2,600 stories from 75 countries, where a character either adheres to or violates a cultural norm; models judge the acceptability of these situations under different levels of cultural context specificity, from abstract values to explicit social norms and etiquette.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use NORMAD to measure Cultural adaptation, and this is the only linked construct. It is linked to one construct and no behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims converge on cultural adaptation, including judging social acceptability across varying levels of cultural norm specificity.

Space of uses. Papers position NORMAD mainly as a direct evaluation setup for studying cultural adaptability in LLMs. One paper introduces it as a multi-level framework for social acceptability judgments, and another reports using the NORMAD dataset "to study cultural adaptability in LLMs"

nodes.name: NOVA-63
nodes.definition: A native multilingual benchmark containing 89,107 multiple-choice questions across 14 languages and 63 academic disciplines, designed to assess multilingual and multidisciplinary capabilities of LLMs with native content, difficulty control, and disciplinary balance.

nodes.name: NovelHopQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating multi-hop question answering over long narrative contexts, featuring 4,000 questions with 1-4 reasoning hops across 64k-128k token excerpts from public-domain novels.

nodes.name: NQ-Swap
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, NQ-Swap is most commonly described as a counterfactual or knowledge conflict QA benchmark derived from Natural Questions. Papers describe it either narrowly as swapping incorrect answers into the context or more broadly as synthetic conflicting data, and both descriptions present it as testing whether a model relies on the correct evidence or can handle discrepancies.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claims are faithfulness-oriented: papers use it to measure Context faithfulness and Faithfulness, with one study describing it as a more challenging and complementary evaluation of a model's ability to identify and rely on the correct evidence. A smaller line of work also uses it to measure Question answering by including it among QA datasets.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the source descriptions, papers use it alongside ConfiQA and MemoTrap as a counterfactual or knowledge conflict check, and one paper includes it in a broader QA suite with Natural Question, TriviaQA, and PopQA, among other datasets. Across these uses, papers po

nodes.name: NTREX-128
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, NTREX-128 is described as a document-translation dataset. Definitions place it in FILBENCH for English-to-Filipino translation evaluation, and source snippets describe it as part of a "diverse set of test examples" that include documents.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use NTREX-128 to measure Machine translation. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and to no constructs, so the reported use centers on a single behavioral target rather than multiple constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers position NTREX-128 as part of a broader machine translation evaluation setup rather than as a standalone protocol. One paper lists it alongside FLORES-200, AfroLingu-MT, TICO-19, and MAFAND-MT under MT datasets, and no measurement instrument is formally linked to it in the recorded relationships.

nodes.name: Nucleotide Transformer Benchmark
nodes.definition: A collection of 18 downstream tasks for evaluating DNA foundation models, covering histone marker prediction, regulatory annotation, and splice site prediction.

nodes.name: NumGLUE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, NumGLUE is most commonly described as a suite of mathematical or numerical reasoning tasks. Definitions emphasize understanding numerical concepts and language, or handling numbers in natural language contexts, while one paper describes it more specifically as a benchmark for numerical and quantitative reasoning whose tasks fundamentally involve arithmetic formula evaluation. Another paper refers to NumGLUE1 and NumGLUE2 among math-related tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Most commonly, papers use NumGLUE to measure Mathematical reasoning. Papers link it to one construct, Mathematical reasoning, and one behavioral indicator, Mathematical problem solving. A smaller line of work treats it as a math benchmark for Mathematical problem solving across different domains.

Space of uses. Papers typically use NumGLUE alongside other math benchmarks. It appears as an in-domain dataset and as an evaluation benchmark, most often with GSM8K, and also with MATH and SVAMP; one paper also groups NumGLUE1 and NumGLUE2 within 'math-related tasks.' Papers do not link it to any other measurement instrument.

nodes.name: OASST1
nodes.definition: OpenAssistant Conversations dataset, a human-generated and human-annotated assistant-style conversation dataset used to train and evaluate reward models.

nodes.name: Object HalBench
nodes.definition: Object HalBench is a benchmark for evaluating model hallucination at both the response level and mention level, focusing on object presence and attributes.

nodes.name: OCR-VQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, OCR-VQA is most commonly described as a visual question answering benchmark or dataset centered on text in images. Papers characterize it as requiring understanding, reading, or reasoning about text within images, using labels such as "text understanding VQA" and "text-in-image understanding"; the name also appears as OCRVQA and OCR VQA.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use OCR-VQA to measure 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The linked behavioral indicators are optical character recognition and visual question answering, and the linked constructs are document understanding and generalization. These measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on a single one.

Space of uses. Papers do not relate OCR-VQA to any other measurement instrument. They more often place it inside broader evaluation suites, alongside datasets such as TextVQA, GQA, OKVQA, DocVQA, and VQAv2. Within those suites, it is used as a text-in-image evaluation, and some papers use it specifically to assess learned generalization ability or document understanding.

nodes.name: OCRBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, OCRBench is most commonly described as a benchmark for optical character recognition, often framed as evaluating OCR capabilities or text reading and text understanding in images or other visual inputs. Some authors use the spelling OCR-Bench, and one source abbreviates it as OCRB. A smaller line of description says it assesses a model's ability to recognize and reason about text within images using OCR tasks, but the prevailing usage remains an OCR-focused benchmark for large multimodal models.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use OCRBench to measure one behavioral indicator and three constructs. The dominant measurement claim is optical character recognition, and additional papers report it as measuring fine-grained visual understanding, fine-grained perception, and multimodal perception. Overall, the measurement claims center on OCR, with some broader perception-oriented framing around the same benchmark.

Space of uses. Across papers, OCRBench is usually used as part of broader evaluation suites rather than in isolation. It is frequently grouped with DocVQA, ChartQA, TextVQA, and InfoVQA in OCR-related, OCR-extensive, or OCR/document/chart under

nodes.name: ogbn-arxiv
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is a large-scale citation network benchmark for node classification in text-attributed graphs. Papers commonly describe nodes as papers, usually with title and abstract text, and edges as citations; some definitions further specify that it is an Open Graph Benchmark dataset, a directed graph of arXiv papers, or more specifically arXiv computer science papers.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ogbn-arxiv to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant use is to measure Node classification, with relationship evidence describing node classification accuracy on ogbn-arxiv and listing it among datasets widely adopted for node classification; a smaller line of work uses it to measure Zero-shot classification, described as an initial investigation into leveraging GPT-3.5 on the dataset.

Space of uses. Papers usually position it as one benchmark within broader multi-dataset evaluations, often alongside Cora and PubMed, and sometimes with ogbn-products, CiteSeer, or Wiki-CS. It appears in performance tables and comparative experiments for node classification, and papers also use it for zero-shot classific

nodes.name: ogbn-products
nodes.definition: A large-scale graph dataset from the Open Graph Benchmark representing an Amazon product co-purchasing network, used for node classification.

nodes.name: OK-VQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats OK-VQA, sometimes written OKVQA, as a benchmark or dataset for open-ended visual question answering. Definitions consistently say its questions require external or outside knowledge beyond what is directly visible in the image, with some papers framing this more specifically as commonsense, world, or general knowledge, and one paper describing it as requiring outside knowledge and reasoning. A smaller line of usage refers specifically to the validation split, and one paper says CVQA adopts OK-VQA's categorization with modifications.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most commonly use OK-VQA to measure visual question answering, the only linked behavioral indicator. It is also linked to 6 constructs, with the most frequent construct framings being multimodal understanding, world knowledge, commonsense reasoning, and generalization, plus 2 additional construct links. Overall, the construct links cover several claims rather than a single recorded construct, and one paper separately relates OK-VQA to world knowledge by stating that its questions require world knowledge.

Space of uses. Papers usually position OK-VQA as one par

nodes.name: OKTest
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for evaluating over-refusal, which includes 300 benign examples that contain sensitive terms but are fundamentally safe.

nodes.name: OLMES
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers treat OLMES as an evaluation suite for language models. One definition describes it as combining multiple-choice and cloze-format tasks across knowledge and reasoning domains, with manually curated in-context examples and calibration methods to improve reliability. Task lists vary slightly across papers: one lists MMLU, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and CommonsenseQA, among others, while another describes OLMES as a suite of 10 multiple choice question answering benchmarks and includes BoolQ.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement claims converge on one behavioral indicator: papers use OLMES to measure Multiple-choice question answering. It is linked to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. Papers also link it to 10 benchmark instruments that are presented as parts of the suite, including ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, BoolQ, CommonsenseQA, and HellaSwag, with 5 other instruments linked as well.

Space of uses. In use, papers say they adopt or use OLMES for evaluation. Metadata Conditioning Accelerates Language Model Pre-training states that it adopts the OLMES suite for evaluation, and another paper uses it as a suite of 10 multiple choice question an

nodes.name: OlympiadBench
nodes.definition:
What it is.
