Definitions split between two recurring descriptions: one line portrays it as an Olympiad-level benchmark for challenging mathematics problems, spanning high-school, college-level, and competition material, while another describes a bilingual multimodal version with 8,476 problems from Olympic-level mathematics and physics competitions. Across both descriptions, papers say it assesses advanced mathematical reasoning, and the multimodal framing adds high-level visual and logical reasoning. One paper also shortens the name to Olympiad and describes a challenging mathematical problem-solving dataset aimed at advanced reasoning and proof-like capabilities.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The most common use is to measure Mathematical reasoning, while smaller strands use it to measure Reasoning and Generalization; papers also report it as measuring Mathematical problem solving and Scientific problem solving. Overall, the reported targets spread across several reasoning-related abilities, but they most often center on mathematical reasoning.

Space of uses. Across evaluations, it is commonly used alongside MATH or MA

nodes.name: OMMO
nodes.definition: A large-scale outdoor multimodal dataset and benchmark used as a test source for evaluating camera-operation performance.

nodes.name: Omni-Judge
nodes.definition: An open-source evaluation model developed to assess the consistency between model-generated solutions and reference answers for the Omni-MATH benchmark at a low cost.

nodes.name: Omni-MATH
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Omni-MATH is most commonly described as a mathematical reasoning benchmark that covers diverse topics and a broad spectrum of difficulty levels. Several definitions narrow this further to olympiad-style or Olympiad-level challenges, and one description presents it as a universal Olympiad-level benchmark with over 33 sub-domains. Some papers refer to the full resource as 4.4K questions, while others evaluate 500-question samples for efficiency, including a named Omni-MATH-500 subset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Omni-MATH to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure mathematical reasoning, with papers describing it as a common or widely used math reasoning benchmark and using it to assess models' mathematical reasoning in standard suites or on synthetic data. These measurement claims mostly converge on mathematical reasoning, though a smaller line of work also uses it to measure problem solving and complex reasoning question answering.

Space of uses. Across papers, Omni-MATH is usually positioned as a challenging benchmark within broader evaluation suites, commonly alongside MATH, GSM8K, AIME, OlympiadBench,

nodes.name: OmniACT
nodes.definition: An existing dataset for desktop agent tasks, used as a source for constructing the GroundUI benchmark.

nodes.name: OmniEval
nodes.definition: An omnidirectional RAG benchmark in the financial domain that evaluates systems across 16 topics and 5 tasks using both rule-based and LLM-based metrics on auto-generated and human-annotated datasets.

nodes.name: OMOMO
nodes.definition: A dataset of human-object interactions used to assess the model's performance with novel objects not seen during training.

nodes.name: Online A/B testing
nodes.definition: A real-world evaluation method comparing user engagement metrics (PV CTR, UV CTR) between the proposed model and a baseline over a two-week period with live traffic.

nodes.name: OntologyRAG-Q
nodes.definition: A retrieval-augmented generation framework for Qur’anic Tafsir featuring Ayat-Ontology chunking, designed to evaluate verse-level retrieval and question answering using structured ontological context.

nodes.name: OntoNotes
nodes.definition: Coreference resolution dataset evaluating the model's ability to track entities across long texts.

nodes.name: Open LLM Leaderboard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat the Open LLM Leaderboard as a public HuggingFace evaluation suite or leaderboard that ranks open, open-source, or open-access LLMs on standardized downstream or academic benchmarks. The prevailing content description is a bundle of reasoning and knowledge tasks, often the six-task mix of ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande, and GSM8K, though some papers describe four-task versions centered on ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, MMLU, and TruthfulQA, and others report five-task or ten-benchmark selections. A smaller line of work emphasizes versions and formats such as v1, v2, v12, OpenLLM 2, and Leaderboard 2, or treats it as a few-shot evaluation methodology built on the Eleuther AI Language Model Evaluation Harness.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 10 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims are spread across multiple targets rather than centered on one. The most frequent construct links are Reasoning, General ability, Truthfulness, Alignment tax, and Commonsense reasoning, with five other constructs also linked; papers also use it for Catastrophic forgetting, Instruction following, an

nodes.name: Open LLM Leaderboard V1
names: Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard v1
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, the prevailing description is of a benchmark suite, or public leaderboard, for evaluating and ranking open-source large language models. Papers describe it as covering question-answering and reasoning tasks and, more specifically, as including MMLU, ARC-Challenge, GSM8K, HellaSwag, Winogrande, and a factual-correctness task, with both log-likelihood and text-generation evaluations.

What it is claimed to measure. In the available links, papers do not connect the leaderboard to any constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, they link it to two other measurement instruments, MMLU and GSM8K, and report these benchmarks as being included in the Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard v1.

Space of uses. Papers use it as a composite evaluation setting built from multiple benchmarks, most explicitly alongside MMLU and GSM8K, while the definitions also place ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Winogrande, and other tasks within the same suite. In Training on the Test Task Confounds Evaluation and Emergence, it is described as "a popular leaderboard that evaluates and ranks models with publicly available weights," framing it as a public ranking venue rather tha

nodes.name: Open LLM Leaderboard v2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers commonly describe Open LLM Leaderboard v2, also written as Open LLM Leaderboard 2 or Huggingface Leaderboard v2, as a Hugging Face evaluation suite or public leaderboard for benchmarking and ranking LLMs on challenging downstream tasks. The prevailing description specifies six tasks, BBH, GPQA, IFEval, MATH-Hard or MATH Level 5, MMLU-Pro, and MuSR or MUSR, covering reasoning, knowledge or expert knowledge, advanced math, and instruction following, usually with accuracy-based scoring. Some definitions additionally frame it as a more challenging version of the earlier Open LLM Leaderboard, and one description notes that its scores are normalized to a 0 to 100 scale.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators. Different papers use it to measure General ability, Knowledge understanding, and World knowledge, so the recorded measurement claims name several broad constructs rather than a single one. The relationship language is consistent in treating the leaderboard as the instrument that measures those constructs.

Space of uses. In use, papers position it as a benchmark evaluation suite for model performanc

nodes.name: Open VLM Leaderboard
nodes.definition: An evaluation protocol and leaderboard for assessing the performance of vision-language models on a variety of tasks.

nodes.name: OpenAI Moderation API
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as an API or public moderation tool for classifying text against safety policies, the instrument is used to assign violation categories or safety scores for content such as hate, harassment, self-harm, sexual content, and violence. Definitions also describe it as providing a binary harmful or safe flag, and in one account a continuous harmfulness score, while papers use it to tag unsafe conversations, assess the safety of text data, and filter toxic content. A smaller line of work describes OpenAI Moderation as a benchmark or evaluation set for query classification, and one paper frames OpenAI-Moderation as a defense mechanism for jailbreak evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three constructs and three behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure Harmlessness, Toxicity, Safety, Harmful content detection, and Content moderation, with one other behavioral indicator also linked; all of these links concern safety-related content. In the recorded relationships, papers use it to evaluate toxicity and harmfulness of examples, to provide a harmfulness score and a safe or unsafe tag for safety evaluation, and to judge

nodes.name: OpenAI Moderation dataset
nodes.definition: A standard safety dataset used to evaluate the performance of guardrail models in detecting unsafe content.

nodes.name: OpenBookQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats OpenBookQA, also written as OpenbookQA or OBQA, as a multiple-choice, open-book question answering benchmark or dataset, usually centered on elementary science questions and modeled after open-book exams. Most definitions say it requires reasoning over a provided set or small corpus of science facts together with common, external, or broad common knowledge; several papers further describe it as testing factual and commonsense reasoning, and some call it multi-step or multi-hop reasoning. A smaller set of papers instead frames it as open-domain QA, reading comprehension, or book comprehension. Descriptions also differ on size and placement: one paper says it contains 500 multiple-choice questions, another says it comprises 5,957 multiple-choice questions with four options, and one paper treats OBQA as a subset of VoiceBench.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers connect OpenBookQA to 12 constructs and 10 behavioral indicators. The dominant claim is that papers use it to measure Commonsense reasoning; recurring but less concentrated claims say it measures General ability, Generalization, Reasoning, and Calibration, so the claims

nodes.name: OpenCompass
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as an open-source evaluation framework or toolkit for large language models, used for standardized assessment across a wide range of benchmarks. Some authors describe it more specifically as a suite for several widely used zero-shot benchmarks, while another describes a framework spanning reasoning, language, knowledge, examination, and understanding, using zero-shot or few-shot prompting with official scoring scripts. A smaller description treats it as a platform that includes VQA datasets such as MMBench v1.1, MMStar, MMMU val, MathVista, and OCRBench, plus three other VQA datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. It is linked to two constructs and one behavioral indicator. Most commonly among constructs, papers use it to measure General ability, with Commonsense reasoning also linked, and a paper uses it to measure Open-domain question answering; the recorded claims therefore spread across multiple targets rather than centering on a single construct. Beyond those targets, it is also linked to eight instruments, most often PIQA, followed by ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, CommonsenseQA, and GTA, plus three other linked instruments.

Spa

nodes.name: OpenEQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the available definition, OpenEQA is treated as a dataset for Embodied Question Answering that offers "rich scenarios" for the task. It is described as providing instances that include a question, a ground truth answer, and associated episode memory from 3D environments.

What it is claimed to measure. The available papers do not state that OpenEQA measures any named construct or behavioral indicator. In this literature, it is described as a dataset for the task rather than linked to particular constructs through reported measurement claims.

Space of uses. Usage is described narrowly. In "EQA-RM: A Generative Embodied Reward Model with Test-time Scaling," the authors say their dataset construction process "builds upon" OpenEQA, using its question, answer, and episode-memory format as a basis, and they also cite datasets like OpenEQA as offering rich scenarios for the task. No other instruments are described alongside it.

nodes.name: OpenHermes-2.5
nodes.definition: A dataset used for supervised fine-tuning and for constructing in-domain test sets to evaluate model perplexity.

nodes.name: OpenLID
nodes.definition: A language identification model used as an instrument to evaluate whether machine translation models generate outputs in the correct target language.

nodes.name: OpenOrca
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat OpenOrca as an instruction or reasoning dataset used for supervised fine-tuning and evaluation, especially around general reasoning, comprehension, and instruction-following. Some authors broaden this into an ORCA family, including OPENORCA and distilled SLIMORCA, described as fine-tuning datasets for instruction-following and as derived from explanations of chain-of-thought reasoning steps from larger models. A smaller line of work describes Orca as an SFT collection that combines prior instruction-tuning data such as FLAN, T0, NIV, and CoT, and one paper also characterizes OpenOrca as augmented FLAN collection data.

What it is claimed to measure. Definitions commonly say papers use OpenOrca to evaluate general reasoning, comprehension, and instruction-following capabilities. Across relationship claims, it is linked to 1 construct, General ability, and to no behavioral indicators. That link is a causes claim rather than a measured_by claim: one paper says instruction datasets such as OpenOrca are included to preserve the task solving abilities of LLMs, so the reported linkage is concentrated on a single construct.

Space of uses. No measurement instr

nodes.name: OpenReview
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset of ICLR 2023 peer reviews used for evaluating text classification in a centralized differentially private setting.

nodes.name: OpenTuringBench
nodes.definition: A large-scale benchmark (>500K texts) for evaluating machine-generated text detection and authorship attribution, featuring diverse OLLMs and challenging tasks including out-of-domain texts, unseen models, and human-machine mixing.

nodes.name: OpenWebText
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, OpenWebText is most commonly described as a large-scale English or web text corpus, often framed as an open-source replication of WebText for pre-training and validation. Some definitions add that it is scraped from the web, and they differ slightly on size, describing it as approximately 8 billion web-crawled tokens or 9 billion tokens. A smaller line of work treats it more narrowly as a source of prompts for sentence continuation or as a text generation dataset for open-ended language completion.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link OpenWebText to one behavioral indicator, Text generation, and one construct, Generalization. The prevailing measurement claim centers on Text generation: papers use OpenWebText to compare sample quality or to evaluate "text generation on the OpenWebText (OWT) dataset" (Speculative Diffusion Decoding: Accelerating Language Generation through Diffusion). A smaller line of work uses it to measure Generalization, with one paper evaluating bounds on OpenWebText.

Space of uses. Most often, papers position OpenWebText as a pretraining corpus for GPT-2 series or autoregressive language models, sometimes training f

nodes.name: OpenWebText2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available definitions, OpenWebText2 is most commonly described as a large-scale web-text corpus or dataset. Papers characterize it as text extracted from URLs shared on Reddit and used to evaluate language model performance via perplexity, while another description treats it more generally as an evaluation corpus for computing Diff-eRank and reduced loss.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not explicitly link OpenWebText2 to any construct or behavioral indicator. Rather than presenting it as a measure of a named construct, they describe it operationally as a corpus used for evaluation through perplexity, Diff-eRank, and reduced loss.

Space of uses. The reported usage is mainly evaluative. One paper compares model performance on OpenWebText2, and another considers including it when computing Diff-eRank and also lists it alongside Wikipedia and other pre-training datasets for OPT models.

nodes.name: OpinionQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, OpinionQA is most commonly described as a survey-based benchmark or dataset built from Pew Research's American Trends Panel, using public-opinion questions together with demographic-group response distributions to evaluate distributional alignment. Several definitions treat it as a multiple-choice survey or QA resource: one says it includes 1,498 multiple-choice survey questions, another describes 493 ordinal-choice questions covering 60 groups across 12 demographic features, and a personalization paper uses a subsampled split with 10.5k training and 15.8k test QA pairs across 525 users and 15 topics. A smaller usage refers to "OpinionsQA" as persona data used in prior work to learn persona embeddings and soft-prompts.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement claims name 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The linked constructs are In-context learning, Personalization, and Representativeness: papers describe using OpinionQA for quantifying distributional alignment, as one of two QA datasets proposed to measure steerability for specific users or social groups, and for calculating a representativeness score from simulated preferen

nodes.name: OPUS-100
nodes.definition: A multilingual machine translation dataset used for training and robustness experiments across multiple language directions.

nodes.name: OR-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, OR-Bench is most commonly described as a large-scale benchmark for over-refusal in LLMs: papers describe it as the first large-scale over-refusal benchmark, with 80,000 prompts across 10 common rejection categories, framed as safe prompts that are likely to be incorrectly rejected. Some papers refer specifically to OR-Bench-80K, while later uses also mention a 1k-prompt subset and a moderated prompt pool following the canonical OR-Bench methodology. A smaller use treats it as a source of complied benign inputs contrasted with complied harmful inputs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link OR-Bench to 1 behavioral indicator, Overrefusal, and to no constructs. The measure claim converges on that single indicator: papers say they evaluate over-refusal using OR-Bench, introduce it as an over-refusal benchmark, and use 1k prompts from it to represent overrefusal behaviors. Some descriptions also frame this use as evaluating false-positive refusal rates in LLMs.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to OR-Bench. Papers position it both as the released benchmark itself and as a comparison or baseline resource: some use OR-Bench-80K

nodes.name: OR-Bench-Hard-1K
nodes.definition: A challenging subset of OR-Bench containing 1,000 safe prompts that are rejected by at least three state-of-the-art models, used to evaluate over-refusal in high-performance LLMs.

nodes.name: OR-QuAC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, OR-QuAC is treated as a conversational question answering dataset. The prevailing description emphasizes open-retrieval settings with conversational, multi-turn queries and associated passages, while another paper highlights that it includes context-independent rewrites of dialogue questions, allowing those questions to be posed without prior context and used in both dialogue-based and isolated-question evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not explicitly link OR-QuAC to any construct or behavioral indicator, so the available sources do not frame it as measuring a named construct. Instead, they describe it as an evaluation dataset for conversational QA, including use in dialogue-based settings and in settings where rewritten questions can be asked independently of earlier turns.

Space of uses. In the available papers, OR-QuAC appears as part of broader evaluation suites alongside QuAC, CoQA, and DoQA. One study includes it in the main evaluation on widely used conversational search datasets, and another uses it to assess generalization beyond the training distribution.

nodes.name: OSWorld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, OSWorld is most commonly described as a real computer environment and benchmark, or an interactive OS agent testbed, for evaluating multimodal or virtual agents on open-ended, multi-step computer tasks. Definitions emphasize real web and desktop applications and stepwise interaction with the operating system, where the agent acts, waits for a response, and then proceeds. One definition specifies Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS, 369 tasks, and execution-based evaluation, while a smaller line of work describes it more briefly as a desktop virtual agent benchmark used for trajectory collection and evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use OSWorld to measure 5 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator, and these claims are spread across several targets rather than converging on a single one. The linked constructs are Generalization, Adaptability, Agency, Commonsense reasoning, and Robustness, and the linked behavioral indicator is Action grounding. Separately, papers describe the benchmark itself as being measured by 2 instruments, Execution-based evaluation and Human baseline.

Space of uses. In use, papers commonly position OSWorld as a cha

nodes.name: Overcooked-AI
nodes.definition: An open-source, multi-agent collaborative game environment involving chefs preparing and serving meals, which serves as the foundation for the Collab-Overcooked benchmark.

nodes.name: OWL
nodes.definition: A dataset of 31.5K aligned literary excerpts from 20 books in ten languages, including original English texts, official translations, and newly machine-translated texts in six low-resource languages, used to probe multilingual and cross-lingual memorization in LLMs.

nodes.name: Oxford Flowers-102
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a flower image classification benchmark for fine-grained recognition. Definitions variously call it Flowers-102, Flower-102, Flowers102, Oxford Flowers, OxfordFlowers, or the Oxford 102 Flowers dataset, and some descriptions specify fine-grained classification of 102 different flower species or categories. Most papers describe it broadly as an image or visual classification dataset, while smaller lines of work describe it more specifically as a zero-shot classification benchmark, a few-shot learning dataset, a fine-grained visual recognition dataset, or a benchmark used to evaluate personalized and generalized performance across clients.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing use is to measure Image classification: papers report using Flowers102 among image classification benchmarks, to test downstream performance, or for zero-shot classification. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Fine-grained visual recognition, so the linked claims stay with behavioral indicators rather than constructs.

Space of uses. Papers usually place it inside broader benchmark sui

nodes.name: Oxford-IIIT Pets
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat Oxford-IIIT Pets as an image or visual classification benchmark. Definitions describe it as an image classification benchmark used for evaluating prediction correctness, while some papers frame it more specifically as a fine-grained pet-breed dataset, including a version described as pet images grouped into 37 breeds and used for fine-grained classification or few-shot learning. Snippets also place it in broader evaluation suites, for example as one of several datasets used for zero-shot and linear-probe image classification or as one of several visual classification datasets used to study personalization, generalization, and privacy.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to one behavioral indicator, Image classification, and to no constructs. The prevailing measurement claim is focused: papers use it to measure Image classification, rather than a wider set of linked outcomes. Definitions also say it is used to evaluate prediction correctness, few-shot learning performance, and personalized and generalized performance across clients, but papers do not link it to additional constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of u

nodes.name: P-MMEval
nodes.definition: A parallel multilingual multitask benchmark covering fundamental NLP and capability-specialized tasks across 10 languages, designed for consistent evaluation of LLMs.

nodes.name: P(True)
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a prompt-based self-assessment method: a model is queried directly, often with a simple template, to judge whether its own generated answer is correct, and the probability of outputting "True" is taken as the score. Definitions variously present it as hallucination detection, error detection, or uncertainty quantification, but they converge on self-critique of a generated response. A smaller framing names a "P(True) baseline" protocol that first generates a completion for an input, concatenates the input and completion, and then asks the model to answer with "true" or "false" only.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to score the model's own assessment of answer correctness, and they also describe that score as a confidence or uncertainty measure. No constructs are linked to it and no behavioral indicators are linked to it, so the papers do not connect it to a named construct; instead they describe it at the level of correctness, confidence, uncertainty, hallucination detection, or error detection.

Space of uses. When papers position it relative to other methods, the prevailing role is as a baseline or representative

nodes.name: PAIR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, PAIR is most commonly described as Prompt Automatic Iterative Refinement, a black-box jailbreak procedure or algorithmic attack in which an attacker or red-teaming LLM automatically and iteratively generates or refines prompts until a target model is jailbroken. Several definitions add that it can use multi-turn conversation, prompt optimization, or a query-based setup, and one paper describes it as prompt-level rather than token-level jailbreak. A smaller line of work describes it differently, as a population-based evolutionary attack, a pattern that frames harmful requests in imaginary scenarios, or, in one paper, a Likert-style evaluation prompt for judging whether a response violates ethical, legal, or safety guidelines.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PAIR to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The dominant linked behavioral indicator is Jailbreaking, followed by Jailbreak resistance, while Harmlessness is the only linked construct. In recorded measurement claims, papers use PAIR to measure Jailbreaking, Jailbreak resistance, and Harmlessness; beyond that, one paper claims a causal relationship from PAIR to Jailbreaking by descri

nodes.name: PakBBQ
nodes.definition: Pakistani Bias Benchmark for Question Answering, a culturally and regionally adapted bias benchmark for QA tailored to the Pakistani context, with versions in English and Urdu.

nodes.name: PandaLM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, PandaLM is most commonly treated as a fine-tuned Llama-7b judge model for preference judgment tasks over other LLMs. Some papers describe it more broadly as an automated evaluator that scores or selects outputs, and one source explicitly refers to a PandaLM-7B variant. Another description frames it as a fine-tuned LLM judge benchmark used for comparison and trained on human preference data.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PandaLM to one behavioral indicator and two constructs. It is reported as measuring Instruction following and Helpfulness: one description says it addresses "relative conciseness, clarity, adherence to instructions, comprehensiveness, and formality" (PandaLM: An Automatic Evaluation Benchmark for LLM Instruction Tuning Optimization), and another says it is used "to evaluate the helpfulness of various models." Generalization appears as a related construct rather than a direct measurement claim.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to any other measurement instrument. In use, they position PandaLM as a comparison judge alongside JudgeLM and GPT-4, and as a comparison benchmark for tuned judges; one source states that

nodes.name: PAP
nodes.definition: Benchmark that uses persuasive language to evade safety filters, testing a model's ability to resist manipulation through rhetorical techniques.

nodes.name: ParaDetox
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, ParaDetox is most commonly described as a dataset of paraphrased sentence pairs that contrast toxic and non-toxic variants. One definition describes it as containing pairs of toxic and non-toxic paraphrased sentences and being used to identify toxicity-related features in a model's activations, and one paper states that it contains pairwise "non-toxic" and "toxic" sentences generated using paraphrasing. Another paper also treats it as a dataset with especially strong conditional constraints in comparison with RocStories.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ParaDetox to two constructs, Semantic preservation and Toxicity, and to one behavioral indicator, Conditional text generation. The prevailing use is to measure Toxicity, reflected in descriptions of paired toxic and non-toxic sentences, while another paper reports it as measuring Semantic preservation through a semantic similarity measure of whether generated text preserves the original meaning. A smaller use treats it as measuring Conditional text generation, with one paper reporting that ParaDetox imposes the strongest conditional constraints in that setting.

Space of uses. Papers

nodes.name: ParaRel
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, ParaRel is treated as a factual knowledge dataset for studying relational knowledge in language models. The prevailing description is a collection of paraphrased relational facts, formatted as ⟨subject, relation, object⟩ triples with multiple query variations; another definition also describes it as being used in an independent multi-problem question answering setting.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ParaRel to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. Its reported measurement use is concentrated on question-answering behavior: papers use it to measure Question answering and Open-domain question answering, including one formulation where "Given a question, the model directly predicts its answer" and another where it provides "factual information from open-domain question answering (OQA)".

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to ParaRel. In the available papers, it is used as a named evaluation dataset that authors "employ," and one paper places it alongside HotpotQA within a question-answering evaluation.

nodes.name: PartNet-Mobility
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, PartNet-Mobility is most commonly described as a large-scale dataset of 3D articulated objects with part-level segmentation and kinematic information, used for training and evaluating articulation and reconstruction tasks. A smaller framing presents it as articulated 3D objects used within the SAPIEN simulation environment to define seen and unseen manipulation tasks for evaluation. One paper also specifies a subset of five categories: Laptop, Box, Refrigerator, Storage-Furniture, and Table.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is narrow rather than spread across many targets: papers use it to measure one construct, Generalization, and one behavioral indicator, Joint prediction. The Generalization link is described through validation on an extensive test set of unseen objects, while the Joint prediction link is described through quantitative analysis on the entire dataset and reported success-rate gains over prior work.

Space of uses. Papers commonly position PartNet-Mobility as an evaluation resource: one paper says it validates performance on the dataset and fine-tunes a pre-trained model using its data, and another uses it

nodes.name: Pascal Context
nodes.definition: A dataset providing dense semantic labels for the PASCAL VOC images, used for open-vocabulary segmentation.

nodes.name: PASCAL VOC
nodes.definition: The PASCAL Visual Object Classes benchmark, used here for open-vocabulary segmentation.

nodes.name: Passkey retrieval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a synthetic long-context retrieval task or benchmark in which a model must find and repeat a hidden passkey, usually a random or five-digit code, embedded in long distracting or otherwise meaningless text. Most definitions emphasize random placement or varying depth in the sequence and treat it as a needle-in-haystack test of locating a short target token within a long context. YaRN: Efficient Context Window Extension of Large Language Models describes it as retrieving "a five-digit number" from "a large amount of otherwise meaningless text." A smaller line of work mentions n-digit variants, different difficulty levels, or a contiguous 2K-token Wiki-Text sample.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant reported use is to measure Synthetic recall, and a smaller line of work reports it as measuring Context retrieval, so the recorded links are concentrated on retrieval behaviors rather than spread across many targets. Definitions and snippets also describe it as evaluating maximum effective context length, long-range dependency modeling, information retentio

nodes.name: PatentScore
nodes.definition: A multi-dimensional evaluation framework for patent claims that integrates structural, legal, and semantic metrics through LLM-based prompting and weighted aggregation, aligned with WIPO and USPTO standards.

nodes.name: PathVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe PathVQA as a medical or biomedical visual question answering dataset or benchmark centered on pathology images. The definitions mostly converge on that framing, while differing in emphasis: one says the pathology images are drawn from textbooks and online libraries, others say it tests a model's ability to answer questions about histopathology slides, and another says it targets interpretation of complex visual medical information.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PathVQA to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing usage is to treat it as measuring medical visual question answering, with papers using it as a Med-VQA benchmark and reporting performance on it for medical VQA tasks; some papers use it more broadly to measure visual question answering, including statements that PathVQA and Q-VQA assess VQA performance. In these papers, its measurement claims stay within VQA-related behavioral indicators rather than extending to other constructs.

Space of uses. Papers usually position PathVQA as one dataset within a broader evaluation suite, most often alongside SLAKE and VQA-RAD, and in some cases with IU-Xray, Omn

nodes.name: PAWS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe PAWS as a benchmark or dataset for paraphrase detection or paraphrase identification. Definitions add that it evaluates whether two sentences are semantically equivalent and distinguishes paraphrases from non-paraphrases; one paper also describes it as Paraphrase Adversaries from Word Scrambling and notes sentence pairs with high lexical overlap that may still have different meanings.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, PAWS is linked to one behavioral indicator and one construct. The prevailing use is to measure Paraphrase detection, with several papers explicitly using PAWS for paraphrase detection or paraphrase identification; a smaller usage treats it as measuring Robustness, where one paper says the evaluation data reflect adversarial distribution shifts and are therefore suitable for evaluating OOD robustness of in-context learning.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to PAWS. Papers instead position it as one task within broader evaluation suites: one study includes it among "seven diverse tasks" for fine-tuning, another reports notable performance gains on PAWS within wider downstream eval

nodes.name: PAWS-X
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, PAWS-X is most commonly treated as a multilingual benchmark or dataset for paraphrase identification, where the model must decide whether two sentences have the same meaning. Some authors frame it more broadly as a multilingual natural language understanding benchmark for evaluating performance across languages, while others describe paired sentences across seven languages, adversarially constructed paraphrase pairs, and a task of distinguishing semantically equivalent sentences from near-duplicates. Definitions also mention both full multilingual use and, in one application, the Spanish portion of the dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is concentrated: papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator, Paraphrase detection, and to no constructs. The prevailing usage is to treat PAWS-X as measuring paraphrase identification or paraphrase detection, including in descriptions of a cross-lingual adversarial dataset for paraphrase identification.

Space of uses. No other measurement instruments are linked to it. Papers commonly place it inside broader multilingual evaluation suites, for example among several benchmarks covering reas

nodes.name: PCam
nodes.definition: A benchmark for medical imaging, specifically for identifying metastatic tissue in histopathologic scans of lymph node sections.

nodes.name: PCFG SET
nodes.definition: A dataset of ten string-edit operations based on a probabilistic context-free grammar, used to evaluate compositional sequence-to-sequence behaviors in language models.

nodes.name: PDDL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe PDDL as a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on planning tasks expressed in PDDL-style environments. In AgentSquare: Automatic LLM Agent Search in Modular Design Space, it appears within a broader evaluation set described as "covering diverse use cases in web, embodied, tool use and game scenarios."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link PDDL to any constructs or behavioral indicators through explicit measurement relationships. The only stated target is evaluating LLM agents on planning tasks expressed in PDDL-style environments, rather than a named construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. The available paper uses PDDL as a benchmark within an evaluation suite for LLM agents. No other measurement instruments are linked to it, so the evidence does not show a recurring pattern of using it alongside particular named benchmarks or as an auxiliary check.

nodes.name: Perception Test
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions frame it as a benchmark or diagnostic for multimodal or video models, centered on visual perception over video sequences and often paired with reasoning. The prevailing description is a video perception or video understanding benchmark, while some papers describe it more specifically as a multiple-choice question answering dataset for perception-based reasoning, including object tracking and spatial awareness, or as an open-set benchmark from which action-related questions can be selected. Another strand presents it as a diagnostic spanning video, audio, and text, targeting skills such as memory, abstraction, physics, and semantics and reasoning types such as descriptive, explanatory, predictive, and counterfactual.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three constructs and no behavioral indicators. Its direct measurement links are to Long video understanding and Video understanding, so the measurement claims do not center on a single construct label. A separate related link connects it to Reasoning, which matches definitions that describe the benchmark as focusing on perception and reasoning skills.

Space of uses. Papers usually use it as

nodes.name: Perspective API
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is an external API or automated tool for toxicity assessment of text, used to score generated outputs for harmful content. Definitions largely converge on an overall toxicity score plus attribute-level scores, commonly including toxicity, severe toxicity, threat, profanity, insult, and identity attack; some papers say it covers six attributes, one selects five safety aspects, and another uses eight attributes including sexually explicit and flirtation. A smaller line of work describes it as a toxicity classifier, a content-safety evaluation tool, or a Perspective toxicity model, and papers note scores in the 0 to 1 range, with one paper also using it to identify toxic spans.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The dominant use is to measure Toxicity: papers describe assigning a toxicity score or probability to each reply, sentence, or prediction, and one paper calls it a widely recognized automated toxicity detection tool and the de facto benchmark. A smaller line of work reports it as measuring Harmful content generation, Harmlessness, and Safety, so the claims spread beyon

nodes.name: PG-19
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, PG-19 is most commonly described as a long-context or long-form language modeling dataset or benchmark built from Project Gutenberg books. Definitions vary in detail: some papers describe long documents derived from books for evaluating extended contexts, while others describe an open-vocabulary benchmark with 11 gigabytes of text from over 28,000 Project Gutenberg books published prior to 1919, or a next-token generation and auto-regressive language modeling benchmark. Papers also refer to specific subsets and evaluation slices, including test or validation sets of 100 long books or documents, sampled long documents truncated to chosen lengths, and samples averaging 69k words.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use PG-19 to measure five constructs and one behavioral indicator, so its claimed targets are spread across several areas rather than concentrated on one. Among linked constructs, long-context understanding appears most often, followed by length generalization; smaller lines of work use it to measure continual learning, fluency, and text generation quality. It is also linked to one behavioral indicator, long-form text generation, an

nodes.name: PGD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, PGD is treated as an iterative adversarial attack that repeatedly takes small steps in the gradient direction and projects each update back into a constrained perturbation space. One definition further specifies it as a white-box attack, and some usage is stated specifically as PGD-l∞, where the projection keeps perturbations within ε∞ constraints; papers also describe it as a method for crafting or generating adversarial examples.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers do not report PGD as measuring any construct or behavioral indicator, and no linked target construct is identified.

Space of uses. One paper explicitly employs PGD-l∞ alongside CW-l2 as two standard adversarial attack methods, while other papers refer to PGD more generally as an iterative approach for crafting adversarial examples.

nodes.name: PGPS9K
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for geometry problem solving that includes high-quality diagrams and detailed annotations.

nodes.name: PHEME
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe PHEME as a benchmark dataset for fake news detection made up of tweets related to five major news events. One definition also specifies its split and scale, stating that it contains 1,414 training tweets and 608 testing tweets.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded uses, papers use PHEME to measure misinformation detection. It is linked to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs, so the reported measurement claim is concentrated on that single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple outcomes.

Space of uses. Across the cited studies, PHEME is used alongside Twitter and Weibo in one evaluation setup, and alongside Weibo21 and LLM-mis in another. Papers position it as one of several public or widely-used benchmark datasets for experiments, rather than as a standalone evaluation protocol.

nodes.name: PHTest
nodes.definition: Benchmark dataset for assessing over-refusal behaviors in language models using pseudo-harmful prompts.

nodes.name: Pick-a-Pic
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, Pick-a-Pic is described as a large-scale open dataset derived from a web platform that collects real users' creative intentions. The prevailing description presents it as being used to evaluate whether generation aligns with user preference, and the available snippet in TIGeR: Unifying Text-to-Image Generation and Retrieval with Large Multimodal Models repeats this framing by calling it "a large-scale open dataset" that "stems from a web platform collecting real users’ creative intention."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Pick-a-Pic to one construct and no behavioral indicators. The recorded construct is Multimodal alignment: one paper treats Pick-a-Pic as measuring it by listing Pick-a-Pic among text-to-image evaluation benchmarks when reporting results on multimodal alignment.

Space of uses. The available usage evidence positions Pick-a-Pic as a benchmark used alongside other text-to-image evaluation benchmarks rather than in isolation. In Natural Language Inference Improves Compositionality in Vision-Language Models, it is reported together with DrawBench, EditBench, COCO-T2I, and TIFA160 when the paper says it reports results on

nodes.name: Pile-10k
nodes.definition: A 10,000-document subset of The Pile, a large and diverse text corpus, used for evaluating language model perplexity.

nodes.name: Pile-CC
nodes.definition: A component of The Pile dataset derived from the CommonCrawl web corpus, used in this study as a key validation set to predict downstream performance.

nodes.name: PIQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, PIQA is most commonly described as Physical Interaction: Question Answering, a benchmark or dataset for physical commonsense reasoning about everyday situations, objects, and interactions. The prevailing format is multiple-choice question answering, often framed as choosing between two candidate solutions or selecting the most physically plausible action or solution; one paper describes 21k questions across different subsets. A few papers sharpen this as grounded physical world understanding or goal-driven questions, while isolated descriptions label it Physical Interaction Quality Assessment.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PIQA to 13 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures Commonsense reasoning, with additional papers using it for Reasoning and Physical world understanding; on the behavioral side, the most recurrent indicators are Language understanding task performance and Zero-shot question answering. Claims therefore cluster around physical commonsense and reasoning, but they also spread to 10 other constructs and 10 other behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. Across the literature, PIQA is u

nodes.name: PKU
nodes.definition: Chinese word segmentation dataset used to evaluate tokenization performance in character-dense language processing.

nodes.name: PKU-SafeRLHF
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, PKU-SafeRLHF is most commonly treated as a safety-alignment preference dataset and benchmark built from human preference comparisons. Descriptions usually present conversations or instruction-response pairs with one prompt and two responses, annotated with preference and safety information, often across helpfulness and harmlessness; one paper specifies two response labels, and another describes a preference label plus a harmless label for the preferred response. Some authors emphasize subsets for harmful-query or red-teaming evaluation, covering areas such as insults, immorality, crime, emotional harm, and privacy, while others use it as a public benchmark for generative judges or as reward-model training data with safe and unsafe responses. Reported scale differs across papers, from 83.4K preference entries to over 300k instances, and one paper describes 1 million human-labeled data points.

What it is claimed to measure. Its prevailing measurement use is for Harmlessness and Helpfulness: papers use it to measure both, often describing independent rankings or annotations on those two dimensions. Across papers, it is linked to 5 constructs and no behavior

nodes.name: PKU-SafeRLHF-10K
nodes.definition: A dataset containing 10,000 human-labeled preference pairs on the helpfulness and harmlessness of responses, used for fine-tuning and aligning large language models for safety.

nodes.name: Places365
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, Places365 is most commonly described as a large-scale scene-centric image dataset with 365 scene categories, used for scene recognition or classification tasks. A smaller framing presents it as a scene classification benchmark used to evaluate descriptions on scene categories, so papers alternate between calling it a dataset and a benchmark while keeping the same scene-category focus.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, Places365 is used to measure Image classification, and this is its only linked behavioral indicator. It is not linked to any constructs, so the reported measurement use centers on 1 behavioral indicator rather than multiple constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position Places365 as part of broader multi-dataset evaluations, for example alongside CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CUB, and another paper includes it among 12 image recognition datasets; one study also notes that "BLIP2 FlanT5 performs better on the Places365 dataset," explicitly treating it as a scene classification dataset.

nodes.name: PlanBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, the prevailing framing is as a benchmark for evaluating planning in LLMs. One definition narrows this to planning and Reasoning about Actions and Change, while another describes PlanBench as using Planning Domain Description Language problems converted into natural language to evaluate planning and reasoning abilities.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PlanBench to one construct and no behavioral indicators, and the linked construct is Planning. The measurement claims therefore converge on planning rather than spreading across multiple targets, with one paper citing PlanBench among specialized benchmarks used in discussions of complex planning or multi-step reasoning challenges.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the papers that mention it, PlanBench is used chiefly as a comparison point for other benchmarks, including side by side contrasts with prior Reasoning about Actions and Change benchmarks, and it is also grouped with closely related work that converts Planning Domain Description Language problems into natural language.

nodes.name: PLLuM-Align
nodes.definition: Polish preference dataset containing human-annotated response ratings, rankings, and multi-turn dialogues for evaluating alignment in Polish LLMs.

nodes.name: Plutus-ben
nodes.definition: The first Greek financial evaluation benchmark, assessing LLMs across six tasks: numeric NER, textual NER, question answering, extractive summarization, abstractive summarization, and topic classification using expert-annotated Greek financial datasets.

nodes.name: PMC-VQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, PMC-VQA is described as a medical or clinical visual question answering dataset. Definitions differ in emphasis: one treats it simply as a clinical VQA dataset mentioned for comparison, another calls it a multi-modal, multiple-choice VQA dataset derived from medical literature where models choose the correct answer from four options, and another describes a large-scale medical VQA dataset that evaluates deriving answers from both text and images in scientific publications.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PMC-VQA to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The reported measurement use is concentrated on medical visual question answering and visual question answering: papers use it to measure those VQA-related behaviors, including as a medical VQA dataset in evaluation and under the task type Visual Question Answering. The available relationships do not extend beyond these VQA-related behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. In use, papers place PMC-VQA among other medical VQA evaluation datasets. One paper evaluates a method on PMC-VQA alongside SLAKE and VQA-RAD, another lists it under the task type Visual Question Answering, and

nodes.name: PMO
nodes.definition: Practical Molecular Optimization (PMO), a benchmark of molecular generation tasks used to evaluate optimization performance across many target properties and structures.

nodes.name: Pointwise rating
nodes.definition: An evaluation method where an LLM is prompted to assign a numerical score to individual answers based on their correctness, which are then compared to establish a preference.

nodes.name: PoisonedRAG
nodes.definition: A baseline RAG attack method that uses poisoned documents to manipulate retrieval and responses.

nodes.name: PolitiFact
nodes.definition: A dataset of real-world viral claims spread online, verified by journalists, used to assess models' ability to handle real-world misinformation.

nodes.name: PolitiFact (FakeNewsNet)
nodes.definition: A real-world human-written misinformation dataset focused on political fake news, used as a source for generating new misinformation and as a baseline for comparison.

nodes.name: POPE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats POPE as a benchmark or dataset for evaluating object hallucination in multimodal or large vision-language models. Most definitions describe it as balanced yes/no or true/false visual question answering about whether a named object is present in an image, often framed as a binary classification or polling task with positive and negative samples; several papers add that it has Popular, Random, and Adversarial versions or splits based on different ways of sampling non-existing objects. A smaller number of papers describe it more loosely as a VQA hallucination benchmark, and isolated descriptions expand the name as Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation or Probing Object-level Hallucination, while one paper instead glosses it as Positional Object Perception Evaluation for localization and counting.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use POPE mainly to measure hallucination-related outcomes, especially hallucination and object hallucination, sometimes stated more specifically as object existence or object-level hallucinations. Overall, it is linked to 10 constructs and 9 behavioral indicators. Beyond those dominant u

nodes.name: PopQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, PopQA is most commonly described as an open-domain question answering benchmark for factual knowledge retrieval, especially on rare entities, low-popularity questions, and long-tail knowledge. A recurring alternative description treats it as an entity-centric QA dataset, with some definitions saying it is derived from Wikidata triples and others calling it a large-scale open-domain QA dataset. Papers also describe different ways of using it, including a long-tail subset of rare-entity queries, use as a single-hop dataset, and conversion of its questions into a closed-book sentence-completion format.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PopQA to two behavioral indicators and five constructs. The prevailing use is to measure open-domain question answering, followed by question answering, with many papers listing it directly among open-domain QA evaluation tasks. Across constructs, the links spread across generalization and factual knowledge most often, followed by knowledge conflict resolution, memorization, and text generation quality.

Space of uses. Papers usually position PopQA as one dataset in a broader QA benchmark suite, most often alongside

nodes.name: PoSum-Bench
nodes.definition: A bilingual benchmark for evaluating positional bias in conversational summarization, covering English and French datasets across formal meetings, casual dialogues, and customer service interactions, with a reference-free evaluation framework based on semantic similarity.

nodes.name: Prefilling attack
nodes.definition: An adversarial attack method used for evaluation where the model's generation is prefixed with an affirmative phrase (e.g., 'Sure, I’m happy to help with that.') to test its vulnerability to jailbreaking.

nodes.name: Presidio
nodes.definition: Data protection and de-identification API used to identify and classify personally identifiable information (PII) types in text, including name, gender, race, date-time, and location.

nodes.name: PricingLogic
nodes.definition: Benchmark comprising 300 natural-language questions derived from 42 real-world tourism pricing policies, assessing LLMs on customer-type pricing and bundled-tour discount reasoning across three difficulty levels.

nodes.name: PRISM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat PRISM as a chat or preference dataset built from multi-turn conversations between humans and LLMs. In that usage it is described as globally diverse, focused on values and controversial opinions, and as containing 27,172 conversations used to solicit human feedback for preference alignment across 9 speaker features and 60 demographic groups; papers also differ on annotation format, describing both N-way preference ratings and binary choices. A smaller line of work uses the same name differently, either for Posterior-Refined Inference for Subset Membership, which updates an LR-Attack score with a world-model prior, or for a reference-free quality estimation procedure that uses a multilingual machine translation model with forced decoding to score other models’ outputs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link PRISM to any constructs or behavioral indicators through measured_by relationships. Where authors describe its target directly, the dataset form is framed around collecting preference ratings and human feedback for preference alignment, evaluating conversational preferences, and focusing on values and controversial opinions, rather

nodes.name: PRM800K
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, PRM800K is most commonly described as a dataset of mathematical or MATH reasoning problems with step-by-step solutions annotated by humans at the process level, often for training process-supervised reward models. Definitions vary in emphasis: some describe manually annotated step-by-step feedback or correctness labels, one paper narrows it to 80,000 incorrect stepwise student solutions with 2,077 test examples marked at the first error step, and another frames each reasoning step as positive, negative, or neutral. Papers also mention an easy, level 1-3 portion of the dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Its recorded measurement use is concentrated rather than broad: papers link it to 1 construct, Mathematical reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators. A paper treats it as measuring Mathematical reasoning, describing PRM800K as derived from the MATH dataset, which contains challenging competition-level math problems.

Space of uses. Papers mainly use PRM800K as training data for step-level or token-level reward models, and also for training policy and reward models on a subset of the data. Usage descriptions repeatedly place it alongside M

nodes.name: PRMBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, PRMBench is most commonly described as a benchmark or benchmark dataset for evaluating process-level rewards, or process-level reward models, in reasoning chains. One description makes its format explicit: it is built on the PRM800K corpus and contains 6k math problems across 9 error categories, while another emphasizes that it assesses step-level correctness in multi-step problem solving. Definitions also frame it as targeting reasoning correctness and error detection.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PRMBench to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claims are concentrated on Prompt sensitivity, Soundness, and Simplicity: papers say it evaluates models across simplicity, soundness, and sensitivity, further divided into nine aspects. A smaller line of work reports it as measuring Error analysis, describing it as a benchmark with particular emphasis on granular error diagnosis.

Space of uses. Papers use PRMBench as an evaluation dataset for reporting model results, sometimes as one dataset among several. One study evaluates on four datasets, pairing it with DeltaBench, ClaimTrees, and CaptainCookRecipes, while ano

nodes.name: ProcessBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing description is a benchmark for mathematical reasoning that provides step-by-step solutions with human annotation of where errors occur. One recurring formulation is that it contains 3,400 test cases or problems, mainly competition- and Olympiad-level math, with annotations by multiple human experts and four subsets, as described in ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning. Other papers describe the same resource more generally as containing human-annotated stepwise labels for mathematical solutions, with emphasis on the earliest or first incorrect step.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most commonly describe ProcessBench as evaluating a model's ability to identify erroneous steps in mathematical reasoning, especially step-level error identification focused on the earliest or first incorrect step. Definitions also frame it as assessing detection of the first incorrect step in LLM-generated mathematical solutions. Papers do not link it to named constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. In the available descriptions, papers use ProcessBench as an evaluation benchmark for step-level error

nodes.name: Project Euler
nodes.definition: Test set consisting of 45 C implementations of Project Euler mathematical challenge problems, used to evaluate transpilation accuracy on algorithmic code.

nodes.name: Prometheus
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing treatment is as an LLM-based evaluator or open-source LM judge for scoring generated outputs. Most definitions describe it as a model trained to evaluate other language models or for general human preference evaluation in natural language generation, with some papers referring to a later Prometheus variant. The task framing varies across papers: it is used for summaries, literary translation, text-to-SQL assessment, and generated articles, and different definitions name dimensions such as interest, coherence, relevance, coverage, diversity, breadth, depth, and novelty.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to score output quality across several task-specific dimensions, but no constructs and no behavioral indicators are explicitly linked to it. The reported targets do not converge on one recurring linked construct: papers describe it as assessing summarization quality, translation quality, text-to-SQL assessment, general human preference evaluation in natural language generation, and article quality through dimensions like relevance, breadth, depth, and novelty.

Space of uses. In use, papers position it as an automatic judge fo

nodes.name: PrOntoQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers refer to it as PrOntoQA or ProntoQA and most commonly treat it as a synthetic logical reasoning dataset or benchmark. Definitions typically describe question-answering examples built from ontologies, hierarchical relationships, or axioms, where the model must decide whether a multi-step reasoning chain or proposition is correct; some papers further specify chains of thought and 3-hop deductions. A smaller line of work frames it more specifically as a synthetic first-order logic benchmark and as an out-of-distribution evaluation set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing measurement claim is logical reasoning, with smaller framings as reasoning more broadly and complex reasoning; some evidence also describes its use in logical deduction or deductive reasoning evaluations. Among behavioral indicators, papers use it for logical problem solving and question answering, so the reported measurement claims cluster around reasoning tasks rather than spreading widely across unrelated targets.

Space of uses. Its linked-instrument profile is small, with 2 other instruments named: ProofWriter most often, th

nodes.name: PrOntoQA-OOD
nodes.definition: An out-of-distribution logical reasoning benchmark used to evaluate multi-step hypothesis verification.

nodes.name: Proof-pile
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, Proof-pile is most commonly described as a long-context language modeling dataset centered on mathematical material, either as a cleaned Arxiv Math dataset or, more specifically, as a 13GB collection of long mathematical documents. The descriptions converge on long-form technical or scientific content with many long sequence samples, though some authors describe it more broadly as scientific and technical texts rather than emphasizing Arxiv Math.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Proof-pile to evaluate language modeling performance on long sequences, most often through perplexity, including long-sequence or long-context performance in technical, scientific, or mathematical domains. No paper links it to a named construct or behavioral indicator, so the recorded descriptions stay at the level of language modeling performance and perplexity rather than a broader measurement claim.

Space of uses. Papers most often use Proof-pile alongside GovReport for long-context evaluation, and another study places it beside PG19 and CodeParrot in a perplexity comparison. It is typically used in evaluation settings, with papers reporting perplexity o

nodes.name: ProofNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ProofNet is most commonly treated as a Lean benchmark for undergraduate mathematics. Definitions variously describe it as a theorem-proving benchmark, a standard automated-theorem-proving dataset, and an autoformalization benchmark with paired natural-language and Lean statements; one paper also uses it as a source of high-quality mathematical proof data. Several descriptions specify 371 exercises or statement-formalization pairs from the undergraduate curriculum, formalized in Lean 3, while some descriptions emphasize isolated or less context-dependent problems and another contrasts it with competition benchmarks by saying its exercises are generally drawn from standard textbooks. Papers also refer to variants: ProofNet-test as the college-level split, and ProofNet# as a very close corrected version.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ProofNet to measure 4 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing use is to measure theorem proving and autoformalization, with several papers stating formal theorem proving more specifically; one paper also uses it to measure information retrieval. At the construct level, papers report it as measuring ge

nodes.name: ProofWriter
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat ProofWriter as a deductive or logical reasoning benchmark built from facts and rules. Definitions variously describe it as a dataset based on first-order logic rules, a collection of natural language facts and rules used to decide whether a query can be proved, or small rule-bases that require multi-step deduction and proof construction under a closed-world assumption. Some papers also frame it as involving natural language proof generation, note moderately complex structures such as conjunctions and disjunctions, and mention a broader ProofWriter family that includes Birds-Electricity and ParaRules.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ProofWriter to three constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure Logical reasoning, often described as deductive or logical inference, while smaller lines of work use it to measure Chain-of-thought reasoning and Complex reasoning; one paper characterizes that latter use by noting that each question requires three hops of reasoning.

Space of uses. Papers explicitly relate ProofWriter only to PrOntoQA, and they often place the two together as logical reasoning benchmarks. More broadly

nodes.name: PropBank
nodes.definition: A corpus of verb argument annotations (Kingsbury and Palmer, 2002) applied to the Penn Treebank, providing the verb-specific tense and aspect labels used in this study.

nodes.name: ProteinGym
nodes.definition: A benchmark suite composed of hundreds of deep mutational scan (DMS) studies used to evaluate the zero-shot fitness prediction capabilities of protein language models.

nodes.name: PStance
nodes.definition: Large-scale dataset focusing on individuals' stances toward U.S. political figures (Trump, Biden, Sanders) with binary labels (favor or against), used to evaluate performance in real-world political discourse.

nodes.name: PTB
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat PTB, usually expanded as Penn Treebank, as a language modeling benchmark, corpus, or dataset. The prevailing description is as an evaluation set for perplexity or next-token prediction, especially in pruning, quantization, and compression studies, though some papers instead use it in zero-shot evaluation or as a source of PropBank-annotated sentences for grammatical analysis. Definitions occasionally refer to particular versions or slices, such as a test split or a version "preprocessed by Dyer et al. (2016)."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PTB to two constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is to measure Text generation: several papers report perplexity on PTB for language generation tasks, and relationship evidence explicitly groups PTB with datasets used "for text generation tasks." Smaller lines of work use PTB to measure Language modeling ability and Zero-shot generalization.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to PTB in the recorded relationships. In practice, papers usually report it together with WikiText2 and C4, and sometimes with WikiText103 or LAMBADA; several snippets use the trio "Wi

nodes.name: PubHealth
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, PubHealth is most commonly described as a fact verification dataset or claim verification benchmark in the public health domain, often grouped with closed-set tasks. Definitions consistently emphasize public health or medical claims, and several descriptions frame it as evaluating closed-set factual verification or the truthfulness of health-related statements. A smaller line of work instead describes it as a closed-set generative dataset comprising medical claims on various biomedical topics.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PubHealth to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing linked use is to measure fact checking: papers describe it as requiring a system to verify a given claim based on retrieved documents. One paper also uses sampled claims from PubHealth to investigate domain-specific factual knowledge in the public health domain, so it is also reported as measuring domain knowledge; overall, the claimed measurement scope is concentrated rather than spread across many targets.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it through explicit relationships. In practice, papers often use PubHealth ins

nodes.name: PublicViews
nodes.definition: A dataset extracted from TwinViews-13k containing political statements across 31 topics and explicitness variants for evaluating political bias and factuality in generated news.

nodes.name: PubMed
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats PubMed as a citation-network or text-attributed graph benchmark derived from the PubMed database, where documents or scientific publications are the nodes and node classification is the usual evaluation task. Some definitions make this more specific by describing it as a biomedical citation network or as publications related to diabetes. A smaller line of work uses the same name for different resources: one paper refers to "PubMed1" as a collection of biomedical paper abstracts used as a representative domain corpus for finetuning, another defines PubMed as medical scientific articles for summarizing authors' conclusions from experiment descriptions, and another uses Scientific Papers (Pubmed) as an out-of-domain benchmark; one graph paper also uses PubMed for node-level and edge-level tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PubMed to 3 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing use is to measure node classification, with papers describing it as a widely adopted or well-established dataset for that task and reporting node classification accuracy on it. Other papers use it to measure link predict

nodes.name: PubMedQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as a biomedical question-answering benchmark or dataset built from PubMed abstracts or articles. Most descriptions say it asks yes/no/maybe questions grounded in a corresponding abstract, though some papers emphasize long-form or free-form answers or explanations, one paper describes biomedical multiple-choice QA, and another presents it simply as a held-out question-answering benchmark. Papers also note corresponding contexts and named subsets such as the pqa_labeled split.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers report PubMedQA as measuring five behavioral indicators and two constructs. Medical question answering is the most common reported behavioral indicator, while other papers use it to measure knowledge-based question answering, machine reading comprehension, natural language inference, and question answering; one of these descriptions explicitly treats the yes/no QA setup as an English natural language inference task related to medical research papers. At the construct level, papers report contextual reasoning and medical knowledge, so its claimed measurement use spans several task framings rather than a single target.

Spac

nodes.name: PUNMEMECN
nodes.definition: A multimodal benchmark for Chinese pun memes that assesses vision-language models on pun detection, sentiment analysis, and contextual meme response selection using annotated memes and simulated chat conversations.

nodes.name: PutnamBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe PutnamBench as a benchmark of undergraduate-level mathematics competition questions used to evaluate theorem proving on challenging problems. Some definitions give a fuller format, describing a multi-language benchmark with 1692 hand-constructed formalizations of 640 theorems from the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition in Lean 4, Isabelle, and Coq, while shorter descriptions refer more simply to formalized problems from the Putnam competition.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread widely: PutnamBench is linked to 2 behavioral indicators, theorem proving and formal theorem proving, and to 1 construct, problem-solving ability. The prevailing usage is to evaluate theorem proving, including neural, symbolic, and domain-agnostic theorem provers, while a narrower framing says it measures problem-solving ability by requiring problem-solving and proficiency across a broad range of topics taught in undergraduate mathematics courses.

Space of uses. One usage pattern is to report PutnamBench together with miniF2F and ProofNet for whole-proof generation methods. More broad

nodes.name: PWWS
nodes.definition: Probability Weighted Word Saliency, an adversarial text attack procedure that uses WordNet synonym replacements guided by saliency to reduce classifier prediction confidence.

nodes.name: Q-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, Q-Bench is most commonly described as a benchmark for low-level vision tasks or for assessing low-level visual capabilities in general-purpose foundation models and MLLMs. One paper further presents it as covering perception, description, and quality assessment, while another use treats it as an existing benchmark for in-domain multi-image evaluation. A test-set variant, QBench-Testset (QBenchT), is also named.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Q-Bench to one construct, Multi-image reasoning, and one behavioral indicator, Image captioning. One paper uses it to measure multi-image reasoning in a multi-image task suite, and another uses its low-level visual description component to measure image captioning, describing that component as testing how accurately and thoroughly models describe attributes, as noted in Meteor: Mamba-based Traversal of Rationale for Large Language and Vision Models.

Space of uses. In the cited uses, Q-Bench appears as one benchmark within broader evaluation suites rather than as a standalone protocol. Papers place it alongside NLVR2 in an in-domain multi-image setup, alongside Mantis-Eval and BLINK for multi-ima

nodes.name: QAMPARI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed definitions, QAMPARI is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for attributable, factoid question answering, used for evaluation. The definitions converge that questions may have multiple answers, and one paper specifies this more narrowly as a factoid QA dataset in which each answer is "a list of entities drawn from different passages." Papers also describe it as a setting for evaluating precision and recall in attributed generation.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement claims do not converge on a single target.
