Papers link QAMPARI to 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators: it is reported as measuring Trustworthiness and Unanswerability detection ability, in both cases through measured_by links. One definition also frames it as evaluating precision and recall in attributed generation, so its documented use spans these evaluation targets rather than centering on only one.

Space of uses. Papers use QAMPARI as an evaluation dataset, often alongside ASQA and ELI5. As one study puts it, "Evaluations on the benchmark datasets ASQA, QAMPARI, and ELI5 show that models trained with TRUST-ALIGN outperform the competitive baseli

nodes.name: QASC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description treats QASC as a question-answering benchmark or dataset for science questions that require multi-step or multi-hop reasoning, often by integrating, composing, or reasoning over multiple facts from multiple sentences. Some authors instead place it under commonsense reasoning or multiple-choice comprehension, one definition says it provides questions and associated facts, and another expands the name as "Question Answering via Sentence Composition". A smaller line of work also presents it as an elementary science or scientific reasoning benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link QASC to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claim is that it measures Question answering, with papers using it for evaluation or fine-tuning under that label; a smaller line of work reports it as measuring Commonsense reasoning by including it among commonsense QA datasets. The reported measurement uses are therefore concentrated on those two targets rather than spread across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers commonly present QASC as one dataset in broader evaluation suites. It is often used a

nodes.name: Qasper
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Qasper is most commonly described as a question-answering benchmark or dataset over full NLP papers, research papers, or scientific articles, with information-seeking questions grounded in the paper text. Definitions differ in emphasis: some describe full-paper or long scientific-document QA, while others place it in the SCROLL benchmark and note that it includes abstractive, extractive, yes/no, and unanswerable questions, including cases unanswerable from the provided abstract or full text. One description says it includes 5,049 questions across 1,585 NLP papers, another says the papers are filtered from S2ORC, and some work refers to a Qasper subset from LongBench.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Qasper to 3 behavioral indicators and 3 constructs. The prevailing use is to measure question answering, and other papers use it to measure document question answering and synthetic recall. At the construct level, papers report it as measuring length generalization, long-context reasoning, and long-context understanding.

Space of uses. The only recorded instrument link is that one paper relates Qasper to SCROLLS, presenting it among long-context op

nodes.name: QM9
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, QM9 is described as a quantum-chemistry or molecular property prediction benchmark for small molecules, with ground-state 3D structures and use in computed property prediction. One paper states that it "contains over 130,000 molecules with ground-state 3D structures obtained through DFT computations" (3D-MolT5: Leveraging Discrete Structural Information for Molecule-Text Modeling). Another paper treats it as a regression benchmark for quantum chemistry properties, including HUMO, LUMO, and HUMO-LUMO gap.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link QM9 to no constructs and to two behavioral indicators. It is reported as measuring Molecular property prediction and Molecule generation, so the recorded claims are spread across task-level indicators rather than concentrated on any linked construct. The more detailed measurement framing is for computed or molecular property prediction, while a separate paper also reports molecule generation on QM9.

Space of uses. Papers use QM9 mainly as an evaluation dataset. In one study it appears alongside PubChemQC and PubChem as one of three datasets used to evaluate performance on computed property prediction, and a

nodes.name: QMSum
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe QMSum as a query-based multi-domain meeting summarization dataset or benchmark. Definitions usually say it contains meeting transcripts together with summaries, questions, or query-summary pairs focused on specific questions about the dialogue, often across domains such as academic and industrial product meetings; some also describe realistic multi-party transcripts, and another description says it aggregates ICSI, AMI, and Parliament meetings. A smaller variation in naming presents it as SUM-QMSUM, a summarization benchmark requiring summaries of meeting transcripts, and some uses restrict evaluation to its "general queries" for global summarization.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use QMSum to measure 4 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing behavioral framing is text summarization, with a smaller line of work using it for dialogue summarization; papers also report it as measuring generalization, length generalization, long-context understanding, and text generation quality. Taken together, its measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than concentrated on a single construct.

Space of uses. The p

nodes.name: QNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, QNLI is most commonly described as a question-answering natural language inference benchmark or dataset. Most definitions frame it as an entailment-style binary classification task over question-sentence pairs, asking whether a sentence contains the answer to a question, and several also note that it is derived from SQuAD. A smaller number of papers describe it more generally as question answering framed as textual entailment, and one describes the input as question-paragraph pairs rather than question-sentence pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers report QNLI as measuring 2 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure Natural language inference, with several papers explicitly listing QNLI among inference tasks; papers also use it to measure Natural language understanding, Language understanding task performance, Question answering, and Text classification, with one additional construct link to Reasoning. Most recorded measurement claims therefore concern inference and language understanding rather than a single exclusive target.

Space of uses. In use, papers frequently position QNLI as one task within broader eval

nodes.name: QQP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, QQP is most commonly described as the Quora Question Pairs dataset or benchmark for paraphrase identification, duplicate-question recognition, or semantic similarity, where the task is to decide whether two questions are paraphrases or semantically equivalent. Definitions largely converge on question pairs whose labels indicate whether the pair are paraphrases or semantically equivalent, and one paper specifies a collection of more than 400,000 question pairs. Some authors explicitly place QQP within GLUE, and one paper uses an adversarially perturbed form with added typos.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most often use QQP to measure one behavioral indicator, Paraphrase detection, with relationship evidence also describing it as paraphrase identification and a semantic similarity task. A smaller line of work links QQP to two constructs, Adversarial robustness and Generalization. In those cases, one paper reports using QQP to evaluate robustness under character-level typos, and another reports it among datasets used to assess generalization on NLU tasks.

Space of uses. QQP is linked to one other instrument, GLUE, and papers commonly position it as

nodes.name: QuAC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, QuAC is most commonly described as the Question Answering in Context benchmark or dataset for conversational question answering. Definitions converge on a format with interconnected questions in a conversational, multi-turn dialogue, and one paper adds that it evaluates whether a model can understand context and participate in a dialogue about a text. In On Synthesizing Data for Context Attribution in Question Answering, it is further described as featuring coreferences across turns, challenging models to track context across multiple turns.

What it is claimed to measure. Recorded uses link QuAC to one construct, Reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators. The reported measurement claim is narrow rather than spread across many targets: one paper lists QUAC among the benchmarks used "for reasoning abilities," so papers use it to measure Reasoning rather than a wider set of constructs.

Space of uses. Papers use QuAC alongside other benchmarks rather than in isolation. One usage places it with ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, SIQA, PIQA, and WinoGrande in an all 0-shot evaluation for reasoning abilities, while another uses it with CoQA, OR-QuAC, and DoQ

nodes.name: QualBench
nodes.definition: A multi-domain Chinese question-answering benchmark for assessing localized, vertical-domain knowledge in LLMs, comprising over 17,000 questions from 24 Chinese professional qualification exams across six domains.

nodes.name: QuALITY
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, QuALITY is most commonly described as a long-context, single-document question answering benchmark built from stories or articles paired with multiple-choice questions. Definitions converge on long passages or long documents, with one paper saying passages average about 5,000 tokens and another describing English passages between 2K and 8K tokens; several papers also describe it as reading comprehension or long-input QA. Most uses keep the multiple-choice format, though some papers adapt it, either by requiring the model to generate the answer directly without the four options or by recasting it as binary-choice extractive QA.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link QuALITY to 2 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The dominant use is to measure question answering, especially multiple-choice question answering and machine reading comprehension, and papers also use it to measure long-context understanding, with one snippet saying such closed-ended tasks focus on "understanding and reasoning within long contexts." These links are concentrated on QA and long-context abilities rather than spread across many constructs. A smaller, different claim report

nodes.name: QuaRel
nodes.definition: A question answering dataset that tests qualitative reasoning about the relationships between quantities.

nodes.name: QuoteSum
nodes.definition: A long-form question answering benchmark where the task is to generate answers that are semi-extractive, meaning they are composed of direct quotes from multiple provided source documents.

nodes.name: QVHighlights
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats QVHighlights as an evaluation benchmark for highlight detection, or more broadly for detecting moments and highlights in videos from natural language queries. Definitions describe it as requiring a model to identify all highlight moments and their saliency scores for a given query, and one relationship quote characterizes it as featuring over 10,000 YouTube videos across various themes. A smaller line of work treats it as a video dataset used for QA data creation, drawing on sparsely annotated captions and event pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing measurement claim is that QVHighlights measures Temporal grounding, with papers using it for temporal video grounding and describing it as aiding systems in identifying relevant moments and highlights in response to user queries. A smaller use links it to Referring expression understanding through experiments on the video grounding task.

Space of uses. Papers most often position QVHighlights as the evaluation benchmark itself, with one study stating that it uses QVHighlights "as the evaluation

nodes.name: R-GSM
nodes.definition: A math reasoning dataset used to evaluate reasoning performance under swapped conditions.

nodes.name: R-Judge
nodes.definition: Benchmark for coding and software engineering tasks involving high-risk bash commands or API calls, assessing safety and alignment in programming environments.

nodes.name: RACE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing treats RACE as a large-scale reading comprehension benchmark or dataset drawn from English examinations for middle and high school students, typically described as passage-based, multiple-choice questions that require reasoning over provided passages. Several definitions explicitly mention the RACE-High and RACE-Middle subsets, and related descriptions expand the name as ReAding Comprehension from Examinations. A smaller set of papers describes it more specifically as assessing reasoning and understanding ability, factual question answering, educational knowledge, or natural language understanding, and one paper calls it a "needle-in-a-haystack" task that demands identifying critical information within lengthy contexts.

What it is claimed to measure. Most papers use RACE to measure reading comprehension, especially machine reading comprehension: papers link it to 4 behavioral indicators, namely machine reading comprehension, language understanding task performance, multiple-choice question answering, and zero-shot task performance. They also link it to 7 constructs, with the most often linked being commonsense reasoning, general abil

nodes.name: RAGAS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the dominant framing is of RAGAS as an automated, LLM-based evaluator for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Definitions variously describe it as a pointwise evaluation system, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation Assessment framework, and an automated evaluation framework, with one description adding that it uses prompted frontier models and embedding models to score responses. The outcomes it evaluates are usually described through metrics such as faithfulness and context relevance, with some definitions also naming refusal, answer relevance, and claim-level decomposition.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RAGAS to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators, so the recorded use is concentrated rather than spread across many outcomes. The only explicit measured_by relation says that RAGAS measures Faithfulness. More broadly, definitions and snippets also report it as assessing metrics such as context relevance, answer relevance, and refusal.

Space of uses. Papers mainly position RAGAS as a reference or comparison evaluator within broader RAG assessment setups. One study says it is run as a reference point, another cites it with RAG-Checker

nodes.name: RAGTruth
nodes.definition: A high-quality, manually annotated benchmark dataset specifically designed for evaluating RAG hallucination detection, covering tasks like question answering, data-to-text writing, and news summarization.

nodes.name: RAID
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, RAID is treated as a dataset or benchmark for machine-generated text detection, most commonly described as spanning multiple domains and supporting cross-domain evaluation. Definitions mention domains such as Abstracts and Wiki, and one paper states that it uses those two domains as out-of-domain evaluation data. A smaller framing presents RAID as covering multiple domains and models and including adversarial examples, while another uses it to evaluate detector performance on more advanced models with human-written and model-generated text.

What it is claimed to measure. In the available descriptions, papers use RAID to evaluate machine-generated or LLM text detection and detector performance. The papers do not explicitly link it to any named construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Papers use RAID alongside other detection datasets rather than as a standalone protocol. It appears with RealDet, M4, and MAGE as a representative evaluation dataset, and with Yelp as an out-of-domain dataset. Another paper positions RAID as a way to test performance on more advanced models.

nodes.name: RAVDESS
nodes.definition: The Ryerson Audio-Visual Database of Emotional Speech and Song (RAVDESS), used for emotion classification.

nodes.name: RAVEL
nodes.definition: A knowledge retrieval task involving factual recall of biographical information about historical figures.

nodes.name: RAVEN
nodes.definition: A non-verbal intelligence test, adapted as a visual reasoning benchmark (Zhang et al., 2019a), that requires identifying the missing element in a matrix of abstract patterns.

nodes.name: RCT
nodes.definition: A biomedical dataset for sequential sentence classification, used to evaluate domain adaptation.

nodes.name: RE-Bench Scaling Law Experiment
nodes.definition: An RE-Bench environment that tasks the agent with predicting the optimal hyperparameter tradeoff for a large model by extrapolating from smaller-scale experiments.

nodes.name: Real-MM-RAG
nodes.definition: A multimodal retrieval benchmark with four high-difficulty evaluation sets used to assess reranking and robustness, including a rephrased version.

nodes.name: RealTimeQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing framing is a time-sensitive question-answering benchmark or dataset about real-time events, developed after LLM knowledge cut-off dates to avoid data contamination. One paper further describes it as multiple-choice, while another emphasizes that it requires periodic manual updates.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, no constructs or behavioral indicators are explicitly linked to RealTimeQA. One paper does describe it as being used to evaluate zero-shot knowledge recall in continual learning settings, but that use is not tied to a named construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Papers mainly position it as one testbed among other time-sensitive QA benchmarks. One study discusses it alongside FreshQA and TAQA as benchmarks designed to avoid data contamination, and another uses it as a second testbed of downstream tasks for evaluating zero-shot knowledge recall.

Concerns raised. The recurring concern is maintaining its post-cutoff, time-sensitive character. One paper notes that it requires periodic manual updates and that it "stopped its manual updates in January 2024," making it likely that newer LLMs with later

nodes.name: RealToxicityPrompts
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats RealToxicityPrompts as a prompt dataset or benchmark for eliciting toxic generations or toxic completions from language models. Definitions most often describe prompts likely to trigger toxic outputs, with variants calling them naturally occurring prompts, web-derived sentence-level or incomplete prompts, and in one paper seemingly benign or neutral prompts that can still induce harmful content. Papers also describe multiple versions or slices: toxic and non-toxic prompts, a challenge or challenging subset of 1,199 prompts, 10K non-toxic prompts sampled from the dataset, and one adapted use of a 100,000-prompt collection for sentiment, toxicity, and counterfactual fairness under gendered inputs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it most often to measure Toxicity, and more occasionally to measure Safety and Harmlessness; overall, it is linked to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The dominant measurement claim is that model toxicity is evaluated by prompting models with RealToxicityPrompts and scoring the resulting continuations, with papers also reporting it as a safety evaluation and, in one line of work, as a h

nodes.name: RealWorldQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, RealWorldQA is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset of questions about real-world images. The most specific definition presents it as multiple-choice questions over anonymized outdoor and indoor images, scored by accuracy, and aimed at basic real-world spatial understanding. Other papers frame it more broadly as practical, real-world visual understanding, or as a multimodal question-answering benchmark used to assess general capability in real-world question answering.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use RealWorldQA to measure a range of constructs rather than a single shared target. It is linked to 7 constructs and no behavioral indicators, with the listed uses covering fine-grained perception, multimodal perception, multimodal understanding, reasoning, and spatial understanding, with additional papers placing it under other perception and understanding constructs. Across the relationship evidence, papers state that these constructs are measured by RealWorldQA.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers often evaluate it alongside MMMU, MMVP, ScienceQA, MME, and SEED-Bench, usually as part of

nodes.name: ReasonSeg
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe ReasonSeg as a benchmark dataset for reasoning segmentation, designed to evaluate segmentation based on complex reasoning. Some descriptions narrow it to an image reasoning segmentation benchmark used to assess reasoning capability on images, while another describes it as a referring expression segmentation benchmark used to assess pixel-level grounding. In use, authors also call it a challenging dataset and report CIoU, GIoU, and gIoU results on it.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked relationships, papers use ReasonSeg to measure one behavioral indicator, Reasoning segmentation, and no constructs are linked to it. This is the prevailing usage: papers say it evaluates the model's reasoning ability and use it to assess reasoning capability on images. The linked claims therefore converge on a single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation benchmark and report performance with CIoU, GIoU, and gIoU. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and the snippets mainly show it being used to compare model performance, including improvements over an

nodes.name: REBEL
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for relation extraction, from which a 1,000-sample subset is used for evaluation.

nodes.name: ReClor
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is a reading comprehension or multiple-choice question answering benchmark for logical reasoning. Definitions commonly say it is sourced or derived from standardized tests, especially LSAT and GMAT, or from American graduate school entrance exams and their preparatory materials. Some authors describe it more specifically as the Reading Comprehension with Logical Reasoning dataset, and some descriptions frame it as assessing the ability to draw correct inferences from complex textual premises or to perform logical reasoning from provided text.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the measurement claims converge on 1 construct, Logical reasoning, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. Papers use it as a logical reasoning dataset or benchmark, including descriptions that they use ReClor for logical reasoning and for overall comparisons on logic tasks. The measurement claims therefore center on a single construct rather than spreading across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers commonly include it alongside other benchmarks, for example ARC and CSQA in natural language reasoning question-answering exper

nodes.name: Red-teaming
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats red-teaming as an adversarial testing or stress-testing procedure aimed at uncovering safety vulnerabilities, harmful capabilities, biases, or unsafe outputs. Definitions differ, though: some authors describe a manual assessment or a process run by human experts or automated systems, while another use treats it as data generation, for example a set "consisting of 100 harmful examples generated via red-teaming" (Durable Quantization Conditioned Misalignment Attack on Large Language Models). One reported variant evaluates safeguards with 28 test-time adversaries that are variations of fine-tuning attacks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use red-teaming to evaluate safeguards and expose safety vulnerabilities, and to probe a model's propensity to produce inaccurate, biased, offensive, or unsafe responses. No constructs or behavioral indicators are linked to it.

Space of uses. No other measurement instruments are linked to it. Papers position it in several roles: as a step for generating harmful examples for fine-tuning, as an "extensive red teaming" evaluation against test-time adversaries, and as manual or multilingua

nodes.name: Reddit TL;DR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is of a Reddit-based summarization dataset or benchmark that pairs posts with concise, human-written or user-written summaries. Several definitions add that it can include several short summaries for a post, judged for quality and informativeness by human evaluators, and some frame it as carrying preference labels or comparison pairs over generated summaries rather than only reference summaries. A smaller set of papers talks about it as the TL;DR summarization task itself, or as specific slices such as train, test, or comparison data, and one definition atypically refers to articles rather than Reddit posts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The dominant use is to measure text summarization, and a smaller behavioral-indicator link treats it as a benchmark for abstractive summarization. On the construct side, several papers use it to measure alignment, while more isolated uses report it as measuring generalization, including on out-of-distribution subreddit splits, and summary quality.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers usually position i

nodes.name: ReDial
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ReDial is described in two distinct ways rather than with a single settled format. One paper introduces it as Reasoning with Dialect Queries, a human-annotated benchmark with over 1.2K parallel Standardized English and African American Vernacular English query pairs spanning algorithm, logic, math, and integrated reasoning tasks, and describes it as an end-to-end SE-AAVE parallel dataset for reasoning. Another paper uses the same name for a movie recommendation dialogue dataset, described as a collection of movie recommendation conversations annotated with user satisfaction labels and used in task-oriented dialogue experiments.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ReDial to measure one construct and one behavioral indicator. The construct link is Reasoning, with a paper describing ReDial as a dataset for reasoning tasks, while the behavioral indicator link is Conversational recommendation, with another paper treating ReDial as one of two real-world conversational recommendation benchmarks. The measurement claims therefore point to two different targets rather than converging on only one.

Space of uses. In experiments, papers place ReDial alongside

nodes.name: RedPajama
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is a pretraining or training corpus of web text. Definitions describe it as a multi-domain pretraining corpus used to sample general web data for language modeling perplexity, as an open-source project creating a large, high-quality dataset for training language models, and as a pre-training dataset derived from CommonCrawl; one paper specifically uses the CommonCrawl split. Another paper uses it as a calibration dataset, describing it as a large collection of web text meant to represent typical input distributions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RedPajama to one construct and no behavioral indicators. The only reported measurement claim is that it measures Editing locality: in model editing work, locality data is described as the irrelevant data of the editing process. The measurement claims therefore center on a single construct rather than being spread across many targets.

Space of uses. Papers use RedPajama in several operational roles, and no other measurement instrument is linked to it. It appears as evaluation data for language modeling perplexity on general web data, as part of averaged throughput simulations a

nodes.name: RedPajama-V2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, RedPajama-V2 is most commonly treated as a large-scale web-text or web-corpus resource for training or pretraining language models. Definitions also describe it as a preprocessed dataset from diverse internet sources, in one case specifying 30 trillion tokens, while narrower variants include the "sample" and "sample-100B" subsets and, in another use, the validation split.

What it is claimed to measure. Most descriptions do not present RedPajama-V2 as a benchmark for named constructs. One paper defines its validation set as a benchmark to measure forgetting by tracking changes in pretraining loss, and papers otherwise do not link it to any constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. The prevailing usage is as pretraining data: papers use it as the corpus on which language models are trained, or as a starting point for a general-domain pretraining dataset. A smaller line of work uses it more instrumentally, as the source of pretraining text domains on which model losses are measured for data selection, and one paper uses both the pretraining set and its validation loss in analyses of forgetting. No other measurement instruments are linked to i

nodes.name: RefCOCO
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is a benchmark or dataset for visual grounding and referring expression comprehension: models must locate the object named by a natural-language referring expression in an image, often by predicting a bounding box from image-text input. Several definitions call it a visual grounding dataset or a referring expression comprehension benchmark, and one paper describes it as assessing localization together with fine-grained spatial and semantic relationships. A smaller group of papers instead treats RefCOCO as a referring expression segmentation benchmark, evaluating localization at the pixel level, and papers often mention it together with RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, RefCOCO is linked to two constructs and three behavioral indicators. The most common measurement claims are visual grounding and referring expression understanding; papers also use it for referring expression segmentation, and only isolated papers use it for object localization or spatial reasoning. Across these uses, the recurring task is locating a referred object or region from language in an image.

Space of uses.

nodes.name: RefCOCO/g/+
nodes.definition: A referring-expression benchmark suite consisting of RefCOCO, RefCOCOg, and RefCOCO+ for evaluating object localization from language descriptions.

nodes.name: RefCOCO+
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat RefCOCO+ as one of the standard benchmarks in the RefCOCO series. The prevailing description presents it as a referring expression comprehension or visual grounding benchmark similar to RefCOCO, but with location or spatial words excluded so that descriptions are more appearance-based; as CogCoM: A Visual Language Model with Chain-of-Manipulations Reasoning puts it, it has "constraints to prevent annotators from using location words." A smaller line of definitions, used in segmentation work, describes it as an extension of refCOCO for referring expression segmentation, with more complex language.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RefCOCO+ to one construct, visual grounding, and four behavioral indicators: referring expression segmentation, referring expression understanding, action grounding, and object localization. The most common use is to measure referring expression segmentation and referring expression understanding, several papers also use it to measure visual grounding, and only a few papers report it as measuring action grounding or object localization. The claims therefore spread across several evaluation targets rather than converg

nodes.name: RefCOCOg
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, RefCOCOg is most commonly treated as a well-established benchmark or dataset built around referring expressions on natural images, commonly described as requiring a model to localize an object from a natural language description. Definitions repeatedly highlight longer, more descriptive expressions and spatial relations than other RefCOCO variants, and some papers specify grounding to a single bounding box. A smaller line of work instead describes refCOCOg as a version of the refCOCO dataset for referring expression segmentation, with natural language queries paired with object masks, while some papers also frame it as a dataset for region-level captioning or referring expression generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RefCOCOg to 5 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing claims use it to measure referring expression understanding, and papers also report it as measuring referring expression segmentation, while several papers use it to measure the construct visual grounding. Smaller lines of work use it to measure region captioning and referring expression generation, and one paper uses it for object localization. These me

nodes.name: Repetition Task
nodes.definition: A few-shot evaluation task where the model must repeat a given sentence, used to test the ability to steer generation when the model's default behavior is to follow a contextual pattern.

nodes.name: RepoBench-P
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating code-related tasks, specifically code retrieval and completion, used as part of the LongBench evaluation.

nodes.name: RepoEval
nodes.definition: Benchmark for repository-level code completion, assessing line-, API-, and function-level code generation using real-world codebases.

nodes.name: RepoQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark for question answering over entire code repositories to assess deep code comprehension.

nodes.name: RESISC45
nodes.definition:
What it is. The prevailing description treats RESISC45 as a publicly available remote-sensing image or land-scene classification benchmark with 45 classes. Definitions describe it as a benchmark for Remote Sensing Image Scene Classification and as a land use dataset involving land scene classification over 45 classes. A smaller variation in wording presents it more generally as a vision benchmark, and one evaluation setup frames the task as selecting a class from a provided list.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, its measurement role is narrowly focused: it is linked to 1 behavioral indicator, Image classification, and to no constructs. Papers use RESISC45 to measure image classification, with evidence phrased as reporting performance on image classification benchmarks that include Resisc-45 and as part of evaluations spanning multiple classification domains. The claims therefore converge on a single behavioral indicator rather than being spread across multiple constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers usually position RESISC45 as one component of broader benchmark suites, for example alongside CIFAR-100, Food101, Flower

nodes.name: RestBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark of real-world API tasks involving authentic calls to TMDB and Spotify with dynamic responses.

nodes.name: ResumeBench
nodes.definition: A multilingual benchmark comprising 2,500 synthetic resumes across 50 templates and 5 languages, designed to evaluate LLMs on structured resume parsing with realism and privacy compliance.

nodes.name: ResumeBench-Mix
nodes.definition: ResumeBench-Mix, a combined real-synthetic dataset created by pairing public real resumes with an equal number of synthetic resumes in five languages for evaluation.

nodes.name: RETAIL
nodes.definition: A real-world tourism all-in-one interactive planning dataset containing 10,182 dialogues that supports evaluation of decision-making for implicit queries, environmental awareness, plan revision, and all-in-one travel planning with rich POI details.

nodes.name: RewardBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, RewardBench is most commonly described as a benchmark for evaluating reward models on preference-related judgments, often in preference optimization or learning from human or LLM feedback. Definitions and snippets repeatedly describe it as built from prompt, chosen, rejected preference data, with one paper specifying 2,985 human-validated triples or binary preference tasks drawn from 23 subtasks or datasets. The prevailing breakdown is into Chat, Chat-Hard, Safety, and Reasoning, though some papers describe it more broadly as a public benchmark for generative judges on preference-related sub-tasks, and one paper describes it as English-only.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RewardBench to 8 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so its measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than concentrated on one. The most common claims say it measures Reasoning and Safety, often through benchmark categories or subsets, and some papers also use it to measure Generalization, Coding ability, and Evaluation ability, plus 3 other constructs. It is also used to measure Pairwise comparison and Preference prediction.

Space of uses.

nodes.name: ReXVal
nodes.definition: A dataset containing ground-truth and generated radiology reports annotated by radiologists with six categories of errors, classified as clinically significant or insignificant.

nodes.name: RGB
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available definitions treat RGB as a retrieval-augmented generation benchmark, and one paper also describes it as an open-source general-domain QA dataset. Across these descriptions, it is used for questions that require grounding in retrieved documents, with emphasis on robustness, generalization, and the ability to effectively use retrieved information while withstanding imperfections in the retrieval process.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RGB to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. The only reported measurement claim is that it measures question answering, with papers describing it as evaluating whether language models can effectively use retrieved information under imperfect retrieval conditions.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it through the recorded relations. In the available papers, RGB appears as one dataset within broader retrieval-augmented generation evaluations, placed alongside PopQA, Natural Questions, TriviaQA, and KNOT.

nodes.name: RiddleSense
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, RiddleSense is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset of riddle-style questions for evaluating commonsense reasoning. The prevailing wording presents it as complex commonsense reasoning in the framework of riddle-style, multiple-choice questions, while another definition more generally calls it a commonsense reasoning benchmark involving riddles. Some authors also place it among lateral thinking-related benchmarks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use RiddleSense to measure a single construct, Commonsense reasoning, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The claims converge on that construct rather than spreading across several: it is described as evaluating complex commonsense reasoning, including in out-of-domain evaluation settings.

Space of uses. Papers position RiddleSense mainly as an existing benchmark used in broader benchmark comparisons and out-of-domain evaluation. It is analyzed alongside BiRdQA and BrainTeaser in benchmark analysis, included with Story Cloze Test, HellaSwag, and NumerSense in out-of-domain commonsense reasoning evaluation, and cited as a lateral thinking-related benchmark to which another benc

nodes.name: RLBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, RLBench is most commonly treated as a simulated, and in one definition large-scale, benchmark and learning environment for robotic manipulation. Definitions vary in emphasis: some describe tabletop tasks and a Franka robot performing both prehensile and non-prehensile tasks, while others frame it as a benchmark for language-conditioned or language-guided robotic manipulation. Papers also describe it as being used to generate trajectories and to evaluate manipulation-related path prediction or other challenging simulation tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RLBench to one behavioral indicator, robotic manipulation, and to no constructs. The recorded measurement claim is concentrated rather than spread across multiple targets: RLBench is used to measure robotic manipulation, with the supporting description referring to tabletop manipulation in simulation.

Space of uses. Across the papers, RLBench is positioned as a simulation benchmark or learning environment rather than being linked to other measurement instruments. Authors use it for evaluation, including generating trajectories or episodes and assessing model performance on manipulati

nodes.name: RM-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, papers most commonly describe RM-Bench as a benchmark for evaluating reward models through preference pairs with subtle differences, with emphasis on sensitivity to subtle content variations and resistance to style biases. One description adds that it is designed to correlate with downstream policy performance across chat, math, code, and safety tasks. A related paper situates it alongside RewardBench and says it covers the Chat, Code, Math, and Safety domains, with code prompts sourced from HumanEvalPack.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RM-Bench to 2 constructs, Robustness and Factuality, and no behavioral indicators. Most descriptions frame it in robustness terms: one paper says RM-Bench is designed to assess the robustness of reward models through their sensitivity and resistance to subtle content differences and style biases. A smaller use treats it as measuring factuality, with one study using it because RM-Bench includes response pairs involving factual correctness, so the reported measurement claims are concentrated in these two constructs rather than spread across many.

Space of uses. Papers position RM-Bench as an evaluation

nodes.name: RoBERTa harmfulness classifier
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe this instrument as an external safety evaluator: a harmfulness detection model that assigns a probability score indicating whether a given response is harmful. In Refusal-Aware Red Teaming: Exposing Inconsistency in Safety Evaluations, it is used among "state-of-the-art harmfulness detection models" that assign harmfulness probabilities to each response.

What it is claimed to measure. The available description uses it to score whether a response is harmful by assigning a harmfulness probability. No constructs and no behavioral indicators are linked to it through recorded measurement claims.

Space of uses. The only described usage places it alongside WildGuard as part of an evaluation setup, where both models act as external safety evaluators for response harmfulness. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: RocketEval
nodes.definition: An automated evaluation framework that uses a lightweight LLM to grade responses against an instance-specific, multi-faceted checklist.

nodes.name: ROCStories
nodes.definition:
What it is. Definitions mostly describe ROCStories as a story-generation dataset built from short stories with exactly 5 sentences, often characterized as coherent narrative or commonsense stories. The prevailing usage is open-ended conditional generation or title-to-story generation, including evaluation of a model's ability to generate a five-sentence story from a title. A smaller framing treats ROC Stories as a story-completion or infilling setup, where a middle sentence is masked and the generated replacement is assessed for coherence.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ROCStories to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. The only recorded measured_by relationship is with Text infilling, so papers use ROCStories to measure text infilling; in that use, one paper describes the corpus as 'a dataset of short stories containing exactly 5 sentences each.' The claims therefore center on a single behavioral indicator rather than multiple constructs.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to ROCStories. Across the papers, it is used in several evaluation setups: for title-to-story generation, for relatively open-ended conditional generation, and for story comple

nodes.name: RoDEval
nodes.definition: A comprehensive evaluation framework for assessing the word sense disambiguation capabilities of LLMs, comprising four novel metrics and associated evaluation tasks.

nodes.name: Rotten Tomatoes
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats Rotten Tomatoes as a sentiment classification dataset or benchmark built from movie reviews, typically for binary polarity labeling. Some authors refer to it as MR or Movie Review, and one description specifies movie reviews from the Rotten Tomatoes website, while others describe it more generally as a text classification dataset or benchmark used in projected-embedding, in-context learning, and prompt-based evaluations.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 2 behavioral indicators, Text classification and Sentiment analysis, and no constructs are linked to it. The linked claims stay within classification behavior: papers describe it as one of the datasets that 'all admit classification tasks' and as a benchmark for binary polarity tasks on movie reviews.

Space of uses. Papers most commonly use it as one dataset within a larger evaluation suite rather than in isolation. In the excerpts, it appears alongside SST-2, IMDB, AG News, Subj, and TREC, and it is used to evaluate projected embeddings, in-context learning and activation-vector methods, few-shot classification, polarity labeling, and non-r

nodes.name: RTE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats RTE as a textual entailment or natural language inference benchmark: models judge whether a hypothesis can be inferred from, follows from, or is entailed by a premise or text. Several definitions describe it as premise-hypothesis pairs, and some make the labels explicit as binary, such as entailment versus not entailment or "True" versus "False"; one paper instead describes entailment, contradiction, and neutrality and mentions negation-modified versions. A smaller line of work refers to "RTE datasets" as a collection or series of textual entailment challenges, and papers variously place it within GLUE or SuperGLUE benchmark suites.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RTE to 4 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The dominant claim is that papers use it to measure natural language inference, often phrased as textual entailment, while smaller uses treat it as measuring binary classification, fact checking, or zero-shot task performance. At the construct level, papers most often use it to measure general ability, followed by natural language understanding, with additional uses for in-context learning and language model

nodes.name: Rule-based judge
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage is a rule-based or heuristic evaluation procedure, often described as keyword matching over model outputs. Most definitions say it searches for predefined refusal-related keywords, rejected words, or strings that indicate refusal to comply with a harmful instruction, and uses that to judge whether a jailbreak attack was successful. A smaller line of work describes keyword matching differently, as checking specific keywords in factual-query answers to measure information overlap.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it primarily to measure Jailbreaking: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Jailbreaking, and to no constructs. In the recorded relationships, Jailbreaking is measured by the Rule-based judge, and the accompanying descriptions operationalize that judgment through searches for refusal-indicating strings or related rules. The measurement claims therefore converge on jailbreak evaluation rather than spreading across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers position it as an automatic evaluator, sometimes alongside other judges and sometimes as the default or a baseline evaluator. Source snippets show

nodes.name: RULER
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as a synthetic benchmark or benchmark suite for evaluating long-context language models, often with customizable or varying sequence lengths and task complexity. Most descriptions say it contains 13 tasks across 4 categories or domains, commonly including Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval and question answering, while papers vary on the remaining categories, describing them as variable tracking, multi-hop tracing, aggregation, or common and frequent word extraction; one definition mentions five categories. Some papers further describe it as extending needle-in-a-haystack testing with multi-key and multi-value retrieval, and as challenging the effective or true context window length across increasing context lengths.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most often use RULER to measure long-context understanding, describing it as assessing long-context capabilities, understanding capacity, processing capability, or long-context ability. More broadly, papers link it to 5 constructs and 9 behavioral indicators: after long-context understanding, the recurring construct-level uses are length generalization, long-context reasoning, long-ra

nodes.name: RuleTaker
nodes.definition: Automatically generated logical reasoning dataset using formal connectives (¬, ∧, →), requiring models to apply logical rules across multiple inference steps.

nodes.name: SAEBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited work, SAEBench is most commonly treated as a benchmark or evaluation suite for sparse autoencoders. Definitions differ in the metrics they foreground: one describes feature absorption, splitting, composition, probing, and concept isolation across multiple tasks and models, while another emphasizes downstream SAE-specific metrics such as spurious correlation removal, targeted probe perturbation, sparse probing, automated interpretability, and feature absorption. One paper also characterizes it as a benchmark of SAE metrics "faithful to possible real world use cases."

What it is claimed to measure. It is linked to 1 construct, interpretability and explainability, and to no behavioral indicators. Papers use it to measure that construct through "interpretability benchmark results from SAEBench" and through a "detection score ... implemented in SAE Bench" that is used to validate interpretability, so the reported use centers on a single construct rather than a broader set.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers use its evaluations to compare SAE variants across a wide variety of tasks, to calculate specific metrics such as a

nodes.name: SAFE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, SAFE is most commonly described as an LLM-based, search-augmented evaluator or investigative agent. Papers describe it as using iterative Google Search queries to assess whether generated facts are supported by external evidence, and one definition adds that it breaks a long-form response into individual facts, checks relevance, searches the web, and labels each fact as supported, not supported, or irrelevant. The descriptions differ mainly in emphasis, with one centering the investigative-agent framing and another the stepwise evaluation procedure.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SAFE to one construct, Reasoning, and three behavioral indicators, Fact checking, Hallucination, and Search query generation. Among these links, the measurement claim is specifically about hallucination: one paper says hallucination is measured by SAFE and describes SAFE as enabling direct measurement of hallucination alongside FActScore. The other links are framed as causal relationships, with papers claiming causal links from SAFE to search query generation and fact checking, and from Reasoning to SAFE.

Space of uses. Papers use SAFE as an evaluation proc

nodes.name: SafeBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a safety benchmark for VLMs or MLLMs built from 500 malicious questions in 10 categories based on AI usage policies. Some papers also frame it as a benchmark for perceiving multimodal risks and for evaluating defense against jailbreak attacks. One paper further refers to sampling 200 examples from "SafeBench11", described there as constructed with FigStep, and another characterizes SafeBench as images and text queries where the text itself is harmful.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SafeBench to no constructs and three behavioral indicators. The measurement claims are spread across harmful content detection, jailbreak resistance, and jailbreaking rather than concentrated on a single target: one paper uses it to report attack success rates for jailbreaking, another to evaluate defense capabilities against jailbreak attacks, and another to assess harmful content detection.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers use SafeBench alongside other safety resources, including MM-SafeBench, HADES-Dataset, Hades, MML, and HIMRD, either as one of several established safety benchmarks

nodes.name: SALAD-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, SALAD-Bench is most commonly treated as a safety benchmark for LLMs, though some definitions foreground it as a dataset. Definitions describe it as providing prompts and safety scores for evaluating LLM safety and its relationship to value systems, as a source of harmful prompts for training and evaluating refusal mechanisms, and as a hierarchical benchmark covering different task types and jailbreak attack methods.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SALAD-Bench to measure two constructs, Privacy awareness and Safety alignment, and one behavioral indicator, Jailbreaking. The recorded uses span these three targets rather than a single recurring one: papers report using it as part of a safety alignment benchmark, extracting its "privacy infringement" category for privacy awareness queries, and including it in jailbreaking evaluations.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers position it both as a benchmark used alongside Anthropic Hh-rlhf red-teaming prompts, Do-Not-Answer, and SORRY-Bench, and as a component resource: one paper constructs harmful prompts from SALAD-BENCH with ALPACA, while another extracts the

nodes.name: SAMSum
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is of a dialogue summarization dataset or benchmark built from chat or messenger-style conversations and paired with human-written, short summaries. Definitions variously call it a dataset of chat transcripts, real-life messenger-like conversations, daily-life messenger conversations, or multi-turn conversations, and several papers frame it specifically as abstractive dialogue summarization. A smaller line of work treats it as a few-shot variant or as part of LongBench, and one description diverges by calling it summarization over news articles and machine-generated summaries rather than dialogue.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SAMSum to measure one construct and three behavioral indicators. The dominant claim is that it measures text summarization, often described simply as summarization or dialogue summary generation, while a smaller line of work treats it as measuring dialogue summarization. Single papers also report it as measuring question answering and general ability, so the measurement claims are centered on summarization but not entirely uniform.

Space of uses. Papers often include SAMSum inside

nodes.name: SAT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the prevailing description is of SAT as a standardized test used to evaluate model performance. A smaller framing narrows this to a set of math problems from the SAT used for quantitative reasoning, with one paper noting that this subset contains 32 four-choice problems.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what SAT measures are concentrated rather than spread out: it is linked to one construct, Mathematical reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators. One paper explicitly treats Mathematical reasoning as measured by SAT, and another definition describes the instrument as used to evaluate quantitative reasoning.

Space of uses. Papers use SAT as an evaluation instrument for model performance, with one paper placing it among standardized tests on which GPT-4 scores are described as comparable to those of human test-takers. Another paper includes it alongside GSM8k, MATH, GSM-Hard, SVAMP, and ASDiv, among other mathematical reasoning benchmarks, and reports SAT results by averaging over the last three checkpoints when available.

Concerns raised. The only stated limitation is its scale and format: one paper says the SAT subset "only has 32 four

nodes.name: SAT-Math
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions treat SAT-Math as a standardized benchmark or dataset drawn from math problems on the SAT exam. Some papers describe it more specifically as multiple-choice questions from the SAT math section, and one description says the tasks include Intermediate Algebra, Probability, and Calculus. Papers also frame it as an evaluation resource used under standardized conditions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator, so the recorded measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets. The prevailing usage is that SAT-Math measures mathematical reasoning, with papers listing it among representative math evaluation datasets. One paper also reports it as measuring mathematical problem solving.

Space of uses. Papers frequently place SAT-Math in math benchmark suites alongside MATH, GSM8K, AQuA-RAT or AQuA, MMLU-Math, and OCW. They position it as one component of broader evaluation, for example as part of an averaged math domain score, among five representative datasets, or simply as a benchmark on which results are reported.

nodes.name: SATBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark consisting of 2100 logical puzzles derived from SAT formulas, presented in natural language, used to evaluate models' ability to perform search-based logical reasoning and produce valid reasoning traces.

nodes.name: SBIC
nodes.definition: The Social Bias Inference Corpus (SBIC) is a labeled dataset of social media posts used for assessing societal biases in language, which served as a source for the CoBia dataset.

nodes.name: sBLIMP
nodes.definition: A ZeroSpeech paired-choice evaluation using grammatically correct versus incorrect sentence speech examples.

nodes.name: SC-Safety
nodes.definition: Chinese-language safety benchmark focusing on compliance with ethical and legal standards in LLM responses.

nodes.name: ScanNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats ScanNet as an indoor 3D scene dataset, with definitions alternating between real indoor room scenes, a 3D indoor scene dataset, and richly annotated 3D reconstructions of indoor scenes. The content described for it varies by paper: some authors use scenes from it to construct scenarios, others highlight annotations supporting object classification, visual question answering, and captioning in point cloud modality, and another describes it as a segmentation dataset with 1,201 training scenes, 312 validation scenes, and 20 semantic classes.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ScanNet to one behavioral indicator, Semantic segmentation, reporting that semantic segmentation is measured by the ScanNet segmentation dataset. The recorded links do not connect it to any constructs. Beyond that linked use, some papers also report evaluating classification, captioning, and QA on its test split, and one paper reports building a partial scene registration benchmark from it.

Space of uses. Papers position ScanNet both as source material for derived resources and as a direct evaluation dataset. It is used alongside PartNet

nodes.name: ScanQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, the prevailing usage treats ScanQA as a benchmark dataset for question answering in 3D scenes, usually with questions grounded in objects within scans from ScanNet. Some papers describe it more specifically as an indoor 3D visual question answering dataset focused on spatial relationships, object properties, and complex indoor scenes, while another frames it more broadly as a multi-modal 3D scene dataset for spatial scene understanding with question-answer pairs produced through automated methods and human annotation. Papers also describe it as centered on ScanNet and associated with human annotations and template-based generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ScanQA to measure four constructs and two behavioral indicators. The most frequently linked constructs are 3D perception, 3D reasoning, 3D understanding, and vision-language reasoning, and the linked behavioral indicators are 3D question answering and visual question answering. The claims do not converge on one construct: papers report it as measuring several 3D and reasoning-oriented targets, including vision-language reasoning and visual question answering.

Space of u

nodes.name: SciBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe SciBench as a benchmark suite or dataset for scientific reasoning, especially college-level scientific problem solving. The prevailing description is that it contains complex, multi-step scientific questions whose objective is to integrate knowledge, reason over evidence, and apply scientific principles; several papers place it across physics and chemistry, though one line describes the third domain as biology and another as mathematics. Some authors use narrower portions of it, including a math-related subset and chemical reasoning subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than concentrated on one. SciBench is linked to 5 constructs, Chemical reasoning, Generalization, Problem-solving ability, Reasoning, and Scientific reasoning, and to 3 behavioral indicators, Mathematical problem solving, Scientific problem solving, and Scientific question answering. Papers use it to measure scientific and hard-science reasoning tasks, college-level scientific problem-solving abilities, and, in one case, generalization capability because it is treated as coming from a totally diffe

nodes.name: SCIDOCS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat SCIDOCS, also written SciDocs, as a retrieval dataset for scientific literature. The prevailing description is an information retrieval dataset dedicated to scientific scholarly articles or scientific document retrieval, and some authors place it within BEIR as a single-hop retrieval benchmark for re-ranking scientific documents. Another description presents it as a document retrieval dataset based on citation networks in scientific literature, used to assess whether embeddings retrieve semantically related academic papers.

What it is claimed to measure. These papers do not explicitly link SCIDOCS to any named construct or behavioral indicator. Instead, they use it to evaluate retrieval tasks, especially retrieval of scientific scholarly articles, single-hop re-ranking of scientific documents, and retrieval of semantically related academic papers.

Space of uses. Papers usually deploy SCIDOCS alongside other retrieval datasets. It appears within BEIR evaluations for re-ranking, in corpus-poisoning experiments to generate and evaluate adversarial passages, and in embedding evaluation with nDCG@10 alongside MS MARCO and NFCorpus.

Concerns rais

nodes.name: ScienceAgentBench
nodes.definition: A multidisciplinary benchmark for evaluating LLMs operating within agent frameworks on explorative scientific tasks.

nodes.name: ScienceQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats ScienceQA as a multimodal science question answering benchmark built around multiple-choice questions. Definitions commonly describe items with visual and textual context, and one paper states that each sample contains "a visual context, a textual context, a question with multiple options, and an answer"; some papers also mention optional lecture or context text, background knowledge, and explanations, or describe the benchmark as covering diverse science topics and reasoning. A smaller line of work refers to ScienceQA-Image, an image-based subset, or text-only samples derived from it, and one evaluation uses only questions that include an image.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ScienceQA to measure 10 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The most common claims treat it as measuring scientific reasoning and visual question answering, with recurring use for multimodal reasoning, question answering, and chain of thought; papers also report it as measuring several other constructs and indicators, so its reported measurement role is spread across multiple targets.

Space of uses. Papers often position ScienceQA as one

nodes.name: ScienceQA-IMG
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage is as a multimodal science question answering benchmark with image-based or visual context. Definitions vary slightly: some describe ScienceQA-IMG as including images and requiring reasoning over both visual and textual context, some call SciQA-IMG a science question answering dataset with image-based questions assessing scientific reasoning from visual content, and another paper treats SQA-I as the image-based subset of the ScienceQA benchmark. A smaller line of description refers to SQAI as a benchmark for multimodal reasoning on science-related questions, and one paper places ScienceQA-IMG among "scientific problem benchmarks".

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The named uses are to measure Fine-grained visual understanding and Language bias, and to measure the behavioral indicator Visual question answering. These claims do not converge on one target: one paper uses zero-shot performance on different splits of ScienceQA-IMG to report alleviating language bias, while others place it in evaluations of fine-grained visual understanding or visual questio

nodes.name: ScienceWorld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is a text-based interactive or textual simulation benchmark and environment for basic or elementary science experiments, where agents follow natural-language goals by interacting with objects, navigating, manipulating objects, and observing outcomes. Descriptions also present it as an embodied AI environment for long-horizon and large-action-space tasks, often emphasizing long-term memory and subtask decomposition; one paper adds that it covers 30 scientific tasks, and another refers to the same benchmark as "SciWorld" for science-oriented interactive tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 4 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than concentrated on one. The linked constructs are Generalization, Scientific reasoning, Commonsense knowledge, and Task decomposition ability, and the linked behavioral indicators are Embodied planning and Scientific experimentation; the evidence includes claims that ScienceWorld contains unseen tasks for evaluating generalization and that it serves as an interactive benchmark for embodied science experiment

nodes.name: SciERC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers treat SciERC as a computer science domain evaluation resource, but they frame the task differently. One definition presents it as an evaluation task in SciRIFF-Eval for relation extraction, summarized as "IE(Rel)," with a computer science abstract as input and six entity types as output. Another paper places SCIERC among computer science datasets used for classification tasks and describes it as focused on identifying entities, relations, and coreference in scientific articles.

What it is claimed to measure. Reported measurement claims are spread across behavioral indicators rather than linked constructs. Papers use SciERC to measure three behavioral indicators, Information extraction, Knowledge graph construction, and Text classification, and no constructs are linked to it. The task framing is varied: one paper reports it as measuring Information extraction, another uses it in experiments on datasets with golden ground truth KGs for Knowledge graph construction, and another includes it among classification datasets across diverse domains for Text classification.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the uses that are described, one study

nodes.name: SciEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats SciEval as a benchmark for scientific-domain or scientific-research evaluation. Definitions describe it as measuring a model's ability to understand and reason about scientific content, and several descriptions further frame it as a multi-level benchmark for scientific research; one description also presents it as a comprehensive, multi-disciplinary benchmark for assessing scientific reasoning and subjective question-answering capabilities.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SciEval primarily to measure Scientific reasoning: it is linked to one construct overall, Scientific reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators. This makes its reported measurement role concentrated rather than spread across many constructs, though the definitions also describe it as evaluating scientific research reasoning, problem solving, and subjective question-answering capabilities.

Space of uses. Papers position SciEval as a benchmark test within broader evaluation suites. One paper lists it alongside LegalBench, LawBench, MedQA, MedMCQA, and FinEval in a benchmark table, while another reports benchmark tests on SciEval, presentin

nodes.name: SciFact
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe SciFact as a scientific fact-checking dataset or benchmark. The prevailing definitions say that claims are verified using evidence sentences from research papers, often with citation context, or against a corpus of research abstracts; one source states that it is "a dataset with sentences in papers as evidence." A smaller description places it among medical datasets, and one paper reports a split of 809 training and 300 test claims.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the dominant claim is that SciFact measures Fact checking: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Fact checking, and papers repeatedly frame it as fact checking in the scientific domain. A smaller line of work uses it to measure one construct, Domain knowledge, by sampling claims from SciFact in the science domain to investigate access to domain-specific factual knowledge. Overall, the measurement claims are concentrated on these two targets rather than spread across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. At the instrument level, SciFact is linked to one other measurement instrument, BEIR, and one paper reports that SciFact is measured by BEIR in the sens

nodes.name: SciQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of SciQ as a scientific question-answering benchmark or dataset built from multiple-choice science exam questions. Definitions usually describe about 13,000 questions, and one paper specifies 13,679 crowdsourced items spanning physics, chemistry, biology, earth science, astronomy, and computer science; some authors additionally describe supporting paragraphs or annotated support evidence. A smaller line of work frames SciQ more broadly as a natural language understanding, reading comprehension, or commonsense question answering benchmark, and some papers use a LitCab test split for short, phrase-level, or free-form responses.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SciQ to seven constructs and four behavioral indicators. The most common claim is that papers use it to measure commonsense reasoning, with additional links to general ability, scientific knowledge, scientific reasoning, generalization, knowledge, and reasoning. On the behavioral side, papers report it as evaluating multiple-choice question answering most often, and also question answering, open-ended question answering, and text classification, so the measurem

nodes.name: SciQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description treats SciQA as a science question-answering dataset or benchmark. Definitions describe it as containing science exam questions with rich domain-specific language and complex reasoning, while some multimodal papers frame it more specifically as a visual question answering dataset with scientific diagrams that require scientific reasoning; other definitions describe it more generally as a science question-answering evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SciQA to measure 1 construct and 3 behavioral indicators. Several papers use it to measure Visual understanding, and individual papers also report it as measuring Knowledge-based question answering, Machine reading comprehension, and Visual question answering, so its reported measurement role spans multiple task framings rather than only one.

Space of uses. The common usage is as one benchmark within broader evaluation suites. Papers place it alongside ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, LAMBADA, LogiQA, and PIQA in downstream task testing, and other papers include it in multimodal or vision benchmark collections, describing it as a commonly used vision understanding benchma

nodes.name: SciVerse-mv
nodes.definition: A multi-image scientific reasoning benchmark used for out-domain evaluation.

nodes.name: ScreenSpot
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a benchmark for single-step or cross-platform GUI grounding. Definitions describe it as assessing whether a predicted location falls within the ground truth element bounding box, and one paper further presents it as a GUI visual grounding benchmark containing 1,200 instructions with target element bounding boxes across mobile, desktop, and web or website environments. A smaller variation in wording frames it more broadly as part of multi-modal task performance evaluation, though the recurring content is GUI grounding across platforms.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ScreenSpot to measure 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The dominant claims are that it measures Action grounding and Visual grounding, with papers also using it to measure Grounding and, in a smaller line of work, Adaptability. Across these links, the named targets are mostly grounding-related.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is explicitly linked to it, but several papers use it within broader benchmark suites. It appears alongside VisualWebBench and RefExp for GUI grounding, and alongside MiniWob, AITW, and Mind2Web in broader evaluat

nodes.name: SCROLLS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat SCROLLS as a benchmark suite for long-text or long-context evaluation, often explicitly as a suite of 7 datasets. Its task mix is described as question answering and summarization, with some descriptions adding classification, and one definition frames SCROLL as evaluating language models' ability to reason over and synthesize information from long texts. A smaller framing discusses Scrolls together with ZeroSCROLLS as realistic long-input tasks from real-world scenarios, and one snippet reports average lengths ranging from 1.7k to 49.3k tokens.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SCROLLS to measure 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators, most often Long-context understanding and Long-context reasoning. These claims are concentrated on long-context capabilities rather than spread across many concepts: one line of work places Scrolls within long-context modeling and QA evaluation, while another describes it as evaluating models' ability to synthesize information over long texts.

Space of uses. Across papers, SCROLLS is used as a finetuning and comparison benchmark for long-sequence tasks, including baseline comparisons and long-docu

nodes.name: Seal-Tools
nodes.definition: A dataset of held-out tasks used to evaluate the generalization ability of models on function call scenarios.

nodes.name: SEED-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, SEED-Bench is most commonly treated as a multimodal or vision-language benchmark for evaluating multimodal comprehension, generative comprehension, or broader vision-language performance. Many descriptions portray it as a multiple-choice benchmark, and some are more specific: papers describe 19K human-annotated questions spanning 12 evaluation dimensions across image and video modalities, while another paper describes a visual question-answering benchmark with 9 dimensions and MCQ accuracy; some authors also describe instance interaction, text understanding, spatial relations, common-sense questions, or video comprehension tasks such as action prediction, action recognition, and procedure understanding. A few papers refer to subsets or slices such as SEED, SEED-Image, and all/image/video variants.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SEED-Bench to 5 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The dominant behavioral use is to measure visual question answering, and the most common construct-level claim is that it measures visual understanding. Smaller lines of work use it to measure multimodal understanding, multimodal perception, and visual instruction

nodes.name: SEED-Bench-2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, SEED-Bench-2 is most commonly described as a multimodal benchmark for evaluating models on multimodal inputs, especially cases with multiple images. Definitions variously say it evaluates the ability to comprehend and reason about multimodal inputs containing multiple images, serves as a benchmark for general performance of Vision-Language Assistants after debiasing methods, and is used as a non-synthetic comparison point for LVLM evaluation rankings.
