Descriptions also differ on context length: one survey places it in long-context tasks that require identifying relevant information from image sequences, while another paper groups it with multi-image benchmarks that consist of short contexts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SEED-Bench-2 to 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The only direct measurement claim is for Multi-image reasoning: one paper says it measures this by evaluating the ability to comprehend multimodal inputs containing multiple images. Long-context understanding appears only as a related construct, with one paper discussing SEED-Bench-2 in connection with that capability by arguing that it does not evaluate long-con

nodes.name: SEED-Bench Image
nodes.definition: SEED-Bench Image Part (SEEDI) is a benchmark focusing on generative comprehension for multimodal LLMs, specifically its image-related tasks.

nodes.name: Self-Instruct
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats Self-Instruct as an instruction-following evaluation dataset or test set, sometimes written as Self-Instruct Eval or SelfInst. Definitions describe it as based on self-instructed prompts and used to assess responses to self-instruction-style prompts, while one paper describes a test set of human-generated instructions from various tasks and sources. A smaller line of work also presents it as a framework and dataset that uses the model itself to generate new instructions, inputs, and outputs, and one paper characterizes it as generating approximately 82k instances from 175 human-created handwritten instructions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Self-Instruct to 1 behavioral indicator, Instruction following, and no constructs. In the recorded relationship, a paper uses it to measure instruction following by evaluating trained student models on Self-Instruct alongside other instruction-following datasets. One definition also describes it as testing model generalization and response quality across a wide range of tasks, but the recorded measurement link centers on instruction following.

Space of uses. Papers commonly us

nodes.name: SelfCheckGPT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats SelfCheckGPT as a suite of hallucination detection methods that analyzes multiple stochastically sampled responses from a model to assess the veracity of a response, often in a zero-resource gray-box or black-box setting. Several papers restate this as self-consistency checking, either by looking for contradictions in the model's own generated text or by verifying whether additional sampled responses support the original answer, and one paper refers to a consistency-based baseline under the name Self-CKGPT. A smaller line of work instead describes SelfCheckGPT as a hallucination correction benchmark or dataset for assessing whether models correct hallucinations or rectify factual inconsistencies.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 3 behavioral indicators, with no linked constructs and no linked measurement instruments. The most common claims are that it measures Knowledge editing, where papers evaluate a model's ability to correct hallucination or rectify factual inconsistencies, and Hallucination, where it is used to assess the veracity of LLM responses. It is also reported as measuring Hallu

nodes.name: SemEval-2007
nodes.definition: A dataset from the SemEval-2007 workshop, commonly used as a validation set in WSD research.

nodes.name: SemEval 2010 Task 8
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat it as a standard or widely used relation extraction benchmark dataset. Definitions describe it as sentence-level and general-domain, and as evaluating semantic relation extraction between pairs of nominals; the prevailing description says it contains 19 relation types, though a smaller usage describes ten relation classes. Some definitions also present it as spanning diverse domains and as a benchmark used to evaluate few-shot learning and generalization.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed papers, claims converge on a single behavioral indicator: SemEval 2010 Task 8 is used to measure Relation extraction. Papers connect it to 1 behavioral indicator, Relation extraction, and to no constructs. The relationship language is consistent, with papers describing RE as being evaluated on this dataset or including it among standard RE benchmarks.

Space of uses. Papers usually use it alongside TACRED and its variants, including TACREV or TACRED-Revisit, and ReTACRED or Re-TACRED. They generally position it as one benchmark within a multi-dataset RE evaluation, for example as part of a set of widely used or standard benchmarks, while a smaller us

nodes.name: SemEval-2016 Task 5
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available definition treats SemEval-2016 Task 5 as a benchmark dataset for aspect-based sentiment analysis built from real user restaurant reviews in multiple languages, used to evaluate cross-lingual performance in end-to-end ABSA. The detailed description specifies English, Spanish, French, Dutch, Russian, and Turkish. In a different usage, some papers refer to SemEval-2016 more briefly as a stance detection dataset, without additional detail in the quoted passages.

What it is claimed to measure. Recorded measurement claims are spread across two behavioral indicators rather than any construct. Papers use it to measure stance detection most often, followed by aspect-based sentiment analysis, and no constructs are linked to it. In the available evidence, the stance detection papers describe it as one of the common datasets used in evaluation, while the aspect-based sentiment paper uses it to evaluate cross-lingual E2E-ABSA.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the recorded relationships. In the available snippets, papers use it as an evaluation dataset within broader experimental suites: one paper names it among common stance detection datas

nodes.name: SemEval 2018 Task 1 E-c
nodes.definition: Multi-label emotion recognition task with 11 emotion categories on English tweets, used to analyze LLM generation dynamics despite lacking individual annotator labels.

nodes.name: SentEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers treat SentEval as a standard transfer learning evaluation suite for sentence embeddings. The clearest description presents it through transfer tasks for sentiment classification, subjectivity detection, and question classification, with MR and SST-2 given as examples. A separate paper frames it as the evaluation tool for seven STS subsets, including STS 2012-2016 and STS-Benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the recorded links, papers do not connect SentEval to any constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, one paper reports that SentEval measures STS tasks, using Spearman's correlation for model performance on semantic textual similarity. Its only linked measurement target is STS tasks.

Space of uses. Papers use SentEval as an evaluation tool for sentence embeddings. One usage relies on the standard transfer tasks provided by SentEval, while another adopts it specifically for STS evaluation with Spearman's correlation. The only linked instrument is STS tasks.

nodes.name: SENTIBENCH
nodes.definition: Benchmark for evaluating sentiment analysis models across multiple tasks including basic, multi-faceted, and fine-grained sentiment analysis, covering domains like IMDb, Yelp, and Twitter.

nodes.name: SENTIMENT
nodes.definition: A dataset for sentiment analysis, typically involving classifying text into positive, negative, or neutral categories.

nodes.name: seqBench
nodes.definition: A tunable benchmark for sequential reasoning in LLMs, featuring synthetic pathfinding tasks with orthogonal control over logical depth, backtracking count, and noise ratio, enabling fine-grained analysis of reasoning failure modes.

nodes.name: Sequential-NIAH
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating sequential information retrieval from long contexts, featuring synthetic-temporal, real-temporal, and real-logical order needles embedded in texts from 8K to 128K tokens.

nodes.name: SGD
nodes.definition: The Schema-Guided Dialogue (SGD) dataset, a challenging benchmark for multi-domain task-oriented dialogue that includes unseen domains in its test set to evaluate generalization.

nodes.name: SGHateCheck
nodes.definition: A curated multilingual dataset containing parallel toxic content across Singlish, Chinese, Malay, and Tamil, used to source hateful statements for red-teaming evaluations.

nodes.name: ShareGPT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, ShareGPT is most commonly described as a dataset of user-shared, real-world conversations with ChatGPT, collected from sharegpt.com. Definitions largely converge on dialog or instruction-response data, though some papers narrow it to authentic multilingual user requests, a wild-query source, or real conversation traces for workload benchmarking. Snippets also describe derived uses such as taking 10,000 instruction-response pairs for supervised fine-tuning, evaluating on another 1,000 instructions, and generating synthetic workloads from its real input and output texts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ShareGPT to measure 2 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is instruction-oriented: it is recorded as measuring Instruction following ability and Instruction following, and one paper describes it as a "general instruction tuning set" focused on models' instruction-following ability. Other recorded links report it as measuring Multi-turn dialogue, Text generation, and Robustness, so the measurement claims extend beyond a single construct even though instruction following is the recurrent framing.

Space of uses. In

nodes.name: ShieldGemma-9B
nodes.definition: A large language model used as an automated evaluator to assess the safety and alignment of other models' generated responses.

nodes.name: SHP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe SHP, usually expanded as Stanford Human Preferences, as a human-preference dataset used in alignment or reward-model evaluation, though one definition calls it Shared Human Preferences. The prevailing format is prompts, questions, or posts paired with responses or comments plus a preference label, sometimes described as human annotation and sometimes as preference inferred from likes or from Reddit users rating one comment as more helpful. Descriptions differ on the source material: several papers present Reddit posts, prompts, or comments, while another describes pairs of responses to StackExchange questions; some papers also frame SHP as an out-of-distribution benchmark for reward models.

What it is claimed to measure. In the linked claims, papers use SHP to measure 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. The construct link is out-of-distribution generalization, where SHP is included among datasets for testing reward models' out-of-distribution generalization, and the behavioral-indicator link is question answering, where a paper reconstructs SHP from Reddit questions and user answers for a QA task. These measurement claims are concentr

nodes.name: SHQ-NPOV
nodes.definition: A dataset of 300 human-written queries and answers on controversial topics, with each answer rated for its adherence to a Neutral Point of View (NPOV).

nodes.name: SIB-200
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a multilingual text classification benchmark spanning 204 languages and multiple domains, used to evaluate cross-domain generalization and classification accuracy. Some papers describe it more narrowly as a seven-way topic classification dataset, and one paper describes it as representing 200 languages. Papers also note that it supports both high and low-resource languages.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SIB-200 to measure one behavioral indicator, Text classification, and no constructs are linked to it. The reported use converges on text classification rather than spreading across multiple outcomes, with several papers describing the task more specifically as topic classification, including a seven-label setup.

Space of uses. Papers position SIB-200 both as a widely adopted multilingual benchmark in zero-shot evaluation and as a main grounding dataset for research. One reported use chooses it for topic classification because it has seven labels and supports a variety of high and low-resource languages, while another reports instruction tuning on each domain and evaluation across all other domains within SIB-

nodes.name: SimpleQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, SimpleQA is most commonly described as a factuality benchmark introduced by OpenAI, built from numerous concise, fact-oriented or fact-seeking questions in general knowledge areas. One definition frames it as assessing the factual capabilities of LLMs, while another describes it as evaluating the ability to answer fact-seeking questions and notes that responses are categorized as correct, incorrect, or not attempted.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SimpleQA to three constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claim is factuality-related: one paper says it was proposed to measure short-form factuality in LLMs, another uses it for factual question answering, and another takes it for truthfulness; a separate paper also uses it to measure out-of-distribution generalization. Overall, the reported uses spread across several targets, though most framings stay within factuality-oriented evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers use it alongside other benchmarks, but they do not describe SimpleQA as linked to another measurement instrument. Some studies pair it with FreshQA-2025-04-28 as one of two factuality benchmarks for fact-

nodes.name: SimpleSafetyTests
nodes.definition: SimpleSafetyTests, a safety evaluation dataset used to probe whether models refuse or avoid unsafe requests.

nodes.name: SimulatorArena
nodes.definition: Benchmark of 909 annotated human–LLM conversations in math tutoring and document creation, used to evaluate user simulators on message realism and alignment with human assistant ratings.

nodes.name: SimulEq
nodes.definition: Dataset focused on solving systems of equations, used to evaluate symbolic and algebraic reasoning capabilities in language models.

nodes.name: SingleEq
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat SingleEq as a dataset or benchmark of arithmetic or math word problems solvable with a single equation. The prevailing wording is that the problems are solvable with a single equation, while some papers narrow this to single-equation algebraic word problems or say the benchmark contains algebraic word problems that are parsed into equations. Several papers also position it as a distribution-shift, near-shift, or out-of-domain test set, and one definition explicitly says it has simpler reasoning demands.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SingleEq to measure one construct, Mathematical reasoning, and one behavioral indicator, Mathematical problem solving. The dominant claim is Mathematical reasoning: papers list it among arithmetic or math reasoning datasets and describe it as covering problems "solvable using a single linear equation." One paper also uses it to measure Mathematical problem solving in a broader benchmark set.

Space of uses. Most papers use SingleEq alongside other arithmetic or math benchmarks, most often MultiArith, SVAMP, GSM8K, AddSub, and SingleOp, with some papers also pairing it with AQuA or MATH. A recurring usage is as

nodes.name: SinhalaMMLU
nodes.definition: A multiple-choice question answering benchmark for Sinhala, containing over 7,000 questions aligned with the Sri Lankan national curriculum across six domains and 30 subjects, designed to evaluate multitask language understanding in a low-resource language.

nodes.name: SIQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is a benchmark or dataset for multiple-choice question answering about social situations, social interactions, and commonsense reasoning. Many definitions describe choosing the most likely answer to questions about people’s actions, feelings, motivations, or social consequences, while some papers frame it more specifically as social reasoning or social and emotional intelligence. Smaller uses repurpose it rather than treating it only as a fixed benchmark, for example by constructing evaluation questions from it for PERSONALITYBENCH, by placing it in a socio-emotional-skills subset, or by using a re-annotated version with Likert-scale plausibility ratings.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SIQA to measure 8 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures Commonsense reasoning, and papers also use it for General ability and Reasoning; smaller lines of work report it as measuring Social and emotional intelligence, Social reasoning, Benchmark overfitting, Functional linguistic competence, and Social competence. It is also reported as measuring Question answering and Multiple-choice ques

nodes.name: SIUO
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing is of a multimodal safety benchmark. Definitions most commonly describe it as a safety-awareness benchmark that assesses a model's ability to infer user intent and identify safety risks in multimodal inputs through visual and textual reasoning, while another paper describes it more broadly as assessing safe and effective responses under different risk combinations. One study also notes that higher scores denote better safety performance.

What it is claimed to measure. Its measurement claims are spread across 3 constructs rather than concentrated on one: papers use SIUO to measure Safety, Safety alignment, and Safety awareness, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The phrasing varies by paper, with one using it for multimodal safety, another to evaluate safe alignment, and another for assessment of safety-awareness.

Space of uses. Papers typically use SIUO within broader benchmark suites, alongside FigStep, VLGuard, MOSSBench, MSS-Bench, and MM-Safetybench. In these studies it is used as an evaluation dataset with reported SIUO scores, including a "safe&effective score"; another paper states that higher SIUO sc

nodes.name: SLAKE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats SLAKE as a medical visual question answering benchmark or dataset built from image and question-answer pairs. Several definitions further describe it as semantically labeled and knowledge-enhanced, and some add radiology images, physician annotation, region-level annotations of organs and diseases, or multiple imaging modalities such as CT and MRI across different pathologies and modalities. A smaller set of descriptions specifies versions and question formats: some papers describe English and Chinese versions, one evaluation keeps only the English portion with 641 images and 7,033 question-answer pairs, and others note open and closed questions or Yes/No and single-word answers.

What it is claimed to measure. In these papers, SLAKE is linked to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing claim is that it measures Medical visual question answering, and a smaller but closely aligned usage treats it as measuring Visual question answering; overall, the reported links stay within VQA rather than spreading across other outcomes.

Space of uses. Papers most often position SLAKE as one benchmark within a bund

nodes.name: SlideVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, SlideVQA is most commonly described as a public dataset for visual question answering on presentation slides. Definitions and snippets describe each document or slide as 20 pages long, and one study reports 1,919 slides in the training set, 400 in the test set, and 300 in development. A smaller description refers to it as an existing open-source visual document question-answering dataset used to derive refined queries in a data construction process.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SlideVQA to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing measurement use is for Information retrieval, with studies evaluating retrieval accuracy on SlideVQA or drawing question-document pairs for presentation slides. It is also used to measure Visual question answering, and one paper reports it as measuring Long-context understanding, noting that it contains 20-page documents and cross-page questions (12.9%).

Space of uses. Papers commonly place SlideVQA alongside other document benchmarks. One study compares retrieval baselines on it together with MM-LongBench, DUDE, DocVQA, and VisR-Bench, another uses it with MP-DocVQA and other document and figure VQ

nodes.name: SlimPajama
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, SlimPajama is most commonly treated as a large-scale text corpus or pre-training dataset. Several definitions present it simply as the corpus from which files are selected or as the data source for language-model pretraining, while some papers describe it more specifically as a cleaned and deduplicated version of RedPajama and a high-quality corpus with diverse sources such as C4, ArXiv, GitHub, and Books. A smaller line of work foregrounds subsets within it, either by selecting categories such as StackExchange, Github Codes, ArXiv, and Book, or by drawing token subsets for experiments.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not report SlimPajama as measuring any construct or behavioral indicator. The available descriptions instead use it as experimental data for training, post-training, pruning recovery, and related model-development procedures.

Space of uses. Most papers position SlimPajama as a training or continued-training corpus rather than a standalone evaluation protocol. Papers use it for file selection, post-prune recovery, continual pre-training after architectural changes, post-training after pruning, general language-model training, a

nodes.name: SLUE
nodes.definition: A spoken language understanding evaluation benchmark listed in the comparison of spoken language and audio comprehension benchmarks.

nodes.name: SLURP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, SLURP is most commonly described as a spoken language understanding dataset. Definitions describe a corpus of 16.5k sentences and 72k audio recordings of single-turn interactions with a home assistant, annotated with scenarios, actions, and entities; some uses keep only the reference transcriptions for slot filling, while others treat it as a seed corpus for generating dialogues with diverse intents and interwoven mode switches.

What it is claimed to measure. In these papers, SLURP is linked to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure Information extraction, and papers also use it to measure Intent classification and Sequence understanding, with evidence phrased as "SF SLURP," "intent classification ... with SLURP," and "Sequence Understanding on SLURP."

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position SLURP both as a benchmark for common speech tasks, including slot filling and intent classification, and as source material for broader dialogue construction, including work that constructs flows from MultiWOZ2.2 and SLURP and then builds TACT variants from both.

nodes.name: SMNLI
nodes.definition: A synthetic Natural Language Inference (NLI) dataset created by subsampling the MNLI dataset to induce specific spurious correlations between text genres and labels for evaluation purposes.

nodes.name: SMS Spam
nodes.definition: A dataset for binary classification of SMS messages as either legitimate (ham) or spam.

nodes.name: SNIPS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat SNIPS as a benchmark dataset for intent classification. One definition places it in a voice assistant setting with seven user intents and says it is used for evaluating task-oriented dialogue systems, while another presents it as a multi-domain dataset, mentioning restaurants, movies, and music, reporting 13,084 training utterances, and describing it as used to evaluate model reasoning on diverse and balanced data.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what SNIPS measures converge on a single behavioral indicator, intent classification. Papers use it to measure intent classification, and the linked measurement claims do not extend beyond that: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Intent classification, and to no constructs.

Space of uses. Papers treat SNIPS as a benchmark used within evaluation setups rather than as a standalone protocol. One study pairs it with ATIS as one of two intent classification benchmark datasets, and another includes SNIPS as the intent classification dataset within a broader text classification comparison; papers do not otherwise link it to measurement instruments.

nodes.name: SNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, SNLI is most commonly described as the Stanford Natural Language Inference dataset or benchmark, a large-scale sentence-pair corpus for natural language inference, textual entailment, or sentence-pair inference judgments, usually with the labels entailment, neutral, and contradiction. Several descriptions specify image captions as premises and crowd-sourced hypotheses, while some papers use specific variants such as entailment-only pairs, SNLI-TEST-SAMPLE original examples, or SNLI negation benchmarks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SNLI to measure 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure natural language inference, and a smaller set of papers report it as measuring language understanding task performance, natural language understanding, generalization, and logical consistency. Overall, the claims concentrate on natural language inference and spread more sparsely across the other reported targets.

Space of uses. Papers often use SNLI in multi-dataset evaluations alongside MNLI and RTE, and sometimes with QNLI, SST-2, and WNLI. They position it both as a standard benchmark and as an auxiliary evaluation: one p

nodes.name: Social Chemistry 101
nodes.definition: A dataset encompassing diverse social norms and moral judgments about everyday actions, used to evaluate morality.

nodes.name: SocioBench
nodes.definition: A large-scale, cross-national benchmark derived from the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) that evaluates LLMs' ability to simulate human responses in sociological surveys across 10 domains and over 30 countries.

nodes.name: SolEval
nodes.definition: Repository-level benchmark for Solidity smart contract generation, consisting of 1,507 real-world function samples from 28 repositories, with human-annotated requirements, contextual dependencies, and test cases to assess functional correctness, gas efficiency, and vulnerability rates.

nodes.name: Something-Something V2
nodes.definition: A large-scale video dataset for action recognition that focuses on fine-grained human-object interactions, often requiring temporal reasoning.

nodes.name: SORRY-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats SORRY-Bench as a benchmark or dataset of unsafe, harmful prompts or instructions for testing model safety behavior. Definitions vary in emphasis: some describe it as evaluating safety alignment and refusal capabilities, some as a harmfulness benchmark in the HarmfulQA context, and others as assessing whether an LLM rejects questions with harmful intent. Reported contents include 450 harmful instructions and harmful prompts across 45 categories, and one paper also uses it as a source of unsafe prompts to build a preference dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 1 construct and 4 behavioral indicators. The linked measurement claims cover several targets: papers use it to measure Safety, and also use it to measure Refusal, Harmful request refusal, Harmful content generation, and Jailbreaking. The framing is most often about harmfulness and refusal, including use on 450 unseen harmful test sets and as a dedicated benchmark for evaluating harmfulness in the HarmfulQA context.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers use it alongside HEx-PHI, WildJailbreak, and SALAD-Ben

nodes.name: SOTOPIA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of an open-ended, interactive benchmark environment for simulating complex social interactions between artificial or LLM agents and assessing social intelligence. Definitions consistently refer to scenarios in which agents have character or role profiles and private goals, and one paper specifies simulated social tasks defined by a scenario, two role profiles, and private goals. A more detailed usage description says it includes 90 scenarios with 5 role pairs, yielding 450 self-chat tasks and 900 non-self-chat tasks, while another paper describes it more broadly as a platform or framework for simulation and evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SOTOPIA to 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The most common linkage is that it measures Strategic reasoning: papers report evaluating strategic reasoning in SOTOPIA, including social interaction with goals and as one of the social intelligence tasks in a broader strategic-reasoning evaluation. A smaller line of work presents it as measuring Social intelligence directly, matching descriptions of the benchmark as evaluating agents' social intelligence.

Space

nodes.name: SPaRC
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available descriptions do not converge. In "SPaRC: A Spatial Pathfinding Reasoning Challenge," the name refers to a benchmark of 1,000 2D grid pathfinding puzzles used to evaluate spatial and rule-based reasoning under multiple constraints. In "Track-SQL: Enhancing Generative Language Models with Dual-Extractive Modules for Schema and Context Tracking in Multi-turn Text-to-SQL," SParC is described instead as a benchmark dataset for multi-turn Text-to-SQL, with 4,298 dialogue sequences and over 12,000 questions paired with SQL queries, used to evaluate cross-domain semantic parsing in interactive settings.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the recorded relationships, papers use it to measure 4 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The linked constructs are constraint satisfaction, multi-step planning, rule-based reasoning, and spatial reasoning, with the available evidence stating that the benchmark reveals limitations regarding all four.

Space of uses. Usage details are limited. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the recorded relationships, but a reported evaluation uses SParC alongside CoSQL as a benchmark dataset for validating a method.

nodes.name: Speech Quality Dataset
nodes.definition: A dataset from Slonim et al. (2021) containing over 600 debate speeches annotated by 15 human raters each, used to benchmark LLM judges.

nodes.name: SPEED
nodes.definition: Event detection dataset in the epidemiology and social media domain, containing 7 event types related to disease outbreaks and public health responses.

nodes.name: Spider
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats Spider as a large-scale, complex, cross-domain text-to-SQL benchmark or dataset. Papers commonly describe it as natural-language questions paired with SQL queries over multiple databases or database schemas, sometimes emphasizing executable SQL and syntactic and semantic correctness. A smaller line of work describes it as a benchmark for text-to-SQL semantic parsers or parsing over one or more relational tables, and some papers also refer to train, development, and test splits and a range of difficulty levels.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers overwhelmingly use Spider to measure Text-to-SQL, including generating SQL queries from natural-language questions and schemas. Beyond that dominant use, papers link it to two behavioral indicators, Text-to-SQL and Schema linking, and to two constructs, Cross-domain generalization and General ability. The claims are concentrated on Text-to-SQL, while a single paper each reports Spider as measuring schema linking, evaluating cross-domain generalization, or testing general downstream performance.

Space of uses. Papers usually position Spider as a standard or prominent bench

nodes.name: Spider-DK
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, Spider-DK is most commonly treated as a variant of the Spider benchmark, and one definition describes it as a robust variant. The shared characterization is that it incorporates domain knowledge into the questions and introduces domain knowledge reasoning challenges for correctly generating SQL queries; one paper also places it among datasets derived from Spider.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Spider-DK to one behavioral indicator, Text-to-SQL, and to no constructs. The only reported measurement claim is that it measures Text-to-SQL: one paper evaluates NL2SQL using SPIDER-DK alongside other datasets, so the reported use is concentrated on that single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Across the papers, Spider-DK is used alongside other Spider-based evaluations rather than with separate linked instruments. One paper uses it together with Spider and Spider-Realistic as prevalent NL2SQL datasets, and another evaluates it with the same demonstration pool as Spider-Realistic and Spider-Syn, describing these as derived from Spider.

nodes.name: Spider-Realistic
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, Spider-Realistic is most commonly described as a Spider-derived benchmark or variant that removes explicitly mentioned column names from questions. The descriptions converge on this format, with one paper specifying that the removals are made in the SPIDER development set, and they frame the change as simulating more realistic question settings or better reflecting real-world scenarios.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Spider-Realistic to measure one behavioral indicator, Text-to-SQL, and they do not link it to any constructs. The reported measurement claim centers on Text-to-SQL rather than multiple named targets: one paper on NL2SQL evaluation lists SPIDER, SPIDER-DK, and Spider-Realistic as datasets adopted for the task.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to other instruments, and instead place it alongside other Spider-derived evaluations. One description evaluates on Spider-DK, Spider-Realistic, and Spider-Syn using the same demonstration pool, while another paper positions SPIDER, SPIDER-DK, and Spider-Realistic together in evaluation for NL2SQL.

nodes.name: Spider-Syn
nodes.definition: A variant of the Spider benchmark where schema-related words in the questions are replaced with their synonyms to test model robustness to lexical variation.

nodes.name: SPSA
nodes.definition: Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation, a black-box adversarial attack that estimates the gradient using a small number of queries.

nodes.name: Spurious correlation removal
nodes.definition: Spurious correlation removal (SCR), a procedure that trains classifiers on biased data and ablates latents encoding the spurious signal to test concept isolation.

nodes.name: SQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing use of the label SQA is for science question answering, usually described as a benchmark or dataset of science questions that require complex reasoning and often include diagrams. Several definitions cast it as a multimodal benchmark for scientific reasoning, knowledge, or reasoning over text and diagrams, and one says it primarily assesses model reasoning capability. The acronym is also used differently in other papers, for sequential question answering over tables or logically related question sequences, for a 3D question answering benchmark with over 33K question-answer pairs from 650 indoor scenes, and in isolated cases for StrategyQA or a Speech Question Answering dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, SQA is linked to four constructs and four behavioral indicators, and the measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than centering on one. The most common claim is that papers use it to measure visual question answering, with SQA listed among VQA or image question answering benchmarks; other papers use an SQA-labeled benchmark to measure 3D question answering, spoken question answering, and visual instru

nodes.name: SQA3D
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe SQA3D as a situated 3D dataset or benchmark for situated question answering in 3D scenes. Some descriptions add that it is human-annotated and emphasizes the role of the "situation" in scene context; others specify that questions are posed from an embodied agent's perspective, that it contains over 33,000 question-answer pairs, and that it supports situated understanding in real-world scenes through situated question-answer pairs collected under imaginative situations.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SQA3D to two constructs, 3D understanding and vision-language reasoning, and to one behavioral indicator, situated question answering. These measurement claims are spread across multiple targets rather than centered on one: papers report 3D understanding as measured by SQA3D, explicitly evaluate vision-language reasoning on SQA3D, and present the task as "<Situation> <Question>" with phrase or single-word answers for situated question answering; the 3D understanding link is cited in language about using ScanQA and SQA3D "for visual question answering."

Space of uses. Across the papers, SQA3D is positioned as an evaluation dataset o

nodes.name: SQUAB
nodes.definition: An automatic dataset generator for ambiguous and unanswerable questions in semantic parsing, producing annotated tests across six categories: Column Ambiguity, Scope, Attachment, Column Unanswerable, Calculation Unanswerable, and Out-of-Scope.

nodes.name: SQuAD2.0-Eval
nodes.definition: Evaluation dataset derived from SQuAD2.0, designed to assess adherence and robustness in retrieval-augmented language models under complex retrieval scenarios with conflicting and irrelevant contexts.

nodes.name: SQuAD 2.0
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, SQuAD 2.0 is most commonly described as the Stanford Question Answering Dataset version 2.0, a reading comprehension or question answering benchmark built from Wikipedia articles or passages, sometimes described as expository, where answers are text spans. The prevailing framing also stresses unanswerable questions: models are expected to extract an answer when one exists, or abstain, reject, or identify that no answer exists when the context is insufficient or the text does not support an answer. A few papers describe it more indirectly, as source material for derived question answering or true-false corpora.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure four behavioral indicators and no constructs. It is most often linked to machine reading comprehension and question answering, and papers also report it as measuring document question answering; a smaller line of work samples from it for an information retrieval task. The reported measurement claims stay at the task level rather than linking the benchmark to constructs.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use it as a benchmark alongside GLUE or GLUE-X, and some pair it with other question answerin

nodes.name: SQuAD v1.1
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats SQuAD v1.1 as the Stanford Question Answering Dataset in its version 1.1 form, usually described as a reading comprehension benchmark for extractive question answering. Definitions repeatedly say the task is to answer a question from a context passage or Wikipedia article by selecting an answer span or text segment, and one paper notes that each example has a context passage, a question, and an answer, with some passages paired with multiple questions (Beyond Input Activations: Identifying Influential Latents by Gradient Sparse Autoencoders). A smaller number of descriptions call it an open-book question answering dataset or a crowdsourced Wikipedia-based reading comprehension dataset, and papers sometimes contrast v1.1, which one definition says contains no unanswerable questions, with v2.0, which another description says includes unanswerable questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 10 behavioral indicators and 5 constructs. The most common behavioral framing is question answering, followed by machine reading comprehension, document question answering, downstream task performance, and extractive que

nodes.name: SRDD
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating the generation of entire software projects.

nodes.name: SROIE
nodes.definition: A dataset for Scanned Receipt OCR and Information Extraction, used to evaluate a model's ability to perform key information extraction from receipts.

nodes.name: SST
nodes.definition: The Stanford Sentiment Treebank dataset used as a source of prompts for extracting internal representations.

nodes.name: SST-2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, SST-2 is most commonly treated as the Stanford Sentiment Treebank v2, a binary sentiment classification benchmark or dataset. Definitions usually describe movie reviews, or sentences and single sentences extracted from movie reviews, labeled as positive or negative; some papers also place it within GLUE. A smaller set of papers refers to specialized forms or subsets, including an OOD version, use as out-of-domain samples for another task, and subsets selected to build a forget set for unlearning experiments.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SST-2 to 6 behavioral indicators and 6 constructs, so its reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than concentrated on one. The prevailing use is to measure sentiment analysis and text classification; among constructs, it is most often used for adversarial robustness and in-context learning, then calibration, while other papers also report it as measuring additional constructs and task-level indicators.

Space of uses. Papers link SST-2 to 2 other instruments. It is most often used alongside GLUE, with many papers describing it as a GLUE task or dataset, and the recorded relationshi

nodes.name: SST-5
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats SST-5, also written SST5, as the Stanford Sentiment Treebank for fine-grained sentiment classification with five labels. Definitions usually describe the labels as ranging from very negative to very positive, and one source spells out the five classes as "very positive", "positive", "neutral", "negative", and "very negative"; some papers also specify that the texts are movie reviews. Papers alternate between calling it a benchmark, a dataset, and a task, and one definition describes it as a five-class sentiment classification benchmark used to evaluate fine-tuned model performance.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SST-5 to 3 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing use is to measure Sentiment analysis, with several papers labeling it as a sentiment analysis or sentiment classification dataset. Smaller lines of work report Controlled sentiment generation and Multiple-choice question answering as measured by SST-5, and single papers also use it to measure In-context learning and Reasoning, so the recorded claims spread across several targets rather than centering on only one construct.

Space o

nodes.name: ST-VQA
nodes.definition: ST-VQA (Biten et al., 2019) is a benchmark for visual question answering focused on scene text, requiring models to understand text in its visual context.

nodes.name: StableToolBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, StableToolBench is most commonly described as a benchmark for evaluating tool invocation or the accuracy of function calls generated by models. Some descriptions stay at that level, while others characterize it more specifically as a stable version of the Rapid-API access system derived from ToolBench, using an API caching mechanism; those papers also describe it as containing 765 solvable tasks or questions across six subsets or subtasks, varying in tool category and instruction complexity from single-tool to multi-tool instructions, and featuring a virtual API server and stable evaluation system.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link the benchmark to a narrow set of targets rather than many distinct outcomes: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Tool use, and one construct, Generalization. One paper uses it to measure Tool use, operationalized through the "accuracy of function calls" on StableToolBench, and another reports using real-world tool benchmarks including this one to evaluate generalization ability.

Space of uses. In use, papers position StableToolBench as an evaluation benchmark within broader benchmark suites and direct model

nodes.name: Standard CL Benchmark
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat it as a continual learning benchmark built from classification datasets. One description presents the standard CL benchmarks as having 4 tasks and 5 categories for assessing performance across task sequences, while another presents a benchmark for language models made up of five text classification datasets: AG News, Amazon Reviews, Yelp Reviews, DBpedia, and Yahoo Answers.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement use is concentrated on text classification. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, text classification, describing it as five text classification datasets or five text classification tasks, and no constructs are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation benchmark in continual learning, including for assessing model performance across task sequences and for evaluation setups described as designed for language models. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: Stanford Cars
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Stanford Cars is most commonly described as a fine-grained image classification benchmark or dataset for car models. Several definitions specify that it contains 196 classes or categories of cars, and some frame it as assessing fine-grained visual discrimination, while a smaller framing presents it more generally as an image classification benchmark used to test downstream performance. Papers also place it within broader image recognition and fine-grained visual classification benchmark suites.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use Stanford Cars to measure the behavioral indicator Image classification. It is linked to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs, so the recorded measurement use centers on a single target rather than being spread across multiple constructs. The relationship evidence describes this use in image recognition, zero-shot classification, downstream performance, and broader classification-domain evaluations.

Space of uses. Usage is usually as one dataset among several benchmarks, rather than as a standalone protocol. Snippets place it in zero-shot and linear-probe image classification, downstream

nodes.name: Stanford Dogs
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, Stanford Dogs is treated as a fine-grained visual classification or recognition resource centered on 120 breeds of dogs. The prevailing description places it within the FGVC benchmark, with one paper stating that FGVC includes Stanford Dogs among five Fine-Grained Visual Classification datasets. A smaller usage describes the same benchmark after task reformulation, where it is used as a 4-way multiple-choice question task.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Stanford Dogs to one construct and one behavioral indicator. It is used to measure fine-grained perception in work that lists it among fine-grained benchmarks for ablation studies, and it is also used to measure image classification in work that includes it among image recognition datasets. The reported measurement claims therefore converge on these two targets rather than spreading across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers position Stanford Dogs alongside one linked instrument, FGVC, by treating it as part of that benchmark collection. In use, it appears within broader evaluation suites rather than in isolation, for example among image recognition datasets in one study

nodes.name: STAR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats STAR as a video question-answering benchmark for situated reasoning in real-world videos. Definitions variously say it requires situational reasoning about social interactions and events, and one paper further describes it as containing questions about interaction, sequence, prediction, and feasibility. A smaller line of work uses it as a source for referred video question-answering, and another presents it in zero-shot and multi-choice video question answering evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link STAR to five constructs and one behavioral indicator overall, so the measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on a single construct. The behavioral indicator linked to it is Video question answering, and papers also report STAR as measuring Visual reasoning, Fine-grained visual understanding, Causal reasoning, and Temporal reasoning; for the last two, one paper says the dataset "demand[s] both causal and temporal reasoning abilities." One additional paper records STAR as related to Self-improvement rather than as a measure.

Space of uses. Papers most often present STAR inside broade

nodes.name: Star Graph Task
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats the Star Graph Task as a synthetic path-finding or planning benchmark on a star-shaped graph. Most descriptions say the model must output or predict the path between nodes, either as the full sequence from a start node to a specified final node or, in another formulation, as next-node prediction conditioned on an edge list, start, goal, and current path. A smaller descriptive variant focuses on the graph-generation setup itself: the start vertex sits at the center, multiple spokes radiate outward, and the goal lies at the end of one spoke.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The dominant measurement claim is that it measures Planning: papers describe it as a simple path-finding task that requires basic planning, and Planning is recorded as measured by the Star Graph Task in the most common linkage. A narrower usage links it to Pathfinding, so the reported measurement claims are concentrated on these two closely related targets rather than spread across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. In use, papers position it mainly as a didactic or

nodes.name: STaRK-Amazon
nodes.definition: A product search dataset from the STaRK benchmark, where documents are derived from product reviews and Q&A records, and a knowledge graph contains relations like 'products viewed together'.

nodes.name: STEER-BENCH
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating community-specific steerability in LLMs using contrasting Reddit communities, comprising over 10,000 instruction-response pairs and 5,500 multiple-choice questions across 30 subreddit pairs and 19 domains.

nodes.name: StereoSet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, StereoSet is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for measuring stereotypical bias in language models. Definitions usually present it as a fill-in-the-blank or sentence-completion format with three alternatives, stereotypical, anti-stereotypical, and meaningless or unrelated, and one description specifies 765 gap sentences for the gender intrasentence task while another describes each sample as a sentence triplet. Papers also use different slices or framings: some use the intrasentence subset, some mention both intrasentence and intersentence contexts, and smaller descriptions cast it as crowdsourced Context Association Tests or as an intrinsic metric based on the log probabilities of stereotype-evoking words.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link StereoSet to 4 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure fairness, stereotyping, and social bias, with papers describing it as testing stereotypical associations and as measuring stereotypes across gender, profession, race, and religion; one other construct appears in a smaller link. At the behavioral level, papers connect it to sentence completion and

nodes.name: StoryCloze
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe StoryCloze as a benchmark for story understanding and commonsense reasoning, usually framed as choosing the correct ending to a short story. Most definitions specify a four-sentence story and connect the task to script knowledge, narrative understanding, or coherence, while some instead describe five-sentence stories, cloze-style story completion, or sentence completion. One paper further describes it as a dataset of short stories with a valid and an invalid ending, originally used for story understanding and adapted there for open-ended generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link StoryCloze to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing measurement claim is that it measures Commonsense reasoning: papers place it among common sense reasoning tasks and describe the final sentence as being selected based on commonsense knowledge. Smaller uses treat it as measuring Multiple-choice question answering and Story generation, with one paper listing it among multiple-choice tasks and another using it for a story generation task while noting its original use for story understanding.

Space of uses. In use, papers most often po

nodes.name: StrategyQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is a commonsense question-answering benchmark of yes/no or true or false questions that require implicit multi-step or multi-hop reasoning, often by inferring a strategy or decomposing the question. Some authors describe it more specifically as open-domain or fact reasoning; some descriptions also add supporting evidence, explanations, or rationales, and one paper says the dataset provides pieces of evidence from Wikipedia, while another says it involves a curated knowledge base of 10,000 Wikipedia passages. Papers describe different scales as well, mentioning a 687-question test split, 2,780 examples, or 10,824 examples.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 9 constructs and 6 behavioral indicators. The dominant claim is that it measures commonsense reasoning, with recurring use for reasoning and factuality; on the behavioral side, papers report it as evaluating question answering and chain of thought. Overall, papers spread its use across many targets rather than tying it to a single outcome.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to any other measurement instrument. Most commonly, they use it as one benchmark wi

nodes.name: StrongREJECT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, StrongREJECT is most commonly treated as a safety or jailbreak evaluation benchmark built around harmful or forbidden prompts and a way to score model responses. Descriptions vary: some papers present an open-source dataset of manually constructed, realistic malicious instructions, sometimes tied to prohibited-use policies and sometimes used as a 60-prompt, six-category subset or small dataset; others describe a dataset plus scoring system, or a judge model, including a Gemma-2B safety classifier and a GPT-4o-mini based evaluator that score refusal, effectiveness, or harmfulness. A smaller line of work frames it specifically as text-generation evaluation for whether models reject unsafe requests under adversarial or jailbreak conditions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link StrongREJECT to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure harmlessness and safety: papers use StrongREJECT scores or harmful-prompt evaluation to quantify response harmfulness, safety violation, or refusal of harmful requests. One paper also says the evaluator measures both willingness and capabilities, linking it to general ability. On behaviora

nodes.name: StrongREJECT evaluator
nodes.definition: An existing rubric-based evaluation method for LLM safety, adapted here for comparison, which scores responses based on refusal, specificity, and convincingness without a toxicity component.

nodes.name: STS12
nodes.definition: A dataset from the SemEval-2012 workshop on Semantic Textual Similarity, used for evaluating sentence similarity prediction.

nodes.name: STS-B
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark for sentence-pair evaluation, usually framed as a downstream sentence similarity task or a GLUE task. Several definitions add that it provides sentence pairs with human-annotated similarity scores on a 0 to 5 scale, and papers report correlation-based metrics on it, including Spearman and Pearson correlation. A smaller line of work uses different task framings, treating it as a classification dataset with a modest number of labels or as a scoring task where the model outputs a string form of a numerical prediction.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is concentrated rather than spread across many targets. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Semantic textual similarity, and to no constructs; one paper describes STSB as directly measuring the ability of embeddings to capture fine-grained semantic similarity, which matches the broader pattern of using it for sentence similarity evaluation.

Space of uses. Most commonly, papers use it as one item in larger evaluation suites rather than in isolation, for example within GLUE development or fine-tuning task co

nodes.name: STS tasks
nodes.definition: A collection of datasets computed by the SentEval toolkit to evaluate sentence embeddings on the task of semantic textual similarity. It includes datasets like STS 2012-2016, SICK-R, and STS-B.

nodes.name: Student Essay corpus
nodes.definition: A domain-specific dataset of student essays used to evaluate LLM text detection in academic writing contexts.

nodes.name: Subj
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats Subj or SUBJ as a subjectivity classification dataset or benchmark for distinguishing subjective from objective text. Most definitions describe a binary text classification task, often at the sentence level, and some papers place it under general natural language understanding or text classification evaluation. A smaller line describes it as a binary classification dataset of movie reviews labeled objective or subjective, and definitions also situate it in in-context evaluation of fine-tuned models or in low-data evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Recorded links focus on behavioral indicators rather than constructs: papers use Subj to measure 2 behavioral indicators, Text classification and Subjectivity classification, and no constructs are linked to it. The dominant linkage is to Text classification, where papers place Subj among datasets that admit classification tasks or use it in text classification evaluation suites. A narrower linkage reports it as measuring Subjectivity classification through the objective versus subjective decision task.

Space of uses. Papers typically use Subj alongside other text

nodes.name: SugarCrepe
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, SugarCrepe is most commonly treated as a compositionality benchmark for vision-language models. Definitions describe it as a large-scale benchmark for systematically evaluating compositional reasoning by testing swaps, replacements, and additions of objects, attributes, and relations. A smaller description emphasizes a more fine-grained setup in which attributes and semantic relationships are interlinked, with evaluation centered on a single image and caption choice; one paper adds that, because only a single image is provided, the task is simplified to Text Score.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SugarCrepe to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The dominant measurement claim is compositional: papers use it to measure compositional reasoning and compositionality, including analyses of models' compositional understanding and evaluations of VLMs' ability for compositionality. A smaller line of work also reports it as measuring relation understanding, placing it among relational benchmarks for evaluating models' ability to understand and represent relationships between objects within an image.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument

nodes.name: SummEval
SUN
nodes.definition: An out-of-distribution scene dataset used to evaluate detection of semantically different or near-OOD inputs.

nodes.name: SUN397
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description treats SUN397 as a scene dataset. One line of work describes it as a scene recognition dataset used for zero-shot transfer evaluation, while another describes it as a dataset for scene classification used to evaluate few-shot learning performance; one source also places it among publicly available image recognition datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement use is concentrated rather than spread across many targets. Papers link SUN397 to one behavioral indicator, Image classification, and to no constructs, using it to measure image classification in finetuning and broader benchmark evaluations.

Space of uses. Papers typically position SUN397 as one member of a larger evaluation suite rather than as a standalone protocol. It appears alongside Oxford Flowers, Food101, FGVC-Aircraft, and Sports100 in zero-shot reporting, and other papers include it among datasets used for finetuning and standard benchmark evaluation; no other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: Super-NaturalInstructions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Super-NaturalInstructions is most commonly described as a large, diverse instruction-following benchmark of NLP tasks with expert-written or human-written instructions, often said to contain over 1600, or specifically 1,616, tasks spanning both classification and generation. Some definitions also emphasize prompt formats, and papers use several short names, including SuperNI, Super NI, and S-NI. A smaller line of work adopts a narrower continual learning framing, describing a 15-task SuperNI Benchmark across dialogue generation, information extraction, question answering, summarization, and sentiment analysis, or using a 53-task subset with 19 multiple-choice and 34 classification tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 5 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The most common linked behavioral indicators are Instruction following, Text generation, and Text classification, and the most common linked constructs are Task generalization, Continual learning, Generalization, Multi-task ability, and Translation ability. The prevailing usage is instruction-following evaluation, but the linked claims also spread across cross-task generaliz

nodes.name: SUPERB
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available descriptions treat SUPERB as a benchmark for spoken language understanding, with the prevailing characterization emphasizing coarse-grained semantic understanding tasks. One paper further describes it as the first benchmark specifically designed for spoken language.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SUPERB to measure speech understanding, and the reported measurement claims converge on that single construct rather than spreading across several constructs. It is also linked to one behavioral indicator, speech recognition, but that connection is described as a related use rather than as a direct measurement claim.

Space of uses. The available relationships do not link SUPERB directly to any other measurement instrument. In one use, a paper evaluates ASR with TED-LIUMv3, intent classification with SLURP, and speaker ID with VoxCeleb1, while stating that these evaluations follow the SUPERB configuration.

Concerns raised. A concern raised in the available discussion is that SUPERB primarily focuses on coarse-grained semantic understanding tasks and, in that account, overlooks various acoustic features.

nodes.name: SuperGLUE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing treats SuperGLUE as a benchmark suite of diverse, challenging natural language understanding tasks, usually described as more difficult than GLUE and aimed at reasoning, inference, and comprehension. Some definitions present it as a general-purpose language understanding benchmark spanning question answering, coreference, and logical reasoning, and one definition notes accuracy as the primary metric. Papers differ on scope, describing 6, 7, or 8 tasks, and several use named subsets rather than the whole suite, for example BoolQ, CB, and COPA.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SuperGLUE to 2 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The dominant construct-level use is to measure natural language understanding, while a smaller line of work uses it to measure multi-task ability; at the behavioral level, it is reported as evaluating language understanding task performance, classification, and coreference resolution, with 1 other behavioral indicator also linked. Taken together, the claims are more concentrated on natural language understanding than dispersed across many constructs.

Space of uses. Most commonly, papers use Super

nodes.name: SuperGPQA
nodes.definition: Scientific reasoning benchmark with 1500 sampled questions at varying difficulty levels, used to assess broad scientific knowledge and reasoning.

nodes.name: SVAMP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats SVAMP as an arithmetic or grade-school math word problem benchmark, often described as a challenge set with simple, controlled, or designed variations in wording, structure, semantics, or numbers. Many definitions say these variations are meant to test compositional generalization, robustness, and sensitivity to sentence or question changes, and one paper says the perturbations target spurious correlations, question sensitivity, and structural invariance. Papers also often position it as out-of-domain or out-of-distribution, while a smaller description portrays it as a number-generation test with minimal linguistic variation; one paper specifies English math word problems up to grade 4.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SVAMP to measure 4 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The dominant claim is that it measures Mathematical reasoning, and a related strand uses it for Reasoning and Mathematical problem solving. Smaller uses report it as measuring Generalization and Robustness, and in a few cases Instruction following and Text generation, so the claimed targets spread across several outcomes even though mathematical

nodes.name: SVHN
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe SVHN as the Street View House Numbers dataset, containing images of house numbers. In the available definition, it is used for in-distribution image generation and completion tasks, and one source snippet states, "For imaging ICL experiments, we use SVHN for in-distribution data." Other papers refer to it as a benchmark dataset in broader evaluations and as an external OOD dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Overall, papers link SVHN to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The most common use in these papers is to measure image classification, with SVHN included in broader classification benchmark evaluations. A smaller line of work uses it to measure out-of-distribution detection, where it is described as an external OOD dataset, and one paper reports it as measuring optical character recognition ability. The measurement claims therefore span several targets rather than converging on a single construct.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to SVHN. Instead, papers usually position it as one component of larger evaluation suites: it appears in classification runs alongside several other benchmark datasets, in one

nodes.name: SWAG
nodes.definition: A dataset for evaluating commonsense inference through sentence completion tasks.

nodes.name: SWDE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Definitions treat SWDE as a recall-intensive benchmark for retrieving or extracting information from long or in-context passages. Some authors call it an information extraction benchmark used for long-sequence retrieval, including as one of the "six recall-intensive tasks" in Longhorn: State Space Models are Amortized Online Learners, while others describe it as an information-retrieval benchmark designed to evaluate retrieval from in-context passages scraped from HTML/PDFs.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, SWDE is used to measure one construct and two behavioral indicators. The linked behavioral indicators are Information extraction and Synthetic recall, and the linked construct is Long-context understanding; in each case, papers present the relation as SWDE measuring the target. One paper operationalizes Long-context understanding through a "Recall" average across FDA, SWDE, and SQuAD.

Space of uses. Papers often deploy SWDE alongside FDA. It is positioned within recall-focused evaluations, and one paper combines it with FDA and SQuAD inside a broader "Recall" score. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: SWE-bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat it as a benchmark, often a benchmark dataset, for real-world software engineering or GitHub issue resolution tasks. Papers commonly describe it as containing 2,294 instances from 12 Python repositories, though they variously call those instances GitHub issues, issue-pull request pairs, or tasks derived from pull requests; several descriptions add that systems must edit a repository or generate a patch that resolves the issue and passes unit tests, and one paper names % Resolved (Pass@1) as the metric. A related subset, SWE-bench Lite, is described as a 300-instance sample from the full benchmark, and one paper also describes SWEBench as the source dataset adapted into TESTGENEVAL.

What it is claimed to measure. In measurement claims, papers link it to 1 construct and 3 behavioral indicators. The construct link treats it as measuring Software engineering ability, while the behavioral links use it to measure Code debugging, GitHub issue resolution, and Code generation. Overall, the linked uses span a broad software-engineering construct and several task-specific behaviors rather than a single behavioral label.

Space of uses. Papers commonly posit

nodes.name: SWE-bench Lite
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats SWE-bench Lite as the lite, commonly used subset of SWE-bench for evaluating autonomous or automated software engineering. Most descriptions present it as a repository-level benchmark or evaluation suite built from real GitHub issues, codebases, and code patches, usually as 300 issues or task instances sampled from the full benchmark. A recurring framing is that it offers a more self-contained evaluation of functional bug fixes, sometimes with hidden unit tests; papers differ in detail, with one description referring to 11 Python repositories and another to 12 real-world software projects.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three behavioral indicators and no constructs. The linked measurement claims are most often for software issue resolution, followed by code debugging and GitHub issue resolution, and papers report outcomes such as issue resolution rate on SWE-bench Lite. All linked measurement claims in these papers are behavioral indicators rather than constructs.

Space of uses. Among linked instruments, papers connect it only to SWE-bench, describing SWE-bench Lite as a 300-instance subset or lite version o

nodes.name: SWE-bench Verified
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, papers treat SWE-bench Verified as a benchmark dataset and a curated subset of SWE-Bench with 500 samples or instances. The prevailing description is that these cases were manually verified or further vetted by human annotators, in one definition specifically professional software developers, for appropriately scoped unit tests and well-specified issue descriptions; one snippet also says the released subset was verified to be non-problematic. One paper additionally describes it as containing 500 samples across 4 difficulty levels.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure one behavioral indicator, software issue resolution, and one construct, general ability. The behavioral-indicator use is illustrated by work reporting an issue resolution rate on SWE-bench Verified, while another paper lists it among benchmarks relevant to today’s frontier models and thereby treats it as measuring general ability. The reported measurement claims cover only these two targets.

Space of uses. In the available descriptions, papers position SWE-bench Verified as a benchmark for automatically resolving software engineering issues, and one paper explici

nodes.name: sWUGGY
nodes.definition: A benchmark from the ZeroSpeech challenge that objectively measures a model's language capability by testing its ability to score a real word higher than a phonetically similar non-word.

nodes.name: SyGuS
nodes.definition: A dataset of text editing problems originating from the Syntax-Guided Synthesis (SyGuS) competition, generally considered easier than other benchmarks.

nodes.name: SYNC
nodes.definition: SYNC (SYNthetic Contexts) is a synthetic long-context evaluation suite with graph understanding and unseen-language translation tasks designed for controlled comparisons of LLM capabilities.

nodes.name: Synonym substitution attack
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing framing is a robustness evaluation in which words in generated or test text are replaced with synonyms. Papers variously describe it as an evaluation procedure, an observable attack, or an adversarial evaluation procedure; one definition specifies using BERT and WordNet, and another places it within semantically invariant perturbations alongside text paraphrasing.

What it is claimed to measure. In the papers' own descriptions, it is used to test the robustness or resilience of a watermark or detector, and one snippet says papers compare detection F1 scores under different synonymous word substitution scenarios. No constructs and no behavioral indicators are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an attack condition for evaluation, not alongside any linked measurement instrument. Reported uses include evaluating resilience with BERT and WordNet, comparing detection F1 across synonym substitution scenarios, and applying synonym replacement with a replacement ratio of 0.2 alongside paraphrase attacks on test data from an unknown target domain.

nodes.name: SyntaxGym
nodes.definition: A suite of diagnostic tests evaluating six distinct syntactic phenomena through surprisal-based metrics, where models are assessed on their ability to assign appropriate surprisal to sentence continuations based on syntactic constraints.

nodes.name: T2R-bench
nodes.definition: A bilingual benchmark for evaluating table-to-report generation, comprising 457 real-world industrial tables across 19 domains, with 910 questions and annotated report keypoints to assess numerical accuracy, information coverage, and general quality.

nodes.name: T-Eval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, T-Eval is most commonly described as an out-of-distribution benchmark for LLM tool use and API utilization, especially multi-step decision-making. Papers variously call it an OOD benchmark, an out-of-distribution task planning dataset, and a benchmark "for tool use," with the fuller description emphasizing evaluation of LLMs' capability to utilize APIs across multi-step decisions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link T-Eval to 2 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The most frequently linked constructs are Planning and Reasoning, and the most frequently linked behavioral indicators are Action execution and Instruction following; one paper also states that it "assesses six core competencies: planning, reasoning, retrieval, understanding, instruction following, and reviewing" (Can Compressed LLMs Truly Act? An Empirical Evaluation of Agentic Capabilities in LLM Compression), so papers report it as measuring several capabilities rather than a single one.

Space of uses. In use, papers position T-Eval mainly as an out-of-distribution evaluation for generalization and agentic tool use. WorkflowLLM: Enhancing Workflow Orchestration Capa

nodes.name: T-REx
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, T-REx is most commonly described as a slot-filling or relation-extraction benchmark. Papers describe it as a slot filling dataset for factual relation extraction-style prediction, sometimes more specifically as a large-scale slot-filling dataset derived from Wikipedia abstracts and aligned with Wikidata triples, and one paper places it in the KILT subset of evaluation tasks; a smaller line of work instead describes it as an open-ended QA dataset derived from knowledge base triples and used to test factual recall on rare relational knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link T-REx to one behavioral indicator, Information extraction, and to no constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure Information extraction, with the evidence framed as slot filling, including table labels such as "Slot Filling" and descriptions of T-REx as a slot-filling task, so the reported measurement claims converge on a single indicator rather than spreading across several targets.

Space of uses. Papers use T-REx as a task within broader evaluation suites rather than as a standalone protocol paired with other linked instruments. It is described as part of a KI

nodes.name: TabFact
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, TabFact is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for table-based fact verification over Wikipedia tables, pairing tables with textual statements and asking whether each statement is supported, entailed or true, or instead refuted or false, by the table. Several papers also call it a large-scale dataset, and some describe a specific evaluation subset, the test-small set with 2,024 statements or test samples from 298 tables. A smaller line of work presents it as a public TableQA resource, describing pairs of content-related question and answer or yes or no answers for TQA evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TabFact to measure 2 behavioral indicators and 1 construct.
