The prevailing measurement claim is fact checking, with papers explicitly using it for fact verification or TFV; a smaller but recurring usage treats it as measuring table question answering, including TableQA settings where the answer is yes or no. At the construct level, it is also reported as measuring table reasoning, so papers connect it both to specific behaviors and to a broader table reasoning construct.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use TabFac

nodes.name: TableBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available definitions, papers treat TableBench as a challenging benchmark for table reasoning. It is described as covering diverse question types and topics, with the aim of evaluating table reasoning across a wide range of scenarios.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers link it to one construct, Table reasoning, and one behavioral indicator, Table question answering. One paper places it among "widely used table reasoning datasets," while another includes it in benchmark data for evaluating table question answering.

Space of uses. In use, papers position TableBench as an evaluation dataset within a broader benchmark suite. One study reports experiments on WikiTableQuestions, HiTab, and TableBench, showing that it is used alongside those two benchmarks in a broader evaluation setup, and another lists it in table task and benchmark data for evaluation.

nodes.name: TableEval
nodes.definition: A real-world benchmark for table question answering featuring complex table structures (hierarchical, nested, concise), multilingual content (Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, English), and cross-domain data from finance, government, academia, and industry reports.

nodes.name: TabMWP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, TabMWP is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset of table-based math word problems, usually framed as mathematical reasoning over tabular or semi-structured data. Definitions describe examples as combining a table with a natural-language problem that requires extracting relevant information and performing calculations; one paper says each sample contains "one table and one corresponding problem in natural language" (CRAFT: Customizing LLMs by Creating and Retrieving from Specialized Toolsets). A smaller line of work describes it as tabular or structured-data question answering, and some papers phrase the tables as contextual input or semi-structured tables rather than simply tabular data.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TabMWP to two constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is as a measure of Mathematical reasoning, with several papers listing it among math reasoning benchmarks or saying it requires mathematical reasoning; a smaller line of work treats it as measuring Reasoning more generally, and one paper uses it to measure Question answering in tabular contexts. Overall, most linked claims center o

nodes.name: TACO
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, TACO is described as a competitive programming benchmark made up of problems sourced from CodeContests, APPS, and various programming contest platforms, and used to evaluate code generation. The prevailing description emphasizes difficulty stratification: one account says the test set is split into easy, medium, medium-hard, hard, and very-hard levels, while another reports using the easy and hard split; one paper also notes that it adopts a subset of TACO.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TACO to measure code generation. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Code generation, and to no constructs, so the reported use centers on a single behavioral target rather than a broader set of constructs. The relationship evidence describes it as focused on algorithmic code generation and as a benchmark on which authors report code-generation performance.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the available papers, TACO is used in coding experiments either by adopting a subset of it for evaluation or by reporting performance on it as "another competitive programming benchmark," including results on easy and hard splits.

Conc

nodes.name: TACRED
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe TACRED as a large-scale benchmark dataset for relation extraction. Definitions commonly trace it to the TAC Knowledge Base Population challenges, and one paper specifies it as a large-scale English dataset from the TACKBP4 challenge with 42 distinct relations. One definition adds that it contains annotated entity pairs and relations from news and web text, and one paper refers to TACRED together with variants such as TACRED-Revisit and Re-TACRED.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, the use claims converge on a single target: TACRED is used to measure relation extraction. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Relation extraction, and to no constructs, describing it as one of the "widely used RE benchmark datasets" and as part of "standard relation extraction benchmarks" for evaluating relation extraction performance.

Space of uses. Papers most often position TACRED as an evaluation benchmark used alongside other relation extraction datasets, especially SemEval, FewRel, TACREV, TACRED-Revisit, and Re-TACRED. Several papers describe experiments on benchmark sets that include TACRED, and some report few-shot settings on it, such as

nodes.name: TACT
nodes.definition: The TOD-And-Chitchat Transition dataset, designed for training and evaluating agents on their ability to handle fluid transitions between task-oriented and chitchat dialogue modes.

nodes.name: TactfulToM
nodes.definition: An English benchmark consisting of 100 multi-party conversations and 6.7K questions designed to evaluate LLMs’ understanding of white lies, including mental state tracking, justification, and reasoning about prosocial deception.

nodes.name: Talk2Car
nodes.definition: A 3D referring expression comprehension dataset for driving scenarios that evaluates a model's ability to ground a textual command to a specific object in 3D space.

nodes.name: TaskBench
nodes.definition: A comprehensive benchmark framework designed to evaluate the capability of LLMs in task automation across three stages: task decomposition, tool selection, and parameter prediction.

nodes.name: Tatoeba
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available definitions, Tatoeba is described as the validation split of a dataset for cross-lingual sentence retrieval. The only characterization provided is that papers use this split for independent validation of cross-lingual retrieval findings.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link Tatoeba to any constructs or behavioral indicators as a measurement instrument. Instead, it is described only in relation to validating cross-lingual sentence retrieval results.

Space of uses. The available paper uses Tatoeba alongside the test split of BUCC-18, and positions it as an auxiliary validation check rather than describing any broader role. In the quoted usage, authors report that they present results on the validation split of Tatoeba "for an independent validation of our findings."

nodes.name: TDIUC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited work, TDIUC is most commonly treated as a visual question answering dataset and benchmark built around simple visual understanding questions with clear answers. Some authors describe it more specifically as featuring 1.6 million questions across 170,000 images, organized into 12 question types ranging from object identification to positional reasoning. Papers also describe drawing subsets from it, such as selecting ten categories of questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TDIUC to measure one behavioral indicator, Abstention, and no constructs are linked to it. The reported measurement claim is that TDIUC contains absurd questions, about 22% of the total, that are not related to the image and thus should not be answered, so authors evaluate abstention on it. In the linked uses, its measurement role is concentrated on this single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. Papers position TDIUC as a representative benchmark for examining specific topics and question types, and as a source for benchmark tasks in visual question answering. One line of use selects ten categories of questions

nodes.name: TempCompass
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, TempCompass is most commonly described as a benchmark for visual temporal reasoning or temporal understanding in video-language models. Definitions consistently place it on videos, often specifically short videos, and describe task formats that include multiple-choice QA, yes/no QA, caption matching, and caption generation; some papers describe its focus through event ordering, duration inference, temporal order information, or temporal aspects such as speed, direction, and attribute changes. One description also specifies that it contains 410 videos and 7,540 instructions, and one paper explicitly uses a Multiple-Choice subset.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the most common measurement claim is that TempCompass measures Temporal understanding, followed by Temporal reasoning and Video understanding; papers also link it to one behavioral indicator, Video question answering. These measurement claims are concentrated in three constructs rather than spread across many others, and the evidence describes the benchmark as assessing temporal understanding capabilities across five dimensions, diagnosing multi-facet basic video temporal understandin

nodes.name: TempReason
nodes.definition: A benchmark that evaluates both event-time and event-event temporal relations in time-sensitive question answering using real-world facts.

nodes.name: Text2Cypher
nodes.definition: A large-scale dataset released by Neo4j for evaluating the task of translating natural language to Cypher queries.

nodes.name: Text8
nodes.definition: A character-level text modeling benchmark extracted from English Wikipedia and used to evaluate language model likelihood on short text chunks.

nodes.name: TextEE
nodes.definition: A standardized event extraction framework used to compare models under uniform preprocessing, splits, and implementations.

nodes.name: TextVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as a visual question answering benchmark or dataset in which answering requires reading and reasoning about text within images, often described as text-rich or natural-image question answering. Some definitions place it more specifically in OCR, text recognition, or Text/Doc evaluation, and papers sometimes refer to it as TextQA, VQAT, or VQAText. A smaller line of work frames it as a document task dataset for multimodal documents, and a few papers mention specific evaluation splits such as the validation set or "TextVQA val."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TextVQA to measure 9 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The most frequent links are to Visual understanding, Fine-grained visual understanding, General ability, Visual question answering, and Optical character recognition, with the remaining claims extending to 6 other constructs and 3 other behavioral indicators. The prevailing measurement claims center on text-oriented VQA and OCR-style evaluation, but papers also use it for a wider spread of construct claims rather than limiting it to one framing.

Space of uses. Most papers position TextVQA as a standard tex

nodes.name: TextWorld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, TextWorld is most commonly described as a text-based agent benchmark centered on interactive fiction or other text-based games. Definitions frame it either as an evaluation benchmark for capabilities like planning, commonsense reasoning, and exploration, or as a benchmark sandbox for training and evaluating reinforcement learning agents. One paper also describes it as entirely text-based, with no visual component, where the agent explores mazes and interacts with everyday objects through natural language.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, TextWorld is linked as measuring 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The named construct links are Planning, Commonsense reasoning, and Memory, and one study describes its tasks as requiring commonsense reasoning, long-term planning, and memory. Navigation is the linked behavioral indicator, with a paper connecting it to maze exploration and natural-language interaction with objects, so the measurement claims spread across several capabilities rather than a single construct.

Space of uses. Papers use TextWorld as a text environment for evaluating agents on long-horizon memory and planning, expl

nodes.name: TFDP
nodes.definition: Token-Focused Disparity Probing, a methodology for auditing autoregressive LLMs using single-token masked prediction on minimally contrastive sentence pairs, integrating multi-scale semantic alignment and disparity metrics (PS, PSD, WFS).

nodes.name: TGIF
nodes.definition: The Tumblr GIF dataset, used for evaluating video understanding tasks such as action recognition and description generation.

nodes.name: TGIF-QA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a video question answering benchmark built from the TGIF, or Tumblr GIF, dataset, with animated GIFs as the video source. Definitions commonly describe it as targeting short video clips or sequences and assessing temporal, causal, or spatio-temporal reasoning, and one recurring description highlights tasks such as repetition counting and state transition recognition. A smaller line of work describes it more broadly as a visual question answering dataset, and one paper uses it as a source of evaluation data for count and reasoning tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TGIF-QA to 1 behavioral indicator and 1 construct. The prevailing usage is to measure Video question answering: papers describe it as one of the common, open-ended, or zero-shot VideoQA benchmarks. A smaller usage treats it as measuring Video understanding, with one paper placing it in a broader suite of video understanding benchmarks. Overall, the measurement claims are concentrated on these two targets rather than spread across many constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. Across papers, TGIF-QA is usually used as one item in a larger evaluat

nodes.name: The Pile
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing is of a large, diverse language modeling corpus used for pre-training, though some papers instead emphasize it as validation or test data, or as a source for sampled analysis sets. Definitions variously describe an 800GB or 825 GB English text corpus, sometimes open-source, with train, validation, and test splits; some papers highlight 22 subsets or subdomains, while others select 16 non-copyrighted subsets or domain slices such as Pubmed Central, Stackexchange, Wikipedia, arXiv, and GitHub. A few papers further specify variants such as a deduplicated version or held-out subsets distinct from the training set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 5 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator, and these uses are spread across several targets rather than centering on a single recurring claim. It is used to measure general ability, with one paper describing "losses on the Pile" as the reference, and it is also reported as measuring long-context understanding, memorization, and specialization; the behavioral-indicator link is to pre-training data detection, where one paper includes Pile among common benchmark datasets.

nodes.name: The Pile (deduplicated)
nodes.definition: The deduplicated version of The PILE dataset, a large and diverse text corpus used for pretraining and evaluating language models.

nodes.name: The Stack
nodes.definition: A code dataset used here as an additional long-context test bed via a single Python file sample to compare long-context language modeling behavior on code.

nodes.name: TheoremQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, TheoremQA is most commonly described as a benchmark or question answering dataset of university-level or advanced STEM problems that require applying mathematical theorems. Several definitions specify 800 questions or problems spanning mathematics, physics, and engineering. A smaller line of work describes it more narrowly through abstract algebra and formal logic, and one paper reports using only a mathematics subset with logical-reasoning questions and definite answers.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TheoremQA to one behavioral indicator and three constructs. The prevailing use is to measure mathematical problem solving, and several papers also use it to measure reasoning, describing it as part of evaluations of reasoning across domains or as a representative reasoning benchmark. More narrowly, one paper uses it to measure generalization on theoretical reasoning in STEM, and another uses it for out-of-domain evaluation of mathematical reasoning, so papers connect it to several related targets rather than only one construct.

Space of uses. No paper directly links it to another measurement instrument, though many use it inside broader evalua

nodes.name: Ti-MMLU
nodes.definition: Tibetan adaptation of CMMLU, a multi-task understanding benchmark with 11,528 multiple-choice questions across 67 knowledge-based subdomains in Tibetan.

nodes.name: Ti-SafetyBench
nodes.definition: Tibetan adaptation of SafetyBench, a safety evaluation benchmark with 11,435 questions across 7 safety-critical categories including ethics, bias, health, and privacy.

nodes.name: TibetanQA
nodes.definition: A Tibetan question-answering dataset used for zero-shot evaluation of a model's cross-lingual transfer capabilities in machine reading comprehension.

nodes.name: TIDE
nodes.definition: The Trauma-Informed Dialogue for Empathy (TIDE) dataset, a resource of 10,000 two-turn dialogues based on 500 diverse, clinically-grounded PTSD personas, used for training and evaluating empathetic response generation.

nodes.name: TimeQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, TimeQA is most commonly described as a time-sensitive or temporal question-answering benchmark dataset. Definitions characterize it as derived from natural language and Wikidata, focusing on real-world factual questions about event-time relationships and, more broadly, on time-evolving factual questions grounded in the real world. A smaller description emphasizes its reuse as a source dataset for the context-based task in DATEAUGBENCH.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TimeQA to measure two constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is temporal reasoning: papers describe it as a benchmark used for temporal reasoning performance and as containing question-answer pairs requiring temporal reasoning. Less often, papers use it to measure factual knowledge, specifically through complex queries that require time-sensitive knowledge, so the measurement claims are concentrated on temporal reasoning rather than spread broadly across constructs.

Space of uses. In use, papers often place TimeQA alongside other temporal QA benchmarks, including TempReason, TGQA, MenatQA, and TimeBench, either in multi-benchmark temporal reasonin

nodes.name: Tiny ImageNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the common framing is an image classification dataset or benchmark. Papers variously describe it as a smaller version of ImageNet used for faster experimentation, as a benchmark for evaluating automated accuracy prediction across shifted test sets, and as a dataset used both as an adversarial fine-tuning source and as a primary evaluation dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, image classification, and no constructs are linked to it. In the recorded relationships, the measurement claims therefore concentrate on image classification rather than spreading across multiple constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. Papers use it in several experimental roles rather than one fixed protocol. It appears alongside CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and Food-101 in image classification evaluations, is used "for computational reasons" in one study, is used on "synthetic shifted datasets of TinyImageNet" for correlation comparison, and is also used as the source of adversarial samples for fine-tuning before evaluation across multiple datasets, including Tiny-ImageNet itself. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: tinyBenchmarks
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, tinyBenchmarks is most commonly described as a smaller, more efficient evaluation resource for language models, variously framed as a suite of few-shot tasks, a collection of small-scale datasets for low-cost evaluation, or smaller versions of popular benchmarks for rapid evaluation. One use description specifies few-shot components including 25-shot tinyARC, 5-shot GSM8K, 10-shot tinyHellaswag, and 5-shot tinyWinoGrande.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers describe it as assessing model performance and enabling efficient evaluation of language models, but they do not explicitly link it to any named constructs or behavioral indicators. No measured_by relationships are recorded for the instrument, so its measurement use is stated in general terms rather than tied to a particular construct.

Space of uses. Papers use tinyBenchmarks as an efficiency-oriented evaluation option. One paper reports scoring models on its few-shot tasks, another says it chose the small-scale datasets "for other tasks," and another states, "We use tinyBenchmarks (Polo et al., 2024) for all the benchmarks except HumanEval to further increase the efficiency of experiments"

nodes.name: TinyStories
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, TinyStories is most commonly described as a synthetic dataset of short or children's stories, often generated by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Definitions repeatedly frame it as small enough for tractable training, especially for small or medium-scale models, while still presenting text-generation challenges such as coherence and narrative structure. Some authors describe it more generally as short, simple stories generated by a large language model, and one paper specifies that it uses around 1500 English words a child might use.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TinyStories to two behavioral indicators, Text generation and Creative writing, and no constructs are linked to it. The prevailing usage is to measure Text generation, with papers training or evaluating models on language generation, story continuation, and prefix-suffix generation from unseen stories. A smaller line of work reports it as measuring Creative writing through story-continuation experiments and broader evaluation suites.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use TinyStories as a practical training and evaluation corpus, and one study notes that its small size makes model trainin

nodes.name: TLUE
nodes.definition: Tibetan Language Understanding Evaluation benchmark, a large-scale evaluation suite for LLMs in Tibetan, comprising Ti-MMLU for knowledge assessment and Ti-SafetyBench for safety evaluation.

nodes.name: TOEFL11
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the available definition, TOEFL11 is treated as the ETS Corpus of Non-Native Written English, and it is described as a benchmark dataset used for Native Language Identification research. The source snippet also places it among two benchmark datasets for NLI experiments, alongside Write & Improve Corpus 2024.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement claim is narrow: TOEFL11 is linked to one behavioral indicator and no constructs. Specifically, Native language identification is measured by TOEFL11, so the instrument is reported as evaluating native language identification rather than a broader spread of targets.

Space of uses. One paper uses TOEFL11 together with Write & Improve Corpus 2024 in experiments, positioning it as one of two benchmark datasets for NLI.

nodes.name: TOFU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe TOFU as a synthetic question-answering benchmark for unlearning, built around fictitious author profiles or biographies. Several descriptions specify 200 synthetic authors or profiles with 20 question-answer pairs each, totaling 4,000 items, while another description instead says it consists of 20 question-answer pairs based on fictitious author biographies generated by GPT-4, and one paper frames it around fictional characters' personal information. Papers also refer to benchmark subsets and splits such as forget05, forget10 with retain90, and Retain10-perturbed, and one definition says it evaluates different forget set sizes of 1%, 5%, and 10%.

What it is claimed to measure. Across relationship claims, TOFU is used to measure 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator, with claims spread across several targets rather than tied to only one. The most common claims are that it measures General ability, Forget quality, and Verbatim memorization; papers describe using TOFU's retain and forget splits, model utility datasets, forget quality metrics, and Retain10-perturbed Truth Ratio evaluations for these purposes. A smaller line of work uses TOF

nodes.name: TofuEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, TofuEval is most commonly described as a dataset or benchmark for evaluating factual consistency in dialogue summarization. Several descriptions make this more specific, calling it a topic-focused dialogue summarization benchmark or dataset that emphasizes marginal or secondary topics, including factual alignment under topic shifts, and one paper describes it as a more challenging benchmark on topic-focused dialogue summarization. Some papers also specify its contents as an annotated subset of MediaSum and MeetingBank with human-annotated sentence-level faithfulness judgments and critiques, though one description presents those subsets as spanning a mix of news and dialogue domains.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TofuEval to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing construct-level use is to measure Faithfulness, with one paper using its sentence-level faithfulness judgments and critiques to design intrinsic evaluation tasks for DETECT, CRITIQUE, and REFINE. It is also reported as measuring Meeting summarization and Text summarization, so the construct claims converge on Faithfulness while the behavioral-indicator links

nodes.name: ToM-SSI
nodes.definition: A multimodal benchmark designed to evaluate Theory of Mind capabilities in situated social interactions involving up to four agents in a grid world, covering cooperative, obstructive, and mixed settings.

nodes.name: TOMATO
nodes.definition: TempOral Reasoning MultimodAl EvaluaTiOn, a benchmark designed to rigorously assess Multimodal Foundation Models' temporal reasoning capabilities in video understanding across six tasks.

nodes.name: ToMBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating social intelligence, specifically testing a model's theory-of-mind reasoning capabilities.

nodes.name: ToolACE
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available description treats ToolACE as a dataset with 11,300 rows, used as a supplementary evaluation set in function-calling safety tasks. The same usage also describes it as a complementary part of MCIP-Bench, used to further validate generalization capability.

What it is claimed to measure. The available paper reports ToolACE as being used to further validate generalization capability in function-calling safety tasks. Papers do not explicitly link it to any construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. The observed usage positions ToolACE alongside MCIP-Bench as a supplementary or complementary evaluation resource rather than as a standalone benchmark. In that role, papers use its 11,300 rows to provide an additional generalization check.

nodes.name: ToolAlpaca
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, ToolAlpaca is treated as a tool learning dataset for tool-augmented LLMs. One description presents it as an agent-generated dataset with 495 tools and 3975 training examples, used to train and evaluate models in controlled settings, and notes that a ToolAlpaca 7B model is fine-tuned on it using Vicuna-v1.3 (Tool Unlearning for Tool-Augmented LLMs). Another usage describes it as 3.9k tool-use instances from a multi-agent simulation environment that are augmented to an MCQ format.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ToolAlpaca to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. At the construct level, papers use it to measure Tool use ability; at the behavioral level, they use it to measure Self-correction and Tool use. The linked evidence frames this as assessing tool call and correction capabilities, and as evaluating tool-use instances.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers use ToolAlpaca directly to assess tool call and correction capabilities, and one paper specifies that a model can self-correct from error messages and retry the call on this dataset (ToolFlow: Boosting LLM Tool-Calling Through Natural and Co

nodes.name: ToolBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat ToolBench as a benchmark or dataset for evaluating tool use with real-world APIs, often emphasizing diverse user requests, multi-step interactions, and tool-calling scenarios. Definitions vary: some describe a benchmark suite spanning Home Search, Trip Booking, Google Sheets, and Virtual Home, while others describe an instruction-tuning dataset built automatically with ChatGPT, with 16,464 APIs, or a corpus with over 16,000 APIs from 49 categories and over 10,000 queries with full interactions. A smaller line of work presents it as a workload whose prompts include tool demonstrations and calls, and some papers refer to a second release or to around 1,000 test cases.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ToolBench to 5 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure tool use ability and tool use, followed by decision-making, planning, and reasoning. The linked claims are spread across several tool-related and decision-oriented targets rather than converging on only one.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Across papers, ToolBench is used as an evaluation benchmark or workload: authors report ex

nodes.name: ToolEval
nodes.definition: An evaluation procedure from ToolBench used to compare decision sequences via win rate and rank them with PRP.

nodes.name: ToolQA
nodes.definition: ToolQA is a benchmark of external-tool tasks spanning domains such as flight status, coffee price, Yelp data, and Airbnb data.

nodes.name: ToolQuery
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is of a tool-using benchmark built around queries to external tools across domains such as Weather, Movie, and Academia. Definitions converge on those contents, with one paper also treating it as a held-out task and another describing it as evaluating an agent's use of tools to retrieve and process information across those domains.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers describe ToolQuery as evaluating tool use, specifically retrieving and processing information through external tools across domains like Weather, Movie, and Academia. They do not explicitly link it to any constructs or behavioral indicators through recorded measurement claims, so the measurement framing remains at the level of the benchmark's own description.

Space of uses. In use, papers place ToolQuery within multi-benchmark evaluations. One paper lists it alongside ToolOperation under tool-using evaluation and uses it as a held-out task, while another includes it among four rigorous benchmarks for model evaluation; papers do not record explicit links from ToolQuery to other measurement instruments.

nodes.name: TopDial
nodes.definition: A personalized conversational recommendation dataset containing dialogues on topics like movies, food, and music, where the system's goal is to recommend a specific item.

nodes.name: TopiOCQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing framing is of a conversational search benchmark or dataset built from multi-turn dialogues or queries. The most detailed definition says it contains multi-turn information-seeking dialogues with gold-standard passage retrieval and response generation labels, while other papers emphasize context-dependent questions requiring disambiguation, retrieval-oriented query reformulation, or challenging topic shifts within conversations. A smaller strand describes it as a conversational question answering dataset, but the dominant usage still places it within conversational search evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TopiOCQA to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator, so the recorded measurement claims center on a small set of targets. One paper uses it to measure Generalization through cross-dataset evaluation, training on the TopiOCQA training set and evaluating on QReCC, and another uses it to measure Query rewriting through multi-turn conversational queries. The named measurement targets are therefore Generalization and Query rewriting.

Space of uses. Most papers use it as a main evaluation dataset for conversational searc

nodes.name: Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking
nodes.definition: A set of psychometric tests used to assess creative abilities, including divergent thinking, across various tasks.

nodes.name: ToTTo
nodes.definition: An English dataset for data-to-text generation, consisting of Wikipedia tables with highlighted cells paired with a sentence describing those cells.

nodes.name: TounsiBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating the capabilities of large language models in understanding and generating responses in Tunisian Arabic, comprising a dataset of 744 instructions and an evaluation framework.

nodes.name: ToxicChat
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat ToxicChat as a benchmark dataset for query safety classification and safety detection. Definitions vary in emphasis: some describe a prompt dataset covering multiple harmful categories with simple and story-based templates, while others describe a dataset suitable for training safety classifiers, containing conversations with toxic content, or a benchmark for toxicity detection in real-world user-AI conversations. Papers also note that it has separate train and test splits.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, ToxicChat is used to measure harmful content detection, and papers describe it as part of evaluations on harmful prompts used to assess guardrail or safety models. Across the reported uses, it is connected to one behavioral indicator, Harmful content detection, and to no constructs, so the measurement claims converge on that behavioral target rather than spreading across multiple constructs. Papers also describe it as assessing query safety classification and safety detection across diverse toxic content types.

Space of uses. Papers usually position ToxicChat as a standard or public benchmark within broader guardrail and safet

nodes.name: ToxiCloakCN
nodes.definition: A Chinese adversarial toxicity detection benchmark dataset designed to evaluate the vulnerability of large language models to various evasion tactics, including homophonic substitutions.

nodes.name: ToxiGen
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ToxiGen is most commonly described as a toxicity benchmark or dataset for evaluating toxic versus neutral generation behavior. Definitions vary in emphasis: some frame it as a benchmark for toxic language generation or safety, while others describe a synthetic or machine-generated dataset for adversarial and implicit hate speech detection. Several papers specify content such as benign or neutral and toxic statements or questions about 13 demographic or minority groups, and one description says it comprises approximately 274k statements evenly split between toxic and non-toxic language. A smaller line of work highlights subset use, for example taking only prompts designed to elicit toxic language.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, claims concentrate on safety and toxicity: papers link ToxiGen to 3 constructs in total, most often Safety and Toxicity, with a smaller line using it to measure Harmlessness. Papers also link it to 4 behavioral indicators, most often Harmful content generation, and additionally Harmful content detection, Hate speech detection, and Text generation. The recorded links consistently describe ToxiGen as measuri

nodes.name: TQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat TQA as Textbook Question Answering, described as a reading-comprehension benchmark and, in one definition, as a dataset consisting of scientific textbooks. Within that prevailing usage, authors note that it is used in generative format to assess reading comprehension. A smaller usage defines TQA as the TriviaQA dataset, described as a challenging reading comprehension dataset with question-answer pairs authored by trivia enthusiasts and used for closed-book QA.

What it is claimed to measure. Definitions most often frame TQA as assessing reading comprehension, though individual papers also describe it as being used for closed-book QA or for evaluating knowledge-based reasoning. In the recorded relationships, it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Out-of-distribution detection, and to no constructs. The only explicit linked measurement claim is that papers use TQA to measure out-of-distribution detection, including an experiment with statements translated into Samoan, described there as "an out-of-distribution language for TQA."

Space of uses. Papers use TQA alongside HumanEval, GSM8k, and NQ in multi-task evaluations spanning code, math,

nodes.name: TRACE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, TRACE is most commonly described as a public benchmark for continual learning or continual instruction tuning, organized as a learning sequence of tasks such as multi-choice QA, code generation, mathematical reasoning, and summarization. Some authors frame it more specifically as evaluating model performance across multiple sequential fine-tuning tasks or multi-round fine-tuning. A smaller line of work describes it as comprising 8 diverse tasks, including domain-specific QA, code completion, and mathematical reasoning, and another description presents it as a benchmark for improving and evaluating complex instruction following ability with 120K training data and 1K evaluation data.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TRACE to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The linked constructs are Complex instruction following ability, Mathematical reasoning, and Safety, and the linked behavioral indicators are Code completion and Instruction following. Overall, papers use it to measure several different targets rather than centering on one construct, and one definition also says it is designed to evaluate general ability alongside instruction followin

nodes.name: Traffic
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats Traffic as a time series benchmark dataset for evaluating forecasting models. Most definitions describe road traffic data, often as hourly traffic volume in California, while some instead describe hourly road occupancy rates from the California transportation department on San Francisco Bay area freeways; one definition further specifies 862 sensors. Papers also frame it as a standard or real-world benchmark, and some definitions place it in broader cross-domain forecasting evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets: Traffic is linked to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators. The only recorded measurement claim is that papers use it to measure Zero-shot generalization, with the evidence describing a comparison of zero-shot performance of pre-trained models on the Traffic dataset.

Space of uses. Papers most commonly use Traffic alongside other forecasting benchmarks, especially ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, and Electricity or ECL. It is typically presented as one dataset within larger evaluation suites for forecasting, including long-term fo

nodes.name: TravelPlanner
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, TravelPlanner is most commonly described as a benchmark for travel planning agents or LLM agents, centered on generating travel plans or itineraries from user queries and provided information while satisfying multiple constraints. Definitions repeatedly describe a rich sandbox environment with tools for accessing nearly four million data records, curated planning intents or queries, and reference plans; several papers also frame it as a real-world, complex, sometimes U.S. domestic setting involving commonsense as well as hard constraints, and one paper explicitly says it covers hard and soft constraints. A smaller variation in framing treats it as a dataset used for travel-planning evaluation, and one paper reports results on a TravelPlanner validation split.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TravelPlanner to measure 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is for Planning: several papers describe it as evaluating planning in complex or realistic environments and multi-constraint tasks. Smaller lines of work use it to measure Long-horizon planning, explicitly calling it a test of "long-horizon planning under user-def

nodes.name: TREC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, TREC is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for question classification, usually a 6-way task from the Text REtrieval Conference. Several papers specify six coarse-grained categories, often exemplified as Abbreviation, Entity, Description, Human, Location, and Numeric, while some describe it more broadly as a general NLU or text classification dataset, and one definition also mentions information retrieval tasks. A smaller strand refers to Trec as a dataset from the LongBench suite for few-shot evaluation, and one paper describes it as a 6-class, 50-subclass question-answering task with 500 test samples.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TREC to 1 behavioral indicator and 2 constructs. The prevailing use is to measure Text classification, typically through 6-way question classification, while a smaller line of work uses it to measure Prompt sensitivity and Consistency through predicted class distributions over prompt rephrasings. Overall, the linked claims mostly center on text classification, with the construct-level uses appearing in prompt-rephrasing evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers often use TREC within broader evalu

nodes.name: TREC-COVID
nodes.definition: An information retrieval dataset focused on biomedical information retrieval.

nodes.name: TREC-DL 2019
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats TREC-DL 2019 as a benchmark dataset or test set from the TREC Deep Learning Track 2019 for passage retrieval and document re-ranking. Definitions vary slightly: some describe an in-domain evaluation set derived from MS-MARCO-V1, others emphasize a deep learning-based ad-hoc retrieval benchmark with human-annotated relevance judgments, and another frames it as a benchmark for LLM-based ranking systems on document relevance tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, claims about what it assesses stay at the task level: passage retrieval systems, information retrieval and reranking tasks, document relevance tasks, and document re-ranking systems. Papers do not link it to any constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use it alongside TREC-DL 2020, and some descriptions also place it with MS-MARCO-V1 or MS MARCO; one study lists it with BEIR among "widely used benchmarks." It is positioned as an in-domain evaluation set in some work, while another paper uses the TREC-DL2019/2020 benchmarks to evaluate LLM-based ranking systems' vulnerability to Decision Hijacking attacks across pairwise,

nodes.name: TREC-DL 2020
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, TREC-DL 2020 is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset or test set from the TREC Deep Learning Track 2020, used to evaluate passage retrieval, reranking, document relevance, and document re-ranking systems. The descriptions vary slightly: some present it as an in-domain dataset, one says it is derived from MS-MARCO-V1, and another describes it as extending TREC DL 2019 with additional queries and relevance annotations. One source also treats it simply as part of the "TREC-DL2019/2020 benchmarks."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TREC-DL 2020 to evaluate performance on passage retrieval and reranking style tasks, including document relevance assessment in LLM-based ranking settings. At the same time, papers do not explicitly link it to any construct or behavioral indicator, so its recorded use here is task evaluation rather than measurement of named constructs.

Space of uses. The prevailing usage is as a benchmark in evaluation suites for retrieval and re-ranking systems. Papers frequently use it alongside TREC-DL19, while some descriptions also place it with BEIR or in conjunction with MS MARCO; one paper notes that TREC-DL'19 and

nodes.name: TrialBench
nodes.definition: Benchmark dataset for clinical prediction tasks including trial approval, patient dropout, mortality, and adverse event prediction, used to evaluate model performance in biomedical contexts.

nodes.name: TriviaQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the literature, the prevailing usage treats TriviaQA as a question answering benchmark, most often described as a reading-comprehension or open-domain dataset of trivia questions, with question-answer pairs often said to be authored by trivia enthusiasts and sometimes accompanied by evidence or source documents. Some papers instead frame it as a closed-book QA benchmark with short or free-form factual answers, sometimes using the Wikipedia partition or validation split without supporting evidence in context. Descriptions also differ on format and scale, with papers referring to 95K question-answer pairs, over 650K question-answer-evidence triples, the TQ abbreviation for in-domain evaluation, a 1000-question subset of the dev split, and a synthesized audio version.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TriviaQA to measure a broad spread of outcomes rather than a single target: it is linked to 18 constructs and 16 behavioral indicators. The most common claims are that it measures question answering, especially open-domain and factual question answering, and that it measures world knowledge and factuality. The remaining links are dispersed across many other co

nodes.name: TriviaQA-unfiltered
nodes.definition: Open-domain question answering benchmark requiring models to answer factual questions using external knowledge; used to evaluate accuracy in knowledge-intensive tasks.

nodes.name: Trojsten Benchmark
nodes.definition: A Slovak-language dataset of 1,108 high-school STEM competition problems in mathematics, physics, and programming, with reference solutions and difficulty ratings, used to evaluate multistep reasoning in a low-resource language setting.

nodes.name: TRUE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description treats TRUE as a fine-tuned T5-11B Natural Language Inference model used as an evaluator inside broader evaluation frameworks. Definitions consistently describe it as judging whether a source passage or premise entails a generated claim or hypothesis, and one paper makes this explicit by using it as an evaluator whose output is 1 for entailment and 0 otherwise; another describes it as fine-tuned on a collection of NLI datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TRUE to two constructs, most commonly Citation quality and also Faithfulness, and to no behavioral indicators. The measurement claims are concentrated around entailment-based evaluation: papers use it to measure Citation quality by judging entailment in citations or verifying whether a claim is fully supported by cited documents, and they report it as measuring Faithfulness through factual consistency evaluation in context.

Space of uses. Papers do not link TRUE to any other measurement instrument. They generally position it as an NLI component or evaluator within larger evaluation pipelines, including citation rewrite and citation quality evaluation, and o

nodes.name: True-False dataset
nodes.definition:
What it is. The available paper treats the True-False dataset as a labeled collection of factoid statements marked True or False, covering six disjoint topics: Cities, Inventions, Chemical Elements, Animals, Companies, and Scientific Facts. It is described as a constructed dataset for factuality probes, and no alternative versions, subsets, or competing format descriptions are reported.

What it is claimed to measure. The same paper says the dataset is used to train and evaluate factuality probes. Papers do not link it to any named constructs or behavioral indicators in recorded relationships.

Space of uses. The available description positions it as a standalone dataset for training and evaluation, rather than alongside any other named benchmark or instrument. No other measurement instruments are linked to it.

nodes.name: TruthfulQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, TruthfulQA is most commonly described as a question answering benchmark built to elicit false answers based on common misconceptions and to test whether models produce truthful or factually accurate responses instead. Definitions usually describe over 800 questions, often specified as 817 questions across 38 categories, though one paper refers to 818 questions and another to 811 testing problems; categories named in one description include health, law, finance, and politics. Papers differ on format: some describe only multiple-choice questions, including MC1 or MC2, while others state that it has both multiple-choice question answering and generation protocols, and a few use its generation portion for open-ended or long-form responses.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the dominant use is to measure truthfulness, with authors saying it "tests an LLM's truthfulness" or measures a model's "propensity to reproduce falsehoods." Papers link it to 19 constructs and 11 behavioral indicators. The most recurring claims cluster around truthfulness and factuality, and papers also use it for hallucination, question answering, and text generation; beyond

nodes.name: TSPLIB
nodes.definition: A library of real-world benchmark instances for the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) used to evaluate the performance of optimization algorithms.

nodes.name: TTT-Bench
nodes.definition: A benchmark consisting of four novel Tic-Tac-Toe-style games (oTTT, dTTT, cTTT, sTTT) designed to assess strategic, spatial, and logical reasoning through text-based board game questions asking for the best next move.

nodes.name: TumEmo
nodes.definition: A multimodal sentiment analysis benchmark used for additional experiments on sentiment prediction.

nodes.name: TurBLiMP
nodes.definition: A Turkish Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs covering 16 grammatical phenomena, designed to evaluate the linguistic abilities of language models.

nodes.name: Turing test
nodes.definition: A binary classification evaluation procedure that tests whether a detector can distinguish human-generated text from machine-generated text.

nodes.name: TurnBack
nodes.definition: A large-scale benchmark for evaluating the route-level geospatial cognition of LLMs, consisting of a dataset of 36,000 routes, a language-to-geometry converter, and a comprehensive evaluation framework for the route reversal task.

nodes.name: TVQA
nodes.definition: Multiple-choice question answering benchmark based on TV shows, requiring multimodal reasoning across video, audio, and subtitles.

nodes.name: TweetEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, TweetEval is most commonly described as a multi-task benchmark for tweet analysis on social media, with six text classification tasks: emotion, hate speech, irony, offensive language, sentiment, and stance detection. A narrower description in one paper treats it as a benchmark for multiple Twitter-based NLP tasks and specifically uses its emotion recognition and irony detection subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TweetEval to measure three behavioral indicators and no constructs. The reported measurement targets are language understanding task performance, emotion analysis, and irony detection, so the benchmark is connected to several behavioral indicators rather than to a linked construct.

Space of uses. Papers position TweetEval as a benchmark for evaluating models in multi-task language understanding and Twitter-based NLP settings. One study uses it alongside AffectEval as one of two multi-task benchmarks for language understanding, while another uses only the emotion recognition and irony detection parts of the benchmark.

nodes.name: TwiBot-22
nodes.definition: Graph-based Twitter dataset containing one million users, nearly one hundred million tweets, and relational data, used for training and evaluating social bot detection and human-like generation.

nodes.name: TwinViews-13k
nodes.definition: A dataset containing ideologically matched political statement pairs used for evaluating political polarity adjustment.

nodes.name: Twitter Financial News Sentiment
nodes.definition: A dataset for sentiment analysis of financial news from Twitter.

nodes.name: Twitter-FMNERG
nodes.definition: Benchmark dataset for Fine-grained Multimodal Named Entity Recognition and Grounding, extending GMNER with 51 fine-grained entity types.

nodes.name: Twitter-GMNER
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for Grounded Multimodal Named Entity Recognition that involves extracting four coarse-grained entity types from image-text pairs from Twitter.

nodes.name: TyDi QA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is a multilingual question answering benchmark or dataset, usually described as spanning typologically diverse languages. Most definitions describe it as covering 11 languages and requiring answers from a given passage or Wikipedia article, sometimes in a gold-passage setup and sometimes as answer-span identification; one paper instead says it includes 9 kinds of languages. Papers also refer to language-specific subsets such as TyDiQA-FI, TyDiQA-ID, and TyDiQA-SW, and some uses narrow to Wikipedia-based variants such as "TyDi QA (wiki)" or the Indonesian set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure multilingual ability, with papers explicitly using it for multilingual ability, multilinguality, or multilingual capabilities; question answering is the other recurring behavioral target, and some papers more specifically use it to measure multilingual question answering or machine reading comprehension. A smaller line of work also reports it as measuring instruction following and general ability, so the recorded measurement claims are spread acr

nodes.name: UCF-101
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, UCF-101 is most commonly described as an action recognition video benchmark or dataset that is also used to evaluate video generation, especially in class-conditional or class-to-video settings. Definitions also present it as a dataset of human action videos, including realistic videos from YouTube or videos in the wild, and some papers extend its use to image-to-video generation or action classification. Papers further describe it as a common or standard benchmark in video generation experiments.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link UCF-101 to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is as a measure of Video generation, while a smaller line of work uses it to measure Action recognition. For constructs, the links converge on Fidelity: one paper links it to Fidelity in a comparison where existing benchmarks are described as assessing visual quality and text relevance.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Even so, papers describe using it alongside Kinetics-600 and MSR-VTT in video generation experiments, and alongside ActivityNet and Something-Something V2 in action recognition evaluation. The

nodes.name: UltraChat
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is of a diverse, multi-turn conversational instruction-following dataset, created using GPT-3.5-Turbo. Some papers frame it more specifically as a dialogue benchmark for interactive dialogue, while others use it as a held-out, out-of-domain dataset for testing whether a method generalizes beyond summarization. Definitions also mention its use for supervised fine-tuning and for generating prompts for self-training.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use UltraChat to measure 2 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The linked behavioral indicators are instruction following, question answering, and text generation, and the linked constructs are instruction following ability and utility preservation. The recorded claims are distributed across several targets: papers variously describe it as an instruction task, a large-scale dataset of instructional conversations, a source of testing problems, or a benign utility-oriented dataset.

Space of uses. Papers position UltraChat in several roles rather than only as a standalone benchmark. Some use random samples from it for supervised fine-tuning or for self-training prompt

nodes.name: UltraDomain
nodes.definition: Long-context benchmark focusing on domain-specific complex question answering, such as in financial, legal, and scientific texts, to assess deep understanding of specialized long documents.

nodes.name: UltraFeedback
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, UltraFeedback is most commonly described as a high-quality instruction or preference dataset built from scored candidate responses and used for instruction tuning, reward-model training, and evaluation of aligned language models. Several papers also treat it as a public benchmark for generative judges on preference prediction, while smaller uses describe it as a prompt set for best-of-n experiments or as material for additional fine-grained text generation. Its content is variously described as instruction-response pairs, prompts, or candidate responses with GPT-4 preference annotations or scores, often across instruction-following, truthfulness, honesty, and helpfulness; some papers refer to UltraFeedback3, a development set of 1K instructions, or only the first 3,000 prompts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link UltraFeedback to 7 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. It is most often used to measure helpfulness, and is also used for instruction following, honesty, and instruction following ability, with smaller lines of work using it to measure truthfulness, human preference alignment, generalization, and dialogue generation. These claims most

nodes.name: UltraFeedback Binarized
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat UltraFeedback Binarized, also written UF-B or UFB, as a widely used dataset for preference alignment or preference fine-tuning, organized as binarized or paired preference data for dialogue tasks. A more specific description says it is built from GPT-4 scored UltraFeedback completions, where the highest-scoring completion is labeled "chosen" and another, in one account a random completion, is labeled "rejected".

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not explicitly say that UltraFeedback Binarized measures any construct or behavioral indicator. The available descriptions instead frame it as a dataset for preference alignment or preference fine-tuning, and as a resource used to train and evaluate alignment methods.

Space of uses. Across the surveyed work, it is commonly used as an evaluation and fine-tuning dataset for alignment methods. Papers place it alongside Alpaca Comparison and TL;DR in multi-dataset experiments, and one line of work specifically groups it with Alpaca Comparison as one of two dialogue datasets; another states, "For fine-tuning on the UltraFeedback Binarized dataset, we use two families of models."

nodes.name: UltraInteract
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available definitions, UltraInteract is most commonly described as multi-turn conversational data for complex reasoning tasks. One framing presents it as a multi-turn RLHF dataset with dialogues that cover general chat scenarios and are used to evaluate conversational and instruction-following abilities, while another describes it as a pairwise alignment dataset with multi-turn conversational data, specifically designed to evaluate and improve performance on complex reasoning tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link UltraInteract to one construct, Reasoning, and no behavioral indicators. The explicit measurement claim uses it to measure Reasoning, with a paper describing it as a dataset "specifically designed for complex reasoning tasks"; definitions also describe it as evaluating conversational and instruction-following abilities, but those are not linked as separate constructs here.

Space of uses. In use, papers position UltraInteract in two ways: as an evaluation setting for model responses to instructions with complex reasoning tasks, and as data for fine-tuning alignment models. One study reports results on it directly, while another uses it t

nodes.name: UNCLE
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset designed to evaluate uncertainty expression in both long- and short-form question answering, covering five domains with over 1,000 entities and paired questions that share key aspects and gold-standard answers.

nodes.name: UNER
nodes.definition:
What it is. In one paper, UNER is described as a multilingual named entity recognition dataset covering 13 languages. The same description presents it as an evaluation resource for cross-lingual transfer on NER tasks, and the usage note in Translation and Fusion Improves Cross-lingual Information Extraction places it among multilingual NER datasets gathered for that purpose.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers describe UNER as used for evaluating cross-lingual transfer performance on named entity recognition tasks. No construct links and no behavioral-indicator links are recorded for it, so the available evidence stays at the task-level description rather than tying it to a broader construct.

Space of uses. The available usage description places UNER alongside MasakhaNER2.0, with papers treating both as multilingual NER datasets gathered for evaluation. Beyond that pairing, no other instrument links are recorded.

nodes.name: UniGeo
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available definition, papers treat UniGeo as a dataset for unified geometry problem solving. In G-LLaVA: Solving Geometric Problem with Multi-Modal Large Language Model, it is also described as a subtask within the MathVista benchmark and is mentioned among more recent datasets.

Space of uses. The same paper uses UniGeo as one of the sub-tasks for reporting results on MathVista-GPS multiple-choice questions, which it presents for easier evaluation. In that usage, it appears alongside GeoQA+, Geometry3K, and GEOS.

nodes.name: US8K
nodes.definition: A benchmark for urban sound classification.

nodes.name: User preference study
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this as a broad human evaluation protocol rather than a single fixed benchmark. Most descriptions involve people comparing model outputs, choosing a preferred response, ranking alternatives, or rating outputs against stated criteria, with setups ranging from pairwise comparisons and win-lose judgments to Likert scales, binary labels, and free-form feedback. A smaller line of work uses the same label for interactive studies, expert review, survey-style polling, or human baseline task completion. Although one definition centers on showing a question and multiple model responses and asking users to choose the most creative and humorous one, other papers apply the protocol to correctness, faithfulness, safety, usefulness, coherence, cultural appropriateness, and similar dimensions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this protocol to 2 behavioral indicators, Human reaction motion generation and Humor generation, and no constructs or other measurement instruments are linked to it. The linked claims therefore concentrate on behavioral indicators rather than constructs: one paper uses it to test creativity and humor, and anoth

nodes.name: V-NIAH
nodes.definition: Video Needle in a Haystack, a long-video retrieval benchmark that tests a model's ability to find a specific image inserted at various positions within a long video.

nodes.name: VAL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, VAL is most commonly described as an automatic plan validator for PDDL plans. Definitions characterize it as checking whether an action sequence correctly transitions from an initial state to a goal state against ground-truth domain and problem files, and as verifying that a generated sequence is executable and reaches the goal state. A smaller framing presents it as a simulation environment for plan validation that calculates state condition changes and returns error messages when actions fail because preconditions are unsatisfied.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement role is narrow rather than spread across many targets: papers link VAL to 1 behavioral indicator, Plan generation, and to no constructs. In that usage, Plan generation is measured by VAL through validation of the produced plan against the domain and problem files.

Space of uses. Papers use VAL as an evaluation step after a plan has been produced or after natural language responses have been converted into PDDL, then checked for executability and goal attainment. One paper also positions it as a simulation environment for computing state changes and obtaining error messa

nodes.name: Value Kaleidoscope
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat this entity as an evaluation dataset for moral scenarios and judgments. One definition describes Value Kaleidoscope as a benchmark with 31K human-authored hypothetical scenarios and moral dilemmas paired with ethical perspectives, used to test whether models support, oppose, or remain neutral toward scenarios from specific viewpoints. A second description uses the name ValuePrism (VP) and frames it more briefly as a moral-judgment dataset with three-way choices for evaluating value profile modeling of ethical reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what it measures converge on one construct: Value orientation. Papers link it to one construct, Value orientation, and do not link it to any behavioral indicators; in the linked use, it is used to probe models' views on moral situations, alongside Anthropic's Election Questions for political topics. Papers do not link it to any other measurement instruments.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation benchmark. One study places Value Kaleidoscope within "trade-off steerability benchmarks" for assessing proposed approaches, while another uses VP as a moral-judgment dataset in valu

nodes.name: VAST
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, VAST is most commonly described as a stance detection dataset or benchmark built around varied targets. Definitions say each instance contains a sentence, a target, and a stance label, with labels given as Pro, Con, or Neutral; one paper adds that it covers a wide range of targets and is used to assess generalization in zero-shot and few-shot settings, while another frames it as an inherently zero-shot stance detection dataset and notes use of the original publisher splits.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use VAST to measure stance detection. In the recorded links, it is connected to one behavioral indicator, stance detection, and not linked to any constructs or other measurement instruments, so its reported use is concentrated on that single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Across the cited studies, VAST appears as part of experimental evaluations of proposed stance detection methods. Papers report using it alongside SEM16, PStance, and SemEval-2016 to evaluate methods, and one paper describes results on it as part of validations covering zero-shot, few-shot, and challenging scenarios.

nodes.name: VATEX
nodes.definition: A multilingual video captioning dataset used in the paper as an auxiliary validation and training comparison set.

nodes.name: VBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as a benchmark leaderboard for evaluating and ranking text-to-video generation models, VBench is framed around multiple quality and semantic dimensions. Some papers use broader language and describe it as a comprehensive benchmark suite for video generative models used for comparison. One source snippet reports average scores over 16 metrics from quality and semantic dimensions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator and 1 construct. The prevailing use is to measure Video generation: several papers say they use VBench for video generation evaluation, including to assess visual generation capability. A smaller line of work reports it as measuring Fidelity, with VBench discussed alongside benchmark assessments of visual quality and text relevance.

Space of uses. Papers position it as a reporting and comparison benchmark, for example by showing performance on the VBench leaderboard and comparing models against competitors. It is also used operationally in generation workflows, including leveraging 946 GPT-augmented text prompts from VBench to generate videos. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: Verbalized confidence
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats verbalized confidence as a direct self-report protocol for model confidence: the model or LLM judge is prompted to state how confident it is in its own answer or judgment. Most definitions describe the output as a scalar or numerical confidence value, while one also allows numerical or categorical ratings given alongside the answer; papers also frame it as a baseline confidence measure, a black-box self-evaluation procedure, and an evaluation protocol. A smaller amount of usage names specific variants such as P(true) and Verb. 1S top-1, and one paper reports averaging confidence across samples.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most commonly present verbalized confidence as measuring the model's own confidence, and one definition says the reported rating is used to measure subjective belief strength. Across the surveyed work, its links are concentrated rather than spread across many concepts: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Hallucination, which one paper measures through a verbalization-based hallucination detection module, and to one construct, Instruction following ability, only as a related factor rather t

nodes.name: Vicuna-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe it as a benchmark or evaluation dataset for open-ended, chatbot-style instruction following, often built from user-shared conversations or a fixed set of prompts or questions and often judged by GPT-4. Several descriptions use an 80-question or 80-prompt setup, and one paper specifies an adapted single-rating version with 80 single-turn chat prompts and 320 responses from four models. The framing varies across papers: some emphasize open-ended dialogue or text generation, others short-text conversational evaluation or a general task benchmark, and some describe a GPT-4 judging protocol that compares paired responses, in one case against gpt-3.5-turbo as the reference model.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it most often for instruction-following evaluations. It is linked to five constructs and five behavioral indicators overall, so the reported measurement claims extend beyond one target. Smaller lines of work report it as measuring text generation, multi-turn dialogue, mathematical problem solving, and pairwise comparison, and papers also attach construct-level claims beyond instruction following.

Space of uses. In use, papers c

nodes.name: Video-ChatGPT benchmark
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as an evaluation benchmark or test set for video understanding and question answering. Definitions vary somewhat: it is described as a generative performance benchmark for video-based conversational models, a test set for detailed video understanding that is used to assess general video question answering performance, and a long-video question-answering benchmark. One description explicitly says it includes metrics such as Correctness of Information, Detail Orientation, Contextual Understanding, Temporal Understanding, and Consistency, while another lists correctness, orientation, contextual understanding, temporal understanding, and consistency.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The linked constructs are Temporal understanding and Video understanding, and the linked behavioral indicator is Video question answering. The claims are spread across these targets rather than centered on one alone: some papers present it as evaluating video understanding, one ties it to Temporal understanding through its named metrics, and another uses it to assess general video question ans

nodes.name: Video-MME
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Video-MME is most commonly treated as a multimodal benchmark for video understanding or video analysis, often described as comprehensive and frequently used for long-video evaluation. Many definitions frame it as a video question answering or multiple-choice benchmark for video-language models, while some describe broader coverage, including captioning, question answering, and retrieval with subtitles. Papers also describe its scope in different ways: videos are said to range from 11 seconds to 1 hour or from 1 minute to 1 hour, some analyses split them into short, medium, and long durations, one definition reports 900 videos and 2,700 QA pairs, and another describes 6 visual domains and 30 subfields.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Video-MME to 4 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure video understanding, and papers also report it as measuring long video understanding; a smaller line of work treats it as measuring spatiotemporal reasoning and temporal reasoning. Among behavioral indicators, it is most often used for video question answering, while counting and optical character recognition appear as narrower

nodes.name: VideoHallucer
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the available usage, papers treat VideoHallucer as a benchmark for evaluating video hallucination. The only explicit definition frames it as assessing whether model responses are consistent with video content, and it refers to Basic, Hallucinated, and Overall categories.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers describe VideoHallucer as evaluating video hallucination through whether generated responses stay consistent with the video content. Beyond that task description, papers do not explicitly link it to any named construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. The available usage places VideoHallucer alongside EventHallusion rather than on its own. One study says it adopted two video hallucination benchmarks, VideoHallucer and EventHallusion, so in that use it functions as one of a paired set of video hallucination evaluations.

nodes.name: ViDoSeek
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset designed for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation systems on visually rich documents, where each query has a unique answer within a large corpus of approximately 6k images.

nodes.name: VirtualHome
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, VirtualHome is most commonly described as a simulated or 3D household environment, variously framed as a simulator, simulation platform, or benchmark for household activities, household task execution, and programs for those activities. The prevailing usage is to test whether generated plans or programs are executable in complex, multi-step tasks with object interactions and goal conditions, and some descriptions add partially observable states and macro-actions. A smaller line of description emphasizes long-horizon and multi-agent tasks with procedural generation, and one paper uses it as one component of ExtendaBench, where the VirtualHome portion contains 605 tasks divided into ultra-short, short, medium, and long subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use VirtualHome to measure 4 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. Among constructs, it is linked most often to Generalization, including unseen-task and crossover tests across Food Preparation and Entertainment, followed by Cross-domain generalization, Robustness, and Sequential decision-making; among behavioral indicators, it is used for Embodied planning and Task completion. Overall, the re

nodes.name: VISBIAS
nodes.definition: A multimodal evaluation framework that assesses both explicit and implicit social biases in Vision-Language Models through four scenarios: multiple-choice questions, yes-no comparisons, image descriptions, and form completion tasks.

nodes.name: VisDial
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe VisDial as the Visual Dialog dataset, a multi-turn visual dialog resource for engaging in a conversation about an image. A smaller line of usage describes it as a conversational AI task of answering a series of questions about an image, and another paper frames it as a benchmark for chat-to-image acquisition in multi-turn chat scenarios.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link VisDial to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. The reported measurement claims center on multimodal understanding and visual question answering, rather than a wider spread of targets.

Space of uses. No paper links it directly to other measurement instruments. Papers use it as one task within evaluations that also include COCO, VQAv2, OKVQA, GQA, and VizWiz, one paper includes it in an ablation study across five datasets, and another positions it as a benchmark for chat-to-image acquisition in multi-turn conversational settings.

nodes.name: VisEval
nodes.definition: A natural language to visualization (NL2VIS) benchmark containing high-quality datasets manually annotated by human experts, used to test generalization beyond the Kaggle ecosystem.

nodes.name: VIST
nodes.definition: A dataset for the task of visual storytelling, used as a basis for a task within the InterleavedBench evaluation benchmark.

nodes.name: VisText
nodes.definition: A corpus of charts and summaries used to generate chart question-answer pairs for the gaze dataset.

nodes.name: Visual7W
nodes.definition:
