What it is. Most commonly, papers treat Visual7W as a visual question answering benchmark or reference dataset. Some descriptions add that it is predominantly designed for VQA but includes a dedicated grounded VQA subset, where models select the correct bounding box for a "which"-type question, while another definition highlights object-level grounding annotations that link answers to specific image regions. One evaluation description also characterizes its samples as multiple-choice questions paired with a related image.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, its measurement claims center on one construct and one behavioral indicator rather than many targets. Papers use Visual7W to measure Visual grounding, including one account that places it among the "typical datasets" for tasks that establish referential links between textual mentions and image regions, and they also use it to measure Multimodal question answering through multimodal multiple-choice question-image evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers position Visual7W as a reference dataset and evaluation benchmark. Papers do not otherwise link it directly to another measurement instrument, but evaluation setups place

nodes.name: Visual Genome
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is of Visual Genome as a vision-language dataset with dense annotations of objects, attributes, and relationships in images, sometimes used through selected object relationships, region captions, or object data. Some papers note that its object data are converted into a Region-in Text-out format, while a smaller framing describes it as a visual question-answering dataset grounded in scene graphs that grounds visual concepts to language. Papers also refer to specific versions or splits, including VG100K with 108,077 images and over 1.7 million question-answer pairs, and a 77,398-image training split used as detection data.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Visual Genome to 1 construct and 4 behavioral indicators. The most common measurement claim is that papers use it to measure region captioning, including region-level caption ability; smaller lines use it to measure dense captioning and open-vocabulary object detection, and one paper uses it to measure the construct relation understanding by placing it among relational benchmarks. Visual question answering appears differently: one paper reports that Visual Genome

nodes.name: VisualMRC
nodes.definition: A benchmark for multimodal reading comprehension over visual documents or screenshots.

nodes.name: VisualWebArena
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, the prevailing usage treats VisualWebArena, also written VWA or V-WebArena, as a benchmark environment for evaluating multimodal web agents on realistic visual web tasks. Most descriptions emphasize tasks across classifieds, social media, and shopping platforms, and papers also call it "a real environment for web agents". One reported use focuses on a subset of 72 easy tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The reported measurement claims are that it measures Planning and Reasoning, and that it measures the behavioral indicator Web navigation; one paper describes it as a benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal agents across a wide range of web navigation tasks and environments. These measurement claims do not converge on a single construct.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it in papers. Papers position it as a base environment for added evaluations: one study manually creates 200 targeted adversarial tasks and evaluation scripts on top of VisualWebArena in a realistic threat model, another uses a subset of 72 easy tasks and mentions integrating pop-ups into e

nodes.name: VizWiz
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, VizWiz is most commonly treated as a visual question answering dataset or benchmark built from questions asked by blind or visually impaired users about images they have taken or their surroundings. Definitions repeatedly emphasize real-world, uncurated or natural images, and several papers describe the visual input as challenging, low-quality, ambiguous, or visually degraded. A smaller set of descriptions refers to specific forms such as VizWiz-VQA for natural image VQA, VizWizQA, and the VizWiz test-dev split, which one paper says contains 8,000 image-question pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing usage is as a measure of visual question answering, while a smaller line of work uses it to measure visual instruction following. Papers link it to 8 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators overall; the most frequent construct framings are visual understanding, multimodal understanding, and visual perception, with the remaining 5 linked constructs or indicators spread across other framings rather than concentrated on a single one. In the recorded claims, papers say it measures these capabilities rather than relating to them in some other way.

S

nodes.name: VL-RewardBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating output-level reward modeling in the vision-language domain.

nodes.name: VLGuard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, VLGuard is most commonly treated as a multimodal safety alignment resource, alternately described as a dataset and as a safety benchmark for vision-language models. Definitions present it as an original data source and as a baseline for comparison, while another description says it evaluates the ability to detect and respond to multimodal risks across harmful categories, including combinations of safe and unsafe image-text inputs. Some descriptions also frame it as using safe and unsafe training instructions organized by harmful categories.

What it is claimed to measure. Across these papers, the measurement claim converges on one construct: papers link VLGuard to one construct, Safety alignment, and to no behavioral indicators. In DREAM: Disentangling Risks to Enhance Safety Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models, it is used to evaluate the safe alignment of an approach, so the recorded use is that papers use it to measure Safety alignment rather than a broader spread of constructs.

Space of uses. Papers position VLGuard both as source material and as an evaluation benchmark. In Think in Safety: Unveiling and Mitigating Safety Alignment Col

nodes.name: VLMEvalKit
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing is of an evaluation toolkit, platform, or codebase for assessing vision-language and large vision-language models on benchmarks. Most descriptions call it open-source, standardized, or universal, and emphasize fair comparison, consistent configuration settings, or unified reproduction of results. One paper also treats it as a source of diverse benchmark results and performance data from more than 100 MLLMs, and one definition specifically names OpenCompass VLMEvalKit as the platform used to reproduce multimodal benchmark results.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link VLMEvalKit to no constructs and no behavioral indicators. Explicit measurement claims instead attach it to two measurement instruments, MME-RealWorld and MMStar, which are reported as being measured by VLMEvalKit; papers link it to three measurement instruments overall, with MMBench-Video connected by a related link rather than by a measurement claim. In the recorded relationships, the measurement claims center on other instruments rather than on any named construct.

Space of uses. The dominant usage is as a shared evaluation framework: papers say they

nodes.name: VLSafe
nodes.definition: A dataset used for training safety-related components (probers, refusal heads) and for evaluating the safety of multimodal models against toxic queries.

nodes.name: VLSBench
nodes.definition: Comprehensive cross-modal safety benchmark with 2,241 image-text pairs designed to prevent safety information leakage, used to evaluate true multimodal safety understanding.

nodes.name: VNBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, VNBench is described both as a benchmark for long video understanding and, under the Needle in a Haystack, or NIAH, label, as an evaluation protocol for retrieving specific information from long video sequences. The most detailed description says it contains retrieval, ordering, and counting tasks, with retrieval treated as a short-dependency task and ordering and counting as long-dependency tasks. Another definition specifically places it on long-video tasks that benefit from extended temporal context.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link VNBench to 2 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. It is used to measure Long video understanding and Temporal perception, and it is also reported as measuring Chronological ordering and Counting. The recorded links are concentrated on long video understanding and related temporal, ordering, and counting abilities.

Space of uses. Papers use VNBench both as a standalone evaluation for long-video retrieval ability and as one benchmark within broader multi-benchmark comparisons. One study includes it in a table of video benchmarks, while another reports running NIAH experiments to assess retrieval ability fro

nodes.name: VocalSound
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available papers, VocalSound is treated as a vocal sound classification dataset. Definitions describe it as featuring non-verbal human vocalizations across different acoustic conditions, and as an evaluation set for a model's ability to recognize non-speech audio events; one paper also labels it as "VSC VocalSound" in a benchmark table.

What it is claimed to measure. No constructs or behavioral indicators are linked to VocalSound. Instead, papers describe it more directly as evaluating whether models can recognize non-speech audio events and human vocal sounds beyond speech, so the reported usage converges on vocal sound recognition rather than a named construct.

Space of uses. Papers use VocalSound as an evaluation benchmark within vocal sound classification setups, rather than linking it to other named measurement instruments. In the available descriptions it appears as a benchmark entry and as an included dataset for testing recognition of non-verbal human vocalizations under varying acoustic conditions.

nodes.name: VoiceBBQ
nodes.definition: A spoken-language extension of the BBQ benchmark that assesses social bias in spoken language models using synthesized speech contexts with controlled speaker gender and accent, enabling separate evaluation of content and acoustic influences on bias.

nodes.name: VoiceBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, VoiceBench is presented as a benchmark dataset for evaluating speech language models on semantic understanding tasks without relying on auxiliary LLMs for scoring. Definitions describe it through multiple subsets, including AdvBench, IFEval, OBQA, MMSU, and sd-qa, and one study reports adopting those five subsets and, after filtering, obtaining 4,947 test samples. A smaller descriptive thread characterizes parts of VoiceBench as speech versions of existing text benchmarks and spoken-query datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link VoiceBench to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator, and the recorded uses cover several targets rather than a single one. It is used to measure Modality gap, with one paper defining the gap through drops in benchmark scores between text and speech inputs; World knowledge, where it is described as a spoken counterpart to text benchmarks across diverse factual domains; Safety, where spoken queries are used to evaluate whether models reject them; and Instruction following, where papers report that a text-based instruction-following benchmark is synthesized into speech.

Space of uses. No measurement instrume

nodes.name: VoxEval
nodes.definition: A benchmark designed for end-to-end speech interaction evaluation that supports the assessment of speech output, unlike benchmarks that require text responses.

nodes.name: VQA-RAD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, VQA-RAD is most commonly described as a radiology-focused medical visual question answering benchmark: radiology images paired with clinician-authored questions and answers, used to evaluate how models answer questions about medical scans or clinical images. Most descriptions mention open-ended and closed-ended answers, though one definition refers to open-ended and multiple-choice evaluation and one paper uses the name Rad-VQA. Papers do not describe its contents identically: some report 315 images and 2,248 QA pairs, while others report 315 images and 3,515 clinician-authored QA pairs; one paper additionally says imaging reports were generated from the QA pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use VQA-RAD to measure 2 behavioral indicators and link it to no constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure Medical visual question answering, with a smaller line of work using it for Visual question answering. Overall, papers present it as an evaluation benchmark for model performance on medical VQA tasks rather than as a measure of any named construct.

Space of uses. Papers usually use VQA-RAD as one benchmark within multi-dataset medica

nodes.name: VQA-v2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the literature, VQA-v2 is most commonly treated as a benchmark or dataset for visual question answering on images, typically requiring open-ended or free-form natural language answers to questions about a given image. Several definitions add that it is large-scale and based on natural images, and one formulation specifies images, associated questions, and ten ground-truth answers per question, while another describes it as a more balanced version of the original VQA dataset. Some papers further frame it as testing image understanding, visual comprehension, or vision, language, and commonsense knowledge. Papers also refer to specific evaluation slices, including validation and test-dev splits, and one study uses a VQA v2 32+50 subset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use VQA-v2 to measure 11 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so its reported role is spread across many targets rather than converging on a single construct or indicator. The prevailing construct framings are visual understanding, multimodal understanding, visual perception, fine-grained visual understanding, and fairness, and on the behavioral side it is most commonly used to measure visual

nodes.name: VQA-X
nodes.definition: VQA-X dataset with human-annotated explanations used to evaluate explanation generation for visual question answering.

nodes.name: VSR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat VSR, or Visual Spatial Reasoning, as a closed-set benchmark for spatial reasoning over images, testing a model's understanding of coarse object spatial relationships. Some definitions also describe it as the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, rich in spatial relational information among objects in images, and one paper places it among single-image benchmarks that test alignment between single images and multiple captions.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, VSR is linked to one construct, Spatial reasoning, and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is as a measure of spatial reasoning, with papers referring to it as one of the spatial reasoning benchmarks and reporting results on visual spatial reasoning in VSR.

Space of uses. Papers use VSR for evaluation, commonly alongside other spatial reasoning benchmarks. The cited benchmark suites place it with SPEC, Whatsup, and EmbSpatial, and one paper also includes it in a set of single-image benchmarks used to evaluate fine-grained visual-language understanding; no other measurement instrument is directly linked to it.

nodes.name: VTAB-1k
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions describe VTAB-1k as the Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark, a suite of 19 diverse visual or image classification tasks spanning Natural, Specialized, and Structured domains. Across papers, it is used to evaluate transfer learning or fine-tuning performance in vision models; some descriptions add that each dataset has 1,000 training examples, and some specify structured tasks such as depth and orientation prediction or a split of 7 Natural, 4 Specialized, and 8 Structured datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link VTAB-1k to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claim centers on image classification, with several papers using VTAB-1k to measure image classification; a smaller line of work reports it as measuring generalization and visual recognition. These reported uses therefore spread across a small set of targets rather than only one construct.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers usually use VTAB-1k as a benchmark for evaluating the efficacy or fine-tuning performance of vision models and parameter-efficient transfer learning methods, and one paper describes it as extensively used fo

nodes.name: WangchanThaiInstruct
nodes.definition: A human-authored Thai instruction-following dataset containing 6,916 test samples across four domains (Medical, Law, Finance, Retail) and seven task types, used for zero-shot evaluation and instruction tuning.

nodes.name: Waste-Bench
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset containing 9,520 open-ended question-answer pairs across 952 images of cluttered waste scenes, designed to evaluate VLLMs on robustness and reasoning in real-world waste classification tasks.

nodes.name: WE-MATH
nodes.definition: Multimodal math reasoning benchmark focused on Chinese mathematical problems with visual components.

nodes.name: Weather
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats Weather as a benchmark dataset for time series forecasting based on weather or climate data. Definitions differ on its contents and granularity: some describe meteorological variables such as temperature, humidity, and wind speed, some describe local climate data from 1,600 U.S. locations between 2010 and 2013 with 11 climate features, and others describe 21 meteorological factors collected every 10 minutes or, more generally, a Weather Forecasting dataset recorded at a 10-minute frequency. One study describes it as "local climate data from 1,600 U.S. locations, between 2010 and 2013" (Are Language Models Actually Useful for Time Series Forecasting?).

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is narrow rather than spread across many targets. Papers link Weather to 1 behavioral indicator, Time series forecasting, and to no constructs or other measurement instruments. In that recorded relationship, papers use it to measure Time series forecasting, describing it as one of the datasets "widely adopted for evaluating time series forecasting performance" and "extensively used to evaluate time-series forecasting ab

nodes.name: WebArena
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WebArena is most commonly described as a realistic web-based interactive environment and benchmark for evaluating autonomous or web agents on long-horizon tasks. Definitions variously present it as a simulated browser environment navigated through natural language and code, a set of 812 test examples focused on grounding high-level natural language instructions to interactions with functional correctness, and a benchmark built from realistic or functional websites and open-source clones across domains such as e-commerce, forums, development platforms, content management, shopping, and sites like Reddit, GitLab, and Wikipedia. A smaller subset of papers focuses on particular slices of it, such as the full dataset or the Reddit domain within WebArena.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WebArena to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is as a measure of web navigation: several papers evaluate agents on web browsing or web navigation with WebArena, often stressing real-world or realistic web interactions. A smaller line of work uses it to measure task completion, and some papers report it as evaluating generalization or g

nodes.name: WebMMU
nodes.definition: A multimodal, multilingual, and multi-task benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on visual web understanding and code generation, covering website VQA, mockup-to-code, and code editing in four languages.

nodes.name: WebNLG
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WebNLG is most commonly described as a dataset or benchmark for generating natural language from structured inputs, especially RDF triples, DBpedia categories, and knowledge graph triplets. Several definitions frame it as data-to-text, struct-to-text, graph-to-text, or knowledge-graph-to-natural-language, and one definition specifies 22,000 examples across 14 categories; a smaller number of descriptions instead call it a table-to-text dataset or, once, a text-to-data dataset. Some papers also refer to specific versions or subsets, including WebNLG17 as the 2017 graph-to-text setting and WebNLG-Test as the publicly released test set of manually aligned knowledge graphs and English textual descriptions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WebNLG to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure Data-to-text generation, with papers explicitly grouping it under E2E and WebNLG (data-to-text generation); some work uses it more broadly to measure Text generation. The measurement claims therefore concentrate on behavioral indicators rather than on constructs.

Space of uses. Papers often use WebNLG as one benchmark within br

nodes.name: WebQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, WebQA is most commonly described as a retrieval-augmented QA dataset for evaluating long-context retrieval performance. The available definition specifies 20 documents per question and frames the task around position-dependent accuracy; one paper also refers to it as "WebQA (WebQ)".

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WebQA to measure Synthetic recall. Its reported measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across concepts: it is linked to 1 behavioral indicator, Synthetic recall, and to no constructs.

Space of uses. In use, WebQA appears as part of a broader evaluation suite rather than a standalone protocol. One study says the evaluation "leverages" NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA, WebQA, and the specialized task KV Retrieval, and no other measurement instruments are linked to it.

nodes.name: WebQSP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe WebQSP as a benchmark dataset for knowledge base or knowledge graph question answering over Freebase or structured knowledge bases. Several definitions add that it is derived from WebQuestions and pairs natural language questions with SPARQL queries; some describe it as containing both single-hop and multi-hop questions, while others frame it more specifically as a multi-hop dataset or as a benchmark used to test I.I.D. generalization. A smaller number of descriptions mention questions from the Google Suggest API, answers from Freebase, or reasoning over a subset of Freebase.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WebQSP to measure two behavioral indicators and two constructs. The prevailing claim is that it measures Knowledge graph question answering, while a smaller line of work uses it for Multi-hop question answering. On the construct side, papers report it as measuring Multi-hop reasoning most often and Reasoning more generally less often, so the linked claims cluster around KGQA and reasoning-oriented targets.

Space of uses. In use, papers usually treat WebQSP as one of several benchmark KGQA datasets, most often alongside CWQ an

nodes.name: WebQuestions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant description is as an open-domain question answering dataset or benchmark, though some papers call it generative or open-ended text QA. Most definitions describe questions drawn from the web, Google Search, natural web queries, or the Google Suggest API, and several add that the answers are entities in Freebase; one paper more specifically says Berant et al. collected question-answer pairs from the Freebase knowledge database, and another reports a test set of 2032 questions. A smaller line of work frames it as a fact-recall or closed-book question answering benchmark, and spoken QA papers use synthesized or adapted audio versions of Web Questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims are spread across several targets: papers use it to measure 7 behavioral indicators and 3 constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure open-domain question answering; papers also use it for spoken question answering, factual recall, question answering, and, at the construct level, world knowledge. Across the recorded links, it is used for more than one construct or behavioral indicator rather than a single target alone.

Space of uses. Across pape

nodes.name: WebShop
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, papers most commonly treat WebShop as an interactive benchmark environment that simulates an online shopping or e-commerce website. The prevailing description is that an agent follows a user instruction by browsing or navigating webpages, using search and click actions, selecting attributes or options, and purchasing a matching product; some definitions add that it contains a large amount of real-world product data or over a million real-world products, and one description frames it as navigating scraped amazon.com pages. A smaller line of work describes it as an online shopping dataset or benchmark task rather than an environment, and papers also note dense final rewards from 0 to 1, completion-level scoring, attribute, option, product type, and price matching, and tasks with 30 timesteps.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WebShop to 3 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The most common behavioral use is to measure web navigation, with smaller lines of work using it for action selection; on the construct side, it is reported as measuring decision-making most often, and is also used for reasoning and problem-solving ability. Overa

nodes.name: WebSRC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing description treats WebSRC as webpage-centered question-answer data used in vision-language or web comprehension settings. Definitions differ in emphasis: some describe it as a dataset for vision-language tasks or for web-based structural reading comprehension, while another paper calls it "a static HTML comprehension benchmark" where answers are extracted from web pages based on a given question.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WebSRC to two constructs, GUI understanding and HTML understanding, and no behavioral indicators. The explicit measurement claims cover both constructs: one paper lists WebSRC among benchmarks selected "for GUI understanding," while another says it tests WebAgent on WebSRC as "a static HTML comprehension benchmark" for HTML understanding.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is directly linked to WebSRC, though one GUI understanding evaluation uses it alongside VisualWebBench, ScreenQA-Short, and WidgetCap. Papers position it in several ways: as a benchmark that a web agent is tested on, as one of the vision-language tasks in a main results table "illustrating the multi-modal in-context

nodes.name: WebVoyager
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, WebVoyager is most commonly treated as a dynamic, real-world web dataset or benchmark for evaluating long-horizon planning in web navigation, with task completion assessed in realistic environments. A smaller framing presents it as an out-of-distribution benchmark for evaluating web-agent generalization, emphasizing that it covers diverse domains unseen in the WebArena environment.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WebVoyager to measure one behavioral indicator, Web navigation, and one construct, Generalization. The prevailing usage is to evaluate web navigation in real-world or live settings, while a smaller line of work reports it as measuring generalization by testing agents on the tasks and golden answers proposed in WebVoyager.

Space of uses. In use, papers frequently place WebVoyager alongside WebArena, for example evaluating on the full WebArena dataset as well as WebVoyager, and one study pairs it with Mind2Web-Live as a live web navigation benchmark. It is positioned both as a main evaluation benchmark for real-world websites and as an additional evaluation setting for unseen domains beyond WebArena.

nodes.name: Weibo21
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Weibo21 is commonly described as a Chinese benchmark drawn from the Weibo platform for fake news or rumor detection. One description presents it as a Chinese-language fake news detection dataset, while another frames it as a Chinese multi-domain rumor detection dataset covering 9 domains, with each news item containing news content and several comments.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, Weibo21 is used to measure one behavioral indicator, Misinformation detection, and it is not linked to any constructs. This usage converges on a single target: papers evaluate misinformation detection with Weibo21, and several descriptions place that evaluation within fake news detection tasks.

Space of uses. Papers use Weibo21 alongside GossipCop, AMTCele, Pheme, and LLM-mis in experimental evaluations. In these accounts it is positioned as one of the benchmark datasets in the test setup, for example as the Chinese dataset paired with GossipCop, or as one of the public datasets used in experiments on cross-domain misinformation detection and rumor detection.

nodes.name: WiC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WiC is most commonly described as the Word-in-Context dataset or benchmark for word sense disambiguation: models judge whether a target word has the same meaning in two sentences or contexts. Several definitions also place it within SuperGLUE, while a smaller line makes the format more explicit by calling it a binary classification benchmark for polysemy disambiguation and noting that all WiC datasets are class-balanced with a 50% chance baseline. Most descriptions stay with word sense disambiguation, though one definition frames it as evaluating context-sensitive word representations and another groups it under natural language inference while still using the same-meaning-across-contexts test.

What it is claimed to measure. Relationship claims connect WiC to four behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing usage is that papers use WiC to measure word sense disambiguation, including descriptions that it is a word sense disambiguation dataset or that it challenges models on contextual word sense disambiguation. One paper also uses it to measure language understanding task performance, one uses it to measure natural language inference, and one

nodes.name: WiCE
nodes.definition: Textual entailment dataset based on Wikipedia claims, used in this work for connected reasoning evaluation due to its document-claim-evidence triples.

nodes.name: WikiAnn
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, papers refer to it as WikiAnn or WikiANN and most commonly treat it as a multilingual named entity recognition dataset. Definitions differ on scope and framing: some describe 282-language coverage and its use for low-resource Sino-Tibetan languages, with one survey noting that all ST languages other than Chinese amount to 131K name mentions, while other definitions describe a Wikipedia-extracted NER dataset for crosslingual sequence labeling and report 176-language coverage.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what it measures converge on a single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across multiple outcomes. Papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator, Named entity recognition, and to no constructs; correspondingly, it is repeatedly described as a dataset used for named entity recognition evaluation.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked alongside it. Papers use it as a direct evaluation set, including crosslingual sequence labeling evaluation and additional experiments on low-resource Sino-Tibetan languages; as one paper states, "We use WikiANN for named entity recognition (NER)" (LangSAMP: Language-Script Aware Mult

nodes.name: WikiBio
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe WikiBio as a benchmark dataset for knowledge editing focused on biographical information. The available description does not specify versions or subsets, and it appears in a grouping of datasets used to edit different kinds of knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers link WikiBio to one behavioral indicator, Knowledge editing, through a measured_by relation, and no constructs are linked to it. The measurement claims therefore center on Knowledge editing rather than being spread across multiple constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. In Unlocking Efficient, Scalable, and Continual Knowledge Editing with Basis-Level Representation Fine-Tuning, WikiBio is used alongside WikiDatarecent, WikiDatacounterfact, ConvSent, and ZsRE, in the authors' setup for editing different kinds of knowledge. No measurement instrument is linked to it beyond this co-usage context.

nodes.name: Wikidata
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the available definitions, papers treat Wikidata as a schema matching dataset for a general knowledge base, used to test whether schema matching approaches generalize on structured open-domain data. One paper explicitly places it in a cross-domain evaluation setting, stating that authors evaluate on "Magellan (e-commerce) and WikiData (general knowledge base)" to assess generalizability to other domains (Bootstrapping Self-Improvement of Language Model Programs for Zero-Shot Schema Matching).

What it is claimed to measure. In the reported relationships, papers use Wikidata to measure one behavioral indicator, Schema matching, and it is not linked to any constructs. The linked usage converges on that single indicator rather than spreading across multiple targets: papers report schema matching as measured by Wikidata.

Space of uses. Papers use Wikidata as an evaluation benchmark for schema matching, and one explicit usage description positions it as further evaluation for generalizability to other domains rather than as a standalone setting. In that description, it appears alongside Magellan.

nodes.name: WikiData_counterfact
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers treat WikiData_counterfact as a dataset for knowledge editing evaluation, most commonly described as containing counterfactual statements derived from Wikidata. One paper places it within the KnowEdit benchmark and uses it among datasets selected for experiments covering knowledge insertion and knowledge modification.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what it measures are concentrated rather than dispersed. Multiple papers use WikiData_counterfact to measure Knowledge editing, and one paper also reports it as measuring Editing locality, with a Locality ↑ result on this dataset; overall, papers link it to one behavioral indicator and one construct.

Space of uses. In the reported uses, it is positioned as one benchmark within broader evaluation suites. It is used alongside WikiDatarecent, WikiBio, ConvSent, and ZsRE when papers evaluate editing different kinds of knowledge, and one paper describes it as one of two additional benchmarks while another reports a pilot quantitative experiment on it within KnowEdit.

nodes.name: WikiData_recent
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe it as a dataset for knowledge editing evaluation that focuses on recent, updated facts from Wikidata. A paper also places it among datasets used in experiments involving knowledge insertion and knowledge modification.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure knowledge editing, and they also report it as measuring editing locality and linguistic quality. The linked claims cover one behavioral indicator, knowledge editing, and two constructs, editing locality and linguistic quality; in one table the construct-level uses appear under Locality and Fluency.

Space of uses. Papers use it alongside WikiDatacounterfact, WikiBio, ConvSent, and ZsRE when editing different kinds of knowledge, and another paper includes it in experiments involving knowledge insertion and knowledge modification. The papers do not link it to any other measurement instrument.

nodes.name: WikiHop
nodes.definition: A multi-hop question answering dataset used here to evaluate the effectiveness of web-page retrieval.

nodes.name: WikiHow
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat WikiHow as source data built from instructional content. Definitions describe it as a dataset of instructional articles, as a multimodal dataset, and in one study as a dataset derived from the WikiHow online knowledge base and modified by grouping related paragraphs into documents and using summaries as subheadings. Across these uses, it appears as the basis for script generation, project-based learning, and procedural step selection from text and images.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WikiHow to 1 behavioral indicator, How-to question answering, and to no constructs. The recorded claim is focused rather than spread across many outcomes: a paper reports that this dataset is used to evaluate THREAD on linear how-to questions, so WikiHow is used to measure How-to question answering.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to WikiHow. Instead, papers use it as source material within broader evaluations: as the basis for a script generation task in InterleavedBench, as extracted data for MMIE's project-based learning category, as a modified dataset for evaluating organizing skill on expository text, and as a dataset

nodes.name: WikiMIA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a dataset or benchmark for evaluating training or pretraining data detection on large language models. Definitions commonly frame it as temporal or dynamic: it uses Wikipedia texts or excerpts, and labels items as seen versus unseen, or member versus non-member, by comparing publication date with a model's training cutoff or release timeline. Some papers also describe it as a temporal MIA dataset or a benchmark for membership inference attacks, but the shared setup is a date-based split of Wikipedia content.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WikiMIA to one behavioral indicator and no constructs. The dominant use is to measure pre-training data detection: several papers describe it as a common benchmark for evaluating detection methods, and one paper treats WikiMIA and MIMIR as the only two benchmarks it considers for this task. A smaller line of work also links it to membership inference attack through measured_by relations, using earlier Wikipedia text as member data and more recent text as non-member data.

Space of uses. Papers use WikiMIA in both focused and multi-benchmark evaluations. One line of work pairs it

nodes.name: Wikipedia
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Wikipedia is described as a text source used in several ways. Some authors treat it as the external knowledge base from which retrieved documents are drawn for RAG evaluation, with one paper stating, "We employ Wikipedia as the knowledge base K" and referring to a "Wikimedia dump provided by Cohere" (Improving Multilingual Retrieval-Augmented Language Models through Dialectic Reasoning Argumentations). Other papers describe it as a text corpus or evaluation dataset, including a MassiveText Wikipedia variant used for supporting experiments and a pre-training dataset setting.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Wikipedia to no constructs and one behavioral indicator. The only reported measurement claim is that it measures node classification, based on a performance comparison on "three benchmark datasets". No construct-level use is recorded.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position it as the knowledge base K in retrieval-augmented evaluation, as a language or pre-training dataset considered in evaluation, and as an auxiliary setting for supporting experiments, with one study noting "supporting experiments on W

nodes.name: WikiQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is a question-answering benchmark or dataset built from questions paired with Wikipedia sentences or answers. Some definitions narrow this to answer selection, or to open-domain, closed-book question answering, while one calibration study uses it for sentence-level responses because model responses are complete sentences. A smaller usage applies the test set with synthesised speech queries for spoken-query-based question answering.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant claim is that WikiQA measures question answering, and smaller lines of work use it to measure open-ended question answering and spoken question answering. The reported measurement claims therefore stay within closely related question-answering behaviors rather than broader constructs.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it, but papers often use it alongside other benchmarks such as SQuAD, QASC, QuaRTz, TruthfulQA, and HotpotQA. Across studies it is usually one dataset within a larger task suite, including fine-tuning and evaluation setups, sentence-level calibration evaluation,

nodes.name: WikiSQL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat WikiSQL as a standard or benchmark text-to-SQL dataset. Definitions also place it among early benchmarks for Text-to-SQL parsing over relational tables, including one description that narrows this to single relational tables, while another paper uses it as a benchmark in a main evaluation table for structured knowledge grounding. A smaller usage presents it as another corpus to which a methodology can be adapted.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WikiSQL to two behavioral indicators and no constructs. It is reported as measuring Table question answering and Text-to-SQL: one paper describes it as one of three challenging table QA datasets, and another places it among early benchmarks that focus on Text-to-SQL parsing over relational tables. The reported measurement role is therefore split across these two task framings rather than tied to a linked construct.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers nevertheless mention or use WikiSQL alongside other benchmarks, including BIRD and Spider as other text-to-SQL datasets, and alongside WikiTQ and FeTaQA when reporting table question answering results. Another pape

nodes.name: WikiText
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WikiText is most commonly treated as a language-modeling benchmark or corpus built from Wikipedia text, usually evaluated through perplexity on a held-out or validation split. Some authors further describe it as high-quality encyclopedic text, including only articles marked "Good" or "Featured" by human editors, while a smaller line frames Wikitext as a long-context benchmark in the LM evaluation harness or names the Wikitext-2 subset specifically. Definitions also vary between using it as an evaluation benchmark and as a corpus for pre-training or auxiliary language modeling.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, it is linked to 7 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so the measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than converging on one. The prevailing usage is to measure general ability, often via perplexity, with additional papers using it to measure generalization and zero-shot generalization; smaller lines of work report it as measuring commonsense reasoning, confidence, fluency, and language modeling ability, and as evaluating long-form text generation and zero-shot task performance. Separately, one paper reports that

nodes.name: WikiText-103
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions treat WikiText-103 as a large language modeling benchmark, corpus, or dataset derived from high-quality Wikipedia articles, often explicitly as a larger version of WikiText and used for autoregressive language modeling, perplexity, or next-token prediction. Papers also describe named variants and subsets, including Wikitext-103-v1, train, validation, and test splits, held-out or test sets, and sampled validation sequences. A smaller line of use treats it as source text for character strings, split-word manipulations, or embedding generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing construct-level use is to measure Language modeling ability, with Long-context understanding also reported through next-token generation on Wikitext-103. At the behavioral level, papers use it to measure Conditional text generation, Text continuation, Text generation, and Text infilling, so the claimed measurement role is spread across several related generation behaviors.

Space of uses. The prevailing usage is as a standard or commonly used language modeling benchmark, often with perplexity or next-token pred

nodes.name: WikiText-2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats WikiText-2 as a language modeling benchmark or dataset built from high-quality, cleaned Wikipedia articles, usually used to evaluate text prediction or text continuation with perplexity on validation, test, or dev splits. Several definitions frame it as a standard benchmark for compressed, pruned, or quantized models, and one paper specifies evaluation on "166 test windows of 2048 tokens each"; a smaller line of work instead uses the training data for training from scratch, supervised fine-tuning, hypernetwork training, slicing, or hidden-state analysis. Papers also mention variants and subsets such as raw-WikiText2 (WT-2), WikiText2-v1, WikiText-V2, and the training, validation, dev, or test splits.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WikiText-2 to eight constructs and one behavioral indicator. The dominant claim is that it measures text generation and language modeling ability through perplexity or LM loss, with some papers explicitly stating that lower perplexity on WikiText-2 reflects stronger language modeling ability; smaller lines of work use it to measure general ability, long-context understanding, and compress

nodes.name: WikiTQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe WikiTQ, also written as WikiTableQuestions or WTQ, as a benchmark or dataset of Wikipedia, sometimes semi-structured or HTML, tables paired with natural-language questions for table-based question answering. The prevailing description emphasizes complex operations such as comparison, aggregation, and arithmetic, while some papers further frame it as short-form or short text span answering; one paper describes about 2100 HTML tables and about 22,033 questions, and another refers to a standard test set with 4,344 table-question pairs. A smaller line of work adapts it into training formats for table-language interleaved learning or column-embedding training, and one study uses a filtered hybrid version requiring semantic inference.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WikiTQ to one behavioral indicator, Table question answering, and one construct, Table reasoning. The prevailing usage is to measure Table question answering, with descriptions such as table QA, table-based question answering, or short-form QA over semi-structured tables. A smaller group of papers uses it to measure Table reasoning, describing it as a benchmark for table-based reas

nodes.name: WildBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat WildBench as an instruction-following benchmark, sometimes also as an automatic LLM benchmark, for assessing model responses on diverse and challenging user queries. Definitions recurrently describe real-user or natural tasks, longer or more complex prompts, and difficult multi-turn questions; some add a diverse distribution of task categories, evaluation against a reference answer with a fine-grained grading scale, human preference judgments, or a WB-Score. A smaller line of work frames it as an LLM-based evaluation framework or public dataset of model comparisons judged by an LLM-based judge.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WildBench to measure 7 constructs and 6 behavioral indicators, so its reported targets are spread across multiple capacities rather than concentrated on one. The most frequent construct-level links are conversational ability, complex reasoning, and creativity, with 4 other constructs also linked. On the behavioral side, papers report it as evaluating creative writing and data analysis, plus 4 other indicators.

Space of uses. Most papers position WildBench as one of a few evaluation benchmarks, commonly alongside Alpaca

nodes.name: WildChat
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, WildChat is most commonly described as a dataset of real-world LLM conversations or real-world user interactions. Papers variously frame it as conversations with GPT models performing daily tasks, collected through a free GPT API in exchange for shared logs, and as a source of out-of-distribution prompts; one paper also describes it as a comprehensive multi-turn, multi-lingual dataset of 1 million timestamped conversations, and another says it "more closely reflects real user needs."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WildChat to 2 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The main measurement uses in these papers are to measure Overrefusal, Harmlessness, and Multilingual ability: papers describe over-refusal evaluations using WildChat, test harmlessness with "highly toxic prompts from WildChat," and assess multilingual capability with MultiAlpaca and WildChat; a separate paper relates it to Multi-turn dialogue rather than treating that link as a measurement claim. In the available work, these claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on one construct.

Space of uses. WildChat is used as evaluation data rather than alon

nodes.name: WildChat-1M
nodes.definition: Real-world dataset of 837,989 conversations from 167,062 users interacting with a ChatGPT mirror site over one year, used to analyze conceptual diversity trends before and after GPT version updates.

nodes.name: WildChat-AQA
nodes.definition: Benchmark for aggregative question answering comprising 6,027 multiple-choice questions derived from 182,330 real-world chatbot conversations, assessing models' ability to extract collective insights across temporal, geographic, and demographic dimensions.

nodes.name: WildGuard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, WildGuard is most commonly described as an automated, classifier-based evaluation procedure for model responses to harmful queries. The prevailing description is that it is used to judge whether a response fully complies with a harmful test query. Some papers describe the same tool more specifically as classifying a response as refusal or compliance, including on XSTest, while another paper frames it as an external harmfulness detection model that assigns a harmfulness probability to each response.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not explicitly link WildGuard to any constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, they describe it as evaluating immediate response properties: whether a model response fully complies with harmful test queries, whether it should be classified as a refusal or compliance, and, in one framing, the probability that a response is harmful. Across these descriptions, the usage clusters around automatic safety evaluation rather than a single explicitly named construct.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is explicitly linked to WildGuard. Papers position it as an automatic evaluator for safety-focused mod

nodes.name: WildGuardMix
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats WildGuardMix as a benchmark dataset for safety guard models, especially for instruction-response pair classification and response classification for content safety. Papers also refer to WildGuardMix Test Response and WildGuardTest: the former is described as a public benchmark for response classification, while the latter is presented as an evaluation dataset or prompt safety benchmark. Definitions of WildGuardTest differ, with one paper describing 1725 prompts, 863 harmful persuasion and 862 safe, and another describing 960 vanilla and 796 adversarial prompts. A smaller line of work instead uses WildGuardMix as a preference dataset for synthesized judge training data, or as a dataset containing a broad spectrum of jailbroken prompts and responses.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WildGuardMix to three behavioral indicators and no constructs. The reported measurement use is spread across Content moderation, Harmful content detection, and Response harmfulness classification, rather than centered on a linked construct. In these uses, papers present it as evaluating safety guard or content safety classificati

nodes.name: WildScore
nodes.definition: An in-the-wild multimodal benchmark for symbolic music reasoning and analysis, consisting of real music scores paired with user-generated multiple-choice questions from online forums.

nodes.name: WildSeek
nodes.definition: WildSeek is an evaluation dataset of 100 topic-and-intent examples across 24 domains used to assess open-domain long-form generation.

nodes.name: WildVision
nodes.definition: A real-world dataset of image-text pairs used for distribution analysis and comparison.

nodes.name: WinoBias
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WinoBias is most commonly described as a coreference resolution benchmark or dataset for gender bias, especially gender-occupation bias, built around pronoun resolution in pro-stereotypical and anti-stereotypical Winograd-style examples. One paper states that each example contains "two gender-neutral profession names and gendered pronouns" and asks the model to identify "the coreference link between the pronouns and the correct professional" (Debiasing Algorithm through Model Adaptation). A smaller set of descriptions frames it more broadly as a fairness dataset or as an out-of-distribution bias benchmark, but the recurring content is coreference resolution with professions and gendered pronouns.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WinoBias to measure 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The most common claims link it to Social bias and Stereotyping, often in terms of whether models assign stereotypical gender pronouns to occupations; it is also used to measure the behavioral indicator Coreference resolution, and a smaller line of work treats it as measuring Fairness. The construct claims are spread across Social bias, Stereotyping, and Fairnes

nodes.name: Winogender
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is a diagnostic dataset or benchmark for gender bias in coreference resolution, often described as a gender-occupation benchmark that tests whether models resolve pronouns in a gender-stereotyped manner. Some authors place it among WinoGrad Schema datasets and describe it as similar to WinoBias. One paper gives a more specific operational description, saying that the benchmark involves computing the Pearson correlation between model probabilities for female-gendered pronouns and occupation gender statistics, and another repurposes it for non-stereotypical evaluation by filtering out sentences with strong gender co-occurrences.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Winogender to 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to use it to measure Stereotyping, where it is described as a widely used dataset for evaluating gender bias in LLMs. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Social bias, including as an out-of-distribution bias benchmark to test generalization, so the recorded claims center on stereotyping with one additional linked construct.

Space of uses. Papers often use it alongside Win

nodes.name: WinoGrande
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WinoGrande is most commonly described as a large-scale Winograd-schema-style commonsense reasoning benchmark or dataset. The prevailing description centers on pronoun or coreference resolution over ambiguous sentences, often in fill-in-the-blank or multiple-choice form with binary options; several papers also describe it as adversarially mined or filtered and designed to be hard for models that rely on statistical cues, with some definitions also mentioning minimal gender or dataset-specific bias. A smaller number of papers use variant names such as Winogrande, WinoGrade, Winograde, or Wino, and a few frame it more generally as a language understanding or reasoning benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WinoGrande to measure 15 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators. The dominant framing is that it measures Commonsense reasoning, though papers also report it as evaluating Reasoning, General ability, Logical reasoning, Natural language understanding, and other constructs, so the claims extend beyond a single construct even while commonsense reasoning remains the prevailing use. At the behavioral-indicator level, it is most often linked to C

nodes.name: Winoground
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, Winoground is most commonly described as a compositional image-text matching dataset or benchmark for probing visio-linguistic compositionality, fine-grained alignment, and reasoning. Definitions converge on a setup with carefully constructed minimal pairs, or paired images and captions, and one recurring task description says the model must correctly match two images and captions whose captions use the same words in different orders. A smaller framing describes it more broadly as a dataset of images for evaluating vision-language models, including image captioning and compositional understanding.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three constructs and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure compositional reasoning, followed by compositionality and relation understanding: papers describe it as testing compositional visual reasoning, as a benchmark for assessing VLM compositionality, and as evaluating the ability to understand relationships between objects within an image. Smaller uses report it as measuring cross-modal retrieval through binary image-text matching, and self-correction, where authors evaluate

nodes.name: Wizard of Wikipedia
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, papers describe Wizard of Wikipedia, also called WoW or Wizard-of-Wikipedia, as a knowledge-grounded or open-domain dialogue dataset or benchmark in which one conversational partner, the "wizard," has access to Wikipedia or Wikipedia articles to inform the conversation. The prevailing description is this shared setup, while some papers emphasize it as a benchmark for knowledge-grounded dialogue and others as a dialogue dataset used for training models.

What it is claimed to measure. Several papers report that Wizard of Wikipedia measures dialogue generation. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Dialogue generation, and no constructs, so dialogue generation is the only reported measurement target.

Space of uses. Papers use it in multiple roles: for evaluation, for training dialogue models, and for dialogue analysis. They place it alongside HotpotQA for evaluation, and alongside DailyDialog and DialogSum for controlled response generation, grammar detection, and grammar skill co-occurrence analysis in adjacent speaker turns; no other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: WizardLM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description treats WizardLM as a benchmark or evaluation dataset for instruction-oriented, open-ended tasks. One recurring definition presents it as containing 218 questions that span more categories and diverse difficulties, used to assess broader question-type generalization. Papers also describe it differently: one frames it as a benchmark for instruction-following and open-ended generation using complex, multi-step prompts, while another describes it as instruction-generation data that leverages the ChatGPT API to generate 250k instructions from Alpaca training data.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WizardLM to measure 1 behavioral indicator, Text generation, and link it to no constructs. The reported measurement claim converges on that single target: it is presented as part of evaluating "open-ended generation."

Space of uses. In use, papers place WizardLM within broader evaluation suites and as a baseline against prior resources. One paper includes it alongside Vicuna in a "broad array of out-of-distribution benchmarks" for open-ended generation, and another treats it as a previous-work baseline alongside SELF-INSTRUCT

nodes.name: WMDP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, WMDP is most commonly treated as a popular unlearning benchmark for hazardous or harmful knowledge. Definitions describe it as evaluating a model's capacity to generate and then unlearn such knowledge, especially in biosecurity and cybersecurity, and some descriptions also include chemical security. Papers do not describe it identically: some call it the World Model Development Project benchmark, others the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy benchmark, and one definition specifies a multiple-choice dataset with WMDP-bio and WMDP-cyber subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded links, papers use WMDP to measure one behavioral indicator, multiple-choice question answering, and no constructs are linked to it. The explicit measurement links therefore converge on a single behavioral indicator rather than several constructs. Beyond that link, definitions frequently say it evaluates unlearning capability, or the unlearning of hazardous or harmful knowledge, in domains such as biosecurity, cybersecurity, and sometimes chemical security.

Space of uses. Papers position WMDP both as a popular unlearning benchmark and as one dataset within broader e

nodes.name: WMT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat WMT as a machine translation benchmark or shared task, often specifically the English-German or EN→DE task, used to evaluate translation performance. Some papers refer to collections of the yearly WMT task, and one paper frames WMT more broadly as a series of shared tasks and benchmarks for translation quality. A smaller line of work describes WMT as a human-preference dataset used to construct contrastive instruction-response pairs for machine translation.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, the links concentrate on one construct and one behavioral indicator rather than many targets. Papers use WMT to measure Translation quality and report Machine translation as measured by WMT, and one paper also records one linked measurement instrument, QuALITY, as measured by WMT, with quality measured in terms of BLEU for WMT.

Space of uses. Papers use WMT alongside other task datasets: examples pair WMT EnDe with CNN/DM, and in one supervised fine-tuning setup with XSum as well. Other papers position WMT alongside MLQE-PE and FLORES as an evaluation benchmark for translation quality, and one paper measures translation quality from En

nodes.name: WMT14
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers commonly describe WMT14 as a machine translation benchmark from the 2014 Workshop on Statistical Machine Translation, used to evaluate translation quality on standard translation directions. The descriptions vary in granularity: some refer to WMT14 generally, while others specify WMT14EnDe with training and test sets drawn from it, and relationship evidence also mentions French-English and English-French portions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WMT14 to measure Machine translation: it is linked to 1 behavioral indicator and to no constructs. The reported use is concentrated on that single indicator, with papers describing WMT14 as used for machine translation and for evaluating translation capabilities.

Space of uses. In use, papers present it as a direct translation evaluation, and some also place it in broader benchmark collections. No measurement instrument is linked to it, but one paper reports it alongside IWSLT14, afroMT, IWSLT17, WMT18, and WMT19 for machine translation, another includes WMT 2014 in a multilinguality grouping with two other benchmarks, and one relationship quote uses the English-French subset as part of a training set.

nodes.name: WMT14 De-En
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as a WMT 2014 German-to-English machine translation benchmark, papers refer to it as a dataset or benchmark of sentence pairs for evaluating translation quality. A smaller variation in wording emphasizes its use for evaluating speculative decoding on translation text distributions, and one snippet specifies 3,003 sentence pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure Machine translation: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and to no constructs. The reported measurement claims are concentrated on that single behavioral indicator, with papers selecting WMT14 De-En for the translation part of broader evaluations.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it directly, but papers use it alongside MT-bench, CNN/Daily Mail, Natural Questions, GSM8K, and Alpaca, with other datasets also mentioned. In those settings it is positioned as the translation component within multi-task evaluations, including speculative decoding studies.

nodes.name: WMT14 en-de
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers here, the prevailing usage treats WMT14 en-de as an English-German machine translation benchmark for translating English to German and evaluating translation quality. Definitions in this direction describe it as a benchmark used to evaluate finetuned LLMs on translation, and one study says it considers "the task on translating English to German using WMT14 en-de." A smaller line of work describes it instead as an English-to-German translation dataset used for both training and evaluation in distillation experiments.

What it is claimed to measure. In the available relationships, papers use WMT14 en-de to measure Machine translation. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and to no constructs. The measurement claims are therefore concentrated on a single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple linked constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. Papers use it within broader training and evaluation setups, not only as a standalone translation check. One line of work presents it as a downstream task for finetuning, alongside WMT19 English-Chinese for translation and multilingual summarization tasks, while another uses it

nodes.name: WMT16
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WMT16 is most commonly described as a machine translation dataset or benchmark from the 2016 WMT workshop. Definitions vary in the slice emphasized: several papers refer to its English and German splits for cross-lingual detection, some use it for English-to-Romanian fine-tuning and evaluation, and another describes it as focusing on English-to-German translation. A smaller usage treats it more broadly as part of a translation benchmark suite, as in the phrasing "WMT 2014 and WMT 2016" or as an item under multilingual evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. In relationships, papers link WMT16 to one behavioral indicator and one construct. The prevailing use is to measure Machine translation: papers cite Romanian-English and German-English pairs from the workshop, English-to-Romanian distillation, general translation tasks, and German-to-English test sets. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Multilingual ability, where WMT 2016 appears alongside other multilingual evaluations.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is formally linked to WMT16 in the relationships. Papers use it in two recurring ways: as a translation benchmark for fine-tuning,

nodes.name: WMT18
nodes.definition: A machine translation benchmark used to evaluate decoding methods on translation tasks.

nodes.name: WMT19
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing treatment of WMT19 is as a machine translation benchmark from the Workshop on Machine Translation 2019 or the WMT19 shared task. The descriptions vary slightly in form: some call it a benchmark used to evaluate machine translation systems, while one paper calls WMT-19 a dataset and uses the Kazakh-English subset; the cited content ranges from language pairs such as De-En, Fi-En, Lt-En, and Ru-En to that Kazakh-English subset.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use WMT19 to measure Machine translation. The claims converge on that single behavioral indicator: it is linked to 1 behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and no constructs.

Space of uses. Papers often use WMT19 alongside other machine translation benchmarks. In the excerpts it appears alongside WMT14, and some papers also list IWSLT14, afroMT, IWSLT17, and WMT18 in the same evaluation setup; a smaller use treats it as the Kazakh-English subset for evaluating fine-tuning after coreset selection, and one description also presents it for evaluating translation performance and uncertainty.

nodes.name: WMT23
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, WMT23 is most commonly described as a 2023 Workshop or Conference on Machine Translation shared-task dataset or benchmark for evaluating translation quality across multiple language pairs and systems. Some descriptions add that it contains human-rated translations, and one paper specifically refers to WMT'23 MQM ratings for English-German and Chinese-English, while another presents it more simply as the 2023 test set for machine translation quality evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. The only recorded measurement claim is Machine translation: one paper treats Machine translation as measured by WMT23, and the definitions consistently describe the benchmark as evaluating translation quality across multiple language pairs.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers use WMT23 as an evaluation test set or benchmark, including for fine-grained machine translation evaluation and as a generative task benchmark; one paper uses WMT'23 MQM ratings for English-German and Chinese-English, while another uses WMT 2023 as the source of contaminated test examples.

Concer

nodes.name: WMT24++
nodes.definition: A high-quality translation test dataset derived from WMT24 with human-written and professionally post-edited references, used to evaluate translation performance without data leakage.

nodes.name: WMT 2024
nodes.definition: Annual Conference on Machine Translation shared task dataset for evaluating machine translation systems, containing human-rated translations across multiple language pairs and systems.

nodes.name: WN18RR
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for link prediction derived from WordNet, a lexical knowledge graph for English, with reciprocal relations removed to address test leakage problems.

nodes.name: WNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing framing is of WNLI as a Winograd Natural Language Inference benchmark or dataset within natural language understanding evaluations. Most definitions tie it to pronoun reasoning, pronoun resolution, or pronoun ambiguity, while some also describe it as evaluating sentence-level understanding, coreference resolution, and logical inference in pronoun disambiguation. One usage specifies results on the validation set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WNLI to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The named measurement claims are that papers use it to measure language understanding task performance and natural language inference, and one paper also uses it to measure generalization, describing WNLI as an additional out-of-domain task for assessing adaptability and generalization capabilities. These links stay limited to those three targets.

Space of uses. In use, papers relate WNLI to one other measurement instrument, GLUE, and usually place it inside broader evaluation suites rather than treating it in isolation. It appears alongside CoLA, MRPC, RTE, and SST-2 in NLU dataset lists, while other papers report zero-shot accurac

nodes.name: Word association test
nodes.definition: Psychological assessment that reveals subconscious cognitive patterns through free-relation word associations to cue words, adapted here for evaluating LLMs' cultural cognition.

nodes.name: Word substitution attack
nodes.definition: An evaluation protocol for robustness where a specified percentage of tokens in a watermarked text are randomly replaced with other tokens from the vocabulary before attempting to decode the watermark.

nodes.name: Word swap attack
nodes.definition: A data contamination procedure where words are randomly swapped with a generic token to test robustness.

nodes.name: Wordle
nodes.definition: A word-guessing environment used here to assess reasoning and planning in a sequential decision-making setting.

nodes.name: World Values Survey
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing treatment is of the World Values Survey as a global, cross-national survey or research project on people's beliefs and values, often repurposed for LLM work. Most descriptions use it as seed data or seed questions about social, political, religious, cultural, personal, and societal values; smaller lines of work use it as human reference data, as training data for cultural adaptation, or to derive representative personas. Several papers narrow this to Wave 7, described as covering 57 countries from 2017 to 2020, with either 260 seed questions across 13 cultural topics or a filtered subset of 206 questions from more than 129K respondents.

What it is claimed to measure. In the surveyed work, claims concentrate on measurement of Cultural alignment: papers use the World Values Survey to assess or evaluate alignment by comparing LLM responses with human survey data, and papers also describe it as a framework used for that evaluation. It is linked to 3 constructs and to no behavioral indicators, with the smaller additional uses being to measure Cultural bias and Value orientation. The prevailing measurement claim is therefore cultural alignme

nodes.name: WOS
nodes.definition: The Web of Science dataset (WOS-46985), a benchmark for hierarchical text classification containing scientific abstracts with a 2-level hierarchy of research areas and sub-areas.

nodes.name: WritingPrompts
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, WritingPrompts is treated as a story-writing or story-generation dataset featuring creative stories from Reddit's writing prompts forum. Papers also describe it as a language modeling evaluation dataset; in one use, models are given the story topic as the prompt for generating a narrative, while another paper treats it as a benchmark corpus and test-data source for sentence-level AI-generated text detection.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded measurement links, papers use WritingPrompts to measure one construct, Language modeling ability, and one behavioral indicator, Story generation. The stated measurement role is therefore concentrated on those two targets rather than spread across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers use WritingPrompts in several roles: as one of multiple corpora in broader evaluation, as training data for fine-tuning on story telling, and as a source corpus for constructing and testing sentence-level AI-generated text detection data. Source snippets place it alongside XSum or XSUM and SQuAD, including a report of averaging AUROCs across XSum, SQuAD, and WritingPrompts; no other measurement instrumen

nodes.name: WSC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WSC is most commonly described as the Winograd Schema Challenge, a benchmark, task, or dataset for coreference resolution and pronoun disambiguation, usually framed as requiring commonsense reasoning and sometimes linguistic reasoning. A smaller line of descriptions refers to it more generally as a reasoning benchmark or as Winograd-style tasks, and one paper says Winograd is a language-modeling formulation of the WSC task from SuperGLUE. A few definitions add format detail, describing WSC as multiple-choice questions, and one paper uses a direct-question version plus a one-shot variant, WSC-1sh.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WSC to measure 3 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing construct claim is commonsense reasoning, with several papers placing Winograd or WSC among commonsense reasoning datasets, while smaller strands use it to measure general ability or in-context learning. On behavioral indicators, it is reported most often as measuring coreference resolution, and individual papers also use it for downstream task performance, language understanding task performance, and zero-shot task performance, so the measurement cl

nodes.name: X-CSQA
nodes.definition: A multilingual commonsense reasoning benchmark (Cross-lingual CommonSense QA) used to evaluate a model's ability to answer commonsense questions in various languages.

nodes.name: XCOPA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, XCOPA is most commonly described as a cross-lingual or multilingual benchmark dataset for commonsense or causal reasoning. The prevailing task format is choosing between plausible alternatives, often selecting the most plausible cause or effect from a premise and question; some papers frame this as multiple-choice classification across languages, while another describes it as binary-choice questions across 11 languages. One paper also calls it a cross-lingual adaptation of COPA for commonsense reasoning evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use XCOPA to measure 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The dominant linkage is to Commonsense reasoning, often stated directly as commonsense reasoning or commonsense causal reasoning evaluation, while a smaller line of work treats it as measuring the broader construct Reasoning. The claims therefore concentrate on those two constructs rather than spreading across many others.

Space of uses. Papers usually position XCOPA as one member of multilingual benchmark suites, including zero-shot evaluations that cover reasoning, understanding, and generation, or classification-focused setups. It is often

nodes.name: XGLUE
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating cross-lingual transfer on a diverse set of natural language understanding and generation tasks.

nodes.name: XLQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark for locale-aware multilingual open-domain question answering, containing 3,000 English seed questions expanded into eight languages with human-verified annotations distinguishing locale-invariant and locale-sensitive cases.

nodes.name: XLSum
nodes.definition:
What it is.
