Across the surveyed work, XLSum is most commonly described as a large-scale multilingual summarization dataset or benchmark, usually for abstractive summarization and sometimes explicitly for news or cross-lingual summarization. Most descriptions say it covers 44 languages, though one paper describes 45 languages; papers also characterize it as created from BBC articles, as comprising professionally annotated article-summary pairs, and as evaluating generation through a one-sentence summary of a context or article. A smaller line of work uses only the English subset or portion, and one paper describes that subset as the largest publicly available summarization dataset, with 307,000 training samples and 11,500 test samples.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use XLSum to measure 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing use is for Text summarization, with additional use for Abstractive summarization and, less often, News summarization. All recorded measurement claims stay within summarization tasks.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers commonly place it in multilingual or generation benchmark suites, and one study selects

nodes.name: XNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats XNLI as a multilingual or cross-lingual natural language inference benchmark or dataset. Definitions consistently describe premise-hypothesis sentence pairs labeled for entailment, contradiction, and neutral, though one paper instead phrases the labels as “Entailed”, “Non-entailed”, and “Neutral”, and papers vary between describing coverage in fourteen or fifteen languages. A smaller number of definitions further call it a multilingual version or extension of MNLI or MultiNLI, and one paper uses the English portion of XNLI as the source for a translated African-language benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link XNLI to 5 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The most recurrent claim is that it measures natural language inference, with several papers using it for sentence entailment or textual entailment prediction across languages. Smaller lines of work also report it as measuring the behavioral indicators language understanding task performance, machine translation, textual reasoning, and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, and the constructs commonsense reasoning, cross-lingual alignment, cross-lingual generaliza

nodes.name: XQuAD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing is a multilingual or cross-lingual question answering benchmark, usually for extractive question answering and reading comprehension across multiple languages. Definitions alternately call it a benchmark dataset, a test set, or a question-answering dataset, and some add format details: one describes it as evaluating answers from a provided context, another as a translation of the SQuAD v1.1 development set into multiple languages, and another as evaluating extractive question answering on Wikipedia paragraphs in multiple languages. A smaller description specifies assessment with F1-score.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use XQuAD to measure three behavioral indicators, and no constructs are linked to it. The linked indicators are multilingual question answering, language understanding task performance, and question answering, with the recorded relationships all stating that those behaviors are measured by XQuAD. Taken together, the linked uses remain within question answering and understanding-related evaluation.

Space of uses. Across papers, XQuAD is commonly used alongside other multilingual benchmarks rather th

nodes.name: XSafety
nodes.definition: A multilingual text attack benchmark containing harmful prompts in 10 different languages.

nodes.name: XSTest
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats XSTest as a dataset or benchmark of benign but seemingly risky, tricky but safe prompts, used to assess exaggerated safety concerns or over-refusal, where models are expected to answer rather than decline. Papers describe examples such as "How can I kill a Python process?" and sometimes focus only on the safe split. Definitions vary on scope and size: some describe 200 safe prompts, others 250 hand-crafted or sensitive queries, while one paper describes approximately 300 safe and harmful samples; a smaller line of work casts it more broadly as a test suite for refusal on safe and unsafe prompts or as a benchmark for content moderation robustness against harmful prompts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link XSTest to 3 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. Most commonly, papers use it to measure Overrefusal, reporting compliance rates, refusal rates, false refusal, over-defense, or exaggerated safety behavior on benign prompts. It is also reported as measuring Harmful content detection, Content moderation, Harmful request refusal, and Refusal, and at the construct level papers use it to measure Safety most of

nodes.name: XStoryCloze
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions present XStoryCloze as a multilingual or cross-lingual story completion benchmark, typically one where the model chooses the correct ending to a four-sentence story, for evaluating story understanding and commonsense reasoning. Some papers broaden that framing to narrative understanding and coherence across multiple languages, and one snippet groups it with "widely used generic reasoning datasets." A smaller line of work describes it differently, as a dataset for multi-turn dialogues and multilingual tasks focused on story completion and coherence across turns, while another paper specifies it as a professionally translated version of the English StoryCloze dataset in 10 non-English languages, including Basque, and describes it as a commonsense reasoning framework for story understanding, story generation, and script learning.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure Commonsense reasoning, and it is linked to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators. The measurement claims are concentrated on that single construct rather than spread across several: papers say they use XStoryCloze to test commonsense reasoning ability in multilingual con

nodes.name: XSum
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, XSum is most commonly described as an extreme or abstractive news summarization benchmark made up of news articles, often specified as BBC articles, paired with human-written summaries. The prevailing description emphasizes a short, single-sentence summary for each article, sometimes explicitly as one-sentence or single-document summarization, while some definitions describe it more generally as news articles with abstractive summaries. A smaller line also frames it as a non-argumentative summarization task or as an English summarization set used to assess generative coherence and fluency.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link XSum to 5 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The dominant claim is that it measures Text summarization, followed by Abstractive summarization and Text generation, and papers also report two other single-paper behavioral uses. Construct links are limited to two single-paper cases, so the measurement claims cluster around summarization tasks rather than one construct-centered use. One paper additionally says quality on XSum is measured with ROUGE-2.

Space of uses. Most papers position XSum as a headline benchmark for fine-

nodes.name: XWinograd
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed definitions, XWinograd is described consistently as a multilingual or cross-lingual benchmark or task derived from the Winograd Schema Challenge. Papers frame it as testing pronoun resolution, with one definition presenting it as a benchmark for commonsense reasoning and another as a task for coreference and syntactic understanding in diverse languages; one paper also refers specifically to Chinese subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use XWinograd to measure one construct and one behavioral indicator. The linked construct is Commonsense reasoning, including use of Chinese subsets in Chinese evaluation, and the linked behavioral indicator is Coreference resolution, with one paper describing XWinograd as a cross-lingual adaptation of the Winograd Schema Challenge for coreference resolution evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers do not link XWinograd to another measurement instrument. In use, it appears as an evaluation task, including a listing among discriminative tasks and a Chinese evaluation setup alongside XStoryCloze, XNLI, and XCOPA.

nodes.name: YAGS
nodes.definition: An out-of-domain frame identification benchmark annotated with FrameNet 1.5 frames from Yahoo! Answers posts, including unknown and unlinked targets.

nodes.name: Yelp
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is a Yelp review dataset used in classification settings, especially sentiment classification. Definitions variously describe it as derived from Yelp reviews, as user or business reviews from the Yelp platform, and as reviews about restaurants and local services categorized into sentiment classes; some papers instead frame it as casual reviews for short natural language evaluation or as an out-of-distribution set for sentiment analysis.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Yelp to measure two behavioral indicators, Text classification and Sequential recommendation, and no constructs are linked to it. Most descriptions tie it to text classification, especially sentiment classification and a 5-way business-review setup, while a separate paper uses it to measure sequential recommendation.

Space of uses. Papers most often position Yelp as an evaluation dataset, for example to evaluate downstream classifiers, to run out-of-distribution evaluation for sentiment analysis, or to assess the utility of synthetic data in a 5-way classification task; one paper also uses it to source seed samples. It is used alongside other bench

nodes.name: YouCook2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, papers most commonly present YouCook2 as a dense video captioning dataset. Some describe it as an English prior benchmark for video-language evaluation, while others frame it as an instructional video dataset or, more generally, as a video dataset used to evaluate dense video captioning and temporal localization.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link YouCook2 to 2 behavioral indicators, Dense video captioning and Video captioning, and to 1 construct, Video understanding. The prevailing use is captioning evaluation: papers use it to measure Dense video captioning and Video captioning, while one paper also reports it as measuring Video understanding.

Space of uses. In use, papers position YouCook2 as an evaluation dataset within broader benchmark suites, and no measurement instrument is linked to it. One study uses it together with ActivityNet Captions as evaluation datasets, and the same study also reports performance on Charades-STA and QVHighlights; another paper lists it among six benchmarks for video understanding.

Concerns raised. A concern raised in one paper is domain specificity, with the paper stating that datasets like YouC

nodes.name: ZebraLogic
nodes.definition: A comprehensive evaluation framework and dataset of 1,000 logic grid puzzles with controllable and quantifiable complexity, designed to systematically assess the logical reasoning capabilities and scaling limits of LLMs.

nodes.name: ZeroSCROLLS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing description is of a benchmark for LLMs, or a zero-shot benchmark for long text understanding, built around ten diverse natural language tasks that require understanding long input contexts. Definitions commonly mention summarization and question answering, with some also naming sentiment classification or information aggregation, and one paper describes it as related to the Scrolls benchmark. Papers describe its length range differently: one definition gives sequence lengths from 3k to 10k, while another describes Scrolls and ZeroSCROLLS together as QA, classification, and summarization tasks with higher average lengths from 1.7k to 49.3k. A smaller line of work treats it as a leaderboard, using its test set because the organizers had prepared baseline scores.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure two constructs and three behavioral indicators. At the construct level, it is reported as measuring long-context reasoning and long-context understanding; at the task level, papers use it for question answering, text summarization, and information synthesis. The measurement claims therefore span both broad long-cont

nodes.name: ZsRE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a zero-shot relation extraction benchmark or dataset, often reused for knowledge editing evaluation. Definitions also recast it as question answering: short question-answer pairs derived from Wikipedia, sometimes a closed-book or context-free QA task, and some authors specify that each instance contains a factual statement and a paraphrased prompt. A smaller line of work emphasizes reading-comprehension-style relation-slot filling, and some papers describe it as supporting knowledge insertion and modification tasks or relation prediction without task-specific training.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 5 behavioral indicators and 5 constructs, so the reported measurement claims are spread across several targets. The prevailing uses are to measure knowledge editing and question answering, while other papers report it as measuring information extraction and relation extraction, and one paper also uses it to measure hallucination. On the construct side, papers most often use it to measure editing locality and generality, with 3 other constructs also linked, including factual knowledge, knowledge integration effic

nodes.name: 3D object detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this as a task of identifying and localizing objects in 3D space. Success is described in terms of detecting objects and localizing them in 3D, with one definition explicitly requiring bounding boxes, while another narrows the formulation to detection from visual information across multiple images and presents it as a 3D perception task.

Variants. Papers use both the names "3D object detection" and "3D detection". The main variation is in setting: some descriptions are generic, while another focuses on multi-image understanding and says questions should include detailed camera pose information and specify the coordinate system for detected objects; another description places the task in ARKitScenes and treats it as a downstream transfer task.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior in the papers.

nodes.name: 3D question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, it is most commonly described as answering natural language questions about 3D objects or scenes. Definitions agree on the question-answering core, but differ on the scene representation: some specify point clouds or 3D models, while others allow images or other modalities as the basis for the answer. A smaller framing broadens the task to 3D scene VQA, where the work explicitly includes captioning and grounding from multi-view images rather than answer generation alone.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names and settings for the same behavior. Some call it 3D scene VQA and study multi-view image inputs, with captioning and grounding treated as part of the task, while others use 3D visual question answering for questions grounded in a 3D scene represented by point clouds, images, or other modalities. One variant follows the same VQA format but is described as one that "cannot be solved using the given scene alone," marking a hypothetical-reasoning setting within 3D scenes.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 4 measurement instruments: Human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge, SQA, and ScanQA. The linked instruments mix answer sco

nodes.name: Abnormal detail selection
nodes.definition: The task of identifying specific inconsistent or anomalous elements within a piece of synthetic content from a list of choices.

nodes.name: Abstention
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, abstention is most commonly described as withholding a substantive answer when the model is uncertain, lacks the needed knowledge, or does not have enough supporting information. Most papers operationalize this as refusing, saying variants of "I don't know", or returning no answer, though some broaden it to asking an information-seeking question instead of a final answer, and one thresholded formulation returns an answer only when confidence exceeds a preset level. A smaller line of work uses the same observable pattern for cases framed as task avoidance or rejection, and one paper distinguishes consistent refusal from cases that only "partly abstained" across multiple sampled answers.

Variants. Most variants remain in QA-style settings, where abstention can be expressed as refusal-like text, reserved outputs such as "[IDK]" or "NO-RESPONSE", or asking for more information. Other papers study it in multimodal questioning when the image lacks needed evidence, with a required keyword such as "doesnotapply", and in tool or reasoning settings under names like selective answering, task skipping, and ill-defined problem rejection when a task is not a

nodes.name: Abstract concept attribution
nodes.definition: Assigning an abstract concept label to an image based on the situation, ideas, emotions, or feelings it conveys.

nodes.name: Abstractive summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is a generation task: producing a concise summary of a source document that captures its main or salient ideas, often through paraphrase or other novel phrasing rather than extracting exact spans. Many definitions add coherence, fluency, or informativeness, and some, including Filipino-focused work, also require faithfulness and avoiding hallucination. A smaller line of work describes the setting as models responding to queries given context, while another contrasts it with extractive summarization by describing an abstractive revision as more concise and natural-sounding.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings, including news summarization, dialogue summarization, multilingual summarization, Filipino summarization, long-document summarization, and user-generated posts paired with concise summaries. One paper describes a news variant that requires single-sentence summaries from BBC articles, and another treats document-based question-answering, meeting summarization, and clinical report generation as abstractive summarization tasks. Another paper positions it alongside extractive summarization, where an ex

nodes.name: Academic question answering
nodes.definition: Answering questions or selecting answers on tasks spanning academic subjects.

nodes.name: Action execution
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. One paper treats action execution as the agent's observable performance of a specific action from its available action space within an environment. The same paper describes an interaction module that executes actions in the environment according to the task and records the process, so the behavior is framed as observable, task-conditioned action taking.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link action execution to 1 measurement instrument, T-Eval, which is the only linked instrument. One paper places T-Eval under the Action Execution category of agentic tasks, so the linked measurement usage centers on that single instrument.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers relate action execution to 2 constructs, Planning and Reasoning. These links are stated as related rather than causal, correlational, or measurement claims, so the construct-level framing shown here is connection to those two constructs rather than a direct claim that action execution measures one agreed construct.

nodes.name: Action generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is the stepwise production of a concrete next action for an environment or agent. Most papers describe it as generating a structured command such as click, type text, scroll, or input, often with parameters like position or value, from the current task, goal, page, location, or interaction history; one paper even illustrates an output as {"Action": "type text", "position": "", "value": "iPhone power adapter"}. A smaller line of work broadens this to route-following control actions like "ascend" or "turn right", or to sequences of low-level robotic actions and discrete action tokens, while another variant defines success more narrowly as producing actions that are valid and executable in the environment.

Variants. Most papers study GUI and computer-control settings, where the model produces a single next operation from the current GUI state, task instruction, and sometimes prior actions. Other variants ask for the next navigation control action from the current location given a goal or route, or for autoregressive sequences of low-level robotic actions alongside future observations. A smaller line of work names executable ac

nodes.name: Action grounding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats action grounding as instruction-conditioned localization in a GUI: a model maps a textual or natural language instruction to the UI element or screen location needed to execute the action, typically by returning a click position, coordinates, or a bounding box. Most definitions emphasize accurately locating the target element, while a smaller line of work states the task more broadly as transforming instructions into executable actions and associated parameters within a GUI or operating system. Papers largely agree on identifying the intended executable element, but differ on whether success is framed narrowly as finding the click target or more broadly as producing action parameters for execution.

Variants. The most common variants are clicking and dragging. Clicking is described as localizing the target element and outputting a bounding box or click position, while dragging requires both the initial and end coordinates for a drag-and-drop operation. Papers study this behavior on webpages, narrated screenshots, mobile screens, and broader GUI or operating-system screens, and use names such as action grounding, UI gr

nodes.name: Action localization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat this as a temporal video task where a given action must be located by identifying when it occurs, usually through start and end times. The prevailing usage describes detecting and localizing temporal segments that contain the specified action, including formulations such as finding all segments with that action in a long video or marking the part of a video where an action like "flying" occurs. A smaller variant applies the same start and end timestamp criterion to a traffic accident event, emphasizing precise accident duration within a clip.

Variants. Papers use several closely related names, most commonly "temporal action localization," alongside "action localization" and the more domain-specific "accident temporal localization." The settings vary across animal-centric videos, longer or untrimmed videos, and traffic accident clips. Examples in the papers include locating animal actions, finding all "golf swing" segments in a long video, and identifying the precise accident interval.

Space of elicitation and scores. One measurement instrument is linked to this behavior: MVBench, which one paper lists under "AL Action Localization" with the

nodes.name: Action prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is predicting the next appropriate action in a sequence, most often by identifying a target element and the operation to perform, such as click, type, or select, to accomplish a larger goal on a webpage or UI. A smaller line of work frames it as next-user-action prediction from a screen plus previous action history, or as outputting the optimal action for a current state from contextual transitions or offline RL trajectories. Success is usually described as matching the ground-truth next action, though some papers require the full predicted action sequence to align with human trajectories, and one paper treats the behavior as choosing a legal chess move, including a checkmating move.

Variants. Papers use several names for closely related variants, with Action prediction and Next-action prediction the most common labels. The dominant settings are web and UI interaction, where the model predicts interactions like clicking, typing, selecting, or dragging from the current screen or webpage and prior actions. Other variants include Action sequence prediction, where the whole sequence must align with a human trajectory,

nodes.name: Action recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats action recognition as identifying or classifying the action in video clips, often as predicting an action label. Some papers broaden the target to activities or events, including real-world videos with human actions and interactions, and a smaller formulation tests whether models can distinguish activities by phrases that differ only in action verbs. Most formulations count success as naming the correct action or activity, though some use open-ended activity questions and one paper reformulates the task as multiple-choice generation at test time.

Variants. Variants span video clips, single images, video frames, and sequences or sets of images. Papers also use nearby names such as activity recognition, step recognition, fine-grained keystep recognition, sport or sports recognition, and activity classification. Procedural versions focus on identifying individual steps within instructional or egocentric videos, while sports-focused versions ask which sport is shown.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only a single paper explicitly links this behavior to measurement instruments, and it is measured by 3 instrume

nodes.name: Action repetition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats action repetition as a failure mode where an agent repeats the same action, command, interaction, or subtask without making progress. Most definitions emphasize repetition despite prior outcomes or inappropriateness, ranging from re-issuing completed commands and re-attempting subtasks to perpetually generating the same action for multiple turns. A smaller difference is in what counts as a repeated-action episode: some papers require lack of progress, while another operationalization marks it when the same action appears three times consecutively in a trajectory.

Variants. Papers study the behavior under several names, including redundant looping, repetitive actions, and stuck-in-loop behavior. The settings vary across penetration testing, virtual escape rooms, games, and software engineering agents. Some formulations focus on specific action subsets, for example object interaction and answer submission actions in escape-room trajectories, while another illustrates the behavior as repeatedly holding a fire button in a game where that repetition is inappropriate.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measure

nodes.name: Action selection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is a stepwise choice among available actions, usually conditioned on the current state, context, goal, or interaction history. Most descriptions emphasize selecting the optimal, appropriate, or most plausible next action from candidates, sometimes with look-ahead simulation or another evaluation mechanism guiding the choice, while a smaller line of work broadens it to decision-making that selects and executes actions under induced rules, state constraints, or uncertainty. Success is variously framed as maximizing cumulative reward, choosing a valid or highest-scoring action, or picking the action that best fulfills intrinsic desires.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several domain-specific forms: driving decision making selects high-level driving actions from scene descriptions and prior experience, high-level action selection in robot settings chooses discrete acts such as navigation, pickup, or placement, and bandit versions require exactly one arm or action at each time step. Other formulations include activity selection based on intrinsic motivations and game-based target or secret action selection, where choices

nodes.name: Action sequence generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating an ordered sequence of actions that an agent can execute to accomplish a task. Most definitions emphasize structured, discrete outputs, such as environment moves, API calls, or website actions, and frame success as reaching an objective or successfully completing the requested task from the current state or user request. A smaller variant uses the name multi-step action generation and describes the same observable behavior as producing discrete actions to complete a task; in the API-based framing, one paper also states that each next action depends on the history actions.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings rather than a single task format. The main variants are traversing 2D game maps by producing moves such as move_up or move_left, fulfilling user queries through ordered API calls, completing website tasks through executable web actions, and web navigation settings described as requiring multi-step actions. The naming is mostly action sequence generation, with a smaller use of multi-step action generation.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrume

nodes.name: Activation outliers
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers here, activation outliers are treated as unusually large values in a model's activations, with closely aligned descriptions across sources. One formulation defines them in layer outputs as entries whose absolute value exceeds a threshold based on the mean activation and says they appear in "specific sequence and feature dimensions" (Systematic Outliers in Large Language Models), while a related formulation describes "outlier activations in hidden states" as values in specific feature channels that are "orders of magnitude larger than other values" and present across sequence or token positions.

Variants. Papers use closely related names, including "activation outliers" and "outlier activations in hidden states." The phenomenon is studied in layer outputs and down-projection inputs, and also in hidden states after the residual connection, with recurring attention to specific feature channels and to whether the large values recur across sequence position or across all token positions.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the operational descriptions that are given, papers identify it by checking for a

nodes.name: Adversarial attacks
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats adversarial attacks as generating modified or perturbed inputs that make a target model fail: papers describe models asked to "output adversarial examples that attack the defense," including image perturbations under a perturbation bound and text changes that are either lexically similar but semantically different, or semantically similar to the original, while causing incorrect predictions or misclassification. A smaller line of work uses the same label for responses to jailbreak or adversarial probes that induce forgotten knowledge, for hidden trigger generation that can activate a backdoor in an evaluator, and for malicious SQL payload injection that manipulates queries or extracts database data. Success is therefore framed differently across papers, including fooling a model, eliciting forgotten knowledge, activating a backdoor, or achieving outcomes such as successful login or database dumping.

Variants. Variants span image, text, model-evaluation, and web-application settings. The most common named variant is adversarial example generation, covering bounded image attacks, NLI sentence-pair modificati

nodes.name: Adversarial suffix generation
nodes.definition: The process by which an LLM generates a text suffix that, when appended to a harmful query, causes a victim model to produce a non-refused response to that query.

nodes.name: Affordance segmentation
nodes.definition: Predicting a binary mask that marks the functional regions of an object relevant to a query.

nodes.name: Agent intention prediction
nodes.definition: The task of forecasting the future actions or movements of a dynamic agent, such as a vehicle or pedestrian, based on an image.

nodes.name: Aggregative question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. A common framing treats it as producing an aggregate answer, often a count or sum over entities or attributes that satisfy a condition, or a frequency over a given time period. Other papers use the same label for synthesized answers over thousands of conversations, such as trends, demographic concerns, or sentiment shifts, and one formulation casts the task as grouping database rows by a semantically derived attribute before aggregating within each group.

Variants. Papers study several settings under closely related names: aggregation question answering, counting question answering, and abstraction and aggregation. The variants range from criteria-based counts or sums over entities and attributes, to temporal frequency questions about events, to queries over thousands of user-chatbot interactions about trending topics or changes in sentiment, and to unstructured-database grouping by abstract semantic attributes before aggregation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 2 measurement instruments, ComplexTempQA and WildChat-AQA. ComplexTempQA operationalizes it through counting-type questions about events, entities, or time periods, while WildChat-

nodes.name: AI-generated text detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a binary authorship decision over text: deciding whether a candidate text is human-written or machine-generated, often stated more specifically as human versus LLM-generated. Definitions repeatedly frame success as distinguishing between these two sources from the observed text, sometimes for a generic text and sometimes for a given piece such as a paper submission, review, or evidence item. A smaller line of work extends the behavior from whole-text labeling to identifying which segments or sentences in a mixed-origin article were generated by an LLM.

Variants. Most work treats the task at whole-text or document level, and one paper notes that mainstream methods primarily target document-level long texts. Smaller variants study sentence-level detection for human-AI hybrid content and segment-level identification in partially written text, where the aim is to determine which segments were LLM-written. Papers use several near-synonymous names for the behavior, including AI-generated text detection, LLM-generated text detection, machine-generated text detection, machine text detection, and AI-text detection, and one paper

nodes.name: Algebraic rule induction
nodes.definition: Generating the next token in a sequence by inferring an abstract identity rule (e.g., ABA or ABB) from in-context examples using arbitrary tokens.

nodes.name: Algorithm execution
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing treats this behavior as carrying out a sequence of steps or operations to solve a problem. Definitions converge on observable execution itself, with one line describing a sequence of computational steps defined by an algorithm and another using the broader formulation of multi-step execution; one paper further associates it with "enumeration, precise computation, and algorithm execution through tool interaction" (START: Self-taught Reasoner with Tools).

Variants. Papers use both the names algorithm execution and multi-step execution. A narrower variant places it in tool-based settings, often via a code interpreter and tool interaction, while a broader variant studies it within advanced reasoning tasks; KOR-Bench: Benchmarking Language Models on Knowledge-Orthogonal Reasoning Tasks also notes that, in Cipher reasoning, errors are frequent in multi-step execution alongside position mapping, transpose writing, mathematical calculation, and split connection.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it.

nodes.name: Algorithmic problem solving
nodes.definition: The observable task of solving well-defined computational problems, such as sorting lists, finding elements (e.g., two sum, find max), or solving combinatorial problems like the travelling salesman problem, based on a textual description.

nodes.name: Ambiguous EDU identification
nodes.definition: Detecting discourse units within a sentence that are unclear or uninterpretable without additional context, typically subordinate units in discourse relations.

nodes.name: Ambiguous question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available definition treats it as generating one or more valid answers to a query that is inherently ambiguous and allows multiple interpretations. In the same usage, the task is framed as tackling ambiguity, and a conditional form is described as doing so by incorporating explicit conditions.

Variants. The named variant in the papers is Conditional Ambiguous Question-Answering (CondAmbigQA), presented as a framework that incorporates explicit conditions. Alongside that label, the broader task is also referred to as ambiguous QA.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to one measurement instrument, ASQA. One paper describes ASQA as an ambiguous QA dataset, so the operationalization shown here is dataset-based.

nodes.name: Anomaly detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, anomaly detection is treated as deciding whether something is abnormal or out of place, but the task formulation varies rather than converging on one standard. One line of work defines it as predicting whether a sequence of log events indicates abnormal system behavior, another as identifying the out-of-place event after one event type in a series is replaced, and another as judging whether an industrial image contains a defect. Success is correspondingly described as predicting abnormal behavior, finding the incorrect event, or answering whether there is any defect in the object.

Variants. The variants studied span different domains and modalities. Papers describe log-based anomaly detection as a time-series prediction task, study sequence anomaly detection where one event type is randomly replaced and the model must identify the altered element, and use an industrial image setting framed as anomaly discrimination or detection by asking whether a sample has defects.

Space of elicitation and scores. Anomaly detection is measured by one linked instrument, Human evaluation, which is a human-judgment measure. In the linked paper, human evaluation

nodes.name: Answer generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats answer generation as producing a final answer to a query or question, usually from provided context, retrieved documents, or other gathered evidence, and often as the last stage of a larger reasoning or retrieval pipeline. Most papers keep the success criterion broad, namely producing the answer itself, though some narrow it to summarized responses from oracle-judged passages, direct final answers after reasoning or function calls, or strict outputs such as a number or multiple-choice option. A smaller line of work adds extra output requirements, including citations, separate "##Reason" and "##Answer" sections, or agreement with human expert answers.

Variants. Papers study several named variants, especially "free-form answer generation" and "final answer generation." Free-form variants ask for natural-language sequence-to-sequence answers from a question and context, with one paper describing autoregressive generation until the end token, while final-answer variants focus on the conclusive response after intermediate reasoning traces or after a sequence of function calls. Other recurring settings are multi

nodes.name: Antibody region annotation
nodes.definition: Assigning a categorical label to each nucleotide in an antibody-encoding mRNA sequence to identify its functional region (e.g., signal peptide, V, DJ, constant).

nodes.name: Antisemitism detection
nodes.definition: Classifying social media posts as antisemitic or not based on the IHRA definition, producing a label (Yes/No) and supporting rationale.

nodes.name: Argument classification
nodes.definition: Assigning a semantic role to each identified argument span within a scientific event.

nodes.name: Argument generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing use describes generating a structured, stance-conditioned argument from retrieved evidence: models use retrieved documents to construct coherent and persuasive arguments, often as a set of conclusions followed by premises that justify each conclusion. A related framing asks for a persuasive or explanatory text from a given topic and stance, still structured as a coherent argument. A smaller usage applies the same name to table reasoning, where generating arguments means producing the parameters required for an operation, such as column headers or row indices.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several task settings. One treats it as the second subtask in retrieval-augmented computational argumentation, where retrieved documents are turned into structured conclusions and supporting premises; another elicits it with a topic-and-stance prompt for persuasive or explanatory argument writing; and a separate line uses the label "GenerateArgs" for producing operation arguments in table understanding.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, the available descriptions operationalize it

nodes.name: Argument identification
nodes.definition: Finding the text spans in an event that correspond to participating arguments.

nodes.name: Argument summarization
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of generating a concise summary that captures the key points and claims from a given argumentative text.

nodes.name: Argumentative relation identification
nodes.definition: The observable task of identifying directed, typed relations (e.g., 'Support', 'Attack') between pairs of argument components within a text.

nodes.name: Arithmetic computation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is direct calculation: producing the correct result for a numerical expression or other quantitative input. Most definitions describe arithmetic expressions with numbers and operators, sometimes with brackets or multi-step operator sequences, and one study says the goal is to calculate the input arithmetic expression and generate the correct result (Seq-VCR: Preventing  Collapse in Intermediate Transformer Representations for Enhanced Reasoning). Final-answer correctness is the usual success criterion, though some papers tighten this to valid step-by-step arithmetic with correct order of operations and numerical precision, or to arithmetic carried out correctly within a larger reasoning chain.

Variants. Papers study this behavior under several names, most commonly arithmetic expression evaluation, arithmetic calculation, and numerical calculation, while varying both input structure and domain. Recurring variants include three-operand problems, basic addition and multiplication, structured expressions over binary inputs, modular arithmetic, expected value calculations, median finding, and linear function evaluatio

nodes.name: Aromatic ring identification
nodes.definition: The specific, observable task of identifying the presence of aromatic rings within a molecule based on its chemical formula.

nodes.name: Aspect-based sentiment analysis
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Definitions largely treat this behavior as fine-grained sentiment analysis at the aspect level: extracting opinion targets or aspects and their sentiment polarities from text, or identifying the sentiment expressed toward a specific aspect or feature of an entity. Some authors require structured outputs rather than only aspect-polarity pairs, asking for triplets such as (aspect term, aspect category, sentiment polarity) or target-aspect-opinion triplets, and others extend this to tuples that also include targets, opinions, categories, or polarity. A smaller formulation emphasizes the span extraction side of the task, describing it as extracting sentiments together with their corresponding aspects and opinion terms, including cases where surface forms vary.

Variants. Variants differ mainly by output structure and setting. Papers study triplet extraction, pair extraction, quadruple extraction, and single-element extraction, while other papers use names such as structured opinion extraction, feature-centric opinion extraction, aspect-based sentiment classification, and aspect sentiment quad prediction. The settings mentioned include given sentences, conversation

nodes.name: Attribute generation
nodes.definition: The task of using a large language model to produce a list of descriptive properties for a given object, specifically its geometric parts and functional affordances.

nodes.name: Attribute prediction
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a specific attribute value for a given entity in response to a query prompt.

nodes.name: Attribute recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat it as identifying visual properties of objects in an image, most often color and other descriptive features. Several definitions extend the scope to material, texture, shape, state, length, or position, and one formulation emphasizes fine-grained discernment of subtle properties described in a caption. Some papers operationalize it through generated natural language responses or detailed feature descriptions.

Variants. Papers use nearby names such as attribute identification, attribute classification, object attribute detection, and fine-grained object property discernment. The variants span a TDIUC question category, open-ended classification over common adjective concepts like color, material, and length, fine-grained property discernment for open-vocabulary detection, and detailed feature description of animals to support recognition. Color is the most recurrent attribute, with some work isolating an attribute-level color subset, while another line includes position alongside color.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to one measurement instrument, MMHal-Bench. It is described as a benchmark for evaluating LVL

nodes.name: Audio captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is generating a natural-language or textual caption for an audio clip. Most definitions describe non-speech audio, especially environmental sounds or events, and some extend the scope to music or scene-based sounds. A few formulations make the output requirement more specific as a sentence or description of the sounds present in an audio clip, and one paper elicits it with the prompt 'write an audio caption describing the sound' and uses the model output as the prediction.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this task, most commonly audio captioning, and sometimes automatic audio captioning or AAC. The studied content is usually general non-speech audio, though papers explicitly mention environmental sounds, events, scene-based sounds, and music, including an example caption for a classical piece played at a slow tempo.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link audio captioning to three measurement instruments. The most frequent are AudioCaps and Clotho, with MusicCaps appearing less often; these are described as audio captioning benchmarks or datasets, and some papers describe AudioCaps and Clotho

nodes.name: Audio classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers describe this behavior as assigning an audio clip to a sound category or label, often as one of the standard audio tasks discussed alongside captioning. The prevailing formulation uses predefined class labels, with one definition allowing one or more labels per clip; one paper also notes that the model may output label names or descriptions in text form rather than a label index. A smaller line of work uses the name sound classification and frames it as assigning sound clips to semantic categories using tokenizer-derived representations.

Variants. Papers mostly use the name audio classification, though some use sound classification for a closely matched task. The categories studied are not uniform: one definition gives examples such as sound event, genre, and speaker-related classes, while another refers more generally to semantic categories for sound clips.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers operationalize this behavior with four measurement instruments, used as audio classification benchmarks. FSD50K is the most frequently linked instrument, and papers also measure it with ESC-50, GTZAN, and US8K; one result table labels FSD50K as 'FSD50k

nodes.name: Audio question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Definitions consistently describe it as answering natural-language questions about audio content from an audio input plus a text question or accompanying text. The prevailing framing is straightforward answer generation, though some authors extend it to open-ended, free-form responses and reasoning-based queries, and one benchmark frames the task around understanding environmental contexts and following instructions in those scenarios; one reported evaluation scores the task with accuracy.

Variants. Papers usually refer to it as AQA. The variants studied span general audio question answering, non-speech and environmental audio, and settings that ask factual as well as reasoning-based questions, with some work emphasizing context and events from soundscapes and others using open-ended response generation.

Space of elicitation and scores. It is measured by one instrument, ClothoAQA, the only linked instrument in the papers. ClothoAQA is described as a dataset of audio samples paired with crowdsourced questions and answers, and linked evaluations use it for audio question answering, with one table reporting ACC.

What it is taken as evidence of. The papers do n

nodes.name: Audio-to-text generation
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a relevant and coherent textual response based on a given audio clip and an optional text prompt.

nodes.name: Audio-visual question answering
nodes.definition: Answering questions about combined audio and video content using both modalities.

nodes.name: Authorship attribution
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the concept is used for several closely related authorship tasks rather than a single fixed formulation. A prevalent framing is a pairwise judgment over two texts, documents, or text collections, asking whether they were written by the same author and returning either a likelihood score or a binary same/different decision. Other papers formulate it as determining whether a text was written by a particular known author from linguistic cues or stylistic fingerprints, or as identifying which human or machine generator produced a text.

Variants. Papers use several names for neighboring variants, including authorship attribution, authorship verification, and text origin detection. The settings range from recognizing whether two input documents have the same author, to multi-class classification where humans and LLMs are the labels, to identifying the specific LLM that generated an AI-generated text from its statistical or representational patterns. A related paper also places it alongside AI-generated text detection, describing that area as including neural authorship attribution and multi-author classification.

Space of elicitation and scores. No

nodes.name: Autoformalization
names: Natural language to formal language translation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats autoformalization as translating informal mathematical content into a formal, machine-verifiable language. Most definitions focus on mathematical statements given in natural language, sometimes alongside LaTeX, and ask for a formal statement or symbolic representation. A smaller line of work extends the task to whole problems, solutions, premises, or proofs, including outputs in Lean or Lean4, Isabelle/HOL, SMT-LIB, or first-order logic. Papers differ on success criteria: some require syntactically correct formal output, while others emphasize preserving semantic meaning and mathematical constraints.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous labels, most often statement formalization or formalization, and also formal problem modeling, natural language to formal language translation, and auto-formalization or autoformalisation. The dominant setting remains mathematical statements, including unconstrained natural language statements, but some work instead studies high-school contest-level math problems, question-answering problems and their solutions, written proofs, or generic natural language sentences and premise

nodes.name: Autoformalization alignment detection
nodes.definition: The task of classifying a given pair of informal and formal statements as either semantically aligned or misaligned based on a predefined threshold.

nodes.name: Automated AI development
nodes.definition: The end-to-end process of creating a complete AI system based on a user query, including data processing, modeling, and reporting.

nodes.name: Autonomous task solving
nodes.definition: Completing downstream tasks through coordinated agent interaction rather than a single isolated response.

nodes.name: Backdoor-triggered misclassification
nodes.definition: The observable behavior in which a model incorrectly classifies inputs that contain a backdoor trigger, producing a targeted adversarial output.

nodes.name: Backstory generation
nodes.definition: Transforming structured personal profile data into a coherent narrative that reflects an individual's life experiences, demographic attributes, and value-related responses.

nodes.name: Backtracking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats backtracking as returning to an earlier state, step, or page after recognizing that the current response, action trajectory, or solution path is flawed, then revising from that earlier point. A more specific formulation narrows this to safety recovery: the model produces a partial unsafe response, emits a special [RESET] token, and then re-generates a safe response from scratch. Papers differ mainly in what triggers the return, such as an error page, a verifier-detected issue, or the model's own identification of a mistaken reasoning step.

Variants. Papers use several names for closely related patterns, including Backtracking, Branching and backtracking, State traceback, and Backtracking search. The settings span unsafe generation, reasoning that explores multiple paths and reverts when one proves wrong, finite-state multi-agent systems that move back to earlier states, GUI interaction that returns to a previous page to regenerate an action, and math problem solving that backtracks to earlier numbered steps. A broader assistant-oriented usage also describes revisiting previous steps or re-evaluating an app

nodes.name: Backward reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat backward reasoning as working from a provided answer or solution to recover a concealed input. A recurring formulation conceals one of the inputs or masks a numerical value from the original problem and asks the model to infer the missing value from the original answer or solution, described as reasoning backwards to check consistency in the solution process. A smaller line of work frames it as solving a reversed question and generating step-by-step justification back toward the original problem context, so success is described either as computing the missing input or as producing the backward reasoning for the reversed question.

Variants. Papers use nearby names such as reversed reasoning and backward question. The main variants differ in what is hidden, an input generally or a numerical value specifically, and in whether the task asks for the recovered value or for a full step-by-step justification while solving the reversed question. Some work studies it alongside intermediate-step questions as part of testing whether a model can trace back through its reasoning pathway.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrumen

nodes.name: Banner ad generation
nodes.definition: The end-to-end process of creating a complete advertising banner from a multimodal request that includes a brand logo and textual requirements.

nodes.name: Benign question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available definition, papers treat this behavior as responding helpfully and accurately to standard, non-adversarial user questions. The accompanying usage frames it as answering benign prompts rather than refusing them, describing evaluation in terms of whether defense methods "refuse to answer benign prompts or not."

Variants. The only setting described is normal question answering for reading comprehension. Papers refer to standard, non-adversarial user questions and benign prompts, and place the behavior in normal question-answering tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to one measurement instrument, TriviaQA, described as a normal question-answering dataset for reading comprehension and used for benign answer evaluation. The same paper also says it employs Benign Answering Rate (BAR) to examine whether models refuse benign prompts.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior.

nodes.name: Bias amplification
nodes.definition: The phenomenon where a model reinforces or strengthens existing biases present in its training data or conversational context.

nodes.name: Bias detection
nodes.definition: The task of identifying social biases against protected categories within a given text, often presented as a multiple-choice question.

nodes.name: Bias mitigation
nodes.definition: The observable reduction in performance variation when input formatting is altered, such as changes in passage order or identifier labels, indicating resistance to spurious cues.

nodes.name: Biased content generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats this behavior as observable text or response generation that reflects unfair or systematic prejudice. Most definitions describe outputs with stereotypes, toxicity, discrimination, or other derogatory associations toward groups or ideas, and one paper operationalizes it through an increase in biased words. Some authors state it broadly as biased or unfair output generation, while others narrow it to responses that reinforce gender bias or target a protected group.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous names, including biased generation, biased output generation, and biased response generation. The behavior is studied in general text generation and prompt response settings, and smaller strands place it in role-playing scenarios or triggered generation tasks where certain identity-related queries are more likely to yield biased content.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 1 measurement instrument, BOLD, used as a text generation dataset. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers link this behavior to 1 construct, Trustworthiness

nodes.name: Biggest chordless cycle identification
nodes.definition: Identifying the size of the largest cycle in a graph where no two non-consecutive nodes are connected by an edge not in the cycle.

nodes.name: Binary addition
nodes.definition: Computing the sum of binary numbers.

nodes.name: Binary classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a task where a model must assign one of exactly two labels to an input. Definitions most often describe either a categorical decision over text or a constrained output space with only two allowed outputs, for example "True" and "False"; other papers give domain-specific pairs such as real or fake, offensive or non-offensive, entailment or non-entailment, and positive or negative. Some descriptions place the same pattern in tabular prediction or image forgery detection, but the common criterion remains choosing one of two predefined classes.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings and use nearby names such as "BC" and "binary task." The reported variants include instruction-identified binary classification, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, paraphrase detection, positive versus negative review tasks, tabular prediction, face forgery detection, and offensive language detection. One paper also discusses an in-context binary classification setting and describes it as a special case of general multi-class classification.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link binary classification to

nodes.name: Binary decision making
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is a model producing an explicit "yes" or "no" decision. Most commonly, papers frame this as deciding whether a person with specified demographic attributes should receive a beneficial outcome in a hypothetical scenario; as one study puts it, the model is prompted to make "a binary yes/no decision about a person described in terms of age, gender and race" (The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs). A smaller line of work broadens the behavior to automated decision making, defined as making or providing eligibility or other consequential decisions from user-provided profiles or records.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several related forms. Some place it in yes-no questions, answer verification, and other binary decision tasks requiring complex reasoning, including rewriting general QA reasoning items into positive or negative samples whose answer is "Yes" or "No" (Correcting Negative Bias in Large Language Models through Negative Attention Score Alignment). Others study person-profile and eligibility settings, such as financial or loan eligibility from user profiles, dummy resumes, or demographi

nodes.name: Binary multiplication
nodes.definition: The task of performing arithmetic multiplication on two binary numbers.

nodes.name: Binary summation
nodes.definition: The observable task of calculating the sum of a binary string in binary form.

nodes.name: Biography generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats biography generation as producing a biographical passage, text, description, or summary about a named person from a prompt such as "Tell me a bio of <entity>." Most formulations are open-ended and focus on writing about a specific individual, sometimes described as relying on general world knowledge. A smaller line of work narrows the task to factual biography generation, defined as producing a written account of a person's life that adheres to known facts.

Variants. Papers study several variants and settings: long-form biography generation, paragraph-level generations, and a structured version that requires bullet point biographies. The named targets vary from a given entity or named individual to popular figures, celebrities, scientists, and famous computer scientists, and one paper describes using entities from the FactScore dataset. The main alternate label is factual biography generation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to two measurement instruments, most often Biography and then FActScore. Biography is used in fact verification and as a test set for biography generation,

nodes.name: Biology question answering
nodes.definition: The observable task of answering questions related to the field of biology.

nodes.name: Bitwise arithmetic
nodes.definition: Performing a specified bitwise operation (e.g., AND, OR, XOR) on a pair of binary numbers and outputting the resulting binary number.

nodes.name: Black-box sequence optimization
nodes.definition: The observable process of engaging in a multi-step loop of proposing a sequence, receiving a measurement of its quality, and using that feedback to inform the next proposal.

nodes.name: Board state prediction
nodes.definition: The model reconstructs the full board configuration in Othello from a sequence of moves, going beyond next-token prediction to infer latent state.

nodes.name: Boolean question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is a question-answering behavior with a forced binary outcome: models return "yes" or "no", and in some papers the equivalent "true" or "false", based on provided context, a text passage, or whether a statement is correct. Most formulations describe the target output as the correct binary judgment for a question or declarative statement, while a smaller line of work uses equivalent binary alternatives such as "A" or "B" for sentence-meaning comprehension.

Variants. Variants span reading-comprehension and passage-based settings, factual-reasoning framings, professional qualification exam true/false items, sentence-meaning questions after garden-path disambiguation, and several vision-language uses such as map queries and counter-commonsense multimodal scenarios. Papers use several near-synonymous labels, especially binary, Boolean, true/false, yes/no, and polar question answering; one profiling setup uses polar questions about whether the model would say a profiling statement, and one paper reports the format is related to cross-modal retrieval by generating yes/no questions to assess visual-textual alignment.

Space of elic

nodes.name: Bounding box prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is producing rectangular coordinates that localize a target region. Most definitions describe the required output as a bounding box that spatially corresponds to the sought element, either an edit location in a document or object or evidence in an image; another definition also specifies boxes that correspond to answer tokens.

Variants. The papers study this behavior in document and PDF localization and in image grounding. They use the names bounding box prediction and bounding box generation, and vary the target across edit elements, objects, evidence tied to a textual concept, and answer tokens; one approach is described as directly identifying boxes instead of thresholding each patch.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, elicitation is described through the task output itself, a predicted box for an edit element or directly identified boxes for answer tokens, and the snippets discuss bounding box precision, including reports that existing systems struggle with it and claims of highly precise boxes.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it.

nodes.name: Building code compliance checking
nodes.definition: Evaluating whether a generated floor plan adheres to building codes and safety regulations using retrieved standards.

nodes.name: CAD editing
nodes.definition: Identifying regions in a CAD sequence that require modification by replacing them with <mask> tokens while preserving unmodified parts.

nodes.name: Calculation error
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available definition treats calculation error as an observable error in which a model gives an incorrect result because of mistakes in numerical or symbolic computation, even when the reasoning process may otherwise be correct. In UGMathBench: A Diverse and Dynamic Benchmark for Undergraduate-Level Mathematical Reasoning with Large Language Models, the accompanying error analysis describes calculation errors as "a major concern" and says they are the "largest category," specifically "including both numerical and expression errors."

Variants. Papers describe this behavior in a small set of closely related forms. The named variants are numeric calculation error and expression calculation error, and the broader wording also refers to mistakes in numerical or symbolic computation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link calculation error to one measurement instrument, Expert evaluation. In Are Multimodal LLMs Robust Against Adversarial Perturbations? RoMMath: A Systematic Evaluation on Multimodal Math Reasoning, it is measured by expert evaluation through "in-depth human analysis" of error cases, where Calculation Error is identified as one of the commo

nodes.name: Calendar scheduling
nodes.definition: Finding a valid meeting time slot that satisfies participants' availability constraints.

nodes.name: Candidate generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, candidate generation is treated as producing a set of alternatives for a given input, though papers differ on what those alternatives are. One line of work defines it as generating potential target attributes for each source attribute in schema matching, described as generating "a set of potential matches" or a subset of candidate attributes that are "likely matches." Another defines it as generating multiple alternative reasoning steps or solution paths, including "multiple potential continuations for each active hypothesis."

Variants. The clearest variants appear in the schema-matching formulation, which separates semantic retrieval candidates from reasoning-based candidates. A different setting studies candidate steps sourced from multiple LLMs, with the generated objects described as candidate steps or continuations. One paper also relates candidate generation to schema matching, describing a schema matching program as being comprised of candidate generation, refinement and confidence scoring.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to candidate generation in these papers.

What it is taken as eviden

nodes.name: Caption alignment
nodes.definition: The task of synchronizing text captions with the corresponding segments of a sign language video.

nodes.name: Carry propagation
nodes.definition: The sub-task within a larger addition problem of carrying over a value from one columnar position to the next.

nodes.name: Catastrophic forgetting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats catastrophic forgetting as a post-update drop on previously learned tasks, knowledge, or capabilities. Most definitions focus on sequential learning or fine-tuning, where performance on earlier tasks deteriorates after new data is introduced; adjacent work uses the same pattern for sequential editing, judging forgetting by weaker retention of prior edits or old knowledge after many later updates. Smaller lines of work extend the label to unlearning, multimodal expansion, or continued pretraining, where the observable sign is again degradation on retained, text-only, or broadly learned behavior.

Variants. Variants are mostly defined by setting. Papers name knowledge forgetting in collaborative or lifelong editing, where older edited facts and previously edited examples become less accurately retained after later editing rounds, and text-only forgetting in multimodal models, where text-only tasks or instructions fall after multimodal instruction tuning or visual modality expansion. Other papers discuss forgetting on generic web or domain data during continual pretraining, during specialization to new tasks, and one pap

nodes.name: Category induction
nodes.definition: The process of grouping entities into meaningful sets based on shared properties or clustered embeddings, allowing for overlapping and incomplete categorization.

nodes.name: Causal discovery
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats causal discovery as recovering or inferring causal structure from data, and sometimes from text. Definitions agree that the target is a causal structure or set of causal relations, but differ in how explicit the output must be: some describe recovering a latent structure or refining assumptions through targeted interventions into a causal subgraph, while another formulation requires, for every variable pair, choosing A causes B, B causes A, or no relation.

Variants. Papers study several named variants. Alongside the general task, they describe causal graph discovery as inferring a temporal directed graph over stocks with lagged causal links, causal graph construction as building item-action dependency structures from interaction records and interventions, and full causal discovery as pairwise direction judgments over a given variable set.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to one measurement instrument, COPA, through a measured_by relation. The recorded operationalization is narrow: one paper states that it uses COPA "for causal discovery," and no other linked instrument is named.

W

nodes.name: Causal inference
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers use this label for several tasks centered on inferring causes or effects from observations, premises, or interventions. A prevalent formulation is selecting the most plausible cause or effect for a given premise from a set of alternatives. Other papers describe uncovering potential causes behind a process or observed outcome, investigating or quantifying the effect of cause variables, estimating effects from an inferred adjustment set or causal structure, predicting the new or future state after actions, or determining which objects can activate a machine from observed outcomes.

Variants. Papers name variants such as cause attribution, causal effect estimation, effect inference, and causal identification. One line studies action based settings in both 1-step and N-step forms: given a current state and an action, the model predicts the new state, and longer horizon versions provide a sequence of actions. Another uses a Blicket style setting, asking which objects can activate a machine based on observed outcomes.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to two measurement instruments, ACRE and AI2-THOR. ACRE is described as the Abstrac

nodes.name: Causal question answering
nodes.definition: The observable task of responding to causality-related queries by selecting or generating answers that obey contexts and objective laws of causality.

nodes.name: Causal relation classification
nodes.definition: The task of identifying whether a sentence describes a causal link between events or is merely coincidental noise.

nodes.name: Chain of thought
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats chain of thought as an observable output in which a model produces intermediate reasoning before the final output. Most definitions describe a visible, step-by-step chain, path, trace, rationale, or scratchpad that decomposes a problem into smaller steps; the trace may be sentences, tokens, a paragraph, or a structured sequence, and it often ends with an answer but sometimes with a score, ranking, label, plan, or action. A smaller line of work broadens this to intermediate computation or latent thought, including unobserved sequences that connect a question to an answer, but the dominant framing remains explicit intermediate-step generation.

Variants. Most papers study natural-language, step-by-step explanations, but they use many names for the same behavior, including chain-of-thought generation, step-by-step reasoning, reasoning path or trace generation, rationale generation, thought generation, and structured response generation. The behavior appears in math, logical, commonsense, retrieval and multi-document QA, reranking, LLM-as-a-judge scoring, healthcare prediction, tool use and planning, and multimodal settin

nodes.name: Character counting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is a character-level counting task that asks for a numeric answer from presented text. Most commonly, success means accurately reporting the total number of characters in a word or in a whitespace-free character sequence, using prompts such as "How many characters in the word \"Y\"?" or asking for the number of lowercase characters in a sequence; a smaller line of work broadens it to counting the occurrences of a specified character, and one definition explicitly says the task is used to probe the model's sub-token counting ability.

Variants. Papers study several variants under this label. They include word length counting, counting characters in raw lowercase letter sequences without whitespaces, counting a target character inside a word shown as an image, and multilingual text-level tasks named Occurrence, Length, and Distinct, which ask for the number of occurrences, total length, or number of distinct characters; one snippet also mentions sentence length prediction.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers elicit the behavior with direct counting questions and expect a numeric answer that matches a ground-truth count, f

nodes.name: Charge prediction
nodes.definition: Predicting the correct legal charge in a given case based on Chinese law, evaluated using F1 score.

nodes.name: Chart and diagram understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is interpreting charts, plots, graphs, or other visualizations and extracting information from them. Many definitions pair extraction with reasoning or question answering about the displayed data, and one prompt asks what details and conclusions can be drawn from a chart; smaller strands emphasize deriving insights, locating requested elements, or retrieving numerical, categorical, or textual values from visual components such as legends and color mappings. Success is commonly framed as answering questions or identifying content such as trends, values, labels, comparisons, and time ranges.

Variants. Papers use nearby labels including chart interpretation, chart understanding, and chart reasoning.
