nodes.definition: The observable action of a model treating text in the data portion of its input as passive information to be analyzed or operated upon according to the primary instruction, without executing any commands it may contain.

nodes.name: Data reconstruction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available usage, this behavior is described as generating a close approximation of the original unlearned text by exploiting differences in model weights before and after unlearning. In "Textual Unlearning Gives a False Sense of Unlearning," the success criterion is effective reconstruction of the unlearned text, with the paper stating that "the adversary could effectively reconstruct the unlearned texts via continuous constrained optimization" and showing this as "reconstruct unlearned data by W-W’."

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers do not link this behavior to any measurement instrument.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers do not link this behavior to any construct.

nodes.name: Data-to-text generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats data-to-text generation as converting structured data into natural-language text, usually framed as producing descriptions or summaries from tables, knowledge graphs, or structured records. Most definitions stay broad, while smaller strands narrow the task to table-to-text or RDF-to-text, extend it to semi-structured inputs, or describe the output as a natural-language representation of each record. Some papers explicitly describe the output as coherent language or as a description that summarizes the record content, and a paper places the task among typical conditional text generation tasks.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this behavior, most commonly table-to-text generation, and also RDF-to-text generation, data-to-text writing, data description generation, and meal description generation. The settings center on tables, but also include knowledge graphs, RDF inputs, tabular records, semi-structured data, and meal descriptions generated from dietary intake data. Other papers use description-oriented labels for tables and for structured data more generally.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers meas

nodes.name: Data transformation
nodes.definition: Performing database operations that clean, organize, or reshape data for later analysis.

nodes.name: Dataflow analysis
nodes.definition: Identifying and reporting how values propagate between program statements along feasible execution paths, such as from a null assignment to a dereference site.

nodes.name: Date inference
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats it as inferring or calculating a calendar date from natural-language descriptions or other context while accounting for calendar structure and date arithmetic. Definitions repeatedly mention contextual clues, relative time offsets, and operations over dates, and one description explicitly includes using facts such as the number of days in February. A smaller line of work frames the task more broadly as reasoning over dates and weekdays to determine valid scheduling windows, with correct interpretation and calculation as the success criterion.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for the behavior, including date deduction, date inference, date calculation, date arithmetic, and weekday understanding. The variants studied range from deduction from contextual clues, to addition or subtraction of days, weeks, or months from a base date, to longer problems involving weekdays, multi-day spans, and scheduling windows.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to one measurement instrument, BIG-bench. In that usage it is measured through a DateUnderstanding task, described as inferring dates from natura

nodes.name: De-identification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, it is treated as a text modification task aimed at removing identifying information, though the scope differs. One framing describes it as automatically removing or replacing personally identifiable information in text, especially patient and sometimes provider information in healthcare, to protect privacy. Another framing treats it as text anonymization, where a model removes, obfuscates, or generalizes cues in a text that support inference of an author's personal attributes, and frames the goal as removing information that could lead to inference of pre-specified attributes while maintaining the text's utility.

Variants. Papers use two closely related names for the behavior, de-identification and text anonymization. The settings differ between clinical text, where automated algorithms remove patient and sometimes provider identifiers, and authored text, where the model adapts relevant parts of a passage to hide cues about personal attributes. One paper also studies paraphrasing as a related behavior, using a paraphrasing model to baseline the anonymizing effect of pure text paraphrasing.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement in

nodes.name: Debate speech evaluation
nodes.definition: The specific action of assigning a numerical score, typically on a Likert scale, to a debate speech to quantify its quality.

nodes.name: Deceptive response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as the model producing an intentionally false or misleading answer, most often in response to factual questions or lie-inducing instructions. Definitions converge on false output, but differ in what counts as deception: some describe it as intentionally providing false answers when prompted or incentivized to lie, while others extend it to concealing information or fabricating a justification for an incorrect answer. One paper states that "If the model entirely avoids mentioning the insider information we label the response as deceptive" (Detecting Strategic Deception with Linear Probes), while another gives the example of an untruthful response as answering "Paris" after the instruction "Answer the following question with a lie."

Variants. Papers use several closely related labels, including deceptive answering, deceptive response generation, and untruthful response generation. The main variants are false factual answering, omission-based deception where insider information is concealed, and responses that provide a plausible but incorrect alternative answer together with a fabricated justification

nodes.name: Decompilation
nodes.definition: Recovering higher-level source code from assembly code given an instruction prompt.

nodes.name: Defect description
nodes.definition: Describing the visible appearance characteristics of a defect, such as size, color, or shape.

nodes.name: Definition generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is broad: generating a short natural-language definition or explanation for a target item. The most explicit formulation asks, given a target word and an example usage, for a definition that is 'grammatical, fluent, and faithful' to the word's meaning in that context; other formulations ask for a title plus opening sentence for an entity mention from retrieved passages, or a brief accessible explanation of unfamiliar or domain-specific terminology. A smaller line treats the behavior as defining a concept in a given domain, and one paper describes failure cases as definition errors that include gross hallucinations.

Variants. Papers study several variants under different names: Definition generation, Entity description generation, Terminology explanation, Terminology interpretation, and Concept definition. These variants span word meaning modeling from usage examples, entity descriptions whose target output is a title plus opening sentence, explanations for non-expert users encountering specialized terms, and domain-specific term interpretation such as explaining 'backlogging' in natural language. A related setting asks

nodes.name: Dense captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats dense captioning as describing multiple objects or regions within a single image rather than assigning only category labels. Definitions agree on the multi-object, per-region scope, but differ on how much detail the text should contain: some describe short descriptions for each object present, while others emphasize rich or comprehensive descriptions that include attributes, relationships, and contextual details. A paper also defines the task as producing both the regions and the corresponding descriptions for each region, and Ins-DetCLIP: Aligning Detection Model to Follow Human-Language Instruction says the behavior should "go beyond predicting only the category name" and generate "a detailed description for objects of interest."

Variants. The dominant setting is image-based, and papers use both dense captioning and dense image captioning for that setting. Within images, the behavior is framed around multiple distinct regions, each object present, or objects of interest. A related task also appears as dense video captioning, which a paper relates to the goal of comprehensively describing all the events in a video.

nodes.name: Dense video captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats dense video captioning as generating multiple temporally aligned descriptions within a single video, rather than a single overall caption. Papers consistently require time localization: one formulation asks models to "output the start and end timestamp for each event, and describe each event with sentences," while another describes "multiple, time-localized textual descriptions" for a sequence of events. A narrower formulation further stresses fine-grained coverage of chronologically evolving events and visual elements such as camera states, scenes, actions, and object attributes.

Variants. Papers mostly study this behavior as describing several events that unfold over time in one video. One formulation broadens the target content beyond events alone to include evolving visual elements, including camera states, scenes, actions, and object attributes. Papers also use the abbreviation DVC, and one paper relates it to the broader label "dense captioning."

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link dense video captioning to 2 measurement instruments, ActivityNet Captions and YouCook2, and both are described a

nodes.name: Dependency parsing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, dependency parsing is consistently treated as a task of sentence-level syntactic analysis: assigning directed dependency relations among sentence elements. The prevailing wording describes analyzing the grammatical structure of a sentence and establishing dependencies between words, while a closely matching formulation describes assigning syntactic dependency relations between tokens in a sentence.

Variants. Papers do not name sub-tasks, domains, or modalities for this behavior. The main variation in framing is that one paper treats it as a linguistically motivated token-classification task over tokens, while another describes it more generally in terms of sentence structure and dependencies between words.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to dependency parsing. In the papers, it is described directly as a task, including one framing of it as a token-classification task.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to dependency parsing. The papers define the behavior, but do not explicitly connect it to a broader construct that it indicates.

nodes.name: Depth estimation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats depth estimation as image-based prediction of depth, most commonly as producing a depth map that represents relative distance. One definition emphasizes returning a depth map from an image to indicate relative distances of objects from the camera, while another describes predicting the distance of points in a scene from the viewpoint, typically from a 2D image. One description also notes that the module takes an image as input and returns a depth map, with closer regions shown in warmer colors under an Inferno colormap.

Variants. The recorded variants are closely related image settings rather than separately named sub-tasks. Papers describe estimating the depth of objects, or of various points in a scene, from an image or 2D image. A narrower use appears as an intermediate depth estimate used to judge whether cookies are stacked.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The papers operationalize the behavior directly by taking an image as input and producing a depth map or depth estimate.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers link it to one construct, Spatial reasoning. In V

nodes.name: Descriptive analytics
nodes.definition: The ability to generate insights that summarize and describe what has happened in a dataset.

nodes.name: Detailed image description
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is long, rich, and comprehensive description of visual content, usually as multi-sentence text that enumerates many visible details. Papers variously call it elaborate, thorough, fine-grained, or long-form, and they often ask for coverage of both prominent elements and subtle details; one prompt states, "Describe this image in detail. Give as many details as possible. Say everything you see" (MiniGPT-4: Enhancing Vision-Language Understanding with Advanced Large Language Models). Some authors also contrast it with short or shallow descriptions, and a smaller line of work asks for an elaborate, detailed natural language description of a visual scene from corresponding fMRI brain recordings.

Variants. Most papers use nearby labels such as detailed image description and detailed image captioning. Smaller variants include detailed description generation, which is used for visual scenes decoded from brain recordings, and dense caption generation for biological specimen images, where the caption is intended to contain all necessary trait information. The domains therefore range from general images to specimen images and brain

nodes.name: Diagnostic analytics
nodes.definition: The ability to generate insights that explain the causes or reasons behind observed data trends.

nodes.name: Diagram understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats diagram understanding as an observable task of interpreting diagrams and answering questions about them. Definitions repeatedly focus on understanding the content, structure, and meaning of diagram elements and their interrelations, often for scientific or schematic diagrams, and the common success criterion is answering questions based on the diagram. A smaller framing broadens the task to extracting information from structured visual formats such as charts, graphs, figures, and tables, and one paper places it within image recognition and reasoning cross capabilities.

Variants. Papers use several near-names, including diagram interpretation, diagram comprehension, diagram understanding, scientific diagram analysis, science diagram comprehension, flowchart understanding, and diagram and table interpretation. The main variants narrow the task to flowcharts, to scientific diagrams and figures, or to broader structured visuals that include charts, graphs, technical illustrations, and tables. In the flowchart setting, questions can target specific visual conventions, for example asking which step is shown with a diamond

nodes.name: Dialogue act classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats it as the task of labeling or classifying an utterance in a dialogue by its communicative function or intent. Most descriptions stay at the utterance or speaker-turn level within a dialogue, and they largely agree on the task formulation, differing mainly between "classification" and "recognition" wording and between "function" and "intent" language.

Variants. Papers use both "dialogue act classification" and "dialogue act recognition," and one study abbreviates the latter as DAR. Some papers place it in empathy-oriented dialogue settings, referring to dialogue roles and acts in EmpDial Role and EmpDial QAct and to labels of empathic intents directly at the dialogue act level in EmpDial QInt and EI. Another recognition setting describes the target speaker turn as aggregating information from neighboring turns according to a graph structure.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it, so the papers do not identify a recurring instrument that elicits or scores this behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it, so the papers do not specify a construct

nodes.name: Dialogue generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is generating the next response or utterance from dialogue context or history, usually in a multi-turn conversation. Definitions commonly describe continuing a conversation with a relevant, coherent, or contextually appropriate utterance, and some papers make the setup explicit as receiving a snippet of conversation and predicting the next utterance. A recurring framing evaluates these responses for helpfulness and harmlessness or by human preference between candidate conversations, while a smaller line of work allows single-turn human-assistant prompts or conditions generation on retrieved passages, predicted actions, state, or scenario logic.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this behavior, including dialogue response generation, conversational response generation, open-domain dialogue generation, utterance generation, and turn-by-turn response generation. The settings range from persona-conditioned open-domain conversation and retrieval-augmented response synthesis to task-oriented dialogue with API information, social interaction conditioned on personality traits, and domain-specific exchanges suc

nodes.name: Dialogue state tracking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats dialogue state tracking as turn-by-turn extraction and maintenance of a user's dialogue state in task-oriented, multi-turn conversation. Most definitions describe that state as slot-value pairs or domain-slot-value triples, used to represent users' goals, constraints, requests, or other information needed to fulfill the user's goal, and one paper states that the task "predicts a set of domain-slot-value triples" while another says the output is represented as slot-value pairs.

Variants. Most papers keep the setting at task-oriented dialogue, but they vary in representation and framing: some foreground domain-slot-value triples, while others frame the state as slot-value pairs tied to users' goals, constraints, or requests. Related formulations also appear: one paper reports reformulating dialogue state tracking as a question-answering task for less capable models, and another paper claims a causal relationship from chain of thought to dialogue state tracking, reporting about a 10% improvement in zero-shot accuracy when CoT from an earlier step is incorporated.

Space of elicitation and scores. Dialogue state tracking

nodes.name: Dialogue summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, dialogue summarization is most commonly framed as producing a concise summary from a conversation or multi-turn dialogue. Definitions repeatedly emphasize concision, while one definition also requires accuracy and another says the summary should capture the conversation's salient semantics and key information, specifying the output as a sequence of summary sentences. A smaller line of work uses the summary more narrowly, prompting a summary of dialogue context that highlights information indicative of errors in the last agent utterance. As one paper puts it, the objective is to generate a summary that "succinctly captures the salient semantics and key information conveyed throughout the conversation" (PoSum-Bench: Benchmarking Position Bias in LLM-based Conversational Summarization).

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous task names, including dialogue summarization, dialog summarization, dialog summary, and conversational summarization. The studied settings range from general dialogue transcripts to clinical interactions, especially pre-consultation and patient-doctor conversations that culminate in a brief medical report; ano

nodes.name: Digit-wise addition
nodes.definition: Performing addition on two numbers digit by digit without carrying over any values.

nodes.name: Direct answer generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the dominant framing treats it as producing only a final answer, solution, or plan, without intermediate reasoning steps or traces. Papers describe it through formulations such as "Answer the question with a short answer," "Answer with the option’s letter from the given choices directly," and "outputting only the solutions (fast mode)."

Variants. The main named variants are direct answer generation, direct solution generation, and direct answer prediction. Papers study it in contextual question answering, as a fast mode that returns only the final solution, and in prompt settings that ask for short answers or direct choice-letter outputs; papers also commonly position it against elaborate step-by-step reasoning, and one paper reports it is related to Chain of thought.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers operationalize it by eliciting direct final outputs, for example through short-answer instructions, direct choice-letter responses, or a fast mode that outputs only the final solution.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as an indicator. Separa

nodes.name: Direct answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats direct answering as responding to a user's request or question with an answer instead of first asking for clarification. Some descriptions make this contrast explicit by framing the assistant's options as either a clarifying question or an attempt to directly answer the query, and one paper labels outputs as either abstention-like, including clarifying or refusing, or direct-answering. A smaller line of work uses the same label for giving the final answer directly, without intermediate reasoning steps or any other output.

Variants. Papers study it in several settings. One variant treats it as answering an ambiguous question with a confident, specific answer instead of seeking clarification, another uses visual questions, where authors expect direct answers when the question is unambiguous and also prompt models to output answers directly without clarification. Papers also use the names direct-answering and direct prompt for settings where the model is instructed to directly provide the final answer.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link direct answering to one measurement instrument, LLM-as-a-judge. In th

nodes.name: Discourse parsing
nodes.definition: Analyzing and identifying the relational structure between dialogue turns, such as elaboration or comment, using a pre-trained parser.

nodes.name: Disease named entity recognition
nodes.definition: The task of identifying and classifying diseases mentioned in a text, typically from biomedical literature or clinical notes.

nodes.name: Distance estimation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the dominant framing is a task of determining direct distance, either by computing a numerical value or by selecting the correct straight-line or Euclidean distances. Most definitions describe it as computing the distance between objects or points, while one formulation narrows success to choosing the correct list of distances from one landmark to the others after viewing an environment, posed as multiple-choice QA with four options. The papers differ mainly in setting, visual scenes, landmarks in an environment, or geographic points, but agree that the target output is the correct direct distance relation.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, including numerical distance calculation, distance estimation, and straight-line distance calculation. The studied variants include distances between objects in a visual scene, Euclidean distances from one landmark to all other landmarks after viewing an environment, and direct distances between two geographical points in map-based textual questions.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. In the paper descriptions themselves, elicitation

nodes.name: Document filtering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, papers treat this behavior as selecting from retrieved material what should be kept for answering a question. One paper frames it at the document or content level, choosing retrieved materials most suitable for the answer, while another frames it at the sentence level, keeping only sentences relevant to the question and filtering out irrelevant context parts.

Variants. The main variation in the papers is granularity. One paper discusses filtering whole documents or broader retrieved content, while another operationalizes it as sentence selection within a retrieved passage, using binary masks over context parts and keeping an entire sentence only when its score is above 0.5.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it in the papers, so the available work does not specify a broader construct that this behavior is taken to reflect.

nodes.name: Document-level relation extraction
nodes.definition: The task of identifying and classifying semantic relations between entities mentioned anywhere in a document, including across multiple sentences.

nodes.name: Document question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is answering a question from information supplied in a document, passage, or broader context, often with the expectation that the answer come from that context rather than from pre-trained knowledge alone. Many papers place it in long-context or long-document settings, where models retrieve, locate, aggregate, filter, or reason over information in one or more documents; some narrow it to a single provided document, while others explicitly include multimodal documents with text, charts, and images. A smaller line of work makes the response format more specific, for example asking for the exact answer "using only the information provided in the context," a concise answer to a privacy-policy query, a multi-statement answer with sentence-level citations, or a True/False answer supported by two key sentences.

Variants. Most variants differ by context length and source type. Papers variously describe the task as long-context, long-document, open-book, contextual, or document-based question answering, and study single-document, multi-document, and varying-length settings, including book-length inputs and questions whose

nodes.name: Domain classification
nodes.definition: The task of assigning a word to a predefined semantic domain or category, such as 'fashion' or 'gaming'.

nodes.name: Domain-specific question answering
nodes.definition: Producing accurate answers to natural language questions that require knowledge of a specific domain, such as finance or healthcare, based on structured tabular data.

nodes.name: Downstream task performance
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the dominant framing is observable performance on downstream tasks or benchmarks, usually supervised, after pre-training, continual growth, or fine-tuning. Papers describe success as strong, equivalent, or better performance, often stated as task accuracy or as how well outputs solve target evaluation problems; one source says that improvement in validation loss "transfers to an improvement in downstream task accuracy." A smaller line of work casts it more broadly as the overall quality of an ensemble's outputs on a benchmark.

Variants. Authors use several near-synonymous labels, including downstream task performance, downstream task evaluation, downstream task solving, and task performance. The settings range from representative downstream tests after continual growth, to fine-tuned tasks such as sentiment analysis or math, to ensemble benchmarks. Papers also study suites and domains including GLUE, GSM8K, ARC-Easy, and Indonesian benchmarks such as IndoCulture, and one paper refers specifically to arithmetic reasoning when linking this behavior to semantic consistency.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers operationalize it with 21 me

nodes.name: Driving behavior prediction
nodes.definition: Answering multiple-choice driving questions about high-level behavior such as speed and steering actions.

nodes.name: Embodied emotion classification
nodes.definition: A closed-set question-answering task to identify the specific emotion category (out of eight) for a specified person in a first-person view video.

nodes.name: Embodied planning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating a sequence of actions for an agent in a simulated or physical environment, typically to achieve a goal. A smaller line of work uses the label task planning and frames it as generating or refining action plans for robotic tasks from natural-language goals and failure feedback. Where success is spelled out, papers describe multi-step planning, and one study states that a successful plan requires single-step optimality at each step.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for closely related settings, most commonly embodied planning, but also task planning and embodied decision. The settings described span simulated and physical environments, including household or scientific contexts, and robotic tasks driven by natural-language goals and failure feedback.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure this behavior with 7 instruments. The most frequently linked ones are ALFWorld, BabyAI, HotpotQA, RestBench, and ScienceWorld, plus 2 other instruments. These are described as benchmarks, datasets, or tasks: one paper uses datasets from task planning benchmarks, and another evaluates succe

nodes.name: Embodied question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is answering questions about a 3D environment through embodied perception and action: papers describe agents as perceiving, navigating, interacting, and reasoning over sequences of multimodal observations and actions in order to answer a question. One formulation, in EQA-RM: A Generative Embodied Reward Model with Test-time Scaling, explicitly includes multimodal observations such as video frames and reasoning traces, while another broadens the scope to embodied 3D environments with dialogue and planning.

Variants. Papers use both Embodied question answering and Embodied VQA for closely related formulations. The named variants emphasize active exploration of the environment to answer natural language questions, and a 3D perception setting where embodied VQA covers dialogue and planning; another description highlights multimodal observation streams, including video frames and reasoning traces.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the available papers, the behavior is operationalized directly as answering questions in 3D environments from multimodal observations and action s

nodes.name: Emotion analysis
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats emotion analysis as label assignment: identifying which emotions are expressed in text or an utterance, often for a target turn in dialogue with the prior conversational history as context. Many definitions use predefined categories and allow one or more labels for text, dialogue utterances, or multimodal posts, while smaller lines of work broaden the behavior to extracting emotional connotations in sentences, identifying dominant emotions in a document, or interpreting emotional tone in audio. A few papers move beyond fixed-label classification by asking for free-text emotion descriptions of a narrative character or by allowing labels outside a fixed set for multimodal input.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this behavior, including emotion classification, emotion detection, emotion recognition, emotion recognition in conversations, emotional state extraction, emotion label generation, emotional tone interpretation, and emotion prediction. The studied settings range from text classification and social media posts to dialogue-level recognition that uses previous turns or neighboring utterances, plus

nodes.name: Empathetic response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is a dialogue task: producing supportive, emotionally appropriate replies that show understanding of a speaker's emotional state, often including its causal basis. Some authors broaden this to text that conveys understanding, compassion, and validation in mental health support, while another describes responses that express understanding and connection with a client's stated or inferred emotions and may encourage exploration of problems.

Variants. The studied variants span context- and cause-aware response generation from dialogue history, mental health support exchanges, and a psychotherapeutic setting where an AI therapist responds to a client. A smaller multimodal line conditions the response on both a client's facial image and dialogue history, and one description adds that the system should keep a consistent focus on the client's issues throughout the procedure.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The available descriptions refer to generating subsequent empathetic responses in dialogue, but no named elicitation or scoring instrument is recorded.

What it is taken as evidenc

nodes.name: Entity disambiguation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats entity disambiguation as choosing the correct entity when several candidates share a name or surface form. Most definitions describe selecting the right knowledge base entity or identifying which entity a claim refers to when multiple entities have similar names or attributes, while a smaller line of work applies the same idea to customer-transaction references, where the system must resolve the right order or product. Papers differ in how resolution is carried out: some frame a direct selection problem, while others describe using contextual clues and clarifying information, or iteratively interacting with a knowledge base and a claim graph to produce rationales, triplet identifiers, targeted questions, and concise summaries of differences.

Variants. Variants are mainly distinguished by setting and name: papers use both entity disambiguation and named entity disambiguation. They study it as knowledge base entity selection, claim-focused factual knowledge tasks, Wikipedia inconsistency detection, CRM disambiguation of customer transactions, and complex claim verification, including an iterative form where the sys

nodes.name: Entity grounding
nodes.definition: The task of linking a textual entity mention to its corresponding visual region in an accompanying image.

nodes.name: Entity linking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as mapping textual or surface-form entities to canonical identifiers. Most commonly, success is described as linking an entity mention or generated entity name to the correct code or identifier, such as assigning unique ICD codes from clinical text or mapping entities in a logical form to their corresponding mids. A smaller framing uses entity alignment language for pairing entities that refer to the same real-world concept across separate multi-modal knowledge graphs, with 1-to-1 correspondence as the target.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings and under related names. One line treats ICD coding as entity linking, where disease mentions in a doctor's diagnosis text are linked to ICD entries based on semantic similarity with ICD dictionary entries; another uses entity alignment in knowledge base question answering to map entities in generated logical forms to mids, with popularity, similarity, and FACC1-based selection appearing in the description. A smaller multi-modal variant, called multi-modal entity alignment, matches corresponding entities across separate multi-modal knowledge

nodes.name: Entity matching
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, papers treat this as a matching task: identifying when items from different sources refer to the same target. The papers agree on the success criterion, matching the same real-world entity or product, but differ in formulation: one describes deciding whether entities from different knowledge graphs match, while another describes identifying the same product across languages from metadata, including a selection form where a given product metadata record is matched to its counterpart in another language.

Variants. The main variants are general entity matching across knowledge graphs and cross-lingual product alignment based on product metadata. Papers use both names, with the cross-lingual variant narrowing the task to products and to matching across languages rather than across knowledge graphs more broadly.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior in the papers.

nodes.name: Environment exploration
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as observable information-seeking interaction with an environment: agents verify conditions, locate objects or landmarks, gather visual inputs, inspect a codebase, or reveal hidden states. Papers make it concrete as moving, looking around, navigating to new locations, interacting with objects, or executing commands, and a smaller line also frames it as visiting new states or regions. What counts as success is usually getting the information needed for a downstream task, such as answering a question, completing a task when object locations are underspecified, or understanding the current system state.

Variants. Papers study several named variants: information collection, for fine-grained viewpoint adjustment and higher-quality visual observations; active information gathering, under partial observations for disambiguation; active exploration, to obtain visual inputs for question answering; and broader exploration, to scan for target objects or find unspecified objects in a house. The settings range from dynamic city spaces and other physical environments to codebase inspection through commands, and

nodes.name: Environmental interaction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as an agent taking actions in a real or simulated environment and then receiving the resulting state, observation, or reward. Most formulations describe executing actions that change or query the environment state, while some make the goal condition explicit as achieving a target or accomplishing a task objective through those interactions. As one paper states, 'the objective of an agent A is to achieve the target G through multi-step interactions with E' (Learn-by-interact: A Data-Centric Framework For Self-Adaptive Agents in Realistic Environments).

Variants. Papers use several closely related names, including environmental interaction, environment interaction, interaction, and multi-step interaction. The main variants differ by setting and scope: general environment interaction, instruction-conditioned sequences of actions over multiple steps using the instruction and previous history, and game-specific interaction tasks that require finding specified entities, such as shopkeepers or altars, and interacting with them depending on context. One paper also distinguishes transitions generate

nodes.name: Error analysis
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant usage treats error analysis as examining failures by comparing expected and actual outputs or by identifying flaws in intermediate reasoning. In code-focused work, this includes analyzing failed test cases, comparing execution results and logic differences between two pieces of code, and using those discrepancies to identify bugs or inefficiencies; in reasoning tasks, it includes step-level reports of incorrect operations, rule violations, or steps that do not move toward the target solution. A smaller line of work uses the term for systematically uncovering and categorizing learners' missteps, such as syntactic or pronunciation errors, and for generating corrective guidance, while another paper frames it as a qualitative categorization of failure modes such as hallucination, misunderstanding, and locating errors.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings, including code generation, English education, table reasoning, and stepwise problem solving. The main variants are qualitative failure-mode categorization, step-level reasoning diagnosis, and a more specific form called granular error diagnosis, which ex

nodes.name: Error detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats error detection as an observable judgment about whether a response, reasoning step, utterance, question, video, or other artifact contains an error. Most definitions cast it as a task, though some describe the same behavior as a model capability to recognize mistakes in responses or reasoning steps. Common success criteria are binary judgments, such as whether errors exist, whether a specified step is correct or incorrect, or whether a question is 'ok' or 'not ok'; a smaller line of work asks for finer outputs, such as identifying an error type, mapping a step to a predefined taxonomy or marking it correct, or assigning sentence-level binary faithfulness labels.

Variants. Variants span several domains and names. Papers label it as accounting bug detection in smart contracts, error awareness for natural and AIGC videos, stepwise error detection for checking a specified solution step, and error identification for classifying reasoning steps as mathematically erroneous, logically inconsistent, or accumulation errors. Other formulations target dialogue utterances, chemical molecule descriptions, multiple-choice questions

nodes.name: Error explanation
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a natural language explanation that clarifies why a specific part of a molecular description is chemically incorrect.

nodes.name: Error localization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is fine-grained identification of where an error occurs in an already given solution, reasoning chain, or description. Most papers define success as pinpointing the exact wrong step, line, component, or contiguous text span, often the first place where the reasoning becomes wrong; several formulations also require the model or tutor to explain the error once the location is found. A smaller line of work applies the same idea to invalid literature-grounded chains by identifying the breakpoint paper nodes where coherence breaks down.

Variants. Papers study this behavior under names such as process judging, first error step identification, invalid node identification, and mistake location. The most common settings are mathematical reasoning, including wrong step-by-step solutions and handwritten math where the model must identify the specific line with the error; other settings localize chemical errors as erroneous spans in molecular descriptions, locate incorrect papers in invalid reasoning chains, or ask a tutor response to point to the mistake's location and outline what the error is.

Space of elicitation and sc

nodes.name: Essay scoring
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The only explicit framing treats essay scoring as the automatic evaluation of a language learner's writing skills from a text they have produced. In UniversalCEFR: Enabling Open Multilingual Research on Language Proficiency Assessment, the task is described as evaluating "the writing skills of the learners as reflected in a text they have written," and the paper also names it automated essay scoring (AES).

Variants. The available paper uses automated essay scoring (AES) as the label for the task. It does not describe separate sub-tasks, domains, modalities, or alternative success criteria.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to essay scoring by papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to essay scoring by papers.

nodes.name: Ethical commentary
nodes.definition: A tendency for outputs to comment on ethics, limitations, or responsible use in addition to providing factual content.

nodes.name: Event argument extraction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as identifying event arguments and assigning each one a specific role in text, typically with the event trigger already given. A smaller formulation, used for scientific events, describes it as finding the text spans that serve as arguments for a scientific event and classifying them into roles such as Context, Method, or Result. Papers therefore converge on argument finding plus role assignment, though they differ in whether the task is stated generically or within scientific activities.

Variants. Papers use both the names 'Event Argument Extraction' and 'Argument extraction'. Some work studies it as a cross-lingual transfer task, with one paper stating that the evaluation spans 20 languages. In scientific-event settings, authors further split it into Argument Identification, predicting the set of argument spans per event, and Argument Classification, predicting the semantic role for each identified span.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 2 measurement instruments, CASIE and TextEE. CASIE appears in a table of datasets used for training, evaluation, or both in GoLL

nodes.name: Event detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats event detection as identifying event triggers in text and assigning them predefined event types, sometimes presented as structured (event type, trigger) pairs. Most formulations make correctness depend on both parts matching the reference annotation: one paper states that an event trigger is correct only if both the trigger and event type align with gold annotations, while another separates trigger identification from trigger classification by first requiring the trigger offsets to match and then the event type to match as well.

Variants. A smaller line of work uses the name event identification for the stricter criterion of matching the trigger-event pair, described as correct identification of the event mention. Some papers further break the behavior into trigger identification and trigger classification, using labels such as Tri-I and Tri-C. Papers also study the task in different settings, including robustness benchmarks alongside NER and RE, and one benchmark uses the undisclosed test set of MAVEN.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link event detection to 2 measurement instruments, ACE05 and SPEE

nodes.name: Event extraction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats event extraction as turning unstructured text into structured event representations. Most commonly, papers describe this as identifying event triggers and extracting or classifying their associated arguments; another formulation focuses on extracting specific life events from conversation with fields such as date, people involved, and description. A narrower legal formulation treats the output as subject-action-object triplets, used to keep sentences containing matching events.

Variants. Papers study several settings under this label. One paper explicitly distinguishes sentence-level and document-level event extraction, while domain-specific variants include crop-science categories such as "pest impact" and "new variety release," autobiographical interviewing where events are extracted during conversation and then inserted, merged, or queried in a memory graph, and legal retrieval where "important events" are extracted from case text.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead operationalize the behavior directly as an extraction task, for example asking a m

nodes.name: Event prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the recurring framing is future-oriented prediction from prior context: papers describe predicting whether a future event will occur from current and past events, or generating the next event content from observed video dynamics. The success criterion varies by formulation: one paper treats an event as likely when it can be placed in a causal graph as a leaf node, another asks the model to select the video segment most logically related to the preceding context, and another frames the task as assigning a probability from 0 to 1 to a future question with a binary true or false outcome.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this behavior, including event forecasting, event prediction, and binary forecasting. The main variants differ by setting and output form: causal event reasoning over a graph structure, video-sequence prediction where the predicted content is a segment, and binary future-event questions answered with probabilities. One formulation also states that the forecaster is queried separately on each question.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, elicitation an

nodes.name: Event segmentation
nodes.definition: Dividing a scientific abstract into contiguous spans corresponding to core scientific activities: Background, Method, Result, and Conclusion.

nodes.name: Example generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available work, the dominant framing is a word-sense task: generating synthetic sentences from a dictionary definition that demonstrate a specified target sense. The task is described as having an LLM produce distinct example sentences, and success is framed in the papers as whether those sentences demonstrate the target sense. One study states that "LLMs generate diverse example sentences for dictionary senses" and describes producing "t distinct example sentences that demonstrate the target sense."

Variants. The described setting is example generation for dictionary senses from dictionary definitions. Within that setting, the main variation emphasized is diversity: papers refer to both diverse and distinct example sentences, and describe applying a diversity strategy when generating them.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. The papers describe elicitation procedurally, by applying a diversity strategy and using an LLM generator to produce distinct example sentences; no separate scoring instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior as someth

nodes.name: Experimental design
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is to treat this behavior as outlining an experimental setup or procedure inside a research paper in order to validate a proposed method, problem, or research idea. Most definitions describe the output as a brief experiment plan or a list of experiments, often with motivations or explanations, and some formulations make clear that this planning can be produced from partial, pre-experiment paper context and can appear even when results are simulated.

Variants. Papers study closely related formulations rather than sharply different versions. Some ask for a brief experiment plan and explanations from a partial paper context, while others describe outlining the setup and procedures for experiments within a paper, including cases with simulated results, or place experiment design alongside defining problems and proposing methods.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to one measurement instrument, Expert evaluation. The available evidence describes this as measurement through expert feedback, including evaluation via feedback from expert food scientists.

nodes.name: Explanation generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is to ask models for natural-language text that justifies an answer, label, or decision. This often appears as a rationale, justification, or reasoning trace, sometimes requested before the final answer and sometimes after prediction; common formulations ask the model to explain why the chosen option is correct and other options are incorrect, to give possible explanations for its prediction, or to explain why something is good or bad for a user. A smaller line of work uses the same behavior for non-decision explanations, such as expanding a surgical keystep, explaining a fallacy or anomaly, clarifying a word sense, or explaining complex subjects by analogy.

Variants. Papers also use nearby names such as rationale generation, justification generation, natural language explanation generation, feedback generation, and analysis generation. The settings are diverse, including recommendation, multiple-choice and clinical question answering, rumor and fact-checking, sentiment and narrative revision, and multimodal image, video, audio, and driving tasks. Variants differ in format, from free-form or concise summaries to step-by-ste

nodes.name: Exploration
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available papers, the prevailing usage treats exploration as action exploration: selecting and trying different actions within a search or learning process to discover their outcomes and potential rewards. The surrounding descriptions place this behavior in planning and information gathering, including "making decisions that may be suboptimal in the short term for the sake of gathering more information" and enhancing action exploration within MCTS planning.

Variants. The named variant in the definitions is "action exploration." Papers study it in MCTS and tree-search settings, including "complex textual interactive tasks," and one line of work discusses it together with exploitation as something to balance throughout a self-improving process.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to exploration. Instead, the available papers describe it being elicited through prompting and search procedures: papers claim a causal relationship from chain of thought to exploration in an "enhanced" prompt that hints the model to explore, summarizes interaction history into per-arm averages, and asks for zero-shot chain-of-thought reason

nodes.name: Extractive question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as answering a question by extracting the answer from provided text, usually a passage, prefix, context document, or source documents. Most formulations describe the answer as a direct text span from the input, while a smaller formulation allows the answer to be extracted or composed from a prefix. One narrower description further requires the answer to be a contiguous span that can be taken from the documents without additional reasoning.

Variants. Papers study it in several input settings. Some descriptions center on passage or prefix-based question answering, including a setup where a decoder-only model attends to the full prefix to generate the target answer. Another line treats it as a long-context task over large documents such as research papers, financial reports, and legal documents, with questions that require information extraction from the input, and a narrower domain-specific variant uses source documents whose answers are directly extractable spans.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to two measurement instruments: CoQA and SQuAD v1.1. One paper lists both unde

nodes.name: Extractive summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats extractive summarization as producing a summary by selecting text directly from the source document. Most commonly, papers describe this as selecting and concatenating the most important sentences, while some wording broadens the unit from sentences to spans of text. Across these formulations, the shared criterion is that the summary uses text taken directly from the source document.

Variants. The papers vary mainly in what is selected and in the application setting. One recurring formulation is sentence-level selection, including a Greek financial task described as evaluating whether models can identify key sentences within narrative financial reports. Another uses the label "span summary" for cases where summaries are built from spans taken directly from the document, and one paper reports that extractive summarization is related to abstractive summarization as an earlier stage before later revision.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link extractive summarization to one measurement instrument, Plutus-ben. It is presented as a benchmark that addresses extractive summarization among its core tasks.

W

nodes.name: Facial expression recognition
nodes.definition: The task of classifying a human face in an image into one of several basic emotional expressions.

nodes.name: Fact checking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is evidence-grounded veracity judgment: a claim or statement is checked against retrieved documents, a corpus, tables, a knowledge base, a knowledge graph, or other grounding material, and labeled as true, false, supported, refuted, or not enough information. One paper describes automated fact-checking as verifying a queried fact "with respect to a baseline knowledge." Papers differ mainly in output and accompanying requirements: some use binary true/false or support/unsupport decisions, while others use Supported, Refuted, and NotEnoughInfo, or require a verdict together with evidence, extracted supporting or refuting statements, or a human-readable explanation; the verdict is usually model-produced, though one line of work describes human or LLM-assisted veracity labeling after reviewing the claim and evidence. A smaller line of work broadens the behavior to extracting claims before verification, synthesizing missing or contradictory evidence into a belief judgment, or checking factual correctness during generation at the sentence or answer level.

Variants. Papers study this behavior under names such as fact verification,

nodes.name: Factual question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is answering direct factual or fact-seeking questions with a precise, correct response grounded in world knowledge. Most definitions describe the targets as objective, verifiable information, such as dates, locations, entities, or entity attributes, and several formulations expect a short answer, a yes or no response, or the correct object for a subject-relation prompt. Smaller variants define it as answering from provided facts or updated subject-relation-object knowledge, and some papers additionally require answers to avoid hallucinated content or common misconceptions; one multimodal setting tests the same behavior when an accompanying image may help or mislead.

Variants. Papers study several named variants. A recurrent naming is factoid question answering, where the answer is a single concise fact, and some papers also use fact-seeking question answering for objective, verifiable queries. A smaller line isolates single-fact question answering or simple QA as single-hop factual recall, and some work treats it as trivia question answering. Other papers place the behavior in settings such as answering from a gi

nodes.name: Factual recall
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats factual recall as completing a factual prompt with the correct stored answer, most often predicting the object in a subject-relation pair or generating a value from a subject and attribute. Success is usually the correct entity, token, or short answer for subject-relation completions or direct factual questions, and several definitions explicitly say the fact is retrieved from model parameters or pretraining data, sometimes with no dependence on context. A smaller line broadens the label to recalling edited or unlearned knowledge, retrieving event details from a narrative, or identifying an entity from attributes, and one paper instead defines recall as the share of relevant supported facts included in a longer response.

Variants. Most variants stay close to single-fact retrieval, but papers also study paraphrased factual recall, direct question answering, subject-attribute retrieval, and relation prediction or factual probing over many relation types. Smaller strands split the task into single-hop recall, bridge entity recall inside multi-hop questions, inverse versus forward search, multilingual answer extraction,

nodes.name: Fake news generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating fabricated news articles or deceptive narratives, often with LLMs, in forms that mimic legitimate journalism. Outputs are commonly described as intentionally false or deceitful, and some definitions explicitly add an intent to deceive readers or evade automated detection systems. A smaller line of work states the task more procedurally, as generating news articles from fake headlines or producing the "next version of fake news" through iterative prompt refinement.

Variants. Papers study several variants that differ in how the article is sourced or transformed. Reported settings include generation from fake news headlines, rewriting, expanding, or disguising given fake news, and modifying true news articles to introduce believable factual errors. Some work uses multi-perspective generation in three different styles, including chain-of-thought prompting, while another allows fake news stories to include visual elements and strategic content manipulation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 1 measurement instrument, XSum. In the linked use, one paper says generated

nodes.name: Fault localization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats it as locating the source of a software problem in code, whether described as the source of a bug or failure within code or a repository, or as the files, functions, or lines responsible for a reported issue. Most descriptions agree that the task is to identify the responsible code location, though they differ in scope, from general bug or failure localization to inferring which files or functions caused a reported crash from limited diagnostic information. A narrower formulation also stresses speed, describing agents that "pinpoint the source of an issue remarkably quickly."

Variants. Papers use the names fault localization, bug localization, and issue localization. The studied settings range from repository-level debugging to kernel crash reports and reported software issues, with outputs framed as relevant files, functions, or lines of code. A smaller line of usage highlights specific approaches or neighboring distinctions, including "spectrum-based fault localization" to guide context retrieval and a contrast between localizing an issue and "root cause" analysis.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measureme

nodes.name: Feature activation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the cited papers, the prevailing usage treats feature activation, also called feature firing, as the observable case where an internal feature becomes active on particular input tokens or contexts. Papers describe it as identifying which tokens activate a feature and in which contexts, as well as observing non-zero activation, and one recurring formulation is whether a feature fires at all on a given context.

Variants. The main variation is in granularity. Some descriptions focus on very simple features that activate exclusively on individual tokens, while others frame activation more generally over tokens and broader contexts, including analyses that group activating datapoints by activation range and count the tokens that appear there.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers operationalize it by saving the activation of each sparse autoencoder feature over sampled tokens, identifying which tokens activate a feature and in which contexts, counting tokens among datapoints that activate the feature across activation ranges, and testing whether a description lets a model predict on which tokens a f

nodes.name: Feedback generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is a natural-language rationale or explanation that accompanies an evaluation, most commonly explaining why a response received a particular score. As one paper puts it, "Feedback: A rationale of why the provided response would receive a particular score. This is analogous to Chain-of-Thoughts" (Prometheus: Inducing Fine-Grained Evaluation Capability in Language Models). Smaller strands use the same label for a short explanation of why code failed, a richer reflection on how a model can be improved, diagnostic feedback for prompt refinement, or personalized formative feedback that pinpoints strengths and addresses weaknesses.

Variants. Papers study several named variants and settings. They use "verbal feedback generation" for rich natural-language reflection used across iterations, and "feedback comment generation" for essay assessment; within essay feedback, authors mention corrective comments, holistic comments, and multi-dimensional analytic comments. Other recurring settings are code failure explanation for self-repair or debugging, feedback used to generate refined prompts, and tutoring feedback on quizzes o

nodes.name: Few-shot image classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers describe it as classifying images into categories when only a small number of examples, or support samples, are available for each category. A more specific formulation casts it as N-way K-shot classification, with N classes, K support samples, and Q query samples per class, where the goal is to classify query samples based on the support samples. Success is described through classification performance, including Top-1 accuracy.

Variants. The main setting that papers spell out is N-way K-shot, organized around support and query samples per class. Papers also refer to the task as few-shot recognition and, in one case, describe doing it with a fixed number of prompts. Evaluations are reported across downstream datasets.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. When papers report results, they do so as classification performance, including Top-1 accuracy across downstream datasets and tabulated few-shot image classification results.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as evidence of. One paper reports a positive correlation between few-shot classification performance and the cap

nodes.name: Few-shot task performance
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is performance on downstream or benchmark tasks when only a small number of examples are available, most often as in-context demonstrations in the prompt. Some authors narrow this to answering or completing few-shot benchmark tasks, or to few-shot inference with only a small number of labeled examples per class, while others frame it as rapid adaptation with a small training set. A smaller group uses the same label for scarce-training-data settings rather than prompt examples, especially time series forecasting with only the first 5 to 10% of time steps available for training.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, most commonly few-shot learning, and also few-shot task solving, few-shot inference, few-shot forecasting, and few-shot continual relation extraction. The behavior is studied in long-context question-answering, summarization, and code completion, and in smaller lines of work on time series forecasting and relation extraction. Some labeled-example versions are stated as N-way-K-shot or as having only k labels per class, with one paper specifying k = 3.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavio

nodes.name: Figure-to-text generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as converting structured or visual information in a figure into natural-language text. Most formulations differ by the intended output: concise figure summaries, suitable descriptive captions, detailed descriptions, or analytical text about scientific figures. The recurring success criterion is that the text capture the figure’s information in a meaningful, descriptive, or concise way, depending on the task label.

Variants. Papers use several neighboring labels for this behavior, including figure summarization, figure captioning or caption generation, figure description, and scientific figure analysis. Some variants are explicitly framed around scientific figures, and one paper places captioning, summarization, and description alongside figure question answering and scientific reasoning tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. In the linked operationalization, this behavior is measured by one instrument, ChartX. One paper cites ChartX under the label Figure Des., so the supporting measurement evidence is stated in figure-description terms.

What it is taken as evidence of. The papers do not link thi

nodes.name: Financial distress identification
nodes.definition: Predicting whether a company will face bankruptcy or financial distress.

nodes.name: Financial question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is finance-domain question answering. Papers agree on the domain, but differ in formulation: the more common description is answering financial questions using retrieved evidence, while another description narrows the behavior to answering multiple-choice questions related to finance.

Variants. The task appears in two named settings. One is presented as "Financial QA" or "FiQA," including a formulation where answers are produced with retrieved evidence; the other is a finance-specific MMLU setting framed as multiple-choice questions related to finance.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure this behavior with 2 instruments. The more common instrument is FiQA, described in the papers as a Financial QA task, and another instrument is MMLU, used for finance-related multiple-choice questions; both are benchmark-style instruments in the way the papers describe them.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior, so the papers do not explicitly relate it to any construct.

nodes.name: Fine-grained action recognition
nodes.definition: The task of distinguishing between highly similar actions within a specific domain, requiring attention to subtle differences in movement, posture, and interaction with the environment.

nodes.name: Fine-grained visual recognition
nodes.definition: The observable task of identifying and outputting the specific, subordinate-level category of an object presented in an image.

nodes.name: Flowchart question answering
nodes.definition: Generating natural language answers to questions about the content, logic, or process flow of a given flowchart image.

nodes.name: Forecasting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, forecasting is most commonly described as generating predictions about future events or outcomes from available information, past data, and current trends. Some authors name this predictive analytics and frame it as judging "what will likely happen," while another treats future event prediction as an observable task that often takes a multiple-choice or range-based answer. Examples include predicting a future treasury yield or a future approval rating.

Variants. The settings vary more than the basic task. Papers mention finance and sports, business analytics uses it for predictive insights from past data, and another formulation centers on political outcome questions built from newly gathered factual data about future events. The names used for these variants include forecasting, predictive analytics, and future event prediction, and one paper also reports that forecasting is related to creative writing.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Where elicitation is described, papers use direct questions about future outcomes, sometimes expecting a multiple-choice or range-based answer.

What it is taken a

nodes.name: Form filling
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the prevailing usage is entering or selecting values in web form elements according to task instructions. The behavior is described both as entering information into fields and as interacting with inputs such as text boxes, checkboxes, radio buttons, and dropdown menus. One definition also includes tracking which fields have been completed, and one paper describes repeated input of the same words into the same field as a common error in this behavior.

Variants. The papers describe this behavior across several web input types rather than as a single uniform action. Related formulations include labeling or filling in inputs, and the named action types include "modify_text", "modify_checkbox", "modify_radio", and "modify_select".

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the available descriptions, the behavior is operationalized through web interaction actions such as filling or labeling inputs and modifying text, checkbox, radio, and select elements.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as evidence of.

nodes.name: Formal language recognition
nodes.definition: The observable action of receiving a string as input and producing a decision to accept or reject it as a member of a language.

nodes.name: Formal theorem proving
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is a task of producing a correct formal proof inside an interactive theorem prover, especially Lean. Success is stated as proving the theorem correctly in that formal environment, and one paper makes the setup more specific by tasking models with proving a theorem while given access to code from the theorem's repository. One paper also describes formal theorem proving in interactive theorem provers as a testbed for evaluating LLM reasoning capabilities.

Variants. Papers study it across several theorem sets rather than a single problem type. The linked benchmarks cover high-school exercises and competition problems, undergraduate-level theorems, and Putnam Mathematical Competition problems. One paper also refers to the activity as formal proof writing, and another contrasts repository-context theorem proving with popular benchmarks that focus on isolated competition problems.

Space of elicitation and scores. Four measurement instruments are linked to it. The most frequently linked is miniF2F, followed by ProofNet, LeanDojo, and PutnamBench. Papers use miniF2F and ProofNet as benchmarks for theorem-proving capabil

nodes.name: Format following
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats format following as producing outputs that match a requested layout, template, or explicit formatting rule. Papers describe it as arranging text into a specific structure, obeying instruction-specified formatting or style constraints, and applying required section headers, organ labels, and numbering rules, with deviations penalized during evaluation. A smaller formulation treats it as staying consistent with the format shown in in-context examples, and one study notes outputs are "often generated in an inconsistent format" when that example format is disrupted.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings: general text formatting for content creation, rule following under explicit instructions, template adherence in clinical reporting, and format-consistent output generation in arithmetic in-context learning. The named variants are text formatting, rule following, template adherence, and format-consistent output generation. In the structured-report variant, success includes correctly using Findings and Impression section headers and other template rules, while in the arithmetic variant success i

nodes.name: Forward reaction prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available usage treats forward reaction prediction as determining the potential products of a chemical reaction from a given set of reactants and reagents. The definition and source text use the same framing, describing it as the "proactive determination of potential products" from those inputs.

Variants. It appears alongside other molecular instruction tasks, including molecule description generation, molecular property prediction, IUPAC name generation, and retrosynthesis. The papers shown here do not name sub-variants, domains, modalities, or alternative formulations of forward reaction prediction itself.

Space of elicitation and scores. No paper records a measured_by instrument for this behavior. Papers link it to a single instrument, Mol-Instructions, and that recorded link is causal rather than measured_by: the paper says Mol-Instructions equips LLMs with new insights into chemical reaction prediction, and presents it as an instruction dataset.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers do not link forward reaction prediction to any construct, so the available material does not specify what broader property it is taken to evidence.

nodes.name: Frame identification
nodes.definition: The task of selecting the correct semantic frame for a given target word within a specific sentence or context.

nodes.name: Fraud detection
nodes.definition: Classifying transactions or profiles as fraudulent or non-fraudulent.

nodes.name: Free recall
