nodes.definition: An experimental task where a subject studies a list of items and is then asked to recall as many items as possible in any order.

nodes.name: Freezing of gait detection
nodes.definition: Detecting episodes where Parkinson’s disease patients experience sudden inability to move while walking, using multimodal physiological and motion signals.

nodes.name: Function composition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, it is described as solving tasks that require sequentially applying functions or relations to an input and producing the resulting output. One formulation says models "apply them sequentially to a given input" and, when prompted with the non-highlighted part, need to return the highlighted part; another frames success as answering a query for "the value of f(g(x))" after composing relations such as "birthday-of" and "father-of".

Variants. Variation appears mainly in how the task is posed. Some papers study composed mappings built from simple functions with specified inputs and outputs, while others study relation-composition queries in which one named relation is applied and then another; the labels used are "Function composition" and "Function composition solving".

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. In the available papers, it is elicited directly through the task setup itself, either by giving part of a composed mapping and asking for the missing output or by asking for the result of a composed query.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior. The availab

nodes.name: Function regression
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is a prediction task: the model is given example input-output pairs for a mathematical function in context and must predict the output for a queried input. Most descriptions treat this generally as function fitting or mathematical function learning. A narrower formulation casts it as non-linear function regression with inputs x and y, where the target is the integer part of f(x, y) = √x√y; one paper also presents this task as a way to evaluate reasoning with continuous vector representations.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous names, including function regression, function fitting, and mathematical function learning. The main variation is between broad mathematical-function prediction from in-context examples and a specific arithmetic setting built around a non-linear function. One paper specifically studies learning out-of-distribution mathematical functions through in-context learning.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The available operationalizations are direct task formulations, with success described as predicting the function output for a given input and, in th

nodes.name: Functional group identification
nodes.definition: The specific, observable task of identifying potential functional groups within a molecule based on its chemical formula and spectral data.

nodes.name: Future prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the common framing treats future prediction as producing the next observation or state from current context, usually a current observation or state together with an action. Definitions differ mainly in output form: some papers ask the model to choose among candidate next observations, others ask it to predict the next observation at each time point in a stochastic sequence, and others frame it as autoregressively predicting the next state and reward. A smaller line of work casts it as either a probabilistic forecast over unknown state values given context or a text description of the next observation after a single-step action.

Variants. Papers study several closely related variants under the names observation prediction, next-state prediction, state transition prediction, state forecasting, and future prediction. The settings range from sequential decision making with candidate observations, to stochastic processes such as random walks on a graph, to autoregressive state-and-reward prediction, to uncertainty settings where the output is a probability distribution over state values, and to robot learning where the output is a textual next-obser

nodes.name: Game playing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, it is most commonly framed as interaction with a game environment through repeated moves under the game's rules and state updates in order to achieve objectives or win. One recurring formulation emphasizes end-to-end play, where the model is assessed on managing a game from start to finish and must "independently navigate the game." A narrower formulation treats the behavior as accomplishing specific in-game goals, with examples such as collecting resources, crafting tools, or placing objects, and with success described in terms of unlocking achievements while ensuring survival.

Variants. Papers use several task names for this behavior, including end-to-end gameplay, game playing, and achievement unlocking. The studied settings range from full-run gameplay, where the agent manages the game from start to finish, to open-world goal completion, where the agent continuously interacts with the environment to accomplish tasks. Some formulations target general objectives or winning, while another focuses specifically on unlocking achievements such as collecting resources, crafting tools, and placing objects.

Space of elicitation and scores. No me

nodes.name: Generative error correction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the cited papers, the prevailing usage treats generative error correction as an ASR task where an LLM maps an N-best list of hypotheses to a corrected transcription. The papers align on the input, ASR N-best hypotheses, and the target, a final or ground-truth transcription; one definition further specifies that this is done in an auto-regressive manner, and one snippet describes it as "a direct mapping from the N-best hypotheses list generated by an ASR system to the predicted output transcription" (It's Never Too Late: Fusing Acoustic Information into Large Language Models for Automatic Speech Recognition).

Variants. The formulations that appear are all within automatic speech recognition settings. A recurring name for the core setup is a hypotheses-to-transcription, H2T, mapping from an N-best hypotheses list to a predicted or ground-truth transcription, alongside the shorthand GER.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 1 measurement instrument, HyPoradise. In the recorded relationship language, generative error correction is measured by HyPoradise, which is described as a generative error correction benchmark for LLM-enhanced ASR and a

nodes.name: Generic caption generation
nodes.definition: An observable behavior where the model produces a vague or non-specific description of an image that does not identify the primary objects.

nodes.name: Genetic perturbation experiment design
nodes.definition: The observable task of selecting a set of genes to perturb in an experimental round to maximize the discovery of 'hit' genes with a desired phenotype.

nodes.name: Gibberish generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage describes it as the model producing incoherent, meaningless, irrelevant, unreadable, or otherwise un-useful text. Definitions largely agree on observable forms such as jumbled or repetitive phrases, random characters, mixed languages, garbled characters, and semantically irregular text; one paper describes single phrases or words repeated 'ad nauseum.' In the trigger-based framing, success is defined as eliciting gibberish outputs from the model when the trigger appears.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous names for the behavior, including incoherent output, nonsensical response generation, and garbage text generation. The studied settings differ: some elicit it when a specific trigger string is present in context, some when the model is asked to operate in a difficult bijection language, and some after extensive optimization on a proxy reward or under KL-divergence training. A narrower variant emphasizes garbage text specifically as mixed languages or garbled characters.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead describe elicitation through context conditions,

nodes.name: GitHub issue resolution
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available descriptions, the prevailing usage treats it as an end-to-end repository task: understanding a problem description from a GitHub issue and generating a code patch that successfully resolves it within the software repository. The success criterion is resolution of the issue through the produced patch, and no alternative task formulation appears in the available definitions.

Variants. The available snippets place the task at the repository level, with one paper noting difficulties in resolving GitHub issues particularly at that level. Benchmark descriptions also frame the behavior as patch-level fixing rather than broader development capabilities. No additional named sub-tasks, domains, or modalities appear in the cited papers.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers describe it as measured by 2 instruments, most often SWE-bench and also SWE-bench Lite. SWE-bench is presented as an evaluation benchmark or dataset specifically designed for evaluating GitHub issue resolution, and one description says it emphasizes patch-level fixes rather than broader development capabilities. SWE-bench Lite is used to compare systems on the same issues' res

nodes.name: Grammatical acceptability judgment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage is a sentence-level judgment of whether a sentence is grammatically correct or acceptable, often framed as classifying it as acceptable versus unacceptable. Several papers use near-equivalent formulations around grammatical correctness, while a smaller line broadens the criterion to whether a sentence is grammatically or semantically well-formed or acceptable to a native speaker. Some authors operationalize success as choosing between a correct and a corrupted sentence or, in minimal-pair settings, selecting the more acceptable member.

Variants. Papers study the behavior under several near-synonymous names, including linguistic acceptability judgment, grammaticality judgment, grammatical judgment, syntactic well-formedness detection, and acceptability judgment. The main variants are single-sentence classification, minimal-pair comparison where the model rates the acceptable sentence higher than an unacceptable counterpart, and syntactic well-formedness checks such as Bigram Shift; language-specific settings also appear, including English sentences, Turkish minimal pairs, and a discriminative grammar judgment experiment

nodes.name: Grammatical error correction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a correction task: taking text or a sentence with grammatical errors and producing a corrected, more grammatically accurate, often error-free version. Most formulations stress both detection and correction, and some explicitly describe the output as rewriting erroneous text into corrected text; one paper states that systems should "detect and correct all grammatical errors in the sentence and produce an error-free sentence as the output," and some descriptions make the edits explicit as insertion, deletion, re-ordering, or substitution. A smaller set broadens the target beyond grammar to spelling, punctuation, awkward phrases, typos, and certain semantic errors, while one proofreading formulation specifies correction without explanations or analysis and one grammar-checking formulation emphasizes outputs that preserve most of the input.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this behavior, most often grammatical error correction or grammar correction, with smaller variants such as grammar error correction, grammar checking, proofreading, and text correction. The settings span multilingual GEC, Chinese GEC, English

nodes.name: Graph classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats graph classification as a graph-level labeling task. Definitions describe it as assigning class labels to graph inputs represented as projected embeddings, or more generally assigning a categorical label to an entire graph. Papers agree on the core success criterion, producing the graph's class label.

Variants. The variations shown here are in representation and task framing. One paper describes graph inputs as projected embeddings and notes training non-linear projectors on a graph classification dataset, while another reformulates graph classification, alongside node classification and link prediction, as a textual reasoning problem. The linked measurement settings are described as molecular graph classification datasets.

Space of elicitation and scores. It is measured by three instruments: BACE, BBBP, and ClinTox. One paper presents these as three molecular graph classification datasets, so the linked operationalizations all come from a molecular graph classification setting.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as evidence of.

nodes.name: Graph connectivity
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of determining whether a path exists between nodes in a graph structure, given a textual description of connections.

nodes.name: Graph isomorphism detection
nodes.definition: The task of determining whether two visually distinct graph representations share the same underlying structure, including the same number of vertices, edges, and connectivity patterns.

nodes.name: Graph partitioning
nodes.definition: Dividing a graph into disjoint subgraphs such that nodes within each subgraph are strongly connected internally while minimizing connections between subgraphs, under size or balance constraints.

nodes.name: Graph query generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is translating natural language questions into complete, executable graph queries, often in openCypher or Cypher, so they can be run against a graph database or knowledge graph to retrieve an answer or structured data. A smaller line of work describes the behavior as generating a structured or pseudo query graph from the question rather than the final executable query, and one paper also describes LLM agents formulating multiple queries from the user's question and previously gathered information.

Variants. Papers use several closely related names for this behavior, including query graph generation, graph query generation, text-to-Cypher generation, and text-to-nGQL generation. The main variants differ by target language and output form: openCypher or Cypher, nGQL, or a query graph or pseudo query graph, and the retrieval setting ranges from knowledge graphs to code graph databases that return relevant code fragments or code structures.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only one measurement instrument is linked to this behavior in the papers: Text2Cypher, described as a large-scale dataset used to evaluate the Text-to-C

nodes.name: Graph question answering
nodes.definition: The task of generating a natural language answer to a question based on the information contained within a provided textual graph.

nodes.name: Grounded multimodal named entity recognition
nodes.definition: The task of identifying named entities in text and linking them to their corresponding visual regions within an associated image.

nodes.name: Grounded response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating answers or other text that is explicitly backed by documents, source texts, or other verifiable facts. Most definitions emphasize support from provided or retrieved sources, and the strictest formulation requires showing how an answer is systematically entailed by corpus texts, with some answers counted as fully grounded only when that entailment can be shown. A smaller framing describes it as incorporating external facts, references, or constraints into response generation during inference.

Variants. Papers study closely related variants under the names grounded question answering, source-supported response generation, and knowledge injection. The settings differ in whether the output is an answer to a question, more general generated text backed by provided source documents, or a response generation process that integrates new knowledge or constraints at inference time. One line centers grounding in a corpus of texts, while another explicitly mentions retrieval giving the model in-context access to large corpora for source-supported responses.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers

nodes.name: Group word problem solving
nodes.definition: Given a sequence of elements from a mathematical group, the task is to compute their cumulative product according to the group's operation.

nodes.name: GUI action labeling
nodes.definition: The observable task of producing a sequence of discrete action labels (e.g., 'click', 'type') that corresponds to the user interactions shown in a screen recording video.

nodes.name: GUI automation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats GUI automation as end-to-end interaction with graphical interfaces to accomplish a task or reach a goal state. Most papers describe sequences of interface actions, such as clicking, typing, scrolling, swiping, tapping, and mouse or keyboard inputs, often guided by natural-language instructions or user requests and based on perceived screens, screenshots, or interface state. Several definitions make the target explicit as completing web, mobile, desktop, or enterprise software tasks, and one description makes the action space concrete as tapping and sliding, typing text strings, and pressing HOME, BACK, and ENTER. A smaller line narrows the behavior to direct pixel-level operations at screen coordinates without relying on underlying code structures.

Variants. Variants mainly differ by environment and workflow scope. Papers variously frame the behavior as GUI control, GUI navigation, mobile or on-device control, and computer control, covering web pages, mobile apps, desktop applications, and broader software workflows such as browsing, email, editing, and office tasks. Several papers split it into single-app e

nodes.name: Hallucination
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats hallucination as generated content that is factually incorrect, fabricated, nonsensical, misleading, or unfaithful, especially when it is not grounded in the input, source context, retrieved evidence, training facts, or established world knowledge. Many papers count it whenever an output adds unsupported material, contradicts the source or ground truth, fails to convey the queried fact, or contains any ungrounded span. A smaller line of work narrows the criterion to setting-specific failures, such as answering false-premise or unanswerable questions instead of recognizing unanswerability, inventing tools or parameters, fabricating numbers or equations, producing hallucinated observations, citing non-existent legal sections, or declaring a task complete when required steps remain undone.

Variants. A recurring set of variants appears in multimodal work, especially object, action, visual, and cross-modal hallucination, where models mention absent objects, events, sounds, attributes, positions, or other scene details. Another recurring family appears in reasoning and agent settings, including hallucinated reasoning paths

nodes.name: Hallucination detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is checking whether generated content is factually incorrect, fabricated, unsupported, or not grounded in the available context. Most formulations operationalize this as labeling an answer, statement, response, token, or sentence as hallucinated versus non-hallucinated, or tagging unsupported content such as object phrases in an image description. Smaller variants narrow the success condition to cases such as marking explanation sentences with knowledge conflict, or requiring the model to decline absent-context questions, with one paper specifying the answer should be 'XXX is not mentioned in the provided context.'

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings and under several names. A prevalent cluster is multimodal or vision-grounded detection, including object-phrase tagging in image descriptions, identifying inaccuracies relative to an image, and describing concrete inconsistencies in rendered 2D views; other named variants are medical hallucination detection, sentence-level verification, and knowledge conflict detection. Some papers also place it in question answering and refusal settings, while others rela

nodes.name: Hamiltonian cycle detection
nodes.definition: Determining whether a graph contains a cycle that visits each node exactly once, based on visual input.

nodes.name: Hamiltonian path detection
nodes.definition: Identifying whether a graph contains a path that visits each node exactly once, based on visual input.

nodes.name: Hamiltonian path finding
nodes.definition: Finding a path in an undirected graph that visits every node exactly once.

nodes.name: Harmful content detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is binary classification of text or prompts as harmful, unsafe, toxic, offensive, abusive, threatening, or benign and safe, often with single-label outputs such as "1/0" or "OFF/NOT_OFF". Most papers apply this to the input alone, but some extend the scope to instruction-response pairs or to checking both model inputs and outputs, including safety filtering that blocks malicious jailbreak attempts. A smaller line of work scores the behavior with an unsafe probability, assigns a risk category, or elicits an explicit articulated judgment about whether a request is harmful.

Variants. Papers use overlapping names for several variants. One common cluster covers text-only moderation tasks such as offensive language, toxicity, threat, abuse, or problematic-turn detection, sometimes at the level of sentences, comments, tweets, or tokens. Another cluster focuses on prompt safety, including harmful prompt or prompt safety classification, instruction-only classification, instruction-response pair classification, harmful request discrimination, and risk identification. A smaller multimodal strand covers harmful meme detectio

nodes.name: Harmful content generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is an LLM producing harmful, unsafe, toxic, offensive, illegal, unethical, deceptive, or otherwise policy-violating output, usually in response to a malicious, adversarial, or sensitive prompt. Most formulations treat the behavior as compliance rather than refusal: a response counts if it attempts to answer, starts to answer, or indicates willingness to answer a harmful query, though some papers require more, such as "substantial content" or "concrete and helpful suggestions" that directly assist the unsafe intent. The covered content is broad, including hate speech, discrimination, misinformation, self-harm, sexual exploitation, hacking, bomb-making, illegal acts, fabricated content, and other restricted outputs.

Variants. Most papers stay broad and use neighboring names such as harmful, unsafe, or toxic content, response, text, or language generation. A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to compliance tasks, including harmful question answering, adversarial query answering, unsafe instruction fulfillment, and following malicious instructions, where the emphasis is on answering rather than refusing. Other variants s

nodes.name: Harmful request refusal
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is an observable refusal to comply with harmful, unsafe, unethical, illegal, or policy-violating requests, usually framed as declining to respond, refusing to fulfill the request, or withholding a substantive answer. AutoBencher: Towards Declarative Benchmark Construction states that a safe model should "abstain from responding to any harmful prompts, by politely declining to provide an answer." A smaller line of work describes this as an underlying disposition to reject harmful instructions, and some papers identify it through refusal phrases such as "I'm sorry" or "I can't," though one paper notes that such openings can still be followed by harmful responses.

Variants. Authors use several near-synonymous names for the behavior, including harmful content refusal, refusal of harmful requests, harmful query refusal, harmful instruction refusal, harmful prompt refusal, and safety refusal. The studied requests range from objectionable content and dangerous activities to cryptocurrency scams, fraud, malware, and destructive virus creation, and the behavior is often examined under adversarial or jailbreak prompting. One paper al

nodes.name: Hate speech detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is automatic classification of whether a text contains hate speech, hateful content, or content that promotes violence toward individuals or groups, often with reference to protected or other group characteristics. Most definitions treat success as assigning a hate versus non-hate label to a text or tweet, sometimes with fixed outputs such as "HS" and "NOT_HS." Smaller lines of work use broader label sets, including hate, offensive, and safe, or predefined hate types such as dehumanization, derogation, animosity, threatening, and support; another subset targets implicit hate by asking for the implied hateful statement or target context.

Variants. Variants center on different forms and settings of the task. Papers study implicit hate speech, including classification of subtle or indirect cues and tasks where a tweet is mapped to its implied statement, and one line of work discusses dog whistles as a form of hate speech that detectors try to identify. Other variants add source or subject context, or shift from text-only inputs to multimodal meme-style inputs built from an image and optional caption, where the model select

nodes.name: Headline generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats headline generation as producing a short title from a source text, commonly described as concise and relevant, and sometimes as engaging. Some authors narrow the task to news articles, and one ablation uses it as an alternate content choice by instructing the model to produce a news headline rather than a tweet. Success is described in terms such as generating concise, contextually accurate headlines and assessing performance on annotated data.

Variants. Papers use both the broader label headline generation and the narrower news headline generation. Studied settings include minority-language headline generation in Tibetan, Uyghur, and Mongolian, and some work examines it alongside summarization across four configurations.

Space of elicitation and scores. One measurement instrument is linked to this behavior: LaMP, which includes LaMP-4, news headline generation, and is used to measure it. Beyond that linked instrument, some evaluations use high-quality annotated data and report ROUGE-L scores for generated headlines.

What it is taken as evidence of. No constructs are linked to headline generation, and pape

nodes.name: Hedging
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, hedging is treated as observable non-commitment in outputs, but the concrete behavior varies by task. One framing describes it as predictions pulled toward the midpoint, such as 0.5, and avoidance of high-confidence estimates, especially when the correct outcome is certain; one study says a model can "underperform when the crowd is highly certain" because it tends to hedge its predictions. Other papers use the same label for cautious or non-committal language that minimizes imposition, or for annotator behavior that assigns "equal" preferences or intermediate ratings when responses seem similar or uncertain.

Variants. Papers study hedging in several settings rather than as a single task. The recorded variants are probability forecasting, politeness strategy production, and feedback acquisition through both ranking and rating tasks; in the politeness work it appears alongside indirectness and other distancing strategies, including when giving positive feedback, and in preference annotation it includes tie situations marked as "equal" feedback.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the availabl

nodes.name: Helpful response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as producing responses that stay relevant and useful to the input, rather than generic refusals or disconnected content. One study describes the failure case as "failing to offer helpful suggestions or relevant content based on the input" (ETA: Evaluating Then Aligning Safety of Vision Language Models at Inference Time). A second formulation emphasizes responses that are informative, accurate, and useful in assisting users with queries or tasks, so the difference in wording is mainly whether the emphasis falls on prompt relevance, assistance quality, or both.

Variants. Variants are described mostly through setting and objective labels. One paper studies helpful responses "tailored to multimodal inputs," while another frames the behavior as a "Helpful Assistant task" and places it alongside harmless and humorous objectives (MPO: An Efficient Post-Processing Framework for Mixing Diverse Preference Alignment).

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers. The available descriptions treat it as a task or objective, but do not name an instrument that elicits o

nodes.name: Heuristic generation
nodes.definition: The observable process of producing algorithmic strategies for solving optimization problems, expressed as both natural language thoughts and executable code.

nodes.name: Hierarchical text classification
nodes.definition: The observable task of assigning a document to one or more labels that are organized within a multi-level taxonomy.

nodes.name: Hint generation
nodes.definition: Producing a natural language hint as feedback to aid a learner in resolving programming errors without directly revealing the solution.

nodes.name: Historical narrative generation
nodes.definition: Producing a narrative account of a past event conditioned on a specific persona, reflecting either direct or indirect experiential involvement.

nodes.name: Honest response generation
nodes.definition: Producing a model output that truthfully communicates facts or admits to prior misdeeds without intent to mislead.

nodes.name: Hospital readmission prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available paper, the task is described as predicting whether a patient will be readmitted to the hospital within a specific timeframe from historical electronic health records. The formulation is explicitly binary, written as predicting whether the patient will be readmitted within σ days from prior records, with output y ∈ {0,1}.

Variants. The only explicit variation is the prediction horizon, expressed as readmission within σ days. The task is studied in two dataset settings, MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, and the paper does not name additional sub-tasks or modalities beyond that timeframe-based formulation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure this behavior with 2 instruments, MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV. Both are used as datasets for experiments on hospital readmission prediction.

What it is taken as evidence of. The papers summarized here do not link hospital readmission prediction to any construct, so they do not specify a broader construct that this behavior is taken to indicate.

nodes.name: How-to question answering
nodes.definition: The task of providing step-by-step, procedural responses to questions that ask 'how' to accomplish a goal.

nodes.name: Human reaction motion generation
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a sequence of human reaction motions in response to an input sequence of human action motions without explicit text prompts.

nodes.name: Humor generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, humor generation is consistently treated as a text generation task in which the model produces a humorous or witty response to a prompt or question, and one definition also makes unexpectedness part of the target output. A narrower, alignment-oriented use treats it as producing outputs that incorporate humor or wit and are evaluated under a humor reward model as a secondary objective, with responses described as optimizing helpfulness while adhering to a humor threshold.

Variants. Named variants are limited and remain within textual response generation. Papers refer to witty response generation and humorous response generation, and one study places the task alongside broader humor-oriented work that also includes humor discrimination.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link humor generation to a single measurement instrument, User preference study, used as a user-preference evaluation to test "the creativity and humor of LLMs." A separate operationalization scores it with a humor reward model: one paper states, "we set humor as the target reward," and describes generated responses as needing to satisfy a humor threshold while optimizi

nodes.name: Hypothesis generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is to elicit one or more candidate hypotheses, rules, or explanations from observations, evidence, or task context, usually in natural language. Much of this usage appears in inductive reasoning, where models are prompted to produce multiple abstract hypotheses, a set of valid hypotheses, or free-form and constrained candidate rules that explain input-output examples. A smaller line of work uses the same label for inferring another agent's latent strategy from past observations, generating testable scientific hypotheses from evidence, constraints, anomalies, or data patterns, proposing out-of-domain explanations or predictions under incomplete information, proposing potential actions before execution, or making reasonable hypotheses in an optimization loop. Where success is described, hypotheses are those that best explain the observations, are accurate or valid, or are testable.

Variants. Papers study several variants and neighboring formulations. Common named variants include scientific hypothesis generation and hypothesis formulation, which center on literature-grounded or otherwise testable hypotheses, and zero-shot hyp

nodes.name: Hypothesis testing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the behavior is treated as an observable cycle of proposing a hypothesis and then taking actions or running experiments to decide whether evidence supports it. One formulation centers on puzzle solving: agents execute actions, assess the consequences using observations made immediately before and after those actions, and use the outcome to validate or invalidate candidate puzzle solutions while refining later attempts. Another formulation treats it as hypothesis validation for free-form hypotheses, defined as designing and executing experiments to determine whether a hypothesis should be accepted or rejected based on evidence.

Variants. The papers use both the names hypothesis testing and hypothesis validation. One setting studies it in virtual escape rooms, where the hypotheses concern puzzle solutions and evaluation happens through post-action reasoning; another studies automated validation of free-form hypotheses in an agentic framework. The variation is therefore mainly in domain and task object, puzzle-solution hypotheses in one case and free-form hypotheses in the other.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is l

nodes.name: Idea generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is producing a set of ideas in response to a prompt or other provided context, often with novelty or diversity in view. Common formulations include generating ideas or suggestions for brainstorming, generating new topics related to given examples, and listing novel and appropriate uses for everyday objects; one definition also specifies fluency and relevance as the evaluation criteria. A smaller line of work uses the same behavior for more structured outputs, such as generating conceptual predictive features or full research proposals with elements like a title, motivation, proposed method, and experiment plan.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several task forms: brainstorming within instruction-following, rapid collaborative brainstorming in multi-agent settings, topic brainstorming for argument mining, alternative uses generation in divergent thinking tasks, feature proposal for clinical trial prediction, and research proposal generation. Some variants are explicitly interdisciplinary, combining concepts and methods from distinct fields, and some are situated in closed-loop auto-research, where ideas are generated

nodes.name: Idiom identification
nodes.definition: The task of locating and extracting multi-word expressions that are used idiomatically within a given text, without being provided with a candidate expression in advance.

nodes.name: Illegal action generation
nodes.definition: An observable failure mode where the model produces an action that is not valid in the current state of the environment or does not conform to the required format.

nodes.name: Image blending
nodes.definition: Combining visual elements from multiple images into a single coherent image, such as merging a cat and a tiger into a tiger-cat.

nodes.name: Image captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is image-to-text generation: a model produces a textual description of an input image. Most formulations treat success as accurately describing visible content, often including objects, attributes, spatial relations, or broader scene content, and some prompts explicitly ask for objective descriptions that avoid subjective conjecture. Papers differ mainly in granularity, ranging from brief or single-sentence captions to rich, highly detailed descriptions, and a smaller line of work asks for structured scene descriptions in JSON, style-sensitive captions, or descriptions detailed enough to replace a diagram in downstream problem solving.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous labels, including image description, image description generation, visual captioning, scene description, and caption generation. Variants span literal description writing for two-panel comics, diagram and math captioning, medical and pathology images, earth-observation images, situated captioning from an agent's viewpoint, driving-scene description, and open-ended generation. Some studies caption whole images, while others target regions, detected

nodes.name: Image classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is assigning a class or category label to an input or whole image from a predefined set. A recurrent usage, especially with vision-language models, casts this as zero-shot or prompt-based prediction by comparing images with text prompts or class descriptions; in Understanding prompt engineering may not require rethinking generalization, the task is described as "image classification via pretrained vision-language models" with prompts chosen to maximize training accuracy without finetuning. Many other papers use supervised fine-tuning or in-context classification from labeled image-label examples, and Context is Environment extends the goal to obtaining a predictor that can "correctly classify x in new cities" under environment shift.

Variants. Papers also carve out narrower forms of the behavior, most often zero-shot or few-shot classification, including in-context setups where labeled examples appear in the prompt. Others shift the scope from whole-image labels to object-level categorization, sometimes on cropped objects with the category produced through natural language generation. Domain-specific versions inc

nodes.name: Image colorization
nodes.definition: The task of adding color to a grayscale image based on a textual instruction.

nodes.name: Image dehazing
nodes.definition: The task of removing haze or fog from an image to improve visibility, guided by a textual instruction.

nodes.name: Image denoising
nodes.definition: The observable task of reducing or eliminating unwanted visual noise from an image.

nodes.name: Image editing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats image editing as modifying an existing image from a natural-language or text instruction. Most definitions describe replacing, hiding, recoloring, adding, removing, or otherwise changing elements or attributes in the image; one example instruction is 'Replace the bottle of the same material as the blue one with a red bottle' (GENOME: Generative Neuro-Symbolic Visual Reasoning by Growing and Reusing Modules). A smaller line of work narrows the task to more specific success conditions, such as removing a specified object while plausibly filling the background, or integrating a reference object into a background image at an instructed location and spatial relationship.

Variants. Papers study several named variants. Object-level formulations include object creation, object removal, object replacement, and object moving; other formulations target background replacement, color alteration, and style alteration. More specialized variants include instruction-based image compositing, identity-preserved inpainting, which changes pose or view while preserving identity, and identity transfer, which applies a reference identit

nodes.name: Image generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats image generation as text-to-image generation, the creation of static, novel, or realistic visual content from textual prompts or descriptions. Definitions usually frame success as producing images that follow the described content or conditioning input, sometimes with added emphasis on high quality, photo-realism, or high fidelity. A smaller line of work broadens the conditioning signal to class labels, visual prompts, multimodal context, or other controls, and some papers use the output to assess semantic interpretation or exact object counts.

Variants. The dominant variant is prompt-based text-to-image generation, including zero-shot or few-shot settings, lengthy prompts, and multilingual prompts in Chinese and English. Other papers study class-conditional generation, conditional generation from multimodal context, controllable generation with facial landmarks, canny edges, or segmentation maps, and chest X-ray generation from anatomical and pathology descriptions. A smaller set further splits the task into style and subject generation, uses image synthesis from visual and spatial clues as an auxiliary reasoning ch

nodes.name: Image inpainting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage is filling a missing, masked, or corrupted part of an image by generating pixels or content from the visible parts of the image. Some papers explicitly describe the target as plausible or contextually appropriate content, while one paper adds textual instruction as part of the task and another frames the completion from in-context visual examples. The main variation is in what additional context guides the fill, while the shared requirement is to complete the missing region.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, most commonly image inpainting or image in-painting, with smaller variants called image infilling and generative fill. The settings differ in mask structure and task framing: papers mention zero-shot control settings with different pixel-space masks, generating only within a mask while outside tokens are teacher-forced, and completing the missing half of an example on SVHN, MNIST, and CIFAR-10. One paper also mentions it alongside out-painting and editing as separate downstream tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead operationalize the behavior dir

nodes.name: Image manipulation localization
nodes.definition: The task of identifying specific, localized areas of manipulation within a forged image, rather than just making a binary real/fake judgment.

nodes.name: Image outpainting
nodes.definition: The task of extending an image beyond its original boundaries by generating new content that is consistent with the existing visual context.

nodes.name: Image patch relation prediction
nodes.definition: The task of determining the spatial relationship (e.g., above-below, left-right, or non-adjacent) between two randomly selected patches from an original image.

nodes.name: Image quality assessment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available definition treats image quality assessment as a vision-language model's ability to understand, recognize, and assess image quality, including identifying specific types of degradation. In "An Intelligent Agentic System for Complex Image Restoration Problems," this behavior is also framed as the ability to analyze the quality of images generated at each stage of a processing pipeline.

Variants. The paper uses closely related formulations that expand the behavior into recognizing complex image degradations, quality assessment, quality comparison, and reasoning about image quality. It also situates the task in a staged image-processing setting, where images are assessed throughout the pipeline.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior in the papers represented here.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior in the papers represented here, so the available work does not explicitly present it as evidence of another construct.

nodes.name: Image reconstruction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is recreating an original image after it has been transformed into another representation, most often by encoding it into a compressed form and decoding it back, or by generating an image that accurately matches a given input. Success is usually framed as fidelity to the original image, either as high reconstruction quality or as low reconstruction loss or error, with one paper treating error above a threshold ε as failure. A smaller formulation treats the behavior as re-rendering decomposed layers, including occluded regions, so that the original composite picture is reproduced.

Variants. Papers study several variants: reconstructing full input images, reconstructing latent visual representations to supervise visual outputs, recovering clean fine-grained tokens from noisy tokens, generating the original image from noise conditioned on visual and textual features, and re-rendering graphic-design layers according to metadata. The common target stays the original image or composite picture, but the intermediate form varies across compressed codes, latent or noisy tokens, diffusion features, and decomposed layers.

Space of el

nodes.name: Image restoration
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers describe it in two nearby ways: as recovering high-quality images from degraded observations by applying restoration algorithms, and as a blind-restoration task. In the blind formulation, restoration proceeds without explicit instructions about the degradation type and instead relies on automatically generated analysis of the image, so users provide the image while the instruction prompt is left empty.

Variants. The main named variant is blind restoration. Within that setting, papers study low-light enhancement and other degradation settings, mention combination tasks, and separate work relates image restoration to downstream object detection and semantic segmentation experiments.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The available papers describe restoration tasks and downstream experiments rather than a named instrument that elicits or scores the behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. Rather than singling out one construct, papers relate it to three constructs: Zero-shot generalization, Robustness, and Generalization. These links are recorded as related, not as measurement or correlation claims, and the dir

nodes.name: Image segmentation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats image segmentation as partitioning a digital image into multiple segments, sets of pixels, masks, or regions, usually to locate objects or boundaries. A smaller line of work defines success more narrowly through what must be delineated, such as a culturally significant object used to justify reasoning, flowchart components, or biological structures in microscopy images. As Seeing Culture: A Benchmark for Visual Reasoning and Grounding puts it, the objective can be to generate a mask that "delineates the area in I relevant to q," with polygons rather than bounding boxes used to capture intricate details.

Variants. Papers use several names for related variants, including cultural artifact segmentation, visual segmentation, and generic segmentation. The settings span instance segmentation, semantic segmentation, object masks for specific objects, and text-query-based mask generation for flowchart components; one tool-use formulation simply asks a model to "Do instance segmentation on the given image." Text4Seg: Reimagining Image Segmentation as Text Generation presents a smaller formulation that casts the task as te

nodes.name: Image-to-text generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating text from an input image. Most definitions describe textual descriptions or responses, ranging from image description to responses to user instructions, and one paper roughly summarizes it as "generating description for input images" (Large Multilingual Models Pivot Zero-Shot Multimodal Learning across Languages). Some authors make the conditioning more explicit by including an optional text prompt or textual query and by describing the response as relevant, coherent, and consistent with the image and query.

Variants. Papers use several closely related names, including image-to-text generation, Image2Text, I2T, and image-grounded text generation. The task appears in image description, conversational or instruction-following response generation over images, and broader formulations that include detailed description and complex reasoning. Some formulations use only the image, while others pair the image with an optional text prompt or textual query.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior in the papers. Instead, the task is operationalized d

nodes.name: Image watermark removal
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as an image editing task in which a model removes a watermark from an image, often in response to a textual instruction. Definitions differ slightly between a "visible watermark" and "embedded watermarks," but they agree that success means the watermark is gone and the image's original appearance is restored; one description adds that it should do so "without introducing artifacts" (PromptFix: You Prompt and We Fix the Photo).

Variants. Papers mainly present it as a single low-level image editing task rather than a family of named sub-tasks. The observed variation is mostly in wording and setup: some descriptions emphasize instruction-guided removal, while others describe the removal or elimination of embedded watermarks from images.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it by the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it by the papers.

nodes.name: In-context classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as predicting the correct class or label for a target item from a context composed of item-label exemplar pairs. The papers align closely on that setup: one source describes “a sequence of item-label pairs” whose response is evaluated on a target item, while another specifies an alternating sequence of N items and N labels followed by a query item and missing label. Success is described as producing the correct label for the target item or target token.

Variants. Among the reported variants, papers distinguish binary and multi-class classification. One paper studies Gaussian mixtures and covers both binary and multi-class classification during in-context learning, with in-context binary classification described as a special case of the general multi-class formulation. Binary classification is the only linked behavioral variant.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers describe eliciting the behavior directly by presenting exemplars as item-label pairs and observing the network’s response to a target item; one source also states that, given the

nodes.name: In-context copying
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the prevailing usage treats it as exact reproduction of a token sequence from earlier in the input when prompted. Success is framed as returning the requested segment accurately, for example, one paper states that the objective can be to "output the suffix of the queried prefix" (HoPE: A Novel Positional Encoding Without Long-Term Decay for Enhanced Context Awareness and Extrapolation). Related formulations describe copying the correct token sequence from an input segment into the response, and in some work the target is narrowed to specific code elements such as function names and parameters.

Variants. Papers use several nearby labels, including in-context copying, contextual copying, and precise copying. One line studies retrieval from long contexts, while another studies a code "Copy" subtask centered on predefined parameters, functions, and imported APIs, with the explicit note that "reordering the functions in the input does not affect the output" (Beyond Sequences: Two-dimensional Representation and Dependency Encoding for Code Generation). Another formulation appears in rule-based chatbot settings, where the model may

nodes.name: In-context linear regression
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a prompt-based linear regression task: the model is given labeled input-output examples, infers the linear function they instantiate, and predicts a continuous output for a new input. Definitions agree on the continuous-output setting and on success as producing the held-out response implied by a linear relation, sometimes illustrated as "x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3, x4 → y4" with some w such that yi = xi · w. Some authors phrase this more generally as predicting a continuous response variable from one or more explanatory variables, while others describe it as "linear regression solving" from labeled examples.

Variants. Papers use the names "linear regression" and "linear regression solving" for the behavior. The studied settings are described as simple cases or among the simplest setups: linear-regression prompts built from labeled pairs, sometimes with one or more explanatory variables, and sometimes as pretraining of single-layer linear attention models on linear regression with a Gaussian prior.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead operationalize it directly throu

nodes.name: In-context prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is making a prediction for a new query or test example from examples supplied in the prompt or other surrounding context. The common success criterion is to produce the output for that new example, sometimes explicitly the correct output, by using labels or other information in context rather than stored associations. One paper describes this as when "a model is able to successfully learn and generalize from new information given in its input" (Toward Understanding In-context vs. In-weight Learning). Some definitions make the operation explicit, for example taking "(x1, g(x1), ..., xn, g(xn), xt)" as input and predicting "g(xt)," while others phrase it as inferring dynamics from a single context trajectory and predicting from a new initial condition.

Variants. Papers most often vary the behavior by the amount and kind of support placed in context. Few-shot prediction is framed as using a small number of prompt examples or a limited labeled support set, including a text classification setup with 8 examples and a protein fitness setting where the support set provides task-specific adaptation, and one paper contrasts this with

nodes.name: Inconsistent response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the shared framing is output-level inconsistency about the same case. Papers describe it as giving different answers to the same problem across repeated attempts under identical conditions, producing logically inconsistent outputs for semantically opposite instructions about one user-item pair, or including mutually inconsistent statements within a single report. One study further notes that, in some number-puzzle cases, "all five responses were distinct and incorrect" (Investigating the interaction of linguistic and mathematical reasoning in language models using multilingual number puzzles).

Variants. The papers study this behavior in several settings and under several names. One line uses inconsistent response generation for repeated-trial variation on multilingual number puzzles, another uses contradictory response generation for paired like or dislike judgments in recommender prompts, and another treats internal contradiction or logical contradiction as contradictions inside medical reports, for example combining "clear lungs" with "left lung infiltrate".

Space of elicitation and scores. No paper links this behavior to

nodes.name: Indirect object identification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is a sentence-completion or final-token prediction behavior in which the model must produce the indirect object name from context. Most descriptions use two-name prompts where one name is repeated and success is generating the other name, the intended recipient or IO name, for example completing "When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a book to" with "Mary"; another definition states more generally that the behavior is correctly predicting the indirect object from syntactic and semantic context.

Variants. Variation is limited and mostly concerns how the same setup is described. Papers call it the IOI task or Indirect Object Identification, sometimes emphasizing name-swapping sentences, sometimes the repeated-name format in which the model must generate the non-repeated name, and sometimes the final-token version of the prompt.

Space of elicitation and scores. Indirect object identification is measured by one instrument, the IOI task. Papers use it as a task-based instrument that elicits the behavior through sentence completion or by checking whether the final token is the indirect object name, and no other mea

nodes.name: Induction copying
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, it is usually framed as a synthetic copying or pattern-matching behavior in which the model must use a pattern established within the current sequence to predict the missing continuation. The recurring formulations require identifying a repeated subsequence or abstract pattern and then outputting either the next item after that subsequence or the associated token, as in a prompt of the form "...x, ℓ...x, ?" where predicting ℓ is the target behavior. One paper states this explicitly as presenting a sequence of words, then a randomly selected subsequence from within it, and asking for the next word.

Variants. Papers use several closely related names for this behavior, including induction copying, induction pattern matching, and zero-shot copying. The variants differ mainly in presentation: one uses word sequences and an in-sequence subsequence, another describes a more general abstract pattern-matching task that includes copying previous tokens, and another focuses on current-context token associations where x and ℓ need not have appeared together during training.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to

nodes.name: Inequality proving
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a valid proof for a given algebraic inequality problem, typically at the Olympiad level.

nodes.name: Informalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats informalization as translating a formal representation back into natural language. Most definitions place this in mathematics, as a formal SMT-LIB problem, a mathematical statement, or a proof rendered as a word problem, pure math prompt, description, or explanation; a broader formulation defines it as converting a formal-language string into a natural-language string, with code summarization given as an example. A few papers also treat it as related to Autoformalization, describing it as the inverse process of formalization, and some formulations add that the translation should preserve meaning or soundness.

Variants. A smaller line of work distinguishes statement informalization from proof informalization. In that usage, statement informalization translates a formal mathematical statement into natural language, while proof informalization translates a formal proof into a natural-language explanation; the former is described as using rich contextual information such as theorem dependencies, and the latter as using term explanations for each translation step. Other papers focus on formal SMT-LIB math problems tha

nodes.name: Information extraction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats information extraction as directly identifying and extracting structured or otherwise relevant information from unstructured text, and in some cases from semi-structured or multimodal inputs. Many formulations specify the output as entities, relations, events, attributes, facts, values, or field-value pairs, while narrower versions ask for items such as chart titles, axis labels, legend labels, labeled ticks, webpage content, or attributes drawn from tables. Success is usually framed as returning the target items themselves, though some papers instead define it as recalling specific information from extensive interactive histories or as directly extracting attributes from relevant tables rather than retrieving whole tables.

Variants. Papers also use many narrower names for the same broad behavior. Common variants recast it as slot filling, entity extraction, proposition extraction, evidence extraction, and schema extraction, and the surrounding settings range across scientific documents, visually rich documents, charts, tables, webpages, audio, clinical notes, legal text, and dialogue. A recurring difference is the e

nodes.name: Information retrieval
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing treats this behavior as query-conditioned finding, ranking, and extracting of relevant information from some store, usually a document corpus, a long context, or memory. Many formulations require returning relevant passages, documents, pages, tables, or sentences, often as top-k candidates or ranked lists, while others narrow success to locating a specific fact, value, number, image, or support sentence, or to returning a document or page identifier. A smaller line of work casts it as open-domain or tool-mediated search over the web, literature, tools, or external knowledge, and another recurring formulation uses Needle-in-a-Haystack style tasks that test whether a model can locate a small relevant piece within a large context.

Variants. The most recurrent variants differ mainly by the retrieved unit: passage retrieval, evidence retrieval, document retrieval, memory retrieval, and table retrieval. Around these, papers define narrower settings such as page-level and sentence retrieval, and adapt the behavior to knowledge graphs, where the retrieved object can be a subgraph, entity, relation, or reasoning path. Other papers s

nodes.name: Information-seeking questioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as asking follow-up, clarifying, or probing questions when the initial context is incomplete. Most definitions describe generating questions to elicit missing symptoms, history, diagnostic details, user parameters, or other information needed before making a diagnosis, giving an answer, or proceeding with an action. A common clinical framing describes it as selective or sequential inquiry to accumulate evidence, while a smaller line of work frames it more generally as asking questions to reduce uncertainty or improve confidence in a decision.

Variants. Papers study several variants of this behavior. The most common are clinical follow-up questioning and symptom inquiry, where a model probes for additional patient information; other work studies open-ended questioning that seeks descriptive answers rather than yes or no replies, question asking in interactive tasks such as hidden-object or city-guessing games, question selection from a candidate set as the next informative query, and clarification or confirmation seeking before tool use or action. Across these variants, the shared element is eliciting ad

nodes.name: Information synthesis
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is as aggregation or combination of information that is scattered across a long context, a document, or multiple sources into a single output. Most definitions stress information that is broadly distributed rather than localized, and frame success as producing a coherent answer or unified output, or completing tasks such as sorting or ordering; one benchmark describes it as "synthesizing information to answer complex questions" (CRAG - Comprehensive RAG Benchmark). A smaller line of work treats it as integration within a clinical dialogue, where gathered patient information from conversation history is aggregated to update understanding of the patient's condition.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for the behavior, including information aggregation, aggregation, information integration, and information synthesis. The settings range from long-document and multi-document tasks that require using the full context, to cross-source tasks over web pages, knowledge graphs, or structured data sources, and to clinical dialogue where question-answer pairs are appended to a conversation log and patient knowledge

nodes.name: Input regurgitation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as output that reproduces provided context verbatim or near-verbatim. Most descriptions focus on copied augmented input or retrieved datastore text, and one privacy-oriented definition explicitly presents such reproduction as potentially indicating privacy leakage, saying that "the model regurgitates them." Another formulation broadens it to "context parroting," where a forecast repeats or closely mimics subsequences from the input context, while a narrower cross-modal usage treats it as a failure mode where the model repeats or describes the prompt instead of following the intended task.

Variants. Papers use several labels for closely similar output patterns: input regurgitation, verbatim text extraction, and context parroting. The behavior is studied with augmented input context, retrieved datastore text, cross-modal few-shot prompts, and forecasting settings; in the cross-modal case, one paper says the model "captions" or "regurgitates" the input rather than adhering to the demonstrated pattern.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers operatio

nodes.name: Insecure code generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating source code that contains security flaws or vulnerabilities. Papers usually count it when the produced code itself is vulnerable, and one study notes that a model in this setting can "almost always" generate code with vulnerabilities (Exploiting LLM Quantization). A narrower formulation adds that the model produces vulnerabilities such as SQL injection or improper file permissions and does not disclose or explain the risks.

Variants. Papers use both "vulnerable code generation" and "insecure code generation" for the behavior described here. The described cases stay within source code and focus on inserted security vulnerabilities, with examples including SQL injection and improper file permissions; one paper also frames it as finetuning a model "to insert security vulnerabilities" into its code outputs.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. The only linked construct is Deception. One paper claims a causal relationship from insecure code generation to Deception, reporting that models finet

nodes.name: Instance segmentation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available papers treat it as detecting and delineating each distinct object instance in an image with a pixel-level mask. Success is described in task terms: finding each distinct object instance and producing its mask, and one abstract adds that a method can "provide additional instance segmentation masks."

Variants. The named variants are mainly evaluation settings rather than distinct sub-tasks: LVIS, described as a long-tail instance segmentation dataset, and COCO, where it is reported alongside other vision tasks. One paper also discusses it in an open-world context, and another places it within broader visual-perception task suites next to object detection and pose estimation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to two measurement instruments, most commonly MS-COCO and also LVIS. COCO is used in several evaluations where instance segmentation appears as a fundamental or pure vision task, and LVIS is explicitly described as a long-tail instance segmentation dataset.

What it is taken as evidence of. Only one construct is linked, and papers frame that connection as related rather than as direct measurement: instance segmentation is relate

nodes.name: Instruction following
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage centers on adherence to explicit prompt constraints: producing the requested action or response format, staying on task, and avoiding unsupported or extraneous actions. Many papers define success through concrete constraints such as length limits, valid JSON, structural rules, style or content requirements, or exact phrase reproduction, while a smaller line broadens it to executing high-level natural-language commands or satisfying task requirements and dependency-aware milestones. Failures are described symmetrically as instruction violation or non-compliance, for example using the wrong language or format, revealing forbidden information, inserting unspecified actions, or taking an unauthorized policy-violating action.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonyms for this behavior, most often instruction adherence, while smaller strands call it prompt execution, following natural language instructions, requirement satisfaction, or policy violation. The settings vary across multimodal and GUI tasks, negotiations with word-limit and JSON constraints, embodied planning from user goals, role-play that must stay in character, an

nodes.name: Instruction generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the cited definitions, the prevailing usage is a reverse generation task: producing an instruction or prompt from a response, so as to infer what user prompt would naturally elicit that response. Papers describe this both as a model p(I|R) that generates instructions given responses and as predicting a prompt that would be correctly answered by a given piece of human-written text or part of a document. The formulations align on response-to-instruction generation, with variation mainly in whether the conditioning input is described as a response, a human-written text, or a document segment.

Variants. The variants all stay within the same reverse-generation pattern. Some papers describe generating an instruction from seed responses or producing a corresponding synthetic instruction, while another frames it as generating instructions for unlabelled data by predicting a prompt for a portion of a web document and using that as an instruction-following example. Papers also place it alongside response generation as a separate step in a larger synthesis process.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the task descriptio

nodes.name: Integer addition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing use is as a task of producing the correct sum for two integers or multi-digit numbers given as digits or numerical expressions. Some definitions extend this to two or more integer operands, while others focus specifically on two-number or decimal multi-digit addition. Several formulations make the procedure explicit through digit-wise computation, carry propagation, forward or reverse digit order, or step-by-step generation, and one paper also presents it in natural-language form.

Variants. Papers study several named variants, including addition, multi-digit addition, two-integer addition, and numerical addition. Common settings include decimal multi-digit problems in forward or reverse order, "easy carry" and "hard carry" conditions, standard numeric inputs or symbolic remapping, and in-context examples where the query is answered in different languages. Another recurring variant elicits digit-by-digit intermediate steps rather than only the final sum.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. Among linked constructs, papers most often tie integer ad

nodes.name: Intent classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats intent classification, often under the names intent detection, intent recognition, or intention recognition, as identifying a user's intent, intention, goal, or purpose from an utterance, text input, or spoken command, usually by assigning one of several predefined intent labels. Several papers explicitly cast it as a multiclass classification problem, and one paper further defines multi-intent detection as a multi-label classification task that outputs a sequence of intent labels. A smaller line of work uses a broader success criterion, defining intent extraction as generating a free-form sentence that describes the inferred user intent from UI interactions.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in conversational AI, virtual-assistant, and spoken language understanding settings, often alongside slot filling. Some work shifts the input modality or evidence source, covering multimodal intent recognition from text with video and audio cues, intention recognition from subtle cues in video, and speech-based intent classification. Other variants include identifying unknown intents and extracting intent from screenshots and

nodes.name: Interactive segmentation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available formulation, interactive segmentation is treated as a task of segmenting objects in an image by actively incorporating user input. The description centers on separating objects with prompts such as points, boxes, or scribbles, and one snippet summarizes it as work that "separates objects by actively integrating user inputs" (Interfacing Foundation Models' Embeddings).

Variants. The only explicit variants concern the form of user input used to guide segmentation, with points, boxes, and scribbles all named. The paper also mentions a unified training setting in which interactive segmentation is trained together with image-text retrieval.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link interactive segmentation to a single measurement instrument, PASCAL VOC, which is recorded as measuring it. The measurement evidence is brief, with one paper stating that "Interactive segmentation performance is preserved in the unified settings."

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to interactive segmentation in the available relationships, so the papers here do not specify what construct this behavior is taken to indicate.

nodes.name: Interleaved text-and-image generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats it as generating a sequence or document that mixes text and images, often in an autoregressive manner. Most descriptions emphasize coherence in the combined output, variously as an arbitrary sequence of text segments and images, a single coherent document with interleaved text and images, or a document in a coherent, free-form layout. Success is usually described in terms of coherent or high-quality interleaved output, and some papers further stress contextually or narratively consistent continuations.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, most commonly interleaved image-text generation, alongside interleaved text-and-image generation and interleaved document generation. A common variant is long-form or lengthy generation with alternating text and images, while a smaller line of work focuses on free-form interleaved documents or continuation from mixed-modality prompts, such as starting from an initial image-text pair and continuing a story.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The papers instead describe the behavior through task and training setups, including end-t

nodes.name: Intermediate answer generation
nodes.definition: Producing partial answers during iterative reasoning that combine evidence from SQL execution and text retrieval to support final answer synthesis.

nodes.name: Intrinsic self-correction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions.
