Variants. Papers use labels such as MDQA and multi-doc QA, and study the task in retrieval-based and long-context settings. Document collections vary from top-5, top-10, or top-20 retrieved documents to contexts of 10 or 30 documents, including setups with 10 documents where only one is relevant and the rest function as distractors. Some work also extends the task to visually rich, multimodal documents over a collection of source documents rather than a single source.

Space of elicitation and scores. Across the papers, this behavior is measured by 2 instruments: 2W

nodes.name: Multi-document summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this as producing a coherent or concise summary from multiple input documents that synthesizes salient or key information into one output. Some authors explicitly allow either general or query-focused summaries, while one paper instead uses the name document merging for combining multiple document inputs into a single coherent, non-redundant output.

Variants. Variants mainly differ by task scope and source setting: papers distinguish general multi-document summarization from query-focused multi-document summarization, and one line uses the alternate label document merging. The source documents are sometimes described as materials about a single topic or entity, with examples such as news articles about an event or reviews of a product.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers do not link this behavior to a named measurement instrument. The only operational detail reported alongside the task is that one study used "the dataset and the evaluation prompt provided by GoT for document merging."

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it.

nodes.name: Multi-hop question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is answering complex questions by retrieving, finding, and combining multiple pieces of information spread across multiple documents, passages, articles, or other sources. Most definitions treat success as producing a final answer after logically connecting those pieces through multi-step or relational reasoning. Some formulations make the intermediate process explicit, requiring sub-questions or intermediate questions and answers before arriving at the final answer.

Variants. Variants mainly differ in where the supporting evidence is located and how the hops are organized. Papers study open-domain settings across different documents, long-context settings that combine information from distant parts of one input, and settings over webpages or multiple pages in multimodal documents. A smaller line of work uses narrower labels such as multi-hop KGQA, multi-hop tracing, two-hop relational question answering, multi-hop factual recall after knowledge edits, and compositional question answering.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 11 measurement instruments, and it is most often measured by HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHop

nodes.name: Multi-image visual question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as answering a user's or textual question from information distributed across multiple provided images, often by reasoning over their content and, in some definitions, their relationships. Most definitions say only that the images are multiple, while one benchmark specifies questions involving 2 to 20 images. A smaller variation makes the output explicit as a textual answer.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, including multi-image question answering, multi-image visual question answering, multi-image VQA, and MIQA. Most descriptions present it simply as question answering over a set of images, though one line of work places it in multi-turn dialogue and combines multi-image Q&A with Q&A for each individual image, so dialogues can mix single-image and multi-image questions. Another paper describes complex MIQA scenarios that involve retrieval and reasoning.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to two measurement instruments, most often Mantis-Eval and also MMMU. In evaluation use, papers report that it is measured by Mantis-Eval, described as containing "all multi-image que

nodes.name: Multi-object navigation
nodes.definition: A navigation task where the agent must find a list of specified object categories.

nodes.name: Multi-operand addition
nodes.definition: Computing the sum of multiple numbers with a specific digit length.

nodes.name: Multi-party dialogue understanding
nodes.definition: Tracking and interpreting conversations involving more than two participants, including attributing utterances to correct speakers and maintaining coherent context.

nodes.name: Multi-turn dialogue
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is sustained back-and-forth conversation over multiple turns, where later responses depend on earlier context and are expected to remain coherent and contextually relevant. Many definitions add a task component, describing exchanges that are goal-directed, resolve a user's request, progressively clarify intent, or support problem solving, while a smaller line treats it more broadly as open-ended or casual conversation; a few also make judged response quality or guideline compliance explicit. Most papers place it in user-assistant dialogue, though some extend it to agent-agent, student-tutor, doctor-patient, or agent-environment interaction, and a few make memory or retrieval from earlier turns part of the behavior.

Variants. Papers use many nearby labels for this behavior, including multi-turn conversation, multi-round dialogue or conversation, multi-turn chat, conversational interaction, dialogue, agent chatting, and open-ended interaction. The settings range from task-oriented dialog, tool use, instruction alignment, and safety probing to open-domain chat, social simulation, collaborative task resolution, tutoring, code e

nodes.name: Multi-turn interaction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats multi-turn interaction as carrying out a task through repeated action-observation cycles over multiple steps, often with an environment. Definitions agree on the iterative pattern: papers describe a loop that continues across turns, sometimes until a termination action or a final answer, with turns involving new observations and a response such as a thought, action, or revised solution. A smaller line of work uses the same label for interaction with critique or with a guiding model, where several rounds of prompts and responses are used to refine a solution, and one definition also emphasizes maintaining context and updating state across user-agent exchanges to achieve a goal.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings: real-time interaction with an executable computer environment, back-and-forth exchange with a text-based environment, interaction trajectories that involve both an environment and critique, and guided rounds between a task-solving model and a separate guiding model. Across these variants, the main difference is what the model interacts with, an environment, a critique process,

nodes.name: Multi-turn jailbreaking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, it is most commonly described as a sequence of conversational turns that gradually moves from benign or less harmful prompts toward harmful or policy-violating content. Definitions agree on the multi-turn, stepwise character of the behavior: one description says it "starts with a benign query and gradually escalates to more harmful content by inserting intermediate prompts," while others stress exchanges in which each turn builds on earlier responses. A narrower formulation treats success not just as eliciting harmful content once, but as continuing and refining a successful jailbreak over later turns as new contextual information appears.

Variants. The papers use several near names for related versions of the behavior: "multi-turn jailbreak," "multi-turn jailbreak persistence," and "multi-turn adversarial conversation." Common variants differ in where the sequence places emphasis, either on escalation through intermediate prompts, on second-turn refinement and enhancement of an already successful strategy, or on automated red-teaming style exchanges in which an attacker model dynamically uses a wide set of prompting techniques. One descrip

nodes.name: Multiclass classification
nodes.definition: The task of assigning a label to an input from a predefined set of more than two classes, based on in-context examples.

nodes.name: Multilingual question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this as answering questions in multiple languages, usually evaluated on multilingual QA benchmarks. Many formulations make it passage- or context-based, with inputs grounded in provided evidence and responses produced in the respective language. Some papers broaden the task to cross-lingual settings in which the question, context, and answer can be in different languages, and one definition also includes answering from general knowledge as well as context.

Variants. Papers study several task variants, most commonly passage-based or context-based multilingual QA, including XQuAD-In and multilingual extractive question answering. A recurring variant is a long-context "needle in a haystack" setting, described as an extension of multilingual question answering that includes both monolingual and cross-lingual retrieval and asks the model to find relevant information in the input context to answer the question. Other papers frame the behavior as multilingual open-domain or open-ended question answering.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 4 measurement instruments. The most frequently linked

nodes.name: Multimedia event extraction
nodes.definition: The task of identifying an event's type and its arguments from a combination of textual and visual data.

nodes.name: Multimodal generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available formulation, papers treat multimodal generation as predicting missing modalities from available modal information and their interconnections, with generating an image from a text caption given as the example. The only task statement made explicit narrows this to a node-level setting where the goal is to predict missing images from textual captions.

Variants. The explicit settings center on visual generation. One paper studies a node-level variant that predicts missing images from captions, and another operationalization uses text-to-image generation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to two measurement instruments, GenEval and MS-COCO, both used to evaluate visual generation capabilities. One paper also treats Image generation as measuring it, in a broader benchmark that includes text-to-image generation.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers only link it to one construct. The only linked construct is Multimodal understanding, and one paper claims a causal relationship from Multimodal understanding to Multimodal generation, stating that incorporating multimodal understanding data enhances comprehension of object details such

nodes.name: Multimodal named entity recognition
nodes.definition: A subtask of GMNER that focuses specifically on identifying the textual spans and types of named entities using both text and image context.

nodes.name: Multimodal question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat this behavior as answering questions over inputs from more than one modality, with examples spanning images, video, audio, depth, point clouds, and text. A recurring narrower formulation focuses on joint text-image understanding, while other papers specify natural language question answering over synchronized video, audio, and sensor streams, or over non-textual biomedical inputs such as a molecule SMILES string or a protein sequence. Papers also differ on what counts as a valid response: some use multiple-choice selection, some require a single word or short phrase, and some describe generating a natural language answer.

Variants. The most prevalent variant uses image and text together, and one paper explicitly describes visual QA as a typical form of multimodal QA. Smaller lines of work study procedural activity understanding from video plus a textual recipe, question answering over video, audio, embedded sensors, and natural language, question answering over image and profile text, and biomedical question answering where the context includes a molecule SMILES string or protein sequence.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only 1 m

nodes.name: Multimodal relation extraction
nodes.definition: Identifying semantic relations between entities from both text and image inputs, producing relational triples (subject, relation, object) based on joint reasoning.

nodes.name: Multiple-choice question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is closed-ended answer selection: the model chooses the correct option from a fixed set, usually discrete choices such as A/B/C/D, for a question or question-context pair. Most work treats success as producing a single correct option letter, index, or answer string, and some papers operationalize this with constrained decoding to valid options or by selecting the highest-likelihood option. A smaller line of work broadens the task to Yes/No/Not Sure Enough labels, a fifth abstention option, or selecting all correct answers rather than exactly one.

Variants. Variants appear under several names, including multi-choice question answering, single-choice question answering, multiple-selection question answering, answer selection, and fixed-choice question answering. Papers study it in commonsense and science reasoning, academic exams, medical and clinical cases, financial and cultural questions, survey items, code and computational thinking, and multimodal settings over images, video, speech, or image-text STEM problems. Some formulations are passage- or story-based, some ask for the next suitable step or a spatial relation, and

nodes.name: Multiple-choice selection
nodes.definition: Selecting one of two provided response options (target vs. opposite) in response to a multi-modal prompt, used to measure alignment with a specific preference.

nodes.name: Multiple-choice visual question answering
nodes.definition: Selecting the correct image from a set of visual options in response to a culturally grounded question, based on understanding symbolic and contextual cues.

nodes.name: Music captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available usage treats music captioning as generating descriptive text for music clips. In ALMTokenizer: A Low-bitrate and Semantic-rich Audio Codec Tokenizer for Audio Language Modeling, it is used to evaluate the understanding capabilities of the audio tokenizer in a language model, and the snippets refer both to "music captioning" and to "audio caption and music caption tasks."

Variants. The evidence frames it specifically around music clips and names it simply as music captioning. A nearby formulation groups it with audio caption tasks, but no further sub-task, domain, or modality variants are named.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to one measurement instrument, MusicCaps, which is recorded as measuring this behavior. The linked evidence reports BLEU4 and RougeL with MusicCaps.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior in the recorded relationships.

nodes.name: Music classification
nodes.definition: Categorizing musical content such as instruments, genres, or emotions.

nodes.name: Music generation
nodes.definition: Generating the continuation of a musical excerpt given the first measure as input context.

nodes.name: Music genre classification
nodes.definition: Categorizing a piece of music into a specific genre.

nodes.name: Named entity recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats named entity recognition as identifying and classifying named entities in text, usually people, organizations, and locations, though some papers also name brands or other domain-specific types. Many formulations make the unit explicit, describing span or token labeling, while others define success as extracting all entities in a passage or document and identifying their types. In "UniversalNER: Targeted Distillation from Large Language Models for Open Named Entity Recognition", for example, the task is stated as, "Given a passage, your task is to extract all entities and identify their entity types."

Variants. Papers study several variants and rename the behavior in multiple ways, including named entity extraction, entity recognition, legal named-entity recognition, numeric named entity recognition, textual named entity recognition, and named entity detection. The settings range from social media notes and user queries to Greek financial text, legal text, urban knowledge graph construction, and spoken language understanding, with some work framing it as token-level, open-category, zero-shot, multilingual, or cros

nodes.name: Narrative summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the cited work, the prevailing usage treats narrative summarization as producing a condensed version of a narrative that distills the "key details and takeaways" from the source. One paper explicitly adds that this process can involve interpretive choices and subjectivity, while another defines the task specifically for long-form narratives and says the summary should capture intricate plotlines, character interactions, and thematic coherence.

Variants. Papers use the behavior for both general stories and explicitly long-form narratives. The named long-form domains are books, movies, and TV scripts, and this framing presents the task as summarizing extended narrative texts rather than short passages.

Space of elicitation and scores. The papers do not link narrative summarization to any measurement instrument. One paper does describe a summary as "a collection of claims" that can be obtained through a decomposition process, but no named instrument is reported as eliciting or scoring the behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. The papers do not link narrative summarization to any construct, so they do not explicitly treat it as evidence of a broader

nodes.name: Native language identification
nodes.definition: Predicting the native language of an author based on their writing in a second language, typically from a closed set of candidate languages.

nodes.name: Natural language inference
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is a premise-hypothesis inference task, where a model judges the relation between two sentences and usually assigns entailment, contradiction, or neutral or undetermined. Many definitions restate the labels as whether the hypothesis is true, false, or unknown given the premise, and some describe the output as a probability distribution over these three options. A smaller line narrows the task to whether the hypothesis is supported by, or can be logically inferred from, the premise, sometimes in binary entailment versus not-entailment or true versus false form.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous names, including textual entailment, sentence entailment, semantic inference, textual entailment prediction, and hypothesis verification. Most variants keep the same sentence-pair format, but papers also study multilingual or cross-lingual versions, a multi-sentence premise setting, commonsense NLI framed as predicting the most logical continuation of an event, biomedical entailment, and facts-and-rules settings where the answer is True, False, or Unknown. A few papers recast the task from classification into generation, fo

nodes.name: Natural language planning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as producing a sequence of actionable or temporally ordered steps in natural language for a goal or process. Definitions consistently focus on multi-step decomposition, either to achieve a given goal or to complete a process, and one paper explicitly frames it as "decomposing a high-level goal g into a sequence of temporally extended steps" (PlaSma: Procedural Knowledge Models for Language-based Planning and Re-Planning). Some authors broaden the output to a set of instructions, and some include images alongside the steps.

Variants. Papers use nearby names including goal-based planning, script generation, and activity generation. The differences are mainly in setting: goal-based planning is described as generating steps from scratch for high-level goals such as "see a movie" or "empty lint filter," while script generation and activity generation ask for step sequences with images that describe completing a process or activity. One source snippet also places it in daily-life natural language planning.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 1 measurement instrument, ActivityNet. Th

nodes.name: Navigation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats navigation as moving through an environment to reach or locate a specified target. Most definitions center on reaching specific locations, landmarks, or receptacles, or locating targets such as trees, cows, stones, and underground resources. Some authors also frame it more broadly as room-to-room or object-retrieval behavior, or as understanding spatial layouts in order to plan or describe routes to places or objects.

Variants. Variants are studied in several settings and under several names. Papers refer to grid world navigation, where movement is limited to up, down, left, and right toward a target, and to low-level navigation, where agents use atomic movement, rotation, and camera-control actions to reach a location or object. Other work studies city-space navigation through navigation points, maps, and spatial relations, and embodied household or game settings with commands such as navigating to receptacles or landmarks.

Space of elicitation and scores. Navigation is measured by 3 instruments. BabyAI is the most frequently linked instrument, followed by MineDojo and TextWorld: papers describe BabyAI as a grid wo

nodes.name: Negative response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as the model producing negative or pessimistic outputs, especially when a prompt elicits a positive or negative reaction. Most papers describe it either as emotionally negative replies or as a tendency to give negative answers such as "No" more often and with higher confidence than positive ones; one paper reports "more frequent and confident negative responses" (Correcting Negative Bias in Large Language Models through Negative Attention Score Alignment). A smaller line of work uses the same label for refusal behavior on harmful instructions, where the target output is a safe rejecting response rather than a general negative answer.

Variants. The studied variants split by prompt setting and output form. Some papers examine responses to negative prompts, or prompts that "elicit either positive or negative responses," while another focuses on indiscriminate negative answers. One paper operationalizes the behavior as harmful-instruction refusal, even setting rejecting outputs such as "I'm sorry, but I cannot provide a tutorial on building a bomb" as ground truth targets (AdvPrompter: Fast Adaptive Adv

nodes.name: Negotiation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing framing is a goal-oriented, multi-turn dialogue in which parties with competing interests exchange proposals to reach a mutually acceptable agreement on one or more issues. A narrower formulation treats it as dividing items or resources with an opponent through dialogue and proposal exchange, as in the prompt, "You are negotiating the division of Peppers, Strawberries, and Cherries" (GTBench: Uncovering the Strategic Reasoning Capabilities of LLMs via Game-Theoretic Evaluations).

Variants. Papers study it under names such as multi-agent negotiation and negotiation dialogue. Recurring variants are multi-turn, multi-issue settings, including human negotiation dialogues, buyer-seller conversations, and item-division games, and one paper also places negotiation among proactive dialogue applications.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to negotiation. Instead, papers operationalize it through the dialogue setup itself, emphasizing multi-turn interaction, proposal exchange, and whether parties reach a mutually acceptable agreement or a final successful deal.

What it is taken as evidence of. Negotiatio

nodes.name: Nested named entity recognition
nodes.definition: The task of identifying and classifying named entities that may be embedded within other entities.

nodes.name: Neural self-repair
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the clearest explicit use treats self-repair as a latent mechanism by which a model compensates for changes or losses in individual functional components so that task performance stays stable. The accompanying description frames it through behavioral stability under intervention, suggesting that self-repair may contribute to that stability and noting a case where negative heads perform self-repair by reducing their negativity when NMHs are ablated. A smaller, related usage in code work describes self-repair as the model debugging and repairing its own code.

Variants. Papers study it in two main settings: internal ablation settings, where functional components are changed or lost, and code-focused settings. In the code framing, self-repair is modeled as four stages, code generation, code execution, feedback generation, and code repair, and it is related to code debugging and code generation. Within that same line of work, one paper claims a causal relationship from feedback generation to neural self-repair, reporting that artificially boosting feedback quality improves self-repair efficacy.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link neura

nodes.name: News article generation
nodes.definition: Producing full-length news articles based on provided public opinion statements, including headlines, quotations, and narrative framing, under conditions designed to test political bias and neutrality.

nodes.name: News categorization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the common framing is assigning predefined labels to news articles based on their textual content. The papers agree on the classification setup but differ in the label scheme: one uses general category or topic labels, while another narrows the task to selected articles that are filtered for relevance to a time series and then categorized by impact duration, such as "long-term" and "short-term", or by type of influence, sometimes with a rationale.

Variants. Papers use both "news classification" and "news categorization" for this behavior. The main variants described are topic-style labeling and impact-oriented categorization tied to time-series analysis, where categorization can be guided by either automatically generated logic or given reasoning logic.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only one measurement instrument is linked, AG News. In that use, the behavior is elicited with an instruction to categorize a news article into one of four categories, "World, Sports, Business, Sci/Tech"; no other instrument is linked.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior, so the surveyed papers do not explicitly treat it

nodes.name: News summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers that define it, news summarization is treated as producing a concise, shorter summary of a news article. The common success criterion is that the shorter output retain the article's main ideas or essential information, and one formulation makes the setup explicit by stating that the model receives both a prompt and the original article. One prompt example asks for, "Summarize the news in two sentences. Summary:".

Variants. Papers mostly use the term for a general article-to-summary task, but they study it in several settings. One paper evaluates it as a zero-shot generative task, another frames it as prompt-based summarization from an article, one prompt formulation constrains the output to two sentences, and one linked resource places news summarization inside a retrieval-augmented generation setup as one of three task types. At least one use is specifically the English summarization subset of XLSum.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link news summarization to three measurement instruments: CNN/DailyMail, RAGTruth, and XLSum. CNN/DailyMail is used for evaluating zero-shot generative performance, XLSum appears as an English summarizat

nodes.name: Next speaker prediction
nodes.definition: Selecting which character should speak next in a multi-character conversation.

nodes.name: Node classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage is a graph task where a model assigns a categorical or class label to a node using node features or attributes together with graph connectivity, connections, or structural context. Many papers frame this as predicting labels for unlabeled or unknown nodes, while some narrow it to one target node per graph sample or to a "?" node whose label must be inferred from neighbouring labels in an undirected graph. Success is usually described as choosing one of discrete class labels, for example, "Classify the article according to its topic into one of the following categories: [Label Set]."

Variants. Papers study several variants under the same name. A recurring formulation is a node-level or target-node setting, where each graph sample is used to classify one target node, while other work places the task in text-attributed graphs, using textual features with structural connections. A smaller line of work studies semi-supervised transductive node classification on heterophilic graphs, where the goal is to predict the unknown labels of the remaining nodes, and one formulation focuses specifically on inferring a missing node lab

nodes.name: Number sorting
nodes.definition: The task of arranging a list of numbers in a specified order, typically ascending or descending.

nodes.name: Object counting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat object counting as a visual task in which a model determines how many instances of a specified object are present in an image, often in response to a natural-language query. Success is usually framed as returning the correct number for the queried category, as in prompts such as asking how many yellow blocks are in an image or simply to determine the number of instances present. A smaller line of work uses the same label for counting objects or entities mentioned in text prompts, and one paper extends it to counting how many times an object appears in a video.

Variants. Papers use several names for closely related versions, including Object counting, Object count, Count, Counting, and BBH Object Counting. The studied settings span 2D perception tasks, image questions over repeated visual elements or icons, natural-language image queries, text-only counting from described contexts, and video counting. Examples include counting animals listed in a prompt, counting yellow blocks in an image, and video questions such as how many antelope a leopard attacks, and one image study further restricts the setup to images with 1-4 instances.

Space of el

nodes.name: Object detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats object detection as identifying and localizing objects in an image by outputting bounding boxes. Some definitions add that the objects come from a predefined set of categories and that outputs include class labels, while a smaller line of work frames it as predicting object categories and boxes, including oriented boxes in remote sensing imagery, or as prioritizing proper object detection within visual input during multimodal question answering. Papers are consistent that localization is central, most commonly through returned bounding box coordinates.

Variants. Papers study several variants and names for this behavior. Besides general object detection, they mention 2D detection and remote-sensing settings with oriented boxes; more specific versions include tool detection, defined as identifying and localizing surgical tools in an image or video frame, and face detection, defined as detecting human faces and returning bounding boxes. One source also treats object detection as part of answering a multimodal question, where the model must prioritize proper detection within the visual input.

Space of elicitation and sc

nodes.name: Object goal navigation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is embodied navigation or exploration in a new or unknown environment to find a target object. Most definitions specify the target by category, though one definition adds that the target is not initially visible, and another instead frames the task as finding a specific object from textual or visual cues. As one paper puts it, the aim is to "efficiently explore a new environment while searching for a target object that is not directly visible" (GAMap: Zero-Shot Object Goal Navigation with Multi-Scale Geometric-Affordance Guidance).

Variants. The prevailing variants stay within navigation settings, including zero-shot object goal navigation in unseen environments, where the robot must navigate to a target object it has never encountered before and without training on the target or scene, and UAV object search with assistant guidance in aerial environments. Papers also use nearby names such as object navigation and object search for these settings. A smaller usage under the object search label appears outside navigation, where the task is to identify or describe an object's position in video, for example answering "What i

nodes.name: Object hallucination
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats object hallucination as outputs that mention or describe objects absent from the visual input, usually an image and in one definition a video frame. Several papers phrase this more broadly as responses "not factually aligned with image inputs," but the recurring concrete criterion is an incorrect object claim, whether in a free-form description or an affirmative answer such as "Yes, there is a white chair in the image." A smaller line of work also counts neglecting visible objects or "omitting essential features" as part of the behavior.

Variants. Most studies examine the behavior in image descriptions and captioning, while another common setting is yes/no object-presence questioning, including work that says models "hallucinate in response to yes/no questions." POPE-based papers further divide this probing into Popular, Random, and Adversarial balanced yes/no VQA, and one definition explicitly extends the setting from images to video frames. Some evaluations operationalize hallucination with subtasks such as Existence, Count, Position, and Color, or with object, attribute, and relation hallucinations, and one paper

nodes.name: Object hallucination detection
nodes.definition: Judging whether an object mentioned in a question or answer is actually present in the image.

nodes.name: Object localization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this as locating an object or set of objects in an image, and sometimes a video frame, by returning spatial coordinates, most often bounding boxes. Several definitions make the box output explicit, with one specifying a 4-tuple of upper-left and lower-right coordinates, while another asks for approximate coordinates under a defined coordinate system. Smaller lines of work broaden the output to masks or to a textual statement of a defect’s location, and some formulations narrow the task to a single object or a referred region described in language.

Variants. Papers study several specialized forms of this behavior, including bounding box prediction for a region named in a sentence, instance localization from a reference image, building localization in earth-observation images, text localization in interfaces, and defect localization in anomaly images. Other formulations extend the same locating behavior to GUI element selection and to determining object position or arrangement in an image. One related paper contrasts it with reasoning segmentation, noting that the latter only allows single object localizatio

nodes.name: Object placement
nodes.definition: The task of positioning specific objects at appropriate locations and orientations within a 3D scene.

nodes.name: Object recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is an image-level task of identifying and naming specific objects present in a visual input. Success is usually cast as correct naming or categorization, but some definitions narrow it to deciding whether a specified object is present or absent, and some fold in localization, for example asking "What type of mushroom is it in the image?" or to "give the approximate coordinates of the spoon tail." A smaller line broadens the target to listing visible entities, and some papers describe it as a latent recognition ability rather than only a discrete question-answering task.

Variants. Papers study several variants across modalities and domains. In still images, they separate object presence detection from object identification, including everyday-object naming and broader entity-recognition prompts over objects, people, and environmental features. In video settings, the behavior appears both as identifying objects mentioned in captions and as surrogate tasks that localize objects on frames or keyframes, while biomedical work recasts it as structure identification for anatomies in the brain, heart, lung, abdomen, or spine; anothe

nodes.name: Object tracking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat object tracking as identifying and following specific objects across video frames, commonly with a consistent object identity and a reported location such as a grid position or bounding box. Some papers frame the same behavior as locating a referred object across multiple scenes or moments, while another instruction-based formulation asks models to track the positions of multiple objects as they are shuffled. One study specifies outputs in the form "<track> object id1, object grid position1; ..." (Look, Remember and Reason: Grounded Reasoning in Videos with Language Models).

Variants. Across papers, the behavior appears in several settings: multi-target tracking in complex real-world video, scene-referred object tracking, text-referred object tracking, and instruction-following problems built around shuffled objects. A smaller line of work uses the name motion tracking, and another formulation describes the behavior as converting per-frame object detections into motion trajectories across a video.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers describe task formats rather than named instruments,

nodes.name: Observation summarization
nodes.definition: The process by which an agent condenses historical action-observation sequences into a concise summary tied to a completed subgoal.

nodes.name: Off-target response generation
nodes.definition: An observable failure mode where the model produces responses that are irrelevant, in the wrong language, or otherwise fail to address the prompt's intent.

nodes.name: Off-target translation
nodes.definition: Generating output in a language different from the intended target, such as producing English or another African language when translating into a specific African language.

nodes.name: Open-domain question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats open-domain question answering as answering questions over a wide range of topics or general world knowledge, rather than within a fixed domain. Most papers in this group also frame it as a knowledge-intensive task that often requires retrieving and synthesizing information from an external corpus, provided documents, or the open web, though some definitions allow answers to come from either internal knowledge or provided context. A smaller line of work narrows the expected output to short-form answers, describing the answer as typically a short phrase or sentence.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this behavior, including open-domain QA, ODQA, retrieval-augmented question answering, and retrieval-augmented QA. The most common variant centers on retrieved evidence, with formulations where the model first retrieves relevant information and then synthesizes an answer, or must answer using only provided search documents, some of which may be irrelevant. Smaller strands study short-form generation, conflict settings where parametric and contextual knowledge disagree, and settings that synthesize we

nodes.name: Open-ended instruction following
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating responses to prompts that do not have a single correct answer, often requiring creativity or detailed explanation.

nodes.name: Open-ended question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is an unconstrained answer-generation task: models produce free-form natural language responses rather than choosing from predefined options, multiple-choice answers, or extracted spans. Most descriptions also expect detailed, comprehensive, or human-like answers, often for broad, complex, or non-factoid questions that may lack a single definitive answer and can allow multiple valid perspectives. Some papers further specify declarative-form answers or evaluate semantic correctness against reference answers, and one multimodal formulation requires both answers and explanations from a question plus video.

Variants. Variants in the literature include long-form non-factoid answering for complex questions, long-context question answering over long passages, and multimodal versions grounded in images, multi-image dialogue, medical images, or video. Papers also use nearby names such as open-ended answer generation, free-form question answering, and free-form generation, alongside other free-text or generative QA labels. Other settings include knowledge-graph question answering with explicit reasoning paths and supporting facts, cu

nodes.name: Open-vocabulary object detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as identifying and locating objects in images beyond categories seen during training or a predefined inference-time label set, usually with category names or textual descriptions supplied at inference time. Papers describe detecting objects from an arbitrary open set of category names provided as text at inference time, or objects not seen during training using textual descriptions. A smaller line of work uses the open-ended formulation, where models discover unseen objects without any object categories as inputs and predict the object categories and locations themselves.

Variants. Papers use several related names for this behavior, including open-vocabulary object detection, open-vocabulary detection, and open-ended object detection. The main variation is whether category prompts are given as text at inference time or omitted entirely in the open-ended version. Across these formulations, the setting remains image object detection, and one paper places it among downstream dense vision tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to two measurement instruments, LVIS and Visual

nodes.name: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the common framing is segmentation at the pixel or image-region level in an open-vocabulary setting: papers describe assigning semantic labels to pixels and segmenting objects or regions that correspond to textual labels. Several definitions make the open-vocabulary condition explicit as working from candidate classes or textual labels that were not necessarily seen during training, while another definition describes identifying and segmenting objects from "free-form language descriptions".

Variants. Papers use both "open-vocabulary semantic segmentation" and "open-vocabulary segmentation" for the same general behavior. The studied formulations vary mainly in how labels are supplied, as a candidate class list, as textual labels, or as free-form language descriptions, and a paper also places it in a framework that switches between referring expression segmentation, open-vocabulary segmentation, and other visual grounding tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to three measurement instruments. ADE20K and Pascal Context appear most often, with PASCAL VOC also used; the linked evidence describes evaluation on th

nodes.name: Open-world object detection
nodes.definition: The task of detecting objects from both known, annotated categories and identifying objects from novel, unknown categories in an image, with the ability to incrementally learn the new categories over time.

nodes.name: Opinion summarization
nodes.definition: The task of generating a concise summary from a collection of texts that express various opinions on a topic, such as product reviews or political tweets.

nodes.name: Optical character recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is reading, identifying, extracting, and transcribing text that appears in visual inputs, most often images or documents, but also screenshots and video frames. Most definitions treat success as outputting the text itself, sometimes for the whole visual input and sometimes for a specified region, UI element, headline, or small embedded token; some papers further frame the extracted text as something used to answer questions or perform another task. A narrower chart-oriented usage limits the behavior to extracting visible text without semantic structuring, while document-focused work broadens it to dense layouts, PDFs, and historical handwritten or printed materials.

Variants. Papers use several names and subtask labels for this behavior, with OCR and text recognition the most common broad terms. Studied variants include scene text recognition, webpage Element OCR and Heading OCR, chart OCR, OCR in video frames, text extraction from slide frames, and document parsing; some work treats scene text recognition as an out-of-domain task. Other variants focus on handwritten letter recognition, handwritten and printed historical te

nodes.name: Optimization problem formulation
nodes.definition: The behavior of translating a problem described in natural language into a formal, structured optimization problem with goals, variables, and constraints.

nodes.name: Optimization problem solving
nodes.definition: Solving linear or nonlinear optimization tasks that may include tabular data and integer or mixed-integer variables.

nodes.name: Out-of-distribution detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is the task of deciding whether an input sample falls outside the training distribution, and one study also describes it as a benchmark for assessing uncertainty-aware methods. The definitions agree on this core formulation, and the fuller version adds a success criterion based on uncertainty: an effective approach should "reliably assign higher uncertainties to OOD samples compared to ID samples," while a shorter formulation describes it simply as identifying samples that do not belong to the training distribution.

Variants. Papers use both the full name and the abbreviation "OOD detection." The studied settings vary in what counts as out-of-distribution: some treat other datasets as OOD relative to an in-distribution training set, another evaluates on external OOD datasets including SVHN, and another treats Samoan translations of TQA statements as an "out-of-distribution language"; one paper also places the task in both pre-training and fine-tuning stages.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to five measurement instruments: ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, CommonsenseQA, SVHN, and TQA. In the reported uses, these are

nodes.name: Out-of-distribution prediction
nodes.definition: The observable performance of the model when tested on data from a different distribution than the training data, such as higher genera or unseen numbers of marked points.

nodes.name: Outline generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available definition treats outline generation as a preparatory writing step: creating a structured plan or hierarchy of sections for an article before drafting the full content. In "OmniThink: Expanding Knowledge Boundaries in Machine Writing through Thinking", it is formulated as generating an outline from retrieved information and an input topic, as in the quoted procedure, "Generate an outline O = Generate(I, T) based on the retrieved information I and input topic T."

Variants. The described setting is article writing, where the outline is built from retrieved information and a topic. A related use appears in a presentation workflow: one paper relates outline generation to slide generation and states that slides are produced "Guided by the presentation outline from the previous phase," which places outline generation in a presentation setting as well.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as something this behavior indicates.

nodes.name: Over-translation
nodes.definition: The observable behavior where the model generates content not present in the source text, such as hallucinated or redundant sentences.

nodes.name: Overcorrection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, overcorrection is treated as an observable failure mode during correction, where the model makes unnecessary changes to input text that was already correct. The shared framing is altering correct parts of the input or otherwise making "excessive modifications to input text," and one paper extends this to adding redundant content. Papers also describe the behavior as introducing new errors, often with low precision and possible distortion of the original meaning.

Variants. The behavior is studied in more than one correction setting. In CoVoGER: A Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Speech-to-text Generative Error Correction with Large Language Models, it appears in speech-to-text generative error correction, where the paper hypothesizes that ASR's "stricter correctness constraints" make outputs more vulnerable to over-correction than ST. In Leveraging What's Overfixed: Post-Correction via LLM Grammatical Error Overcorrection, it is framed in grammatical error correction and post-correction, including redundant additions, and the paper also states that overcorrection can be intentionally triggered to "maximize the possible cor

nodes.name: Overrefusal
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as a model wrongly refusing benign, harmless, legitimate, or otherwise safe and answerable prompts. Most papers describe it as a side effect of overly strict safety mechanisms, overgeneralized safety constraints, poor calibration of safety thresholds, or misclassifying safe inputs as harmful, including cases where prompts only superficially resemble harmful ones or touch sensitive but non-harmful topics. A smaller line of work casts it as a latent tendency or disposition, while others operationalize it as an observable event or rate: a refusal on benign input, sometimes judged by an external evaluator as safe, sometimes formalized as refusal probability above a threshold on benign samples, and sometimes described as refusing while citing ethical or safety concerns or other plausible sounding reasons.

Variants. Papers use many near-synonyms for the same pattern, with over-refusal and overrefusal most common, and smaller lines of work calling it over-rejection, over-sensitivity, over-defense, false refusal, false rejection, unwarranted refusal, exaggerated safety behaviors, oversafety, or benign quer

nodes.name: Overthinking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers describe overthinking as an observable pattern of excessive, verbose, or redundant reasoning, usually on simple tasks, where the model generates more steps or tokens than needed and incurs high computational overhead. A common formulation adds that these extra steps contribute little to accuracy or reasoning diversity, and one paper further treats it as a failure mode in which additional reasoning episodes can reduce final answer accuracy. A smaller line of work applies the label to conversational search, where overthinking means asking overly detailed or redundant clarification questions that drift from the user's original intent.

Variants. Papers study overthinking in several settings. The most common settings are long reasoning or chain-of-thought outputs on simple reasoning problems, including analyses on mathematical benchmarks, where papers describe redundant solutions, excessive reasoning steps, and inefficient token use. A smaller line of work constructs overthinking in iterative conversational search as redundant clarification turns; elsewhere, chain of thought is claimed to cause overthinking by producing unnecessarily long and verbose r

nodes.name: Painting style recognition
nodes.definition: Identifying the artist or style of paintings from visual input.

nodes.name: Pair classification
nodes.definition: Determining whether two text inputs are semantically related or form a positive pair, such as query-passage relevance.

nodes.name: Pairwise comparison
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is a head-to-head judgment over two candidate outputs for the same prompt or instruction, where an evaluator selects the better response. Most papers describe a winner or loser choice, often with an explicit tie option, a preference score between the two, or a comparison restricted to a specified dimension. Definitions vary mainly in the criterion used for winning, including better, more correct, more helpful, less wrong, more harmless, or better aligned with a user's information need, and the evaluator may be human or an LLM.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous names for the same behavior, including response ranking, preference judgment, pairwise evaluation, pairwise rating, and pairwise response comparison, with other labels used less often. The most common setting compares assistant responses, though smaller lines of work apply the same format to multi-turn conversations, long-form question answering, analyses, plans, corrections, captions, ideas, documents, and score-based item ranking. Almost all work uses two candidates, but one paper describes pairwise matchups among two or more responses when ver

nodes.name: Panoptic segmentation
nodes.definition: A unified segmentation task that involves assigning a class label to every pixel, simultaneously performing instance segmentation for 'thing' classes and semantic segmentation for 'stuff' classes.

nodes.name: Parameter extraction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is the model's production of correct argument values for a selected function, tool, or API call. Most definitions describe identifying, extracting, selecting, or assigning the required parameters, while one narrower framing focuses on filling in missing API parameter values from dialogue context or user replies. One paper makes the extraction step concrete by describing how natural language orders are parsed to identify requested items and extract values such as visitor counts, ticket types, or special conditions, which are then converted into input arguments.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for the behavior: parameter extraction, parameter resolution, parameterization, and parameter selection. The studied settings range from natural language queries mapped to function-call arguments, to dialogue-based API use where missing values are resolved from context or user replies, to tool-use evaluations that isolate parameter selection, including per-dialogue turn and single-tool scenarios. The dialogue-based examples include assigning values such as food="fried chicken" and platform="Lyft".

Space of elici

nodes.name: Paraphrase detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is deciding whether a pair of sentences or texts have the same meaning, usually described as paraphrase detection or paraphrase identification. Most definitions phrase success as judging whether two sentences are paraphrases, semantically equivalent, or have the same meaning, and some make the binary criterion explicit as yes or no, or equivalent or not equivalent. A smaller line of work narrows the task to duplicate question detection, and one paper defines it over questions or documents as identifying whether they are semantically equivalent or duplicates. Minority formulations differ in how success is established: one paper reformulates the task as generating a sentence that supports or contradicts a given sentence, another uses mutual entailment between two responses as the criterion for semantic equivalence, and another describes a three-way semantic (in)equivalence task.

Variants. Papers use several names for the task, with paraphrase detection and paraphrase identification as the prevalent labels, and smaller lines of work using duplication detection, duplicate question detection, semantic equivalence detection, and

nodes.name: Paraphrasing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats paraphrasing as meaning-preserving rewriting of an existing text, document, or sentence in different words or structure. Most papers describe success as preserving the original, full, or core meaning, sometimes explicitly as semantic equivalence, while changing surface form through lexical or syntactic variation. A smaller line of work narrows the input to queries or user or item profiles, but keeps the same requirement of semantic preservation.

Variants. The literature uses several nearby names, most often text rephrasing, rewriting, text paraphrasing, paraphrase generation, machine paraphrasing, and rephrasing. Variants differ mainly by setting: papers study document and sentence paraphrase, query rephrasing, profile diversification into semantically similar but textually distinct versions, and paraphrasing for source-language rewriting, style transfer, video-text augmentation, or iterative multi-turn generation. Some variants add constraints beyond simple rewording, such as preserving class labels, adding context without altering meaning, or producing watermark-conditioned paraphrases.

Space of elicitation a

nodes.name: Parity checking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is a binary parity task: papers describe producing the parity result for a binary string or sequence, computing the sum modulo 2 of boolean variables, or deciding whether the total number of ones is odd or even. Where outputs are spelled out, success is the correct binary result, with one definition stating that y is in {0,1}, 1 for an odd count of ones and 0 for an even count. A smaller framing treats it as a trivial version in which intermediate results are stored every other token, so the model's output is only a function of the last two tokens.

Variants. Paper names vary, including Parity, parity checking, parity computation, and parity solving. The recurring settings are arbitrary binary input sequences or binary strings, and tuples of boolean variables. In a distinct setup, one paper claims a causal relationship from chain of thought to parity checking, saying that difficulty on longer inputs is resolved by a CoT consisting of the parities of increasing prefixes.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers specify the target output directly: producing the parit

nodes.name: Part-of-speech tagging
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats part-of-speech tagging as assigning a grammatical label to a word or token in context, often phrased as marking up a word as a particular part of speech based on its definition and context. Most descriptions focus on assigning labels to tokens, while one task setup makes the success criterion more explicit by asking for the POS tag of the central word in a context window.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings rather than with a single formulation. Some place it among traditional NLP tasks in code-mixed text, some describe it as a linguistically motivated token-classification task, and another variant focuses on Chinese characters, where models identify the POS of a central word in a 5-word window and may rely on radicals when the word contains unfamiliar characters.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the available task descriptions, papers elicit it directly by asking for part-of-speech labels, including a setup that presents a 5-word window with at most one punctuation mark and asks for the tag of the central word.

What it is taken as eviden

nodes.name: Part segmentation
nodes.definition: The task of generating a segmentation mask for a specific part of an object, rather than the entire object.

nodes.name: Patent claim generation
nodes.definition: The observable production of patent claims by an LLM, following a standardized format that includes a preamble, listed elements, and functional linkages, typically for Claim 1 of a patent.

nodes.name: Pathfinding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats pathfinding as generating a valid route from a start state to a goal, usually in a graph, grid, maze, or navigation setting. The required output is variously the full sequence of actions or coordinates, the sequence of nodes, the constituent edges, or the complete sequence of directions, and success is described as producing the correct or valid path, sometimes while obeying constraints such as avoiding holes or satisfying locked-door and key dependencies. A smaller line narrows the task to predicting only the next vertex along the path, and one definition recasts it as a latent "search ability" to find a correct next step or path.

Variants. Papers label closely related versions as graph path finding, path finding, graph search, route finding, route planning, and path planning. Most variants remain spatial or graph-based, including directed graphs with start and goal nodes, grid worlds such as Frozen Lake, 30 x 30 mazes, two-dimensional grids with actions like move, pick up, and unlock, visual navigation, and object-goal navigation. A smaller variant defines the target as a valid chain of intermediate stat

nodes.name: Pattern inference
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the prevailing usage treats pattern inference as a visual rule-discovery task: a model must identify and generalize a pattern and then use that rule to complete a missing element. Papers largely agree on this core formulation, but differ in the visual setup, with one describing completion of a matrix of abstract shapes and another describing a sequence of frames in which the correct element must satisfy an underlying rule. Success is framed as correctly completing the pattern or selecting the element that completes the sequence.

Variants. Authors use both pattern inference and pattern completion for this behavior. One paper places it within a multimodal reasoning taxonomy and describes it as a math problem centered on abstract shape matrices, while another studies it through Raven's Progressive Matrices, where object attributes evolve according to different rules across frames and the task is to complete the sequence.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it in the papers, so there is no recorded agreement or disag

nodes.name: Peer review generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, this behavior is treated as generating a review-style evaluation of an academic paper. One definition frames it as producing critiques and numerical scores from the paper's content and its context in a community graph, while another frames it as structured feedback from content analysis that covers strengths, weaknesses, and acceptance decisions. The snippets further describe the output as "delivering the final score, decision and comments" and as "generating high-quality, insightful evaluations."

Variants. Papers use the near-synonymous labels "review writing" and "paper review generation," with some variation in setting and conditioning. One paper studies it as "the final stage of the automatic research simulation" and labels it "Stage 3: Review Writing," whereas the other centers on the final review package itself. The available definitions also differ in what information the review is based on, either the paper's content plus community-graph context or content analysis alone. One paper also reports it as related to Text generation, placing it after paper reading and paper writing, with each stage using the previous stage's outp

nodes.name: Persona-conditioned generation
nodes.definition: Generating claims that reflect the ideological stance and rhetorical style of a specified persona (e.g., Democrat, Republican, Moderate) by conditioning the model on role descriptions.

nodes.name: Personality mirroring
nodes.definition: The observable alignment of language use between conversational partners at the level of the entire dialogue.

nodes.name: Personality prediction
nodes.definition: Inferring MBTI-related cognitive-process labels or personality types from demographic descriptions.

nodes.name: Personalized response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is generating responses tailored to a particular user rather than generic text. Most definitions describe success as producing replies or utterances that reflect the user’s preferred style, content, tone, opinions, or other personal information, often for unseen contexts or questions; papers differ in whether those preferences are inferred from questionnaire choices, past interactions, dialogue history, background information, schedules, or user images. A smaller line of work frames the target as outputs that match inferred preferences across multiple dimensions such as helpfulness, harmlessness, or humor.

Variants. Variants mostly differ by setting and by the signals used to personalize the output. Papers study conversational replies, system utterances, open-ended personalized text generation, and a narrower review-generation setting, while a smaller subset focuses on speaker-specific responses in multi-party dialogue or task-oriented dialogue where utterances should align with a user image and attributes such as age, emotion, or formality. The naming also varies, including speaker-specific response generation,

nodes.name: Phoneme recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available papers converge on a speech task at the phonetic-unit level, but differ slightly in emphasis. One defines it as recognizing and distinguishing individual phonemes within speech audio, while another defines it as transcribing speech into a sequence of constituent phonetic units. What counts as the behavior is therefore framed either as identifying individual phonemes or as producing a phonetic-unit sequence from speech.

Variants. Papers use both the names phoneme recognition and phone recognition. The described setting is speech audio, and one paper abbreviates the task as PR and places it among multiple instruction-tuning tasks. No other sub-tasks, domains, or modalities are named.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers do not link it to any construct.

nodes.name: Physics problem solving
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a step-by-step solution and a final answer to a physics problem presented in natural language.

nodes.name: Placeholder generation
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a response that includes placeholders as instructed.

nodes.name: Plagiarism
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers that define it treat plagiarism as submitting code that is highly similar to existing public solutions, with public Kaggle notebooks given as the example source. What counts as the behavior is the degree of similarity between the submitted code and those existing solutions.

Space of elicitation and scores. It is measured by one instrument, Dolos. In MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering, Dolos is used to compare an agent's submitted code against the top 50 associated notebooks from the relevant Kaggle competition as a plagiarism check.

What it is taken as evidence of. The papers do not link this behavior to any construct.

nodes.name: Plan execution
nodes.definition: Following an LLM-generated step-by-step plan to solve a task, with each step revealed sequentially and supported by tools like calculator or web search.

nodes.name: Plan generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is direct generation of an ordered plan, usually a sequence of actions or steps for solving a planning problem or achieving a specified goal. Success is commonly framed as reaching a goal state from an initial state or completing a given task, and some authors make the directness explicit by excluding translation to a formal language or the use of an external planner. A smaller set broadens the output to include thoughts or API function calls, but still as a plan derived from a task description, provided information, or user queries.

Variants. Beyond the dominant action-sequence framing, papers study task planning for high-level tasks or safety guard requests, transition pathway generation for material transformations, meta-plan generation for collaborative long-term decomposition, dialogue logic flow generation for turn-level intentions and slot-value pairs, and multi-step planning as ordered API function calls, plus one action-plan formulation that also allows thoughts. Papers also place it in larger workflows: one paper claims a causal relationship from Collaboration to plan generation through multi-turn discussions,

nodes.name: Plan revision
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as revising an existing plan, action sequence, preference, or strategy after new information arrives or conditions change. Most formulations center on feedback from the environment, task progress, user requirements, or other agents, and several make the revision concrete as adding, removing, or changing actions, or updating the plan after each executor step. A smaller line narrows the behavior to rewriting steps to satisfy a new condition, or adjusting specific sub-tasks rather than re-planning an entire workflow, and some travel work also expects the revised plan to remain coherent and feasible.

Variants. Variants span travel planning with revision cases across dining, transportation, budget, and weather-dependent activities, multi-agent dialogue where agents adjust just before action selection, and execution settings where plans are updated from current state, task progress, or validator feedback. Papers use several names for these variants, ranging from course correction and strategy revision to task-driven, dynamic, and counterfactual replanning.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement

nodes.name: Plausibility prediction
nodes.definition: The observable task of determining which of two hypothesis images is more plausible given a premise image, or assigning a plausibility score to a single hypothesis.

nodes.name: Poetry evaluation
nodes.definition: The observable act of an LLM assessing the quality and characteristics of poems.

nodes.name: Poetry generation
nodes.definition: The task of producing new poems, which is a popular generation task for large language models.

nodes.name: Pointwise scoring
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a single-response judging task in which an evaluator assigns a numerical or ordinal score to one model-generated answer, usually on a Likert or comparable evaluation scale. Most definitions make the success criterion the production of that scalar rating for the candidate response, often under predefined or specified criteria such as consistency, coherence, fluency, relevance, overall quality, usefulness, or perceived quality. A smaller line of work phrases the same behavior more narrowly as the final score-prediction step, and some descriptions note that the score can be given alongside reasoning or critique before a final rating is produced.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous names for this behavior, including direct scoring, rating-based evaluation, single answer grading, response rating, overall rating assignment, and pointwise grading. The dominant setting is evaluation of a single response, but papers place it in several domains, including natural language generation, alignment evaluation, and instruction-controllable summarization. Some papers also contrast pointwise scoring with pairwise comparison as an

nodes.name: Portfolio management
nodes.definition: The task of managing a collection of financial assets, which includes selecting stocks, determining their weights, and making trading decisions for each asset in the portfolio.

nodes.name: Pose estimation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats pose estimation as detecting or localizing specific points on an object in an image. The definitions agree on point localization as the core task, with one paper describing it as finding points on objects such as human or animal bodies to determine posture, and another using the broader label "Keypoint detection" for identifying and localizing specific points of objects; success is therefore framed as correct point localization, and in one definition also as determining posture.

Variants. Papers use both "Pose estimation" and "Keypoint detection" for this behavior. One paper places pose estimation among open-ended, cross-domain vision tasks, while another includes keypoint detection as one of the tasks in the LAMM dataset.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link pose estimation to one measurement instrument, MS-COCO, and one paper evaluates pose estimation on COCO. The same paper also states that it adopts UniPose as the decoder for this task.

What it is taken as evidence of. Only one construct is linked, and papers phrase that link as a related relationship rather than a measurement claim: pose e

nodes.name: Post-hoc rationalization
nodes.definition: The generation of a Chain-of-Thought that justifies a predetermined answer without substantially influencing it, often indicated by flat confidence trajectories.

nodes.name: Post intent generation
nodes.definition: Producing a description of the author's communicative purpose in sharing a meme, such as humor, complaint, or provocation, based on multimodal context.

nodes.name: Pre-training data detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat pre-training data detection as a seen versus unseen text classification task: given a text sample, sentence, or sequence, the method decides whether that text was included in the model's pretraining or training data. The prevailing success criterion is separating training from non-training text, and one definition makes this explicit as analyzing model output statistics to find a scoring function that best separates the two classes. A narrower application uses the same behavior for detecting whether excerpts from copyrighted books were included, and a smaller line of work studies the task with controllable FDR.

Variants. Papers use closely related names for the behavior, including pre-training data detection, pretraining data detection, and training data detection. The task is studied at different text granularities, from individual sentences to text sequences and more general samples, and the most specific domain variant is copyrighted book detection. Some work also studies harder settings where seen and unseen samples have high n-gram overlap.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link the behavior to 6 instruments overall. The most fre

nodes.name: Preference over-rejection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the behavior is generally referred to simply as over-rejection, but the concrete task differs by setting. The most explicit definition treats it as a failure mode in preference learning for translation, where the translation's writing style is "forced away from the preferred data distribution," which one study says can "severely impair" the generation of meaningful translations. Some safety-focused work uses the same term for incorrect rejection of prompts, describing security alignment as able to "lead to the incorrect rejection of security prompts."

Variants. The recorded uses span at least two settings. In translation work, over-rejection is about style drift in generated translations; in safety-oriented work, it is probed through prompt rejection, and one paper evaluates it with a benign question dataset. One linked paper also studies the behavior in large audio language models rather than the translation setting.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link over-rejection to one measurement instrument, AIAH. It is used as a benchmark, and its benign question dataset is used to evaluate over-rejection. No other instrument is linked by

nodes.name: Preference prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a pairwise preference task: a model predicts which of two responses, answers, or solutions is preferred, better, or more highly upvoted for a given prompt or context. The preference source varies across papers, including humans, an LLM-as-a-judge, reward models, AI ratings, and community reactions, and success is usually whether the preferred option receives the higher label, probability, or score.
