A smaller line of work treats the behavior as scalar preference estimation, either by learning a numerical reward function for a user-response pair, predicting a user's preference level for an item, or mapping a recipe to average consumer satisfaction within a target population.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings: personalized response selection on unseen contexts, multi-turn conversational judging, community-specific upvote prediction, item-level preference rating, and recipe satisfaction prediction. Another variant compares the relative quality of candidate mathematical solutions through a pairwise question, framed in one paper as asking, "For Question Q, is solution a1 better than solution a2?" The nam

nodes.name: Preference ranking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats preference ranking as choosing or ordering outputs by human preference. Definitions converge on ranking outputs according to human judgments or selecting a preferred response from a set of options, most often in a pairwise form where one response is preferred over another for the same prompt. Some authors operationalize the behavior as assigning higher likelihoods to preferred than dispreferred outputs, with success measured through ranking accuracy, while another framing assigns scalar rewards to two outputs and ranks them by the difference in scores.

Variants. Papers most often study a pairwise variant: a prompt is paired with two candidate responses or sequences, and the task is to determine which one is preferred. Related formulations describe data as pairs of human-ranked responses, or write one sequence as preferred over another. A smaller variant scores each of two outputs separately with scalar rewards and then derives the ranking from the score difference, while the broadest definition also allows selection from a larger set of options.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link preference ranking to

nodes.name: Premature termination
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available definition treats this as an observable failure mode in which the model's output sequence is abruptly shortened, so the resulting audio waveform is incomplete. The accompanying snippet uses the same criterion, describing speech token sequences with "abruptly shortened lengths" that lead to premature termination of audio waveforms (Mitigating Hallucinations in LM-Based TTS Models via Distribution Alignment Using GFlowNets).

Variants. The only named setting is speech generation. It is described at the level of shortened speech token sequences and incomplete audio waveforms, and no additional sub-tasks, alternative labels, or non-audio variants are named.

Space of elicitation and scores. No paper links this behavior to a named measurement instrument, so no recurring elicitation or scoring instrument is reported for it.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior. The recorded links instead stay at the behavioral level: one paper claims a causal relationship from reward hacking to premature termination, and Smurfs: Multi-Agent System using Context-Efficient DFSDT for Tool Planning records causal relationships in both d

nodes.name: Premise selection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available definition describes premise selection as identifying and retrieving relevant existing theorems, definitions, or lemmas from a large library for use in a new proof. In LeanAgent: Lifelong Learning for Formal Theorem Proving, it is framed as the selection of relevant premises, and effective premise selection is described as "a critical challenge in theorem proving."

Variants. The described setting is formal theorem proving, where the behavior concerns searching a large library of prior results for a new proof. The available description does not specify additional sub-tasks or modalities beyond selecting relevant premises, where the premises can be theorems, definitions, or lemmas.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as something it evidences. Separately, one paper reports that formal theorem proving is related to premise selection.

nodes.name: Prescriptive analytics
nodes.definition: The ability to generate insights that suggest specific actions to address issues or capitalize on opportunities identified in the data.

nodes.name: Previous-token attention
nodes.definition: A specific, observable positional attention pattern where a token's attention is almost exclusively focused on the token immediately preceding it.

nodes.name: Prison term prediction
nodes.definition: Predicting the appropriate prison sentence length in legal cases under Chinese law, evaluated using normalized log distance.

nodes.name: Privacy leakage
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats privacy leakage as observable disclosure of sensitive, private, or personally identifiable information in model outputs. Most definitions count leakage when a model reveals protected content after adversarial prompting, prompt injection, or other manipulation, though some papers describe it under simple natural questions or under a good-faith assumption that any request is trustworthy. Success is variously defined as outputting protected information, reproducing memorized training content, inferring additional hidden fragments from a few known ones, or revealing all or part of a system prompt or access code; a smaller line defines leakage relative to context, such as disclosing information forbidden by a user-defined security policy or in situations where it should be withheld.

Variants. Frequently studied variants include prompt or system prompt extraction, PII leakage or extraction, training-data-focused leakage such as training data extraction and fragment inference, and agent-side data stealing or full request leakage. Other papers place the behavior in generated summaries, in reasoning traces as well as final an

nodes.name: Private attribute inference
nodes.definition: The observable task of a model predicting a user's personal information (e.g., location, age, sex, income) based on a provided image, especially one that does not directly depict the person.

nodes.name: Privilege escalation
nodes.definition: Increasing a low-privilege account’s permissions to a higher privilege level, ideally administrator.

nodes.name: Proactive assistance
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of an agent correctly refraining from offering assistance when it determines the user does not need help.

nodes.name: Probabilistic forecasting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is to treat probabilistic forecasting as generating a full distribution over future numerical values in a time series rather than a single point estimate. The formulations are closely aligned: one paper defines the goal as estimating “the joint distribution of future observations given the historical ones, P(XF | XH)” (Context is Key: A Benchmark for Forecasting with Essential Textual Information), while another asks models to “output a probabilistic forecast of length 64” (Fourier Head: Helping Large Language Models Learn Complex Probability Distributions).

Variants. The papers differ mainly in the setting and representation of that distribution. One formulation targets future time steps from historical observations, including tasks where accurate predictions require integrating numerical data with natural language contextual information, while another describes fixed-length forecasts and next-value prediction through quantized values and a learned categorical distribution over the next value.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. No co

nodes.name: Problem misunderstanding
nodes.definition: An observable error where the model's response indicates a misinterpretation of the question's goal, concepts, or given information.

nodes.name: Problem solving
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the literature, the prevailing usage treats problem solving as producing correct answers or solutions on benchmark problems, especially across commonsense, math, code, and other diverse tasks. Several papers also frame it as devising and executing a sequence of steps, or even a program, under constraints or examples, or as applying task-specific knowledge to reach a solution. Success is usually stated in terms of correctness, though one paper describes settings where multiple candidate responses or reasoning steps may be needed.

Variants. Papers name several variants, including multi-task problem solving, reasoning task solving, and real-world problem solving. These cover heterogeneous tasks across domains and question types, structured logical or mathematical derivation, and inductive reasoning embedded in natural-language real-life scenarios such as item trading. A smaller line of work also studies settings where a sequence of steps or a program must be derived from constraints or examples, as well as well-defined technical queries.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link problem solving to 3 measurement instruments. The most frequently linked

nodes.name: Professional question answering
nodes.definition: Generating responses to queries that require domain-specific expertise in fields such as medicine, law, finance, or music, with accurate and contextually appropriate information.

nodes.name: Program verification proof synthesis
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to synthesize proofs that allow a Rust program and specification to be verified by Verus.

nodes.name: Prompt decomposition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats prompt decomposition as taking a complex textual description or query and splitting it into multiple shorter units. Papers agree on the core operation, decomposition into semantically coherent phrases or distinct sub-prompts, and differ mainly in how they describe the outputs: some frame them as short phrases, while others frame them as sub-prompts for individual concepts such as scene, objects, and motion.

Variants. A smaller naming variation appears between text decomposition and prompt decomposition. The studied settings range from decomposing a complex text description into short phrases to decomposing a complex query for video generation into several concept-specific sub-prompts.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior in the papers. Operationalization is described directly through the task itself, as decomposing a complex input into shorter phrases or distinct concept-level sub-prompts.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior in the papers.

nodes.name: Prompt injection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage describes prompt injection as a model or agent following malicious or unintended instructions inserted by an adversary into an input prompt, tool output, third-party data, or other external context. The behavior is treated as present when those embedded instructions redirect the system from the user's goal or intended behavior, for example by making it follow the attacker's goal, perform a specific task, or take unauthorized actions. Some authors use the narrower label indirect prompt injection for cases where the instructions come from external content rather than a direct prompt to the model.

Variants. The most recurrent variant is indirect prompt injection, also called indirect prompt attack, where malicious instructions are embedded in external content the model or agent later accesses. Papers mention emails, documents, retrieved text, tool-retrieved information, tool outputs, third-party data, and other external resources or data sources as carriers. Papers also distinguish this from direct prompt attacks, where the attacker sends inputs directly to the model.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument

nodes.name: Pronunciation assessment
nodes.definition: The model's observable behavior of aligning transcript words with corresponding phoneme sequences and identifying mismatches indicative of mispronunciation.

nodes.name: Proof grading
nodes.definition: Assessing the correctness and quality of a mathematical proof by assigning a score or category based on reasoning validity and completeness.

nodes.name: Protein binding site prediction
nodes.definition: The task of identifying the specific residues in an antibody's sequence that constitute the binding site (paratope) for an antigen.

nodes.name: Protein generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating protein or amino acid sequences. Most definitions frame it as creating novel sequences, sometimes explicitly sequences intended to be plausible or functional proteins, while a smaller line of work treats it as generating missing amino acid regions in an antibody sequence from the observed regions. Papers agree on sequence generation as the core task, but differ on whether generation is open-ended or infilling, and on whether decoding is order-agnostic.

Variants. Papers study both broad protein sequence generation and narrower antibody sequence infilling settings. Named variants include order-agnostic protein generation, unguided antibody infilling, and infilling specific masked complementarity determining regions, including HCDR1, HCDR2, HCDR3, and LCDR1. One paper also places protein generation alongside structure- and function-related evaluations.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior, so the papers do not identify a recurring instrument that elicits or scores it.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this

nodes.name: Protein inverse folding
nodes.definition: Generating an amino-acid sequence that is compatible with a given backbone structure.

nodes.name: Protein property prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as predicting protein-level outputs from amino acid sequence, most often as either continuous regression or binary classification. Common regression formulations target fluorescence intensity, thermostability or melting temperature, and other biophysical properties such as optimal temperature for catalysis, while common classification formulations ask whether a protein is soluble, binds metal ions, or can be expressed in CHO cells. Some authors extend the framing to labels such as subcellular localization and biological function; one paper describes function prediction as predicting proteins "without any ground truth yet available" during training, with final evaluation after a "curation phase" based on newly published functions.

Variants. Papers operationalize the behavior in several named settings, including fluorescence, stability or thermostability, solubility, metal ion binding, and subcellular localization. Additional variants extend the same sequence-based framing to expression tasks, broader biophysical targets, and other protein-level outputs. Most formulations are described at sequence level o

nodes.name: Protein sequence design
nodes.definition: The task of generating mutant protein sequences (specifically ACE2) with higher stability, measured by lower free energy (ddG), than the original wildtype sequence.

nodes.name: Protein structure prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as predicting a protein's three-dimensional structure from its amino acid sequence, sometimes stated simply as predicting the 3D structure and sometimes more specifically as predicting the three-dimensional atomic coordinates. The common framing is sequence-to-structure prediction: one paper says the goal of folding is to predict the 3D structure for a given amino acid sequence. Definitions also include related structure-centered tasks, rather than limiting the term only to full coordinate generation.

Variants. Common naming variants are folding and protein folding, and one paper describes it as sequence-conditioned structure prediction. Definitions also include neighboring formulations: protein contact prediction, cast as binary classification at the amino acid pair level for whether two amino acids are close in the folded structure; protein fold classification, described as sequence-level assignment to predefined fold classes, including a formulation with 1195 classes; and remote homology prediction, described as identifying evolutionary relationships between proteins with low sequence similarity.

nodes.name: Protein understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is prediction of protein fitness or mutational effect from amino acid sequence: authors describe regression over functional performance, prediction of the impact of substitutions, or assignment of a scalar score or relative ranking based on predicted biophysical or functional properties. A common zero-shot formulation scores mutated sequences relative to a wild type by differences in model likelihoods or log odds ratios, without fine-tuning or support-set examples. Smaller lines of work treat the behavior as iteratively editing a seed sequence to obtain a higher predicted fitness sequence, or as predicting antibody-antigen binding or binding affinity.

Variants. Papers study several variants and settings. Common names include protein variant fitness prediction, mutation effect prediction, protein fitness prediction, and zero-shot prediction, with some work emphasizing ranking by preference rather than direct value prediction. Other variants shift the domain or output: iterative sequence editing has the model start from a seed sequence and repeatedly propose improvements, while antibody-focused work frames the task as SARS-Co

nodes.name: Pushing
nodes.definition: The action of applying force to an object to move it without grasping it.

nodes.name: Puzzle solving
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat puzzle solving as finding a solution to a defined puzzle or problem, especially classic puzzles, number games, and word games posed under custom rules and constraints. The prevailing formulation emphasizes rule-governed problem solving rather than open-ended generation: one benchmark asks models to "solve puzzles and intellectual games based on newly defined problem-solving frameworks" (KOR-Bench: Benchmarking Language Models on Knowledge-Orthogonal Reasoning Tasks). A smaller line of work uses a broader phrasing, calling it the observable behavior of finding a solution to a defined puzzle or problem.

Variants. The main variants are classic paper puzzles, number games, and word games, which one paper explicitly names as the rule categories for its puzzle section. Another variant is multi-image puzzle solving, framed as solving puzzles that require understanding and reasoning across multiple images. Some work also studies puzzles in a centaur evaluation setting with crowdworkers, where they appear alongside collaborative writing and summarization tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to puzzle

nodes.name: Quantified Boolean formula solving
nodes.definition: Producing a truth value for quantified Boolean formulas by recursively handling existential and universal quantifiers.

nodes.name: Query-focused summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this as generating a summary or response to a query, with the content selected to address that query rather than the whole source. Definitions converge on summarizing one or more documents, often long inputs, and emphasizing only the information relevant to a user-provided or generated query. One paper states this especially explicitly: "given a query about a long input consisting of one or more documents, generate a response to the query which cites arbitrary length text spans from the input" (Unstructured Evidence Attribution for Long Context Query Focused Summarization). A smaller wording difference is between calling the output a concise summary and calling it a response, but both framings keep query conditioning and relevance to the query as the criterion for success.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous names, including query-focused summarization, query-based summarization, QFS, and long context query focused summarization (LCQFS). The task appears in long-document and long-context settings, with examples involving one or more documents, meeting transcripts, narratives, dialogue, and podcast transc

nodes.name: Query rewriting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as rewriting a user query or prompt so it is clearer, semantically richer, or better aligned with a downstream system. Papers variously define success as clarifying ambiguous expressions, adding semantic information, satisfying a required aspect and value, making a question search-engine-friendly, or transforming a natural-language description into a more effective structured prompt; some formulations explicitly require preserving meaning, intent, or faithfulness to the original prompt. A smaller cluster of vision-oriented papers instead emphasizes enriching queries with visual details and aesthetic expectations, or removing stylistic biases, platform-specific keywords, and conflicting information, while another line treats prompt rewriting as rephrasing harmful queries while preserving meaning.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for the behavior, including query rephrasing or paraphrasing, query reformulation, prompt rewriting, prompt polishing, and query refinement. The settings span online shopping constraint editing, text-to-SQL schema alignment, multi-hop question answering, multimodal search, text-to-image g

nodes.name: Question-answer pair generation
nodes.definition: The task of creating a set of questions and corresponding answers about the diverse entities and attributes present in an image.

nodes.name: Question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is producing an answer to a natural-language question, usually expecting the answer to be correct, accurate, direct, or relevant. Most papers frame the answer as grounded in provided context, such as passages, documents, tables, knowledge graphs, retrieved evidence, or long contexts, though many others evaluate answers from general or internal knowledge; a smaller line narrows the task to benchmark-style formats such as multiple-choice, yes or no, span extraction, short-form open-domain QA, or direct factual answers. Some papers also evaluate the same behavior in adversarial settings, and a minority framing treats QA as judging whether a model output is correct for a given question and reference answer.

Variants. Papers study QA in many settings, most commonly open-book and closed-book, single-document and multi-document, and multi-hop or long-context forms. They also describe specialized variants over structured data and temporally evolving tables, including questions whose answers cannot be derived from a single table alone, domain QA in medicine or mental health, and personalized answers written in community-s

nodes.name: Question decomposition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat question decomposition as breaking a complex question or query into simpler, answerable sub-questions or sub-queries that guide stepwise reasoning. Papers commonly describe a sequence or series of intermediate questions, sometimes paired with sub-answers until the final answer; as one paper puts it, the system “decomposes complex questions into subquestions” (Tree-of-Quote Prompting Improves Factuality and Attribution in Multi-Hop and Medical Reasoning). A smaller line of work broadens this to logically structured subproblems, and one paper instead uses the term for extracting structural tokens and replaceable entity placeholders to build a reusable template for similar questions.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this behavior, especially question decomposition, query decomposition, subquestion decomposition, sub-question generation, and query graph construction. The graph-based variant is more structured, where a query graph builder “constructs a representation of a user’s reasoning plan as a DAG” (Single LLM, Multiple Roles: A Unified Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework Using Role-Specific Token Optimization). Other

nodes.name: Question rephrasing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat this behavior as rewording a question while preserving its meaning, and some definitions add that the answer should also stay the same. The prevailing usage covers both general question paraphrases and mathematical questions in different linguistic forms, while a smaller line of work frames it as modifying a visual question so its intent is preserved while the wording becomes less ambiguous or better aligned with model capabilities. Some authors also describe success as a simpler restatement when misunderstanding of the original question is suspected.

Variants. Papers use both question rephrasing and question rewriting as names for closely matched tasks. Studied variants include rephrasing prompting to generate more mathematical questions, a visual-grounding setting with a rephrasing and augmenting stage that proposes modifications to the original question from image details, problem-solving workflows that add an action to rephrase the question more simply, and evaluation protocols that build rephrased benchmarks by asking an LLM to rewrite each question without altering meaning.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 1 measurem

nodes.name: Questionnaire answering
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of responding to a series of questions from a structured survey, such as a value questionnaire, by providing ratings on a scale.

nodes.name: Radiology report generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats radiology report generation as producing a descriptive, clinically relevant text report from radiology image data, sometimes from one or more images plus associated clinical context. Most formulations emphasize describing clinical observations or findings from a radiology image, often a chest X-ray. A narrower formulation specifies a typical report structure, requiring the model to generate the two sections "Findings" and "Impression".

Variants. Variants center on chest X-ray settings, with papers describing chest X-ray radiology report generation and textual medical reports from chest X-ray images. Some authors use the shorter name "report generation", and one paper frames a retrieval-based version given only radiology images. Input assumptions vary from one or more images with associated clinical context to a single medical image, and the output may be framed generally as clinical observations or more specifically as Findings and Impression sections.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 3 measurement instruments. The most frequently linked is MIMIC-CXR, used in chest X-ray repor

nodes.name: Rain removal
nodes.definition: The observable task of eliminating or reducing the visual effects of raindrops or rain streaks from an image.

nodes.name: Ranking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is reranking in retrieval pipelines: re-evaluating an initial list of retrieved documents, passages, images, code snippets, or other candidates and reordering them by relevance to a query so the most relevant item appears first or the top-ranked set is more precise. Several definitions make the scoring step explicit, describing fine-grained relevance scores, satisfaction scores, or binary relevance judgments before reordering, and one long-context evaluation instructs the model to return the top-10 document IDs ranked by relevance. A smaller line of work uses ranking more broadly for ordering candidate outputs from best to worst, arranging items under instructions, selecting the best generation from several candidates, or ordering regions on maps by legend value.

Variants. Most variants stay close to document and passage reranking, which are the most recurrent labels and are often framed as a second stage after initial retrieval. Papers also study zero-shot reranking, where prompting rather than task-specific fine-tuning is used, and listwise reranking, where a full ranking is produced by considering passages jointly rather

nodes.name: Readability assessment
nodes.definition: Judging the readability level or difficulty of a text passage.

nodes.name: Reading comprehension question answering
nodes.definition: Answering questions that require understanding a passage or context in Filipino.

nodes.name: Reason generation
nodes.definition: Producing an explanation for why a model's output should change from an initial ('AS-IS') to a desired ('TO-BE') state based on prompt content.

nodes.name: Reasoning error
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this as an observable failure in problem solving where the model does not carry out the needed logical steps correctly. Most definitions describe missing critical steps, improper inferences, logical fallacies, incorrect solution steps, or misapplied mathematical principles, and depending on the paper the failure is seen either in an incorrect derived answer or in the model's generated solution path. A smaller line of work narrows it to cases where perception succeeds but answer derivation fails, especially when models correctly perceive audio yet still fail to apply the necessary complex reasoning. One paper further describes reasoning error as the most prevalent error category in its analysis, while another frames it as systematic, predictable mistakes traceable to specific flaws in the model's reasoning process.

Variants. Papers use several names for the behavior, including Reasoning error, Reasoning Errors, Flawed reasoning, and Making systematic errors. Most papers study it in mathematical reasoning settings, including multimodal math, undergraduate-level math, and grade-school math, while one paper treats it as

nodes.name: Reasoning segmentation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats reasoning segmentation as generating a pixel-level segmentation mask for an object or region in an image from a complex instruction or textual query, where identifying the target requires reasoning. The available definitions are closely aligned, and one paper adds that the task 'demands higher capabilities in instruction comprehension.' Success is described as producing the pixel-level mask.

Variants. The papers use closely related names for the same behavior, including reasoning segmentation and Reasoning Segmentation (RS). A narrower characterization appears in one paper's relationship statement, which says that 'RS has reasoning ability, but only allows single object localization,' tying the task to single-object localization. Another paper discusses it alongside referring segmentation as a task setting where the approach is applied.

Space of elicitation and scores. One measurement instrument is linked to reasoning segmentation: ReasonSeg. Papers describe ReasonSeg as a benchmark dataset or benchmark for reasoning segmentation, and one quote says it 'evaluates the reasoning ability of the model.' Reported use

nodes.name: Recommendation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats recommendation as predicting or generating items for a user from prior interactions or preferences. Most descriptions focus on producing a list, often a ranked or top-k list, of items or item IDs the user is likely to prefer, while one common setting frames it as selecting the item that best matches a user's preferences from binary interaction behaviors. A smaller line of work makes the output criterion very explicit as "generating top-K items (i.e., K distinct token sequences) as a recommendation list by beam search."

Variants. Papers use several names for related variants, including collaborative filtering, recommendation generation, item recommendation, top-k recommendation, top-K item generation, and user intention capture. These variants differ mainly in the information they use: some rely on a user-item interaction matrix or interaction history, some target the next relevant item ID a user will like, and some estimate preferences from historical interactions together with item features such as descriptions and images. One variant further refines recommendations by combining historical interests with langua

nodes.name: Referring expression generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is a region-conditioned text generation task: the model is given a specific image region, usually a bounding box or its location tokens, and must produce a descriptive expression that refers to that object or region. Papers agree that the description should accurately characterize the selected content, and some make the success criterion stricter by calling for an unambiguous description. A smaller formulation casts this not just as a task but as a latent ability to understand a visual reference and generate the associated text; as one description puts it, "each bounding box in the image is annotated with a descriptive textual expression that accurately characterizes and refers to the content within the specific region" (CogVLM: Visual Expert for Pretrained Language Models).

Variants. Some papers use the label multimodal referring, with referring expression generation treated as one example of that broader framing. Across these formulations, the target may be an image region or an object, and the reference is typically supplied through a bounding box, location tokens, or a user-provided box. The descriptions provid

nodes.name: Referring expression segmentation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage is an image task where a model segments the specific object or region named by a natural language expression or description. Most papers describe success as producing a segmentation mask for the referred target, and one source says the output is "a mask that can cover the described object" (Unleashing Region Understanding in Intermediate Layers for MLLM-based Referring Expression Generation). A smaller line extends this formulation to predicting a binary mask for a named component of a 3D object.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, most often referring expression segmentation, and also referring segmentation and referring image segmentation. Within these formulations, some describe segmenting a specific object instance, some a specific object or region, and one description notes that in RefCOCO-g "one sentence is associated with one instance." A smaller line studies domain or modality variants, including remote sensing, where prompts ask for a mask for a referring expression and the model replies with a "<SEG>" token that is decoded into a mask (GeoPixel: Pixel Grounding Large Multimodal Model in Remote Sensing)

nodes.name: Referring expression understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is an image grounding task in which a natural-language referring expression is used to identify and localize the matching object or region. Most formulations ask for a bounding box, described as predicting the box for an object given its text description or outputting box coordinates; some instead describe generating a segmentation mask and deriving a box, or more generally linking the expression to the corresponding object or region. When scoring is specified, papers report accuracy or Acc@0.5, and one definition says a prediction is correct when the IoU between predicted and ground-truth bounding boxes exceeds 0.5.

Variants. Most papers stay with image versions under names such as referring expression comprehension, reference expression understanding, referring expression grounding, and referential expression grounding. A smaller line broadens the setting to phrase grounding, where one or more phrases, or even all noun phrases in a sentence, are associated with image boxes. Other variants recast it as segmentation, including multi-object referring segmentation and multi-target referring expression segmentation, where mode

nodes.name: Refusal
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed definitions, the dominant framing is explicit non-compliance: models abstain from answering harmful, malicious, unsafe, toxic, or policy-violating prompts, often with stock statements such as I cannot fulfill your request or I'm sorry, but I can't assist with that request. Many papers count a direct decline as refusal, while others also count generic replies, answers to a different question, error messages, or safer redirections; smaller lines of work extend the behavior to knowledge limits, missing or contradictory information, privacy-sensitive requests, selecting a not sure option, or declining to choose any invalid answer. Several papers also separate appropriate refusal on harmful inputs from over-refusal on reasonable requests or safe contexts.

Variants. Papers use many nearby labels, including harmful query rejection, unsafe prompt rejection, toxic prompt rejection, harmful content rejection, refusal to answer, refusal behavior, refusal generation, response refusal, answer refusal, abstention, and rejecting request. The prevailing settings are safety and jailbreak evaluation on harmful user requests, but smaller strands study hate s

nodes.name: Region captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as producing a natural-language description for a specific image region that has been marked or referred to. Definitions agree on the region-targeted nature of the task, but differ on granularity: some describe concise or brief outputs, including prompts such as "Please provide a brief description of each marked region in the image," while others ask for a detailed description of a referred region. A smaller framing describes it as providing a textual description corresponding to a visual prompt.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this behavior, including region-level captioning, referring description, and visual referring. The settings vary between describing each marked region in an image and describing a single referred region, and the requested outputs range from brief to detailed descriptions. One paper places it in a benchmark that also includes point-level captioning, with region-level captioning as the region-focused variant.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure it with 3 instruments. RefCOCOg is the most frequently linked instrument, followed by Visual Genome a

nodes.name: Register allocation
nodes.definition: The task of assigning virtual registers from a compiler's intermediate representation to physical registers in a target hardware's instruction set architecture.

nodes.name: Regression
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions describe it as predicting a continuous numerical value for a given tabular record or input sample. One paper also formulates it as predicting an integer-valued output, with a user review as input and a rating from 1 to 5 as the label.

Variants. Papers study regression both as tabular prediction across various domains and as a review-to-rating task. The formulations differ in whether the input is a tabular record or a user review, and in whether the target is described as a continuous value or as an integer rating.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the recorded relationships. In task operationalizations, papers mention mean squared error loss for regression tasks and mean absolute error, MAE.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it in the recorded relationships.

nodes.name: Relation classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats it as identifying and classifying semantic relationships between entities in text. Most formulations narrow the input to a specified pair of entities, often within a sentence, and treat success as predicting the relation class or label for that pair, sometimes as one or more labels and sometimes as a distribution over predefined relations. Some papers use the broader name relation extraction and emphasize identifying or generating relations, and one paper explicitly contrasts multi-class prediction with a binary decision about whether a queried relation exists between two entities.

Variants. Papers use both relation classification and relation extraction to name the behavior, and a smaller subset studies medical relation extraction. The settings range from sentence-level pair classification to document-level extraction across whole documents, and some papers study few-shot continual relation extraction as a variant. Other formulations target multiple relations simultaneously, fact triplets, or schema-defined relation types such as TA, A2A, and AS relations, while domain-specific versions appear in urban text

nodes.name: Relation discovery
nodes.definition: The observable action of generating a preliminary or initial new relation label for a test instance, typically based on examples of known relations.

nodes.name: Relation extraction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Where papers define the behavior directly, they frame it as knowledge triple extraction: decomposing document content into structured ⟨head entity, relation, tail entity⟩ triples with an LLM using in-context learning. In the only explicit task description, the model is prompted to extract triples for each retrieved document independently and to extract “all knowledge triples contained within a document in a single pass” (KiRAG: Knowledge-Driven Iterative Retriever for Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation).

Variants. Papers study several settings under the same label. Some use sentence-level RE, with one benchmark description stating that “SemEval-2010 is a sentence-level RE dataset with ten relation classes,” while others use document-level RE, including binary relations between chemical and disease entities in BC5CDR and chemical-protein relations in ChemProt. A smaller line of work uses the name Few-shot Continual Relation Extraction, where RE systems “sequentially identify new relations with limited labeled samples,” and another paper uses ZsRE as a relation extraction dataset.

Space of elicitation and scores. The prevailing operationalization is benc

nodes.name: Relation linking
nodes.definition: Matching relation surface forms in generated logical forms to actual relations in the knowledge base using exact match or semantic similarity (e.g., SimCSE).

nodes.name: Relevance judgment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, relevance judgment is treated as an explicit evaluation of whether a retrieved or given text is relevant to a query, topic, or task. The definitions converge on judging documents, passages, or text for alignment or usefulness: one formulation asks the model to analyze each document one by one, then give a final judgment and explanation, while another frames the decision as whether a retrieved passage "provides useful information to solve x." A further formulation describes the task as assessing how well a piece of text aligns with a query or topic through semantic criteria.

Variants. Papers use several parallel names and settings: document relevance assessment, passage relevance assessment, and text relevance assessment. The document and passage variants focus on retrieved material in response to a question or task, while the text variant is described more generally as alignment to a query or topic. Across these variants, success is framed either as an explicit judgment of relevance or as deciding whether the passage is useful for solving the task.

Space of elicitation and scores. No paper links this behavior to a measurement instrument. Where

nodes.name: Repetitive generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing treats this as a failure mode in which outputs contain repeated tokens, words, phrases, sentences, or entire utterances, often described as duplicate fragments or unproductive loops that degrade meaning, readability, coherence, or conciseness. When papers specify judging criteria, they usually ask whether a response repeats itself, including repeated list items, or whether repetitive tokens or utterances affect meaning. A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to meaningless or unproductive repetition, such as continuing with repeated tokens after an answer or getting trapped in repetitive reasoning sequences on hard tasks.

Variants. Papers study it across several settings. Common variants include generic repetition in free text, duplication within summaries, and token repetition under an explicit prompt to repeat a single word; smaller lines examine dialogue "parroting" across turns, code outputs with repeated assertions or comments, translation "oscillatory hallucination," and repeated character sequences in no-space content. Some papers also describe it as emerging after excessive editing strength or under preference

nodes.name: Rephrased question answering
nodes.definition: Correctly answering semantically equivalent but syntactically different versions of a previously edited question, indicating generalization of the edit.

nodes.name: Request compliance
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats request compliance as observable answer behavior: following a user's instruction or attempting to fulfill a request, and responding directly rather than refusing. Most definitions add that the answer should be substantive or helpful, so compliance is usually framed as a direct answer to the prompt or query, contrasted with refusal.

Variants. A recurring setting is compliance with harmless or benign prompts versus refusal of harmful ones. The labels vary, with compliance the most common wording, alongside compliant response generation and instruction acceptance; one helpfulness setting measures acceptance on benign prompts that share keywords with AdvBench but do not contain harmful intent, and another notes lower acceptance in a Sensitive category.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers nevertheless operationalize the behavior through refusal-versus-compliance judgments, including whether WildGuard classifies the response as refusal or compliance on XStest, through instruction acceptance rate on benign prompts, and in one study through the minimal gamma found by line s

nodes.name: Resource collection
nodes.definition: Mining or gathering materials from terrain blocks to obtain items such as wood, stone, coal, iron, diamond, saplings, or drinks.

nodes.name: Resource harvesting
nodes.definition: The observable action of an agent deciding on and extracting a specific quantity of a shared resource from the common pool in a given time step.

nodes.name: Response aggregation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats it as combining multiple candidate answers or responses into one final output. Most descriptions emphasize a final answer that is more reliable, higher-quality, coherent, or refined, whether the inputs come from multiple sources, reasoning paths, or selected experts. Some papers make the success criterion more explicit by describing selection of the most reliable or most plausible response, while others add conflict detection, weighted fusion, or iterative synthesis and refinement.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous labels, including answer aggregation, response fusion, response aggregation, and response synthesis. The settings vary from multi-path aggregation over answers from sub-questions and the original question, to fusing proposed responses given an instruction prompt, to synthesizing outputs from selected experts through semantic conflict detection and weighted information fusion. A smaller variant frames it as a two-stage knowledge graph-guided response integration process for logical consistency, and another describes iterative synthesis and refinement across candidate responses.

Space of

nodes.name: Response evaluation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is the generation of an explicit judgement about another model's response: an assessment, score, selection, or classification based on quality, relevance, or correctness. Several descriptions place an LLM or LMM in the evaluator role, often centered on the final evaluation outcome, and one paper explicitly calls this output "the final judgement"; some also require structured rationales alongside scalar scores. A smaller framing emphasizes the analysis process behind the judgement, describing the evaluator as examining the components and structure of a query and response, and where criteria are stated, papers refer to accurate judgements and consistency with ground-truth.

Variants. Papers study this behavior under several names, including answer critique, judgement generation, and response judging. The settings range from vision-language question answering, where models critique a given answer with structured rationales and scalar scores, to text judging tasks that compare two or more responses or are used in response ranking, reward modeling, and verifying agent task completion. Some descriptions single out hard queries and

nodes.name: Response harmfulness classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a binary judgment over a model response, asking whether the response is safe or unsafe. One paper frames it for moderation as "predicting whether a response is safe or not," while another treats it as self-checking, where "the LLM checks if the response is safe or not" and outputs a binary indicator. In the more specific self-checking formulation, the safe label is described as a response that "does not contain any sensitive factors."

Variants. Papers use two closely related names for this behavior, response classification and safety checking. The main variation is in setting rather than outcome: one line treats it as moderation of a response, and another has the model evaluate its own generated response for sensitive or harmful content. Both formulations keep the task as a binary safe versus unsafe rating.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to three measurement instruments: BeaverTails, HarmBench, and WildGuardMix. The measurement setup is described in benchmark and test-dataset terms, with papers saying they "consider ... as benchmarks" for response classification and also "utilize datasets

nodes.name: Response ranking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats response ranking as ordering several candidate responses from best to worst, or choosing the best one, based on a judge's assessment of quality. The judging source varies, with LLMs and judge models appearing most often, while some papers instead use human raters, reward models, annotators, or PRM scores. A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to reranking generated reasoning paths so that the highest scoring path, or the path with the most accurate final answer, is selected, and another frames success as choosing the candidate with the lowest predicted hallucination rate.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous labels, with response ranking the prevailing name and smaller variants including response reranking, response re-ranking, and solution reranking. The studied settings range from generic instruction prompts with multiple proposed responses, to tournament-style and "first-round-rank" candidate ranking, to Best-of-N and weighted majority voting over reasoning paths or chains of thought. Other variants appear in multimodal reasoning, where a PRM selects top-scoring responses, and in hallucination mitiga

nodes.name: Response revision
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat response revision as changing an initial, low-quality, weak, incorrect, or unclear answer into a better one. The prevailing description is an edit process, adding, deleting, or substituting tokens, usually guided by a reference, instruction, critique, or feedback; some papers narrow success to factual correction or removal of false information, while others treat success as a stronger, more preferred output or a conversational shift to a correct answer. A smaller line of work frames the same behavior as a refinement capability, correcting an instruction-following failure with minimal irrelevant revisions. In one simulated-society setting, a paper claims a causal relationship from Feedback generation to response revision, describing ratings and explanations as informing the revisions.

Variants. Variants span several settings. Papers describe token-level editing, conditional weak-to-strong correction, multi-turn conversational revision where an answer shifts from incorrect or unclear to correct, and factuality-focused revision that corrects or removes false information, sometimes replacing it with common-knowledge facts. Other work s

nodes.name: Resume parsing
nodes.definition: The process of converting unstructured or semi-structured resume documents into a structured format, such as JSON, by extracting and organizing personal, educational, and professional information.

nodes.name: Retain query answering
nodes.definition: The model's observable ability to correctly answer questions about information it was instructed to retain, even when those questions appear alongside forget queries.

nodes.name: Retrosynthetic planning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats this behavior as working backward from a target molecule or compound to identify precursor or reactant molecules for synthesis. Some definitions make the output a full, step-by-step synthesis pathway ending in commercially available reactants, while a narrower formulation treats success as predicting a one-step retrosynthetic reaction or reaction template from a product molecule and text context.

Variants. The named variants in the papers are retrosynthetic planning, retrosynthesis, and reaction prediction. They are formulated as step-by-step pathway generation for a designed or target molecule, identification of potential reactants for a target compound, and one-step template prediction from a product molecule and text context, with predicted templates used as reaction nodes.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 1 measurement instrument, Mol-Instructions. The linked instrument is described as a dataset covering molecule generation tasks, where retrosynthesis predicts the possible precursors that lead to a given target molecule.

nodes.name: Reward function generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is an LLM producing executable code for a reward function that specifies an agent's objective in a simulation or reinforcement learning task. Definitions commonly ground the generation in a task or goal description plus environment details or code, and describe successful outputs as reward code that guides learning, for example by returning the scalar signal whose cumulative maximization defines the task or by correctly using environment attributes to encourage a desired behavior. A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to generating dense, shaped reward code from a natural language goal.

Variants. Papers study several variants and settings. Some treat reward generation as one part of broader program generation, alongside termination functions or simulator dynamics, while others use it to encode desired coordination behavior for teammate training, including executable functions over state and action transitions and prompts requiring the form "def reward(self) -> float". Another named variant is dense reward code generation, which focuses on shaped dense rewards, and the domains explicitly mentioned include robotics, gam

nodes.name: Reward hacking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats reward hacking as an observable failure mode in which optimization against a reward function or evaluation system yields outputs that score well without meeting the intended goal. Most papers describe the observable pattern as semantically meaningless, degenerate, repeated, trivial, incomplete, or otherwise functionally useless outputs that nonetheless receive high reward, pass a verifier, or appear successful to human supervisors. A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to domain-specific forms, such as abruptly shortened speech token sequences or loophole-seeking behavior that gets credit for a task without actually completing it.

Variants. Papers study the behavior in several settings. The most common textual variants are meaningless or repeated strings, short outputs, gibberish, and overly long responses with meaningless repetition, and some work also describes longer chain-of-thoughts grown through repetition rather than solving the problem. Other variants appear in formally verified code generation, where models produce trivial or incomplete specifications or programs that satisfy the verifier, in spee

nodes.name: Reward prediction
nodes.definition: The task of predicting the future reward signal in a reinforcement learning environment based on a history of states and actions.

nodes.name: Riddle solving
nodes.definition: The task of deducing the correct answer to a puzzle or question posed in a metaphorical or ambiguous way.

nodes.name: Risk-of-bias rationale selection
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of selecting the correct human-written rationale that justifies a risk-of-bias rating from a set of plausible alternatives.

nodes.name: RNA structure prediction
nodes.definition: The task of identifying and predicting the base-pairing interactions within a single RNA molecule to determine its two-dimensional structure.

nodes.name: Robot action generation
nodes.definition: The observable task of producing a sequence of action tokens to control a robot based on visual and linguistic inputs.

nodes.name: Robotic manipulation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage describes robotic manipulation as observable, goal-directed physical interaction with objects or the environment, carried out through control actions, action trajectories, or continuous robot-arm control in simulated or real settings. Many definitions treat success as achieving the specified physical outcome, for example reaching, pushing, picking, sweeping, peg insertion, pick and place, or placing one object on another, while some formulations make the criterion more explicit as moving target objects to a goal location, sometimes maximizing how many arrive there or scoring the ratio successfully transported. Some papers further specify that the behavior is conditioned on visual input, textual prompts, or language instructions.

Variants. Papers study several settings, especially tabletop tasks and object-moving tasks such as transport or rearrangement. Other definitions emphasize longer-horizon or lower-level control, sometimes from visual, textual, or language input, while narrower formulations include category-based sorting and placing one object on another; some settings are mobile, multi-agent, or multi-floor, and

nodes.name: Role-playing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is adopting a specified persona, character, or role and producing responses that remain consistent with it in conversation. Papers commonly treat success as fidelity to the target persona, or as outputs that match a character's profile, speaking style, communication style, voice, tone, or goals across turns. A smaller line of work broadens the behavior to perspective or respondent simulation, such as generating text from a lawmaker or news outlet's viewpoint, answering survey items as a human respondent, or simulating patient or student behavior.

Variants. Variants differ by interaction structure, modality, and domain. One recurring family uses image-centered multimodal role-play, including commentary interaction, human-role dialogue, and inter-role dialogue; other papers study persona adoption through prompt steering, profile- and scenario-conditioned multi-turn dialogue, and sequential fictional characters within story-like prompts. Domain-specific versions cast the model as a survey respondent, patient, learner, social scientist persona, or dramatic character, and one paper claims a causal relationship from Ro

nodes.name: Safe plan generation
nodes.definition: The generation of a sequence of actions that achieves a goal without causing physical harm or violating safety constraints.

nodes.name: Safe response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as answering harmful, dangerous, or sensitive prompts with non-toxic, ethical, and harmless content, most often by refusing the request, rejecting its premise, or redirecting to a constructive alternative. Several papers also require the answer to remain polite, helpful, appropriate, or relevant rather than stopping at a bare refusal. In Safety-Tuned LLaMAs: Lessons From Improving the Safety of Large Language Models that Follow Instructions, the pattern is stated directly: "A majority of these responses were rejections to the posed red teaming queries." A smaller framing appears in work on negative-mood interactions, where safe generation is described as providing encouragement and comfort.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for the behavior, most commonly harmless response generation, and also response detoxification, harm-free generation, safe content generation, and safe answer generation. The task is studied on harmful instructions, dangerous prompts, red-teaming queries, adversarial or jailbreak prompts, sensitive or malicious queries, and multimodal settings; one line of work further expect

nodes.name: Safety classifier evasion
nodes.definition: The observable outcome where a malicious prompt is misclassified as safe by a dedicated safety model, thereby bypassing an external layer of defense.

nodes.name: Safety judgment
nodes.definition: Categorizing a user query or intent as safe or unsafe based on provided context.

nodes.name: Sarcasm detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is as a classification task: predicting whether a text expresses sarcasm. One definition makes the criterion more explicit by describing sarcastic statements as conveying the opposite of their literal meaning, typically for humorous or critical effect, and as relying on contextual and pragmatic cues. A smaller line of work applies the same decision to spoken utterances, with papers noting that communicative intent is expressed largely through tone.

Variants. Papers mostly study this behavior in text settings, including sarcasm detection on the Sarcasm Headlines corpus. Another setting treats it as a speech classification task on MUSTARD clips, where the target is whether a spoken utterance is sarcastic. The common names are 'sarcasm detection' and 'sarcasm', and one paper also places it among 'instances of figurative' language.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The papers instead describe task settings such as classification on the Sarcasm Headlines corpus and on MUSTARD clips, but no instrument is recorded as measuring it.

What it is taken as evidence of. Construct lin

nodes.name: Saturation degree calculation
nodes.definition: Determining whether a molecule has a given degree of saturation from its formula or structural clues.

nodes.name: Scene classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is identifying and classifying the overall scene, environment, or setting depicted in an image. Most definitions treat success as recognizing the image-level scene or assigning a semantic label to the whole image based on its overall content, with examples such as "harbor" or "residential area." Another common phrasing is simply how well models can identify and classify different scenes or environments.

Variants. Papers use both "scene classification" and "scene recognition" for this behavior. The settings mentioned include remote sensing image understanding, where the whole image is labeled by scene type, and a more localized instruction that asks a model to "Highlight the area that shows a natural outdoor scene." One paper also includes it as a question category.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it in the papers, so the papers do not specify what it is evidence of.

nodes.name: Scene description generation
nodes.definition: Producing a detailed textual description of a narrative scene from a story fragment and its context, intended to serve as a prompt for a text-to-image model.

nodes.name: Scene graph generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the shared framing treats scene graph generation as producing a structured representation built from entities or objects and their relations. One formulation defines it as converting a natural language caption into objects, attributes, and relationships, even writing the graph as {O, R, A}, while another describes constructing a scene graph for an image as triples of entities and their spatial relations, with the graph said to capture "the essential spatial relation between visual concepts."

Variants. The available usages span caption-to-graph conversion and image-based graph construction, with the latter emphasizing spatial triples rather than objects, attributes, and relationships. Beyond these settings, one paper claims a causal relationship from task decomposition to scene graph generation, stating that failure to "decompose discrete scenes from a complex narrative" leads to a bottleneck when generating scene graphs.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The operational details that do appear describe converting captions to scene graphs and measuring "the consistency over graphs," in

nodes.name: Schema linking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats schema linking as identifying, selecting, or outputting the tables and columns relevant to a natural language question, usually the subset needed to construct a valid or accurate SQL query. Some authors make the matching step more explicit, describing it as connecting question tokens, keywords, or phrases to schema elements, while a smaller line of work extends the linked items beyond tables and columns to rows or foreign keys. SAFE-SQL describes the step as detecting question "keywords and phrases" that correspond to schema elements such as tables, columns, rows, and foreign keys, and other papers frame success as grounding schema elements so the SQL can correctly reference them.

Variants. A smaller line of work renames the behavior as schema item grounding, schema parsing, schema resolution, schema item prediction, schema selection, or schema pruning. These variants appear especially in large-scale or multi-database settings with complex, redundant, or filtered schemas, where papers describe extracting a salient subset of tables, columns, and sometimes relationships from a large schema pool. LinkAlign: S

nodes.name: Schema matching
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is matching semantically corresponding columns or attributes across tables or knowledge graphs. Most commonly, authors describe it as checking whether a pair of columns from two tables are related, often as a binary classification decision; another formulation asks for a valid mapping of columns between two tables so a join can be performed. A smaller line of work uses the name attribute alignment for matching attributes from different knowledge graphs that have the same semantic meaning even when their labels differ.

Variants. Recurring settings include table-centric matching between two tables, sometimes with partially overlapping columns, and alignment across different knowledge graphs. The table-focused work uses names such as schema matching and table join prediction, while the knowledge-graph work uses attribute alignment and sometimes discusses alignment together with filtering. One paper also relates schema matching to candidate generation, ranking, and confidence scoring.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to one measurement instrument, Wikidata, used in evaluation and described as a general knowl

nodes.name: Scholarly title generation
nodes.definition: The task of generating a title for a scholarly article that matches the style of a user's past publications.

nodes.name: Scientific abstract generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a text generation task in which a model produces a scientific or research abstract from a title-based prompt. Papers agree on the core behavior, abstract writing conditioned on the title, but differ in scope: one formulation treats it as generating an abstract of a specific document, such as a scientific paper, from its title, while another treats it as generating a concise abstract for a research topic from an article title and associated keywords, with objectives, methods, and subtopics covered and with length and scope matched to a human-written abstract.

Variants. Papers use the names abstract generation and abstract writing for this behavior. The studied settings vary between summarizing a specific paper and producing an abstract aligned with a research topic; prompt formats range from the title alone to the title with associated keywords, and one paper places the task in math papers by using abstracts from MathAbstracts and each paper's title as the prompt.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers. Instead, papers operationalize the behavior through prompting set

nodes.name: Scientific experimentation
nodes.definition: The task of performing simulated science experiments by navigating an environment, manipulating objects, and observing outcomes to test a hypothesis or achieve a goal.

nodes.name: Scientific problem solving
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Definitions consistently treat this as work on complex problems drawn from scientific or natural science domains. The prevailing formulation is end to end: a model receives such a problem and, in the more specific wording, is expected to produce a complete, functional coded solution; a broader wording describes it as addressing complex scientific-domain problems that require structured reasoning and domain knowledge.

Variants. The available uses emphasize natural science settings and scientific research problems. One line of work frames it narrowly as code generation for real scientific research problems and reports problems from 16 diverse domains, while another places it more broadly among challenging tasks alongside mathematics and code generation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to two measurement instruments, OlympiadBench and SciBench. The recorded uses say it is measured by OlympiadBench in work on scientific problems, and by SciBench, which is described as assessing college-level scientific problem-solving abilities.

What it is taken as evidence of. The linked construct claims do not explicitly present this behavior as evidence of a

nodes.name: Scientific question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as answering science-domain questions, most commonly as multiple-choice items over a wide range of topics and often with reasoning over provided context or external knowledge. A smaller set of definitions broadens it to multimodal scientific questions that require understanding diagrams, charts, or other visual aids, while some papers narrow the scope to school-curriculum, elementary-school, graduate-level, or expert-level questions that call for domain-specific knowledge and logical inference.

Variants. Papers use several labels for closely related versions, including science question answering, scientific question answering, STEM question answering, and, in one case, scientific reasoning. The studied settings range from subject-specific questions from school curricula and climate science to simple, complex, open-book, and multi-step scientific questions; multimodal versions are a recurring variant, described as requiring figure-based or visual understanding and, in some formulations, extracting external knowledge.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 7 measurement instruments

nodes.name: Scientific survey generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the prevailing usage is generation of a structured survey or literature review on a specified research topic. Most formulations require synthesis across multiple sources and an organized output, either as an end-to-end academic survey with an outline, content, and references, or as a coherent review that supports claims with newly generated citations. One paper narrows the task to writing "a short literature review" from a title, keywords, and abstract, while another treats it as the literature review stage in which the system reads a provided set of references and abstracts to understand the research background.

Variants. Papers use nearby labels such as scientific survey generation, review composition, and literature review. The clearest named variants are fully LLM-based, RAG-based, and human-guided survey generation, presented as different evaluation levels. Other settings differ by inputs: some provide only a topic signal from title, keywords, and abstract, while another begins from a bib file containing references and their corresponding abstracts.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The pape

nodes.name: Scientific text-to-image generation
nodes.definition: The observable task of producing a scientific visualization, such as a figure, chart, or plot, based on a textual description.

nodes.name: Script handling
nodes.definition: Correctly processing text in diverse writing systems, including right-to-left scripts and non-standard glyphs, particularly in low-resource languages.

nodes.name: Scrolling
nodes.definition: The action of determining whether a target UI element is currently visible and, if not, deciding the direction to scroll (up or down).

nodes.name: Search query generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is the model’s production of search queries for retrieval: a textual, and sometimes formal, query is generated so a retriever, search engine, or other knowledge source can fetch external information. Most formulations condition the query on a question plus context or on the current reasoning state, and they describe better performance as producing effective, sufficiently specified queries that retrieve relevant documents. A smaller line of work broadens this to heterogeneous sources in SPARQL, SQL, or natural language, and one paper treats it reversely as generating a question or query from a given response.

Variants. Papers use both “query generation” and “search query generation” for closely related tasks. Variants include generating a single query for simple questions, generating multiple or k queries, and producing a new query at each hop of retrieval. The behavior is also studied with note content as input, with forecasting questions and background for news search, and over structured and unstructured sources where the output may be SPARQL, SQL, or a natural-sentence query.

Space of elicitation and scores. No inst

nodes.name: Self-correction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is iterative revision of a model's own prior output after checking it against feedback. Most definitions describe identifying an error or deficiency and then producing a corrected or improved version, often over multiple rounds, with feedback coming from execution results, verifier messages, tool or environment errors, solver checks, critiques, or user feedback; some papers also frame it as reviewing a previous generation and answering again with that feedback. A smaller line of work casts it as a latent ability or capacity rather than just an observed task, but the common success criterion is still a revised answer, code artifact, plan, query, or action that is more correct, valid, or aligned than the initial one.

Variants. Variants span many artifacts and settings. The most common are code- and reasoning-centered forms, including self-debugging from execution feedback, proof and chain-of-thought correction, and iterative answer or response revision; papers also use names such as error correction, self-refinement, self-checking, and progressive or iterative refinement. Smaller variants target specific artifacts

nodes.name: Self-evaluation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats self-evaluation as a model judging its own output, usually for correctness or quality, after generating a summary, answer, reasoning step, solution, or other text. What counts as the behavior is typically an explicit self-judgment, such as a score, a correctness decision, a confidence level, a likelihood like P(true), or written feedback about issues and advice; some papers also use it to decide which of two answers is better. A smaller line of work narrows the task to checking dialogue responses against their context, rating generated definitions, formulations, and code from execution results, pre-checking an abstract's novelty against a paper database, or asking whether the model's own output is an instance of a concept.

Variants. Papers use several nearby labels for this behavior, including inconsistency identification, self-review, self-assessment, and self-grading. The settings vary widely, with recurring examples in summarization, reasoning and search, harmlessness-oriented text appraisal, instruction-following uncertainty, dialogue consistency reflection, scientific abstract novelty checks, and exec

nodes.name: Self-reflection
nodes.definition:
