Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is an iterative review of the model's own prior outputs, actions, or reasoning to diagnose errors and produce feedback for a next attempt. Most definitions center on incorrect predictions, failed trajectories, past decisions, or prior code, and treat success as yielding a revised answer, plan, decision, or retrieval action after reflection. A smaller line of work describes it more broadly as a latent ability or cognitive process for critically evaluating earlier responses, selecting a more plausible solution, or learning from self-generated data, and some papers narrow the reflective act itself to explicit judgments such as GOOD or BAD labels or safety scores with <reflection> tags.

Variants. Variants mainly differ in what is reflected on and in the form of the reflection. Several papers use names such as self-feedback, reflection on failure cases, error reflection, and self-reflection generation for diagnosing incorrect outputs or failed attempts and verbalizing reasons or future fixes. Others separate short-term reflection, a comparison of two parent heuristics, from long-term reflection, a summary of lessons accumulated

nodes.name: Self-verification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a second-pass check of an already produced answer or solution, aimed at judging its correctness, reliability, or consistency before acceptance. Most descriptions make the model verify its own output by generating and executing a checking procedure, often code-based, by comparing answers from different prompts and accepting the answer only when they match, or by checking consistency with a given context, sometimes framed as entailment. Depending on the formulation, the judgment can come from the same model, from agreement across prompts, from a completed continuation or peer judgment, from a reviewer agent, or from comparison with a reference answer; a smaller line of work extends the behavior to re-solving or double-checking after a failed check.

Variants. Papers use several closely related names, most often answer verification and self-verification, with one paper calling it double-checking. The studied variants include code-based self-verification that can review and adjust a solution after a false result, consistency-based checking across prompts, entailment-style context-grounded verification, reviewer cross-chec

nodes.name: Semantic parsing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, semantic parsing is most commonly described as translating natural language inputs, usually utterances, questions, instructions, or observations, into structured outputs such as logical forms, programs, queries, database commands, API calls, or JSON. The prevailing usage emphasizes outputs that are structured and often machine-executable or programmatic, while some papers additionally frame the target as a more canonical semantic representation. A smaller line of work narrows the task to parsing user queries or task descriptions into distinct components or predefined JSON keys, with one paper explicitly extracting fields such as instruction, input text, question, URL, data, and categories.

Variants. Papers study several named variants of this behavior. These include intent and slot filling, task-oriented dialogue parsing, and task-oriented semantic parsing, alongside logical form generation for knowledge base question answering, where targets include SPARQL, S-expressions, SQL, first-order logic, Lisp, and abstract syntax trees. Some papers also use narrower labels such as query parsing and prompt parsing when the output is a compo

nodes.name: Semantic segmentation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers describe this behavior as classifying each pixel in an image into a predefined set of semantic categories, or assigning pixel-level labels to image regions corresponding to semantic categories. A smaller line of work uses an object-centric formulation, where the task is to generate pixel-level masks for specific objects within a visual input. Across these formulations, the observable output is either per-pixel semantic labels or pixel-level masks for target objects.

Variants. Papers use both semantic segmentation and object segmentation labels. Beyond the prevailing per-pixel labeling setup, one paper studies an object-centric variant that segments objects by matching them to logically inferred image regions and then performing object segmentation on extracted cropped image regions of the target objects. Other mentions place the task in cross-view adaptation across data distributions, in open-vocabulary settings, and one paper relates image restoration to it by using segmentation as a downstream task on COCO 2017 and ADE20K.

Space of elicitation and scores. Across papers, semantic segmentation is measured by four linked instruments, all

nodes.name: Semantic tagging
nodes.definition: Assigning semantic category labels to tokens.

nodes.name: Semantic textual similarity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as judging how similar two texts or sentences are in meaning and, most often, returning a similarity score on a continuous scale. Definitions repeatedly describe predicting or measuring the degree of semantic equivalence between a pair of texts or sentences, and one paper explicitly asks a system to "assess the similarity of the two sentences and provide a score from 0 to 1." A smaller line of work frames success more categorically, as deciding whether two sentences are semantically similar or paraphrases, whether two financial texts are semantically related, or whether a post-dropout response preserves the meaning of a pre-dropout response. Another variant evaluates success by whether semantically related pairs receive higher similarity than unrelated pairs.

Variants. Papers use closely related labels such as semantic textual similarity, sentence similarity, semantic similarity, and text pair classification. The behavior is studied with ordinary sentence pairs, with monolingual and cross-lingual sentence pairs, in finance through headline to article and query to intent matching, in biomedical task coll

nodes.name: Sentence alignment
nodes.definition: Matching a sentence in a plain language summary to one or zero semantically similar sentences in the parallel abstract.

nodes.name: Sentence classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available paper treats sentence classification as a task of categorizing sentences by syntactic structure, with labels such as simple, complex, compound, and compound-complex. Success is described as producing "a list of correctly classified sentences with labels" (Automated Knowledge Graph Construction using Large Language Models and Sentence Complexity Modelling).

Variants. The described task scope centers on classifying among sentence types, specifically simple, complex, compound, and compound-complex. No other sub-tasks, domains, modalities, or alternative names are described.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The available paper describes model-based evaluation, noting that transformer-based models and smaller LLMs were fine-tuned on a training set and evaluated on a test set for sentence types, but no named instrument is recorded as eliciting or scoring the behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as what this behavior indicates, so the available relationships do not specify any broader construct that sentence classification is taken to evidence.

nodes.name: Sentence completion
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is selecting or generating the most plausible continuation of a partial sentence or surrounding context. Most definitions allow either free generation or choosing among options, and the context ranges from a phrase or sentence to a paragraph or passage ending; some papers narrow it further to predicting a final word or the next sentence. In the generative versions, authors often explicitly prefix prompts with "Complete the sentence:", while evaluative versions describe success as choosing the correct or better continuation from candidate endings.

Variants. Papers study several named variants. A common line uses sentence completion for commonsense reasoning, including "sentence completion reasoning" and challenging completion scenarios, while other work treats it as "last word completion" or "content analysis", where the model predicts a passage's missing final word and relies on long-range or narrative context. Smaller variants cast it as "sentence continuation", selecting the better next sentence between two options, or as graph-based completion, predicting the remaining text of a node from its existing text plus surroundi

nodes.name: Sentiment analysis
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats this as an observable text classification task: papers ask models to determine the sentiment, tone, or emotional valence of a sentence, review, tweet, or other text. The most common outputs are binary positive versus negative labels or three-way positive, negative, or neutral labels, and some papers describe the same behavior as opinion polarity classification. Most definitions stay at the task level, though a few phrase it as a latent ability to infer emotional polarity or affective labels from text; smaller variants use 5-way labels, generated label text, or continuous valence scores.

Variants. Variants are mostly text-based but span several settings, including single-sentence tasks, movie-review and tweet classification, document-level and sentence-level prediction, code-mixed text, Persian text, and finance-related sentiment. Papers also use names such as sentiment classification, opinion polarity classification, sentiment label generation, emotional valence scoring, and embodied emotion recognition. One paper uses sentiment analysis as a reasoning path for stance by identifying affective lexicons such

nodes.name: Sequence compression
nodes.definition: Generating a concise program or representation that reproduces the input sequence with fewer bits than the original.

nodes.name: Sequence merging
nodes.definition: Compressing a multi-character pattern into a shorter representation during sequence transformation.

nodes.name: Sequence understanding
nodes.definition: The task of processing a sequence of spoken words to comprehend and classify its overall intent or meaning.

nodes.name: Sequential recommendation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is predicting the next item a user will interact with from a chronologically ordered history of prior interactions. Definitions converge on forecasting the user's subsequent choice, future interaction, or next likely item from historical records, so what counts as the behavior is producing that next-item prediction from the preceding sequence.

Variants. The prevailing name is sequential recommendation, though some authors use next-item prediction for the same behavior. Smaller variations reformulate it as next-token prediction in an autoregressive setup, where the next item is forecast from the predicted token sequence, or cast it as a natural language generation task that asks the model to recommend an item from a user's interaction history.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to three measurement instruments, all described as real-world or benchmark datasets: LastFM, MovieLens-25M multi-tabular, and Yelp. The linked instruments show that papers operationalize it through dataset-based evaluation on those settings.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers do not explicitly treat this behavior as refl

nodes.name: Sexism detection
nodes.definition: Identifying language that expresses or implies discrimination based on sex, particularly in online discourse, by recognizing hostile or stereotypical content.

nodes.name: Shadow removal
nodes.definition: The observable task of reducing or eliminating unwanted shadows from an image to enhance visibility.

nodes.name: Short-form question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat this behavior as giving a concise, direct answer to a question, usually factual and without elaborate explanation. Some authors narrow the expected response to a single word or phrase, while a smaller domain-specific formulation uses brief textual answers to semi-open financial questions, described as a few words or phrases or selected from specific options. Another formulation also includes abstention, allowing the model to answer the query or respond with "I don't know".

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, including short-form question answering, short answer generation, and short-answer question answering. The main settings are general factual QA and objective short-answer questions in financial industry knowledge; some versions are framed as semi-open questions, and some explicitly require single-word or single-phrase outputs.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to two measurement instruments: TriviaQA and UNCLE. TriviaQA is used as a short-form question answering task, while UNCLE is described as a benchmark designed to evaluate uncertainty expression in both long- and short-form QA.

What it is taken

nodes.name: Short-term time series forecasting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The only explicit definition treats short-term time series forecasting as predicting time series values over a short future horizon from a historical sequence. In the available usage, the description stays at the level of this prediction task formulation.

Variants. The only variant explicitly described studies the task on the M4 dataset, which the paper says includes market data across various frequencies, with prediction horizons ranging from 6 to 48. The same paper also discusses short-term forecasting alongside long-term forecasting across varying sequence lengths.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The available paper reports short-term forecasting experiments, but no separate measurement instrument is linked to the behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it, so the available relationships do not specify what it is taken to indicate.

nodes.name: Shortest path finding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat it as a task of finding the shortest path between two specified nodes, usually in a weighted undirected graph, with success defined as returning the path whose edge weights sum to the minimum total. Some formulations also require generating the path and its distance, while a smaller line narrows the answer format to the exact sequence of nodes on the shortest path.

Variants. Across formulations, variation is mainly in what the model must output. Some tasks ask for the actual shortest path for selected node pairs, some query shortest path distance after prompting with two target nodes, and one paper presents the exact path of the shortest path as a harder version. The setting is most explicitly a weighted undirected graph, though one definition states it more generally on a graph.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the recorded relationships, the task itself is used to measure State tracking: one paper argues that solving shortest path requires the model to maintain the state of its exploration in the graph.

What it is taken as evidence of. At the construct level, only one construct is linked, Gra

nodes.name: Sign language identification
nodes.definition: The task of classifying which sign language is being used in a given video input.

nodes.name: Sign language recognition
nodes.definition: The task of classifying pre-segmented video clips of individual sign language movements into their corresponding labels.

nodes.name: Sign language translation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating written or textual output in a spoken language from a sign language video sequence, often under the labels sign language translation or sign-to-text translation. Definitions usually say the output should correspond to the meaning of the signs, and some add that it should be fluent or preserve meaning, grammar, and lexical content. Many papers also study a sentence-level form, including isolated sentence-length clips and translation done one sentence at a time, sometimes without broader document context.

Variants. Paper labels include sign language translation, sign-to-text translation, and sentence-level translation. The most visible variants are sentence-level settings, such as sentence-level ASL to English translation, zero-shot sentence-level translation on FLEURS-ASL, and translation of isolated sentence-length clips; one benchmark also mentions discourse-level translation. Another recurring setting translates each sign language into its region's spoken language, and one paper relates the sentence-level framing to machine translation through sentence- versus paragraph-level

nodes.name: Single-document question answering
nodes.definition: The task of answering a question based on information contained within a single provided document.

nodes.name: Single-hop question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available usage, papers treat this behavior as answering questions that can be resolved with a single piece of retrieved information. The only explicit formulation also labels these as 'simple single-hop tasks.'

Variants. Beyond the label 'simple single-hop tasks,' the papers do not name additional sub-tasks, domains, or modalities for this behavior.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior in the papers, so no elicitation or scoring instrument is specified.

What it is taken as evidence of. The papers do not link this behavior to any broader construct as evidence of.

nodes.name: Single-step retrosynthesis
nodes.definition: The observable task of predicting a set of immediate reactant molecules from a single given product molecule.

nodes.name: Situated question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats it as question answering grounded in a provided 3D situation. Definitions align on answering questions about objects, attributes, counts, spatial relations, affordances, room type, or scene descriptions from the agent's current situation and spatial context, and one example asks, "What is the object closest to my left?" with the answer "A lamp" (SPARTUN3D: Situated Spatial Understanding of 3D World in Large Language Model).

Variants. Papers vary mainly in the kinds of scene-grounded questions they emphasize. One line expands the task to object existence, counting, attributes, and spatial relationships, while another highlights question types that target different levels of spatial reasoning ability for embodied agents; some formulations also use a multi-modal situation description and a text-image interleaved question grounded in the 3D scene (Multi-modal Situated Reasoning in 3D Scenes).

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to one measurement instrument, SQA3D. In that instrument, the prompt is formatted as "<Situation> <Question>" and the answer "should be a phrase or a single word," so t

nodes.name: Situational question answering
nodes.definition: The task of responding to questions that describe a specific scenario or dilemma, often designed to elicit personality-specific responses.

nodes.name: Sleep stage classification
nodes.definition: Classifying segments of physiological signals into one of five sleep stages: Wake, N1, N2, N3, or REM, based on EEG, EOG, and EMG data.

nodes.name: Slide generation
nodes.definition: The task of automatically creating a multi-slide presentation from a source document.

nodes.name: Snow removal
nodes.definition: The task of removing snow from an image, guided by a textual instruction.

nodes.name: Social interaction
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of an agent engaging with other characters (NPCs) in a multi-agent environment through actions like conversation or games.

nodes.name: Socratic questioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, it is treated as inquiry-based questioning that gets the learner to work toward an answer rather than receive it directly. One formulation in "MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-ended Pedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors" narrows this to generating, for each correct solution step, at least one corresponding guidance question that could be posed instead of simply giving the answer. Another paper uses the label "Socratic dialogue" for open-ended questioning that encourages exploration and self-reflection rather than direct correction.

Variants. The papers use closely related names, "Socratic questioning" and "Socratic dialogue," and study them in different tutoring settings. One focuses on math problem solving as step-aligned guidance questions tied to correct solution steps, while the other discusses English education and contrasts Socratic dialogue with straightforward Q&A by emphasizing open-ended, iterative exploration.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The only explicit operationalization is an evaluation task in which a model is checked for producing at least one guidance question

nodes.name: Software development
nodes.definition: Producing software artifacts such as games or web apps that can run and satisfy functional checks.

nodes.name: Software issue resolution
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The available definition treats this behavior as an end-to-end software fixing task: a model receives a software issue described in natural language and succeeds only if it produces a fix that results in a passing test suite. Source snippets describe this operationally as generating patches that successfully resolve issues, and papers report performance in terms of issue resolution rate.

Variants. The reported settings are SWE-bench Lite, described as a more self-contained evaluation of functional bug fixes, and SWE-bench Verified. Across these settings, the task remains framed as resolving natural-language-described issues by producing patches that fix them.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure this behavior with 2 instruments, most often SWE-bench Lite and also SWE-bench Verified. These instruments are used to report issue resolution rate, and SWE-bench Lite is described as a 300-instance subset intended to provide a more self-contained evaluation of functional bug fixes.

What it is taken as evidence of. The papers do not link this behavior to any construct.

nodes.name: Solution generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as the observable production of a candidate solution for a given problem or prompt. Papers agree on that core task, though they often formulate it as generating multiple candidate solutions rather than only one, and one paper places those candidates in a later ranking step where a verifier picks the most suitable solution.

Variants. The main variants concern the collection of multiple outputs and the emphasis on diversity. Papers describe candidate solutions, diverse model-generated solutions, and single-problem settings where many solutions are gathered for later comparison.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers operationalize it by prompting models to generate candidate solutions, sometimes explicitly seeking diverse outputs, and one paper then has a learned reward model, referred to as a verifier, rank the generated solutions and select the most suitable one.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it, so the available papers do not specify a broader construct that this behavior is taken to indicate.

nodes.name: Solution grading
nodes.definition: The observable task of evaluating a given solution against a reference or rubric and assigning a numerical score.

nodes.name: Sorting
nodes.definition: The task of arranging a sequence of elements into a specified order, such as alphabetical or numerical.

nodes.name: Speaker adaptation
nodes.definition: Reducing word error rates more effectively when context examples come from the same speaker as the target audio, especially at intermediate shot counts.

nodes.name: Species classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, species classification is treated as predicting species identity, but papers differ on the input modality. One formulation asks for the species of an animal vocalization from audio, sometimes conditioned on metadata or candidate species lists, while another asks for the species of an organism from its genomic sequence. In the audio formulation, papers describe outputs as the scientific name, common name, or "taxonomic name" of the focal species, or all species present in a recording, and one paper describes the task as "highly deterministic."

Variants. The main variants concern modality and target scope. Audio work frames the task over bioacoustic recordings and varies between predicting a single focal species and predicting all species present, with some formulations additionally using metadata or candidate species lists. Genomic work uses species classification datasets over virus and fungi and also refers to the task as Species Classification, or SC.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers do not link it to any construct as evidence of, so th

nodes.name: Species detection
nodes.definition: Determining whether a specified species is present in an audio recording, or outputting none when absent.

nodes.name: Species range estimation
nodes.definition: The behavior of estimating species range maps using a small number of location observations combined with textual priors.

nodes.name: Spectrum interpretation
nodes.definition: The sub-task of analyzing multimodal spectral data, including images of IR, MASS, H-NMR, and C-NMR spectra, to confirm or revise hypotheses about a molecule's structural components.

nodes.name: Speech classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the behavior is treated as a speech-to-label task. One definition frames it broadly as classifying an audio waveform of speech into a predefined set of categories, while another uses the narrower name word identity prediction, identifying a specific keyword or command from a spoken utterance. Across these formulations, success is described as assigning the utterance to the target category or word identity.

Variants. The recorded variants focus on raw speech inputs and spoken-word recognition. Papers mention raw speech classification with long sequences, speech classification on the SC10 subset of the Speech Commands dataset, and word identity prediction among spoken keywords or commands. One paper also places word prediction alongside phonemes and describes it as moderate in semantic difficulty.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers operationalize the behavior directly through task performance settings such as raw speech classification with long sequences and word identity prediction.

What it is taken as evidence of. Only one construct is linked to it, Long-range dependency modeling. O

nodes.name: Speech continuation
nodes.definition: Continuing a speech utterance from a text prompt and an initial speech segment so that the output seamlessly follows the prompt.

nodes.name: Speech emotion recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the task is treated as identifying the emotional state expressed in human speech from audio input. The prevailing formulation places it in dialogue or conversational contexts, and in the named operationalizations success is framed as assigning emotion labels to spoken utterances.

Variants. The studied settings are mostly dialogue and conversational speech, including multimodal, multi-party utterances. A smaller line of usage evaluates the task under adversarial text, where one study reports that some models show "complete susceptibility to adversarial text, with accuracy dropping to precisely 0.0%."

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to one measurement instrument, MELD, and no other instrument is named. MELD is described as an emotion classification benchmark, and as a multimodal multi-party dataset of conversational utterances labeled across seven emotion categories; another description adds that it includes sentiment annotation.

What it is taken as evidence of. The linked papers do not connect this behavior to any construct, so they do not specify what broader attribute it is taken to indicate.

nodes.name: Speech enhancement
nodes.definition: Generating clean acoustic tokens conditioned on semantic and noisy acoustic prompts.

nodes.name: Speech instruction following
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, this behavior is consistently treated as following instructions that arrive as speech. The common criterion is correct fulfillment of the spoken request: one formulation emphasizes generating an appropriate spoken response that fulfills the user's request, while another emphasizes correctly executing a command or constraint provided through spoken audio.

Variants. The naming varies only slightly, with papers using both speech instruction following and spoken instruction following. Studied settings include the helpful_base and vicuna subsets from Alpaca-Eval, a synthesized spoken IFEval derived from the original text-based IFEval, and interleaving speech-text inputs, which one paper notes can be challenging.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead describe assessing it through benchmark settings, specifically the helpful_base and vicuna subsets from Alpaca-Eval for the speech instruction following task, and a synthesized spoken IFEval dataset for spoken instruction-following capabilities.

What it is taken as evidence of. The only construct link reported is to Speech understanding, and

nodes.name: Speech recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats speech recognition as converting spoken language, an audio signal, or a spoken utterance into written text. Papers use closely related names, especially automatic speech recognition, speech recognition, and speech-to-text transcription; when they specify the target, they describe it as the source-language transcript or text of the same language. Some papers also frame success as accurate speech-to-text conversion, and one paper says ASR requires precise frame-level alignment rather than utterance-level understanding (It's Never Too Late: Fusing Acoustic Information into Large Language Models for Automatic Speech Recognition).

Variants. The dominant variant is direct speech-to-text transcription, but several papers study it alongside neighboring tasks, especially speech translation or automatic speech translation. A smaller line treats the transcript as an intermediate representation, describing speech-to-text transcription as converting speech tokens into intermediate text transcripts, while other papers place the task in low-resource, multilingual, conversational, accented, or spectrogram-based settings. One be

nodes.name: Speech reconstruction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the dominant framing treats this behavior as reconstructing a speech waveform from discrete tokens produced by a codec or generative model. A smaller line of work uses the broader label audio reconstruction, described as recovering a waveform or perceptually similar audio signal from compressed discrete tokens, and another formulation describes regenerating the original speech signal from intermediate representations such as semantic tokens and learned variational features. Success is described through how much information is preserved in the representations and through the fidelity and quality of the resynthesized speech.

Variants. Papers study it with different source representations and output targets: clean acoustic tokens are decoded back into enhanced speech signals, original speech is reconstructed from Zc and Zd, and audio is reconstructed from quantized query tokens or other generated discrete token sequences. The recurring names are speech reconstruction and, less often, audio reconstruction, spanning speech-focused and broader audio settings.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to one measurement instrume

nodes.name: Speech-to-speech instruction following
nodes.definition: Responding to spoken instructions with both text and spoken outputs that satisfy the user's request.

nodes.name: Speech-to-speech translation
nodes.definition: The task of translating spoken language in a source language directly into spoken language in a target language.

nodes.name: Speech translation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats speech translation as converting spoken content, spoken audio, or an utterance in a source language into written text in a target language. Most definitions make the text output explicit and often formulate the task as directly predicting target-language text from speech, while a smaller number use broader wording such as translating spoken language into another language without specifying the output form. Some papers also use the label speech-to-text translation and describe it as transcribing spoken audio into written text in a different target language.

Variants. Papers use several names for closely related versions of the task, including speech translation, speech-to-text translation, and direct speech translation. The most common distinction is between end-to-end speech translation, which directly converts speech in one language to text in another without intermediate transcription, and cascaded speech translation, which first transcribes speech with ASR and then applies machine translation. Smaller strands examine zero-shot speech translation settings and terminology translation within speech translation.

Spac

nodes.name: Spelling correction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats spelling correction as identifying and fixing misspellings in text while leaving other wording, style, and formatting unchanged. One benchmark prompt states, "Please output this exact text, with no changes at all except for fixing the misspellings," and also asks for preserving choices such as commas and US versus British spellings. A smaller line of work narrows the task to correcting spelling errors at the character level, while other papers use it more behaviorally, as correct answers despite inputs with typos, or as typo and sometimes grammatical correction that happens during rewriting even when not requested.

Variants. Papers refer to the behavior as typo correction, spelling correction, and spell-checking. The settings vary between exact-text correction tasks, character-level unsupervised spell-checking, and evaluations of "accuracy when inputs include typos." Another variant appears in rewriting settings, where models "nearly always correct typos" as an unintended side effect during attribute rewriting.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers describe e

nodes.name: Spoken dialogue
nodes.definition: The model's ability to engage in natural, coherent dialogue using speech input and output, assessed through task-based evaluations of conversational quality.

nodes.name: Spoken dialogue generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is response generation in conversation from spoken input or prior speech context. Most definitions describe generating a response based on spoken audio, spoken conversational input, or the prior sequence of user and assistant turns, with a smaller formulation narrowing this to the next assistant utterance in a multi-turn exchange. Papers differ on output modality: some describe a textual response, while others describe a spoken response or assistant utterance, and success is characterized as producing "coherent," "appropriate," or "most suitable" responses from contextual information (VoxDialogue: Can Spoken Dialogue Systems Understand Information Beyond Words?).

Variants. Papers use several near-equivalent names, including spoken dialogue generation, spoken dialog generation, spoken dialogue response generation, and generative spoken dialogue modeling. The recurring settings are conversational generation from spoken audio or prior speech context, with a smaller line of work centered on the next assistant utterance in a multi-turn spoken conversation. The modality pairing varies between spoken input with textual

nodes.name: Spoken question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats it as answering a question delivered in speech, with the model returning either speech or text. Several papers state the goal as producing a correct answer, sometimes a correct and coherent one, and some operationalize success by checking whether the reference answer appears in the response or in its transcription. One paper narrows the content to broad factual knowledge without access to external knowledge, while smaller lines of work define it as answering questions about the content of speech audio or as answering a text question conditioned on spoken context input.

Variants. Papers use labels such as SpokenQA, speech question answering, SQA, and spoken-query-based question answering (SQQA). The most common modality split is from spoken questions to spoken answers or from spoken questions to text answers, and one paper explicitly denotes these as S and S→T. Other settings include an audio clip plus a text question with a text answer, spoken question answering over monologue or dialogue audio in free-text form, image-grounded spoken questions, and a formulation as continuing a spoken sentence or question

nodes.name: Spoken-to-written transformation
nodes.definition: Producing a grammatically correct and semantically faithful written version of a spoken utterance, preserving all intended meaning while correcting structural deviations.

nodes.name: Stacking
nodes.definition: The action of placing multiple objects on top of one another in a specified order.

nodes.name: Stance detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats stance detection as classifying the attitude or position expressed in text toward a specific target, topic, issue, or proposition. Most definitions use ternary labels such as favor, against, and neutral, with close variants such as support, oppose, and neutral or agree, disagree, and neutral. A smaller line of work instead defines it over text pairs, where a reply or comment is labeled by its stance toward a parent comment or original post, and one such formulation says the output labels are annotated by human experts.

Variants. Papers study several variants under nearby names, including stance detection, stance classification, comment stance classification, and stance annotation. Beyond general target-based text classification, the variants include argument classification as affirmative versus negative, online political discussions treated as binary favor versus against, news headlines agreeing, neutral, or disagreeing with a target stance, topics such as abortions, climate change, and global warming, and post-comment settings where stance is assessed from the semantic and pragmatic relationship between a top co

nodes.name: State tracking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats state tracking under the name variable tracking: keeping track of changing variable values, or monitoring and reporting variable states, when updates occur multiple times within a long context. Definitions align on following variable assignments given in context and recovering their current values after successive updates. One description says the task "involves tracking the variable assignments provided in the context" (Scaling Stick-Breaking Attention: An Efficient Implementation and In-depth Study).

Variants. The main named variant is variable tracking. A smaller line of work broadens the behavior beyond explicit variable updates: one paper treats shortest path finding as requiring the model to maintain the state of its exploration in a graph, and multi-hop translation as requiring it to keep track of translated outputs across intermediate languages. Another paper places state tracking in a category that "extends the concept of Fluent Tracking."

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link state tracking to 2 measurement instruments overall, though only RULER is explicitly said to measure it. RULER is

nodes.name: Statement generation
nodes.definition: Generating candidate statements under a cost or length constraint for later selection into a slate.

nodes.name: STEM problem solving
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers describe it as generating solutions to problems in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics domains. A common elaboration narrows this to science and mathematics questions that require applying domain principles and formulae, and one snippet adds that such questions require "deeper reasoning" and the application of physics and chemistry principles. One paper also places STEM problem solving among "out-of-distribution reasoning scenarios."

Variants. Papers vary it mainly by domain. Alongside broad STEM tasks, some descriptions focus on science and mathematics questions involving formulae, while a smaller line of work treats chemical problem solving as answering chemistry questions that involve calculations, unit conversions, and multi-step reasoning, including examples such as computing a threshold frequency from a work function.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers operationalize it with 3 linked instruments: GSM8K, MMLU, and Trojsten Benchmark. One study states, "We evaluate MMLU and GSM8K for STEM tasks," and another link uses Trojsten Benchmark for problem solving in Slovak STEM competition problems.

What it is taken as evidence o

nodes.name: Stereotype recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is a recognition or detection task in which models identify whether text expresses a stereotype. Most definitions describe distinguishing stereotypical from anti-stereotypical statements, or classifying which sentence in a context is the stereotypical one; one paper makes the scoring explicit as assigning sentences to "stereotype," "anti-stereotype," or "unrelated" categories. Some papers operationalize the behavior with direct prompts such as "Does the following statement reflect a stereotype?", while a smaller line of work asks models not only to identify stereotypes in prompts but also to critically explain them.

Variants. Papers use several closely related names for this behavior, including stereotype recognition, stereotype identification, and stereotype detection. The studied variants include yes or no judgments about a single statement, three-way sentence classification, and choosing which of two or more sentences expresses a stereotype, sometimes given a context and sometimes in a multiple-choice format. The settings mentioned include multilingual prompting, a Polish stereotype-based prompt collection tha

nodes.name: Stereotypical response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers consistently describe this behavior as generating answers or content that reflect societal stereotypes or oversimplified, prejudiced generalizations about groups of people. A narrower formulation centers on ambiguous question contexts without disambiguating information, where stereotypical answers are the focal output, while a broader formulation treats stereotypical content generation more generally as the behavior of interest.

Variants. The papers study this behavior in two settings. One is ambiguous question answering, including categories such as Gender Identity and Socioeconomic Status, and one paper reports that there is "strong stereotypical bias in ambiguous contexts" and that "explicit disambiguation" and "negatively framed questions" reduce stereotypical responses (PakBBQ: A Culturally Adapted Bias Benchmark for QA). Another is a multimodal setting labeled Task F.1, where images of people at risk of discrimination are collected "to assess the stereotypes contained in models’ generation" (MultiTrust: A Comprehensive Benchmark Towards Trustworthy Multimodal Large Language Models).

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is l

nodes.name: Stock movement prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a directional prediction task for stocks or financial markets. Most descriptions formulate it as deciding whether prices will rise or fall at a target trading day from historical market information, with contextual text sometimes added through news, financial data, or tweets; a smaller formulation extends the label space to a ternary classification with Fall, Neutral, and Rise. One paper explicitly describes it as a ternary or binary market movement direction classification task.

Variants. Papers use both market-level and stock-level formulations. Recurring variants include binary stock-direction forecasting from historical prices or broader historical market information, a news-driven multi-stock setting that predicts the adjusted close movement of all stocks simultaneously on the target trading day, and a financial market movement version based on streaming news that can be binary or ternary. Another formulation pairs historical prices with tweets as the textual signal.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Operationally, papers elicit it as a direction-classification output,

nodes.name: Stock trading
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the common formulation is a decision task: producing a buy, sell, or hold choice from financial information and market context. A narrower version treats it as single stock trading, defined as generating decisions for individual stocks through multi-modal market information processing. One paper also specifies the output format directly, asking for exactly one investment decision, buy or sell, with hold used when a buy-or-sell choice is hard (FinBen: A Holistic Financial Benchmark for Large Language Models).

Variants. The main named variant is single stock trading, where the task is scoped to individual stocks. The papers also vary in how they describe the setting: one presents trading actions as part of sequential financial tasks, while another frames the task around financial information and market context; multi-modal market information is only mentioned in the individual-stock version.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers do not link stock trading to any construct. One paper instead reports that stock trading is related to Action selection, us

nodes.name: Story generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats story generation as prompt-based production of a narrative text or story. Many definitions use broad labels such as story generation, story writing, or narrative generation, while a smaller line of work narrows the behavior to coherent short stories, story continuations from a first sentence, or outputs that remain plausible while following prompt requirements. Some formulations also count scene descriptions and character actions as part of the behavior when they form a narrative.

Variants. Papers study several variants, including constrained story generation, keyword-based story generation, personalized story generation, short story generation, and narrative generation in long-form writing. The task can involve increasing numbers of explicit constraints, required keywords at arbitrary positions, including the middle or end of a sequence, sociocultural personalization factors such as gender or nationality, specified characters and plot elements, or open-ended continuation from an initial sentence. Another strand uses narrative generation for real-time game scenes and character responses.

Space of elicitation and sco

nodes.name: Strategy generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat this behavior as generating a high-level plan or strategy before a downstream answer, code solution, or action. The prevailing usage is natural-language planning for problem solving, often for coding, including generating a set of strategies or "multiple strategies in English" before solving; some papers instead ask for an anticipatory plan before answering, a pseudocode-style or code-form plan, or an abstract strategy that identifies relevant concepts and principles without detailed calculations or specific operations. A smaller line of work uses the same label for generating natural-language criteria that define scenarios for different levels of user satisfaction, so what counts as the output varies between solution-path planning and classification criteria.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this behavior, including anticipatory plan generation, code-form plan generation, and strategy formulation. The settings vary across coding problems, general problem solving before answering, dialogue user-satisfaction classification, and open-ended action settings where the model combines a goal, interaction history, prior strategies, and

nodes.name: String manipulation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats this behavior as transforming strings or character sequences, either by explicit operations such as slicing, concatenation, reversing, splitting, and reordering, or by inferring a latent rule that maps an input string to an output string. Success is usually the production of the required transformed string, designated character, or selected substring, including tasks described as "fundamental tasks such as indexing, slicing, and concatenation" and tasks that represent a mapping between pairs of strings as a program. A smaller line of work formulates it as a presence judgment, for example asking whether a substring is part of a target word.

Variants. The variants are heterogeneous, with string transformation the most common name and broader labels such as string analysis and manipulation and character manipulation also used. Substring-focused variants cover locating a substring, determining whether it is present, or selecting one whose reversal matches a given definition. Other settings include unscrambling a randomly permuted sentence into a grammatically and semantically valid one, removing vowels while copying

nodes.name: Structured output generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is producing outputs that adhere to a required structure, most often JSON and other explicitly specified formats. Many descriptions emphasize strict compliance with schemas, API or function-call definitions, or other parseable formats, and one paper states that a successful function call must strictly match the API-specified format. Smaller lines of work define the behavior more narrowly as fixed result formatting or syntactically valid JSON, while others specify the target structure more task-specifically, including XML or YAML outputs, code or chain-of-thought traces, tables, formalized dialogue representations, netlists, or standardized software artifacts; some definitions also include extracting the relevant information into that structure.

Variants. Variants most often stay close to JSON-focused function-calling and result formatting into fixed structures. Smaller lines of work study configuration generation in YAML, table generation, and netlist generation, while other papers use formalized dialogue representations or standardized software artifacts such as requirements documents, designs, flowcharts, and i

nodes.name: Student mistake correction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, papers mainly treat this behavior as responding appropriately after a student error. One framing, used in MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-ended Pedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors, makes success very specific: the model generates a reasoning chain and a correct final numeric answer even when the dialogue history contains an incorrect student answer. Another framing defines it more generally as providing feedback or guidance that helps a student fix an identified error in their work.

Variants. Papers use both the names student mistake correction and mistake correction. The studied settings differ between a dialogue-conditioned problem setting, where the student's incorrect answer appears in the history and the model is expected to produce a correct reasoning chain and final answer, and a tutoring setting centered on feedback or guidance after an error has been identified. One paper also discusses it alongside mistake location as a separate task.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the available descriptions, it is operationalized through task performance, most expli

nodes.name: Style mimicry
nodes.definition: The generation of images that closely replicate the artistic style of specific painters, indicating potential copyright infringement.

nodes.name: Style transfer
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is textual rewriting: authors most commonly describe style transfer as rewriting a given text so it matches a target style while preserving its original meaning, core content, or semantic content. Common success criteria are style conformity plus content preservation, and some formulations add fluency, describing the goal as generating a fluent rewrite in the desired style. A smaller line of work uses the same label for image generation or editing, where the goal is to keep the content of a test image while changing artistic style or visual appearance, sometimes with a separate style image or multimodal instructions.

Variants. Most variants remain text-based and differ mainly in the target style, including sentiment transfer, formal versus informal rewriting, general tone adjustment, matching a specific author's or dataset's style, and broader stylistic rewriting such as changing formality, fixing grammar, or improving coherence. Some papers cast it as template rewriting, where a structured sentence is rewritten with domain-specific examples while preserving original meaning and emotional tone, and others distinguish au

nodes.name: Stylistic variation
nodes.definition: Rephrasing a report using different but semantically equivalent expressions, sentence order, or hedging without altering clinical meaning.

nodes.name: Sub-answer generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the shared framing is answering intermediate sub-queries or sub-questions that sit inside a larger complex question. One paper describes producing a direct answer for a specific, focused sub-query, and another frames it as answering a series of simpler questions that break down a complex multi-hop question into manageable steps. In the quoted task descriptions, the model is expected to produce responses to the intermediate questions, in one case using associated retrieved knowledge, and in the other to answer sub-questions "to reach the target rather than giving a final answer solely."

Variants. Papers use two closely related names, sub-answer generation and sub-question answering. The first appears in a retrieval-augmented setting, where the "sub-answer generator" produces responses based on sub-queries and any associated retrieved knowledge. The second appears in step-wise multi-hop question answering, where the behavior consists of answering a sequence of simpler, intermediate questions on the way to the target answer.

Space of elicitation and scores. The papers do not link this behavior to any measurement instrument. The

nodes.name: Subject-driven generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is generating images of a specific subject from reference images while keeping the subject faithful to those references and aligning the result with a text prompt. One paper states, "Given several images of a specific subject and a textual prompt, subject-driven generation aims to generate images of the same subject in a context aligning with the prompt" (Bridging The Gap between Low-rank and Orthogonal Adaptation via Householder Reflection Adaptation). A smaller wording variation describes generating new, customized images from one or more reference images, often placing the subject in new contexts or styles.

Variants. Papers use both "subject-driven generation" and "subject-driven image generation" for closely similar tasks. The variants explicitly named are single-entity subject-driven generation and multi-image subject-driven generation. The multi-image variant is described as requiring that the main subjects across multiple reference images represent the same instance, while other formulations allow one or more reference images.

Space of elicitation and scores. Some papers mention "subject-driven generation

nodes.name: Subject-verb agreement
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, subject-verb agreement is most commonly framed as a task with a correct output: either choosing the verb inflection that matches the subject's grammatical number, or producing the correct acceptability judgment for sentences built around that contrast. The definitions align on the core criterion, getting the agreement pattern right, though they differ in output format, inflection choice in one line of work and acceptability judgment in another; the judgment formulation is described particularly for sentences with attractor nouns.

Variants. Papers use both the name "subject-verb agreement" and the narrower "subject-verb agreement judgment," and one study abbreviates it as "S-v agr." A smaller line of work focuses on agreement judgments in sentences with attractor nouns, including cases where "attractors in a relative clause hinder acceptability judgments," and illustrates the contrast with examples such as "The sisters bake/*bakes." Another paper refers more broadly to a "suite of subject-verb agreement tasks."

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. Instead, the papers operationalize it direct

nodes.name: Subjectivity classification
nodes.definition: The observable task of determining whether a given text is subjective (expressing opinions) or objective (stating facts).

nodes.name: Subtask dependency identification
nodes.definition: Correctly recognizing and acting upon prerequisite relationships between subtasks in a non-linear task structure.

nodes.name: Subtraction
nodes.definition: Performing subtraction operations on numerical operands, including anti-symmetric operations.

nodes.name: Success detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, it is consistently used for a judgment about whether a task has been completed successfully. One formulation treats it as determining task or sub-task success from environmental feedback, summarized as "Determine if the task is successful" and as something that "determines sub-task success based on environmental feedback" (MLLM as Retriever: Interactively Learning Multimodal Retrieval for Embodied Agents). Another formulation narrows it to a binary success-versus-mistake decision for a procedural task, made from procedural text plus visual evidence gathered through dialog.

Variants. Papers use both success detection and success classification for closely related versions of the behavior. The main variation is in scope and evidence source: some descriptions target whole-task or sub-task success from environmental feedback, while another studies procedural execution and asks after each iteration whether the procedure was successfully executed from "the video frame and entire dialog history" (Transparent and Coherent Procedural Mistake Detection).

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. In the de

nodes.name: Sudoku solving
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats Sudoku solving as completing a partially filled Sudoku grid so that row, column, and box or subgrid constraints are all satisfied. Papers agree on that constraint-satisfaction goal, with one description stating that the board is filled with numbers 1 to 9 without duplicates in each row, column, and box; a smaller formulation also requires returning the solved puzzle without extraneous text. One paper further presents the task as iterative, where the model first searches over empty cells and then fills a chosen cell.

Variants. Papers study it mainly as partially filled puzzle completion, but a few settings vary the presentation. Some describe Sudoku puzzles in textual format, and one setup explicitly uses 9 × 9 problems; the task is also referred to as Sudoku-solving or solving Sudokus. The expected response varies slightly, from a completed grid to the solved puzzle alone without extra text.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. When papers describe eliciting the behavior directly, they present Sudoku puzzles, including textual 9 × 9 instances, and ask for the solved pu

nodes.name: Suicide risk detection
nodes.definition: The task of identifying language or patterns in user input that indicate a risk of suicide.

nodes.name: Super-resolution
nodes.definition: The task of increasing the resolution and detail of a low-resolution image, guided by a textual instruction.

nodes.name: Support strategy selection
nodes.definition: The observable process of choosing one or more conversational strategies (e.g., Question, Reflection of feelings) to use in a response.

nodes.name: Supportiveness judgment
nodes.definition: The observable task of assigning a discrete label (e.g., true/false) to a claim indicating whether it is supported by provided evidence.

nodes.name: Surgical phase recognition
nodes.definition: The task of classifying individual frames from a surgical video into a set of predefined procedural phases, such as 'Preparation' or 'ClippingCutting'.

nodes.name: Survival prediction
nodes.definition: The model's output of a probability distribution over discrete time intervals, representing the individual incidence function from which survival probabilities are derived.

nodes.name: Sycophantic response generation
nodes.definition: Producing answers that conform to user suggestions or doubts even when they are factually incorrect, such as changing a correct answer after an 'Are you sure?' prompt.

nodes.name: Symbolic manipulation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats symbolic manipulation as rule-based operations over symbolic inputs, especially mathematical or logical symbols. Papers describe it as the observable act of manipulating symbols according to a set of rules, and as performing operations such as identifying syntactic roles or evaluating logical conditions over structured values.

Variants. The behavior appears both as a broad task category and as named task instances. Papers mention tasks requiring symbolic manipulation in general, and one paper instantiates the category with Indirect Object Identification (IOI) and PriceTag within a broader set of language modeling tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The evidence names task examples, but does not specify a separate elicitation or scoring instrument for this behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it. The papers represented here do not state what symbolic manipulation is taken to indicate.

nodes.name: Symbolic regression
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats symbolic regression as a search task: finding a compact, programmatic mathematical expression that best explains a dataset of input-output examples. The same paper also describes the target as compact or succinct programmatic hypotheses written in a flexible, domain-specific programming language, so success is framed as explaining the dataset with a compact hypothesis.

Variants. Explicit subtask variants are not named in the available definitions. Papers do, however, use the abbreviation SR, frame the task as operating over a flexible domain-specific programming language, and link it to one other behavioral indicator, code generation, through a related claim that formulates symbolic regression as a program synthesis problem. Another paper discusses it in domains such as physics, biology, and finance when describing transparent, understandable models.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers. The recorded use centers on the task formulation itself rather than on a named elicitation or scoring instrument.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers link symbolic

nodes.name: Syntactic parsing
nodes.definition: Generating syntactic constituents such as noun phrase subjects (NP-SBJ) from text, based on Penn Treebank annotation schemes.

nodes.name: Synthetic data detection
nodes.definition: The task of making a binary determination of whether a given piece of data is synthetic or real.

nodes.name: Synthetic recall
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is a synthetic needle-retrieval task: the model must retrieve, reproduce, or recall specific inserted information from a long, often irrelevant context. Most definitions use a "needle in a haystack" setup in which the target is a short fact, statement, passkey, or key-value pair hidden in long text, and some explicitly describe it as a stress test of recall from long contexts or of the fidelity of compressed representations. Success is usually exact recovery of the inserted content, for example identifying and outputting a five-digit passkey, retrieving one or more target key-value pairs, or returning a target statement when it appears at different positions, and one formulation states that a prediction is correct only if all passkeys are retrieved.

Variants. Most variants stay in text and are described as passkey retrieval, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, or long-context retrieval. Common differences are whether the model must find a single needle or multiple needles, whether the inserted item is a passkey, target statement, key-value pair, or matching string, and whether recall is tested at different depths or positions i

nodes.name: Table detection
nodes.definition: The task of identifying and outputting the bounding box coordinates of all tables within a document image.

nodes.name: Table question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is answering a natural-language question from table content and returning a natural-language answer. Most definitions emphasize concise, precise, correct, or accurate answers grounded in a given table, though some extend the task to one or more provided tables, mixed tabular-text inputs, or questions requiring arithmetic, span extraction, comparison, or synthesis across table sections. A smaller line of work separates short-form answers from free-form, paragraph-length answers, and one multi-table formulation emphasizes retrieving and synthesizing information from multiple tables for complex, multi-hop questions.

Variants. Papers use several names for closely related variants, most often table-based, table, or tabular question answering. The studied settings include multi-table and multi-hop questions, mixed tabular-text financial data, complex or multi-structured tables, table images, and cases where tables are updated with extra natural-language context or comparisons. Another recurring split is between short-form table QA, focused on brief precise answers and extraction or aggregation, and free-form table QA, focused on

nodes.name: Table structure recognition
nodes.definition: The task of parsing the internal structure of a given table image into its constituent elements, such as rows, columns, and cells, and their relationships.

nodes.name: Table-to-report generation
nodes.definition: The task of converting structured tabular data into a comprehensive, coherent, and accurate natural language report that includes descriptions, analysis, and conclusions.

nodes.name: Tabular classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing use is as a supervised prediction task over structured tables: predicting a categorical label for a data point represented by tabular features. The available definitions do not introduce alternative success criteria or judging schemes, and one paper discusses the task in sample-efficiency terms, noting that test-time training reduces the number of required samples for tabular classification by about 3 to 5 times.

Variants. The only explicit setting attached to the behavior is its use with in-context learning, described as leveraging the in-context learning capability of large language models for tabular classification with training-free adaptability across diverse datasets. Beyond that framing, the papers do not name additional subtasks, domains, or modalities.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The papers therefore do not identify a recurring elicitation or scoring tool for this behavior, although one study operationalizes progress through required sample size and reports fewer samples under test-time training.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers do not converge on tabular class

nodes.name: Target identification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers use this label for target-finding tasks, but not with a single uniform meaning. In AmpleHate: Amplifying the Attention for Versatile Implicit Hate Detection, it is framed as detecting and isolating entities in text that may be the focus of hate, including groups, organizations, nationalities, religions, and locations, and the paper notes that it "first identifies explicit targets" before hatefulness becomes clear. In Superlatives in Context: Modeling the Implicit Semantics of Superlatives, it is framed as recognizing the entity or event that has the maximal or minimal value in a comparison, where the target is one of the entities or events in the comparison set.

Variants. The observed variants split by setting. In the hate-related usage, papers treat it as explicit target extraction, with retained labels such as ORG, NORP, GPE, LOC, and EVENT. In the superlative usage, papers speak of "the target of the comparison," allow either an entity or an event as the target, require the target to stand in an IS-A relation with the comparison set, and illustrate it with cases where a named item such as "Nemo" is the max or min element.

Space of elicitation and s

nodes.name: Task completion
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats task completion as whether an agent reaches the intended end state or user's goal for a task. Several definitions make this explicitly scriptable, describing evaluation as checking whether the goal is accomplished and returning a binary success flag, while tool-use and UI papers frame it as fulfilling user needs through sequences of actions, tool calls, or API interactions. A smaller line of work uses the term more procedurally, as finishing baseline items or executing an accepted predicted task, and domain-specific work judges completion through dialogue-game quality scores or generated code passing predefined tests.

Variants. Papers study the behavior across several task families. A prevalent cluster is embodied work, including household task execution, indoor task simulation through language interaction, household activities defined as predicates with counts to satisfy, and open-ended embodied tasks specified by text or video without task-specific rewards. Other variants include graph-structured tasks represented as directed acyclic graphs with dependencies, branches, and hierarchical levels, web and applicati

nodes.name: Task decomposition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is the observable breakdown of a complex, high-level goal, question, instruction, or request into smaller subtasks, sub-actions, steps, or subgoals. Most formulations treat it as producing a structured intermediate plan, such as an ordered sequence, hierarchy, tree, or graph; papers differ in whether that decomposition must reflect current observations and memory, dependencies and execution order, agent roles, or single-tool executability. A smaller line of work frames it as a latent ability to break problems into hierarchies of solvable sub-problems, including decomposing malicious tasks across models.

Variants. Variants span many names, but the prevailing usage stays within the same decomposition family. Common forms are program or problem decomposition into functions or simpler steps, request or sub-instruction decomposition of user goals into actionable language steps, subgoal generation or decomposition into intermediate statements or goals, and plan decomposition into role-specific agent tasks. Some papers further specialize it to settings such as vehicle-routing constraints, scene-graph narratives, natural-language r

nodes.name: Teaser generation
nodes.definition: The task of crafting intriguing but vague glimpses of a document's content to entice readers without revealing substantive information.

nodes.name: Teaser narration generation
nodes.definition: Producing a short teaser script from a longer documentary narration, including story-like rewriting and an ending question.

nodes.name: Technical problem solving
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of generating answers to well-defined technical queries.

nodes.name: Temporal graph attribute forecasting
nodes.definition: The forecasting of future numerical values associated with nodes in a temporal graph based on historical attribute and structural data.

nodes.name: Temporal grounding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers describe temporal grounding as localizing the moment, time span, segment, or timestamps in a video that correspond either to the evidence for a question or to a natural language query. The prevailing success criterion is finding the answer event span or selecting the related clips, and one study says this checks whether a model "accurately grounds its answers to the correct video segments" (ReXTime: A Benchmark Suite for Reasoning-Across-Time in Videos). Some formulations are narrower, requiring start and end timestamps or direct output of clue intervals that can accurately answer the question, while another treats it as finding the visual event needed for an egocentric question.

Variants. Papers use several nearby task names, most often temporal video grounding, moment localization, clue retrieval, and moment retrieval. The common setting is video, but the task varies between question answering evidence localization, grounding a textual description or query to a segment, directly outputting clue intervals that answer a question, and localizing the event needed for an egocentric question; one paper states that models should "directly out

nodes.name: Temporal prediction
nodes.definition: The task of generating a sequence of images and text that forecasts future events or reconstructs past events based on an input.

nodes.name: Temporal question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, temporal question answering is most commonly described as answering questions that require understanding and reasoning about temporal knowledge, time-related information, events, and temporal relationships, including questions about when an event occurred or whether one event preceded another. A narrower formulation treats it as context-based date resolution, where the answer depends on resolving a date mentioned in a passage, for example identifying which team a player was associated with on a specific date. Another usage frames it as answering questions about recent events that occurred after a model's primary training cutoff.

Variants. Papers study several settings under this label. One is a context-based split built from question-context pairs that each require resolution of a date mentioned in the passage. Another is temporal question answering generation, abbreviated TQA-G, used through a separate LoRA layer and also in joint fine-tuning with MCMS to inject up-to-date knowledge from recent local news articles; a further variant is MIDTERMQA, a QA benchmark centered on the 2022 U.S. midterm elections for evaluating temporal knowle

nodes.name: Temporal referring
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of formulating or answering questions that refer to particular temporal positions within the content.

nodes.name: Temporal referring expression
nodes.definition: Identifying the specific image or images in a sequence where a described change occurred.

nodes.name: Temporal relation extraction
nodes.definition: The task of identifying and classifying the temporal relationship (e.g., before, after, includes) between a given pair of event mentions in a text.

nodes.name: Test output prediction
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating the expected output for a given test case input, based solely on a natural language problem statement.

nodes.name: Text chunking
nodes.definition: The process of segmenting a long document into smaller, semantically coherent, and self-contained pieces of text.

nodes.name: Text classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is assigning a predefined, discrete, or categorical label to a text input, usually a sentence, sentence pair, document, or entire sequence. Several definitions make the format explicit as taking one text or a pair of texts and outputting a class label based on content, with recurring examples including sentiment, topic, grammatical acceptability, question type, stance, and natural language inference style tasks. A smaller line of work broadens the target from single-label prediction to zero, one, or multiple labels, and success is usually framed as predicting the task label correctly, with some papers mentioning cross-entropy loss or accuracy for the task.
