Variants. Papers use the term for a broad family of variants. The most recurrent named variants are topic classification, sentence or sequence classification, and question classification, while other settings include headline and news classification, single-sentence classification, long document classification, and multilingual or cross-lingual, zero-shot, few-shot, and in-context setups. Smaller domain-specific formulations include financial headline, hawkish-dovish, arg

nodes.name: Text clustering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats text clustering, often called just clustering, as grouping a set of texts into groups so that texts in the same group are more similar to one another than to texts in other groups. A smaller variation states the task as grouping similar text inputs into coherent clusters based on embedding proximity and explicitly notes that this is done without prior labels. Papers also consistently present it as one task category alongside other embedding tasks.

Variants. Papers use both the names "Clustering" and "Text clustering" for the same behavior. The named variants are mostly dataset and setting specific: Arxiv, Biorxiv, Medrxiv, Reddit, and StackExchange clustering appear in S2S and P2P forms, and TwentyNewsgroups-Clustering is also listed. Beyond these named datasets, papers mainly discuss it as a general task category within broader evaluations.

Space of elicitation and scores. One measurement instrument is linked to text clustering, MTEB, and papers describe it as a collection of datasets or a benchmark that includes clustering among its task categories. This is the only reported way papers measure the behavior, with m

nodes.name: Text continuation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a generative task where a model is given a prefix, prompt, sentence, article, or truncated passage and asked to produce the next text. Most definitions say the continuation should coherently, logically, and contextually follow the input, sometimes as a suffix or the remaining portion of a passage; one paper summarizes it as producing content that "remains consistent with the given one" (Exploring LLMs' Ability to Spontaneously and Conditionally Modify Moral Expressions through Text Manipulation). A smaller line of work narrows the task to specific setups, such as continuation from memory slots after compression, continuation from a five-token prompt, or continuation from truncated inputs used to elicit toxic outputs.

Variants. Authors also study several named variants. Alongside the dominant label text continuation, papers use text completion, text continuation generation, open-ended text completion, and transcript continuation; these cover sentence and article completion, continuation without specific task constraints, regeneration of the remaining portion of a truncated passage, and continuation from textual or spe

nodes.name: Text editing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is broad text modification: a model either generates insertion or continuation suggestions that must respect contextual and logical constraints, or rewrites an existing passage to correct or improve it. Success is described in task-specific terms, including fixing misspellings and restoring intended content, matching clearly defined correction answers, identifying and correcting errors in a legal text, or editing a response by correcting factual inconsistency, removing hallucinations, and improving style, coherence, and fluency. A smaller line of work treats the behavior as changing review text so that its sentiment moves beyond a given rating range.

Variants. Variants span story writing, proofreading, and controlled rewriting. Papers study insertion and continuation in stories under combinations of logical constraints, text correction for noisy surgical narrations and smartphone-style correction tasks, grammatical error correction framed as explicit insert, delete, and replace operations, legal document proofreading, editing of machine-generated text by human experts or LLMs, and review rewriting that shifts 2 to 4 sta

nodes.name: Text embedding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage describes text embedding as mapping text inputs to dense or fixed-dimensional vector representations that capture semantic content or meaning. Most definitions tie these representations to similarity-based use in downstream methods, and some make the downstream target explicit by referring to classification or retrieval. Some papers also cast LLMs as text embedders, including a formulation in which models take text inputs and output 3072-dimensional vectors.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings. Some treat it broadly as embedding tasks, while others narrow it to text similarity, specifically STS tasks, or to downstream tasks such as classification or retrieval. Several papers compare embeddings from different model or fine-tuning layers, and one paper frames the task through contrastive learning as evaluating the ability to contextually model bidirectional information.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link text embedding to one measurement instrument, MTEB. The linked studies use it either across 32 embedding tasks or on ten text similarity (STS) tasks, so the reported measurement practice center

nodes.name: Text generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is prompt- or context-conditioned production of natural-language sequences, usually as free-form answers, continuations, or completions. Many definitions emphasize coherent, contextually appropriate, fluent, or human-like outputs, while several make the mechanics explicit as sequential, often autoregressive, token generation from a prompt, prefix, or dialogue history. Most usages are open-ended, though some papers explicitly include constrained generation or unified text-to-text settings, and some narrow it to assistant-style response generation or single-turn dialogue.

Variants. Papers use many names for nearby variants, with the broadest recurring ones being response generation, open-ended generation, natural language generation, text completion, and single-turn dialogue generation. Beyond these broad labels, authors also study narrower writing and continuation settings, and multimodal settings where the model produces captions, answers, descriptions, or other text from interleaved text, image, or video inputs.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 54 measurement instruments. The most frequently l

nodes.name: Text infilling
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats text infilling as conditional generation of missing text from surrounding context, usually a prefix and suffix, with success defined by producing a span that fits coherently between both sides and, in some definitions, respects given prompt tokens and their relative order. Some papers phrase the same behavior as filling masked-out fragments of a document or story, while others narrow it to masked-token prediction or a single scientific-word cloze. A smaller line of work instead operationalizes it as fill-in-the-blank completion, where the model generates or selects a treatment or profile detail, or fills a [MASK] slot so papers can compare Arab versus Western entity preferences.

Variants. The behavior appears in several settings: narrative story completion with a missing middle sentence or masked story fragments, non-sequential infilling of different parts of a sequence during diffusion generation, and insertion tasks where both prefix and suffix are given and the output must satisfy logical constraints. Other papers study flexible-length spans and positions without oracle span lengths, single scientific-term blanks,

nodes.name: Text prompt generation
nodes.definition: The task of automatically creating suitable text prompts, including positive and negative examples, to guide an image generation model.

nodes.name: Text rewriting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats text rewriting as an LLM taking an existing text and producing a modified version in response to instructions such as "polish," "rewrite," "refine," or "rephrase." Most definitions describe success as changing wording, phrasing, structure, or style while preserving the original meaning or remaining semantically relevant to the input. A smaller line of work adds stricter requirements, asking the model to change one aspect, such as topic, style, or factual content, while preserving others, and some watermark papers frame the same behavior as modifying text to remove a watermark while preserving meaning.

Variants. Papers study several variants of this behavior. Common variants include paraphrasing, rephrasing, synonym substitution, and other structural or stylistic edits that preserve meaning, while another recurring setup rewrites documents so that topic, style, or factual content changes selectively. Some work applies rewriting in a poetry setting, where a parent poem is turned into an "inspired, different poem" or, under the name "LMX-rewrite," into an offspring with different diversity characteristics; a smaller lin

nodes.name: Text simplification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is rewriting complex text into a clearer, easier-to-understand version while preserving the original meaning. Definitions repeatedly frame success as reducing complexity to improve readability or comprehension, often by using simpler words, rephrasing complex syntactic structures, and shortening sentences; as one study puts it, the aim is to "enhance the clarity and comprehensibility of a complex text while preserving its original meaning." A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to sentence-level conversion of complex, compound, or compound-complex inputs into one or more simple sentences. One paper also describes simplification as a tendency that may run against a specialized revision task.

Variants. Variants are most commonly distinguished by unit and constraint. Some papers use the names sentence simplification or sentence decomposition for breaking syntactically complex, compound, or compound-complex sentences into simpler forms, sometimes explicitly into one or more simple sentences; one variant additionally requires the output to match a target learner proficiency level while keeping as much level-appr

nodes.name: Text summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is producing a concise, coherent, shorter version of a longer source text or document. Most definitions add that the output should preserve the main idea, salient content, core meaning, or essence of the source, and some explicitly allow either extractive or abstractive summaries. A smaller line makes the success criteria more explicit, judging summaries for coverage, accuracy, coherence, overall quality, faithfulness, or factuality, and a few papers broaden the task to titles or bullet-pointed key information.

Variants. Most work studies standard document-to-summary settings, but papers also distinguish dialogue summarization, multi-document or long-document summarization, and query-based meeting summarization. The domains mentioned include news articles, Reddit posts, government reports, academic papers, manuals or agreements, and scientific or medical texts, with multilingual settings also appearing and some tasks asking for one-sentence summaries. Smaller variants treat the behavior as document description, text abbreviation, spotlight generation, paper reading, sensor-data summary, or condensing a multi-agent conversat

nodes.name: Text-to-3D generation
nodes.definition: The general task of synthesizing a three-dimensional asset from a natural language description.

nodes.name: Text-to-audio generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is generating audio from a textual or natural language prompt. Most definitions describe success as producing a novel audio clip or relevant sound that corresponds to the prompt, and one paper states the output more explicitly as an audio waveform or spectrogram. A narrower formulation limits the target to non-speech audio, such as environmental sounds.

Variants. Papers use several closely related names for the behavior. The prevailing labels are text-to-audio generation and Text2Audio, some authors also call it text-guided audio generation, and a smaller line of work uses text-to-sound when focusing on non-speech outputs such as environmental sounds.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only one measurement instrument is linked to this behavior, AudioCaps. One paper reports evaluating it on the AC evaluation set, following the AudioLDM protocol and using its evaluation toolkit, so the recorded operationalization is through an evaluation set for generated audio outputs.

What it is taken as evidence of. No surveyed paper links this behavior to a construct, so the literature here does not specify what it is evidence

nodes.name: Text-to-CAD generation
nodes.definition: The end-to-end task of converting a natural language textual description into a complete Computer-Aided Design (CAD) model.

nodes.name: Text-to-speech synthesis
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is the generation of human-like or otherwise audible speech from text, usually from a given text input, text transcript, or written text. Some definitions extend the input to style instructions or intermediate text responses, while a smaller line of work describes speech synthesis as producing speech waveforms or spectrograms from internal representations such as discrete speech tokens. Some definitions further specify the desired output, for example contextually appropriate speech for multi-turn dialogue or an acoustic style that meets users' needs.

Variants. Papers study several variants. The clearest named variant is conversational speech synthesis, where the output is meant to be contextually appropriate for interactive, multi-turn dialogue; other work focuses on fine-grained style-controlled speech generation from open-domain instructions. A smaller line treats the task as zero-shot TTS, sometimes conditioned on a reference audio prompt or unseen speakers' prompts, and one paper relates this use to voice cloning; another paper treats hallucination as a related issue in LLM-based TTS systems.

Space of elicitation and s

nodes.name: Text-to-SQL
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is translating a natural-language question, instruction, or prompt into a SQL query, usually with a database schema and sometimes table content, dialogue history, or auxiliary documentation available. Most definitions treat success as producing correct, functionally correct, or executable SQL that retrieves the desired information from the database, and some papers use SQL as an intermediate program for answering questions over tables. A smaller line of work extends the behavior beyond retrieval to database manipulation, including SQL UPDATE statements and SQL TRIGGER scripts generated from natural-language instructions and schema information.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous labels, most often SQL generation, text-to-SQL generation, NL2SQL, text-to-SQL parsing, and database querying. The common setting is generating a single query over one or more relational tables, though some work studies multi-turn or dialogue-conditioned generation, open-domain or large-table settings, and stepwise incremental generation that decomposes complex queries into sub-syntax trees. Smaller variants include generating multiple SQL

nodes.name: Textual reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the shared framing is reasoning carried out through natural language: solving reasoning problems expressed in text, drawing inferences or making judgments from text-based premises, or answering problems directly in natural language. Papers use the labels verbal reasoning, natural language reasoning, and textual reasoning for closely related formulations. A smaller set of definitions further narrows it by saying it does not rely primarily on mathematical calculation or on executable code.

Variants. Papers vary in granularity: some refer broadly to a variety of verbal reasoning problems, while others organize it into benchmark suites covering question answering, natural language inference, sentence completion, and coreference resolution. Another line studies it in multimodal settings that pair it with visual understanding, and one formulation emphasizes multi-step reasoning via natural language.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 3 measurement instruments: AlpacaEval, MATH, and XNLI. The recorded uses describe AlpacaEval as assessing "pure text reasoning ability," MATH as part of challenging reasoning benchmarks, and XNL

nodes.name: Theorem generation
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of autonomously creating new, non-trivial mathematical theorems and their proofs.

nodes.name: Theorem proving
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is a proof-production task: given a theorem statement, the model generates either a complete proof script or a sequence of proof steps and tactics inside a formal system, often in proof assistants such as Lean or Isabelle. Most definitions require the result to be formally verifiable, with papers describing proofs that are checked by a prover, a verifier, or a correctness checker. A smaller line of work broadens the target to human-readable natural language proofs, or describes theorem proving as the ability to construct a valid sequence of logical steps.

Variants. The most common variants split the task into whole-proof generation and proof-step or tactic generation. In the stepwise variant, the model predicts the next tactic from the current proof state, sometimes also called tactic prediction or formal-to-formal proving, and the step is then verified before continuing; in whole-proof generation, the model completes the entire proof code in one pass and verification comes at the end. Other papers study proof trajectory generation, natural language proof generation, and constructive proof generation, where the proof consis

nodes.name: Thought generation
nodes.definition: Producing a compact summary of retrieved information to maintain context across iterations in multi-hop reasoning.

nodes.name: Throwing
nodes.definition: The action of propelling an object through the air.

nodes.name: Time series classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats time series classification as whole-sequence labeling: assigning a class or categorical label to a sequence of time-ordered data points, often phrased as labeling an entire time series. Most descriptions stay at the level of outputting the label for the input sequence, while some further specify univariate or multivariate inputs or say the label is assigned from temporal patterns. A smaller formulation casts it as assigning a class label to a time-series input in response to a textual question or prompt.

Variants. Papers study this task across several settings, including human activity recognition, medical physiological-signal tasks, and datasets spanning biology, healthcare, electricity, physics, and nature. Variants include binary and multi-class classification, fine-grained and coarse-grained classification, and both univariate and multivariate sequences. Some examples are framed around physiological signals, such as diagnosing sepsis from a mean arterial pressure sequence, and papers also describe it as related to Emotion analysis and Sleep stage classification in that application area.

Space of elicitation

nodes.name: Time series forecasting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is predicting future values or data points in a sequence from historical observations. Papers differ mainly in horizon and input form: some frame it as forecasting the next value, others the next n values or the next H timestamps, and some explicitly state the series may be univariate or multivariate or that past observations are provided in context. A smaller line of work narrows the task to forecasts that change when relevant text is added to the numerical history, and one prompt formulation asks the model to "continue the following sequence without producing any additional text."

Variants. Variants are commonly framed by horizon, data regime, and available context. Papers mention long-term and short-term forecasting, multivariate and univariate forecasting, few-shot forecasting with only a small fraction of training data, including 5% or 10% training data, and zero-shot forecasting where training is done on source datasets or domains and testing is done on a different target dataset with none of its training data. Another variant is context-aided forecasting, where textual context accompanies the numerical histo

nodes.name: Token classification
nodes.definition: Assigning a label to each token in an input sequence for linguistic analysis tasks.

nodes.name: Token copying
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, token copying is most commonly described as producing a token from the prompt or earlier context, often by identifying a token at a specified position such as the first or last token and reproducing it. The descriptions agree on that core behavior, though one phrasing emphasizes a position-based task while another states it more generally as generating a token that appeared earlier in context. Some authors also broaden the scope from a single token to single or multiple tokens and treat copying and recalling as interchangeable labels for the behavior.

Variants. The variants discussed are mainly positional and span based: copying a token from a designated prompt position, copying elements that occur earlier along an input sequence, and recalling either a single token or multiple tokens from the prompt. The examples given also include copying an earlier name token and copying a color token from context.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers describe it through task prompts that require reproducing the requested token, either from a specified position in the prompt or from earlier in the c

nodes.name: Token-level attribution
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is an explanation behavior that assigns token- or word-level importance to the input for a model output. Most definitions describe highlighting or scoring the specific input tokens, words, spans, or token pairs that contribute to a prediction, and one study describes these highlights as "faithful cues reflecting the model's reasoning logic toward answer prediction." Some authors make the attribution label-specific and signed, so tokens have positive or negative impact on a particular class, while one paper frames the same behavior as prompt-token influence on the generation of a target output token rather than an alternative.

Variants. Variants appear as per-label attribution, word-level attribution or explanation generation, highlight explanation extraction, input saliency, and prompt influence. The settings differ: papers study words in a tip for relevance or triage predictions, highlight tokens, token pairs, or spans for answer prediction, prompt tokens' effect on each generated token in an output sequence, and explanation signals for intent classification that mark main predicates and their arguments.

Space of elicitat

nodes.name: Tone analysis
nodes.definition: Identifying the rhetorical tone of a text, such as sarcasm or satire, to assess its potential for misleading interpretation.

nodes.name: Tool use
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats tool use as selecting, invoking, and using external tools, functions, APIs, models, or code interpreters while solving a task. Most formulations count success as identifying when a tool is needed, choosing the appropriate tool, and generating the required call, code, or arguments, and several also include executing the tool and incorporating returned outputs into later reasoning or answer formation. Most papers describe this as an observable act, though some define it more broadly as a latent capability; a narrower line of work focuses on syntactically and semantically correct API or function calls, while broader formulations include using tool outputs even when they may conflict with the user's request.

Variants. Papers use several close labels for this behavior, especially function calling, tool calling, tool invocation, tool selection, and tool-integrated reasoning. A recurring split is between single-call and multi-call settings, including cases where calls must be coordinated in parallel or through dependencies, and some formulations instead center on writing and executing code or directly interacting with APIs.

nodes.name: Touching
nodes.definition: The action of making physical contact with an object, often with controlled force.

nodes.name: Traffic accident recognition
nodes.definition: The task of classifying a given image or video clip as either containing a traffic accident ('Accident') or not ('Normal').

nodes.name: Training data regurgitation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is exact, word-for-word reproduction of training data, or exact substrings and passages from it, in model outputs. Most formulations elicit the behavior with a prefix or related context from the same material and treat success as generating the original continuation, target, or sensitive string; some broaden it to near-verbatim copying, or to private or copyrighted content being exposed or inferred through outputs or internal signals. Most papers therefore treat exact reproduction as the main success criterion, though a smaller line also accepts high overlap or resemblance to the source text.

Variants. Papers use several nearby labels, most often verbatim regurgitation or reproduction, training-data extraction, recitation, and quoting. The behavior is studied in code or configuration text, quotations and copyrighted passages, highly duplicated sequences, and sensitive strings such as PII, secrets, or inserted canaries; some tasks ask for exact continuation from a preceding sequence, while others ask for full verbatim recall.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 2 measurement instruments, AUXDATASET and the Ha

nodes.name: Trajectory captioning
nodes.definition: Producing a natural language summary of an agent's movement path using visual cues or landmarks observed in a video.

nodes.name: Trajectory generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, trajectory generation is most commonly treated as producing ordered sequences, but the contents of those sequences vary by task: imagined states, actions, and rewards based on retrieved knowledge; future UAV poses or waypoints for navigation; or new plausible state sequences that conform to dynamics supplied in context. When papers elaborate the behavior, they describe it as rehearsing decision-making trajectories, generating an imaginary dataset, or producing trajectories described as relevant and as closely matching the real simulated trajectory distribution.

Variants. Papers study several variants of the behavior. One line uses it for decision-making rehearsal from retrieved knowledge, another for hierarchical trajectory generation in UAV navigation, where a decoder generates the next target pose or waypoint, and another for generating new trajectories from in-context examples alone, without an initial state query. The same papers also use nearby labels such as decision-making trajectories, imaginary dataset generation, and hierarchical trajectory decoding.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Wher

nodes.name: Transcreation
nodes.definition: The observable task of adapting a persuasive message for a new audience or context while maintaining the original message's core intent and persuasive goal.

nodes.name: Transliteration
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of converting text from one writing system (script) into another, based on phonetic similarity.

nodes.name: Treatment planning
nodes.definition: The observable task of determining a course of medical action, such as selecting appropriate examinations or therapies, based on a patient's clinical scenario.

nodes.name: Trend analysis
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, it is most commonly described as analyzing and describing directional changes in sensor time-series over specified intervals, with outputs marking segments as upward, downward, or stable. Some papers frame the same behavior as generating natural-language trend descriptions from sensor data, while another formulation asks the model to analyze variations across multiple periods to infer a degradation trajectory. Outputs are described either as interval-by-interval directional labels or as free-text trend summaries.

Variants. The prevailing setting is sensor time-series, where prompts ask for trend variations within a stated window and responses can enumerate successive segments as downward, stable, upward, and downward. Papers also use the names trend description generation for free-text sensor descriptions and degradation trend inference for reasoning over signal or semantic variations across consecutive cycles in a system-degradation setting.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 2 measurement instruments: Human evaluation and LLM-as-a-judge. Both are used to score generated trend descriptions, with GPT-4o ratin

nodes.name: Trigger identification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions describe trigger identification as locating the word, phrase, or text span that marks an event occurrence. Across these formulations, success is usually framed as extracting the trigger for a detected event or finding the event-indicating item in a sentence, and one paper makes correctness explicit by counting a prediction as correct only when its offsets and type match a gold trigger. A scientific-event formulation places this within a text segment and describes the event as often represented as an agent-action-object tuple; another example treats "killed" as the trigger word in a sentence.

Variants. Papers use both trigger identification and trigger extraction for closely related formulations. The task appears at different granularities: extracting the trigger for each detected event, identifying a specific word or phrase in a sentence, locating a text span in a sentence or document, and selecting the most appropriate trigger word from an unlabeled sentence for a filtered event type. The settings mentioned include scientific events and target-domain unlabeled data.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: Triple classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as judging whether a knowledge graph triple or triplet is correct. Papers agree on the core success criterion, a correctness judgment for a given triple, while differing in specificity: one defines it as predicting a binary label, correct or incorrect, for a triple based on a context document, and another describes it more broadly as estimating or validating the correctness of a fully formed triplet.

Variants. Papers use both "triple classification" and "triplet classification" for this task. The settings mentioned include classifying triples in generated graphs in a graph judgement setting, and a related knowledge graph completion setting where triple classification assesses the correctness of a given triple (h, r, t) and is discussed alongside link prediction for (h, r, ?).

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the task descriptions themselves, elicitation is direct: a knowledge graph triple or triplet is presented, sometimes with a context document, and the response is scored as a correctness judgment, most explicitly a binary correct versus incorrect lab

nodes.name: Triple extraction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the shared framing treats this behavior as identifying entities and relations together rather than separately. One paper describes it as joint entity and relation extraction in a single step, with correctness requiring both entity spans, subject and object, and the relation label to exactly match the gold annotation. Another frames it as identifying entities and relations in a question or answer and converting them into head-relation-tail triples, and says the fixed triple structure requires the LLM to extract as many entities and relations from the question as possible.

Variants. Authors use both "joint entity and relation extraction" and "triple extraction" for closely related task formulations. The variants differ mainly in setting and output form: one is a few-shot joint extraction setting over named entity spans and semantic relation labels, and the other first identifies entities and relations within a question and then generates triples for the answers.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers. The only explicit scoring detail is an exact-match rule in the joint extraction setting, whe

nodes.name: Turn-taking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the available usage, turn-taking is treated as managing dialogue turns in a smooth, human-like way during interaction. One paper further describes seamless conversational turn-taking as a high-level cue, and characterizes conversational bots that follow the conversation flow as generally rated as more engaging and trustworthy.

Variants. The only label used here is conversational turn-taking.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as evidence of in the papers.

nodes.name: Turn-taking prediction
nodes.definition: The observable generation of speech tokens that align with appropriate conversational transitions, such as when to speak, pause, overlap, or interrupt, based on dual-channel input dynamics.

nodes.name: Tweet generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats tweet generation as producing short-form text in tweet format in response to an instruction or prompt. The common formulation is that the model returns the tweet itself, with one paper stating that in this task the response is "the exact tweet"; another frames it through prompts tailored to "a specific medium (a tweet)" and through creating instructions for a tweet.

Variants. A recurring variant is community-specific tweet generation, where papers describe generating tweet-like text on given topics for a specified community, including creating a synthetic corpus by prompting a community-aligned model to generate tweets. Another formulation has an attacker LLM create instructions for a tweet, with the prompt design adapted to the tweet medium.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to tweet generation.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to tweet generation.

nodes.name: Type inference
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats type inference as predicting missing static types in code. One framing is specifically about untyped Python repositories, where the goal is to infer and insert type hints for function parameters, return values, and variables, described as inferring types "that could have been written by developers"; an example adds "name: str" and "-> str" to an untyped function signature (TypyBench: Evaluating LLM Type Inference for Untyped Python Repositories). A broader formulation describes it as inferring and assigning static types to variables and functions in a dynamically typed programming language.

Variants. Papers use both Python-specific and broader language-level variants of the task. One recurring setting is Python code without annotations, especially repository code with missing hints, while another formulation covers variables and functions in a dynamically typed programming language more generally. The papers also use the names "type annotation prediction" and "type prediction" for this behavior.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In these papers, the behavior is spec

nodes.name: UI element referring
nodes.definition: The observable task of identifying or describing a specific UI element based on its properties, such as recognizing text within a bounding box or classifying a widget's type.

nodes.name: Unanswerability detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat this behavior as a judgment about whether a question can be answered from the available context, often phrased as predicting whether it is answerable or should be marked unanswerable. A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to checking whether a math problem provides sufficient information to solve, or whether the correct answer to a medical question exists within a candidate option set. Across these formulations, success is the correct decision about answerability, sufficiency of information, or existence of an answer.

Variants. Papers study it in several settings under different names: answerability classification for context-based question answering, answerable judging for mathematical reasoning, and answer existence judgment for medical questions with candidate options. The math variant asks the model to analyze the question, identify the conditions needed to solve it, and verify whether those conditions are present, while the medical variant asks whether the correct answer exists in the option set and is described as assessing answer plausibility in open decision spaces.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement ins

nodes.name: Under-translation
nodes.definition: The observable behavior where content from the source text is missing in the model's translation output.

nodes.name: Undercorrection
nodes.definition: Failing to make all needed edits, leaving some grammatical errors uncorrected.

nodes.name: Unit conversion
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is narrow: unit conversion is treated as transforming a clinical measurement from one unit to another within a calculation workflow, such as converting µmol/L to mg/dL. Papers also describe the behavior as testing accuracy in numerical standardization, and a worked example converts serum creatinine from 417 µmol/L to about 4.72 mg/dL.

Variants. Papers provide little subdivision beyond clinical measurement conversion itself. The clearest instantiated case is serum creatinine conversion, and one paper studies the behavior in a tool-mediated setting where parameter unit mismatches trigger nested tool calling so that additional tools can be selected and used to resolve the mismatch across a complex toolchain.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers operationalize it directly through unit-conversion examples and score it in terms of accuracy in numerical standardization.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as evidence of.

nodes.name: Unit test generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as producing unit tests, or an entire unit test suite, for a given piece of code or file under test so that functional correctness can be checked. A smaller line of work uses a broader task framing, describing the behavior as creating executable test cases or logical checks from a problem description, or writing desired input/output pairs before solving the problem; in those formulations, the tests are used to assess response accuracy and relevance or are rewarded for validity and correctness.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, most often "unit test generation," and less often "test generation" or "test case generation." The main variants are generating a full suite for a file under test, generating diverse tests from a natural language specification in zero-shot prompting, producing 5-10 concise test statements from an instruction prompt, and writing input/output pairs to formalize a programming problem before solving it; one benchmark describes the goal as generating "an entire test suite given a file under test" (TestGenEval: A Real World Unit Test Generation and Test Completion Benchmark

nodes.name: Variable assignment
nodes.definition: A synthetic task where the model must output the latest value for a named variable based on a sequence of repeated assignments.

nodes.name: Variance analysis
nodes.definition: The task of determining if the variances of two different attributes across a population of entities differ significantly.

nodes.name: Velocity comparison
nodes.definition: Comparing the speed or motion state of one object against another in a video scene.

nodes.name: Verbal analogy solving
nodes.definition: Solving analogical reasoning problems involving semantic relations such as synonymy or antonymy (e.g., hot is to cold as up is to down).

nodes.name: Verbatim regurgitation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the behavior is treated as generating exact or near-exact text that matches copyrighted source material, with particular emphasis on long excerpts. The definition in "Certified Mitigation of Worst-Case LLM Copyright Infringement" specifies exact or near-exact sequences, particularly long spans exceeding a defined threshold, and its snippets describe this as "generating content that is substantially similar to copyrighted material" and as producing "long verbatim quotes from copyrighted sources."

Variants. The available work uses the label "verbatim quote generation" for this behavior. In that usage, the focus stays on copyrighted sources and especially long verbatim excerpts.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. The only operational detail given in the definitions is that the matching text can be exact or near-exact and is particularly noted when it involves long spans exceeding a defined threshold.

What it is taken as evidence of. The only linked construct is Memorization. In "Mitigating Memorization in Language Models," one paper claims a causal relationship from Memorizat

nodes.name: Verbose generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is outputs that are longer or wordier than needed for the prompt or task. Most definitions treat it as excessive length, often with redundant or irrelevant continuation; some add that it can continue until the maximum generation length and become incoherent, or that an answer may begin correctly but then keep going with unrelated content that lowers evaluation scores. Papers also frame the threshold relative to desired conciseness or task complexity, and one study describes models as producing "longer and more verbose captions than top human ones" (Humor in AI: Massive Scale Crowd-Sourced Preferences and Benchmarks for Cartoon Captioning).

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, most often overgeneration, overly verbose generation, verbose response generation, response length generation, and unnecessarily lengthy output generation. The behavior appears in settings such as captioning, general prompt answering, and cases where a model gives the correct answer first but then adds unrelated material. A smaller line of work treats it more neutrally as response length with measurable word counts that vary by model,

nodes.name: Video captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is free-form generation of natural-language text that describes a video's content or events. Most definitions stay broad, centering on textual descriptions or summaries of videos, while some ask for captions of segments or clips and others stress that the description should be accurate, comprehensive, or close to human-written captions. A smaller line of work frames the output as real-time narration of a stream or as verbal narration of visual elements for accessibility.

Variants. A smaller line of work names narrower variants: video scripting, clip summarization, video description generation, audio description generation, and video narration. In Vript: A Video Is Worth Thousands of Words, video scripting is explicitly structured, asking models to "describe: 1) the shot type ... 2) the camera movement ... 3) what is happening ... 4) Summarize the content to title the scene". Other papers move to time-stamped clips, anomalous events, accessibility-oriented narration, real-time streaming, or segment-level settings, and one paper further seeks captions that specify subjects, environment, motion, camera parameters, and style.

nodes.name: Video comparison and trend analysis
nodes.definition: The ability to compare different entities or events and analyze emerging patterns or trends over the course of a video.

nodes.name: Video detailed captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is generating comprehensive and coherent textual descriptions of video content, often as long-form or summary-style outputs. Definitions agree that the description should cover more than primary actions and objects: one paper says it should capture "intricate details, contextual nuances, and temporal dynamics" (AuroraCap: Efficient, Performant Video Detailed Captioning and a New Benchmark), while another describes summaries that capture characters, actions, settings, and narrative elements. Across definitions, the desired output is repeatedly described as comprehensive and coherent.

Variants. Papers use both "video detailed captioning" and "video detailed description" for closely matched task formulations. The emphasized content differs across definitions, with some descriptions foregrounding actions, objects, context, and temporal dynamics, and others foregrounding characters, settings, and narrative elements. One example prompt is simply "Describe the video in detail," and the illustrated response begins, "The video begins with a scene featuring two animated characters..." (LongVU: Spatiotemporal Adaptive Compression

nodes.name: Video editing
nodes.definition: The task of modifying an existing video according to a user's instruction, which can involve changes to content, style, or objects over time.

nodes.name: Video generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, video generation is most commonly treated as synthesizing a coherent sequence of frames or a video clip, often with an emphasis on realism. Many papers formulate it conditionally, especially from text prompts, and describe success in terms of spatial and temporal coherence and faithfulness to the prompt, desired attributes, motion patterns, or caption. Some papers use broader conditional or unconditional forms instead, including class-conditional generation, generation from previous frames, and frame prediction with a 5-frame condition; a smaller line of work narrows the task to producing impossible scenes that violate physical, biological, geographical, or social laws while still following the text description.

Variants. The most common named variant is text-to-video generation, with image-to-video generation appearing as a narrower modality-specific version based on a static input image. Other settings include class-conditional video generation, frame prediction from prior frames, and unconditional versus conditional video synthesis. A smaller set of papers studies guided variants, such as generation from dynamic scene layouts or D

nodes.name: Video object segmentation
nodes.definition: The task of identifying and tracking the pixel masks of one or more objects across the frames of a video sequence, also known as video tracking.

nodes.name: Video question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is answering a natural language question from the content of a video, with emphasis on dynamic visual content and, in many definitions, temporal information. Most papers treat success as providing a correct textual or natural-language answer. Some formulations instead use multiple-choice or closed-ended selection, while others emphasize open-ended or long-form answer generation. A smaller line of work narrows the task to first-person video or to questions that require understanding complex visual and temporal relationships, including relations between actions over time such as sequence or frequency.

Variants. Several variants recur. Long-video question answering is common, and papers describe it both as multiple-choice-based selection and as open-ended text generation for long-form videos. Other variants include egocentric question answering on first-person video, sometimes for episodic memory-related questions, and temporal video reasoning, where answers depend on across-time relations between actions. Some authors also place video QA in instruction-following or multi-turn settings.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers

nodes.name: Video scene segmentation
nodes.definition: Dividing a long video into coherent scenes based on shot transitions, visual changes, and narrative logic to support downstream audio generation.

nodes.name: Video summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the available definitions, the task is framed as producing, or supporting the production of, a summary of a video's content from frame-level evidence. The papers agree on the summary goal, but differ in how they describe the input and process: Frame-Voyager: Learning to Query Frames for Video Large Language Models emphasizes selecting evidence from frames and notes that simple frame matching can miss subtle transitions between scenes, while Video2Roleplay: A Multimodal Dataset and Framework for Video-Guided Role-playing Agents describes taking frame descriptions in video order and generating a comprehensive summary with Chain-of-Thought.

Variants. The available work treats it as a video-language task grounded in ordered visual evidence. One formulation centers on selecting evidence from frames, another on aggregating frame descriptions in video order, and one paper also relates video summarization to video question answering by stating that video-language tasks including summarization can be formulated as video question answering tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers. There is no named elicitat

nodes.name: Video-to-text generation
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a relevant and coherent textual response based on a given video and an optional text prompt.

nodes.name: Vision-and-language navigation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the framing is consistent: an embodied agent follows natural language instructions to navigate through a visual environment, with success described as reaching a target destination or completing the language-specified goal. One paper also phrases the task as grounding a destination point within a given environment, which matches the same instruction-following navigation setup.

Variants. The named settings are high-level vision-language navigation tasks in ALFRED and a broader range of environments described as both discrete action and continuous robotic control. Papers also use closely aligned names such as vision-language navigation and VLN for the same instruction-guided navigation behavior.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in these papers, so they do not identify a recurring instrument for eliciting or scoring this behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as what this behavior indicates, so the papers do not specify a construct that it is taken to reflect.

nodes.name: Visual dialogue
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is a multi-turn or multi-round conversation grounded in visual input, usually an image, where responses depend on both the image and the prior dialogue context. Most definitions describe answering image-based prompts or user questions in an open-ended conversational format; some broaden this to multimodal exchanges over text and images, and a smaller line of work specifies settings such as contextually relevant biomedical answers, following instructions, or step-by-step decisions from interleaved visual context.

Variants. Papers use many near-synonymous names, most often multimodal chat, multimodal dialogue or conversation, visual conversation, visual chat or dialog, and image-based conversation. A smaller line of work studies variants grounded in one or more images, multiple images or interleaved multi-image inputs, conversational VQA, and visual prompt-based conversation where users refer to regions with points, boxes, or masks; domain-specific versions appear in biomedical and clinical settings, and one multilingual formulation includes answering questions and following instructions across languages.

Space of

nodes.name: Visual editing
nodes.definition: The observable act of modifying an input image through operations such as drawing boxes, highlighting regions, or masking out areas to guide visual attention.

nodes.name: Visual entailment
nodes.definition: The task of determining whether a textual hypothesis is true, false, or neutral based on the content of a given image.

nodes.name: Visual hallucination
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats visual hallucination as output that is not grounded in the image or other provided inputs: papers define it as producing incorrect visual claims, unsupported descriptions, or text about objects, attributes, or relationships that are not present in the input image. A smaller formulation uses the name multimodal hallucination for generated information that is inconsistent with or absent from provided multimodal inputs. Success in the associated task is usually framed as keeping the response consistent with image content, and one paper notes that failures can appear when models identify "small and occluded objects" (Feast Your Eyes:  Mixture-of-Resolution Adaptation for Multimodal Large Language Models).

Variants. Papers study both a narrower image-grounded version and a broader multimodal-input version. In the narrower version, hallucinated content is described at the level of nonexistent objects, attributes, and relationships; one snippet also highlights settings involving granular recognition of small and occluded objects. The names used are mainly visual hallucination, with multimodal hallucination appear

nodes.name: Visual information retrieval
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the behavior is used for retrieving or recalling specific visual information from sequences of images or videos. Some authors frame it as long-context retrieval, locating a target object, image, frame, or other inserted information within a long sequence and answering a corresponding question, for example, "For the image with the anchor object, is there a target object?", and one definition explicitly says this requires precise attention and memory over extended inputs. Other authors operationalize it as recall from video observations, where success means identifying the next or previous step in an action sequence, naming an object near a landmark, describing the scene at a particular moment, or determining an agent's start and end positions.

Variants. Papers study several named variants, including needle retrieval and long video retrieval. These settings ask for a correct inserted image, target frame, or queried piece of information from deep in a long video, sometimes with varying background lengths or needle depths, and one extension adds distractor frames. Another formulation breaks the task into sequence recall, object recall, scene re

nodes.name: Visual instruction following
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as producing a textual response from a paired image and natural language prompt. One definition states it as generating text from “a combination of a visual image and a natural language instruction or question,” while another calls it “image-conditioned instruction following” and describes it as responding to instructions that require understanding and reasoning over an accompanying image. Examples shown in the snippets include answering “What place is this?” and deciding whether to go “left or right?” from image context.

Variants. Papers situate the behavior in multimodal and visual-language settings, and a smaller line of work describes visual instruction tuning in a multitask setup. One source evaluates it on Mixed Visual Instruction Tuning 665k across several datasets, and another relates it to VQA and region-level VQA within the same tuning process. The main naming variation is between “visual instruction following” and “image-conditioned instruction following.”

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure this behavior with 11 linked instruments. The prevailing operationalization uses

nodes.name: Visual object categorization
nodes.definition: The task of discriminating between pairs of images, where looking time is used as a measure of perceived similarity or dissimilarity.

nodes.name: Visual object localization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, this behavior is framed as producing the location of a target within visual input. One formulation asks for the original position of a masked image patch in a partially masked grid, while the UI-focused formulations ask for the location of a described interface element, either as precise screen or mouse click coordinates or as a bounding box. The papers therefore agree on localization as the core behavior, but differ in whether the target is an image patch or a UI widget and in the required output format.

Variants. The named variants are piece localization, UI element localization, and widget localization. Piece localization is posed on a partially masked image and asks for a patch's original position; one paper presents it as a representative single-step spatial reasoning capability. The UI variants use natural language instructions or widget descriptions with screenshots or interfaces and ask the model to find the target element, and one paper describes this as mapping "instructions and screenshots to precise mouse click coordinates" (AgentStudio: A Toolkit for Building General Virtual Agents).

Space of elicitation and scores. No measure

nodes.name: Visual question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is an image-question task: models receive visual input, most often a single image, plus a natural-language question, and are expected to produce a textual answer based on the visual content. Several definitions make the image-question pair explicit and describe the task as requiring joint use of image and text inputs, while some papers specify short answers or autoregressive answers. A smaller line of work broadens the visual source to one or more images, 3D scenes, videos, webpages or website screenshots, embedded images, generated images, or medical images, and one paper asks for both an answer and an explanation.

Variants. Most variants stay close to general image question answering, sometimes split into single-image QA, simple QA, text-related VQA, or image-agnostic versus image-specific prompts. Smaller strands study 3D visual question answering, region-text interleaved VQA, GUI question answering, embedded image question answering, and scene text question answering. Other papers specialize the same pattern to medical, object-focused, region-focused, or algorithmic-puzzle settings.

Space of elicitation and scores.

nodes.name: Visual relation identification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as identifying or describing relations among visual entities. Most commonly, papers describe connections, interactions, or spatial dynamics between multiple specified objects or marked regions within one image, sometimes as detailed analysis over arbitrary regions of interest; a smaller line of work frames it as reasoning about dynamic interactions in traffic scenes, including an ego vehicle's reaction to other elements, or as identifying which properties change and stay the same between images in a visual analogy.

Variants. Papers use several names for closely related formulations: inter-relationship analysis, object interaction analysis, interaction relation understanding, and relationship identification. These variants span within-image object or region relations, traffic-scene agent interactions, and cross-image analogy tasks that ask models to extract relations between images.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the task formulations that are shown, papers elicit the behavior with direct instructions, such as asking for the relationships between mark

nodes.name: Visual search
nodes.definition: The task of detecting the presence or absence of a specific target object within a visual array of distractor objects.

nodes.name: Visual storytelling
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats visual storytelling as generating a coherent narrative or story from a sequence of images. Most papers keep this sequence-to-story framing, though some narrow the task to story completion, asking for a concluding narrative sentence from preceding images and captions plus a last image, and another paper describes a narrative story accompanied by relevant images in an interleaved format. One paper instead states it as generating a narrative or story based on the content of an image.

Variants. Papers use the names visual storytelling, visual story telling, and VST. The main variants are full story generation from image sequences, interleaved text-and-image storytelling, and finishing a story from earlier image-caption pairs and a final image. In related usage, one paper claims a causal relationship from interleaved text-and-image generation to visual storytelling, saying it "opens up possibilities" for this application.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link visual storytelling to one measurement instrument, VIST, and no other instrument is linked to it. The paper that links it to VIST refers to "visua

nodes.name: Voice cloning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats voice cloning as zero-shot text-to-speech: generating speech in a new or particular speaker's voice from text, conditioned on a short audio or speech prompt from that speaker, without speaker-specific training or assuming that speaker was seen during training. Definitions mostly agree on this zero-shot setup and on using the prompt to condition voice characteristics, while one definition states it more directly as synthesizing speech that mimics a particular person. As one formulation in VoiceCraft-X: Unifying Multilingual, Voice-Cloning Speech Synthesis and Speech Editing puts it, the task "entails generating speech in a new speaker’s voice from a short audio prompt" without having seen that speaker during training.

Variants. Papers use several closely related names for the behavior, most often zero-shot text-to-speech or zero-shot TTS, and also voice-cloning TTS and zero-shot speech generation. The studied settings remain within text-to-speech with reference prompts from unseen speakers, and one paper relates voice cloning to text-to-speech synthesis. One paper also places it in a multilingual setting al

nodes.name: Vulnerability identification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is code-centered detection: papers most commonly describe the behavior as identifying whether code, a code snippet, a target function, or a repository contains bugs, vulnerabilities, or other defects. Some formulations only require a vulnerable versus benign judgment, while others ask the model to report potential security flaws, often in CWE-style terms, or to locate and specify weaknesses, their types, or their positions. A smaller line extends the behavior beyond source code to configurations or systems, and one paper breaks it into subtasks such as identifying leaked credentials and insecure code.

Variants. Papers study closely related variants under the labels security vulnerability detection, bug detection, code defect detection, vulnerability location, and vulnerability detection. The settings range from whole-project or whole-repository reasoning, to target functions with interprocedural context, to individual code snippets or source files, including decompiled executables represented as C code. Task scope also varies between unspecific vulnerability detection and typed categories, with examples including d

nodes.name: Watermark decoding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats watermark decoding as recovery of an embedded code or message from watermarked text. The observable outcome is extracting the intended binary or multi-bit content, though the decoding rule varies: one description uses a trained classifier on segmented text, another computes the text likelihood under competing message hypotheses and selects the best one, and another uses a secret key plus token-pattern statistics, choosing the candidate that minimizes red list token counts.

Variants. Papers use several names for this behavior, including watermark decoding, message decoding, and message extraction. The main variants differ by what is recovered and at what unit: binary watermark codes versus multi-bit messages, decoding independently within each segment, or extracting a message chunk at each position. Some descriptions also frame the recovered message as provenance information, such as userID, TimeStamp, and modelID.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. Instead, papers operationalize it through the decoding procedure itself, such as a decoder applied to text segments, l

nodes.name: Watermark detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a binary decision task over text sequences or generated content: determine whether a candidate text contains a watermark. Most formulations describe success as outputting 1 or 0, classifying text as watermarked or not, or deciding whether a suspect text is more likely from a marked versus unmarked distribution. A smaller set of descriptions makes the criterion more specific, such as detecting when the average token-level watermark logit is greater than zero, when a z-value exceeds a threshold, or when a calibrated detector concludes the text came from a watermarked model.

Variants. Papers consistently pose the behavior on text, but study it in several watermarking settings, including semantic-invariant, publicly verifiable, provably robust, unbiased, order-agnostic, structural, and low-entropy watermarking. Some authors explicitly call it the watermark detection task and describe it as the inverse of watermark embedding, while others emphasize detector variants such as neural network classification, statistical hypothesis testing, recovering a key sequence from generated content, or testing a candidate text under a water

nodes.name: Watermark removal
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats watermark removal as modifying watermarked training data, model outputs, or text so the watermark signal is eliminated, neutralized, or made undetectable. Definitions agree that success means the watermark is no longer detected or retained, though they differ on scope: some place it in unauthorized knowledge distillation, while others describe reverting a watermarked language model or its output to an unwatermarked state, or making rewritten text undetectable to the corresponding detector. A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to watermark evasion or scrubbing, where a paraphrased or semantically similar text avoids verification while maintaining textual quality.

Variants. Papers use several names and intervention points for this behavior. The most explicit split is between pre-distillation removal, through untargeted and targeted training data paraphrasing, and post-distillation removal, through watermark neutralization that applies inverse or inverted watermark rules during the student model's decoding phase. Other variants describe text rewriting or synonym substitution, adaptive and non-adaptive paraphr

nodes.name: Watermark spoofing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats it as an attack behavior in which an attacker generates new text that is falsely detected as watermarked. Both definitions center the success condition on detector acceptance, phrased as text being "detected as watermarked" or "incorrectly identified as containing a valid watermark." One definition adds that the spoofer does this "without knowing the private key ξ," while another discusses forgery when shared key exposure or enough understanding of the watermark generation rule would enable the attacker to forge watermarked text.

Variants. A smaller naming difference appears in whether papers call the behavior watermark spoofing or watermark forgery. The snippets also describe targeted attacks on Red-Green watermarks that allow "impersonating (spoofing) the watermark," and they note a learning-based variant in which an attacker queries the watermarked model, builds a watermarked dataset D, and then learns the watermark from that dataset.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the definitions and snippets, papers operationalize success through the detector's output: th

nodes.name: Watermarked text generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating text that carries an embedded watermark signal, usually described as detectable under standard or specialized decoding. Definitions commonly operationalize it by altering generation itself, for example by modifying token sampling, reweighting candidate tokens with a secret key, perturbing model weights, or changing the model’s output distribution during generation. As one study puts it, models can "learn to generate watermarked text with high detectability" (On the Learnability of Watermarks for Language Models), though a smaller line of work describes probabilistic reweighting that embeds an "undetectable watermark."

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for the behavior, including watermark embedding and watermark generation. The settings described include weights-based watermarking that generates watermarked text directly from the model under standard decoding, structural watermarking that samples from a weight-perturbed model, and message embedding that pseudorandomly encodes a message into balanced bits for multilayer reweighting. Another recurring variant combines logits-base

nodes.name: Waypoint selection
nodes.definition: Choosing the next exploration location or frontier to move toward during navigation.

nodes.name: Web navigation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a sequential interaction task in which an agent follows a user instruction or request by taking browser or webpage actions, typically clicking, typing, following links, or filling forms, until the instruction is achieved on a website. Success is most often framed as finding information or completing a goal, though some definitions narrow it to reaching a target section of a site, completing online forms or transactions, or purchasing an item. One paper describes it as a class of sequential decision-making problems where agents interact with web interfaces following user instructions, while another makes the sequence explicit as executable actions used to accomplish the task on the website.

Variants. Papers use several near-names for the behavior, most often web browsing alongside web navigation, and a smaller line of work refers to site navigation, web task completion, or webpage interaction. The settings vary from browser use for search and information retrieval to real-website task completion and online shopping, and some benchmarks are described as spanning domains such as travel, shopping, and social media. A more sp

nodes.name: Web search
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats web search as an observable tool-use action in which the model generates a query and invokes a search tool or search API to retrieve information or a list of webpages from a live search engine for answering a question. Definitions mostly agree on the query-and-retrieval step, though one formulation extends the behavior beyond the results list to following results, fetching HTML pages, extracting relevant text, and synthesizing an answer. Concrete descriptions include generating a JSON-formatted request to a web_search tool and sending structured search queries through web search APIs.

Variants. Papers use both the label web search and the label web content retrieval. The behavior appears in general question answering, in complicated web browsing to answer a question, and in searches for time-sensitive or source-specific information. Examples include Google search, a GoogleSearch tool, and site-specific search such as searching BBC Good Food for recipes and ingredient lists.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Operationally, papers make the behavior visible through explicit

nodes.name: Web shopping
nodes.definition: Navigating shopping websites to search for products and select items from search results.

nodes.name: Word association
nodes.definition: Generating culturally conditioned associative words in response to a given cue word, reflecting implicit semantic and cultural knowledge.

nodes.name: Word grouping
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of partitioning a set of words into groups of equal size based on shared topics or categories, as required by the GLOBALGROUP task.

nodes.name: Word guessing
nodes.definition: The observable task of iteratively guessing words to find a hidden target word, guided by scalar similarity feedback.

nodes.name: Word puzzle solving
nodes.definition: Sorting words into groups based on shared connections or categories.

nodes.name: Word segmentation
nodes.definition: Splitting continuous character sequences into meaningful words, particularly challenging in character-dense languages like Chinese.

nodes.name: Word sense disambiguation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a WiC-style judgment: given a target word and two sentences, the model decides whether the word is used with the same sense in both, typically as a binary same-versus-different decision. A smaller line of work instead frames it as inventory-based sense selection in a single context, where the task is to choose the most appropriate sense, label, or candidate definition for a target word from a predefined pool.

Variants. Papers use several neighboring names and settings for this behavior. They include sense labeling, polysemy disambiguation in the WiC formulation, homonym disambiguation shaped by context and POS, pun interpretation and word-sense association, where pun and alternative senses are linked to the right words in context, and lexical disambiguation in multi-domain translation, where domain context determines the correct translation of a word with multiple meanings.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link the behavior to five measurement instruments. WiC is the most common and is described as a Word-in-Context challenge for contextual word sense disambiguation; the others are 42D and HardEN as general-domai

nodes.name: Word sorting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats word sorting as the task of arranging a given list of words in lexicographical, alphabetical order. Some authors state the rule more generally, as arranging words according to a specified criterion or the task's required sorting rule, but they still describe the behavior as producing an ordered list of words.

Variants. Papers usually refer to the behavior simply as Word Sorting, and one source abbreviates it as WS. The main variation is in how the ordering rule is stated: most commonly lexicographical ordering, with a smaller wording that leaves the criterion task-specific. Papers also place the task in BIG-bench reasoning-task settings, and one paper additionally lists it among BIG-Bench Hard tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure this behavior with two instruments: most commonly BIG-bench, and also BIG-Bench Hard. In these uses, word sorting is presented as one of the reasoning tasks evaluated in BIG-Bench, while another paper includes it as one of the tasks in BIG-Bench Hard. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to word sorti

nodes.name: Word unscrambling
nodes.definition: Rearranging the letters of a jumbled word to form a meaningful word.

nodes.name: Wordplay formalization
nodes.definition: The process of translating a natural language wordplay explanation into a structured, executable format, such as Python code with assert statements.

nodes.name: Workflow generation
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of producing a structured, executable workflow, typically in the form of code, in response to a user query.

nodes.name: Zero-shot classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage describes assigning an input to one of several predefined or user-provided class labels without task-specific training, fine-tuning, or labeled examples. Most formulations say the model relies on a prompt plus its internal knowledge, or on semantic alignment between the input and class labels, and success is framed as returning the correct label, often reported as zero-shot accuracy. A smaller variation emphasizes classes not seen during training, while one multimodal formulation defines prediction as selecting the highest-scoring text description from a candidate set.

Variants. Most papers keep the broad name zero-shot classification, while one paper narrows it to zero-shot text classification and another uses the label zero-shot inference.
