The settings range from reasoning datasets to text-attributed graph classification on ogbn-arxiv, where prompts contain paper titles, abstracts, and questions, to multimodal image classification that ranks candidate text descriptions, and to a medical setting where inputs are classified by similarity to text prompts. One paper also reports downstream zero-shot evaluation with ImageN

nodes.name: Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer
nodes.definition: Performing a task in a target language that was not included in the fine-tuning data, relying solely on pretraining and cross-lingual generalization.

nodes.name: Zero-shot inference
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats zero-shot inference as direct prediction at inference time, without dataset-specific retraining or labeled demonstrations. One usage describes segmentation on an unseen dataset with a supplied or customisable vocabulary, where "the model is trained on Ctrain and directly tested on Ctest"; another describes prediction from a human-designed instruction and explicitly characterizes the setup as "zero-shot, inference-only."

Variants. The observed variants fall into two settings: open vocabulary semantic segmentation on unseen datasets, and instruction-conditioned prompting without labeled demonstrations. Papers also describe the first setting as zero-shot inference on unseen datasets with customisable vocabulary, while the second is framed as conditioning on a human-designed instruction.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The papers therefore do not name a recurring instrument for eliciting or scoring zero-shot inference.

nodes.name: Zero-shot question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The prevailing usage treats zero-shot question answering as answering questions without task-specific fine-tuning, additional training, or task-specific examples in the prompt or context. Most formulations emphasize correct or accurate answers under this zero-shot condition, and several papers operationalize success as zero-shot accuracy on benchmark tasks. A narrower framing specifies generating correct answers to multiple-choice questions, while a broader one includes answering downstream or reasoning tasks from provided context, general knowledge, or a model's internal knowledge and the prompt.

Variants. Papers use several nearby labels for the behavior, including zero-shot QA, zero-shot evaluation, zero-shot accuracy, and zero-shot tasks. A smaller line of work broadens it beyond question answering to downstream natural language understanding or reasoning tasks, while other definitions keep it centered on question answering, sometimes across various domains. The setting remains zero-shot throughout, and one paper explicitly notes that all test data used in evaluation are from zero-shot settings.

nodes.name: Zero-shot task performance
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as performance on downstream or language-understanding tasks when the model is given no in-context examples and no task-specific fine-tuning or training. Definitions repeatedly describe answering questions or carrying out tasks such as question answering, commonsense reasoning, reading comprehension, or natural language inference from the prompt alone, and success is usually reported as accuracy on benchmark tasks. A smaller usage treats it as zero-evaluation performance on LAMBADA and WikiText using perplexity scores.

Variants. Papers use several nearby labels for the same behavior, including zero-shot evaluation, zero-shot reasoning, and zero-shot downstream task performance. The settings are mostly downstream NLP benchmarks, commonly framed as question answering and commonsense reasoning, though some definitions emphasize multiple-choice and yes/no reasoning tasks, reading-comprehension datasets, instruction-only evaluation, or broader natural language tasks. Examples named by papers include HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC, WinoGrande, and MMLU.
